en: Śrī:
The beginning of the second part of the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra; now begins the section on the Parikara ornament.
When there is an underlying intention (*sābhiprāya*), an embellishment (*alaṃkāra*) may reside in a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Here, the use of the term "embellishment" is intended to dispel the doubt that its function is fulfilled merely by the absence of a defect (*doṣābhāva*); this will be demonstrated later. "With an underlying intention" means preceded by an intention directed toward a meaning that supports the contextual subject matter—that is, that which suggests such a meaning. Thus, the definition should be understood as: "the state of being a qualifying attribute that suggests a meaning supporting the contextual subject matter. The phrase "supporting the contextual subject matter" is included to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the realm of *dhvani*.

The term "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*) is introduced instead of "cognitiveness" (*bodhakatva*) in order to exclude the figure of speech known as *hetvalaṃkāra* (the ornament of cause). The word "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is included to exclude the figure of speech called *parikarāṅkura* (the sprout of the preparatory detail) which will be discussed later; however, since in that case the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is likewise [suggestive], there is no over-extension of the definition.

O you of lightning-hue, though your garment is washed by the luster of your feet, it becomes beautiful through its taking refuge in you; having attained the state of great gold, it achieves a similarity in color with you.

O Vidyudvarṇā! O Rame! [The word] *mahārajana* refers to safflower (*kusumbha*), according to Amara’s lexicon: "The neuter form *mahārajana* means safflower. By taking refuge in you—who are bowed down by the luster of your feet—the wise man, discerning the strength and vigor of himself and his enemy, conducts himself with humility;
such a person does not suffer defeat. [Note: The phrase *sārāsāraṃ balaṃ vīryamātmano dviṣataśca yaḥ* is a citation from the *Hitopadeśa*, which provides the context for the preceding verse.]
In the same way, when a wise man perceives an enemy to be exceedingly powerful, he should resort to the conduct of a reed; this is the defining characteristic of wisdom.

The sense is that, according to the manner described in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, he resorts to the "reed-like conduct" (*vaitasavṛtti*). In the alternative interpretation, the word *mahārajanām* [is explained] because of the resorting to a change of letters (*natatā*), specifically by resorting to the letter *ta* for the letter *na*; that is, by removing the letter *na* and reading the letter *ta* there. [The word] *mahārajata* means gold, as Amara states: "Gold is *mahārajata* and *kāñcana*. It also refers to the state of being the word *mahārajata*. Having approached you, it attains similarity with you (*sāvarṇya*).

In this context, the qualification "having the color of lightning" contains the intention that the saffron robe (mahārajana) is worthy of attaining a hue through the previously described method, following its attainment of the state of great silver (mahārajata).
O Beloved of Śrī, for the sake of this wretched world— which bestows immediate happiness yet leads to many small miseries— I do not even envy Brahmā.

It is so called because it bestows that pleasure which is *ākālika*, meaning "swiftly perishing. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose beginning and end occur at the same time" (*samānakālāv ādyantau yasya*). According to the rule *ākālikaḍādyantavacane*, the suffix *ṭhak* is added to the word *samānakāla* in the sense of "swiftly perishing. For the word *samānakāla*, there is the substitution of *ākāla*; or alternatively, the suffix *ṭhan* is applied by the rule *ākālāṭ ṭhaṃś ca*. It is so called because it contains many (*astokāḥ*)—that is, numerous—paths of affliction (*ārtivartanyaḥ*), which are paths of suffering. The rest is easy to understand. Here, the various epithets of the world are intended to convey its utter worthlessness.
Or as in:

"O Bestower of Boons, O Ocean of Compassion, O Friend of those who bow, quickly rescue me—my heart agitated by hosts of enemies, besmeared with sin, and the onset of whose calamities is endless. (805) Here, the numerous epithets of the speaker are imbued with the intention of his being worthy of pity due to extreme wretchedness; and the numerous epithets of the Blessed One are imbued with the intention that his rescue is necessary because of His affection for His devotees.
Just as I have not narrated the story of Rāma, nor composed the Bhārata in its full extent, nor mastered the Bhāgavata—O Lord, how then can I hope for praise from You? (806)

The three roots *katha*, *cala*, and *kāś* are listed in the *cur*-class (*curādi-gaṇa*) among the non-ṇic-ending roots beginning with *kath*. From these, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*), and the *luṅ* (aorist) is formed in the active voice (*kartari*), the suffix *cli* undergoes *caṅ* substitution according to the rule "ṇiśridrusrubhyaḥ kartari caṅ. Because the *ṇic* here has lost its vowel (*aglopi*), the conditions for the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the reduplication of a desiderative) do not apply. This is because the rule "sanvallaghuni caṅpare'naglope" contains the exclusion "anaglope," which precludes the application of *sanvadbhāva* when there is vowel elision. Consequently, the short *i* prescribed by "sanyataḥ" does not occur in the reduplicated syllable, nor does the lengthening prescribed by "dīrgho laghoḥ."

The word *īśe* is the first person singular present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *īś*. In the phrase *stavasya*, the genitive case is used because, according to the rule *adhogarthadayeśām*, the object is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). Here, the qualifiers such as *nācakatham* (I did not speak) and so forth, by way of negating actions unique to Vālmīki, Vyāsa, and Sūta, contain the underlying intention (*ākūta*) that "I am not Vālmīki," and so on.
O lotus-eyed one, you did not rise up from the fire, nor did you recite the Gītā for my sake; why do you show such compassion toward me, asking "Who is he?", when I was not even born from Vyāsa?

In this context, the qualifiers such as "not having risen from the fire" and so forth, by way of negating actions unique to Draupadī, Dhanañjaya, and Śuka within themselves, contain the underlying intention (abhiprāya) such as "I am not Draupadī," and so on. Here, the distinction is that in the first example cited, there is a single qualifier; in the two immediately following examples, there are multiple word-meaning (padārtha) qualifiers each containing a single intention; and in the final two examples, there are sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) qualifiers containing distinct intentions.

Even though these [figures] possess a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), they do not receive the designation of *dhvani*. This is because, in the cases of gold attaining a luster equal to that of Lakṣmī, the world of the four-faced Brahmā becoming undesirable, the Lord and His devotee respectively being the inevitable deliverer and the one to be delivered, and the absence of a cause for showing compassion toward oneself—the suggested meaning serves merely as an embellishment (*upaskāraka*) of the expressed meaning (*vācya*). For this very reason, since the suggested meaning acts as an accessory to the expressed meaning, this ornament is named *parikara* (the "accessory").

Now, since the inclusion of a purposeless qualification is universally accepted as the fault of "insignificant meaning" (*apuṣṭārtha*), one might argue that a purposeful qualification can at best be considered merely the absence of that fault—like the absence of harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) and so on—and not a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) at all. To this, the ancients reply: when many purposeful qualifications are employed as residing in a single substratum (*dharmin*), a particular aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) arises that is so firmly established by experience that it cannot be denied; therefore, it is rightly included among the poetic figures.

In this regard, there is no fixed rule that *parikara* consists solely in the employment of multiple qualifiers. Since the presence of "unduly elaborate meaning" (*apuṣṭārtha*)—which is considered a defect—is not applicable in cases such as *śleṣa* (punning) and *yamaka* (chiming), the status of these as figures of speech cannot be denied even when only a single qualifier possesses intentional significance (*sābhiprāya*). Thus, even in the example "sudhāṃ śukalitottaṃsaḥ," its establishment as a figure of speech remains unimpeded.

Furthermore, it is universally accepted that *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality) is a figure of speech when based on the cause being a single word-meaning; likewise, they argue that it is entirely appropriate for even a single intentional qualifier to constitute a figure of speech.

Others, however, argue that if one accepts a specific charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) through the employment of significant epithets (*sābhiprāya-viśeṣaṇa*) in instances other than *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and so forth, then its status as an ornament (*alaṃkāratva*) is unavoidable; otherwise, it could equally be asserted that there is no specific charm even in the case of *śleṣa* and the like.

If it is argued that experience (*anubhava*) is the authority in that case, then since that is equally true elsewhere, it cannot be considered a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*). Having thus refuted the opinion of Dīkṣita, [the author] states: "The nature of being a figure of speech consists in being an embellisher (*upaskāraka*) while possessing beauty; the nature of being a non-defect (*doṣābhāva*) consists merely in the absence of anything that detracts from aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). Furthermore, even if these two occasionally coincide in a single instance, one does not establish the other as redundant, because the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) remain distinct even when the things delimited (*upadheya*) overlap.

Just as for a Brahmin, ignorance is a defect while learning is the absence of that defect and constitutes a merit, so too is the case here. Nor should it be argued: "Why is there such a weighty inclusion of *parikara* among the figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*), given that it is obtained merely as the absence of a defect? For this is justified by its dual nature, which serves to demonstrate its distinction from other defects.

Just as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), though already included as a variety of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), is counted again in the enumeration of figures of speech; or just as one who lives in both [floors] is counted again in the enumeration of ground-dwellers even though he has been counted among those living in palaces—so it is here as well, and thus there is no fault. Otherwise, even *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) would not be a figure of speech, because it consists merely in the absence of the defect known as *nirhetu* (absence of a cause). Thus they say.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of the Parikara (the Circumstantial), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Sprout of the Parikara (*Parikarāṅkura*):
"If the substantive (*viśeṣya*) should be endowed with significant meaning (*sākūta*), it is the *parikarāṅkura*."
When the substantive possesses intentional meaning, it is the figure of speech known as *parikarāṅkura*.
Just as in the past, O Trivikrama, you became an arrow upon the bow held by the hand of the Three-eyed Lord and reduced the three cities of the asuras— which were so difficult to assail— to ashes.

The word *trinayana* is listed in the *kṣubhnādi* group; consequently, by the rule "and in the case of *kṣubhnādi* words," the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] does not occur under the rule "after a preceding member, in a proper name, except for *g*. Here, through the etymological derivation "one who has three strides" (*trayo vikramā yasya*), the power of the literal meaning (*yogabala*) manifests his skill in the destruction of Tripura; thus, the substantive *Trivikrama* serves as an embellishment (*upaskāraka*) for the expressed sense (*vācya*).
Or rather:
Who can split the thousand arms of Bali’s son without the thousand-spoked [discus], and who can split the thousand petals of the lotus family without the thousand-rayed [sun]? (809)

Here, the primary meaning of the sentence takes the form of the figure of speech known as *dṛṣṭānta* (simile). In that context, the words *sahasrāra* (thousand-spoked) and *sahasrāṃśu* (thousand-rayed), which serve as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) of two sentence-meanings consisting of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), suggest the capacity for splitting a thousand petals and a thousand arms respectively; thus, they function as embellishments (*upaskāraka*) of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Just as this butter-thief steals my eye, so too does he steal it within the center of my own heart; how might I bind him with a fetter? May I behold this Dāmodara [as he shakes off my bonds].

This son of Nanda, the thief of butter, steals my eye—that is, he captivates my vision—according to the saying: "He who, by his beauty and noble qualities, robs men of their sight and heart. The root *mūṣ* belongs to the *bhvādi* class and means "to steal"; it may also be understood as "he steals away my garment," for the *Ratnamālā* states that the word *netra* can mean both "garment" and "eye. I shall bind this very one, who thus robs my eyes, within the center of my own heart—that is, I shall meditate upon him.

The sense is: "Among those who steal the property of others, I shall bind him too, for he is also a thief. This very Dāmodara, having been brought to such bondage, how indeed could he shake off my own bond of worldly existence (*bhavabandha*)? The sense is: "I shall observe and test what kind of method this man possesses for releasing one from the bonds of my own worldly existence."

Alternatively, the sense is: "How can one who is himself bound remove my bondage? based on the saying, "Alas, how can one who is himself bound be the liberator of another? In this context, the meaning is that he will not be capable of loosening the bond I have created within my own heart. Here, the substantive "milk-thief" (*navanīta-cora*) contains an underlying suggestion (*kūta*) regarding his expertise in thievery, which serves to embellish the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) consisting of the plundering of her eyes.

The term "Dāmodara" is the substantive; containing within it the intention that his bonds be loosened and his hunger satisfied, it serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning by suggesting, "How could he possibly shake off his bonds? Here, the two substantives possess distinct intentions.

In some cases, however, the suggester becomes the substantive (viśeṣya) by the force of conventional usage alone, regardless of its logical connection. As it has been stated in the *Ekāvalī*: "In certain instances, however, because of its well-known status, the substantive—even when employed in a manner that is not [literally] so—manifests the intended meaning as being such."

Just as neither Sutrāman, nor Vidhi, the enemy of Satru, nor even Īśvara can truly protect me, who am surely lying hidden in the cave of the thicket of worldly existence, only the boon-granting Mucukunda is able to save me.
In this context, the substantive "bestower of boons upon Mucukunda" (mucukundavarada) reveals his preeminent role as the protector of those sleeping within the cave.

O Lord of the Mountain, who has cast far away the vision of the Truth and embraced impurity; O Wielder of the Discus, why do you not enter this dense darkness within the small cave here and dispel it? 812.

O Cakradhara! That by which the vision of the virtuous—those who know Brahman—is cast aside is so described. In another sense, it is that by which the vision of the "virtuous"—the stars—is obstructed; for the meaning is that it is impossible to perceive the stars when dense darkness has entered the cave [of the heart]. It is so called because it has accepted impurity, sin, and blackness. Within the small cave (daharaguhā) there is dense darkness; therein exists the quality of tamas itself, which is a thick gloom, or perhaps a blinding darkness caused by the obstruction of clouds.

The construction may be understood as: "Having entered this small cave, why do you not take [it] away? Or, why indeed do you not take it away? In the first construction, the intention is: "For what reason do you not take it away? We do not know. In the second construction, the meaning is: "You certainly do take it away. Here, the substantive *cakradhara* (the Discus-bearer) implies that because the discus is as radiant as ten million suns, it is easy for the Blessed One who bears it to dispel the dense darkness within the cave of the heart.
Or, for example:

"O Vanamālī (the one garlanded with forest flowers), having first utterly dispelled my unbearable and most malignant evil impressions, you have indeed brought about the rise of fragrance in my mind, which was once so lowly.

(813) Here, the substantive "Vanamālī," by manifesting the intended meaning—the propriety of the arising of fragrance through the prior utter removal of evil impressions—enhances the expressed literal sense.

Or, O lotus-eyed one, just as the name "Rāma" which belongs to you is equal to the Thousand Names [of Viṣṇu], who else is capable of proclaiming the greatness of that infinite name without being like it? (814)

The construction [of the verse] is: "Who indeed is capable of describing its greatness? The suffix *tumun* is used here according to the rule: *“paryāptivacaneṣvalamartheṣu”* (Pāṇini 3.4.66), which prescribes it after words expressing sufficiency or capability. Here, the word *anantam* (infinite) serves as the subject (*viśeṣya*). By intending the state of having a thousand heads, it turns toward the meaning of the statement—namely, the skill in describing the majesty of Rāma’s name—which possesses a glory equal to the *Śrī Viṣṇusahasranāma*, as expressed in the saying: *“Rāma’s name is equal to the reality of the Thousand Names.”* Or, for example: "O Sovereign of the World, that one man alone is sufficient to praise your thousand names; or even the leader of the assembly of wind-eaters (the serpents)."

That Supreme Person, renowned as "the thousand-headed Puruṣa," is alone capable of praising You; or rather, Śeṣa—the leader of the assembly of wind-eaters (serpents) and the foremost of the serpent race—is capable—such is the construction. Here, the two subjects, "Puruṣa" and "leader of the assembly of wind-eaters," being pregnant with the intention of His possessing a thousand heads, serve as an embellishment (*parikara*) for the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*), which consists in His capacity to praise the thousand names of Lakṣmī.
In the four preceding examples, there was only one subject possessing an intended meaning (sābhiprāya), but here, however, there are two subjects, and even those share a single intended meaning.
Or rather:

"O Giver of Boons, I do not speak thus of you because of the suffering of Abhimanyu, nor because of the hundred-fold torment of Indra; for what compassion have you shown toward an elephant? How then can I describe you? (816)

In this passage, there are four distinct subjects (*viśeṣya*) each containing a different underlying intention, which distinguishes it from the previous example. The two subjects "Abhimanyu" and "Śatamanyu" (Indra) suggest that they must be respected because he is his nephew and his brother respectively, and even more so because of the power of their yoga and their extreme state of wretchedness; the subject "the elephant" suggests that it is to be disregarded because it is a wild animal and lacks any connection [to him]; and the subject "the granter of boons" (Varada) suggests his utter foolishness due to granting boons without discriminating between self and other. Thus, the distinction lies in these four subjects harboring divergent intentions.

"I have bestowed my compassion upon you who are indeed free from negative consequences (*ananubandhin*), in preference to those who possess them"—by this statement, "What am I to you? the reproach is expressed. Here, it should be understood that *parikarāṅkura* cannot be a separate figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). For, having defined *parikara* as "the arrangement of words with an intended meaning," its twofold division into "qualifying" (*viśeṣaṇa*) and "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) words makes it possible for this [figure] to be merely a sub-variety thereof.

For the distinction between figures of speech (alaṃkāra) depends on the distinction of their aesthetic charm (vicchitti); it does not exist merely because of the presence of intentional words within a single sentence. Moreover, this figure has been defined by the author of the *Ekāvalī* and others, whereas the earlier writers, such as the author of the *Prakāśa*, did not define it.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh lake, the Parikarāṅkura, in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Śleṣasaraḥ:
Śleṣa (punning) rests upon both the subject and the non-subject, and relies upon multiple meanings.

The *śleṣa* (punning) consists in the arrangement of words with multiple meanings. It is threefold: pertaining to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), pertaining to what is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*), and pertaining to both the subject and the non-subject (*prakṛtāprakṛta*). Each of these three types is further divided into two—those with a word-break (*sabhanga*) and those without (*abhaṅga*)—making six varieties in total. Among these, the first type is as follows: "May the Lord of the Mountain of Serpents (Śiva), whose conduct is pleasing to the heart, who is the source of the daughter of the Ocean (Gaurī), and who is the sustainer of the worlds; may he, the doer of good, abundantly bestow prosperity upon us who are weary, as we wander in this world. (817)

Regarding the Lord (Bhagavat-pakṣa): He whose heart-pleasing state of being—that is, whose disposition—is fixed upon that best of mountains named Śeṣa, the Lord of the Ahigiri, is so described. Regarding the Goddess (Śrī-pakṣa), however, she is one whose mode of existence—that is, her dwelling—is "heart-reaching," having reached the chest of Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the Ahigiri, the leader of Veṅkaṭādri. She is the bringer of auspiciousness to the worlds and the sovereign—the mistress—of Udanvatsutā, Lakṣmī. This [latter] is the predicate in the case of the Lord; in the other case, it means "the doer of good" (kalyāṇakarī).

The construction is "the overlord (*adhibhū*) of the worlds. This means she is the sovereign (*adhīśvarī*) of the universes (*bhuvanāni*). "The daughter of the ocean, the delighter of the rivers, Śrī"—this is the subject (*viśeṣya*). The rest is easy to understand.
As it is said in my own *Rāmeśvaravijaya* and *Raṅkharājavilāsa*, two works in the *campū* style:

"May one ever contemplate that ancient abode named Turaṅgarāja, which shines like a diamond within the heart, which is noble and always grants the attainment of speech, and which bestows all desired objects. (818)

I constantly meditate upon—that is, I contemplate in my heart and mind—the one who possesses a radiant couch that is the king of serpents himself; who is noble, generous, and bestowing what is beneficial and supreme good (*śreyas*); or, alternatively, "noble" (*udāra*) is an epithet for "beneficial," meaning *niḥśreyasa* (the highest beatitude). He is the ancient abode known as Raṅgarāja. The word "tu" is used for emphasis, according to Amarasimha’s lexicon: "Words such as *evaṃ*, *tu*, *punar*, and *vai* are expressers of emphasis. Thus, the meaning is "He alone is the abode. I always strive to attain Him through my speech.

In the phrase "anyatra hṛdaye," the division is "hṛt aye. Here, *hi* is a separate word used in the sense of well-known fact (*prasiddhi*). "Aye hṛt! means "O heart! It is resplendent like a king, shining in the orb of the moon, or as bright as the moon. The division is "añca mudā araṃ. It bestows, in a mere moment (*kalayā*), that which is desired and sought—the ancient abode known as the King of Horses, namely Śrī Hayagrīva. The construction is: "Always, for the attainment of speech, go with joy (*mudā añca*)."

The meaning is "propitiate. This is the second person singular present imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *añc*. In these two examples, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the two subjects under discussion—Śrī and Śrīnivāsa, as well as Śrīraṅgarāja and Hayagrīva. It should be noted that in the first example, this *śleṣa* is "unbroken" (*abhaṅga*), whereas in the second it is "broken" (*sabhaga*). This should be observed accordingly in the examples to be cited hereafter. Other points to be discussed will be explained further on. As for example: [Example follows]

I meditate in my heart upon that Sudarśana, the king of noble discs, who is honored by the foremost, whose splendor is like the rising sun, who wields great weapons, and whose navel resembles a lotus. 819.

In this instance, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the two subjects under discussion, namely the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) and the Sudarśana [discus]. To illustrate: in the case of the Blessed One, *prathimne* means for the sake of greatness—that is, for the sake of proclaiming his renown. The compound is formed according to the rule *caturthī tadartha* ("the fourth [case-ending] when it has that as its purpose"). Alternatively, it may mean "beneficial by way of greatness" or "beneficial through renown. In the case of the Sudarśana, *prathi* refers to the rim (*nemi*); it is "honored by the rim" (*prathimahitam*). As Amara states: "The word *nemi* is feminine, while *prathi* is masculine."

"Whose friend is the flash of light belonging to the cloud—that is, the dark rain-cloud (*ghanāghana*)—which manifests and expands at the onset of the monsoon; this means he is as dark as the rain-cloud of the rainy season. Alternatively, he whose radiance is like that of Mitra (the Sun), who is rising, dense, and of unimpeded brilliance; this means his luster resembles the rising sun, for it is said: 'Sudarśana is equal to ten million suns.'"

"Mahāyudham" means one who possesses great weapons, such as the discus (*cakra*) and others; alternatively, it refers to one for whom there is a great battle (*yut*)—as Amara states, "the words *samiti*, *āji*, *samit*, and *yudh* all mean battle. Or else, it may mean one for whom there is a great battle on the side of the Lord alone. In the case of the Sudarśana [discus], however, the meaning is that he is the bearer of many weapons, according to the description: "bearing the conch, the discus, the bow, the axe, the sword, the arrow, the trident, the noose, the goad, the fire, the thunderbolt, the shield, the plow, the mace, the club, and the spear."

[He is] one whose navel possesses a lotus with a stalk (*sārasa-padmam*). Because *gaḍu* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇas*, the locative case is placed at the end of the compound. In the context of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), this is the predicate noun. Alternatively, [the term *sanābhi* may be analyzed as follows]: that which exists together with spokes (*ara*)—that is, with pins (*śalākā*)—fixed all around, is called *sāra*. This is based on such descriptions as "extremely intense with a thousand throbbing spokes" (*sphuratsahasrāraśikhātitīvram*), and the *Medinīkośa* states: "*araṃ* means 'swift' and 'a part of a wheel'. That which exists together with the navel—the central cavity—is *sanābhaḥ*. The suffix *ac* is applied here by splitting the rule *ac-pratyanvava-* into two parts, namely, by the application of *ac* alone.

In both cases, there is a *saha-pūrvapada-bahuvrīhi* compound. "Sārasanābham" is a *viśeṣaṇobhayapada-karmadhāraya* (a karmadhāraya with two qualifying words), meaning "that which is both essence (*sāra*) and navel-like (*sanābha*). Thus it is so described. Regarding the interpretation for the Lord (Bhagavat): "Sudarśanam" means beautiful to behold; "Cakrarājaḥ" means the king of the multitude (*cakra*) of the virtuous (*sādhu*, i.e., the *sat*s); thus, "I contemplate that Sārasanābha who is the Sudarśana, the King of the Multitude of the Virtuous. Regarding the interpretation for the Sudarśana [discus], however: "Cakrarāja" means the king of discs; "Sudarśanam" refers to the divine weapon of the Lord by that name. In this case, this very term is the subject (*viśeṣya*).

The construction is: "I shall consider it in such a way that it may be correct. The word *sudarśana* is taught as being masculine as well, for the *Nāmanidhāna* states: "In the sense of a discus, *sudarśana* is not feminine. Furthermore, according to the *Medinī* and *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*, it is masculine only: "*Sudarśana* is masculine when referring to Viṣṇu’s discus, the Meru tree, or the Jambū tree; otherwise, it is *sudarśana* [masculine]. Therefore, there is no contradiction even though the *Liṅgānuśāsana* (part of the *Amara-kośa*) contains the reading "the discus is *sudarśana*" in the neuter gender.

In reality, however, even in that case, the masculine reading alone is accepted in works such as the *Amarasudhā*; and it was employed by Māgha in the verse: "This Sudarśana is a kinsman to the worlds. Although here, because the word *sudarśana*—qualified by adjectives such as *prathima* and *hitam*—ends in the nominative singular neuter, the masculine gender is not required since there is uniformity between the masculine and neuter genders in that form;

nevertheless, it should be understood that when the qualifier is *mahāyudham*, analyzed as *mahatī yut yasya* (that which has a great splendor), a difference in form between the two genders necessarily arises, and thus that [masculine usage] was indeed required and demonstrated.

May that certain, most venerable Lord, the support of the five classes of beings, protect you—He by whom the pride of the sons of Danu was destroyed by the roar arising from His close proximity to the wind from Hari’s mouth. 820.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the two subjects under discussion, the Lord and the conch Pañcajanya. For instance: those who have Hari as their mouth are Indra and the other gods; for the *amarakośa* states, "The two words *marut* refer to the wind and the gods. From the *abhitaḥ-saṃstava*—that is, from the excellent praise—of them, there arose a sound (*ninada*) by which was destroyed the pride (*darpa*) of the sons of Danu, that is, the arrogance of the Dānavas; he [the Lord] is thus described.

In the case of Lord Hari, there is an *abhisaṃstava*—meaning a thorough familiarity or constant contact—with the breath from his mouth (*mukhamarutaḥ*), according to the rule that "the word *saṃstava* may mean familiarity" (*saṃstavassyātparicayaḥ*). By means of the sound produced thereby, the pride of the Danavas and their progeny was destroyed; this is the stated meaning. By this, the following is made known: "The sound of him, who is filled by the wind arising from Viṣṇu’s mouth, is the destroyer of the pride of the Dānavas. Regarding "of the five-fold people" (*pañcajanānām*), which refers to human beings, Amarasimha states: "The term *pañcajana* may denote males (*pumāṃsaḥ*)."

They are called *pañcajanāḥ* because they are produced by the five elements (*bhūta*); [the suffix] *ghañ* is applied to the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*). No *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs here due to the rule *janivadhyośca*. It is the substratum (*ādhāra*), that is, the support (*āśraya*). Alternatively, it is the substratum or support of the five classes of beings (*pañcajana*), namely the senses, according to the Vedic revelation: "In whom the five classes of beings and the ether are established. In this alternative view, *pañcajana* is the name of a Daitya; he is the substratum of which [the conch], and it is precisely because of being its substratum that it is designated by the word *pāñcajanya*. As it is stated in the venerable *Bhāgavata*:
"O Lord, I did not seize that great Daitya Pañcajana..."
O Kṛṣṇa, there was an asura dwelling within the water who had assumed the form of a conch shell.
Having begun thus, [it continues]:
"Then, taking the conch-shell produced from his limb, he ascended the chariot.

For this very reason, the word *pāñcajanya*—formed with the suffix *ñya* in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhāva*)—was derived by the Author of the Bhāṣya from the Vārttika on the sūtra *gambhīrāññyaḥ*, which states: "It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *bahiḥ*, *deva*, and *pañcajana*. He, whose great respect is manifest as a king, is some [divine being] of such great majesty as is heard in the Śruti: "From whence words turn back. May that Blessed One protect us. In the alternative interpretation, *bhagavān* is a qualifying epithet [of the author].
May He whose majesty and splendor are unique among the worlds—the *rājanmahas*—protect us; may the conch (*dara*) protect us. Or, for example:

"I take refuge in the auspicious Lakṣmī (*sādhuśrī*), who possesses beautiful armlets (*rucirāṅgadā*), who shines when grasped by the hand of the Lord of Mountains (Śiva), the best of serpents, and who has shaken off the sluggish demons. 821.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) regarding Lakṣmī and the mace (*gadā*), both of whom are introduced as subjects worthy of praise. To explain: by means of the "taking of the hand" (*karagraha*)—that is, by marriage—with Śrīnivāsa, the lord of the mountain of the foremost of serpents; in the other sense, by means of grasping with the hand. [She is] "shining" (*ullasitā*), meaning radiant and manifest. She is one whose younger sibling is "shining with the state of being the moon" (*vidhutā*), that is, one whose younger brother is the moon, meaning she is like the moon (*candrasodarā*).

She by whom the offspring of Danu—the Dānavas—have been shaken off and driven away from her side, and are therefore rendered sluggish and feeble; she who possesses beautiful armlets (aṅgada) and bracelets (keyūra)—to that Śrī, Lakṣmī, one should properly go for refuge with fully developed limbs.

For the word *śaraṇa* is currently used in the sense of "means" (*upāya*), as in the expression "the house and its protector are the refuge. (Note: The term *śaraṇa* here functions as a synonym for "protection" or "means of safety," specifically referring to the Goddess Lakṣmī as the source of shelter.)

This is according to the statement in the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*. The meaning is: "I have taken refuge," that is, I have resorted [to Him] by making the taking of shelter at the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lord my human effort (*puruṣakāra*). In the alternative interpretation, the word *sādhuśriyam* is a compound modifying *gadā* (the mace); it means "that which possesses beautiful splendor. The word *rucirām* is analyzed separately; it means "the lovely" *gadā*, namely the *Kaumodakī*. In this interpretation, the *parasavarṇa* (assimilation) of the anusvāra is optional according to the rule *vā padāntasya*. Thus: "I resort to the refuge."
Or, for example:

"We meditate upon [the Lord] whose body is possessed of the Nandaka sword, who is dark yet radiant, whose splendor is glorious, whose limbs are endowed with beautiful form, and who is embraced by a noble disposition capable of destroying the demon Bali. (822) In this instance, there is a *śleṣa* (pun/paronomasia) between the two subjects, the Lord and the sword Nandaka. In the sense of the Lord, there are five words: *sannandakam*, *asitojjvalam*, *ojas*, *śrīmat*, and *sarūpadheyāṅgam*. The word *śrīmat* means "possessing eternal union with Śrī" (Lakṣmī). Regarding *rūpadheyam*: the suffix *dheya* is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*) according to the rule "after *bhāga*, *rūpa*, and names, the suffix *dheya* is added. Thus, *rūpam eva rūpadheyam* ("form itself is that which is called rūpadheya").

"Accompanied by that" means *sarūpadheya*, which signifies a divine form. That whose body (*aṅga*) or physical frame (*vigraha*) is such is described as "possessing such a body. Regarding the destruction of Bali—the Daitya of that name—meaning his fall from the station of Indra: "Dakṣiṇā" means clever (*dakṣa*). As the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi* states: "The word *dakṣiṇa* refers to one who follows the will of another, to one who is clever, to the right side, and to that which is straightforward. It was "filled with a great hope" (*āśā*), meaning a great longing (*tṛṣṇā*). Furthermore, it is both "black" (*asita*) and "radiant" (*ujjvala*), hence "black-and-radiant" (*asitojjvala*).

The meaning is: "delighting the virtuous," that is, "causing intense joy" and "bestowing bliss. *Ojas* (splendor) is the substantive; it refers to the Supreme Brahman, as heard in the scripture: "That which is the light of lights, the gods meditate upon" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.2.9). "We meditate" [upon this]. In the case of the sword (*Nandaka*), however, there are four words: *sannandakam*, *asitojjvalam*, *ojasśrīmat*, and *tsarūpadheyāṅgam*. *Ojasśrīmat* means "possessing the excellence (*śrī*) of splendor (*ojas*). *Tsarūpadheyāṅgam* refers to that whose limb (*aṅga*) is to be placed (*upadheya*) or set within the hilt (*tsaru*).

In the first interpretation, regarding the word *śrīmattsaru*, there is a doubling of the letter *t* according to the rule *anaci ca*. Amara states: "The word *tsaru* refers to the hilt of a sword and the like. This expression is used because the sword is supported by its hilt (*tsaru*). [The compound means: that which is grasped by the right hand—the great hand (*mahā-śaya*) meaning the hand other than the left—of the Lord, who is the destroyer (*dhvaṃsana*) of the powerful Daityas; the sense is that it is held by the right hand of the Daityas and others. It is radiant (*ujjvala*) due to that blackness (*asitā*), which is the state of being black (*asitā*) derived from the root *as*.
He who is both "existent" (sat) and "delighting" (nandaka) is Sannandaka; that is the object to be qualified. We meditate upon the sword named Nandaka.
Or, for example:

"May that certain great bow (mahāśārṅga), which is inclined toward those who have approached [it] and whose upper end is free from wear by the friction of the string, long remain for my welfare. In this instance, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the two meanings of "bow" (*śārṅga*), both of which are the subject at hand. To explain: "inclined toward those who have approached" (*samupanateṣu pravaṇam*) means dependent upon or devoted to those who have come for refuge; and "that by which weariness has been shaken off" (*vidhūnitajyānighṛṣṭaparakoṭi*) is a compound word analyzed as follows: it refers to that which has dispelled all weariness (*jyāni*)—meaning exhaustion—in the world. Thus, the meaning is "that which has pacified the fatigue of all people."

The meaning of "by whom millions of enemies, the adversaries, were ground and crushed" is that he has destroyed his infinite opponents. Regarding the Lord (Bhagavat), it refers to him who possesses the great *śārṅga* bow. Regarding the *śārṅga* bow itself, however, it refers to that in which arrows (*iṣu*) have come together and are joined. The reason for this is "inclined" (*pravaṇa*), meaning bent. He states the reason for even that: "shaken" (*vidhūnita*). This means shaken or moved; by that [bow], the string (*jyā*, *maurvī*) is rubbed or, in other words, brought into contact.

That which has another end (koṭi)—meaning its peak—is superior in comparison to the limit of its own support. That which is both great and Śārṅga (the bow) is the Lord’s form; may that indescribable reality, which is both that [form] and the other [reality], long be for my welfare. These five verses beginning with "prathimahitam" were composed by me myself as a hymn to the Five Weapons (*pañcāyudha*) using double entendre (*śliṣṭa*).
Or rather:

May the Great Splendor be victorious—He whose bow, renowned throughout the three worlds, was cast with great force by the tip of His arm adorned with excellent qualities, and which now vibrates upon the beautiful hand of Acyuta. 824.

Here too, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the two subjects, Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu) and the bow Śārṅga. To explain: "adhirūḍhāḥ" means grown, manifested, or appearing. [The compound] "suguṇakoṭi" refers to that which possesses millions (*koṭi*) of excellent qualities (*suguṇa*, i.e., auspicious attributes). In the alternative sense [referring to the bow], it is a *bahuvrīhi*-within-a-*bahuvrīhi*: "that whose end (*koṭi*, i.e., the tip or string-end) has a beautiful string (*suguṇa*, i.e., a fine bowstring) mounted upon it. Thus, the meaning is "having a strung tip."

That by which great calamities—the misfortunes of the world—have been cast away and dispelled is "Kṣiptamahāpat. It is renowned throughout the three worlds. In the alternative sense, it is that by which great winged arrows have been discharged; thus, "Kṣiptamahāpattri. It is celebrated in the worlds. That whose abode—meaning its splendor, power, or majesty—is unfailing (acyuta) and auspicious (śubhakara), is so described. That whose Śārṅga bow is quivering and uplifted is so described.

The Śārṅga bow—possessing great splendor (*mahaḥ*) that quivers (*preṅkhat*) within its abode (*dhāma*), which is none other than the auspicious and blessed hand (*kara*) of the Lord Acyuta—is the subject here; it is the Supreme Brahman, as heard in the scripture: "Now, that light which is beyond this heaven" (*atha yadataḥ paro divo jyotiḥ*). May this [Śārṅga] be victorious.
Or, for example:
"May that lotus-eyed one be victorious, who formerly manifested as the Great Boar with haste in order to uplift the eternal earth that had been seized by the enemy of the gods. (825)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between Mahāvarāha and Śrī Hayagrīva, who are introduced as subjects worthy of praise. To explain: by the enemy of the gods, Hiraṇyākṣa—or in the other sense, by the demon named Madhu, the second of the Kaiṭabhas—who carried away the eternal *gā* (earth), or the speech in the form of the *Śruti* (Vedas). To rescue her, he who was previously filled with haste and agitation as Mahāvarāha—or in the other sense, the word should be split as *mahāvarāhas-tu-arānvitaḥ*; here the particle *tu* is used for emphasis and should be construed with "to rescue. (Note: In the second interpretation, *mahāvarāhas-tu-arānvitaḥ* means "the Great Boar, indeed, [is] possessed of spokes," referring to the wheel of the chariot of Viṣṇu.)

The meaning is "precisely for the sake of uplifting. *Arānvitaḥ* means "endowed with the letter *ra*"—that is, being *Mahāvarāha*, he becomes *Mahāvāha*, namely Hayagrīva. The intention is that when the consonant in the form of the letter *ra* is removed from the word *Mahāvarāha*, the remaining *ā* (the initial *ā*) and the *ā* following the *va* undergo a *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution for similar vowels), resulting in the formation of the word *Mahāvāha*. He manifested. May that lotus-eyed one be victorious. By the term "lotus-eyed," this is made to correspond with the description: "having eyes like blossoming lotuses, like those of the Great Boar (*Mahāvarāha*)."

Just as the Lord formerly chose Mucukunda— who was ever free from fear— as the best and most sinless of men, may that Mucukunda, whose second syllable is "Mu" and who dwells in the cave of the heart, reside within my own heart.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the two subjects at hand, Mucukunda and Mukunda. He [the former] is renowned as the son of Māndhātṛ, as a commander-in-chief (*saināpatya*), and as a protector of the gods; he is the sovereign lord (*adhīśa*), the overlord (*adhirāja*), and the universal emperor (*sārvabhauma*)—that is to say, Mucukunda. Long ago, on the occasion of putting Kālayavana to flight, from Dāmodara—from the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the suffix *tasi* is used here after the word *ādya* according to Pāṇini’s rule *pañcamyāstasi*; he received and accepted a boon that was more sinless (*anaghataram*).

"Guha-śayaḥ" means one who dwells in mountain caves; "dvitīya-varṇaḥ" refers to one whose second caste is the Kṣatriya caste—that is, this Mucukunda. In the alternative interpretation, "sadāmodarataḥ" is a single compound word ending in the nominative singular. It means the Blessed One who is "rataḥ"—attached—to the "āmode"—joy—of the "satām"—the virtuous. "Purā-adhīśaḥ": the word "adhīśa" here ends in the genitive singular; it means "of that very Adhirāja," namely Mucukunda. The genitive case is used here in the sense of a general relationship.

The analysis of the phrase is: "I give a boon that is most free from suffering" (*anaghatarām varām dade*). He has given [this]. "Dwelling in the cave" (*guhāśayaḥ*) means situated within the cave of the hearts of all sentient beings, according to such Vedic texts as, "That which is placed in the cave, dwelling in the depths. The analysis of the phrase is: "of the unique syllable" (*advitīyavarṇaḥ*). This one of the unique syllable—meaning Mucukunda, who is devoid of a second syllable, i.e., Mukunda—the meaning being that because of the identity between word and object; may he dwell in my heart, meaning may he become the traveler upon the path of meditation.

However, it should be understood that if the intention is to treat Mucukunda as not being the subject under discussion, this will serve as an example of a pun (śleṣa) between the relevant and the irrelevant.
Or for example:

"O Govinda! Those who have undertaken the vow of the Jayantī festival of the Son of Nanda are dearer to you than even Brahmā, though he may abandon them because they were pierced by the fire of their previous births. (827) In this instance, there is a *śleṣa* (pun/paronomasia) between the subjects at hand—those like Ambarīṣa who are single-mindedly devoted to the Blessed One, and those performers of the Śrī Jayantī vow. To explain: "O Govinda, Son of Nanda!"—this address serves as an embellishment for the meaning that is about to be stated.

"By the fire of existence"—pierced and afflicted by the conflagration of *saṃsāra*, and for that very reason "inauspicious," or "unlucky"—even Brahmā, the four-faced one, they "leave behind" (*jahataḥ*), meaning they abandon him because he is of no assistance to their meditation. If even the four-faced one is abandoned first, then the abandonment of deities inferior to him is established as a matter of course. Alternatively, the word *prāk* (before) is compounded with the word *bhava* (existence); thus, *prāgbhava* refers to beginningless *saṃsāra*, which is like a fire. The rest is the same. Here, [the verse implies] all things situated within the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Living beings are subject to the cycle of existence produced by their own karma.
For all those who are encompassed by ignorance remain within the domain of saṃsāra; therefore, they are of no benefit to meditators in their practice of meditation.
Thus, such authoritative texts as "Everything up to Brahmā is inauspicious" were also kept in mind. These [ascetics] have undertaken their vows;
you who have undertaken that vow—O Purandara, strike me with your thunderbolt or do not strike me at all.
But I, O sir, shall not abandon Govinda to worship anyone else.

Those by whom such a vow (vrata)—of the kind described by Ambarīṣa—is observed; for Amarasimha states: "Vrata is a masculine or neuter term meaning a religious observance, and it consists of merit such as fasting. It is precisely with the intention of this authoritative evidence that the address "Govinda" is used in the root text. This very term serves as the substantive, just like [the epithets] "Pītāmbara" (Yellow-Robed) or "Sāgarāmbara" (Ocean-Clad). For Vāmana has formulated the rule: "The employment of an adjective is for the purpose of identifying the substantive. Being your most beloved ones, they are victorious.

By the term "dearest" (*priyatama*), there is an expression of the state of being chosen by the Supreme Self as stated in the Śruti: "Whomever He chooses. For the commentary on the aforementioned Śruti in the *Laghusiddhānta* states: "Indeed, only one who is dear is worthy of being chosen; and he for whom He has unsurpassed love becomes His dearest."

Except for Brahmā, [the deity of] the Rohiṇī asterism is Prajāpati, because it is heard in scripture that "Prajāpati is the deity of the Rohiṇī asterism," and because of the traditional law (smṛti) stating, "The Ordainer (Vidhātṛ) is the lord of Rohiṇī. Furthermore, even though Bhadrā is inauspicious, she is [referred to as such] because of the rule establishing the names of the lunar days (tithis) in sequence: "Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā are the lunar days in order," which assigns these names respectively to the five groups of lunar days beginning with the first.

The meaning is that for one who lacks the *bhadra* [muhūrta], even if it is pierced by the seventh [tithi], this is the reason for not abandoning it. "Pierced by the purifier of the previous birth" means by the purifier (*pāvaka*)—the constellation Kṛttikā—which exists previously; for it is heard in scripture that its presiding deity is Agni, as in: "The constellation Kṛttikā has Agni as its deity," and because it is said, "Kṛttikā is declared to belong to Agni. "Pierced" means brought to a state of piercing; this is the cause for it being ungraspable. "Leaving" means abandoning.
Jayantī is said to be of two kinds, designated as *śuddhā* (pure) and *viddhā* (pierced).
The pure [lineage] is said to be of two kinds, and the pierced is of four kinds.
Therefore, with every effort, one should observe the vow on the following day, even if it means skipping the seventh lunar day of Kṛttikā by even a single digit.

This is because the authorities have determined that the four types of *vedha*—namely, [the conjunction] of the seventh lunar day with the eighth and Rohiṇī, and [the conjunction] of the eighth and Rohiṇī with Kṛttikā—as expressed in such statements, must be avoided. The phrase "those who have undertaken the vows on Jayantī" (*amī jayantyupāttavratāḥ*) is a compound word. [As stated: "O King, when Rohiṇī is found on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, that is celebrated as Jayantī."
If even for half a *muhūrta* on the ninth lunar day there is the conjunction with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, whether it occurs at the very beginning or not, that day is celebrated as *Jayantī*.

The meaning is as follows: those people who have undertaken—that is, accepted—the vow (vrata), consisting of the observance of fasting and so forth, on a lunar day (tithi) characterized by the aforementioned definitions, and who are thus called "those [who perform the vow],"—namely, those performers of the Jayantī-vrata which is free from the fourfold conjunctions (vedha)—become exceedingly dear to You. In this regard, [it is said]:
"Even without the pure eighth lunar day (śuddhāṣṭamī), or even with a pure asterism (śuddhamṛkṣa)..."
And on the ninth or even the tenth day, the Vaiṣṇava [should perform the rite] with a deer.
If the [asterism] is joined with the seventh lunar day in the first half, or joined with Kṛttikā in the second half,
one should avoid those two days and perform [the rite] on another day.
Thousands of such statements should be investigated. Thus has been illustrated *śleṣa* (paronomasia) having multiple subjects that are exclusively of the primary nature.
An example of one whose objects are many and not the subject at hand:

The row of stars, possessing exceedingly great and pure qualities as they shine within the vast void, with their continuous and supreme radiance, has been eclipsed by the claws of the bull of the mountain that leads [the herd]. (828)

She whose quality—meaning her thread—is *sumahāḥ* (exceedingly great), *śobhanadīptiḥ* (of beautiful luster), *vilasattamaḥ* (most radiant) within the *bileṣu* (cavities or apertures), and *viśadaḥ* (pure and clear). In another sense, she is so described because she possesses an exceedingly great cavity (*sumahābile*) in the sky—as Amaraśeṣa states, "the great cavity is the gateway of the clouds"—and because she has an *atisattamaḥ* (supremely shining) and *viśadaguṇaḥ* (pure white) quality. Furthermore, she is so called because she possesses a *satatam-uttama-sphuraṇam* (constant and most excellent brilliance or shimmering luster).

In another sense, she is "she whose radiance (*prakāśa*) is a supreme flashing forth (*sphuraṇa*) in darkness (*tamas*). Regarding the term *tamassphuraṇā*, one should understand that the sequence of phonemes remains identical in both cases, even when the *visarga* of the word *tamaḥ* is optionally elided according to the rule: "The *visarga* is elided before a *khara* or a *śara*. *Tārāvalī* refers both to a pearl necklace and to a row of stars. The word *tāra* denotes a monkey, purity, a pure pearl, a star, the center of the eye, and is not used in the neuter gender for the formless (*nārūpya*).

Thus, in both cases, the word *medinī* (earth) is used. The rest is easy to understand. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the necklace of pearls and the row of stars, which are not the primary subjects (*aprakṛta*), by virtue of being the standard of comparison for the row of the Lord’s nails. Or, for example:
"May that man, the leader of my arm, be victorious! He who, while separated from heaven, conquered the cloud-bannered Indra by the mere splendor of his radiant form. (829)

[He beheld] him whose station in the sky, the firmament, was appropriate—that is, whose state of abiding was suited to gladdening the world through the act of raining. He states the reason for this with the word "ucca": [he saw] that cloud (*mudira*) from which the waters (*āpaḥ*) were high (*uccāḥ*), meaning abundant; the suffix *ap* is applied at the end of the compound according to the rule "ṛkpūrap... and so forth. The sense is that it was a cloud of the rainy season (*prāvṛṣeṇya*). Regarding *mudira*, Amara states: "ghana, jīmūta, mudira, jalamuṭ, dhūmayoni."

He who surpassed by his very form—that is, by his divine body and its splendor alone—the one who possesses a high bow (in the alternative sense, the one with an uplifted bow), and who possesses a state devoid of the letter *di*—that is, a state that is broken apart from the letter *di*, meaning the cloud (*mudira*), which [when the letter *di* is elided from the word *mudira*] results in the form *mura*. Here, the identity between word and meaning is the accepted principle. He surpassed—that is, he eclipsed—by his "form and splendor," meaning by the power of his prowess in battle.
Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the two non-contextual subjects, the cloud (*mudira*) and Mura.

Just as a mortal, O Mother of All, by beholding you becomes one who has attained well-being and stability, a consumer of nectar, and is celebrated as a foe to the hosts of Dānavas, so too does he attain the state of being honored by the wise. 830.

O Akhilamba! "Martya" refers to a mortal human being; there is also a word-break as "amartya," meaning a god. Through your gaze—that is, by your side-long glance—he becomes one for whom his own wealth (*sva*) and the stable earth (*sthira-bhū*) are thoroughly secured (*prasādhita*), meaning they are brought under his complete control. In the case of the "immortal" (*amartya*), it means one by whom heaven (*svaḥ*) has been secured, that is, adorned. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with an indeclinable ending in *r* as its final member. He is "stable" (*sthira*), meaning enduring for a long time.

"Sudhānyāda" means one who eats "sudhānya"—that is, excellent grain; in other words, one who consumes food such as well-refined rice and grains. Alternatively, he is so called because his "nyāda" (food) consists of "sudhā" (nectar). The suffix *ṇa* is applied to the root preceded by the prefix *ni-* according to the rule "nau ṇa ca. Amara states: "jemana, lepa, āhāra, nighasa, and nyāda all mean food. He is "atyākhyāta" by the water of his gifts—that is, he is exceedingly and universally renowned—and for this very reason, he attains the state of being honored by the wise.

The sense is that [the king] attains the state of being worthy of praise by the learned due to his status as a most noble universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*). In the other case, he is known—by common renown—as the "enemy of the Dānavas," meaning the destroyer of the Daityas headed by Vṛtra; here, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case (instrumental) according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi*. Alternatively, the word *ākhyātaḥ* may be taken as ending in the nominative. He "attains the state of being praised by the wise" means that he enjoys the sovereignty over the gods. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the two subjects—the mortal and the immortal—which are not the primary context, both being favored by the glance of the Mother of the World.

O Lord, Sovereign of the World, just as the prosperity desired by your friends has been attained by you, so too, O Jewel upon the Crest of the Serpents, has munificence been displayed through your acts of giving. (831)

O Blessed One! By you, as a sovereign on this earth, the *avyayībhāva* compound has been employed in the sense of the locative case (*adhibhu bhuvi*). You have brought about—that is, accomplished—the desired prosperity of your friends or well-wishers. Furthermore, through giving—that is, bestowing—you have manifested both generosity and eloquence; for Amara states, "one who is generous is also sweet-spoken. Indeed, those who know the Dharma say: "And having given, one should speak sweetly."

The explicit meaning is that you have made your friends wealthy and have rendered them fond of gifts and kind words appropriate to their status. In the alternative sense, there is a word-division as *amitrāṇām* (of enemies). [The phrase is: "of enemies (*amitrāṇām*), of lords (*adhibhuvām*), of masters (*prabhūṇām*)"—according to Amara, "the lord (*adhibhū*) is the leader (*nāyaka*) or guide (*netṛ*). "Wealth (*vibhavaḥ*)" was acquired "by means of battle" (*kalitaḥ*); the suffix *-tasi* is used here according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi*. According to Amara’s list of synonyms for battle: "encounter (*saṃprahāra*), clash (*abhisaṃpāta*), strife (*kalaha*), conflict (*saṃsphoṭa*), and combat (*saṃyuga*)."

*Chitaḥ* means "cut. It is derived from the root *chā*, meaning "to cut," belonging to the *divādi* class; the suffix *kta* is applied in the passive sense (*karmani*), and the vowel substitution *it* is optional according to the rule *śāccho 'nyatarasyām*. Amara states: "The words *kṛttam*, *dātam*, *ditam*, *chitam*, and *vṛkṇam* all mean 'cut'. Furthermore, *vadānyatā* means "generosity" (*vanyatā*); it is not possessed of the syllable *da*—that is, it is unjoined with or devoid of it. This is a compound with the negative particle *na*. It has been composed (*viracitā*).

The intention is that the enemies were not only deprived of their wealth, but were even reduced to living on forest-gathering (vanyavṛtti). Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the Friend and the Enemy of the Blessed One, both of whom are unmentioned (*aprastuta*). If the intention were for both to be mentioned (*prastuta*), this would be an example of *śleṣa* with multiple subjects under discussion. This should be understood similarly in the previous example as well.
An example of [the paronomasia] between the mentioned (*prastuta*) and the unmentioned (*aprastuta*) is as follows:
"He who bears the dark shadow of beautiful marks, whose nature is recognized by the sun, and who makes the high shoulder of the bull prominent—this Hari spreads his heart-pleasing glory. (832)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the Lord and the Moon, both of whom are the subjects and the non-subjects [of the description]. To explain: he is so called because he possesses a beautiful (*mañju*) mark (*lakṣma*), namely the Śrīvatsa sign or the unique marks such as the conch and discus. By this, his transcendence is indicated:
"The Creator is beyond darkness; he bears the conch, discus, and mace;
the Śrīvatsa is upon his chest; he is eternally glorious, invincible, eternal, and immutable."

This is according to such Vedic passages [as Ṛgveda 10.37.4]. He bears a dark, deep-black luster or radiance. This Hari, O Blessed One, is one whose nature is known for compassion (*ghṛṇin*); he possesses compassion (*ghṛṇā*), thus he is compassionate (*ghṛṇin*). The suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of possession according to the rule for the *vrīhi*-class of words. Amara states: "The words *ghṛṇā*, *jugupsā*, and *karuṇā* mean compassion. Alternatively, he is one whose self is renowned as compassionate; this is according to such Vedic passages as [Ṛgveda 10.86.1]: "Compassionate, with true valor. Or again, he is one whose self is known among those who possess compassion (*ghṛṇiṣu pratītātmā*), meaning he is supremely merciful.

*Ghṛṇī* means one whose nature is an object of trust, since the root *iṇ* preceded by *prati* has the sense of "trust. Alternatively, it may be a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of two adjectives: "one who is compassionate (*ghṛṇī*) and one whose self is recognized (*pratītātmā*). In this latter view, *pratīta* means "delighted. As Amarasimha states: "The word *pratīta* is used for one who is well-known or delighted. The sense is that his mind is thrilled with great compassion in order to revive those residing in the realm of *līlāvibhūti*. By this, he expresses his possession of mercy, which is the cause of his accessibility (*saulabhya*).

For this very reason, by saying "approaching the lofty Vṛṣabhādri, the mountain of the bull," there is an expression of his accessibility (*saulabhya*). By saying "he spreads his heart-stealing glory (*śrī*), which resides upon his chest," the sense is that he demonstrates his own nature as Śrīnivāsa (the Abode of Śrī). Through this, it is shown that even while possessing accessibility, he does not relinquish his transcendence (*paratva*).

He whose nature is well-known through the rays of the sun (ghṛṇi) during its fortnight (pakṣa)—he who bears the dark (asita), beautiful shadow of the earth (kṣmācchāyā); that is to say, the reflection of the earth denoted by the word "hare" (śaśa). For it is stated in the *Harivaṃśa*: "The mark on your body consists of the shadow of the world, resembling a hare"; there is also the reading "on your lap" (*tavāṅke*). And because of the statement of later authors: "Others maintained it was the shadow of the earth."

According to Amara: "Chāyā means the beloved of the sun (shadow), luster, reflection, and non-heat. This *hari* refers to the moon; as stated in the *Ratnamālā*: "'Hari' is used for Yama, the sun, horses, fire, the moon, Viṣṇu, Indra, rays, and parrots. *Tuṅgam* means high. *Vṛṣabhāgam* means the portion of the bull, that is, the third part of the sign of Taurus (*vṛṣa-rāśi*), because that very position is its highest point of exaltation (*paramocca*). As stated by the teacher Varāhamihira: "Aries, Taurus, Capricorn, Virgo, Cancer, Pisces, and Libra are the points of exaltation (*tuṅga*) for the Sun and the other planets respectively."
Those planets are not combust when they occupy ten, three, five, two, twenty-one, nine, and eighteen degrees of their signs respectively.

Thus, being so, he spreads his heart-pleasing splendor—that is, he becomes radiant; or alternatively, it means he extends the abundance of auspiciousness for those born when [the planet] is in its own sign. This is according to the statements in the *Mādhavīya*: "In its exaltation, it is intensely radiant," and "Radiance bestows full auspiciousness."

Victorious is that Lord of the Gods, whose abode is established upon the Bull-mountain (Vṛṣācala), by whom a line of friends— possessing honored and stainless glory and ever placed within the heart— is sustained.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the relevant subject (*prakṛta*), the Blessed One, and the irrelevant subject (*aprakṛta*), Indra. For instance: by which Blessed One [it is said] "she who writes upon the heart" (*hṛllekhā*), meaning she possesses a beautiful writing on the heart (*suhṛllekhā*), that is to say, she is exceedingly heart-captivating. By the rule “*hṛdayasya hṛllekha*” and so forth, the word *hṛdaya* undergoes the substitution *hṛd*. As the *Ratnakośa* states: “*Hṛdya* means heart-captivating; *hṛllekha* means dear to the heart.”

For this very reason, she was *āhitā*—placed or fixed—constantly in the heart and upon the chest; for this very reason, she was *gauravitā*—endowed with respect. This is because the word *gaurava* is listed among the *tārakā*-type words, and the suffix *itac* is applied in the sense of "that has arisen in him" (*tad asya saṃjātam*). Alternatively, she was made *gauravavatī* (possessing dignity); from the causative form of the root *gaurav*, namely *gauravaya*, the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied, and by the rule that the causative base behaves like the primary base (*ṇāviṣṭhavadbhāva*), the suffix *matup* is elided according to the rule *vinmatoḥ*. For this very reason, she *āsa*—shone forth. This is the third person singular perfect (*liṭ*) of the root *as* in the sense of "to shine."

In this context, the analysis of the compound is: *gauḥ avitā saśrīḥ*. By which generous one (*maghavatā*) [the earth] is *saśrīḥ*—possessing splendor, lovely, dear to the heart, and beneficial; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The words *ahitam*, *pathyam*, *gate*, and *dhṛte* mean 'beneficial'. *Suhṛdo lekhāḥ* refers to the gods, as in the *Amara-kośa*: "The *lekhās* are the sons of Aditi. *Gauḥ* means the sky or heaven; the *Medinī* lexicon states: "*Gauḥ* [is used] for heaven and for a bull. *Anavaratam* means a constant protector (*avitā*).

He whose divine abode or auspicious form is established upon the mountain Vṛṣa—*dhāma* meaning "abode," "body," "splendor," or "power" according to Amara; he is the Lord, the sovereign of the gods. Alternatively, the phrase *vṛṣācalāhitadhāmaḥ* may be analyzed as follows: he whose *dhāma* (abode) or *tejaḥ* (splendor/power) is unfriendly (*ahita*) to the mountains (*acala*), meaning the "Mountain-Slayer" (Indra); he is the sovereign of the gods—that Indra, the possessor of the bull (*vṛṣan*), is victorious. As it is said: [The verse continues: Just so... [the example follows].
These excellent gems known as pearls, whose very existence is attained solely through the pure fluid bestowed by the dark clouds, possess such bliss as comes from a shimmering oyster shell.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (double entendre) between the subjects under discussion—the knowers of Brahman—and the unrelated pearls. To explain: by Kṛṣṇa, the Blessed Lord, that which is "thick" (*ghana*)—meaning dense—has been abundantly bestowed (*abhivitīrṇa*) upon Himself, His own domain; this is the exceedingly pure (*atyamala*), clear (*svaccha*) "flavor" (*rasa*), synonymous with affection (*sneha*) and distinct from any other sentiment. Devotion (*bhakti*) is precisely such meditation preceded by that [affection], for it is said: "Devotion is defined as meditation preceded by affection."

The meaning is that those whose existence (*sattā*)—that is, their maintenance of their own nature (*svarūpa-dhāraṇa*)—has been attained and correctly acquired by that very [devotion] alone, are "those whose existence is attained solely through [devotional] relish" (*rasaika-samadhigata-sattā*). According to the process described in the statement, "I give that yoga of discernment (*buddhi-yoga*) by which they come unto Me," they perform the maintenance of their own bodies and so forth solely through the aforementioned meditation bestowed by the Blessed One.

Those who are true jewels—the foremost among the knowers of Brahman—being liberated and thus freed from the bondage of *prakṛti*, are so described; being those for whom the abandonment of sorrow (*śoka*) shines forth (*vilasat*), they are called "those whose abandonment of grief is radiant," because in the Prajāpati discourse [it is said], "He is free from evil," and because of the scriptural hearing that "He is free from sorrow" (*viśoka*). Such is He, from whom words turn back.

"Those whose bliss is such"—meaning their bliss is heard in scripture as being "unattainable even by the mind," thus indefinable by speech and mind; and who are "those whose houses are shining conchs"—this is a *karmadhāraya* compound with two qualifying words (*viśeṣaṇa*). The meaning is that they are far removed from the qualities of the rejectible (such as sorrow) and experience the bliss of the realization of the perfect Brahman.

Except when provided by a dark cloud—a blue rain-cloud—the pure water of the Svāti star, those drops of stainless water from the time the sun traverses the Svāti constellation, fall as raindrops upon that river.
When the sun is in the Svāti asterism, these raindrops remain within oyster shells;
after six months, having become solidified, they are born as pure pearls.
Because of this statement, those whose existence and abiding in their own nature have been attained by that very [truth] are so described.

For this very reason, they are called "liberated" (mukta), meaning they are known as liberated; they are excellent jewels (sanmaṇayaḥ), the finest gems. They have come from—that is, are born from—the "shining oyster shell" (vilasat-śukti), which is the pearl-oyster (muktāsphoṭa). Thus, they are the joys of the eyes (dṛgānandāḥ), meaning they become the causes of delight for the eyes of the beholders.

Just as the great natural union with the primary splendor and the union residing on the exalted plane—alas, these two, like a bird and a serpent, never encounter opposition in any matter whatsoever. (835)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the two subjects under discussion, Garuḍa and Ananta, and the two non-subjects, the words *vihaṅga* and *bhujaṅga*. For instance, "the two very great *vihaṅga-bhujaṅgas*" means Garuḍa and Ananta. They are described as being "in natural association with the primary Lord" (*mukhya-vibhu-sahaja-saṅgau*), meaning that their connection—consisting of the relationship of the dependent and the supported—is natural and inherent, rather than secondary or figurative, as it might be in the case of a king or similar superior. This refers to their relationship with Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Lord.

For this very reason, they have taken refuge in her who possesses an exalted, uplifted, abundant, and great majesty; or rather, she is so called because she is the one whose ground (bhū), the goddess Earth, is exalted (udagrā) and most auspicious (śreyasī). They have taken refuge in that "Mā," which is Śrī. The compound is formed according to the rule "the second member is compounded with 'śrita'" and so forth. In the Vedic texts such as "the wife of Viṣṇu, the Earth," and because the goddess Earth is described as "the dear friend of Lakṣmī" (*lakṣmī-priyasakhī*), the specific excellence of Śrī is expressed here.

Alternatively, the meaning is that Bhū and Mā, who are the divine consorts of the Blessed Lord, have taken refuge [in them]. The sense is that these two are not merely subordinate to the Blessed Lord alone, but also to His divine consorts who are intent upon propitiating Him; thus, they never encounter opposition in any matter whatsoever, even in regard to some purpose such as service (kaiṅkarya).

The meaning is that, O Blessed One, for a certain person, among those various services and so forth established by eternal desire, there arises no intention to perform another [service], and this is due to the power of taking refuge in the eternally faultless Lord. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), "mukhyavibhū" refers to those two letters whose forms are *vi* and *bhu* respectively; and "sahajau" means those two letters which exist together with *ha* and *ja*. In the word *sahaja*, the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs according to the rule "vopasarjanasya."

The two *saṅgau* are those that exist together with the conjunction of the letters *ṅga* and *ṅka*. There is a *dvandva* compound of these three qualifiers: the primary (*mukhya*), the pervasive (*vibhu*), and the innate (*sahaja*) *saṅgau*. They are "resorted to by the *udagrabhū*"—that is, they are resorted to by the letter *ma*, which is the *agra-bhū* (the "final letter") because it exists at the end (*avasāne*) and occurs "at the front" (*agre*) in an excellent manner (*utkṛṣṭaṃ*). Alternatively, *udagrā bhūḥ* means the "ground" (*bhū*) that has risen above (*udgatā*) the "front" (*agra*); that is, the conclusion. Resorted to by that is the meaning of being resorted to by the letter *ma*.

The meaning is that such terms for "bird" (*vihaṅga*) and "serpent" (*bhujaṅga*) do not exist anywhere in the world or in the Veda. The sense is that they have not "incurred contradiction"—that is, a different meaning—in their denoted object (*arthe abhidheye*), because whatever meaning is expressed by the words *vihaṅga* and *bhujaṅga*, exactly the same amount of meaning is expressed by the words *vihaga* and *bhujaga*. In this interpretation, the phrase "very great" (*sumahāntau*) should also be supplemented with the sense of "existing at the end of the word *sumahat*."

The two words *sumahāvihaṅgaḥ* and *sumahābhujaṅgaḥ* result in this meaning: [one who goes] in the sky (*vihāyas*). In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound, by the rule *“gamessupi vācyaḥ”* (the suffix *khañ* is to be stated after the root *gam*), the suffix *khañ* is applied; then, by the rule *“vihāyaso viha iti vācyam”* (the substitute *viha* is to be stated for *vihāyas*), the word *vihāyas* is replaced by *viha*; next, by the rule *“khacca ḍidvā vācyaḥ”* (it should be stated that *khañ* optionally takes the marker *ṭ*), the *khañ* optionally becomes marked with *ṭ*; due to the force of this *ṭ*-marker, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*); and finally, by the rule *“arurdviṣadajantasya mum”* (the augment *mum* is added after *aru*, *dviṣat*, and words ending in a consonant), the augment *mum* is inserted. Thus, the two forms *vihaṅgaḥ* and *vihaṅgamaḥ* are produced, both having the same meaning.

Likewise, from the analysis of the compound *bhujair gacchati* ("he goes by means of his arms"), when the suffix *khac* is optionally treated as having an indicatory *ḍit*, with the elision of the *ṭi* (the *a*) and the insertion of *mum*, the two forms *bhujaṅgaḥ* and *bhujaṅgamaḥ* are derived.
Or for example:

"O Viṣṇu! Indeed, when you—the Great One—attain the state of being the final member [of a compound] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the quality of ending in the suffix *-t* vanishes in the form *sat*. (Verse 836) Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun/paronomasia) between the two subjects—the one under discussion (*prakṛta*), the worshipful knower of Brahman, and the one not under discussion (*aprakṛta*), the word *mahat* itself. To explain: "O Viṣṇu! refers to one who has attained *uttarapadatā*—the state of having the "highest" (*uttaram*) "place" (*padam*) as his final member, according to the Vedic text "That of Viṣṇu" (*tad viṣṇoḥ*). Thus, the meaning is: "by you who dwell in the supreme abode. In this sense, when the Great One (*mahataḥ*) attains the state of being the final member (*uttarapadatām gatena*) through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyāt*) with the word *sat*, the quality of ending in the suffix *-t* (*tāntatvam*) disappears in the form *sat*. This is because the suffix *-t* is elided by the rule *saṃjñāpūrvako vidhiranityaḥ* ("a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name is not always obligatory"). Thus, the word *mahat* becomes *mahān*. Alternatively, the suffix *-t* vanishes in the form *sat* due to the rule *tasya lopaḥ* ("there is the elision of that [suffix]"). In this verse, the *śleṣa* consists in the application of a single set of words to both the subject under discussion (the worshipful knower of Brahman) and the subject not under discussion (the word *mahat*). Specifically, the term *uttarapada* applies to the former as "one whose final member is the highest place," and to the latter as "the final member of a compound. Furthermore, the term *sāmānādhikaraṇya* applies to the former as "grammatical coreferentiality," and to the latter as "having the same substratum" (i.e., being part of the same compound). Finally, the term *tāntatva* applies to the former as "the state of ending in the suffix *-t*," and to the latter as "the quality of having the letter *t* at its end. Thus, the *śleṣa* is established. (Note: The commentary further clarifies that the *śleṣa* involves the simultaneous application of the meanings of the words *mahat* and "knower of Brahman" to the single set of descriptive terms.)

Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with you—that is, because it shares the same substratum—the ablative case is used in the sense of the object when a *lyap*-affix is elided; the meaning is "having attained coreferentiality. When there is a "proper abiding" (*samavasthāna*) in compound, the suffix *ghan* is added to the root *ās* preceded by the prefix *sam*. Of "the Great One" (*mahataḥ*), that is, of some venerable knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*); "real" (*satya*) means non-superimposed and innate (*svābhāvika*). That which is both this [quality] and a "form" (*ākāra*)—namely, the form consisting of freedom from sin and so forth—[the meaning is] that it manifests when that [state] exists.

"Tāntatvam" means exhaustion such as hunger, thirst, and so forth; "astam eti" means it goes to or reaches invisibility. This is because of the scriptural hearing that [the Self] transcends those [qualities]. The sense is: by your grace, for the conscious being who dwells with you in the supreme ether (*parame vyoman*) and in whom the eightfold qualities have manifested, the exhaustion of hunger and the like shall never arise. Elsewhere, the word "O Viṣṇu! is an address specifically to the word *viṣṇu*. This is due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in having a single referent despite a difference in the grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

As they say: "Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the application of words with distinct grounds for their usage (*pravṛttinimitta*) to a single referent. The phrase "having the latter member as its word" (*uttarapadatām*) means having the final constituent of a compound as its word; specifically, it means having a co-referential latter member as its word. When there is a compound with you, the word *viṣṇu*, which has been reached (*gatena*), then—by the rule concerning the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*)—of the final *t* of the word *mahat* (meaning "great"), when the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the *t*], that is, when the state of being *āt* has occurred, [the form *mahāviṣṇu*] comes to be.

In the expression *satyākāre*, the word division is *sati ākāre*.
