The state of ending in *t* (the quality of being *takārānta*) "sets" and is no longer seen; because it has been superseded by the substitution of *ā*, the resulting form is *mahāviṣṇu* and not *mahadviṣṇu*—this is the intended meaning. Here, the meaning of the rule *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇe* should be kept in mind. Or, for example:

"O Viṣṇu, I have always known You as one whose qualities are prescribed by the great seers in the vocative singular (*sadā-saṃbuddhau*). Indeed, due to the elision of the suffix *su* [in the vocative], the *visarjanīya* [the visarga] becomes far removed from You. (837)

Here there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) on both the Lord Viṣṇu and the word *viṣṇu*. To explain: O Viṣṇu! [I bow] to Him whose qualities—such as being the cause of all, omniscience, and supreme excellence—are ordained (*vihita*) or taught by the Great Seer (*maharṣi*). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The term *ṛṣi* refers to the Veda, to sages such as Vasiṣṭha, and in the masculine, it denotes creative intelligence (*dīdhiti*). Thus, He is one whose qualities are established by that [Seer]. As it is said: "He is the cause, the Lord of the lords of the senses; He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving. Viṣṇu is supreme;
from Viṣṇu the universe has emerged, and in Him alone it remains."
He is the singular mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, supreme heroism, and power;
he is the highest of the high, the Lord of the high and the low, in whom no afflictions or other defects exist.

The meaning is: "He whose nature consists of all auspicious qualities," as proclaimed by such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*). He has always known—that is, understood—in his intellect and mind that he was a partaker of true existence (*sadbhāva-bhāk*); for the scripture says, "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing. But one who is not thus, being non-existent, should be abandoned from afar; thus he says, "In you... Here, the word division in *dūre'saḥ* is *dūre asaḥ*. He is "not that" (*asaḥ*), meaning he is not of such a nature; the sense is that he has not known You as described above.

Therefore, because of the loss of "supratyaya"—meaning beautiful knowledge or great confidence—regarding you as the object, you are to be cast far away and abandoned. The particle *hi* indicates what is well-known; the sense is that it is a matter of common knowledge that such a person must be excluded by the virtuous. In another interpretation: "O Viṣṇu! O word 'Viṣṇu'!"—in this case, the analysis of the compound is *sadā-sambuddhau* (always in the vocative).

The term *saṃbuddhau* refers to the singular vocative case as designated by the rule "the singular [case-ending] is called *saṃbuddhi*"; thus, the sense is "when following" that singular vocative. The meaning is that its *guṇa* (vocalic strengthening) has been prescribed by the great sage Pāṇini through the rule "there is *guṇa* for a short vowel," because *guṇa* is ordained when a vocative follows. [I] have always known [this], namely in the phrase "O Viṣṇu, you."

The meaning is that due to the elision of the *sup* suffix in its form as *su*, the *hal* (consonant) of the vocative is elided by the rule "eṅ hrasvāt saṃbuddheḥ. The word *saḥ* is the genitive singular (*ṣaṣṭhyekavacana*) of the *sup* suffix *s*. The *visarjanīya* is the *visarga* prescribed by the rule "kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ," which occurs immediately after the *ru*-substitution [of *s*] by the rule "sasajuṣoruḥ"; this [visarga] is indeed far removed. The point is: if the original substitute (*sthānin*), the *sakāra* itself, is elided, what talk can there be of a *visarga* based on the *ru*-substitution in its place?
Or, for example:

"Just as here the god Viṣvagañcati (the one who faces all directions) has taken refuge on the foremost mountain, the great region; so too this verbal root *añc*, though lacking a suffix (*apratyaya*), is seen everywhere at the end of that [word]. (838)

In this verse, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the subject, Śrīnivāsa, and the two non-subjects, the words *viṣvagdeva*. To explain: the Supreme Lord Vāsudeva is the *dhātu* (creator/source) even without being a *pratyaya* (dependent); for while *pratyaya* means "well-known," it also signifies "beginning with *san*" (as in verbal suffixes), "conduct," "oath," "weakness," and "the cause of dependence in trust. Thus, though not dependent on Brahmā (*dhātu*), He is the source of all. Furthermore, although He is eternally manifest (*pratyaya*), He remains the cause of confidence in conduct, oaths, and the absence of weakness.

Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. The meaning is that He is impossible even for Brahmā to contemplate. Alternatively, the construction may be understood as "the root (*dhātu*) itself being without a suffix. "The foremost mountain" (*agryam adrim*) refers to Śeṣācala, because it is the subject under discussion and because it is said: "This mountain named Śeṣācala is the best among mountains. "The great region" (*mahādeśam*) means a venerable place; the sense is that it is a divine region named Śeṣācala. Having resorted to it, He moves, wanders, or sports here on this mountain, everywhere and on all sides.

Therefore, for that reason—namely, because it is the place where the Blessed One dwelt—this mountain, which has become the site of the Blessed One’s residence, is to be seen from all sides, by people; this is the ellipsis. The meaning is that not only is the Blessed One alone to be beheld, but this mountain as well, being most purifying due to the Blessed One’s traversing of it everywhere, is indeed to be seen by everyone from every direction.

In one alternative, the word *viṣvak*—which consists of the form *viṣvak*—and the word *deva*—which consists of the form *deva*—become *añcatipara*, meaning that which has the root *añc* (the verbal root *añcu*) following it; the term *añcati* is used here as a technical designation by means of the suffix *śtip*. Having become *añcatipara*, it attains (*śrita*), that is, reaches, the substitute *adri*—which exists in the place of *ṭi* (the final letter) at the beginning (*agryam*) [of the word], which consists of the form *adri*, which is great (*mahāntam*), and which is vast (*bṛhantam*) because it contains more than one phoneme (*anekāltvāt*).

Now, one might object: if *viṣvak* and *deva* were to undergo the substitution [of *adri*] when followed by *añcati*, then in the cases of *viṣvagañcanam* and *devāñcanam*, the substitution of *adri* for *viṣvak* and *deva* would also occur. To this, he says: "The verbal root (*dhātu*), even though not a suffix (*apratyaya*). In this view, the word *iha* connects here [to the following]. Here, in the phrase "when followed by *añcati*," the term *dhātu* refers to the verbal root *añcu* itself; and "not having a suffix" (*apratyaya*) means that from which no suffix is present—that is, it ends in the *kvip* suffix.

The meaning is that because the entire *kvip* suffix is elided, it is non-existent; or rather, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound where "apratyaya" means "that for which no suffix exists. Since this functions as a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the sense of "ending in that" is obtained, meaning "ending in a *kvip* whose suffix is non-existent. Otherwise, as in examples such as *viṣvagañcanam*, the substitution of *adri* would not occur. This is the intended point.

Therefore, because of the substitution of *adri* for *viṣvag* and *deva* [in the rule], that which exists correctly at the end on all sides—namely, the word *aga* situated here within the words *viṣvak* and *deva*—is analyzed as *ak-aḥ*. By the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*, the letter *k* becomes *g* through the *jaś*-substitution. This means that the collection of phonemes beginning with *a* situated in the word *viṣvak* (i.e., *ak*), and the vowel *a* situated in the word *deva* (i.e., *a*), are [the referents]. The analysis is thus *adṛśya*.

The meaning is that [the word] is not seen because it has been removed by the present substitution (*ādeśa*). Regarding this, those proficient in the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*) should investigate the meaning of the rule "viṣvagdevayośca ṭeradryañcatāvapratyaye" according to the manner already explained; enough of this digression. Alternatively, there is a threefold division: *samaṃ*, *tataḥ*, and *adṛśya*. *Tataḥ* means after the substitution of *adri*; for that very reason—that is, precisely because of the substitution of *adri*—this aforementioned meaning applies to the two words *viṣvak* and *deva* under discussion, namely the *ak* and *aś*.

"In such a way that it is equal (sama) and identical (tulya), [the substitute] becomes invisible (adṛśya). The meaning is that for both of these words, because the substitution of *ṭeradri* occurs for *ṭeḥ*, and because the *ak* and the *asya* are removed, their invisibility is exactly the same. Alternatively, for that very reason already mentioned, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (*sārvavibhaktika*). Thus, the meaning is "in those two words, namely *viṣvak* and *deva*," this [substitute] which resides in the intellect—namely *ak* and *aś*—is equally and identically invisible.
Just as the absence of qualities in Lakṣmī’s friend, her husband, is well-known to be appropriate, we also know this to be appropriate: that there shall be no absence of conviction. 839.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the subject, the Blessed Lord, and the non-subjects, the words "friend of Lakṣmī" (*lakṣmīsakhī*) and "husband" (*pati*). For instance, by [the term] "friend of Lakṣmī" (*lakṣmyāḥ sakhyuḥ*), his being a well-wishing friend is expressed, thereby illuminating the fullness of his passion (*anurāga*). Furthermore, this designation as "Lord of Śrī" (*śrīpati*)—meaning the husband (*bhartṛ*) of Śrīnivāsa—is intended to manifest that the state of possessing both genders (*ubhayaliṅgatā*), which is to be discussed immediately hereafter, has him as its sole locus.

For this very reason, the venerable commentators on the Bhāṣya stated: "The Lord of Śrī is solely intent upon auspiciousness that is the antithesis of all that is to be abandoned. [The term] *aghī* means one who possesses sin (*agha*); its state is *aghītā*. That which is both that state and a quality is *āghitāguṇa*; the absence of that is what is proclaimed—that is, it becomes well-known—as logical. This is because of such scriptural passages as: "He has risen above all evils; He is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa."

This [term] "pratyaya" (cognition) is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for power (*śakti*), strength (*bala*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and so forth. There is no word-break as "na-abhāvaḥ" (not non-existence). By the two negatives in the phrase "abhāvaḥ na bhavitā," the possibility of the absence of existence is excluded, meaning that "non-existence shall not occur; existence alone shall occur. We also consider this logical, based on such scriptural passages as: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action. The sense is that there can never be a deficiency in His auspicious qualities, which are characterized by knowledge.

By these two preceding and subsequent points, it is shown respectively that He is the adversary of all that is to be discarded—as stated in the scripture, "free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, and free from thirst"—and that He is a mine of infinite auspicious qualities—as stated in the scripture, "whose desires are true and whose resolves are true."

Except for *lakṣmī*, that is, the word *lakṣmī*; there is a superimposition of the femininity residing in the meaning onto the word. This applies to the word *sakhi* [in the case of] *sakhyuḥ*, and the word *pati* [in the case of] *patyuḥ*. Regarding *ghitvābhāva*: *ghitā* means the technical designation *ghi*; by that, the absence of the *guṇa*—namely, the *guṇa* prescribed by the rule "gher ṅiti"—is what is rightly proclaimed [to occur].

Because the word *lakṣmī* ends in a long vowel (*ī*), which is designated as a "river" (*nadī*), the designation *ghi*—which is based on ending in a short *i* or *u* vowel that is not designated as a "river," according to the rule *śeṣo ghyasakhi*—does not apply to it. This is because in that very same sūtra prescribing the *ghi* designation, the word *sakhi* is excluded by the term *asakhi*.

It is correct that the absence of the *guṇa* substitution resulting from the *ghit* designation is well-established for the uncompounded word *pati*, because the *ghit* designation for the word *pati* is restricted by the rule "the word *pati* [receives the *ghit* designation] only in a compound" (*patiḥ samāsa eva*), and thus it does not apply to the uncompounded form. In the phrase "of the suffix *ā* in *bhavitā*," the division is *bhavitā* + *ā-pratyayasya*.

The absence of *nā* for the suffix *āṅ*—that is, the absence of the substitute *nā* prescribed by the rule "āṅo nāstriyām" for the suffix *ṭā* which is designated as *āṅ*—is what we consider appropriate in the case of [the form] *bhavitā*. The sense is that, because the designation *ghisamjñā* itself is absent for the words *lakṣmī*, *sakhi*, and *pati* according to the aforementioned method, the grammatical operation resulting from it (the substitution of *nā*) does not occur. Alternatively, the word *api* expresses censure; the construction is: "We consider even this to be appropriate."

In this view, we understand that it is logical for the substitution of *nā* for *āṅ* (the prefix *ā*) before a suffix beginning with *ā*; however, we do not consider it logical that the substitute *nā* would apply to those words because they lack the designation *ghisamjñā*. Or, for example:
"O Lord, [the self] shines forth by its very nature, renowned for the happiness of the welfare of others, as well as for its own enjoyment, for the sake of all people, and for its own sake. (840)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the subject at hand, the worshipper of the Blessed One, and the non-subject, the word *tvadbhogīna*. For instance: "O Master! *Tvadbhogīnaḥ* means beneficial for Your enjoyment alone and not for one's own; it means being solely intent on accomplishing Your enjoyment, that is, having as its sole essence the state of being subservient to You. Indeed, the definition of a *śeṣa* (subordinate) is: "That whose very nature is to be accepted solely through the desire to bestow excellence upon another is a *śeṣa*."

For this very reason, he is "beneficial to all" (*viśvajanīnaḥ*), meaning conducive to the welfare of every person, and "beneficial to himself" (*ātmanīnaḥ*), meaning his sole activity is the practice of what is beneficial for both self and others. As it has been said: "The teacher is devoted to the welfare of himself and others. Such a Self (*ātmā*)—that is, the conscious being (*cetanaḥ*)—shines forth as one who is celebrated by the bliss (*sukha*) arising from that which is "for the sake of welfare and purpose" (*hitārthasukhena*). Here, "welfare" (*hita*) refers to the means for attaining the Lord, and "purpose" (*artha*) refers to the supreme human goal; the two words "welfare" and "purpose" are intended to signify the knowledge of those [means and goals]. This also implies the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Being celebrated through the bliss or joy (*ānanda*) derived from those two, he shines.

Then, at the end of the body, it shines—that is, it blazes—by its own nature as characterized by the manifestation of the eightfold qualities and so forth. Having as his sole essence the state of being the remainder of [Brahman], he is the benefactor of the world-people who have become his disciples and of himself; he is conscious, perceived here as possessing bliss induced by the knowledge of reality, welfare, and the goals of human life. At the end of the body, with the natural qualities of Brahman such as freedom from sin manifested, he shines through eternally uncontracted knowledge; the sense is that he becomes liberated.
But elsewhere, the word *tvadbhogīna*, the word *viśvajanīna*, and the word *ātmanīna* are all compounds whose meaning is proclaimed as "for the sake of benefit and happiness."

The word *sukha* is formed by the suffix *kha*, prescribed by the rule *tasmai hitam* ("beneficial for that"), applied to the sense of "benefit" (*hita*) in the form of "well-being" (*hitarūpa*). This suffix *kha* is further prescribed by the rule *ātman-viśvajana-bhogottarapadāt-khaḥ*. The substitute *īna* for this *kha* is prescribed by the rule *āyan-ey-īn-īy-īyaḥ*. Being renowned through that [substitute], it shines; thus, [the term] is connected respectively with *tvadbhogīna* and the others. Such an expression is used because the three words beginning with *tvadbhogīna* are produced through the aforementioned grammatical derivation.

Now, with the words beginning with "atha," he demonstrates the specific distinction regarding the word *ātmanīna*. The word "atha" serves to indicate this distinction. The term "ātmā" refers to the word *ātman*, which appears having attained the state of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) as prescribed by the rule "ātmādhvānau khe. It remains in its actual phonetic form and does not undergo the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* portion (*ṭilopa*) as required by the rule "nastaddhite. The suffix *kha* is indeed common to all three words; however, the intended meaning is that the specific distinction lies in the *prakṛtibhāva* occurring in the word *ātman*.

Just as the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), whose abode is the mountain (Garuḍa), clearly manifests attachment, devotion, and the state of being beneficial; so too, in this Supreme Lord, His status as the Sovereign is established through both inference and scripture, possessing specific distinctions. || 841 ||

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the subject, the Blessed Lord, and the two non-subjects, the roots *dhā* (to place) and *bhaj* (to worship). To explain: Śrīnivāsa—whose abode is the mountain of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa)—is attached to and full of affection for the devotee; for it is sung [in scripture]: "I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to me. Therefore, He clearly maintains (*dadhāti*) his state of being beneficial—that is, His quality of acting for the welfare of that devoted person by way of the relationship between means and end; the sense is that there is not even a trace of doubt here.

The analysis of the compound is *svaujasī* (in her own power) or *svā ojasī* (her own power). It refers to that which consists of divine splendor, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "having attained the supreme light" (*ojasi paraṃ jyotir upasaṃpadya*). Alternatively, the analysis is *svā aujasī*; it exists in this Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Brahman, who is all-pervading and unsurpassed splendor, and in whom there is power (*ojas*) or radiance (*prakāśa*) on all sides (*ā*).

"Self" (*sva*) means established by itself; "other" (*para*) means supreme; and "Lord" (*īśa*) means the Sovereign. His state is "sovereignty" (*pareśatā*), which is supreme lordship. This is according to such scriptural passages as, "He is the Lord of the entire world," and "He is the Lord of all. Now, there is an alternative reading: *māgamata iti chedaḥ*. From "contact with Māyā"—that is, Śrī—He indeed becomes possessed of distinction. The meaning is that the natural sovereignty of the Blessed One, the Abode of Śrī, becomes redoubled in its majesty through association with Śrī, just as a golden lotus does through its connection with fragrance and the like.

The particle *nanu* is used here for emphasis. By the second half [of the verse], His transcendence (*paratva*) is shown, and by the first half, His accessibility (*saulabhya*). Alternatively, the meaning of the second half is as follows: "in Him" refers to this Śrīnivāsa, who possesses His own splendor (*svaujas*), that is, whose nature is self-luminous (*svaprakāśasvarūpa*). "Sovereignty" (*īśatā*) refers to His lordship (*aiśvarya*). The word *anumāgamataḥ* is a compound: *anumā* means inference (*anumāna*) or Smṛti, and *āgama* means revelation (*śruti*). Thus, it means "from both inference and revelation. The suffix *-tas* is applied here according to the rule *ādyādibhyaḥ*, functioning like all case endings.

"Beyond" (*para*) means "far removed," according to such scriptural passages as, "from which words turn back. The meaning is that [Brahman] is not an object of those [words]. According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The word *para* is used in the senses of 'distant,' 'other,' 'principal,' 'enemy,' and 'Supreme Self. Alternatively, one may supply the words "stated through inference, scripture, and tradition" (*anumāgamataḥ śrutismṛtibhyām uktā*). The phrase *pareśatā pāramaiśvaryam aviśeṣabhāgi* is to be divided thus. *Aviḥ* means "mountain," according to Amara: "The words *avi*, *śaila*, *meṣa*, and *arka* [mean mountain]. Thus, *aviśeṣa* refers to Śeṣa who possesses the form of a mountain; the meaning is Śeṣa, the Śeṣa-mountain (*śeṣādri*).

She is so called because she "frequents" (bhajati) that [Supreme]. The sense is that all the supreme sovereignty existing in the Supreme Brahman shines forth only in Śeṣādrī, because of its manifestation here [in her]. In this interpretation, the description of both transcendence and accessibility is provided sequentially by the latter half of the verse alone. Alternatively, *svaujasī* means "established in her own majesty"; for Amara states, "Ojas denotes strength and power.
This is because in the *Bhūmavidyā*, in response to the question, "Venerable sir, in what is [the Self] established? the answer is heard: "In its own majesty" (*sve mahimni*).
The gods have taken refuge in Rudra; Rudra has taken refuge in Brahmā;
Brahmā has taken refuge in me, O King, but I have not taken refuge in anyone.
I have no support whatsoever; indeed, I am the support of all.

And because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*): the meaning is that in this Blessed One, [the state of being the Supreme] is established through inference, scripture (*āgama*), and both *śruti* and *smṛti*. The state of being the Supreme Lord (*pareśatā*) is the aforementioned meaning. The "remnants" (*śeṣa*) are sentient beings who have become servants; he who enjoys them is the "enjoyer of remnants" (*śeṣabhāk*). Specifically, one who is an enjoyer of remnants is a "particular enjoyer" (*viśeṣabhāk*); he does not possess such particularity, and thus he is the "non-particular enjoyer" (*aviśeṣabhāk*).

The meaning is that the status of being the sovereign of all (*sarvaśeṣitva*), which is proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti regarding that Supreme Brahman, is not possible in the case of those who are subordinate to Him—such as Brahmā, Rudra, and others, or the eternally perfected ones like Ananta, Garuḍa, and so forth. Alternatively, there is a word-break: *na nu mā āgamataḥ*. *Pareśatā* means "supreme lordship" (*pareśatā* = *parā śreṣṭhā īśatā aiśvaryam yasyāḥ sā*). *Mā* refers to Śrī (Lakṣmī). The meaning stated [previously] applies here as well, with the feminine suffixes *svā* and *jas*.

The sense is this: in this Blessed One, according to the tradition (*āgama*) or by virtue of an eternal connection as taught in the *Pañcarātra-āgama*, He does not possess any distinction—that is, He does not possess difference—but rather becomes one who has attained identity (*tādātmya*). [Regarding the word "viśeṣa,"] the *Ratnamālā* states: "A *viśeṣa* refers to a limb, an individual, a sectarian mark, or an absolute differentiator. Alternatively, *nanu* may be taken as a single word; the division would then be *aviśeṣabhāgbhavati*. The meaning remains the same: he becomes one who has attained identity.
"Know that the relationship between me and my Lord is one of identity (tādātmya), because of their mutual inseparability and their mutual concomitance," as stated in the Lakṣmītantra.

"Because she is included within that, even the Śruti does not designate her separately"—according to this statement by the learned (Abhiyukta). Alternatively, let the state of being the Supreme Lord (Pareśatā) reside in your own majesty; the meaning stated here is precisely this. According to the manner of the scriptural passage, "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives... for the sake of one of noble birth," she is one who possesses distinction (*viśeṣabhāk*). "Distinction" (*viśeṣa*) means the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), that is, the state of being a differentiator (*vyāvartakatva*); [this is derived] from the root *śiṣ* with the prefix *vi-* in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve ghañ*). Indeed, she is so called because she partakes of that [distinction].

The sense is this: by functioning as a qualifier of the Blessed One through the determination of His essential nature (*svarūpa*), [the attribute] effects His distinction from the four-faced Brahmā and others who are suspected of being the cause of the world. Alternatively, while "He" (*asmin*) exists in the nominative case (*svaujas*), the lordship (*īśatā*) of others—such as the four-faced one and so forth—does not indeed possess excellence (*viśeṣabhāk*) or superiority (*utkarṣabhāk*) according to scripture (*āgamataḥ*). The sense is: when the supreme sovereignty of the Blessed One is manifest, how could the sovereignty of others attain superiority when viewed through the lens of the scriptures?

The word *mā* has the sense of prohibition; as stated in the *Ratnamālā* and *Viśva*: “*Mā* is an indeclinable used for prohibition; *mā* is considered an indeclinable in the sense of negation. In the context of verbal roots (*dhātu*), it refers to the *Mahābhāṣya*, the speech of Patañjali on the mountain of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa). "Arising" (*bhavan*) means attaining existence; the suffix *lyu* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent because it belongs to the *nandigrahipacādigaṇa*, or alternatively, by virtue of irregularity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *luṅ* is applied in the sense of the agent. This amounts to saying that it is recited in grammar. In the phrase *dadhātispaṣṭam*, there is a word-break after *dadhāti*.

The optional elision of the *visarga* occurs according to the rule: "When followed by a *khar* consonant that is itself followed by a *śar* vowel or semivowel, there is optionally the elision of the *visarga*. The term *dadhātiḥ* refers to the root *dhā*; this is an indication made by means of the suffix *śtip*. Because it exists together with the *kta* suffix (*ktena*), being thus "joined" (*saktaḥ*), it clearly attains—that is, reaches—the form *hitatām*, which is the form *hitam*. The underlying sense is that when the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *dhā*, the substitution of *hi* for *dhā* is prescribed by the rule: "In place of *dhā*, *hi* [is substituted] when *kta* follows."

In this very verbal root *dhā*, the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present participle suffix (*laṭ*) has been prescribed when *svaujas*—that is, the collective term for *su*, *au*, and *jas*—follows. The analysis of the phrase is *na numāgamataḥ*. It does not possess a distinction—that is, it does not differ—due to the addition of the augment *num*, which is prescribed by the rule "the augment *num* is added after bases ending in vowels other than *dhātu* [roots] that have an *uk* (u, ṛ, ḷ) or the letter *ac* (vowels), before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. The sense is that there is no prohibition of *num* for this suffix by the rule "there is no *num* after a reduplicated base (*abhyasta*) or after the suffix *śatṛ*."

Alternatively, "phaṇīśagiribhava" is a single word ending in the vocative case, while "na" is a separate word. This is an address made by a certain grammarian teacher to a student: "O you who are born regarding the mountain of the Lord of Serpents (the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*)! It is like the address "born among cows" (*goṣu prasūta*) used for one born specifically to experience cows; here, it means one who has been born [to study] precisely the *Mahābhāṣya*.

In the word *bhajat*, when attached (*sakta*) and connected (*saṃbaddha*) to the suffix *śatṛ*—which undergoes the substitution of *śatṛ* for *śatṛ*—the letter *na* belonging to the augment *num* assumes, or indeed possesses, "favorability" (*hitatām*), that is, suitability, when the case endings *su* and *aujas* follow, because the augment *num* is prescribed by the rule beginning with "*ugidacām*" (Pāṇini 7.1.70). This is the intended meaning. In the second half of the verse, there are three words: *na*, *num*, and *āgamataḥ*. In this aforementioned *śatṛ* suffix, *num* is the augment; *āgamataḥ* means either from the letter *ā* (as in *āgamataḥ*) or from the act of coming (*gamataḥ*).

The meaning is that, depending on the possibility, [the rule] *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* prescribes a long vowel (*dīrgha*) when followed by a *su*-affix; [the form in question] does not possess this distinction—that is, it does not undergo such a change. The point is that because the form ending in *śatṛ* ends in *at*, it lacks the status of ending in *at* (as a whole), and thus the aforementioned long vowel is not applicable. For this very reason, the *Kaumudī* text states regarding the form *bhavan*: "But in the case of the *śatṛ*-ending [form], there is no long vowel because it does not end in *at*. Alternatively, the division of the text should be read as *na nu māgamataḥ*.

In this context, the word *bhajan* (partaking), the suffix *śatṛ* contained within it is supplied [from a previous rule]. Does it not partake of a distinction on account of the augment *m*, that is, the augment *m* associated with [the rule] *āne muk*? The meaning is that since the augment *muk* prescribed for the suffix *śānac* does not apply to *śatṛ*, it does not undergo the peculiarity caused by that [augment]. Or, the particle *nanu* is used in the sense of exclusion. Does it not partake of a distinction on account of the augment *m*? Or, the particle *nanu* is used in the sense of an inquiry.
The sense is that it does not exist at all. For this reason as well, those who are attentive should consider that the primary interpretation alone is the natural one.

Just as the suffix *ka* occurs after the root *han* when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it, resulting in the word "khaṭvā" (a bed) which bestows happiness; so too, while that Lord remains awake, how could there be even the prefix *ā*—let alone the suffix *tṛc*—for one who has found refuge? 842.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the subject at hand, the Blessed One, and the two sūtras about to be stated which are not the subject at hand. "Hanta" expresses joy born from reflecting upon the meaning of what is about to be said, or it marks the commencement of a sentence. Regarding "anupasarge": it means in the matter of warding off calamities for the worlds; that is to say, in the absence of an *upasarga*. Hemacandra states: "An *upasarga* [is used] in the sense of calamity (*upadrava*), as well as in the sense of the prefix group beginning with *pra*, and in the sense of a type of disease. "Pratyayaḥ" means cause (*hetu*). Amara states: "The word *pratyaya* is used in the senses of dependent, oath, knowledge, trust, and cause."

And he is the giver of happiness, bestowing the bliss associated with prosperity. Therefore, the meaning is: who else other than this Lord—denoted by the letter 'A' or by the one currently under discussion—could be the cause for removing the calamities of the worlds and for the distribution of happiness?

While that Lord—the leader of the entire world and the protector of the entire world—is awake, having been heard of as "this is the lord of beings, this is the guardian of beings," who could possibly be unprotected in calamity or misfortune? The sense is: even if there were some who might be called unprotected while the Blessed One is the protector, it would be impossible. In this regard, no one is seen to be capable of gathering prosperity or averting misfortune except for that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Thus, the meaning of such authoritative means of knowledge has been synthesized.

In this context, the meaning of the two rules—"*āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*" and "*ātaś copasarge*"—should be examined along with their examples. To illustrate: in the rule "*ātaḥ*," the word "*ākārāntāt dhātoḥ*" (from a root ending in the vowel *ā*) is understood; "*anupasarge*" is transformed into the ablative case as "*anupasargāt*" (when there is no prefix); and "*karmaṇi*" is supplied from the previous rule. Thus, the meaning of the rule is: when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *ka* is applied. He provides an example, beginning with "atha": "And he becomes a giver of happiness (*sukhada*)."

The meaning is that [the word] *sukhada* is derived from the root *dā* (to give) with the suffix *ka*, when the word *sukha* is used as an object (*karman*) and is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, in that well-known case, here—in this instance where it is present and manifest—the suffix *ka* would apply to the word *adhipa* according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. The sense of that rule is that the suffix *ka* occurs after a verbal root ending in long *ā* when a prefix beginning with the vowel *ā* is used as an object (*upapada*).
It should be noted that in this verse, the sequence of the grammatical rules "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" and "ātaś copasarge" has been incorporated exactly as they appear in the sūtras.
Just as this Śeṣa, the mountain that licks Your feet, shines forth pre-eminent in virtues— O Lord of Śrī, by whom has the denial of His virtues ever been heard, seen, or performed?

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the serpent Śeṣa, who is licking the feet of the Blessed One and is the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), and the two words denoting him which are not so (*aprakṛta*). To explain: O Lord of Śrī! this Śeṣa-mountain licks your feet—thus it is "tvaccaraṇalihaḥ," meaning it touches your lotus-feet. Therefore, being "uttaraḥ" (superior) through its qualities such as sanctity and loveliness, it shines or gleams. For such a Śeṣa-mountain, there is a "guṇaniṣiddhiḥ," that is, a negation of the aforementioned qualities.

The word *niṣiddhā* is derived from the root *sidh* with the prefix *ni* and the suffix *ktin*. It means: by which man has it been composed (*klṛptā*), by whom heard, or by whom seen? The meaning is that no one has ever composed, heard, or seen a negation of its purifying qualities and other attributes.

But elsewhere, there are the words *tvaccaraṇaliha* and *śeṣamahīdhra*; the analysis (*chēda*) is "aguṇottara. That is, he is so called because his final member (*uttarapada*)—namely *lihaḥ* and *dhra*—is "guṇa-less" (*aguṇa*), meaning devoid of a *guṇa*. Now, one might ask: why do the *guṇa* substitutions prescribed by the rules for light roots (*laghūpadha-lakṣaṇa*) and for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes not apply to these two words respectively? To this, he says: "By what? (*keneti*).

The meaning is that there is a prohibition of *guṇa* (vocalization) caused by the suffix *ka*, which is applied to the words *liha* and *dhra*—the former by the rule "ig-upadha-jñā-prī-kiraḥ kaḥ" and the latter by the supplementary rule "in the section on *kap*, there is an addition for *mūla-bibhuj* and so forth"—and this is the *guṇa*-prohibition established by the rule "kṅiti ca. [The word *śrutā*] means heard in the scriptures (*śāstra*) and observed in actual usage (*prayoga*).

The meaning is that, since both the words *liha* and *dhraśa* end in the suffix *kap* according to the method stated above, the prohibition of *guṇa* (vowel strengthening) resulting from the marker *k* is both heard and seen. Alternatively, this is an answer identical to the question posed by someone who says, "Your foot-licking Śeṣa and the mountain Dhara both appear devoid of *guṇa* (virtue); by whom has the prohibition of their *guṇa* been made, heard, or seen? This constitutes the poetic figure *citra* (puzzle), which is the specific distinction in this sense.
Or for example:

"O Supreme Brahman! If someone should defile you, let him do so; indeed, at some time or other, there will surely be someone [who restores] you, and thus the elision of the letter 'na' shall occur. (844) Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the two meanings—contextual and non-contextual—of the term *parabrahman*: namely, Śrīnivāsa (the Lord) and the word *parabrahman*. To explain: O Supreme Brahman! [The sense is: "someone" whose heart is unstable... [and so forth].

Regarding You as the object, "supratyayam" means a beautiful knowledge consisting of uninterrupted meditation (*bhāvanā*), being excellent because it is not interrupted by heterogeneous cognitions; this is the meaning of "upāsanam. "Lumpati cet" means if it should break off—if it should interrupt, that is, if it should create an interval—let it do so at will. From that loss of the cognition, [it follows: "O Blessed One! at any time whatsoever," the word *vā* found in the rule *nalopo vā* (Pāṇini 6.3.74) is displaced in order and connects with the word *kaścit*. Thus, "some loss" or "deprivation" shall not occur.

If anyone were to cause an interruption in your meditation, no loss whatsoever could possibly occur to you—who are solely intent upon infinite auspicious qualities that are the antithesis of all that is to be abandoned; on the contrary, it would be for that person alone. As it is said: "For when one perceives even a slight difference in this [Reality], then fear arises for him. Fear indeed arises for the learned man who does not contemplate [it]. "If for even a moment, or even for an instant, Vāsudeva is not meditated upon—that is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is a calamity."
The sense is that there will arise the fear shown by the Śruti and Smṛti as described above.

In this alternative view, the meaning is that there is an address to the word itself as "O Supreme Brahman" (*parabrahman*). The sense is that someone is an expert in grammar (*śabdavid*). Regarding the phrase "in you, the word 'Supreme Brahman'," it means that in you—the word *parabrahman*—there is the suffix *su* (the nominative case-ending), specifically the *su* suffix accompanied by the vocative marker (*saṃbuddhi*) due to the force of the address. If one were to elide [the suffix], the intention is that it would be done by the rule "after a neuter [stem], the suffixes *s* and *au* are dropped" (*svamornapuṃsakāt*). Let it elide; let it be dropped as much as desired.

Therefore, due to the elision (*lopāt*), the elision of the letter *na* (*nalopaḥ*) will occur optionally (*vikalpenaiva*) at any time whatsoever; it is not the case that it will absolutely never occur, as it does in masculine words ending in *n* such as *rājan*. This is because the rule "in the vocative, the elision of the *n* of neuter nouns is to be stated as optional" (*saṃbuddhau napuṃsakānāṃ nalopo vā vaktavyaḥ*) prescribes the optional elision of the *n* in the vocative of neuter words ending in *n*. It should be understood that this [verse] contains the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) of contempt (*avajñā*) which is about to be described.

Just as a cognition, when properly attended to, accomplishes one's desired object according to its specific aim—provided it has set aside the requirement for the actual time of action by means of supplying the appropriate sense—it likewise [fulfills its purpose]. (845)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the name of the Blessed One (*bhagavannāman*) and a technical grammatical designation (*saṃjñā*), both being relevant and irrelevant [to the context] respectively. To explain: the address "O Blessed One" (*he bhagavan*) is obtained from the context. The term *ucitādhyāhārā* means that for which the "supplying of the appropriate sense" (*ucita-samañjasa-arthādhyāhāra*)—namely, the bestowing of the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*)—is fitting; thus, it means "that which bestows all desired human goals. This is because the fruit of chanting the Name has been declared in such passages as: "One desiring dharma shall obtain dharma, and one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth," and so forth.

"‘Ucita’ means measured, appropriate, known, practiced, and consistent," according to the *Ratnamālā*. Your "name" (*saṃjñā*)—of which Amara states, "‘Saṃjñā’ may mean consciousness or a name"—when "recited" (*anusaṃhitā*), that is, proclaimed, fulfills the desired object (*abhīpsitam artham*) for those who proclaim it, according to its designation; the meaning is that it does so without overstepping its assigned purpose, in accordance with the intention of the speakers, following the authority of the cited evidence.

It is said that she not only brings about the attainment of what is desired, but also the warding off of what is undesired; thus he says "dūrī-": she is one by whom the "kārya" (tasks) of "duṣkṛtinaḥ" (the evildoers)—namely, the actions consisting of bringing them to torments—have been "dūrīkṛtaṃ" (driven far away). These are the "pakṣāḥ" (partisans) of "kālasya" (Time), that is to say, the assistants or soldiers of Kṛtānta (the God of Death). Regarding this, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "'pakṣa' [is used] in the sense of half a month or a side," starting from there and continuing until "'in the sense of strength, a friend, or an assistant.'"

The meaning is that by the mere utterance of the Blessed One’s name, all the inauspiciousness of those who perform it ceases; consequently, the power of Yama or his messengers there becomes utterly ineffective. As it is said in the Vaiṣṇava [scripture]: "O lotus-eyed Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, supporter of the earth, Acyuta, wielder of the conch and discus—those who indeed cry out, 'Be my refuge,' O messenger, leave those sinless ones far away."
Thus,
neither the servants, nor the nooses and rods, nor Yama himself,
nor the torments are capable of affecting him whose soul always takes refuge in Keśava.
Passages such as these are also favorable to this very point.

In this context, the technical designations (saṃjñā) taught by the science of grammar—such as the designation "repetition" (abhyāsa) and so forth—remain according to their original location (yathoddeśa), without overstepping their own respective domains. By means of supplying (adhyāhāra) or inferring (ūha) the appropriate meaning—as Amara states, "adhyāhāra is reasoning (tarka) or inference (ūha)," and others say, "adhyāhāra is the introduction of either an additional word or its meaning to fill a deficiency"—they accomplish the desired goal, which consists in the comprehension of the intended meaning of the sentence.

The sense is that, according to the *yathoddeśa* (as-stated) view, it is established by the grammarians (*śābdika*) that a technical term (*saṃjñā*) functions through syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) by supplying the meaning [of the rule] into the sentence. Furthermore, she is one who has accepted the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) view; and as such, she brings about what is desired. The sense is that, because of the *kāryakāla* nature of the technical term, it is established that even through word-level syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*), there is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

It is stated: "The technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) are according to their enunciation (*yathoddeśa*)," and also, "The technical definitions and rules of interpretation are according to the time of operation (*kāryakāla*). Regarding the first alternative: "According to the enunciation" (*yathoddeśaṃ*) means not exceeding the enunciation (*uddeśa*). "Enunciation" (*uddeśa*) refers to the place of instruction (*upadeśadeśa*); this term is derived with a locative sense (*adhikaraṇasādhana*). Thus, the meaning of the first rule is: in whatever place a term is taught, it is precisely in that place—through the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—that its denotative power (*śakti*) is grasped, and likewise the meaning of the rule of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) is grasped; and with these powers and meanings thus grasped, one proceeds throughout the entire treatise.

In this treatise, "place" (*deśa*) is used to refer specifically to the time of pronunciation; this is the summary. As for the meaning of the second *paribhāṣā*: "It is drawn to its own vicinity by the operation (*kārya*); thus it is 'at the time of the operation' (*kāryakāla*). This means that for the sake of its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), there is an attraction of those *paribhāṣās* marked by the signs [of] their own application. The distinction is that under the *yathoddeśa* view, a technical name (*saṃjñā*) belongs to its own place, whereas under the *kāryakāla* view, it belongs to the place of the rule (*vidhideśa*).
Just as Brahmā and Śiva, along with all other lords, are mentioned together by Your Supreme Self, so too those others who preceded them ultimately possess nothing but You alone as their remainder.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the contextual subject—the entities such as Brahmā and others, represented by the four-faced god and so forth—and the non-contextual subject—the meanings of the words "Brahmā" and so on. For instance, O Lord of All (*akhileśvara*), the activities beginning with "maintenance" (*sthiti*) and so forth were mentioned together with you, the Supreme (*para*), in such passages as "the playful acts [consisting of] maintenance and so forth are performed by Hari, Viriñci, and Hara," where they are recited together as the basis for a perceived identity.

The meaning is as follows: those two who are the objects of the suspicion of being the cause—namely, the four-faced Brahmā and Śiva (Śambhu)—are so because of the scriptural declarations: "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose" and "He is neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone is absolute. Those for whom these two are the first are "those headed by them" (*tadādimāḥ*). These are the other gods, such as Indra and others, who are mentioned as being within the scope of the suspicion of being the cause in passages such as: "O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, there is none higher than you, nor any greater."

They too, at the conclusion, on the occasion of determining the meaning of the sentence, [cite] the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *antaḥ* is not feminine; it means certainty, destruction, essential nature (*svarūpa*), front, proximity, and interior. Or, it may mean essential nature. Regarding the compound *bhavadekaśeṣatām*, which means "the state of being a remainder for You alone," we have explained in the *Lakṣmīsahasra-ratnaprakāśikā* that this is a compound belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* class, characterized by having no analysis in its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*).

The sense is that, upon correct reflection, even Brahmā and all others would be determined to have Bhava alone as their ultimate remainder (their final substrate), and never [determined] that you alone are the substrate of all; or rather, at the end—during dissolution—those for whom you alone remain are "those who have Bhava as their sole remainder," and they possess that state.
When Brahmā and the others have dissolved away, when the world of moving and non-moving beings has perished,
and when the dissolution of all elements has arrived such that the Great Principle (Mahat) is merged into primordial nature (Prakṛti),
the one Lord Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the universe, remains alone.
When the world has perished at the end of two parārdhas, when the primary elements have merged into the primordial matter,
and when the manifest has returned to the unmanifest by the force of time, you alone remain, known as Śeṣa.

In the manner described above, the meaning is that they possess the state of having You alone as their remainder; that is, they dissolve into You. It should be understood that the address "O Lord of All" is intended precisely with reference to such a distinction.

In the alternative interpretation (*aprakṛtapakṣa*), however, the word *brahmā* and the word *brahma*, as well as the word *śiva* and the word *śiva*, [become] the word *bhavat*—the word *bhavat* being "supreme" (*pareṇa*) or "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭena*). It should be understood that this excellence of it is due to its being the sole remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) among all when mentioned together, according to the method to be explained. In the context of "mentioning together" (*sahoktau*), this is the locative singular ending in *-i*. The meaning is: "when there is a mention together. At the end—that is, at the conclusion of the compound analysis (*vigraha*)—they assume the state of being the sole remainder of the word *bhavat*; that is, they assume the state of being the sole remainder of the word *bhavat*.

The root *dhā* (meaning "to hold" or "to maintain") belongs to the *bhūvādi* class; from this, we derive the first person singular present indicative (*laṭ*). This [word *bhavān*] connects with each of the two words *brahman* and *śiva*. This is because of the grammatical rule: "Pronouns such as *tyad* and others always remain when combined with any other word. The sense is that in the analytical compounds *brahmā ca bhavān ca* and *śivaśca bhavān ca*, the word *bhavān* alone remains.

Other words such as *tad* and *etad*, which begin with those [pronouns], also—when used in conjunction with *bhavat* (the word for "you"), which is recited later in the *tyadādi* group after all others—attain at the end, that is, upon the conclusion of the analytical compound (*vigraha*), the state of being a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) consisting solely of the word *bhavat*. This is derived from the root *dhā* (meaning "to hold" or "to nourish") belonging to the *jauhotyādi* class, in the present tense, third person plural. According to the rule: "When pronouns beginning with *tyad* are used in mutual conjunction, that which follows is retained."

The meaning is that in the analysis (vigraha) of the phrase "sa ca yaśca eṣa ca bhavāṃśca," the word *bhavantaḥ* remains as the residue precisely because it is the word *bhavat* that follows [the others]. Or, for example: "In the class of roots beginning with *bhū*, there is one whose state is free from prefixes (*upasarga*), which has produced a series of false augmentations (*āgama*), and which ends in *t*; such a root would have fled away. But the second *bhavat* is indeed infinite. (847)

In this verse, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the relevant Lord Śrīnivāsa and the irrelevant Patañjali. O Ananta! O Blessed One! You are the *dhātu*, meaning the sustainer and nourisher, according to the statement: "He is the Ordainer and the Disposer. [The word *dhātu*] is derived from the root *dhā* with the suffix *śatṛ*. He who has been born (*janitā*)—derived from the root *jan* with the suffix *tṛc*—in you, in the world beginning with the earth (*bhūlokādi-loke*), which belongs to the *bhv-ādi* class; that conscious being (*cetanaḥ*) who possesses the arrival of a series of misfortunes (*asadāvalīḍhāgamavān*)—the term *īṭ* here refers to one who is the chief (*pradhānabhūtaḥ*) among the rows (*āvalī*) or lines (*paṅkti*) of the wicked (*asatām*). Thus ends the verse.

The meaning is that he possesses association with them—that is, he is corrupted by association with the wicked. Alternatively, *iḍāḥ* refers to the words (*vācaḥ*) of the wicked; according to Amara, "the earth, cows, speech, lightning, and water are called *iḍā*. Thus, one who possesses their *āgama* (tradition) is one who constantly practices improper discourse; here the suffix *matup* denotes constant connection. Or else, *iḍāḥ* are the words of the wicked, and he is *āgamavān* (possessing tradition) through them—meaning he is learned in the scriptures (*śāstra*) [of those words]. Those very words of the wicked constitute his tradition/scripture, or he is one who possesses them. The sense is that only the words of the wicked serve as the injunctions for his practice. For this very reason, he would indeed be harmful (*ahita*).

The meaning is that, due to a lack of discernment corrupted by association with the wicked—which is itself caused by being subject to the power of long-standing evil deeds—one would indeed harbor hatred toward you. Alternatively, the construction may be: "That which is produced in the *bhvādi* [class of roots], being possessed of the augment (*āgama*) *as* and *l*, is indeed harmful (*ahita*) to you, the root (*dhātu*). The sense remains the same. Since the word *yaḥ* ("which") occurs in the subsequent sentence, there is no necessity for its grammatical form (*vṛtta*) to be explicitly mentioned in the preceding sentence.

That conscious being, whose state—meaning existence, nature, intention, activity, or birth—is sparse due to afflictions; for Hemacandra states: "Upasarga [means] misfortune, and also [prefixes] such as pra-, etc., and a type of disease. "Virala" means thin, delicate, or exceedingly light. And Amara states: "Pelava, virala, and tanu [mean thin]; bhāva [means] existence, nature, intention, activity, self, or birth."

For this very reason, he would become exhausted, weary, and flee; the meaning is that being wretched and finding no place of rest, he would run anywhere and everywhere. The implication is: "Where indeed could prosperity ever accrue to one who hates the Blessed One?"

In this alternative [interpretation], "O Ananta! is an address to Śeṣa, who has descended as Patañjali. The word division is *bhavatā ūhitaḥ ayam* ("this is inferred by you"). It means "inferred" (*ūhita*) or "considered" (*vicārita*) by you (*bhavatā*). Alternatively, the division is *bhavataḥ hitaḥ ayam* ("this is beneficial for you"). Or, it means "known to be beneficial" (*pathya*) for you. The root *hi* (in the sense of "to go") takes the suffix *kta* in the passive sense; those roots meaning "to go" also mean "to know. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *hita* is used in the senses of 'beneficial,' 'gone,' and 'held.'"

The genitive case here is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*), as the prohibition "na loka" (Pāṇini 2.3.69) applies specifically to the genitive of agency (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*). Alternatively, the suffix *kta* is prescribed by the rule "matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.188). In this case, the genitive is an exception to the prohibition "na loka," being governed by the rule "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67). In the *bhvādi* class—that is, the *bhvādigaṇa*—the word *janitā* means "manifested" or "arisen"; that is to say, it means "situated. The term *ayaḥ* refers to the verbal root *ay*. This is an indication made using the *śap* affix.

When the prefix *upa* is intended to be related to itself—that is, when the prefix *parā* [is applied], as will be stated in the word *palāyita*—[the following occurs]: "the state of being *vira*" means that by which the letter *ra* (repha) has been removed (*vigamita*), thus he is *viraḥ*. "The state of *la*" (*labhāva*) refers to the presence of the letter *la*; he in whom this state of *la* exists in place of *vira* is so described. Alternatively, "the state of *la*" (*labhāva*) is the substitution of *la* for *ra* (repha); he in whom this specific state of *ra* and *la* exists is so described. By the word *vi*, the permanence of the substitution of *la* is indicated.

The meaning is that, in every respect, it possesses the letter *l* in place of the letter *r*. "Ending in *ta*" (*tāntaḥ*) refers to the suffix *kta*, from which the anubandha *t* has been dropped; the meaning is "ending in the suffix *kta*. In the phrase "always possessing the augment *iṭ* after a semivowel" (*sadāvalīḍāgamavān*), there are three separate words—*sadā*, *vali*, and *iḍāgamavān*—which are not compounded.

The essential meaning is as follows: when there is a letter *k* belonging to the suffix *kta* which is connected to a *val* (consonant) *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, that letter—which is a member of the *val* pratyāhāra—would always (*sadā*) and invariably (*nityam*) possess the augment *iṭ* and thus "flee" (undergo change). This is because, according to rules such as *ayapaya*, for the root *ayati* (from the *bhvādi* class) preceded by the prefix *parā-* when the suffix *kta* is applied, the rule *upasargasyāyatau* mandates the invariable substitution of *l* for *r*, and the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* mandates the augment *iṭ*; thus, the form *palāyita* is produced.

Just as the Lord is both supreme and subordinate, yet He alone is truly the Sovereign; even when undergoing transformation, He does not truly change, for the quality of lightness inherent in His nature remains far from being affected.

Here there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *bhagavataḥ* and the word *īśvara*. "Another" (*paraḥ*) means different, such as the four-faced Brahmā and others; "inferior" (*avaraḥ*) means lowly. "Cit" means that which perceives, thus "cit" is consciousness. He who is the lord (*īśaḥ*) of this [consciousness] belongs to the Blessed One, the *Īśvara*. Just as in the verse "Under the sovereignty (*īśā*) of Him... (Ṛgveda 7.99.1), this word *īṭ* means "lord. He is not a lord (*īśvara*). The meaning is that because he is inferior in comparison to the Blessed One, he is not his lord (*īśvara*). Alternatively, "another" (*paraḥ*) means different, and "cit" means consciousness.

The word *īśa* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). According to the maxim, "In an unconditioned designation, there is no restriction [of meaning] for the wise; for the relationship between a word and its referent is established," the power of the word is unrestricted; thus, the meaning is "from this Lord of all. Alternatively, *avaraḥ* means "inferior" or "less than. Or else, by carrying the word *asya* back to the preceding part, the construction is *asya īśaḥ avaraḥ*, which has the same meaning: "inferior to him. In this latter view, *īśa* is a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

For this very reason, the meaning is that no other [deity] such as the four-faced Brahmā and so forth is the supreme Lord (īśvara) for this Blessed One; for the Śruti says, "No one is his lord," and so on. This very one—this Śrīnivāsa alone—is the Lord, the Lord of all. Indeed, the word "hi" (indeed) highlights what is well-known from the Śruti, Purāṇas, and other sources, such as: "He is the Lord of all; He is the Ruler of the past and the future; Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of the lords of all. Alternatively, the particle "hi" indicates a reason.

The sense is that this is because He alone is the Lord of all. Furthermore, he states another reason with the words "transformation" (vikṛtim). The meaning is that this Blessed One does not undergo transformation—that is, the six modifications of being such as "is born," "exists," "grows," and so forth—based on scriptural authorities such as, "He transcends old age and death," and "By means of decay and destruction [He is untouched]."

Furthermore, what is this "deceit" (*upadhā*) of the Blessed One, by which others might be outwitted? It is a particular modification of the mind (*cittavikāraviśeṣa*). As Amara states: "Deceit (*kapaṭa*), pretense (*vyāja*), hypocrisy (*dambha*), fraud (*upadhā*), disguise (*chadma*), and trickery (*kaitava*) are synonyms. There is also the usage: "ministers who have passed the test of deceit" (*amātyānupadhātītān*). Even the quality of "lightness" (*laghutāguṇa*)—meaning a quality consisting of mental frivolity caused by passion, hatred, and so forth—is present. Alternatively, the "defect" (*aguṇa*) is that lightness resulting from deceit; thus it is a non-quality (*aguṇa*), meaning an unwholesome quality (*apraśastaguṇa*) or a quality to be abandoned (*heyaguṇa*). Here, the negative particle (*nañ*) denotes lack of excellence (*aprāśastye*).

Because "aprāśastya" (unworthiness) and "virodha" (opposition) are enumerated among the meanings of the negative particle *nañ*, this [term] indicates the general category of qualities to be abandoned (*heya-guṇa*). The meaning is that even that [category] does not touch him from afar. While others might have a connection with such qualities to be abandoned due to their incompleteness, for Him—because of His boundless sovereignty, eternal fullness, and being the adversary of all that is to be abandoned—not even a trace of a connection with them is possible; thus, the implication is that He alone is the Lord of All.

Here, by the mention of being "distant from worldly attachment" (*upadhādūratva*), his straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is demonstrated through the absence of crookedness, owing to the uniformity of the functioning of the three instruments (*karaṇatraya-vṛtti-aikarūpya*) among those who have taken refuge in him. As he himself has said:
"The sky may fall, the earth may shatter, even the Himavat may move, and the ocean may dry up—O Kṛṣṇa, my word shall never be in vain."

Thus, by speaking of the distance from the quality of levity, his steadfastness—characterized by being unshakeable even by those who have committed offenses against him or by those who point them out—is demonstrated. As he himself said to Sugrīva and the others in a spirit of friendship:
"I would never abandon one who has approached me in the state of a friend, even if he should possess faults; for this is not censured among the virtuous."
Thus:

in the [derivation of] *īśa*, the root is *īś* from the verbal root *īśa aiśvarye* (to rule/sovereignty). It is an imitation of the root, as in the case of rules such as *kṣiyo dīrghāt*. *Cit* means the suffix *varac* prescribed by the rule *stheśabhāsapisakaso varac*; *paraḥ* means "following," because of the governing rule *pratyayaḥ, paraśca* (a suffix is that which follows). *Asya* refers to this *varac*. *Iṭ* means the augment *iṭ*. *Na* means it does not occur. This is because of the prohibition in the rule *neḍvaśikṛti*.

This very [root] *īś*, being thus excellent and distinguished, becomes the verbal root *īś*; from this, the word *īśvara* is produced. This word *īśvara*, once so produced, shall not undergo modification; it shall certainly not incur a grammatical change (*vikāra*) due to the absence of the augment *iṭ*. The sense is that because the root and the suffix are heard exactly as they are situated, if the augment *iṭ* had occurred, then its modification would have followed.

Regarding this word *īśvara*, the quality of the penultimate vowel being light (*upadhālaghutāguṇa*)—that is, the grammatical rule "the penultimate [vowel] is that which precedes the final consonant" (*alo'ntyātpūrva upadhā*), and the resulting shortness defined by the rule "a short vowel is light" (*hrasvaṃ laghu*)—is far removed from applying here. This is because the rule "there is guna for a root ending in *pu*, *g*, or *n*, and for one whose penultimate vowel is light" (*pugantalaghūpadhasya*) does not apply, since this word has a long penultimate vowel. The sense is that even if there were no modification caused by the addition of the augment *iṭ*, if guna had occurred, then a modification would have been incurred; yet even that does not happen.

Just as the word *vātāśagi* (wind-eater) attained its place at the beginning of the great and glorious fame of the assembly of the wise, so too does Your praiseworthy and most excellent foot shine forth, O Hari, with its celebrated renown.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the word *pāda*, which is the subject at hand as the Lord’s foot, and the word *pāda*, which is not the subject at hand [meaning "quarter"]. For instance: *budhavrajamahoda!*—this is an address meaning "O You who bestow (*dadāti*) the greatness (*mahaḥ*) or splendor (*tejaḥ*) upon the multitude of the wise (*budhavrajasya*), that is, the host of gods. Thus, O Hari, O Blessed One! "At the beginning" means at the time of the Trivikrama incarnation.

The meaning is that he is one whose *udanta*—that is, his history or account—is *prathita*, meaning well-known; the sense is that his power to traverse all the worlds is established by such Vedic texts as, "Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]; in three places he planted his step. For this very reason, he is *ślāghya* (praiseworthy) through his fame; *sādhīyān* means exceedingly firm (*bāḍha*), that is to say, supremely excellent. From the word *bāḍha*, when the suffix *īyasun* is added, the substitution *sādhu* occurs according to the rule "for *anti* and *bāḍha*, there are *nedas* and *sādhu*."
Your foot—your very step—having reached its place on Vātāśagiri, the mountain of Śeṣa, shines forth; it is so described because it has been set there.

Elsewhere, for the wise grammarians, there is great prosperity—the cause of great exaltation. Its vocative is *he hare*! The meaning is: "O Śeṣa," having descended as Patañjali. According to Amara, "vyālaḥ kumbhīnaso hariḥ. By the power of the qualifier, it should be understood that even the general term *hari* here refers to a specific one. [The word] *ślāghyaḥ* ends in a short vowel.

The word *pāda*—well-known as ending in a short vowel (*hrasva*) and established in the *Kośa* and other works as ending in *ad*—is the term for the word *pāda*. In the context of [suffixes] beginning with *śas*, *śas* is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the second case plural. The phrase "when a suffix beginning with that follows" means when a suffix beginning with *śas* follows. *Vātāśaḥ* refers to the sage Pāṇini. By his "speech"—meaning by means of the sūtras beginning with "padannomās"—he "attained," that is, obtained, the substitute (*ādeśa*) consisting of the form *pad*.

The compound *prathitodantaślāghya* is analyzed by reversing the sequence as *prathita-danta-ślāghya*. It is so called because the letter *d* (the sound *da*) is at the end (*anta*) of it. Since such a state is established when a word undergoes substitution (*padādeśa*), the term *danta* is "praiseworthy" (*ślāghya*); thus, *dantaślāghya* refers to you, the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the *Śabdānuśāsana*. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here in the sense of a general relationship. From the word *sādhu*, the suffix *ayiṣun* is added to form *sādhīyas*, meaning "exceedingly good. Being thus renowned as exceedingly good, he shines resplendent.

The author of the Sūtras has rendered [the word] correct by providing merely the grammatical rule (*ādeśa*); however, the meaning is that you, the author of the Bhāṣya, have made it even more correct by demonstrating the corresponding substituends (*sthānin*) as well. Or, for example: "He is worthy to attain supreme peace; he is to be counted among the Vedas and their knowers, for he is without the augment *iṭ*, since his self, having attained constant self-restraint, is indeed once and for all manifest. (850)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) of both the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) meanings of the word *dhātu*. To explain: "Supreme" (*param*) means unsurpassed; "bliss" (*śam*) means the bliss of experiencing the Supreme Brahman—this is the sense. He is "worthy of attaining" this, and for that very reason he is a "source" (*dhātu*), one who is even reckoned among or praised by Brahmā. Furthermore, he is a "knower of the Veda," a knower of Brahman. He is called "one in whom [it] does not exist" (*aniṭ*); "night" (*niṭ*) signifies ignorance, as it were, and he is one in whom that is not found. The cause for this is his "self-restraint" (*dāntatva*) and so forth.

For indeed, because this knower of Brahman has attained the specific quality of self-restraint—as described in such passages as "He who is peaceful, self-restrained, and withdrawn"—his Self, which is the inner controller, is "once and for all manifest," meaning it is ever-illuminated by being free from obscuration. Therefore, the meaning is that not even a trace of ignorance remains for this knower of Brahman.

Here, the meaning of the scriptural passage occurring in the Dahara-vidyā—“Therefore, having crossed over that bridge, one reaches indeed day even at night, for this world of Brahman is ever-shining”—is summarized. And the meaning of this scripture has been described by the author of the Upaniṣad-bhāṣya as follows: “For one who has attained the Supreme Self, even the night—the dark period—is just like day; because there is no possibility of the arising of ignorance in him, the night is like the day, and there is no distinction between day and night.”
The reason for this is that [the Self] is "always shining forth once and for all," because the manifestation of its nature as Brahman is never obscured.

In this context, he is worthy of attaining the *śa* suffix prescribed by the rule "śaḥ tudādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.77), which signifies excellence beyond himself. The word *veda* is a separate term; it refers to the root *vid*, meaning "to obtain," which is listed among the *tudādi* roots. It is described as *aniṭ*, meaning that its *iṭ* augment is non-existent (*avidyamāna*). Thus, I know (*veda*) that it should be counted (*gaṇyaḥ*) among the *aniṭ* roots.

The meaning is that because the root *vid* is also listed among those that do not take the augment *iṭ*—as stated in the *aniṭ-kārikā* rule, "The roots *vindati*, *candra*, *daurga*, etc., are desired [to be aniṭ], and it is also seen in the *Bhāṣya*"—the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule "from a single-vowel root that is unaccented in its original enunciation" (*ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt*). By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "the root *vid* also," it is implied that just as the two roots *vid* (meaning existence) and *vid* (meaning inquiry)—which are listed with the suffixes *śyan* and *śnam* respectively—are unimpededly subject to the prohibition of *iṭ*, so too is this [root]. For those two roots are likewise recited in the *aniṭ-kārikā* verses beginning with "the root *vidyat* and *vind*."

The text confirms that the root *vid* is anudātta (unaccented) by means of the phrase "the state of ending in *da*" (*dāntatvam*), and so forth. For (*hi*) because it has reached (*īyuṣaḥ*) the state of having the letter *da* at its end (*ante*) incessantly (*aniśam*)—wherein the vowel *a* in the word *da* is for the sake of pronunciation—the nature (*ātmā*) or essential form of this root *vid* shines forth (*vibhātaḥ*) only once (*sakṛt*) with the phoneme *vi*. Since the root *vid* possesses such a nature, it consists of a single syllable; therefore, the stated prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is indeed appropriate. This is the intended meaning.

Just as those which, though being *kuśala*, are not seen to have the suffixes of the *taddhita* class, for this reason these [suffixes] are elided, but these *taddhita* suffixes themselves are not [elided]. 851.

Here there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the subject at hand—those who are not devotees of the Lord—and the meaning of the grammatical rule: "The *la*, *śa*, and *ka* [are elided] when a *taddhita* suffix follows; its [the *lopa* marker's] elision. To explain: those people who, though being *kuśala* (skilled) and *kṛtin* (accomplished); or alternatively, the construction is that those who are *santaḥ* (virtuous), *manīṣiṇaḥ* (wise), and *kuśalāḥ* (skilled)—meaning they are proficient even in the secondary sciences such as the *Ṛgveda* and others;

and who are *taddhitapratyayādayaḥ*: those for whom the *pratyaya* (knowledge) and other qualities beginning with it—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), devotion, detachment, and so forth—are *taddhita* (beneficial) to that aforementioned Lord, bringing about delight.

Those who possess the qualities of knowledge, devotion, dispassion, and so forth as favored by the Blessed One—those who are characterized by such secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) and the like—are not seen; for this very reason, namely the non-perception of such beneficial knowledge and qualities, they "perish," meaning they vanish of their own accord or fall downward. The sense is that in the absence of the knowledge and other virtues favored by the Blessed One, even proficiency in all the arts is of no avail.

However, those virtuous people who possess the knowledge and devotion that bring pleasure to the Blessed One—beginning with the secondary suffixes (taddhita-pratyaya) and so forth—are not lost, because of the scriptural declaration: "My devotee perishes not. This is the intended meaning.

In this context, even though they are present and heard at the time of pronouncing the sūtra, those which are "skillful"—namely the *ka*-group consonants (*kavarga*), *ś*, and *l*—are referred to as "skillful" (*kuśala*) here in contrast to what will be stated in the forthcoming sūtra, *laśakut*. This usage is intended to achieve a desired pun (*śleṣa*). Furthermore, those such as *taddhita* suffixes and so forth, being distinct from *taddhita*, are seen—that is, known—as constituent parts of suffixes other than *taddhita*; in the term *nataddhita*, the word *na* forms a compound [with *taddhita*].

The meaning is that these [sounds] are designated as *it* because the rule "laśakvataddhite" prescribes the *it*-designation for the groups of sounds beginning with *l*, *ś*, and *k* when they constitute the initial element of an affix, excluding *taddhita* affixes. For this very reason, they are elided—that is, they become dropped—because the rule "tasya lopaḥ" prescribes the elision of a sound bearing the *it*-designation. Furthermore, elision (*lopa*) means non-appearance, according to the grammatical maxim "adarśanaṃ lopaḥ. By the phrase "not a *taddhita*" (*ataddhite*), he states the result of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*), beginning with "na," etc.

As for the *taddhita* suffixes and so forth—meaning those *k*, *ś*, and *l* sounds that constitute parts of *taddhita*-designated suffixes such as those prescribed by rules within the *taddhita* section, such as "the suffix *kan* after *ākarṣa* and others," "the suffix *śa* after *loman* and others," and "the suffix *lac* optionally after a word ending in long *ā* when denoting something residing in a living being"—these are not elided.

The meaning is that [the suffixes] such as *ka*, *khaś*, *gha*, *śatṛ*, *śānac*, and *lyuṭ*—which are prescribed by rules such as *āto’nupasarge kaḥ*, *ejeḥ khaś*, *puṃsi saṃjñāyāṃ ghaḥ prāyeṇa*, *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*, and *lyuṭ ca*—do not undergo elision (as the *kādi*-suffixes do). Rather, they are heard [in pronunciation] exactly as they appear in words such as *ākarṣakaḥ*, *lomaśaḥ*, and *jaṅghālaḥ*.

Just as the honorific suffix *maha* is established from the word *mahat* by means of the suffix *atipratyaya* according to the lords of scholars, so too is the augment *num* established when a case-ending (*sarvanāmasthāna*) follows. (552)

Here, there is a conjunction between the Blessed One and the Great Element (*mahaddhātu*). For thus, from that which is supreme—that is, from the knowledge consisting of an uninterrupted stream of memory arising from a preeminent and non-confused cognition of a different class—there is established and attained the Great Light (*mahaḥ*), the venerable splendor, the self-luminous Supreme Brahman described in such passages as "That which the gods know as the light of lights" and "He who is the supreme, great radiance. The text specifies that very light with the words "wherein."

"In the *sarvanāmasthāna* (the locus of all names)" means in that which is denoted by the word "all" (*sarva*), the ultimate ground of all names; or rather, in that which serves as the cause for the manifestation of the names and forms of the gods and so forth. "In whom"—that is, in the Supreme Brahman alone—"the arrival of Mā" (*māgamaḥ*)—meaning the arrival (*gamaḥ*), union (*saṃgamaḥ*), or connection (*saṃbandhaḥ*) with *mā*, i.e., with Śrī—is established (*siddhaḥ*), perfected, or auspicious (*maṅgalakara*). This is because the root *ṣidh* is used in the sense of "establishment in a science" (*śāstre*) and "auspiciousness" (*māṅgalye*); from this root, the suffix *kta* is applied in the agentive sense (*kartari*).

By the word *api* (also/even), it is indicated that the connection of this auspicious [work] with its auspicious deity, Śrī, is itself an intensifier of excellence. Regarding the particle *nu*, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *nu* is used in inquiry, conjecture, contempt, option, entreaty, and the past. The established meaning is that the supreme splendor which constitutes Śrīnivāsa is attained through the practice of meditation by those who know Brahman.

In the view of the wise lords among grammarians, the term *mahaḥ* refers to the verbal root *maha*, which is stated to mean "worship" (*pūjā*). From this root, by means of the suffix *at* occurring after itself—that is, after that which exists subsequent to the root—the form *mahat* is established; the meaning is that the word *mahat* is produced. This occurs precisely when the word *mahat* itself is followed by a suffix designated as a "strong case-ending" (*sarvanāmasthāna*), as prescribed by the rules: "The [suffix] *śi* is called a strong case-ending" and "The augment *suṭ* is added to a non-neuter [stem] before a strong case-ending."

In the expression *numāgama*, the analysis is *num* (the augment) + *āgama* (arrival). Because [the word *pṛṣat*] is treated as ending in a *śatṛ*-suffix by the rule "In the present tense, *pṛṣat*, *mahat*, *bṛhat*, and *jagat* are irregularly formed like the *śatṛ* [participles]," it possesses the property of being an *ugit* [stem]. Consequently, the *num* augment prescribed by the rule "After an *ugit* stem ending in a vowel other than *a*, before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [case-ending], provided it is not a verbal root" applies; that is to say, there is the arrival (*āgama*)—the connection (*gama*)—of the vowel *ā*. This results in the lengthening of the penultimate *n* by the rule "Of a [stem] ending in *s* or *m*, and of *mahat*," which means that this [lengthening] is also established.

Just as here [in this world], one who is attached to primordial nature (prakṛti) does not arise in the supreme state even if permitted by it, so too a person would not exist as such in Brahman; nor is there here any subjugation by the Lord. (853)

Here there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the subject at hand, the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), and the word "Brahman" (*brahman*) which is not the subject. For it is thus: "In this world, a man who has grown great in the supreme realm does not arise again when joined with nature; he is considered [to have reached] Brahman. If it were otherwise, there would be neither mastery nor the state of being honored here"—such is the division of the words.

The word *naraḥ* means a conscious being (*cetanaḥ*) regarding the Supreme Abode (*parabhūmani*), which is characterized by unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśayamahimani*). The meaning is that it is distinguished by supreme vastness, according to the scriptural description: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else—that is the Infinite (*bhūmā*). For this very reason, it is "expansive" (*bṛṃhati*) and "increasing" (*vardhamāne*), meaning it is all-pervasive, according to the scriptural description: "Neither above, nor across, nor in the middle did anyone grasp it.
