Regarding the object, namely Brahman, he is "one who thinks" (*mataḥ*) or "the thinker" (*mantā*); here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent, according to the rule "the suffix *kta* is used after roots meaning 'to think' (*mati*) or 'to understand' (*buddhi*)," and so forth.

The meaning is: one whose nature is contemplation upon the essence of the Supreme Brahman. "Attached to Prakṛti" means due to contact with Prakṛti; "here" means on this earth or in this world. "He does not arise again" means he is not born again. Having attained the Supreme Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*), he does not return. As it is said: "Having come to Me, the great-souled ones do not undergo rebirth—which is a transient abode of suffering—for they have reached the supreme perfection."

The meaning is "because of singing thus. "In that state" means while there is such non-return. "In this man who knows Brahman" refers to one who has brought [the world] under control; "vaśī" means the Lord of all, whose entire world is dependent on his own will. "Vaśī" is so called because he possesses *vaśa* (control); for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *vaśa* may mean dependence, desire, or sovereignty. This is supported by the Śruti: "He is the controller of all, the lord of all," and by the Smṛti: "This entire world, including the moving and the unmoving, exists under the control of Kṛṣṇa."

*Kṛtī* means one for whom something has been done (*kṛtam asyāsti*). According to the manner stated in the verse, "O Pārtha, there is nothing for me to be done," the meaning is that he is devoid of any remaining duties for his own sake. Alternatively, he is *kṛtakṛtyaḥ* (one who has accomplished his purpose) through the protection of those who have sought refuge, as stated in the passage beginning with "And having consecrated... and ending with "...Rāma was then one who had accomplished his purpose. Or else, *kṛtī* means one who possesses a service rendered (*kṛta upakāraḥ asyāsti*), where the suffix *matvarthīya* expresses abundance; the meaning is that he considers even the slightest favor received to be very great.

As it has been said: "He is satisfied by even a single benefit rendered in some way. Regarding the word *kṛtena* here, commentators explain it as: "The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the inception of an action; [it means] by that which has been undertaken to be done.
When Draupadī cried out "Govinda! to me while I was living far away, that cry does not depart from my heart, like a debt that has grown large.

And so it is said. Here, in the verse “*vaśī vadānyaḥ*,” the qualities of self-mastery (*vaśitva*), skillfulness (*kṛtitva*), and gratitude (*kṛtajñatva*) are set forth by the venerable Śrī Yāmunamuni. The compound *vaśikṛtī* is a *karmadhāraya* consisting of two qualifying terms: he who is both self-mastering and skillful. Furthermore, *sa cāsāvīṭ*: *īṭ* refers to the Lord, the Blessed One; *itaḥ* means obtained from Him. Alternatively, it may mean "by whom [the state of] being self-mastering and skillful has been obtained. The state of that [person] is *vaśikṛtīḍitatā*, which signifies the experience of the Supreme Brahman.

The sense is that it is not merely that "it might not be," but rather that it is necessarily bound to happen; by means of these two words which negate the possibility of a negation, the suspicion that such a wise person might fail to experience the Supreme Brahman is cast far away. As Vāmana has aphorized: "In the case of negating a possible negation, there are two negations. In the phrase *nossyāt*, the optional doubling of the letter *s*—according to the rule *anaci ca*—must certainly be accepted for the sake of conforming to the intended meaning.

Alternatively, the sense is: "May there not be mere praise from those who are self-controlled (vaśibhiḥ), whose senses are mastered, who are skillful (kṛtibhiḥ), and wise (vidvadbhiḥ)—that is, may he not merely be extolled as 'this one of great power is a knower of Brahman' (brahmavit); rather, let there truly be such praise. Elsewhere, the word division is as follows: "In this [state] of the vast supreme expanse (bṛṃhati-parabhūmani), may there be for us (naḥ) the attainment (at) which is joined with nature (prakṛti-saṅgataḥ) and approved (numataḥ); may there be no 'ra' in Brahman; likewise, through that state of 'at', may there be 'u'; nor here [is there] the division of words as 'vaśi-kṛti-iḍitatā'."

In the word *bṛṃhatiparabhūmani*, the root *bṛh*—as in the verbal root *bṛh* meaning "to grow" (*vṛddhau*), listed in the *bhvādi* class—is intended here by the mention of *śtip*. Therefore, the phrase means: in that which follows [the root], namely *parabhūḥ* (existing elsewhere), where there is a suffix such as *man* or *mann*; that is to say, in a form derived from *bṛh* by the addition of the suffix *manin*.

In the word *brahmaṇi*, which is the word for Brahman, [the suffix] is connected—that is, joined—to the verbal root *bṛh* (meaning "to grow"), which serves as the base for the suffix *man*. It is derived from the root *at*, belonging to the *bhvādigaṇa* and meaning "to go continuously" (*sātatyagamana*), with the suffix *ac* applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*ecādyac*). The term *numataḥ* means "from that which possesses *num*"; that is, the letter *na* becomes *at* due to the addition of the augment *num*, which is prescribed by the rule "the augment *num* is added to a root ending in *it*" (*idito num dhātoḥ*) because the root *bṛh* ends in *it*. Thus, the letter *na* becomes *at*.

The meaning is that the *n* of the suffix *num* in the root *bṛh* becomes the short vowel *a*, as designated by the grammatical convention "taparaḥ tatkālasya. The intention is that, following the recurrence of the suffix *man* from the rule "sarvadhātubhyo man," the substitution of *a* for the *n* of *num* is prescribed by the Uṇādi-sūtra "bṛṃherno'cca. Likewise (*tathā*) means in exactly this same way; by the substitution of *a* for the *n* of *num* through the change to the vowel *a*, the *u*—that is, the *ṛ* sound following the *b*—[is affected].

From the word *ṛ*, in the *ṅasi* case-ending, there is a single substitute by the rule *ṛta ut*; then, after the substitution of *u* and the subsequent replacement of that *u* by *ra* (via *rapara*), the *s* is dropped by the rule *rātsasya*, resulting in a *visarga* for the *repha*. The construction “*na syāt*” means “it would not be *ra*,” but this is negated by the word “*na*,” meaning “it certainly would be. This is because, with the form *bṛ-a* established, the rule *iko yaṇ aci* prescribes the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *ṛ*.

In this very context, once the word *brahman* has been thus established, [the objection is raised that] by the rule *neḍvaśikṛti*, the augment *iṭ*—that is, the addition of the suffix *iṭ*—would not occur when the suffix *kṛt* (beginning with the *vaś* pratyāhāra) follows; therefore, two words are repeated: *na syāt* (*na bhavet*), meaning "it would not be. This is because of the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *neḍvaśikṛti*. Thus, the meaning of this most difficult verse should be contemplated with a subtle vision, attentively and compassionately, by a multitude of wise and sympathetic scholars who are most proficient in the terminology and methods of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*. As for example:
The God, being free from affliction, bestows his own station upon himself for the sake of those who delight in him; yet he enters there for the sake of another, for whomsoever he may desire.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the subject at hand, the person devoted to Brahman, and the subject not at hand, the element of water (*viś*). To explain: that person who would "deserve" (*abhyarhet*)—that is, become worthy—to attain the supreme station for the sake of another (*parasmai padāya*), where the dative case is used according to the rule beginning with "for the purpose of an action" (*kriyārtha*); to him, who is devoted to his own self (*svajuṣe*), that is, to the conscious self (*ātmane*) which dwells within the human body (*viśe*).

Since it is established by the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that words denoting a body extend to include the possessor of that body (*śarīrin*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words *viśe* and *ātmane*. According to Amarasimha, "the two *viśau* are the Vaiśya and the human. The sense is that the Lord, the Blessed One, being free from affliction (*nirupasarga*), wards off from afar any anxiety as to how this title could be bestowed upon such a person; he grants him a fitting, divine station (*pada*).

And that man also, entering into that supreme state, comes to dwell there with his sole delight in service to Him, having been graced by the Lord with the sovereignty of infinite liberation; this is the intended meaning.

In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the verbal root *viś*, which is listed as "in the sense of entering," would be fit (*abhyarhet*) for the designation of the Parasmaipada—that is, for the *l*-substitutes prescribed by the rule "the *l*-suffixes are Parasmaipada"—because the root *viś* is read among the Parasmaipada roots; this is the intended meaning.

To that *viś*—which is self-enjoying (*svajuṣ*) and which possesses its own co-utterance (*svasamabhivyāhāra*), meaning it is that which enters (*viśadhātu*)—the *deva* impels. A *deva* is so called because he illuminates (*dyotayati*) the meaning of the verbal root; [it is derived] from the root *div* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *ac* (according to Pāṇini 3.1.134). The term *deva* is used here because prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely illuminators (*dyotaka*). The prefix *niḥ* is a specific type of particle (*nipāta*) defined by the rule "prefixes occur in connection with action" (*upasargāḥ kriyāyoge*).

The term *ātmanepada* refers to the affix known as *śānac*, which is designated by the technical name *ātmanepada* according to the rule "taṅānāvātmanepadam. Because the rule "nerviśaḥ" prescribes the *ātmanepada* for the root *viś* when preceded by the prefix *ni*, there is a metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of that designation to the prefix itself. That prefix *ni* is thus characterized by its association with the root *viś*. In this context, the phrase "when that *ātmanepada* follows" is the understood sense. Thus, he becomes one who is entering (*niviśamānaḥ*), and in that same way, he is accomplished (*niṣpadyate*).

The root *viś*, which is naturally *parasmaipada*, attains *ātmanepada* status when preceded by the prefix *ni* according to the method described; thus, the final meaning is "entering" (*niviśamāna*). In this view, regarding the form *ātmanepadaṃ parasmaipadāya*, it should be understood that the fourth case ending does not undergo elision (*aluk*) due to the two rules: *vaiyākaraṇākhyāyāṃ caturthyāḥ* and *parasya ca*.

Just as the king of the earth, having freely renounced his own will while serving the two feet of his lord, always bears the command of that supreme master even in a place of instability, so too does [the yogi] bear the instruction of the True Teacher.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the King of Kings (*rājādhirāja*), who serves the feet of the Blessed One, and the king of the earth (*rājadhātu*), who is both the relevant and the irrelevant subject. To explain: by nature—and not by the instigation of another—he serves the pair of feet of the Lord (*nātha*), namely Veṅkaṭanātha, "at will," meaning according to his own free choice and not in a constrained manner. He is an "overlord of kings" (*adhidharaṇirāja*), meaning one superior to the kings of the earth; that is, a King of Kings (*rājādhirāja*). Furthermore, he is "elegant" (*caṭula*), for he possesses "elegance" (*caṭu*), which here means hymns of praise.

Because the word *caṭu* is listed among the *sidhma*-group [of words], the possessive suffix *lac* is applied according to the rule "sidhmādiṣu ca. Alternatively, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "āto ’nupasarge" [Pāṇini 3.2.3], based on the derivation "one who takes (*lāti*) or receives (*ādatta*) flatteries (*caṭūn*). According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The words *caṭu* and *cāṭu* refer to the praise of kings and the like, as well as to the testicles of cattle. Thus, the meaning is "being praiseworthy. Or else, there is a word-break as *acaṭula*; the meaning is "being not fickle (*acapala*)."

In the phrase "madena kiṃciccaṭulālasānām," Mallinātha has explained that "caṭulāḥ" means "capalāḥ" (fickle). The word "sthāne" means "in the kingdom"; the word "sthitassan" (being situated) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. "Deśam" means the country or realm. "Paramānamatam" means "regarded with supreme honor"—that is, esteemed with the highest respect and dignity—such that it may be so; "sadā" means constantly; and "tathā" means in an indescribable manner. "Dhatte" means he nourishes or sustains. Alternatively, "sadādeśam" may be read as a single compound word.

He upholds—that is, nurtures—the command or edict, which is esteemed with honor and respect even by enemies, being highly regarded and praised for its application according to rule; or rather, he upholds the instruction or order of the virtuous so that it becomes known through great veneration. The sense is that he nurtures his supreme sovereignty with great respect along the path commanded by the good.

Alternatively, the indeclinable *sthāne*, which carries the sense of "proper" or "fitting," should be understood as a separate word placed at the end [of the verse]. The meaning is: "It is proper that he assumes the form of a child for one who serves the pair of the Lord's feet. The rest is exactly the same.

In this context, "O Lord" (*nātha*) is a vocative address. *Adhidharaṇī* is a separate word; it is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of a case ending, meaning "on the earth. The root for *rāj* is stated as *rājṛ* in the sense of "shining," and this is its citation form with the suffix *śap*. By its very nature—and not through association with the *yaṅ* or other such suffixes—it serves both bases at will, according to its desire; that is to say, it is "ubhayapadī" (conjugated in both voices).

The sense is that, by the rule regarding the *svarita* accent, the *ātmanepada* ending is employed when there is a desire to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, while the *parasmaipada* ending is employed when there is a desire to express that it accrues to another. For this very reason, [the verse says] "in such a way as to be praiseworthy" (*caṭu ślāghyaṃ yathā syāt tathā*). "Another" (*param*) means existing beyond oneself. "In the place of *la*" (*lasthāne*) means in the place of *laṭ*. The division is *ānam* and *atam*. By "ānam" and "atam," there is the inclusion of the suffixes *śānac* and *śatṛ*, from which the *anubandhas* have been dropped.

The sense is that when *āna* is in the Ātmanepada, it takes the suffix *śānac*, and when in the Parasmaipada, it takes *śatṛ*, because of the rule "for the present tense (*laṭ*), there are *śatṛ* and *śānac*" (*laṭaśśatṛśānacau*). The sense is that it receives the substitute *sat*, meaning the substitute termed *sat*, because of the prescription of the term *sat* for those two substitutes, *śatṛ* and *śānac*, by the rule "those two [are called] *sat*" (*tau sat*). Thus, [the forms] *dhatte* and *dadhāti* are formed. Since the root *rājṛ* is svarita (circumflex) and thus inherently both-voiced (ubhayapadin), it naturally receives the desired substitutes *śānac* and *śatṛ*—which are termed *sat*—in place of the *l*-suffixes; this is the summarized meaning. Or alternatively:

We worship the divine couple, the form of the Blessed Lord, which shines with mutual union, is sweet through the primacy of both members [of the compound], and possesses the excellence established by Ananta Giri. (855) Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun/paronomasia) between the relevant *dvandva* compound—the divine pair consisting of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa—and the irrelevant grammatical *dvandva* compound. To illustrate: "itaretarayogojjvalam" [shining with mutual union] refers to a couple of equal character, age, and conduct, and of equal lineage and marks; [the rest follows].
Rāghava is worthy of Vaidehī, and she, this dark-eyed woman, is worthy of him.

In the manner described above, the meaning is that they have attained their supreme state through mutual connection; or alternatively, that they have acquired their existence through mutual inseparability (*avinābhāva*). As it is stated in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"I-consciousness (*ahantā*) is the Brāhmaṇa, and I am his eternal Self (*ātmā*);
Hari is remembered as the one who has become the 'I' (*ahambhūta*) within all beings."
I am the egoity of all beings; that I am, the eternal one.
For the object of the "I" (ahamartha) is established only when it is pervaded by the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā).
And that egoity (ahaṃtā) is proclaimed to arise from the sense of "I" (ahamartha),
because of their mutual inseparability and their mutual concomitance.
Know that the relationship between me and my Lord is one of identity.

And so forth. Within the fourfold range of meanings for the particle *ca*—namely, conjunction (*samuccaya*), disjunctive addition (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*)—as prescribed by the rule "the *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of *ca*," [the term] shines brightly, manifesting as a unified whole through the presence of its inherent capacity in the specific sense characterized by mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*).

The following point must be noted here: there is no compound formation in the case of *samuccaya* (conjunction), as in "Worship both the Lord and the Guru," nor in the case of *anvācaya* (sequential addition), as in "Go for alms and bring the cow," because of the absence of the semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) that constitutes syntactic capacity (*sāmarthya*). For instance, while it is necessary for the words constituting a *bahuvrīhi* to possess semantic integration through the inclusion of an object (*karman*) and so forth, and for the words constituting a *dvandva* to possess semantic integration through the inclusion of an additional meaning (*arthāntara*), this is required because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "A word-formation rule applies to what is semantically capable" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*) and the injunction "A *dvandva* compound occurs in the sense of *ca* [and]."

If there were no mutual connection (*itaretarānvaya*), the state of becoming a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) would not be possible for things that are independent of one another, such that conjunction (*samuccaya*) and disjunctive addition (*anvācaya*) would be included within that state of unified meaning. Therefore, a compound occurs in cases of mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*) and collective grouping (*samāhāra*) because of the existence of mutual association (*sāhitya*), but not in the cases of conjunction or disjunctive addition. However, one must distinguish that in mutual connection, association is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the substance (*dravya*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), whereas in collective grouping, association is the primary element and the substance is the qualifier.

With the intention that, even between these two, the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) is superior—because, according to the method to be explained, it primarily emphasizes both word-meanings as substances rather than depending on a collective whole (*samāhāra*) where the emphasis is on their association—it is said: "It shines with mutual conjunction."

They say: "Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the connection of several mutually independent things to a single [action]; subordination (*anvācaya*) occurs when one of them is secondary; mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is the connection of things combined together; and a collection (*samāhāra*) is an aggregate. [The compound] is sweet because both word-meanings are primary; those two word-meanings consist of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and they are delightful through their equal primacy in qualities such as being presided over by the dual majesty (*ubhayavibhūti*), pervasiveness, and lordship.
For the remainder of both her and mine is a power (*vibhūti*) consisting of two natures.
Just as the world is pervaded by me through my own form and essential nature, so too is all this pervaded by her; likewise, she is the sovereign mistress who governs it.
These and other such means of valid cognition have been considered here.

The meaning is that when the action is connected with the [two] members of the compound, it is "charming" because both constituent meanings are primary; for this is the traditional dictum of the ancients: "A *dvandva* is one in which the meanings of both members are predominant. *Bhagavantau* refers to the two Lords (*bhagavatī* and *bhagavān*), who are full of the sixfold perfections such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth; the expression is used thus because both possess the aforementioned qualities in their entirety. *Dvaṃdva* means a pair (*mithuna*).

The meaning is that among the compounds (samāsa), it is the dvandva compound that is enumerated as being a manifestation (vibhūti) of the Lord, who is the primary subject here. This is because [the Lord] is sung of in the chapter on the expansion of manifestations (*vibhūtivistara*) in the words, "And I am the dvandva among compounds" (*dvaṃdvassāmāsikasya ca*). It is precisely because the dvandva is a manifestation of the Lord that it is described here as having the nature of the Lord. "Sāmāsika" means a collection of compounds; among those, I am the dvandva compound.

For it is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Tātparya-candrikā* that "this [Dvandva] is indeed superior to the Avyayībhāva, Tatpuruṣa, and Bahuvrīhi compounds—wherein respectively the prior member, the subsequent member, or another word is predominant—because it has as its primary meaning the objects denoted by both members. It is with this very intention that the sweetness of the predominance of the meanings of both members is mentioned here. Furthermore, he distinguishes the Dvandva as "possessing excellence bestowed by the infinite mountains"; the meaning is that it has attained excellence upon the Śeṣācala (the serpent-hill).

In one sense, [we worship] that which has attained excellence in the *Mahābhāṣya*, the speech of Patañjali on the mountain of Ananta; here, "on the mountain of Ananta" refers to the speech in the form of the *Gītā* of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, in which excellence has been established according to the cited authorities. Therefore, the meaning "having the form of the Blessed Lord" (*bhagavadrūpa*) should also be understood. We worship it.
Or rather:
"O mind, did I not previously place you in the *tatpuruṣa* compound? I see that you are not equal here [in the *dvandva*], yet I perceive you to be supreme elsewhere [in the *bahuvrīhi*]. (856)

Here, the poet describes a *śleṣa* (double entendre) between his own mind and the suffix *ktvā*. To explain: "O mind! O heart! I have previously placed you upon that Supreme Person (*tatpuruṣa*)—the one known by all the world as the Lord of All and so forth; that is, having entrusted the burden of my own protection to Him. In this state, I sit perfectly composed (*samāse*) and have become happy through [His] fullness. The meaning is that I have become blissful by resting completely [in Him].

This is the first person singular present indicative (*laṭ*) in the active voice (*kartari*) derived from the root *ās* preceded by the prefix *sam*. Therefore, in this world, I do not see any person whatsoever who is equal to me.
Those who are devoted to virtuous deeds, the pure, and those likewise learned in Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
do not equal even a ten-millionth part of one who has taken refuge [in the Buddha].

The meaning is: "from such scriptural authority as this. Regarding the phrase "in the other state" (*paratra pade*), I know—that is, I understand—the Supreme Person (*parama-puruṣa*) who is heard of in the scripture, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," to be equal to me, similar to me; for the meaning is that the state of supreme equality has been declared by the scripture, "Being stainless, he attains supreme equality."

In this alternative view, the word division is indeed *itaḥ*. Here, *itaḥ* means "in this" [context] that is present in the mind; the suffix *-tasi-* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). "Not preceded" (*apūrve*) means not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. By the letter *a*, there is an intended reference to the negative particle *nañ* with its *n* elided. And in a *tatpuruṣa*—that is, in a compound designated as a *tatpuruṣa*, but not in just any compound whatsoever—the term *ktvā* refers to the suffix *ktvā* whose *anubandha* has been dropped (i.e., *tvā*), just as in the rule *ānemuḥ* etc., it refers to the suffix *śānac* and so on. The meaning is "the suffix *ktvā*."

The meaning is that he has placed [the suffix] here, in this *ktvā* suffix; that is to say, in its place. It does not mean the three words "na," "tu," and "lyam. The term *lyam* is a reference to *lyap*, which has had its *anubandha* dropped, just as *matup* and so on are used in rules such as "matau bahvacaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.120). The intention is that [the word *lyam*] is not [to be taken literally]. Furthermore, [the phrase] "I do not see, indeed I do not see" is intended to show that *lyap* is prescribed for *ktvā* only when the compound is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*—according to the rule "samāse'nañpūrve ktvo lyap" (Pāṇini 7.1.37)—because *lyap* is not observed in cases like "akṛtvā," where there is a *nañ*-compound.

In cases where a compound is preceded by a word other than the negative particle *nañ* in the subsequent member, I understand the suffix *lyap*; this is because we observe *lyap* in examples such as "having adorned" (*alaṃkṛtya*) and "having paid homage" (*namaskṛtya*). This is the intended meaning.

Or, for example: Even at the end of the aeon (*kalpānta*), the Goddess Śrī remains short-voweled; she would not become "Lakṣmī" [long-voweled]. Even when appearing at the end, she is invariably short-voweled, as she is necessarily joined with many others. (857)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the wealth (*saṃpad*) that is the subject at hand—whether it be the wealth residing in Lakṣmī or obtained through her side-glance—and the words "Śrī," "Lakṣmī," and so forth, which are not the subject at hand. To explain: [the word] *lakṣmyāḥ* means either "belonging to Lakṣmī" (*śrī-saṃbandhinyāḥ*) or "obtained by the side-glance of Lakṣmī" (*lakṣmī-kaṭākṣa-labdhāyāḥ*). In this sense, *lakṣmyāḥ* may be taken as the ablative case (*pañcamī*), with the word "obtained" (*labdha*) understood as the ellipsis. Or, it may be construed as "of Śrī" (*śriyaḥ*) meaning "of wealth" (*saṃpadaḥ*), or "of Śrī" (*śriyaḥ*) meaning "of Lakṣmī. The meaning remains the same as before. Even though the end of the eon has arrived—that is, even during the time of universal dissolution (*saṃvarta-samaya*).

That which has a short vowel as its internal form (antaḥ-svarūpa) is described as such; it is neuter in the general sense. Its state is "having a short final vowel" (*hrasvāntatva*), which amounts to perishability (*naśvaratva*). Hemacandra states: "The word *anta* [is used] in the senses of internal form, proximity, boundary, immobility, and destruction. The *Ratnamālā* also says: "*Anta* is not feminine; it [denotes] certainty, destruction, essential nature, the front, proximity, and interior. It would not be so. The intention is that prosperity associated with Lakṣmī, or obtained through her sidelong glances, would not be perishable even at the end of a Kalpa.

In the word *itarapprasaktā*, [the feminine form] is derived as "attached to others" (*itarāsu*), "residing in other deities" (*itarāsu devatāsu*), or "obtained from other deities" (*itarābhyo devatābhyo labdhā*). Regarding the form *itarapprasaktā*, the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the word *itarā* occurs by the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre*. Furthermore, in this specific sense, the doubling of the letter *p* in *itarappra-*—by the rule *anaci ca*—is necessary to avoid a discrepancy in the phonetic form of the word in its different meanings. Alternatively, it should be understood that if one takes *tara* as the suffix *tarap* (with its *anubandha* dropped), as if it were the comparative suffix *tarap*, then even in a different sense, the doubling of the letter *p* is not necessarily required.

The meaning is that she is *Śrī* (Prosperity). Though she appears as "much" (*bahvī*)—or rather, though she appears as undifferentiated at the time of non-investigation—at the end, at the time of final determination, she becomes "short," meaning quickly perishable. This is certainly and surely true regarding prosperity connected with deities other than the Blessed Lakṣmī, or prosperity obtained through her grace; for although it appears as infinite during the state of non-investigation, at the time of the extraction of reality, it is known to be merely limited. This is the intended sense.

In the alternative view, regarding the state of reaching the end of the *kalpa* (kalpāntagatatve): the word *kalpaḥ* refers to the suffix *kalpa*, and "reaching the end of that" means when it exists beyond its own [base]. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for being followed by suffixes such as *tarap*. The particle *api* is displaced in order and connects with the word *śriyaḥ*. We have stated more than once that there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the femininity residing in the meaning onto the word *lakṣmyāḥ*, that is, onto the word *lakṣmī*. The same applies hereafter. For *śriyaḥ*—that is, for the word *śrī* as well—the state of ending in a short vowel would not occur.

Since the optional shortening prescribed for a feminine noun ending in *ṅī* (whether by the rule *anadyāśśeṣasyānyatarasyām*) and for a monosyllabic word ending in *ṅī* is prohibited by the rule *kṛnnadyā na*, this applies here. Furthermore, the word *lakṣmī* ends in a *kṛt*-derived feminine noun (*kṛnnadī*), because the suffix *ī* is prescribed after the root *lakṣ* by the Uṇādi sūtra *lakṣermuṭ ca*; and because that word is designated as a *nadī* by the rule *yūstryākhyau nadī*.

However, because of the prohibition "neyaṅuvaṅsthānāvastrī," the word *śrī-*—not ending in a short vowel—is not even within the scope of that [rule]. Consequently, forms such as *lakṣmīkalpā* and *śrīkalpā* contain only the long vowel (*ī*), and not the short-vowel forms *lakṣmikalpā* or *śrikalpā*. He states another distinction with the words beginning "bhāntī": the word *bhāntī* is subject to the suffix *tarap*. The particle *api* here has the sense of "even" (*api cet*). *Bhāntī* is the word [ending in] *tarap*.

The term *tarap* refers to that [word] in which the suffix *tarap* is applicable—that is to say, one ending in the suffix *tarap*. Furthermore, when it has reached the end of the *kalpa*, the aforementioned meaning is established. Alternatively, at the end [of the word], it may optionally be short; from the word *hrasva*, the possessive suffix *matup* is applied, and by the rule *arśa-ādy-ac*, the form *hrasvā* is derived. The meaning is that it should be one ending in *hrasvā*. The intention is that, according to the rule *ugitaśca*, the short vowel is optionally prescribed when followed by suffixes such as *gha*, *rūpa*, or *kalpa*. Moreover, this word *bhāntī* ends in an *ugit* vowel.

Furthermore, the sense is that this word [bahvī] is well-known as being a feminine form derived from a masculine base (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), ending in the *ṅī* suffix, and consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāc*). The word *bahvī*—having become subject to the *tarap* suffix—would necessarily be short at the end when it reaches the state of *kalpa*, meaning it would always end in a short vowel; for the sense is that a short vowel is invariably prescribed by the rule: "In the presence of *gha*, *rūpa*, *kalpa*, *cala*, *ḍu*, *bruva*, *gotra*, *mata*, and *hata*, there is a short vowel for a feminine stem (*ṅī*) having more than one vowel."

The meaning of the rule is as follows: "When the suffix *ṅīp* follows a word that has already expressed the masculine gender, there shall be shortening of the penultimate vowel of a multi-syllabic (*anekāc*) stem when the suffixes *gha*, *rūpa*, and *kalpa* follow, as well as when words such as *celaṭ* follow as subsequent members (*uttarapada*). The term *gha* is the technical designation for the suffixes *taraP* and *tamap*, because of the rule establishing that designation: "The suffixes *taraP* and *tamap* are called *gha*."

Thus, when the suffixes *itarā* and *kalpā* follow the word *bhāntī*, the forms *bhāntitarā* and *bhāntikalpā* arise due to the optional shortening of the vowel; however, in the alternative where shortening does not occur, there is masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "in *tasil* and other suffixes," resulting in the forms *bhāttarā* and *bhātkalpā*, and not *bhāntitare* and so forth. When the suffixes *itarā* and *kalpā* follow the word *bahvī*, the vowel is always shortened, resulting in the forms *bahvitarā* and *bahvikalpā*. This should be discerned by those of attentive heart and by the foremost among the grammarians.
Just as a king who has previously eaten bad food regains his appetite upon reaching your assembly, O Hari, so too for this one whose food is infinite, his appetite is never lost, even eternally.

O Hari! Previously—that is, before taking refuge at Your feet—the man who was a consumer of *kadaśana* (wretched food), meaning one who ate contemptible food, was *asūpagata*, which means either "approached by the vital breaths" (*asubhiḥ prāṇaiḥ upagataḥ*) or "one by whom the vital breaths have departed" (*asavaḥ upagatāḥ yena*). The sense is that he sustained his life solely through the consumption of bad food. Alternatively, the construction may be joined as *asūpagataḥ kadaśanabhuk*: "one who had approached the soup" (*sūpaṃ gataḥ sūpagataḥ*), forming a compound according to the rule *dvitīyā śrita-*. Thus, he was one who had reached the state of eating even mere soup.

"He does not become such" means he does not become one who eats bad food—that is, a consumer of inferior fare, eating wretched grains like *yava* and *nāla*, or contemptible foods such as sauces and the like. On the other hand, "one who finds your feet" (*tvatpadavit*)—meaning one who reaches or attains your feet, that is, one who has taken refuge at your feet—becomes a king. This refers to one who was previously a consumer of bad food, but subsequently attains the status of royalty through the grace of the Blessed One.

Furthermore, regarding the food: even when the boiled rice (*odana*) is always devoid of soup, it does not become "soup-less" (*luptasūpa*). The term "soup" (*sūpa*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other condiments as well. The meaning is that one becomes an eater of refined food. It should be noted that in the phrase *annantasya*, the optional *parasavarṇa* (assimilation to the following sound) for the *anusvāra*—governed by the rule *vā padāntasya*—is intended to ensure phonetic uniformity (*śabdaikarūpya*) in the alternative meaning.

In this context, the word *kadaśanabhuk*, the word *prāk*, and the word *tvatpadavic* are each joined with the term “is not *supagata*” (*na bhavati asūpagataḥ*). This means that the *sup* suffix has been elided by the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghātsutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Now, the word *atha* here means "moreover" (*kiṃca*). Furthermore, *atha* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*), auspiciousness (*maṅgale*), doubt (*saṃśaye*), commencement (*ārambhe*), introduction (*adhikāre*), and sequence (*anantare*).

Hemacandra states: "The particle *na* is used in subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), in a proposition (*pratijñā*), and also in the senses of 'afterwards' (*paścāt*) and 'entirety' (*sākalya*). A king is one for whom the word *rāja* exists. Regarding this word *rājan*, which has the collection of phonemes *ann* at its end—that is, that which is so described—it is observed that the syllables *su* and *it* are never (*sadā*) elided; "never" means that there is no elision (*upalupta*) of these two phonemes. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the action (*bhāve*) derived from the root *lup*.

The meaning is that there occurs the elision of the *su* suffix by the rule "halṅyābbhyaḥ" and the elision of the *n* by the rule "nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya. Alternatively, the word "atha" connects with the phrase "nasupraluptam," meaning that there is a complete elision (*sākalyena*) of both the *su* suffix and the letter *k*. By the words "asya punaḥ," a distinction from words such as *kadaśanabhuk* is indicated; for while in those cases there is only the elision of the *su* suffix, in this case there is also the elision of the *n*, and this distinction should be understood.

Here, there is a paronomasia (śleṣa) between the word "kadaśanabhuja" and others, which refers to the subject at hand who has taken refuge at the lotus-feet of the Blessed One, and that which is not the subject at hand.
Or rather, O Lord of the Earth, if there is no faith, then worldly existence itself prevails; how could the state of this sinner, having reached such growth, ever become virtuous? 859.

In this verse, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the contextual person who lacks faith in the Blessed One (*bhagavad-apratyayita*) and the non-contextual verbal root *bhū* ending in the suffix *apratyaya*. To explain: O Lord of Ramā (*rameśa*), if there is *apratyaya*—meaning lack of conviction—in You, who are *svayaṃbhu*, that is, devoid of any other cause and being the cause of all (as per the Śruti: "The Lord, the wise one, the conqueror, the self-existent"), then indeed there is only worldly existence (*bhava*).

The sense is that for one who has not entrusted the burden of self-protection—characterized by great confidence in You—the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) is difficult to abandon. Alternatively, regarding the Self-existent Lord (*svayaṃbhu*), there may be "lack of conviction" (*apratyaya*); here the negative particle (*nañ*) denotes opposition, meaning contradictory knowledge, that is, the cognition of manifoldness (*nānātva*). If such [contradictory knowledge] exists, then for him, "existence alone" (*bhava eva*)—meaning the cycle of worldly existence alone—prevails.
As it is said: "What is here is also there; what is there is also here.
He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity."

Thus, according to the method stated in the Śruti, the meaning is that for one who perceives duality in the Supreme Self, there is only the attainment of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), which is designated by the word "death. "That very reality of the Supreme Self which is the Self here in this world, being realized as 'I', is likewise the Self of those situated in other worlds; therefore, there is no difference in the Self"—this is the meaning. "He who perceives duality, as it were, in this Supreme Self, goes from one state of transmigratory existence to another"—thus the meaning of the Śruti has been described in the Upaniṣad-bhāṣya.

How could the state—meaning the condition, stability, nature, or intention—of this person, who possesses sin that is the very root of such contradictory cognition, become "sādhvī" (excellent)? According to Amara, *bhāva* is used in the senses of existence (*sattā*), nature (*svabhāva*), intention (*abhiprāya*), effort (*ceṣṭā*), self (*ātman*), and birth (*janman*). How could his disposition attain an "excellent" increase—that is, an expansion through exclusive absorption in meditation on the Supreme Brahman? Alternatively, the construction may be: "How could his disposition, having attained an excellent increase, [remain as it is]? By "having attained an excellent increase," it is meant that he has become unconditioned (*aparicchinna*).

"Bhāva" means "vibhūti," that is, "eternal manifestation" (nityavibhūti); this is according to the lexicon *Śeṣa*, which states: "The word *bhāva* is used for a wise man and for manifestation. The sense is that such fortune as has been described is difficult to attain.

In the case of the verbal root *bhū* (to exist) on earth, when the suffix *ap*—as prescribed by the rule *“ṝdorap”* (*ap* is the suffix after roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*)—is applied, resulting in the form *bhava*, it comes into being by itself; the meaning is that it is accomplished independently of any other cause. Here, the term *ghañ* refers to this root *bhū* which possesses the marker *gha* (i.e., the root *bhū* with the elided indicatory letter *gh*), meaning it is a root for which the suffix *ghañ* has not [otherwise] been specifically prescribed.

How could it be that *bhāva* attains the correct grammatical increase (*vṛddhi*) prescribed by the rule "aco ñṇiti"—an increase caused by the suffixes *ñi* and *ṅi*—if the suffix *ghañ* were absent? The meaning is: how could such a form be produced in the absence of *ghañ*? Or, for example:

O Kṛṣṇa, if at any time one is established in the final state of the mind, which is predominantly characterized by goodness (*sattva*), then that alone becomes the complete expiation (*prāyaścitta*); of this there is no doubt. (860)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the penance consisting of meditation on the Lord, which is the subject at hand (*prastuta*), and the word "penance" (*prāyaścitta*), which is not the subject at hand (*aprastuta*). To explain: in the phrase "para iha," the division is "paraḥ iha. O Kṛṣṇa! "paraḥ" means He who is distinct from all sentient beings and supreme over all, according to such scriptural statements as, "Higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme."
Govinda, even when remembered but once, quickly burns away the heap of sins accumulated by men over hundreds of years, just as fire consumes a pile of cotton.

In accordance with the manner described above, you—who are renowned for your power to utterly destroy the impurities of all the world—have been established here in this world, in the heart, within the mind. The sense is that this occurs at some time or other upon the conclusion of the body, and not necessarily at all times. The word *prāyaḥ* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "abundance" (*bhūmani*), according to Amara’s lexicon which states, "the indeclinable *prāyaḥ* is used in the sense of abundance. Thus, the meaning is "frequently. If [you] have remained [there], it means if you have been remembered.

That very state of remaining as one is—entirely and in its totality—constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the means of purification. The word *prāyaścitta* denotes, both by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and by etymological derivation (*yoga*), a dharma capable of averting sin. Traditionalists and authors of legal digests (*nibandhana*) state that the word *prāyaścitta* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for a specific occasional rite (*naimittika-karma*) performed for the purpose of destroying sin. The etymological derivation (*yoga*) has been shown by Aṅgiras:
"Prāya" is said to be austerity (*tapas*), and "citta" is called determination (*niścaya*). That which is joined with both austerity and determination is here called *prāyaścitta*.

Thus, the meaning is that *prāyaścitta* is austerity characterized by the performance of vows, accompanied by the conviction that sin is necessarily removed by the observance of a twelve-year penance or similar rites. This is also defined in another *smṛti*:
"Prāya is said to be sin; *citta* is its purification. There is no doubt, there is no uncertainty here.
Those who know [the law] declare that for great sins the penances are great, and for small sins they are small.
O Maitreya, Svāyambhuva and the other Manus sang these expiations.
Of all the various atonements consisting essentially of asceticism and ritual action,
the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme among them all.

The sense is that, according to the procedure thus described, one should not doubt that this alone constitutes the complete expiation (*akhilaprāyaścitta*). It should be understood that the address "O Kṛṣṇa" was employed in the root verse precisely to remind one of this authoritative source.

"In one alternative" (*pakṣe*) means when there is a desire to express a compound (*samāsa*). "Generally" (*prāyaḥ*): this word *prāya-* ends in -a. In this alternative, the division of the words is *pare iha* instead of *paraih*. "In *citte*" means when the word *citta-* follows; that is, when it exists in the subsequent position. "In *avasitau*" means at the end, in the pause, or at the conclusion. "In one instance" (*ekadā*): the division of the words is *āsthitaḥ*.

If the entire compound is analyzed, it would likely result in only two words, *cittam* and *iti*, which together would constitute *prāyaścitta*. The meaning is that the term *prāyaścitta* is thus established. This is because, according to the rule *prāyasya citticittayoḥ*, the augment *suṭ* is prescribed for the word *citta* when it follows the word *prāya*. Although the augment *suṭ* is indeed an initial element of the word *citta*, this is in accordance with the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "An element marked with *ṭ* or *k* is placed at the beginning or end [of the word to which it is attached]."

Nevertheless, since the word *prāya* is not heard at the end [of the compound], it was stated that the word *prāya* assumes *satva* (the substitution of *s*) in the final position. The change of the *s* in *āgama* to *ś* occurs by virtue of the rule for *ścutva*. However, in reality, because the Bhāṣya reads "or there is the augment *suṭ* after *prāya* when *citti* or *citta* follows," the vowel *a*, which constitutes the final member of the word *prāya*, undergoes the *askāra* (the substitution of *ṣ*); thus, the word *prāya* itself assumes *satva* in the final position, and the aforementioned difficulty need not be followed.

Taking the word *askāra* as the illustrative example (*pratīka*), Kaiyaṭa has explained: "In place of this [short vowel], there is *askāra*; because it belongs to the *śakandhu*-class, there is a substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). The intended meaning of Kaiyaṭa’s text is as follows: *askāraḥ* refers to the making of the letter *a*—that is, the insertion of the short vowel *a*—in place of the final short *a* of the word *prāya*. Having raised the objection that a long vowel resulting from the coalescence of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) might occur in the expression *a askāraḥ*, he states that because it belongs to the *śakandhu*-class, there is a substitution of the subsequent form.
Just as one who,
having attained a higher state of mind, desires even more to perform atonement, generally at the end he must become united with that which was previously his own end.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the word *citta*, which is the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) as the consciousness of one desiring to attain the Blessed One, and the word *cit*, which is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*). The division is *cit taṃ*. He who is *cit*—that is, consciousness—is well known as the one who has made the vow to shake off all the impurities of those who have come for refuge, through such words as: "I shall liberate you from all evils."

Having approached and taken refuge in the Supreme Self—who is heard of as the goal to be attained by the knower of Brahman in the text, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—he desires to become a performer of atonement more intensely, that is, he wishes to be pre-eminently endowed with atonement. The sense is that this is because taking refuge is declared to be an incomparable atonement in the verse: "Those who know the hearts of the foremost among the Raghus and Yadus know that [refuge] to be the peerless atonement for the beginningless and boundless ocean of sin."

"Formerly," at the beginning; "with one whose end is auspicious" means with one whose conclusion or resolve is excellent—that is, with one possessing firm determination. The sense is that he possesses great confidence which cannot be shaken even by those headed by Bṛhaspati. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *anta* (end) is not feminine; it denotes certainty, destruction, essential nature, the front, proximity, or the interior. By that conscious being, "in the end"—that is, at the conclusion of the body—being "united" (*sayujā*), meaning endowed with qualities such as being the refuge, being equal [to Him], and having sin destroyed. The word *yuk* refers to qualities, as it is derived from the root *yuj* ("to be joined").

For a quality is connected to its substratum (dharmin). Vyāsārya states in the Mahāsiddhānta that [the soul] is "associated" because it possesses similar qualities. Alternatively, since there is a single object of enjoyment in the form of Brahman with its attributes (saprakāraka), the soul is "associated" (sayuk) with Brahman by virtue of being the enjoyer; thus it must generally be understood as such. The sense is that one should not doubt this here; the meaning of the Śruti passage, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," should be reflected upon in this context.

If it is argued that, in this case, the simultaneous use of the terms *sāyujya* and *sārṣṭitā* in such scriptural passages as “the union (*sāyujya*) and equality in power (*sārṣṭitā*) with these very deities” would be inappropriate—since both terms have the same meaning, for *ārṣṭi* (or *sārṣṭi*) means eating, which is to say enjoyment—it is replied as follows: *Sāyujya* refers to the absence of any distinction between the two regarding the object to be enjoyed. *Sārṣṭitā*, however, is the absence of any gradation (superiority or inferiority) in that enjoyment. As was stated by the venerable Ācāryas in the section on the experience of the full Brahman: “In this state, *sāyujya* is the non-distinction between the two concerning the object to be enjoyed.”
"Sārṣṭitā is the state therein of enjoyment devoid of gradation.

Elsewhere, the word *prāya*—having reached (*prapadya*) or attained (*prāpya*) the mind (*citta*) existing in the subsequent [state] as the word *citta*—desires more intensely to become the word *prāyaścitta* in its entirety; that is, it desires more intensely to be the term *prāyaścitta*. [In the compound], the word ending in the suffix *su* (the particle *su*) indicates the word *su* [as a whole]; this means that in the state of grammatical analysis (*vigraha*), it is [a word] heard with a suffix ending in *su*.

Therefore, by the word *prāya*, it must generally be [the form] ending in *sa* (i.e., *prāyas*), joined with a following consonant (*sayuj*), and not the indeclinable *prāyaḥ*. This is because, according to the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*, there is an elision of case-endings (*sup*) after an indeclinable; thus, an indeclinable always lacks an audible case-suffix. Furthermore, since it already ends in *s* by its very nature, it would be unnecessary to specifically enjoin that it "ends in *sa* joined [with a consonant]. For it is precisely for the word *prāya* that the substitution of *as* is prescribed by the rule *prāyasya citticittayoḥ*.

It should be understood that even though the word *svataḥ* is already established as ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the qualification *svantena* (by that which ends in a suffix) is stated solely to illuminate the specific meaning already mentioned. Everything else has been explained in the immediately preceding example. Or, for instance: "He who is the single instruction for those who know the six categories (*satpada*), which [instruction] pertains to both what precedes and what follows—by him, even that which was unheard becomes clearly heard."

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the ruler of all who is the subject (*prakṛta*), and the grammatical substitute (*ādeśa*) which is not the subject (*aprakṛta*). To explain: that aforementioned *ādeśa*, which is the cause of the state of "having heard what was not heard," is to be known (*jñeya*)—that is, capable of being known—by those who know the Reality (*satpadavidām*), such as those who have heard the statement "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedam*). [The word] *pada* [is used here]; according to Amara, "pada" means determination, protection, place, mark, foot, and object. This is because the words *ādeśa* and *sat* share a single meaning.

By the use of the verbal root *jñā* in the word *jñeya*, the phrase “he understood that” (*taddhāsya vijijñau*), which occurs at the conclusion of the Sadvidyā, is recalled; for this verse serves to establish the meaning contained within the Sadvidyā. Alternatively, it refers to those who find (*vindanti*)—that is, reach—the *pada*, meaning the station or the foot, of the *sat* (the Real), namely the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavidām*). [The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *vid*. The meaning is: specifically for those who possess the practice of approaching a teacher who knows Brahman. This follows the maxim: “Every sentence implies a restriction.”

The meaning is that this aforementioned instruction is to be understood as intended for those who have realized the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), and not for the arrogant, stubborn ones who merely pride themselves on being learned in the scriptures (*anūcāna*) while possessing only lower knowledge. This refers to Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, who, having resided in a teacher’s house for twelve years and mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga-veda*), became conceited, thinking himself highly esteemed and learned; yet he remained stubborn when he approached his own father, Uddālaka—the foremost among the knowers of Brahman—who said to him: "My dear boy, since you are so highly esteemed, proud of your learning, and stubborn, did you perhaps ask for that instruction?"

It should be understood that this was said with the following intention: when asked, "By what does the unheard become heard?", [Sanatkumāra], his mental pride dissolved by not knowing the answer, came into the presence of [Nārada] and thereby learned such an instruction, and not otherwise. He specifies that very instruction with the words "He becomes," and so forth: he who is the one, non-dual *ādeśa*—whereby something is pointed out (*ādiśyate 'nena*)—of both the prior and the subsequent; that is, of the prior [creator] such as the four-faced Brahmā, and of the subsequent [beings] such as ourselves, he is the *ādeṣṭṛ*, the director or ruler.

"O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable (akṣara), the sun and the moon stand held apart. He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all. There is one Ruler; there is no second Ruler. Viṣṇu is the Ruler of the entire universe, the Controller of all"—from such scriptural authorities as these. [The word *praśāsana* is derived] from the root *diś* preceded by the prefix *pra-*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), according to the grammatical rule: "The suffix *ghañ* is used after roots other than those meaning 'to do' when denoting an agent or an instrument, provided it forms a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*)."

Nor should one suspect a contradiction with the intended meaning—namely, that [the scripture] is the agent (*kartṛ*) regarding the place [of instruction]. For, according to the principle stated by the grammarians, "the application of *kārakas* depends upon intention" (*vivakṣātaḥ kārakāṇāṃ pravṛttiḥ*), it is logical to employ such a usage by intending the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) in the agent itself, independently of any other instrument. He specifies the very place [of instruction] by the word "by which" (*yena*). That is to say, "by which [it is] heard. Even that which was not heard becomes clearly heard, as if it were entirely heard.

This is an elliptical expression for the idea that "by what is heard, thought, and known, the unheard, unthought, and unknown becomes heard, thought, and known. Here, the entire meaning of the passage from the *Sadvidyā*—namely, "But did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard"—is recognized and reaffirmed.

In this context, regarding the statement “by which the unheard becomes heard,” the meaning of the phrase “by which [it] is heard” and so forth has been described in accordance with the passages from the *Muṇḍaka* and *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads*: “O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? and “Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this becomes known. By the expression “by which the unheard becomes heard,” its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is stated, and by the word “instruction” (*ādeśa*), which signifies the role of the ruler (*praśāsitṛ*), its nature as the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*) is expressed.

Thus, the established meaning is that the material cause (*upādāna*), being identical with the Self, is the object known through true knowledge (*vidyā*). Everything else is easy for those learned in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*; therefore, enough of this elaboration.

In the view of those who know the six cases (*satpada*)—that is, those who are learned in the science of correct grammar—that [substitute] is to be understood as the single substitute for both the preceding and the following elements, as prescribed by the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "one [element replaces] both the preceding and the following" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*). There exist single substitutes such as *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *savarṇadīrgha*, as in the rules "guṇa is substituted for *a* and *eC*" (*ādguṇaḥ*), "vṛddhi is substituted for *a* and *eC*" (*vṛddhireci*), and "a long vowel is substituted for *aK* followed by a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*).

By means of such a substitution (*ādeśa*) as has been described, even that which was previously unheard—that is, even that which had not been heard prior to the substitution during the state of non-continuous utterance (*asaṃhitā*)—such as the phonemes *o*, *au*, *ā*, and so forth, becomes clearly heard when continuous utterance (*saṃhitā*) is intended; it becomes audible once the substitution has taken effect. For example, when *upendra* is established, the phoneme *e* is unheard prior to the prescription of the substitution of *guṇa*, but it is heard immediately after that substitution is prescribed.

And just as in the case of *kṛṣṇa* + *ekatvam*, where the vowel *ai* is not heard when [the forms] stand as such, but is heard after the substitution of the *vṛddhi* has been prescribed; and just as in this very verse, where the vowel *ā* is not heard in the state [of the form] *yena aśrutam*, but is heard after the prescription of the substitute—so too should it be understood in other cases.
Or, for example:

"In this *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the subsequent member begins with a vowel other than 'a', [the word] *sadā* becomes *kadā* by rule; and *koḥ* becomes *kad* when followed by *adhipatiḥ* in the sense of place. (863)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the subject at hand, the Supreme Person Śrīnivāsa, and the subject not at hand, the person who is the lord of goats. To explain: in the phrase "ajādau adhipatau," [it refers to] the Lord who is the cause even before Brahmā—the Creator, renowned as "aja" (the unborn)—the sovereign of all worlds without qualification, according to such scriptural passages as "He is the Lord of beings.

Alternatively, in the phrase "ajādau adhipatau," the locative case in "ajādau" is used because of its connection with the word "adhipati" (lord), following the rule "svāmīśvarādhipati... [Pāṇini 1.4.55], meaning the Lord of the four-faced one and others. He is both that [Lord] and a Person; thus, he is the "tatpuruṣa" (that-person).

In Him—Śrīnivāsa, who is renowned as having His abode in the supreme ether according to the scripture, "He who is the overseer in the supreme ether," and who is heard of in scripture as having the entire universe as His body according to the text, "The Person alone is all this"—in Him, here in this form of Śeṣācala, the supreme station, [the Lord] dwells eternally and not merely occasionally; He is indeed ever-present (sat-eva), for the earth is called *ku* in the Amarakośa: "Gotrā, *ku*, and Pṛthivī [are synonyms for earth]."

The meaning is as follows: in this land, here and there, a "bad lord" (kad-adhipati)—a contemptible ruler who considers himself a lord due to possessing a sovereignty that is temporary and dependent—is seen; such is the sense of the censure. But when Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of all lords and the Ruler of all, shines with resplendent glory upon the Śeṣādri mountain, no one on earth who possesses only limited power shall ever shine by way of being a ruler. This is the intended meaning.

The word "only" (eva) here connects with "elsewhere than in a *tatpuruṣa*. The sense is that [the substitution occurs] only when intended within a *tatpuruṣa* compound, and not in a *bahuvrīhi*. Therefore, it should be understood that the substitution of *kad-* which will be mentioned later does not occur in examples such as *kūṣṭro rājā*. [The term] "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau*) means "beginning with a vowel-sound" (*ajvarṇādau*), referring to the word *adhipati*. The qualification "beginning with a vowel" is intended merely to state the actual nature of the thing, since the fact that the word *adhipati* begins with a vowel is self-evident.

When there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), by means of the rule "koḥ kattatpuruṣe’ci" (Pāṇini 7.2.102), which is recognized through the words "anuśāsana," "koḥ," "kat," and so forth, the word *ku* is replaced by *kad*. The meaning is that because the subsequent member implies the preceding member, it refers to that which has become the prior member. When the substitute *kad* occurs—that is, when the substitute *kad* is applied—the meaning is "always" or "perpetually. The sense is that the form *kadadhipatiḥ* would thus be produced; for by the aforementioned rule, the substitution of *kad* is prescribed as being obligatory (*nitya*).

Or rather, just as a single offspring-designation would necessarily arise for a lineage, why would it not likewise arise for Śauri? Otherwise, an undesirable succession of other designations would result at that time. (864)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the meditation on the Blessed One, which is the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), and the patronymic suffix (*gotrāpatyapratyaya*), which is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*). To explain: *gotraḥ* means "one who protects cows," i.e., a cowherd (*gopāla*), according to the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*. In that Lord Vāsudeva, the descendant of Śūra (*śauri*), [meditation] was "fixed" (*āpatya*)—that is, held with respect; the word *yadā* is to be supplied. From the root *pat* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *lyap* is applied after the gerundive suffix *ktvā*. By this rule, a single suffix was made into an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness.

At that time, no undesirable succession of heterogeneous cognitions—which are causes of fear and bring about loss—would arise. For the non-interruption of the stream of memory consists precisely in its being uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions. By the term "undesirable," the meaning of the Śruti passage is indicated: "For when he perceives even the slightest difference in this [Brahman], then fear comes upon him; it is indeed from that [perception of difference] that fear arises for the one who knows but does not contemplate [the unity]."

For this is its meaning: this seeker of liberation (*upāsaka*) experiences fear whenever he creates even a slight interval (*antara*), that is, a break, in his meditation upon this Supreme Self. For the wise one who is steadfast in the worship of Brahman, who does not perform uninterrupted contemplation due to a longing for objects other than That, that very lack of contemplation is fear; indeed, there is no other fear greater than that. And it has been said by the Great Sages: "If Vāsudeva is not meditated upon for even a moment or an instant, that is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is a calamity."

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": Vyāsārya explains that "loss" (hāni) is the loss of what is desired; "defect" (chidra) is the occurrence of the undesired; "error" (bhrānti) is the resulting lapse of the mind; and "distortion" (vikriyā) is the involuntary, improper functioning of the limbs caused by that [lapse].

In the case of a *gotra*—where, according to the rule "the offspring from the grandson onwards is the *gotra*," the sense intended is that of an offspring (*apatya*) in the form of a *gotra*—there is a restriction by the sūtra "only one [suffix] in a *gotra*" (*eko gotre*). This means that if a single *apatya*-suffix (a suffix prescribed for the meaning of offspring) has been applied, then, by that restriction, only one such suffix shall occur in the *gotra*. If [it] has been applied—if indeed it has been applied—then, in the case of the word *śauri* (referring to Śauri), this serves as an illustration for words such as *aupagava* and others.

An undesirable succession of suffixes would not arise. The point is this: in the sense of "the descendant of Śūra’s lineage," when the suffix *iñ*—which is an exception to the *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaśca* and is itself an exception to the *aṇ* prescribed by *bāhvādibhyaśca*—is applied to the word *śūra*, there is no further production of an undesirable sequence of suffixes such as *aṇ* (by the rule *tasyāpatyam*) followed again by *iñ* (by the rule *tasyāpatyam*).

In this way, from *Upagu*—to denote a descendant in the lineage (*gotra*)—the suffix *aṇ* yields *Aupagava*; from that, by the rule *“ata iñ”* (P. 4.1.95), the suffix *iñ* yields *Aupagavi*; and from that, by the rule *“yañiñośca”* (P. 4.1.101), the suffix *phak* yields *Aupagavāyana*. Thus, a succession of undesired suffixes would not arise, because of the restriction “*eko gotre*” (P. 4.1.93).
Here, in the context of the lineage, there is a succession of suffixes numbering one less than itself;
or else, the production of undesired forms would result from [suffixes] numbering two less than itself.
"Offspring should belong to the father alone, and from him [the right] extends even to his ancestors"—
with this and the subsequent sūtra, these two are intended to refute that difference of opinion.
Thus the meaning of the verse is to be reflected upon; here we pause for fear of prolixity.

Just as one who is devoted to the worship of the gods wipes away every blemish from the sacrificial vessel with a purifier held in his own hand, so too is He here intent solely upon bestowing grace upon those who seek it.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the person under discussion—a man devoted to the mantras of the Lord such as Varāha and Nṛsiṃha, mentioned in the context of the *apāmārjana* rite—and another person not under discussion, namely a frequent sacrificer (*yāyajūka*). To explain: in this world, that man who is habituated to the worship of the God—the Lord—through adoration consisting of recitation, praise, and so forth; who is honored by means of speech, according to the saying, "The God is worshipped by the sacrifice of speech";
and who, with devotion, always worships the Lotus-eyed One with hymns.

Because [the text] states that recitation, praise, and so forth constitute forms of worship through such passages as these; he is described as one whose nature or disposition (*śīla*) is the worship of the gods (*devejyā*). According to the *Ratnamālā*, "sacrifice" (*ijyā*) is feminine and refers to sacrifice, giving, worship, and union. He [should perform this] with a *pavitra*—that is, a blade of *kuśa* grass, the singular being used for the species—as it is said: "One who performs the *dālbhya-śānti* should purify all his limbs with the tips of *kuśa* grass. Alternatively, according to the manner stated in: "Having placed in his hand water brought from all sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), which was offered by the Sage," he [purifies himself] with water consecrated by mantras held in his own hand.
The word *pavitra* refers to curd, a water-pot, cow-dung, water, *kuśa* grass, copper, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), and mantras; it is used in the sense of gold.
In three genders, it means "pure," and in the masculine, it denotes Śiva and fire.
Thus ends the *Ratnamālā*. "Akhila" means entire or whole. "Graha" refers to specific types of spirits such as *ḍākinīs* and *pūtanās*;
it is used in the senses of seizing, favoring, persistence, and grasping.
It also applies to the sun and other planets, to *pūtanās* and similar beings, and to Rāhu during eclipses.
Thus says the Medinī; "he sweeps" means, that is to say, he casts it away.
May Narasiṃha, who always has a terrifying face and a great roar,
and who is the benefactor of the world, utterly destroy all the planetary spirits without exception.
May there be peace, may there be auspiciousness, and may whatever is unpleasant perish;
for I have performed this purification with kusha grass arising from the body of Vāsudeva.

The sense is that, by means of the sprinkling with kuśa-water consecrated by great mantras such as those of Vārāha and Nārasiṃha—according to the sequence stated in the chapter on *apāmārjana* (the ritual of cleansing)—one drives away all planetary influences (*graha*). He states the reason for this: "because of the intended [favor]," etc. For (*hi*), since the word "this person" (*asau*) is also to be supplied here, it refers to that man who is devoted to the worship of the gods and who is intent upon bestowing the desired favor; that is to say, toward those intended recipients, namely those who are obedient to his commands and subject to his injunctions.

For the synonyms for "obedient" (*vidheya*) are recited as: "one who accepts discipline, one who stands by one's word, and one who is compliant. Indeed, no one has any desire to speak to people toward whom they feel no affection. "Intent upon that favor" means single-mindedly focused; as Amara states: "‘Ekatanu’ means having no other activity, and it is also synonymous with ‘ekāgra’ and ‘ekāyana’. The sense is that the very act of favoring obedient people is, according to the aforementioned reasoning, the cause for warding off all their misfortunes, such as being seized [by spirits]. By this [verse], it is implied: "Those men who have not propitiated Govinda are partakers of suffering;
what ought to be done for those tormented by suffering by the compassionate?"
Thus, that compassion which was stated as the reason for performing the *apāmārjana* rite of pacification (*śānti*) in response to the question regarding the *apāmārjana* has been summarized here.

In this context, O Lord! that person who is devoted to sacrifice (*ijyāśīla*), a frequent performer of sacrifices (*yāyajūka*), cleanses (*saṃmārṣṭi*)—that is, prepares through the act of cleansing—the entire *graha*, meaning all the specific vessels used for the oblation (*homasādhana*). Now, one might ask: although the singular number is heard in the scriptural statement "he cleanses the *graha*," how can it be said that he cleanses "all the *grahas*"? To this, he says "here," and so forth.

The word division is: *vivakṣitā nu grahaikatā no hi*. For (*hi*), because in this sentence, "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatā*)—that is, the oneness of the cup, the number residing in the cup—is not intended to be significant (*no vivakṣitā*). The meaning is that it is not intended. Regarding the particle *nu*, the *Viśva* lexicon states: "*Nu* may occur in conciliation, in a question, in the sense of an alternative, and also in the past or in conciliation. Since singularity is not intended to be significant, the point stated in the section concerning cleansing (*saṃmārgādhikaraṇa*)—"he cleanses all the cups"—should be applied here.

This principle of *saṃmārga* (cleansing) was deliberated upon in the third chapter of the Jaiminīya-darśana (Mīmāṃsā). To illustrate: in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture, "One cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the cleansing to be performed on one cup, or on all of them? For that purpose, the inquiry is whether the number inherent in the object (*uddeśya*) is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*) or not.

Just as in the case of "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), where the number inherent in the object is intended to be significant by the force of the scriptural mention of singularity, so too here, the number inherent in the object ought to be intended to be significant.

Therefore, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) applies to only one cup, [the siddhāntin replies]: since the connection of the animal with the sacrifice is understood by this very statement, and because the animal is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the sacrifice, there is no repetition of the principal (*pradhāna*) for every instance of the subordinate. Consequently, when there arises an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "by how many animals," the number one is connected as the delimiting factor. Thus, it is logical that the number residing in the thing to be enjoined (*upādeya*) is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*).

However, since the connection of the *grahas* with the sacrifice is understood through another statement, and since in the statement regarding the cleansing (*saṃmārga*), the *graha* is understood to be the primary object (*pradhāna*) relative to the cleansing by virtue of the direct mention of the accusative case, the quality of cleansing must be repeated for each primary object. Consequently, because no expectancy arises as to how many *grahas* are to be cleansed, the number residing in the *grahas* as the objects of reference is not intended to be significant. Therefore, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that all *grahas* are to be cleansed. As it has been said:

If indeed, at the conclusion of the syllable "na," there occurs the word *yadupati-mahilā* (the consort of the Lord of the Yadus), and if the syllable *a* follows it, then he would be one who has attained [the goal]; what doubt can there be in this matter? (866)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the word *lakṣmī* and the lotus-feet (*padāravinda*), as well as between the word *prapanna* and the act of seeking refuge. For instance: "O beloved of the Lord who says, 'Come to me alone for refuge,' etc.! O consort of the Lord of the Yadus!"—by this, her possession of those same attributes is illuminated. Indeed, it is said: "She is eternally one whose nature conforms to His nature. [In the compound] *bhavatprapadi*, the form *prapadi* refers to the tip of Your foot (*pādāgre*); the substitution of the masculine form occurs according to the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre*. Amara states: "The tip of the foot is called *prapada*."

*Niṣṭhātaḥ*: this is the suffix *tasi* used in all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). It means "by being solely intent upon that," or "by having the sole vow of taking refuge in that. Regarding the word *niṣṭhā*, the *Ratnamālā* states: "But *niṣṭhā* [is used] in the sense of destruction, accomplishment, end, intentness, and entreaty. Hemacandra states: "*Niṣṭhā* [is used] in the sense of excellence, determination, affliction, accomplishment, end, completion, entreaty, and vow. [The term] *anaḥ* refers to one who breathes, i.e., a living being; from the root *ana* (to breathe) with the suffix *ac* according to the *pacādi* class.

The meaning is: "He who exclusively upholds the state of being a sole refuge-seeker at Your feet," according to the manner expressed in such passages as, "Just as the *cātaka* bird has surrendered [to the cloud], uphold the dharma of the *cātaka* who is devoted solely to the cloud-bearer that holds the auspicious rain. Alternatively, it means "by means of a petition" (*niṣṭhātaḥ prārthanayā*). The treasury [of definitions] has been stated. The meaning is: "He who has been revived by the five ancillaries (*aṅga*) beginning with favor (*anukūlya*), which are characterized by petition (*prārthanā*)."

If it occurs, then this person who has surrendered (*prapanna*) and is established in independent surrender (*svatantra-prapatti*) "cuts" (*dyati*)—that is, severs—future existence (*bhava*), or birth, or entry into a womb, after the act of surrender; thus he is *bhavadaḥ*. [The root] *dā* [is used here] in the sense of "severing" (*avakhaṇḍane*). Because the vowel *a* is changed to *ā* by the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto'nupasarge*.

Alternatively, [the term] *bhavadaḥ* means "that which bestows (*dāti*) what exists (*bhavam*) before (*agre*). From the root *daip*, meaning "to purify" (*śodhane*), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the previously mentioned method; thus, the meaning is that it purifies rebirth and wipes away its connection. This is because the root *śodhayati* is seen used in the sense of "washing" (cleansing) in such passages as "one whose self is purified of all sins. The sense is that since the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) occurs precisely at the end of that body, there is no possibility for the unimpeded recurrence of rebirth.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [he] becomes foremost," it is indicated that this person, who is steadfast in independent *prapatti*, experiences only that *prārabdha* (commenced karma) which was accepted according to the principle stated as "having fully enjoyed the remainder of the portion of karma that has commenced," until the end of that body; and by the process described as "having his other karmas exhausted," he shakes off the connection with another body for the experience of the partial fruits of *prārabdha* that were not accepted.

By the statement, “‘Exhausting [karma] through renunciation (nyāsa), we do not accept the interruption of what has already begun’,” it is indicated that one who is devoted to *aṅga-prapatti* does not experience subsequent bodies after the commencement of knowledge for the sake of fully experiencing the fruits of commenced karma (*prārabdha-karma*), as is the case with one who is established in [the primary form of] *prapatti*. Furthermore, regarding the word *bhavada* (“becoming”), if the intended meaning is “becoming immediately after the moment of *prapatti*,” then the distinction should be understood: in the former sense (of immediate succession), he is “distressed” (*ārta*) once having surrendered; in the initial sense (of the primary meaning), he is “haughty” (*dṛpta*).

In the verse, "abhavat prapadī yadupatimahile," the word division is *abhavat* (it became). The word *bhavati* is a vocative form. [The commentary asks: "O Bhavati! O venerable one! O Queen of the Yadu-lord! [She was] *prapadī*.
