This is derived from the verbal root *pad* preceded by the prefix *pra*, with the suffix *niṣṭhā*; by the grammatical rule "the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*," the suffix *kta* is applied. Of that [suffix], namely the letter *t* belonging to the suffix *kta*—this word ends in a consonant (*hal*).

[The substitution of] *na* occurs for the preceding dental *d*, both with respect to the suffix *kta* and the initial [root-final] *d*. This [word] also ends in a consonant (*halanta*). If the substitute *na* had occurred, then this word would have resulted as *prapanna*; that is, it would have been established as *prapanna* because of the grammatical rule: “*niṣṭhā-ta* is replaced by *na* after *ra* and *da*, and the *da* preceding them is also replaced,” since there is an injunction for the replacement of the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix and the *d* preceding it by *na* when following *r* or *d*. In this matter, what doubt could there be? The meaning is: there is no uncertainty whatsoever.
Or, for example:

"Let him instruct [others] to praise Hari; the elision of *tu* is never seen here. If he were to say "censure" (*nindā*) instead, then the elision of *hi* would indeed occur first. (667) In this verse, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the two finite verbal forms *stautu* and *ninda*, which are not the primary subjects but are associated with the two primary subjects—the instruction regarding praise and censure directed toward the Lord—which yield good and bad results respectively. To explain: "Let him instruct people to praise Hari"—this is the implied sense.

In this person who acts as a teacher, no loss or diminution of spiritual welfare is ever seen; indeed, it is never seen at all. For one who impels the ignorant toward the utterances of the Blessed One, there is never any loss whatsoever. On the contrary, there is only an abundance of spiritual welfare. Indeed, the fruit of one who gives knowledge and instruction in Dharma to the ignorant is not equalled by even the gift of the entire earth.

This is because of such statements. The word "he" (*janā*) is to be supplied as the object of the verb of censure. "You" refers to the one censuring the Blessed One; *ninda* is the second person singular present indicative of the root *nind*. If one should speak thus, then from this very statement that incites censure, "loss" (*lopaḥ*), meaning ruin, will surely occur "before" (*purā*). This means it occurs immediately, characterized by being directly subsequent. According to Amarasimha, "in the sense of 'imminent,' [the word] *purā* is used. In this sense, there is also the usage: "Go quickly, before the god rains."
The sense is that for one who initiates blame against the Blessed One, the loss of all excellence occurs immediately.
O Great King, we do not know who that person might be— whether it be one who reviles the Beloved of Kamalā or one who causes others to revile him— for which hell he would fall.
Because of this statement.

On one view, let him instruct [the pupil] by saying, "Praise Hari. In this word *stautu*, the elision of the letter *t* (i.e., the elision of the *tu*-portion) is not observed; the meaning is that it is indeed heard, because there is no grammatical rule (*śāstra*) prescribing such an elision. If he should say, "Censure," then in this word *ninda*, the elision of the suffix *hi*—prescribed by the rule *ato heḥ*—occurs "previously" (*purā*), meaning it certainly took place. The use of the present tense (*laṭ*) with the word *purā* refers to the past, according to the rule *puri luṅ cāsme*.

Regarding the substitution of *hi* for the singular imperative suffix *sip* by the rule "serhyapicca," there is the instruction that *hi* following an *at* vowel is elided by the rule "ato heḥ. The point is that the form *ninda* is heard immediately after the elision of *hi*.
Or as in [the verse]:

"If the nectar of the divine story of the Best of Raghus has become a *liḍ* (imperative) on earth, then this person has indeed become such that he is the first and the highest; here, he is certainly not 'middle' (*madhyama*). (868)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the primary subject, a man who tastes the nectar of the Lord’s stories, and the non-primary subject, the verbal root *bhū* (to be/exist), which takes the suffix *liṭ*. For instance: he who licks (*liḍ*) the nectar of the divine stories of the best of the Raghus upon the earth (*bhuvi*) is "one who licks the nectar of the divine stories of the best of the Raghus" (*raghuvaradivyakathāmṛtaliṭ*), formed by adding the suffix *kvip* to the root *lih*.

If this man "was" (*abhūt*), he indeed came into being; he attained existence (*sattā*). For the verbal root *bhū* signifies "existence," as is well known from such examples as "the wise Lakṣmaṇa, deeply devoted [to his brother], will not cease to exist. Existence (*sattā*) is the attainment of one's own self-nature (*ātmalābha*). The sense is that his attainment of existence occurs only through tasting the nectar of the divine narrative of the Blessed One, and not otherwise. The use of the past tense (*parokṣabhūta*) is intended to highlight that such a person is difficult to find in the present day. He further qualifies him with the word "one" (*eka*).

The word "this" (ayam) is supplied [from the previous verse]. This one person—indeed, this singular male—is, by the maxim that "every sentence implies restriction," the supreme (*uttama*) in this world; the word *tathā* here signifies "inexpressible" (*anirvacanīya*), as seen in such usages as "having gone thus" (*tathā gatāṃ tām*). For this very reason, he is the first (*prathama*), the leader of all, and not at all middling (*madhyama*); the sense is: how could such a one be middling?

O best of the Raghus, addressed as such because you possess the divine nectar of stories! If the *liṭ*—prescribed by the rule "the *liṭ* [is used] for the remote past" (*parokṣe liṭ*)—occurred for the root *bhū* on earth, then this root *bhū* has indeed become (*babhūvaiva*). The word *abhūt* is supplied [from the context]. The meaning is that it resulted precisely in the form *babhūva*. The use of the past tense (*bhūta-nirdeśa*) is intended to highlight the indisputable nature of the formation of the aforementioned form.

To address the question of what form the root *bhū* would take even when the *liṭ* [perfect tense] suffix is applied, he says "eka" and so forth. Here, in this context of the root *bhū*, the word "this" (*ayam*) is to be supplied. The meaning is that "this" *liṭ* is the first person singular—the singular number indicator for the first person. This is because the form "babhūva" is derived from the *liṭ* of the root *bhū* by applying the substitution of *ṇal* for the *tip* suffix according to the rule "parasmaipadānāṃ ṇal," and thus this is the very form of the first person singular of the *liṭ*.

It is not only this much; likewise, it becomes the *uttama* (first person) indicative of oneness (*ekatvabodhaka*), just like that [the third person], because even when *mip* is replaced by *ṇal*, the form is produced as *babhūva*. It does not become the *madhyama* (second person); for the singular of the second person does not occur there, since the form would be *babhūvitha* and not *babhūva*.
Just as renunciation, O Soul of All, bestows the same fruit upon all castes—whether born in the inverse order or the natural order—it indeed constitutes the ultimate goal for each. (869)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the subject at hand, "entrusting one's burden" (*bhāranyāsa*) to the Lord, and the non-contextual term "renunciation" (*sannyāsa*). For instance: "O Soul of All! O Blessed One! In You, the Blessed One, resides *sannyāsa*—that is, taking refuge (*prapadana*), or *nyāsa*, which is a synonym for depositing [one's burden], performed with the five limbs.
*Sannyāsa* is said to be renunciation (*tyāga*), and it is also called seeking refuge (*śaraṇāgati*)."

Thus, because the word *sannyāsa* is stated to be a synonym for *prapatti*: "of those established in themselves" (*svaniṣṭhānām*) means those whose steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) is in the Self; that is to say, those who possess exclusive devotion to surrender (*prapadana*). "Of all castes" (*sarveṣāṃ varṇānām*) means those born of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. Whether they are "born in the natural order" (*anulomānām*, i.e., born of women of the same or higher caste) or "born in the inverse order" (*pratilomānām*, i.e., born of women of a lower caste)—in both cases, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *ac-pratyanvava-pūrvāt-sāmalomnaḥ*.

The elision of the suffixal *ṭi* is by the rule *nastaddhite*. Those born from a man of superior caste (*varṇa*) and a woman of inferior caste are *anuloma*-born. Those born from a man of inferior caste and a woman of superior caste are *pratiloma*-born. Thus it is recorded by Yājñavalkya: "From a Brāhmaṇa, a *mūrdhāvasikta* is indeed born on a Kṣatriya woman; on a Vaiśya woman, an *ambaṣṭha*; and on a Śūdra woman, a *niṣāda* or also a *pāraśava*."
From a Kṣatriya man, a Vaiśya woman bears a Māhiṣya son, and a Śūdra woman bears an Ugra son;
from a Vaiśya man, a Śūdra woman bears a Karaṇa son—this is the rule prescribed for women married to men of different castes.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born a Sūta; from a Vaiśya father, a Vaidehaka is recorded;
but from a Śūdra father, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all ritual duties.
A Vaiśya woman bore a Māgadha to a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra woman bore a Kṣattṛ;
furthermore, a Vaiśya woman gave birth to an Āyogava son from a Śūdra.
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
these, born from inverse and natural orders, are to be known as both "untrue" and "true."

Thus, the meaning is that those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) are to be known as non-existent, while those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) are existent. "Bestowing the same goal" means granting the identical human aims; that is to say, it bestows all kinds of desired human aims without depending on the distinctions of the classes (*varṇa*), stages of life (*āśrama*), and so forth.
The qualification for *prapatti* belongs to all castes who possess the quality of *sāttvika* and so forth, even those who lack other means and yet desire what is to be attained;
for that [prapatti] bestows the fruit of all desires upon everyone everywhere.

Thus, because it has been stated that taking refuge in the Blessed One is accessible to all and bestows all human goals, it is precisely with this intention that the Blessed One is addressed in the root text as "O Soul of All."

In this context, the term "sannyāsa" refers to the word *sannyāsaḥ*. Furthermore, because of the optional application of *parasavarṇa* (assimilation to the following sound) by the rule "va padāntasya," the anusvāra of the letter *m* may optionally become a *n*; thus, one must understand the form as having two *n*s (*sannyāsa*). Otherwise, it would be difficult to achieve the equality of sequence between the forward and reverse recitations intended here.

It conveys an identical meaning—that is, it causes the understanding of the same referent—regarding all the phonemes (*varṇa*) residing within itself, whether they are arranged in direct order (*anuloma*) or reverse order (*pratiloma*). In this context, the word "bhavati" (it becomes) is a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*). Whether the phonemes residing within itself are recited in direct order or in reverse order, since the same sequence is observed in both cases, this *sannyāsa* (rearrangement) disregards direct and reverse order; thus, the sense is that the word "śabda" (sound/word) indeed conveys an identical meaning. For example: [Example omitted per instructions]

Or else, this single favorable aspect of Saumya, accompanied by Akrūra and powerful, situated here in the center of the world-protectors, will immediately bring about the destruction of the misfortune.

In this passage, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the subject at hand, the grace of the Blessed One (*bhagavad-anugraha*), and the non-subject, the auspicious planet (*saumya-graha*). To explain: [the Lord] is the helper (*sahāya*)—that is, the protector (*trātṛ*)—of Akrūra, who is named Akrūra. He is powerful (*balavān*), possessing the capacity to revive those who have taken refuge in Him; He is auspicious (*saumya*), meaning gracious (*anugra*). By this, His being easily accessible for the enjoyment of happiness is indicated. He is the Lord (*indra*) even of the world-protectors (*lokapālaka*), such as Indra and others, because of the scriptural testimony that His status as a world-protector is unconditional: "He is the lord of beings, He is the world-protector."

"Having gone to him" means having reached him; that is, belonging to him. "The One" (eka) refers to one who, without dependence on any other companion, is the accomplisher of all his own duties. "Grace" (anugraha) means compassion; the sense here is: "If he should show such grace toward me as he did toward Akrūra. "Destroyer of misfortune" (ariṣṭabhaṅgada) means the uprooter of all kinds of inauspiciousness—such as my failure to do what ought to be done and doing what ought not to be done—which has persisted from beginningless time; he will become so immediately, and not after delay.

"Affliction, longing, delusion, and suffering persist only so long as one does not come for refuge to You, the destroyer of all sins"— according to this principle, the implication is that my contact with inauspiciousness has its limit precisely in Your grace.
In the [ascendant] division, any one of Mercury, Venus, or Jupiter situated in a quadrant is powerful;
even if accompanied by malefic planets, it immediately brings about the destruction of misfortune.

Thus, the meaning of the verse proclaiming the destruction of the calamities of children should be investigated as follows: "O Guardian of the World!"—this is the address to the Blessed One. "Is it perhaps a gentle planet?"—here is the word division. The sense is that a "gentle planet" (saumya-graha) refers to one among Mercury, Venus, or Jupiter.

If a planet is strong—endowed with strength from its position, direction, time, and actions—and situated in a quadrant (kendras), that is, in any one of the first, fourth, seventh, or tenth houses; and if it has malefic planets such as Mars and others as its companions, or is even conjoined with malefic planets, it will immediately bring about the destruction of *ariṣṭa*, meaning infantile mortality (*bālāriṣṭa*). What need is there to mention other unfavorable results? Or rather: "O Lord Moon, those born under these auspicious planets, when they attain high yogas through their positions in the eighth, sixth, or third houses, shall become commanders of armies, ministers, or kings. (Verse 871)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the two subjects, the Blessed One and the Moon, both of whom are relevant and irrelevant [to the context] respectively. For instance: "O Blessed One! O You who are complete in the sixfold qualities! O Vidhu! O Viṣṇu!"—according to Amarasimha, "Vidhu" refers to Viṣṇu as well as the Moon. [The epithet] "by those who are gentle (*saumyaiḥ*), auspicious (*śubhaiḥ*), and by whom the state of being overcome by enemies has been cast down (*astāriparibhavasthitibhiḥ*)" means: by those through whom the condition of being defeated by enemies—that is, the humiliation caused by foes—has been eliminated; or alternatively, by those whose very state of existence is such that the defeat by enemies has been cast away.

The meaning is: "by those who have avoided the host of external and internal enemies. By these "lights" of yours—meaning by your glances (dṛṣṭibhiḥ)—the word *jyotis* being used for light, splendor, and vision according to Amara; and as Medinī states: "The word *jyotis* [is masculine] in the sense of fire and the sun; it is neuter in the sense of vision, a star, and illumination. When there is "intense connection" (*adhiyoge*), meaning an exceeding bond, the people born [therefrom]—namely, army commanders, ministers, and kings—become so as is appropriate. The underlying sentiment is: "What is difficult to obtain for those who have come within the range of the Lord's glance?"

In this context: O Blessed One! O Glorious One! O Moon! O Indu! The meaning is: "of you," regardless of which zodiac sign (*rāśi*) you may be situated in. [Your state is defined] by the conditions of *asta*, *ari*, and *paribhava*: *asta* is the seventh house, *ari* is the sixth, and *paribhava* is the eighth. As stated in the *Mādhavīya*: "The sixth is called *kṣata* or *ari*; the seventh is termed *jāmitra*, *asta*, *kalatra*, *manmatha*, *mada*, or *dyūna*; and they call the eighth the *randhra*, *āyuḥ*, *maraṇa*, *parābhava*, or the place of death."

By those "thus described" gentle and auspicious luminaries—the planets Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—who are situated in those aforementioned places; it is stated in the Kośa: "In Adhiyoga, when all the auspicious planets are located in the sixth, seventh, or eighth houses from the Moon, regardless of where that Moon may be, a royal yoga called Adhiyoga is formed. Those born under that Adhiyoga become, respectively, commanders of armies, ministers, and kings."
When there is an Adhiyoga of the Moon with benefics at the eighth or seventh house,
the birth of an army commander, a minister, or a king occurs in that [yoga].
The meaning is that this is according to the statement of Varāhamihira.

Just as the Supreme Self, the best of poets, having first made even a lowly person attached to a word light, and finally rendered even him free from possessiveness, shows people the further shore that is so difficult to reach. (872)

Here, the Blessed One is the subject under discussion (*prastuta*), while the preeminent poet (*kavivarya*) is not; there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the two. For instance, the "preeminent poet" (*kavivarya*) is one who is to be chosen (*varaṇīya*) by poets (*kavi*)—that is, by the learned—or alternatively, he is the most excellent (*vareṇya*) among poets, because he is the author of the *Pañcarātra*, the *Gītā*, and other works, as stated in the Śruti: "The poet (*kavi*), the wise one (*manīṣī*)."

The Supreme Self—Nārāyaṇa, the inner self of all, who is described in scripture as "in the middle of that crest [of the flame] is the Supreme Self"—having rendered even a base, ordinary person who has sought refuge at His feet free from possessiveness (*nirmama*)—that is, devoid of the sense of "mine" regarding the body and so forth, as it is said, "the two syllables *mama* are death" (where *mama* is an indeclinable resembling a case-ending, analyzed as "he from whom *mama* has departed")—then, for the sake of that very freedom from possessiveness, He [elevates] even such a person who has been made thus.

In the phrase *nirmamantataḥ*, the *parasavarṇa* (substitution with the following sound) occurs by the rule *vā padāntasya*. Regarding *janaiḥ*, [it refers to] common folk (*pāmaraiḥ*), as Medinī states: "The word *janaḥ* means the world, from Maharloka upwards, and also a common person. *Sudurgamaṃ* means exceedingly difficult to reach. *Pāram* [refers to] the further shore; as the Śruti says, "The Blessed One shows the further shore of darkness," he reveals the Self, which is like a fierce sun to the dense darkness of saṃsāra, through the practice of meditation. By the rule *dṛśeśca*, the verb takes two objects (*dvikarmakatā*). The sense is that He makes one a partaker of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*).

In this context, "one whose supreme self is the intellect" (*parama-śreṣṭha-ātmā-buddhiḥ*) refers to one for whom the intellect is the highest essence. "The best of poets" (*kavi-varyaḥ*) means the foremost among those who compose poetry. "Attached to words" (*pada-lagnam*) means connected as one of the elements within words consisting of nominal and verbal suffixes as they are employed. Even a vulgar word (*pāmaram*), such as the word *pāmara* itself, he renders "light" (*laghu*)—the phrase is to be divided as *nirmam antataḥ*. Regarding *antataḥ*, the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *antaḥ* is not feminine; it denotes certainty, destruction, essential nature, the front, proximity, and the interior."

The meaning is: having made the letter *a* exit from *nirmaṃ*—that is, having removed the letter *a* situated in the middle of the word *pāmara*. [Thus one obtains] *sudurga*, which means difficult for people to traverse, i.e., difficult to understand. [The compound] refers to that which has such an *m* (the letter *ma*) as its [final] part. The sense is: once the letter *m* has been removed, how can the letter *m* be heard again? It shows the word *pāra*; the meaning is that it shows the word *pāra* as being what remains when the letter *a* has been removed from the word *pāmara*.

Just as he is known as the supreme lord of the gods, O beloved of the Lord of the Universe, so too is he the sovereign of this land; what more need be said? We shall here declare both the seen and the unseen.

Here, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) between the Blessed Śrī who protects a man and the word *deveśādhīśa*. To explain: O beloved of the Lord of the World! whomsoever you protect (*aveḥ*), the root *ava* being in the imperative middle voice singular; that man shall be known as, or become famous as, the sovereign even over the lords of the gods (*deveśānām*), that is, the guardians of the world (*lokapālānām*). What then need be said regarding his becoming the lord of regions (*deśādhīśaḥ*)—of worldly objects (*deśa* meaning "region" or "object," according to Amara)—that is, a king? Indeed, what more can be said?

The sense is that this is not surprising. Here, regarding this man protected by you, the visible fruit in this world consists in the attainment of sovereignty over the land, while the invisible fruit in the hereafter consists in the attainment of lordship over the Lord of Gods; these should be construed in reverse order. The sense is that we are well-acquainted with your power. We have said—that is, we have spoken.

In the alternative interpretation regarding the phrase "jagadīśavallabhe 'yam," the word *ayam* (this) is the division [of the compound]. The term *deveśādhīśaḥ*—the word *deveśādhīśa*—would indeed be known by you; that is, it would certainly be understood by you. This very term *deveśādhīśa*, as previously stated, when deprived of the vowel *e* (becoming *aveḥ*), results in the word *aveḥ* ending in *e* (as in *aveḥ*, *sayau*, *sayaḥ*). Thus, it would become *deśādhīśaḥ*, resulting in the form *deśādhīśa*.

In this instance, regarding these two words *deveśādhīśa* and *deśādhīśa*, we have observed the syllable *ve*—as in the form *vayam* (we)—derived from the nominal stem *vayam* with the substitution of *ay* for the case-ending *am*, as seen in the word *deveśādhīśa* (heard) and not seen in the word *deśādhīśa* (unheard), respectively. We have thus stated "we have spoken" (*abrūmaḥ*). This [figure] is a blend of *kāvyārthāpatti* (poetic presumption). In the same way, among the examples previously shown, those who possess creative intuition (*pratibhā*) should infer the blending with other figures of speech as far as possible.

Or rather, her praiseworthy ornament shines forth as the "Śrīramyā" known by the name "Saikāvalī," which takes the form of pearls held by a multitude of men who have successfully achieved their goals.

The distinction here is that there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) of three meanings: the subject at hand, Śrī, and the two figures of speech not under discussion, namely *muktāvalī* and *ekāvalī*. To explain: in the sense of Śrī, the analysis of the verse is as follows: "Śrī is lovely; she shines by the name of *ekāvalī*; she is highly praiseworthy in her adornment; she is a well-accomplished series [of virtues]; and she has assumed the form of pearls (*muktā*)"—such is the word-division. She is "lovely" by the splendor (*abhikhyā*) of the *valīs*, that is, the beauty of the three folds of skin (*trivalī*).

That peerless and unrivaled Fortune shines forth, worthy of praise by the wise (kṛtibhiḥ) in such a manner as to be sufficient and complete. He further qualifies her with the word "sādhu" (well). The word "yasyāḥ" is in the ablative case; that is to say, from the presence of that Fortune, or rather, through her grace. The row (śreṇī)—the line—of those who have accomplished their purpose (kṛtārthānām), having fulfilled their means and achieved their ends, becomes one whose form is both grasped and released (gṛhītamuktākṛtiḥ), meaning its nature is both acquired and relinquished, in a truly excellent manner.

In the case of the *muktāvalī* (pearl necklace), however, the analysis is as follows: "That praiseworthy ornament (*alaṃkṛti*), beautiful with splendor (*śrī*), shines under the name *ekāvalī*; it is well-made, its form consisting of pearls (*muktā*) taken from a series of meanings (*arthaśreṇī*). Beautiful (*ramyā*) with the splendor (*śrī*) of loveliness (*lāvaṇya*), that praiseworthy ornament (*alaṃkṛti*)—meaning an adornment (*ābharaṇa*)—shines by the name *ekāvalī*. According to Amara, "*ekāvalī* is a single-stringed necklace" (*ekāvalyekayaṣṭikā*).

It shines, whose form—that is, the nature—of the ornament named *ekāvalī* is such that it has pearls purchased with a great deal of wealth, meaning a vast amount of riches; she is one who possesses such pearls, and it is well accomplished, meaning it has been perfectly produced.

In the view that this is the *ekāvalī* ornament, the caesura (*cheda*) in the first half remains as before; however, in the second half, there is this distinction: "the series of meanings (*arthaśreṇī*), having the form of pearls taken up [and released], has been well-composed. That ornamentation—meaning the poetic excellence (*kāvyalakṣmī*)—shines, being beautiful with its splendor and praiseworthy by the name of *ekāvalī*. Of that ornamentation, the series or row of meanings—that is, the subject matter—has the form of pearls that have been taken up and released. It was "well-composed," meaning it was skillfully fashioned, because of the definition of that ornament: "A *ekāvalī* is considered to be a series of meanings arranged according to the manner of taking up and releasing [pearls]."

Just as the sun, possessing dense energy within its true self due to the dark luster of the form of the supreme deity, shines intensely here with eyes like lotus petals, so too is he renowned as a hero.

In this context, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) among these three: the Lord who is the subject (*prakṛta*), and Indra and Āditya who are not the subject (*aprakṛta*). To explain: in the sense of the Lord, "one whose luster is dark by nature" means one whose radiance (*bhāḥ*) is dark (*asitā*, i.e., *śyāmalā*) by its very essence or nature, as is heard in such passages as, "Standing in the midst of dark clouds, I go from the dark to the variegated," and so forth. "One whose power is dense within the Self of the virtuous" means [residing] in the mind (*ātmani*) of the virtuous (*satām*), namely those who know Brahman; or it may be a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the virtuous Self" (*saṃścāsāvātmā ca*).

The meaning is: "in both ways" refers to when the mind is purified. "Nibiḍaujas" means of dense radiance; for in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā it is heard that [the Self] is graspable by the pure mind and possesses a luminous form, as in the texts: "Consisting of mind, having breath for its body, and light for its form," and "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other deities, nor by austerity or ritual action;
but when one's being is purified through the clarity of knowledge, then one sees Him, the partless One."
While meditating.
For within the body there is indeed a pure one consisting of light, whom ascetics whose defects have been exhausted behold.

Such scriptural passages as these should also be considered. Amara states: "Ātman, effort, fortitude, intellect, nature, Brahman, and the body. He is the *dyumaṇi*, shining like a gem in the sky, that is, in the supreme ether, according to the Śruti: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven. He is renowned as *Śūra*, because his name is listed among the names of Kṛṣṇa in the passage "Śūra, Śauri," etc.; or else, the word *Śūra* is used figuratively for his descendants, just as the word *Yadu* is.

Among the Yadus, who are distinguished by their heroism, he is renowned such that he is called Śauri. By the word *dyumaṇi* (the sun-jewel), his transcendence (*paratva*) is shown; by the words *śūra-vikhyāta* (renowned for heroism), his accessibility (*saulabhya*) is revealed. He is the Supreme among Gods, superior even to the four-faced Brahmā and others, according to such Vedic texts as, "Wherein dwells the God of gods. With eyes like the petals of a lotus—lotus-petal-eyed—the Blessed Lord shines forth most brilliantly here in this world.

In the case of Indra: *svarūpāsitabhāḥ* means one whose power (*bhāḥ*) has been worshipped—that is, seated upon himself or served by him—by the *svaru* (thunderbolt), according to Amara’s lexicon: "The thunderbolt has a hundred edges (*śatakoṭiḥ svaruḥ*). The root *ās* is used here in the sense of "sitting" (*upaveśane*); from this, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the past passive participle (*kta*) is formed in the passive sense. Thus, he is described as one whose power is manifested through the weapon of the thunderbolt. According to the Medinī lexicon: "*bhāḥ* [is used] in the sense of power (*prabhāva*) and radiance (*mayūkha*); it is not feminine. He is a *dyumaṇi*, an ornament of the heavenly world (*svarloka*); according to the Medinī lexicon: "*dyauḥ* [is used] for heaven and the sky, and is feminine."

He whose eyes are like the petals of a thousand-petaled lotus is thus described; the sense is that he is "the thousand-eyed one" (sahasrākṣa). He is both "heroic" (śūra)—meaning valiant—and "renowned" (vikhyāta), meaning his valor is famous for slaying great asuras such as Vṛtra; the sense is that he is the "best of gods" (devottama), the foremost among the immortals. The analysis of the phrase *sadā ātmani biḍaujāḥ* is as follows: *biḍaujāḥ* refers to Indra; the sense is that he should always shine (*bhāyāt*) intensely within the self—that is, within the intellect.

In the sense of the Āditya (the Sun), however, it means "seated" or "established" in its own form or own aspect; or else, it refers to that in which light (*bhās*) is "completely bound" (*sita*)—that is, fixed—by its own nature or essence (*svarūpeṇa*). [The root] *ṣiñ* is used in the sense of "binding," with the suffix *kta* in the passive voice. Amara states: "Bound (*baddha*), fastened (*saṃdita*), and tied (*sita*). The meaning is that its radiance is naturally motionless.

Alternatively, *āsita* means "abiding" (*sthiti*), derived from the root *ās* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the abstract state. Thus, *svarūpāsitabhāḥ* means "shining by means of that abiding in its own nature"; from the root *bhās* with the suffix *kvip*, the meaning is "appearing precisely through the persistence of its own nature. Being one whose vital energy (*ojas*) is dense within the True Self (*sadātman*), he exists within himself—according to Amara, the word *sat* denotes "the true," "the virtuous," "that which exists," "the excellent," and "the venerable. This is the Self, the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), as stated in the Śruti: "This golden person who is within the sun."

Therefore, he possesses dense splendor (*nibiḍaujāḥ*), because of the scriptural teaching that the light of the sun and other luminaries depends upon him, starting from "The sun does not shine there" up to "By his light all this shines. He has eyes like lotus petals (*nalinadalekṣaṇaḥ*): "petal" (*dala*) is derived from the root *dal* (meaning "to split") with the suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *ac*; the suffix *ṇi* is elided according to the rule *ṇeraniṭi*.

Since *dala* and other such words are listed by Bhoja [in the *Kātantra*], the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* applies—because *ghaṭādayo mitaḥ* [states that] *ghaṭa* and others are *mit*—thereby providing an exception to the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) caused by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), resulting in a short vowel. "That which has the sight (*īkṣaṇam* = *darśanam*) of a lotus petal (*nalinadalama*)" is what is meant; the sense is that its appearance causes the blooming of the lotus. The word division is *sutarāṃśuḥ* (the one with very bright rays), known as *ravi*. After the elision of the *ra* by the rule *rori*, the preceding vowel is lengthened by the rule *ḍhralope* in the *saṃhitā* [text].

"Having rays that are *sutarāḥ*—meaning more beautiful (*śobhanatarāḥ*)—is what is meant by that [epithet]. Here, the word *su-* denotes a substance (*dravya*). Therefore, the suffix *nām* (the *na* of *nāmn*) is applied to the comparative suffix *tarap* [in *sutarāḥ*], because of the prohibition: ‘[The suffix *ām* is not applied] after *kim*, a *tiṅ*-ending, an indeclinable, or a word ending in a *ghat* suffix, when excellence of a substance is expressed. He is known as *Ravi*; thus he is called *ravikhyātaḥ*. He is the best of gods (*devottamaḥ*), because he is listed among the synonyms for the Sun as ‘the best of gods, the treasury of light (*dhāmanidhiḥ*)’. He is the jewel of heaven (*dyumaṇiḥ*), the Āditya; may he shine here.
In this case, there is a triple pun (*śleṣa*) just as before; however, it should be noted that the distinction lies in the transposition of the adjective and the substantive."

Just as the son of Sumanas (the God of Love), though always subject to the power of Gaurī’s lotus-footed speech, yet being of noble resolve, fulfills the virtuous desires of those whose minds are fixed upon his own feet; so too does [the Lord] here. 876.

Here, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is the subject under discussion (*prastuta*), while Brahmā, Śiva, and Kāma are not the subject (*aprastuta*); there is a *śleṣa* (punning conflation) of these four. To explain: in the sense of the Blessed One, *aja* means "he who is not born" (*na jāyate sma iti ajaḥ*). Viṣṇu is the Blessed One, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "He is unborn" (*ajāyamānaḥ*). The *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *aja* [denotes] a goat, Hari (Viṣṇu), Brahmā, the moon, Kāma, a king, and Śiva. Regarding Gaurī, she has a golden-yellow complexion (*hiraṇyavat-piśaṅgavarṇā*), as per the *śruti*: "Gold-colored, tawny, wearing a golden garland," and so forth. The *Amara* lexicon states: "*Gaura* [denotes] the ruddy, the white, and the yellow."

By this, her abundance of beauty (*lāvaṇya*) is illuminated; the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule "ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca. She whose constant love (*rati*)—meaning affection directed toward her husband—is virtuous (*sādhvī*) and praiseworthy; by this, her excellence of devotion is expressed. By these two qualifiers, it is indicated that her word is not to be transgressed. She whose feet (*pada*)—meaning her dwelling place—are lotuses (*kamala*); she is "Lotus-footed" (*kamalapadā*), [referring to] Śrī, whose abode is the lotus (*padmālayā*). By this, her extreme delicacy (*saukumārya*) is suggested.

And by that very act of making such a request, his words are implied to be necessarily acceptable, lest they cause offense. He is "under the sway" (*vaśaga*) of speech—that is, subject to the words—of the kind described in the passage beginning with, "Who in this world is thus free from fault? Therefore, being a "remover of the existence of the wise" (*sumanobhavahārī*)—meaning one who removes the worldly cycle (*saṃsāra*) for those possessed of good minds—he [leads] those very same "wise ones" (*sumanasaḥ*) who are attached to his own "foot" (*pada*), whether understood as his feet, his position, or his state; such is the sense.

"Those whose desires are fulfilled" means those whose auspicious qualities have become manifest. He "spreads out": the essential meaning is that the Blessed Lord, rendered helpless by the power of His own words of glory which cannot be transgressed, effects the manifestation of the eightfold qualities for those who have taken refuge in Him, preceded by the complete removal of ignorance.

In the four-faced (Brahmā) interpretation: [he is] under the sway of Vāṇī (Sarasvatī), who has lotus-like feet—referring to Gaurī whose feet are as tender as a lotus—and whose complexion is pure according to the description "she who is white as the kunda flower, the moon, frost, and a necklace of pearls"; she is one whose "delight" (rati)—meaning affection—is always "well-placed" (sādhu) among the "virtuous" (sādhu), that is, among the refined and the learned, because she is the Goddess of Speech. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *sādhu* is used in three senses: appropriate, beautiful, and refined; it is not used for a usurer. She is one who is subject to her (Sarasvatī).

In the *Amara-kośa*, it is stated: "The two *bhavas*—the lotus (*sumana*) and the water-lily (*bisaprasūna*)—are 'removers of birth' (*ajanmaharau*) by virtue of their very birth. Here, *hārī* means "charming"; the meaning is that [Brahmā] was born from the navel-lotus of the Blessed One. *Aja* refers to the four-faced one (Brahmā). He extends the fulfillment of noble desires (*satkāmān*)—meaning those endowed with delightful objects of enjoyment—to those who have reached Satyaloka and are attached to his own feet.

Regarding the phrase *kamalapadāyāḥ*: it is derived from the root *pad* (to go) with the suffix *pacādyac*, hence *pada*. Thus, *kamalapadā* means "she whose feet (*pada*) are like those of a deer (*kamala*)," or alternatively, "she whose mark (*pada*) is the deer (*kamala*). In either case, the meaning is "of her who has a deer as her hand-mark" (*kuraṅgapāṇeḥ*). As Amara states: "The word *kamala* may also refer to a deer; and *pada* [denotes] resolve, protection, place, a mark, a foot, or an object. Although the attribute of having a deer as a hand-mark is most famously associated with Īśāna (Śiva) alone.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this description is made because Umā forms half of his body. For this very reason, the statement that the deer is common to both—“with the hindquarters pursued by their own young fawns acting like lamps”—is consistent. Alternatively, [the name] refers to one whose feet possess lotuses—that is, lotuses in the form of lines indicative of her being a supreme woman. [He is] under the influence of the speech of Gaurī (Pārvatī), who delights in a beloved husband.

"Manobhavahārī" means one who takes away the mind-born [god of love], i.e., Manmatha; "sumanobhavahārī" means one who thoroughly destroys the mind-born, that is to say, the enemy of Kandarpa. There is a contradiction in saying that the unborn (aja) Lord (īśāna) extends (tanoti) those whose desires are good (satkāma)—meaning those possessed of Madana—while being attached to his own feet (nijapadalagna); the resolution of this is that he extends those whose heart's desires have borne fruit (phalita-manoratha).

On the other hand, in the camp of Smara (Kāma), he was perfectly under the control of the speech of Gaurī—she who has feet like lotuses, whose feet are red like the aruṇa-lotus, who is fair-complexioned (*aruṇa-varṇā*), and who is purified by her devotion to her husband; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *gaura* may mean yellow, red, white, or pure, according to its referent. Alternatively, he was perfectly under the control of the speech of Rati, the goddess of pleasure. The meaning is that he was subservient to their commands. Furthermore, he was the one who captivates the mind through his birth—that is, he is the charming one born from the mind (*manasija*), the unborn Smara (Kāma).

The *Kośa* has already been cited. "In its own domains" (*nijapadeṣu*) means in its own objects, that is, in the excitants (*uddīpanavibhāva*) such as the qualities of the object of focus (*ālambana*). It is said to "extend" (*tanoti*) people who are "attached" (*lagnān*), meaning deeply devoted, and who possess "good desires" (*satkāmān*), meaning those whose longing for the enjoyment of a powerful beloved is intense.

May that Hari— who is as heart-stealing as the abundant and true marks of prosperity, who is known by the name Virocana, and whose excellent weapon is capable of shattering the body of Vṛtra— bestow lightning-like splendor upon us.

Here, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is the subject under discussion (*prastuta*), while Indra, the Sun, the Moon, and the light of lightning are the subjects not under discussion (*aprastuta*). The distinction from the previous example lies in the *śleṣa* (punning) of these five. To explain: in the sense of the Blessed One, "Hari" refers to one who is *puṣkala* (abundant) and *atiśobhana* (exceedingly beautiful). Regarding "satī ca sacca," there is a neuter singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām*; thus, "satī" also means that which is worthy of honor (*abhyarhita*).

*Śrī* and *lakṣaṇa* are *śrīlakṣaṇe*; he in whose heart (*hṛdye*) and on whose chest (*uras-sthite*) reside *lakṣmī* and *śrīvatsa* is [the one described]. Regarding the word *śrīmān*, Amara states: "The words *śrīmat*, *śreṣṭha*, and *puṣkala* mean excellent; *sattama* means most beautiful. Medinī states: "'Sat' is used for the good, the wise, and the praiseworthy; it is used in the masculine for the honorable and the true, and in the three genders for 'existing'; as a feminine, it refers to a virtuous woman. Alternatively, *puṣkala* means full or complete, as the *Ratnamālā* states: "'Puṣkala' refers to the full and the excellent."

He possesses praiseworthy marks, endowed with the bodily signs that indicate the status of a Great Man as described in the *Sāmudrika* [treatises]; he is pleasing and charming to the mind. As it is stated in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* and other texts:
"He is firm in three places, long in three, equal in three, and elevated in three."

By such [passages] as these; or else, he is so called because he possesses that which is the heart-captivating name—the very characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of Śrī, the auspicious and virtuous Lakṣmī—which is a mantra for subduing her or the world. The analysis of the compound is: *hṛdayasya bandhanaḥ* = *hṛdyaḥ*. According to the rule "in the sense of binding or in the Veda," the suffix *yat* is applied after the word *hṛdaya* in the genitive case when the Veda is the subject matter. They say that *hṛdya* means a mantra for subduing (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

The sense is that the name of the Blessed One, Lakṣmī, is worthy of constant recitation (*nityajapa*), according to the saying: "It is said that for Nārāyaṇa, your name alone is the most bold [suitable] for constant recitation. *Lakṣaṇa* refers to a mark, a sign, a name, a seal, or bodily excellence.
*Hṛdya* refers to something pleasing to the heart, a mantra for subjugation, or a fragrant unguent.
O beloved of the heart, O benefactor of the heart, O born of the heart... ||

Thus says the *Vaijayantī*. Alternatively, he is so called because the lotus (*puṣkarā*)—that is, Śrī herself—is his "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning the signet ring that makes known his lordship over the world, which is "dear to the heart" (*hṛdyam*), being situated within the heart. He is "Bahuvirocanābhikhya," one whose renown (*abhikhyā*) or fame possesses "abundant radiance" (*bahuvirocana*). This is according to the Vedic text: "His name is great glory. The *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *abhikhyā* [is used] for splendor, fame, and names."

He whose excellent weapons (hetayaḥ)—the *sudarśana* discus and others—are capable of shattering the compact frames (*saṃhanana*) of the Vṛtras; for "Vṛtras" refers to enemies, and their "compact frames" (*saṃhananāni*) refer to their bodies, according to Amara’s definition: "The body (*gātra*), the form (*vapuḥ*), and the compact frame (*saṃhananam*). The term *bhiduraḥ* means "shattering," derived from the roots *vid*, *bhid*, and *chid* with the suffix *kurac*. Thus, *vṛtrasaṃhananabhidurāḥ* means those [weapons] which split the bodies of the enemies of Vṛtra. He is one who possesses such excellent (*varāḥ*) and supreme (*śreṣṭhāḥ*) weapons. Furthermore, "Vṛtras" refers to darkness, enemies, and Dānavas.

Regarding the term *vṛtra*, Amara and Hemacandra state: "Vṛtra [denotes] a cloud, an enemy, darkness, a Dānava, Indra, or a mountain. Regarding *heti*, the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "*Hetir* means flame, ray, or weapon. *Vidyudbhāḥ* means having a luster equal to lightning. This is supported by the Śruti: "All moments (*nimeṣāḥ*) were born from the Puruṣa, from the lightning (*vidyutaḥ*). Alternatively, *vidyut* may be derived as follows: *vit* is knowledge (as in the phrase "to one who knows worldly affairs," etc., where *vit* is formed with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an abstract noun from the root *vid*). That which joins (*yauti*) with this knowledge is *vidyut*; here, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *yudh* in the sense of an agent, signifying "mixing" or "joining."

The augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*. He whose light (*bhās*) or splendor (*tejas*) is like lightning is *vidyudbhās*; the meaning is that he is endowed with splendor expanded by knowledge. Herein, knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor are present in their entirety.

When these qualities have been mentioned, the mention of the first and the last according to the principle of "inclusive abbreviation" (pratyāhāra) serves as an indicator for all four qualities situated in between, beginning with power (śakti). By this, His possession of the complete set of six qualities (pūrṇa-ṣāḍguṇya) is demonstrated. May that Hari be victorious!

In the sense of Indra: *puṣkala* means "abundant"; by resorting to the non-distinction between *ra* and *la*, *puṣkara* means "the sky. Those who sit (*sīdanti*) in the sky are the *puṣkarasadaḥ*, i.e., the sky-dwellers (*dyusadaḥ*), from the root *sad-* with the suffix *kvip*. Of those gods, the "glories" (*śrī*) are the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) such as the parasol and chowrie that signify sovereignty; he who is "charming" (*hṛdya*)—that is, dear to the heart—by means of these is [described]. He whose "many" (*bahu*)—meaning thousands in number—"vilocanāni" (eyes); by resorting to the non-distinction between *ra* and *la*, this refers to the "Vilocanas. He who has such a famous name (*abhikhyā*) is thus called "Bahuvilocana," which contains a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The *saṃhanana* (crushing weapon) of Vṛtra—a specific class of *asura*—is so called because it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for killing (*hanti*), formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*. That which is *bhidura* (cleaving), the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*)—as Amara states, "the cleaver is the thunderbolt"—is his excellent weapon (*vara-heti*). He is thus described as one whose supreme weapon is that very [thunderbolt]. *Vidyut-bhāḥ*: *vid* refers to knowledge concerning grammar; for the Śruti says, "Speech, indeed, was turned away and unmanifested; Indra, having stepped into its midst, manifested it."

Or, the knowledge concerning Brahman is [implied] from the hearing of [the Lord's] instruction to Pratardana regarding Brahman whose body is his own self, beginning with: "He said, 'Know me alone; this I consider the most beneficial for a human being. Furthermore, *vidyudbhāḥ* means "he who shines through battles such as that against Pauloma," according to Amara’s definition: "The word *samit* refers to a battle (*āji*) or a conflict (*yudh*). Alternatively, there is a word-division as *vidi udbhāḥ*; in the sense of *vidi*, meaning the aforementioned knowledge, *udbhāḥ* means "possessing upward-shining splendor," i.e., one whose knowledge is unimpeded. May that Hari, Indra, be victorious!

On the solar side (*sūryapakṣe*), he is one whose name is Virocana—meaning "named Virocana" (as Amara states: *candrāgnyarkā virocanāḥ*)—and who possesses a heart that is dear (*hṛdya*) because it protects (*rakṣaṇa*) the excellence (*śrī*), fortune, or beauty of the lotuses (*puṣkara*); for there is no distinction between the letters *ra* and *la*. Alternatively, his name is Virocana because he possesses a distinguished splendor (*abhikhyā*) of *rocana* flowers—that is, red water-lilies (*raktakahlāra*). The word *bahu* is a separate term that connects with what follows.

The meaning is that it possesses the beauty of the red *kahlāra* lotus; this is confirmed by the *Ratnamālā* and *Vaijayantī*, which state: "The word *rocanā* refers to the red *kahlāra*, the bile of cows, and an excellent woman. The word *bahu* means "in such a way as to be abundant"; this is an adverbial modifier for the action of piercing (*bhedana*). The term *saṃhanana* refers to the collection or assembly of *vṛtras*, that is, the rain-clouds; this is according to the *Śeṣa* lexicon, which states: "*Saṃhanana* [denotes] a limb or a collection."

May that Hari, the Sun, who possesses rays—excellent weapons that have gathered for the purpose of raining upon those [clouds] that are prone to breaking apart—be victorious; for according to the Vedic revelation, "With those very rays by which the Sun shines, Parjanya rains. He is the one whose luster is lightning, and whose color is like lightning. May that Hari, the Sun, be victorious.

On the lunar fortnight (*candrapakṣe*), it is *puṣkala* (abundant) and full; for the wise, it is the protector (*rakṣaṇa*) of the prosperity (*śriyaḥ*) or fortunes, which is "heart-pleasing" (*hṛdya*)—that is, dear to the heart—because he is the lord of the stars (*tārādhīśatvāt*). Alternatively, he is called *puṣkarasacchrīlakṣaṇahṛt*: one who "seizes" (*harati*) the name or the mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the beauty (*śrī*) that resides abundantly (*bahu*) in the lotuses (*puṣkareṣu*). [The suffix] *kvip* is added to the root *hṛ*. Regarding the word *sat*, the *Ratnamālā* states: "In the case of a constellation (*ṛkṣe*), *sat* is neuter. [Thus, *sat* here refers to the constellations such as Rohiṇī. [The compound *puṣkarasacchrīlakṣaṇahṛt* is analyzed as follows: He is the one who seizes the mark or name of the splendor (*śrī*) belonging to the lotuses (*puṣkara*), which is present (*satī*) in them in great measure (*bahu*). The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *hṛ* (to take away).

The meaning is that he shall completely eliminate even the name or the sign of the splendor of the lotus. In this interpretation, the construction of the two words is as follows: "he who has taken away the auspicious marks of Puṣkarasat," and "he who is known by the name Virocana. "Virocanābhikhya" means one whose other name is Virocana. He is the one whose excellent rays (aṃśavaḥ)—which are capable of piercing (bhiduraḥ) the mass (saṃhanana) or collection of darknesses (vṛtrāṇām)—are his weapons. He is the one whose light (bhāḥ) or power shines forth particularly like lightning (vidyut).
May that Hari, the Moon, be victorious!

In the case of the "lightning-flash" interpretation (*vidyutprakāśapakṣa*), however, the adjectives should be applied by changing their gender. She is beautiful (*satī*) like the constellation Puṣkara; or else, she is like the serpent Puṣkara or a stream of water, being present (*satī*) with a curved, slender, long, and radiant form.
*Puṣkara* refers to a lotus, water, a lunar mansion (*bha*), battle, the mouth of a musical instrument, a god, a stream,
an island, a type of medicine, a crane, a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), a snake, and the tip of an elephant's trunk.

Thus ends the *Ratnamālā*. She possesses fortune (*śrī*), hence she is *śrīlā*; the suffix *lac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *sidhma*. Amara states: "One who possesses *lakṣmī* is called *lakṣmaṇa* or *śrīla*. She is charming for a moment (*kṣaṇahṛdyā*), beautiful for a short time because her radiance is fleeting. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound of these three [words]. *Hari* is of a tawny color (*kapilavarṇā*). For this very reason, she has the name *Virocanā*. *Rocanā* is *gorocanā* (cow-bile pigment); she whose splendor (*abhikhyā*) is like that of *rocanā* is *rocanābhikhyā*. One who is especially *rocanābhikhyā* is *virocanābhikhyā*.

Alternatively, "rocana" means those of excellent complexion; she whose "abhikhyā" (splendor) is like theirs is one whose beauty is equal to that of the finest jewels among women—this is the meaning. For this very reason, there is the poetic figure *pratīpa* (the inverse). She whose "varā hetayaḥ" (excellent rays) are "bhidura" (shattering) toward the "saṃhanana" (mass) of "vṛtra" (clouds)—that is, her flames—because she has manifested by piercing through the multitude of clouds. May the splendor of the lightning, the flash of the *taṭit*, be victorious!
"Harin is used for Yama, Anila, Indra, Candra, Arka, Viṣṇu, Siṃha, Aṃśu, and Vājī;
for Śuka, Āhi, Kapi, and Bheka. In three genders, it means 'tawny'. Thus says Amara.
Or for example:
"The King, who is a guardian of the world, victorious, and named Samavartin, being wise and a bestower of prosperity, surely rains down desire upon all sides to an exceeding degree. (878)

Here too, the Blessed One alone is the subject under discussion; Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Candra are the non-subjects (*aprastuta*). There is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) among these six. In the sense of the Blessed One, *jiṣṇu* means "victorious" (*jayaśīla*). Regarding the name *Samavartin*: he who exists together with *Mā* (the goddess Śrī) in his activity is *samavartin*; the meaning is that he exists as one who is "even" (*sama*) and "present" (*vartin*) precisely through his possession of glory (*śrīmattā*).

Alternatively, he is so called because he conducts himself with equality toward all, according to the manner stated in the verse, "I am equal toward all beings. Or else, he is the "Samavartī" because he exists within—having entered all things, whether sentient or insentient—as their internal controller; as the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *samavartī* should be understood as meaning 'equal toward all virtuous persons. His state of being such is *samavartitā*.

By her [name], he was one whose fame was celebrated and whose renown was well-known; he whose mind was preeminent is thus described—meaning "high-minded" (mahāśaya), or rather, "most noble" (mahodāra). And this nobility consists in his delight in giving without regard for the insignificance of the recipient or the magnitude of the gift, following the principle of inheritance (dāyabhāga-nyāya) and being indifferent to any return favor; furthermore, even after giving abundantly, he remains unsatisfied. For this very reason, he is a "bestower of fortune" (śrīdaḥ), granting all prosperity to those who seek refuge, like the King who is "the sole ruler of the world."

"He is the sovereign of the world of Brahmā, O Emperor! Viṣṇu, the great one who consists of Brahman, is the king of kings over all"—according to the manner stated in such passages, he is the supreme ruler of all worlds. He is the Lord whose power is thus renowned, the guardian of the world (*lokapāla*), the protector of the entire universe, as per the Śruti: "He is this guardian of the world. He surely rains down—that is, he most abundantly grants—our desires and heart's wishes, which are directed everywhere and are unimpeded; the word "us" is to be supplied. The particle *nanu* is used for emphasis. Alternatively, it may be read as two words: *na nu*.
The particle *nu* is used here in the sense of inquiry; the meaning is: "Does it not rain even more now? It is indeed raining."

In the case of Indra, he is so described because his name is renowned for its conformity with his essential nature through his appropriate conduct: *pracetāḥ* (the wise), *mahāmanāḥ* (the high-minded), and *śrīdaḥ* (the bestower of prosperity upon those who take refuge in him). He is known as a king (*rājā*), being celebrated as such from scriptural passages such as "Indra is the king of the world" and "To Indra, the king. He is a guardian of the world (*lokapāla*) and victorious (*jiṣṇu*), as Amarasimha states: "The victorious one is the bull among the gods (*lekhārṣabha*). Regarding *sarvatomukha*, it refers to water, as Amarasimha states: "*Puṣkara* is *sarvatomukha* (all-pervading)."
It rains exceedingly so that there may be sufficient desire, because rain depends upon him as the one who carries the rain-cloud.

On the side of Yama, he is victorious (jiṣṇu), characterized by triumph, wise (pracetāḥ), and a bestower of fortune (śrīda)—the meaning of these has already been explained. He is a king, for his kingship is established by the Vedic scripture: "Yama is the king who crushes [enemies] with his armies. His name "Samavartī" is renowned as a celebrated title; he is known as Samavartī. As a guardian of the world (lokapāla), he rains down desires (kāma) most abundantly in every direction—that is, he grants them to those who take refuge in him. This is because it was said by him personally to Naciketas: "Whatever desires are difficult to obtain in the mortal world, ask for all those desires according to your wish. This is the intended meaning.

In the section concerning Varuṇa, *pracetāḥ* is the substantive. *Samavartitā* means "he who exists equally"; this is derived from the root *vṛt* with the suffix *tṛc*. The meaning is the same as before. *Aprathitanāmā* is a separate word. He whose name (*nāma*) is proclaimed (*prathita*) or designated (*vyapadiṣṭa*) by the waters (*adbhiḥ*) is [thus called]; his name is so designated by the waters according to such Vedic texts as, "Varuṇa is the lord of the waters. He is also a king, according to such Vedic texts as, "May King Varuṇa lead you," and "Of whom Varuṇa is the king."

The other qualifiers have meanings exactly as previously stated. It should be understood that because he is the Lord of Waters (salilādhipati), he rains exceedingly in every direction at will; his raining occurs through the agency of the rain-god Parjanya.

In the case of Kubera’s side, "Śrīda" (the Giver of Fortune) is the substantive. The other epithets have the meanings already explained. His status as a king is established by the Vedic text: "Obeisance to Kubera Vaiśravaṇa, the Great King. Thus, although there is no difference in their status as guardians of the world (*lokapāla*) among all eight lords of the directions, the Veda proclaims that Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera alone possess the rank of kingship by virtue of being the lords of the great quarters (*mahādigadhīśa*).

However, it should be noted that this does not apply to the lords of the intermediate directions—Agni, Nirṛti, Marut, and Īśāna—since their sovereignty is not heard of in scripture. Śrīda (Kubera) rains down desire more intensely in every direction, according to the Vedic revelation: "May he grant my desires for me who desires desires; may Vaiśravaṇa, the lord of desire, bestow them."

In the lunar fortnight, however, the World-Protector [Candra], having extracted the eternal portions of Indra, Vāyu, Yama, and Ārka; of Agni and Varuṇa; and of Candra and Vitteśa— Please perform the translation.

Beginning with this introduction and stating, "The king is fashioned from the eight portions of the world-protectors (lokapālas)," the moon also possesses the status of a world-protector. The other epithets have meanings already explained above. The subject to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) is "the king," which here means the moon. His status as a king is established by the Vedic revelation: "Soma alone is our king, so say the Brāhmaṇa subjects. He rains down [his rays] most intensely in every direction—that is to say, without restraint—as he desires, meaning he utterly inflames the god of love (Manmatha).

If it is argued: "But since there is no fixed rule regarding the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) in all these examples you have established, how can this be an illustration of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), given that in examples such as 'May Mādhava, who is always [Sarvada] protect us,' a fixed rule is indeed observed"? To this we reply: "Understand that this is because there is no transgression of the rule that both [sets of words] must be *śliṣṭa* (paronomastic). For the definition of *śleṣa* consists precisely in the paronomasia of both the qualifier and the qualified. There is no insistence that the qualifiers or the qualified must necessarily be of a uniform form across all meanings."
This is because, for them, only the mere necessity of their being connected is required; such is the direction [of the argument]. Thus it should be understood in all cases.

"Just as a great sovereign lady, possessing noble character and having acquired fortune from a multitude of cows, radiant with wealth, attains the highest excellence"—here too, the Lord of Fortune (Viṣṇu) alone is the subject (*prakṛta*), while Bṛhaspati, Divaspati, Paśupati, Grahapati, Vasumatī, and Narapati are non-subjects (*aprakṛta*). There is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) of these seven; for instance, in the case of the "Lord of Fortune" (Śrīpati): "having acquired fortune from a multitude of cows"—the "multitude of cows" (*govisarā*) is a collection of waters (*gavām apām visarassamūhaḥ*), that is, the ocean; "fortune acquired from that" refers to one by whom the Goddess Lakṣmī has been obtained.
The word *go* is used for a cow, a sacrifice, a bull, the moon, speech, the earth, a quarter, and a milch-cow in the feminine;
however, it is used in the dual for rays, eyes, arrows, heaven, the thunderbolt, water, and hair.

Thus ends the *Ratnamālā*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *visara* means a spreading, a multitude, or a herd; *śrī* means the arrangement of dress, beauty, Sarasvatī, or the *sarala* tree; it refers to fortune (*lakṣmī*), the attainment of the three aims of life, various implements and so forth, as well as majesty, movement, and [the goddess] Strī."

"Exalted" (*udāram*) means the most excellent; "being" (*sattvam*) refers to that being which illuminates its own existence and is distinct from the *sattva* that is a *guṇa*. This describes her specific quality. Because of such statements as "That which is *sattva* is the divine Lord Hari," she possesses a non-material, divine, and auspicious form composed of pure *sattva*. Regarding the word "exalted" (*udāra*), it is known to mean "generous," "munificent," or "great. Regarding "being" (*sattvam*), it is used for a *guṇa*, for a *piśāca*, and for "determination" (*vyavasāya*) and "nature" (*svabhāva*).

And the *Ratnamālā* states: "In living beings, however, [the term] refers to the existence of qualities, life-force, strength, mind, and being. *Vasumatta* means that from which the *vasus*—the well-known specific deities—are *matta*, meaning satisfied; thus he is *vasumatta*.

The meaning is: she who shines in the sun—referring to the sun as "aviḥ" (the sheep/wool) because "in him [the sun] he shines," thus he is "dyotā" (the shining one)—and who, according to the method described in the Madhu-vidyā beginning with "This very sun is the honey of the gods" and continuing with "That which is the first nectar, the Vasus subsist upon that with Agni as their mouth; for the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar," is the one shining in the sun, which is the cause of the satisfaction of the Vasus, in the manner stated in the passage "And he who is in the sun."
The word *vasu* refers to a class of gods, to the yoktra (thong), Agni, and the rays of the sun;
it is used in three genders when meaning "sweet," and in the neuter when meaning water, wealth, or a jewel.
Thus ends the *Ratnamālā*. Regarding the word *hṛṣṭa*, Amara states: "It means joyful, intoxicated, or satisfied.
The word *avi* refers to a mountain, the sun, a ram, a mouse, a woolen blanket, a wall, a house, or light; as a feminine noun, however, it denotes a woman in her menses or the earth.

Thus ends the *Ratnamālā*. The Lord Vāsudeva—referred to in the passage, "The clarified butter is for the Great Deity (*mahate daivatāya*); He is the Deity of deities"—attains the supreme limit (*parāṃ kāṣṭhām*) of existence. The meaning is that He alone is the ultimate goal to be attained. For the Śruti says, "That is the limit; that is the supreme goal. Amara states: "The word *kāṣṭhā* [is used] in the sense of excellence, stability, and direction. Furthermore: "*Kāṣṭhaṃ* means wood; *kāṣṭhā*, however, [means] excellence, mere location, direction, turmeric, and also a specific measure of time."
Thus says Hemacandra.

She by whom prosperity (*śrī*)—in the form of the abundance of speech (*vākprasara*) consisting of a multitude of cows (*govisara*) during the fortnight of Bṛhaspati (*bṛhaspatipakṣe*), which is the divine teacher’s (*devācārya*) poetic power—is acquired, is so described. She whose noble (*udāra*), renowned, and virtuous nature (*sattva*) is scholarship (*vaiduṣya*)—according to Amara, "a *sat* is one who is wise, learned, or intelligent"—and whose possession of wealth (*vasumattā*) is brilliance (*tejasvitā*), that is to say, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

And that knowledge—both the knowledge of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, and the knowledge of wealth (*vasumattā*)—is not subject to the rule of the "shorter word first" (pūrvanipāta) here; for the sūtra beginning with *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ* indicates that such a rule is not absolute. Thus, there is no contradiction in placing the word *vidyā*, which has fewer syllables, after [the other term]. The meaning is that she is "woven" (*ūtā*) by the knowledge of wealth; according to Amara, *ūtam* means "sewn" (*syūtam*). This is derived from the root *veṅ* with the suffix *kta* in the passive sense, involving vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). The sense is that she is a great deity (*devatā*), worthy of worship by the gods, named Bṛhaspati.
She rests upon the highest pinnacle, that is, the utmost excellence.

"In the fortnight of the Lord of Heaven" (divaspatipakṣe) means with a multitude of eyes—that is, with a thousand eyes—[in the form of] a shower of rays. "She by whom beauty (śrī) has been acquired" is so described. "Of noble spirit" (udārasattvā) means of great resolve. "Vasumat" refers to those who possess the Vasus, a class of deities; the state of being such is "vasumattā. This is used in the neuter gender for the abstract quality, as in examples such as "the fulfillment of the purpose of autumn" (śaradaḥ kṛtārthatā). She is "illuminated on all sides" (āvidyotā) by that [state of being vasumat], meaning she shines constantly in the company of the Vasus due to her sovereignty over all the gods.

The "Great Deity" (Mahatī Devatā) is so called because she has attained greatness in accordance with the scriptural statement: "He who slew Vṛtra—that is Mahendra’s status as Mahendra. The "Deity" refers to the deity in the form of Indra. "Not the other" (aparām) means not the latter or western one; thus, it means the former or eastern direction. She has fully resorted to that quarter (kāṣṭhā), meaning the direction.

In the sense of Paśupati (Śiva), *go* means a bull; *visarā* means "one who moves about" (*visarati*), formed with the suffix *pacādyac*. *Govisarā* is a separate word, meaning "one who moves like a bull. She by whom *śrī*—meaning poison (*viṣa*)—has been taken up or drunk is so described. *Śrī* [is used] for dress, arrangement, beauty, prosperity, straight trees, speech, Lakṣmī, cloves, poison, and also for the *bilva* tree. .......................... (Note: The ellipsis indicates that the provided text fragment ends mid-definition of the term *śrī*.)

Thus [ends] the *Ratnamālā*. For this very reason, he is called Śrīkaṇṭha. She is so described because she possesses "udāra" (exalted) or great beings, such as *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, and so forth; the sense is that she is the mistress (*īśa*) of these beings. "Vasumān" means one who possesses *vasu*—that is, fire (*agni*). The state of being such is "vasumattā," which means possessing the fire of the eye on the forehead (*phālalocana*). The light (*aviḥ*) which is [produced] by that has been cited as the definition in the lexicon (*kośa*); it should not be forgotten. By that, she is "dyotā," meaning radiant.

Alternatively, *vasuḥ* means the giver of wealth; by that [giver of wealth], she is possessed of wealth (*vasumatā*). On that mountain named Kailāsa, which is thus [wealthy], or rather, on that mountain Kailāsa where the giver of wealth (*vasuḥ*)—the Giver of Wealth—is intoxicated (*mattaḥ*) with joy, she shines; such is the meaning, as both of them (Śiva and Pārvatī) have their abode on Kailāsa. She is a great deity, renowned as Mahādevī, and she takes refuge in the supreme quarter (*kāṣṭhā*), the direction of the North-East (*aiśānī*), which is established in the Smṛtis as the most excellent because of its praise: "The North-Eastern quarter is the best of directions."

The meaning is: she whose glory (*śrī*) is acquired through the expansion—that is, the multitude—of cows and directions on the side of the Lord of Planets (*grahapati*); thus, she is "the illuminator of all directions. The word *ari* means "possessing spokes" (*ara*), with the possessive suffix *ini* added to *cakra*; by virtue of that name, the *kokas* (ruddy geese) are intended here, as Amara states: "The *koka*, *cakra*, and *cakravāka* are named after the wheel (*rathāṅga*). A collection of enemies (*ari*) is called *āra*.

The term *sāmūhika* refers to the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ*. *Ārasattva* means the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) whose essence is noble; she is one by whom that [organ] has been made to shine forth, hence *udārasattvā*. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the elision of the word *lāsita* according to the rule *prādibhyo dhātujasya*. The word *vasu* means rays; he who possesses these is *vasumān*. The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of abundance (*bhūmani*) or excellence (*atiśāyane*).

The state of being that is "wealthiness" (*vasumattā*); by that [wealth], she is "illuminated" (*dyotā*). The sign of Aries (*meṣarāśi*) is called "Avidyota" because she shines therein; this is stated because the sign of Aries is her exaltation (*uccasthāna*), for as astrologers say: "In its own exaltation, it is radiant. She is the "Great Deity," meaning she is named the Sun (*sūrya*), who is worshipped at all three junctions of the day by everyone.

She "resorts to" (*samupāśrayate*) both the supreme eastern direction (*parāṃ... prācīm*) and the western direction (*paścimām... kāṣṭhām*)—the primary directions—in the manner described, for the purpose of rising and setting. This is the intended meaning.

On the side of Vasumatī (the Earth): *gāvaḥ* are cows; *avayaḥ* are sheep; *sarāṃsi* are lakes; *āpaḥ* are waters, meaning other waters such as those of rivers and so forth—or alternatively, the waters of lakes (*sarasām āpaḥ*). The compound *go'visaro'pam* is formed by the collective sense of these [words], with the suffix *ap* added according to the rule *ṛkpūrap* etc. She is described as one by whom *śrīḥ*—meaning beauty—is taken up (*āttā*) through that [compound]. She is one in whom there are *udārāḥ*, meaning great *sattvāḥ*, or living beings. Alternatively, *āraḥ* means Mars (*aṅgāraka*), according to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *āra* occurs in the feminine sense of a leather awl, and in the masculine sense of Mars or Saturn."

She who has that very *sattva* (essence) as her *garbha* (womb/embryo) is *udārasattvā*, meaning one whose essence is noble. The word *sattva* here signifies the embryo; for this reason, the term *āpannasattvā* is heard as a synonym for "pregnant. Indeed, Aṅgāraka (Mars) is said to have arisen from the womb of the Earth (*vasudhā*). He is indeed designated as "the red-bodied son of the Earth" (*rohitāṅgo mahīsutaḥ*). Furthermore, because she possesses wealth—whether in the form of gems or treasures in the shape of hoards—she is called *Vasumatī*. *Avayaḥ* refers to mountains.

She is so called because she shines by means of those who possess wealth (*vasumattā*) and are free from decay (*avaya*), thus being "the one shining through the wealthy and the undecaying. Alternatively, she is "non-illuminated" (*avidyotā*) in the sense that she does not lack illumination; the meaning is that she is eternally radiant due to her possession of wealth and her containing jewels within her womb (*ratnagarbhatā*). She is a great and vast deity in the form of the earth, for in the passage beginning "Come, let me enter these three deities," the earth is heard to be designated as a deity by the word "food" (*anna*). She rests upon the highest pinnacle, meaning she pervades all directions.

She by whom prosperity (*śrī*)—meaning wealth or majesty—has been acquired from the king’s side, from herds of cattle, from the acquisition of various lands, from the extension of her gaze, or from the discharge of arrows; who has brought it forth from the circle of neighboring vassals; she whose noble nature (*sattva*) consists of strength, vitality, or generosity of heart; who is intoxicated or satisfied with riches (*vasu*); who shines with walls (*avi*), palaces, splendors, or indeed with all things; and whose treasury (*kośa*) has been proclaimed as not to be forgotten—she is thus described.

The Great Deity in the form of a king, for it is remembered in scripture: "Indeed, this Great Deity exists in human form. She has fully attained the supreme pinnacle—the highest state, namely the position of sovereign overlordship. Thus it is said.

In this manner, it is possible to compose paronomasia (śleṣa) involving eight, nine, ten, or even more than that many meanings; nevertheless, one desists out of fear that there might be excessive strain for the divine goddess of speech (Bhagavatī Bhāratī).

Thus, the threefold nature of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) has been elaborated by way of its having as its scope the relevant (*prakṛta*), the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*), and both. In that regard, the distinction between the forms of *sabhaṅga* (with word-splitting) and *abhaṅga* (without word-splitting) has been shown in general. Now, its specific divisions are being elaborated. Here, the author of the *Kaustubha* states: "Paronomasia is both *sabhaṅga* and *abhaṅga*. The state of being *sabhaṅga* consists in the presence of another meaning to be understood through the recollection of words possessing a different sequence of phonemes (*vibhinnānupūrvīka-śabda-pratisandhāna*)."

"Non-śleṣa (the absence of punning) consists in the fact that the different meanings understood are not conveyed by words possessing an identical sequence of phonemes (*samānānupūrvīka*). Both types of this *śleṣa* are indeed figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) alone; for even when multiple-meaning words are present, if the other meaning does not connect with the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the designation of *śleṣa* is absent. And the first [type] is eightfold, due to the distinctions of phoneme (*varṇa*), word (*pada*), gender (*liṅga*), language (*bhāṣā*), case-ending (*vibhakti*), stem (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and number (*vacana*)"—so he [Mammaṭa] stated. To explain: "The first [type of] *śleṣa* is said to be eightfold, through phoneme, word, gender, and language, as well as through case-ending, stem, suffix, and number. (77)

And therein, *varṇaśleṣa* (phonetic punning) occurs where, by virtue of case endings and so forth, various phonemes are heard as having a single form; for that is called *varṇaśleṣa* by the learned. (78)
That wherein several phonemes are heard as having a single form through the power of case endings and so forth is called *varṇaśleṣa* (phonemic paronomasia).

Just as my mind delights in the flute that is the cause of the highest good and the ornament that brings auspiciousness, so may my heart be fixed upon you, the Blessed One, the Lord of Gods, who is compassionate toward me.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between Lakṣmī and Śrīnivāsa. Regarding Lakṣmī: "O Goddess of the Gods" (*deveśvari*)—the term *īśānā* means the sovereign of the gods, and this is her vocative address. The suffix *ṅīp* is not applied because the word ends in *varaṭ* according to the rule beginning with "stheśabhāsa. O Blessed One (*bhagavati*), O cause (*hetu*) of all that is auspicious (*śreyasām*). For it is said: "Indeed, for men traveling upon the paths of worldly existence, the imperishable state, or the Vaiṣṇava path, no welfare (*śreyaḥ*) is ever possible without the grace of the beloved of the lotus-eyed Lord's heart."

She is so described because she possesses braids (*veṇi*) which are ornaments that produce beauty; she is one who has such braids (*praveṇī*). This word *veṇi* ends in the vowel *i*. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *veṇṛ*, belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* (meaning "to observe, to play musical instruments, to take, to go, to know, and to think"), the *uṇādi* suffix *in* is applied. Amara states: "Veṇī and praveṇī. The *Nigama* lexicon, in its section on feminine nouns, says: "Karaṇa, śroṇī, and veṇī. And there is the usage of the poet Murāri Miśra: "The goddess gave birth to you, whose binding of the celestial nymphs' braids was crushed by enemies."

In her whose knees shine with the form of a jeweled mirror, so described; in her whose friend is compassion—that is to say, in her who is overcome by compassion—may my mind enter you. The verb *vi-ni-viś* (from the root *viś* preceded by *ni*) takes the Ātmanepada ending according to the rule *nerviśaḥ*.

In the case of Śrīnivāsa, however, there is a word-split (*ccheda*) as *deva* in the phrase *deveśvare*. Thus, it means: O Lord (*deva*), to Him who possesses most excellent (*śreyasyaḥ*, i.e., more praiseworthy) weapons (*hetayaḥ*), that is, divine arms; and to Him whose flute is an ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*) of His auspicious hands (*karayoḥ*, i.e., His two hands)—the meaning being that He holds the flute in His hand for the purpose of singing.

"In him whose wife shines forth (*samullasaj-jāni*) because she possesses a beautiful, divine form"—in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *niṅ* is applied according to the rule *jāyāyā niṅ*, and the semivowel *y* is elided by the rule *lopo vyor vali*. This recalls the Vedic scripture: "To Viṣṇu, the one with a beautiful wife" (*sumajjānaye viṣṇave*). [The word] *dayālu* means "compassionate," derived from the root *day* (to pity) with the suffix *āluc* according to the rule *spṛhi-gṛhi-pati-dayi-ādinā āluc*.

"May the mind be fixed upon You, the Lord, the Blessed One, who possesses uncontracted sovereignty because of Your designation as 'Īśvara' (the Sovereign) without any limiting adjuncts. Herein, in the phrase "in the cause (hetau), in the braid (veṇau), in the knee (jānau), O compassionate one (dayālau)," the words *hetu*, *veṇi*, *veṇu*, *jāni*, *jānu*, *dayāli*, and *dayālu* are phonetically fused (*śliṣṭa*) because their vowel *e* and *o* are identical objects of pronunciation when inflected in the locative case. Furthermore, in the phrase "in the Lord (īśvare), the Blessed One (bhagavati)," a fusion of the vocative and locative case endings is additionally superimposed according to the method to be described below.
