"Or rather: May my heart always cling for a long time to some deity dwelling in the abode of the Ocean of Milk—a divine boat for crossing the ocean of misfortune, [yet] in the case of Śrīnivāsa, one who is 'without arrows' (aśarāru), meaning non-violent, whose nature is grace and who does not employ punishment; whereas in the other case, the word is split as 'āśarārau': the enemy (aru) of the *āśaras* (demons), for Amara states, 'The flesh-eater, the blood-drinker, is the *āśara*. In this instance as well, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) specifically between Śrī and Śrīnivāsa. "Aśarāru" means non-violent, in the sense that he possesses a nature of compassion and does not recognize [the need for] punishment. In the alternative case, the division is "āśarārau. He is the adversary (*aru*) of the *āśaras*, the Rākṣasas; according to Amara, "The flesh-eater, the blood-drinker, is the *āśara*."

"Durgativārāśi" refers to the ocean of misfortune, such as poverty, which is like a vast sea; for it is said [of the Kalpa tree] that it is "the one that carries across the ocean of poverty," and so forth. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "Durgati means hell or destitution. In the alternative sense, "durgati" is hell, which is itself an ocean; the "divyatarau" refers to a divine, marvelous boat (*tari*) for crossing that [ocean].

May my heart always cling to that certain deity—who is of the nature of Śrī and the abode of Śrī (Śrīnivāsa), and who is so described as having his birth, dwelling, and home in the ocean-jar (kalaśodadhi) and the milk-ocean (dugdhajaladhi). Herein, in the phrase "sadā-āśarārau divyatarau," there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) of the phonemes 'u' and 'i' from the words *aśarāru*, *āśarāri*, *divyataru*, and *divyatari* when placed in the locative case.

O lotus-eyed one, O bestower of all, just as the wise, knowing You alone to be the sun that eternally dispels darkness within their own selves, are liberated and attain intense bliss—alas! [so it is]. (883)

The giver of everything is the "Giver of All" (*sarvadātā*); his perfect awakening is *sarvadātaḥ*. According to the scriptural statement, "He who is the giver of self and the giver of strength," and "Viṣṇu is indeed the bestower of all fruits," the meaning is that he has the nature of giving away his entire being, including even his own self. O Lotus-eyed One (*abjākṣa*)! By this, the intended meaning of the Śruti passage, "Just as a lotus is golden-hued, so are his eyes," is recalled. In the atom (*aṇau*), that is, in that which has the dimension of an atom, according to the Śruti: "This Self is atomic."

In accordance with the statement, "Non-selfhood has arisen in the self, while lordship resides in Brahman," the meaning is that [the Lord] impels—that is, urges on—the sleeping sense organs within the inner self (pratyagātman), which is one's own true nature belonging to the Lord. By this, the Vedic mantra "May He impel our thoughts" (*dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*) is recognized.

Alternatively, the meaning is that [the Lord], abiding as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) according to the manner stated in the passage, "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self," impels the intellects that are the means for attaining Himself, in the manner described by the words, "May that God unite us with auspicious mindfulness. In this regard, one should recall the verse: "I give that yoga of intellect by which they come unto Me. It is not merely this; He abides within His own self, which is His own body, according to the Śruti: "He whose body is the sun."

"Self, effort, fortitude, intellect, nature, Brahman, and the body"—thus says Amara. The word division is "sarvadā taraṇau ca udayamānam. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is with "taraṇau ca": You, who are always rising—that is, shining—within the sun (*taraṇi*, the solar orb). By this composition, the scriptural passage from the *Śruti*, "That which is here in the person, and that which is yonder in the sun," is brought to mind. "One" means existing in both places as non-different.

By this, the phrase "He is one" (sa ekaḥ), found in the remainder of the cited scripture, is made recognized. "Knowing" (vidantaḥ) means understanding; by this, the phrase "he who knows thus" (sa ya evaṃ vit) is indicated. "The wise ones" (sudhiyaḥ) means the learned; being liberated, by this, the attainment of the state beyond darkness—preceded by traveling the path beginning with light—is described, as stated in the passage "having departed from this world. "They find intense bliss" (amandamānandaṃ vindanti); by this, the meaning of the scripture, "he reaches this Self consisting of bliss" (etamānandamayamātmānam upasaṅkrāmati), is fully summarized.

The meaning of the cited scripture has been described by Vyāsārya as follows: "Every wise person, having departed from this world, experiences the Supreme Self—the object of enjoyment—which consists of unsurpassed bliss and possesses the collective and individual manifestations beginning with the *annamaya*, while being the enjoyer himself. The exclamation *hanta* expresses the joy born from contemplating such a meaning. Here, as before, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the letters *i* and *u* in the seventh case endings of the words *taraṇi* and *aṇu*.

In the three examples beginning with "sarvadātaḥ," there is a division such as *sarvadā ataḥ* (always from [him]) and *sarvadā taraṇau* (always in the boat/savior), and there is also the concatenation of words to be mentioned later. In these three examples, beginning with "śreyohetau" (in the cause of welfare), there is conformity with the general definition of *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* (pun with word-break), because two distinct meanings are communicated through the recollection of two words of different sequences—such as *hetu* and *hetivaiṇu*, or *veṇu* and *veṇī*—being brought within the scope of a single utterance.

In the rule *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23) and others, although there is no difference in the sequence [of sounds] after the substitution [of *gha* for *ghi*] by the rule *acca gheḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.119), one should observe that the substitute (*ādeśin*) possesses a different sequence [from the original], because a difference is seen in the substituted form itself. This should be inferred in other cases as well.
Word-pun (padaśleṣa) is that pun which is based on a division of words. || 79 ||
May He,

the self-born, protect us— He whose heart is tender with affection for those who have approached Him as His own children, who possesses the ever-present glory of true friends, who plucks the lotus-heart of the sins of the Kali age, and who is an ocean of auspicious virtues.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) on the two Śrīs. In the sense of Lakṣmī (*Śrī*), she is one whose mind is affectionate—that is, characterized by love—toward the Earth-goddess (*Kṣmā-Devī*), who is full of maternal tenderness (*vātsalya*) toward those who have approached for refuge. This is because the Earth is specifically described as "the goddess who is the dear friend of Lakṣmī. She is a true and virtuous friend (*satsuhṛd*), for the *Amara-kośa* states: "The word *sat* is used in the senses of truth, the good, that which exists, the excellent, and the venerable. Her fortune (*śrī*) is eternal.

She is called *suhṛdyā* because she is exceedingly dear to the hearts of the virtuous, or because she is their eternal and imperishable friend (*suhṛd*). She is one whose splendor (*śrī*), beauty, or prosperity is such; she is the remover of the impurities of the Kali age (*kalikalmaṣahṛt*). She is one whose qualities (*guṇas*) are auspicious (*kalyāṇa*). She is self-born (*svabhū*), meaning her birth depends on her own will and is not produced by karma; thus she is "self-born in the ocean" (*ambudhisvabhū*). May that Padmā, Śrī, protect us. Thus [ends the verse].

In the interpretation of Śrīśa (Viṣṇu), however: *vaṃse* means on the chest; according to Amarasimha, "the chest is called *vatsa*. He by whom the *lakṣma*—the mark known as Śrīvatsa—has been "samupanata," meaning attained, is *samupanatavatsalakṣmā*. His mind is affectionate toward the *santaḥ*, those who know Brahman, because of the song: "And he is dear to me. He is so-called because his *hṛdyā*—eternal (*nityā*) because of the statement "This Mother of the World is eternal"—*śrīḥ*, Lakṣmī, resides upon his chest (*vakṣas-sthā*). The word should be divided as *kalikalmaṣahṛt-pām-ā*.

He is so described because his feet—referring to the word *padau* which means "feet" (*caraṇau*) according to Amara’s lexicon (*padaṅghriścaraṇo'striyām*)—are said to remove the impurity of the Kali age.
As long as he touched this earth with his two lotus-feet,
Kali was not capable of embracing the world.

This is what is intended here: "May the Lord Keśava Mādhava, the self-born ocean of auspicious qualities—*svabhūḥ* (self-born) according to Amara’s lexicon—" protect me (*mām*). The construction is *mā mām avyāt*. Even in the case of non-repetition (*ananvādeśa*), the optional substitution of *mā* for *mām* indeed occurs, because it is stated: "These substitutions, beginning with *vām* and *nau*, are optionally prescribed when there is no repetition. In the word *padmā* within the *saṃhitā*, there is no substitution of the nasal *n* for the final consonant, because the rule *yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* prescribes that such a substitution is optional.

In this context, in examples such as "samupanatavatsalakṣmā," the pun (*śleṣa*) is based on the division of words; this very type is called *sabhanga-śleṣa* (pun with word-splitting) by the author of the *Kāvyadarpaṇa*.

The "fusion of genders" (liṅgaśleṣa) is to be understood as occurring through the contraction or expansion of syllables; it consists in the identical form of words belonging to the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders.

The meaning is this: if the identity of gender—whether feminine, masculine, or neuter—is described through short or long syllables, by treating a short vowel as long or a long vowel as short, or through compounds, that is *liṅgaśleṣa* (punning on gender). For example:

"May he who possesses a certain majesty, who leads us to the highest good, who holds a lotus in the tip of his hand, who possesses motherhood for the three worlds, and who is ever awake in fulfilling our desires, [protect us]. (885) [In this verse, the same word *mahaḥ* can be interpreted as masculine (*mahaḥ* = majesty) or neuter (*mahaḥ* = light), and *mātṛtvabhāk* can be read as feminine (*mātṛtva-bhāk* = possessing motherhood) or masculine (*mātṛ-tva-bhāk* = possessing the nature of a mother).]

Here too, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) specifically between the two Lords, Śrī and Śrīśa. [The Lord] is "possessing motherhood" (*mātṛtvabhāk*), meaning he possesses the state of being the mother of the three worlds—that is, the state of being a progenitor—as well as the agency of measuring [the universe] by means of the three steps. [The suffix] *ṇvi* is applied to the root *bhaj*. He is "vigilant" (*jāgrat*) in granting the desired objects to those who are deeply bowed down; [this refers to the form] *jāgarūka*, and in the alternative [grammatical] case, the absence of the nasal augment (*num*) is according to the rule "not after a reduplicated stem before the suffix *śatṛ*" (*anābhyastāc chatuḥ*). He is "bearing" (*dadhāna*) a lotus (*abja*) and a conch (*śaṅkha*) upon the tips of his hands; [this refers to the form] *dadhat*.

Some great light—a reality determined as such by its splendor—is perceived as having the form of Śrī through the power of its attributes; may it lead us, its own people, to the highest good and auspiciousness.

In this alternative interpretation, *mahassvān* is a single word. By the power of its qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), *mahassvān*—meaning "possessing majesty" or "radiant"—is understood to refer to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavān*). The construction is: "May He lead us to some form of ultimate welfare. In the term *mahassvān*, because it is designated as a *bha*-stem by the rule *tasau matvarthe*, the status of being a complete word (*pada*) does not apply, and thus rules such as the substitution of *r* (rutva) do not take effect. In this interpretation, one should understand that the *s* in *mahassvān* undergoes doubling according to the rule *anaci ca*.

May he whose auspicious eyes are enamored of the lotus, whose fame is born from an ocean of nectar-like parrot-speech, and who captivates the hearts of the most radiant Bhāmā, protect us constantly. 886.

Here too, there is a *śleṣa* (punning connection) between Śrī and Śrīśa (the Lord). It should be understood that in the case of Śrī, the adjectives end in the nominative singular; in the case of Śrīśa, they end in the vocative. She whose auspicious gaze is attached to lotuses—that is, she whose eyes are friends to the lotus—is "kamalasuhṛnnayanā. She whose speech is like the speech of a parrot (*śuka*) is "śukavāk. She who is born from the ocean of nectar, produced from the milk-ocean, is "amṛtābdhijā. She who possesses widespread fame is "tatayaśobhāk. She whose luster is greatly brilliant is "mahojjvalabhās."

The analysis of the compound is *mā-maṇihāri-hṛt*. She whose chest (*hṛt*) is so described—meaning it possesses a necklace of jewels (*maṇihāra*)—is *Mā*, that is, Lakṣmī. The sense is: "May she protect us constantly; she must surely guard us, there is no doubt about this."

In the sense of the Blessed One (Bhagavat), [the term] refers to Him whose auspicious gaze is devoted to Padmā, that is, Lakṣmī; this is the vocative address. The speech of Śuka—that is, the great sage Śuka—is the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* itself, which is like an ocean of nectar (*amṛtābdhi*). That which is born from it is "born from the nectar-ocean of Śuka’s speech" (*śukavāgamṛtābdhijam*). He who possesses such widespread fame is so described; this is the vocative address meaning, "O You of vast renown celebrated through the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*! The phrase *mahojjvalabhāmāmaṇihārihṛdi* is a single, compound word.

"Jvalā" means that which burns; it is derived from the root *jval* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). "Mahojvalā" means one who blazes with splendor (*mahaḥ*); according to the rule "anaci ca," there is a doubling of the letter *j*. [O Lord] whose chest (*hṛt*) is captivating (*hāri*, i.e., beautiful) because of that Lakṣmī who is the jewel of beauty (*bhāmāmaṇiḥ*). This is the vocative case. The word division is "pāyāḥ deva. O God! O Blessed One! protect us constantly—this is the imperative sense. The verb *pā* (to protect) is used here in the middle voice, first person singular, in the benedictive mood (*āśīrliṅ*). In the preceding part of the verse, it was used in the second person singular.

In these two verses, because words such as *dadhat* (bearing), which possess both masculine and neuter genders, fall within the scope of a single utterance, there is a "śleṣa of gender" (*liṅgaśleṣa*). Such an example of *liṅgaśleṣa* is provided here in accordance with the illustrations given by the author of the *Alaṅkāra-kaustubha*. In reality, however, according to his own view, this is not an illustration; for he first asserts that the eightfold *śleṣas*—beginning with those of phonemes (*varṇa*)—are "with break" (*sabhanga*), and having refined the definition of "being with break" as "the state of conveying a different meaning through the recognition of words with distinct sequences of sounds," he provides the following example: *unnidrābja-pariṣkṛta-pravara-doḥ-prahvībhavaddaivataḥ*... [and so forth].* (Note: The final portion of the verse cited is incomplete in the source text.)

May the face of the slayer of Kaiṭabha, or the moonlight of the conqueror of Madana, protect us— that face which is like a blooming lotus, resembling a mass of unfolding thick white lotuses, and made radiant by the moonlight of jewels struck against the slopes of the crowns of the guilds of gods.

Having cited this, it was stated: "In this instance, the form of *doḥ* and so forth is the same in the neuter, masculine, and feminine genders. And thus, since in that example there is a single uniform form for all three genders in sequence (as in *dadhat*, etc.), and in our own example there is likewise no difference in sequence between the masculine and neuter genders, this cannot be an example of *sabhaṅga-liṅga-śleṣa* (pun on gender with a break); rather, it is simply an example of *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (unbroken pun), like the word *hari* and others.

Now, one might object: "In words such as *hari* and others, since there is no difference in gender, let it be that the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) is undifferentiated; however, in cases such as *dadhat* and *dadau*, because there is a difference in gender, the sequence must be differentiated. This is not so, for the difference in gender is not the cause of that [differentiation]. What is called "sequence" in words is the state of being the final phoneme qualified by each preceding phoneme through the relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*). And since this is seen to be indeed undifferentiated in the instances shown, where could there be a state of having a differentiated sequence?

Nor can the distinction between those [words] be maintained on the basis of differences in meaning, such as masculine or neuter gender, because even the difference in meaning does not serve as the determinant for that [distinction]. Even if one were to admit that gender is a property residing in the word itself, gender would not be a constituent of the *ānupūrvī* (the sequential order). For what is called "gender" is indeed a certain property residing in the word—consisting of femininity, masculinity, and so forth—which is entirely distinct from the *ānupūrvī*, just like the properties of being high-pitched (*udātta*) or low-pitched (*anudātta*).

For this very reason, the statement in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*—"in words such as *taṭa* (bank) which share the same phonetic sequence (*ānupūrvī*), there are three genders"—is consistent. If one were to admit that gender is also included within the phonetic sequence, then in examples such as "Your face is equal to the *abja*; your eyes are like the *kamala*," the two words *abja* and *kamala* would differ in their phonetic sequence due to the difference in gender, resulting in the undesirable consequence that they would constitute *sabhaṅga-śleṣa* (pun with broken word-structure). And if this were accepted as desired, it would contradict the consensus of all rhetoricians (*alaṅkārika*) that such instances are cases of *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (pun without broken word-structure).

Therefore, grammatical gender (*liṅga*) cannot constitute the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*), because such a distinct sequence is impossible in words like *pravara* and *dora* found in the examples previously shown; thus, it is not appropriate for them to be considered examples of *sabhaṅga-avāntara-liṅgaśleṣa*. However, the example of *liṅgaśleṣa* given by the author of the *Kāvyadarpaṇa*—"May Hari, who possesses the luster of a blue lotus, protect your eye"—is perfectly valid according to that [author's] own system, since there is no contradiction even if that [gender] is subject to *bhaṅga*.

For, having cited the *padaśleṣa* (word-pun) as included within the eightfold classification of *śleṣa*, he stated that this alone constitutes *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* (pun with word-break). However, he did not explicitly state that other varieties are either *abhaṅga* (without break) or *sabhaṅga*. Therefore, his intention is inferred to be that *varṇaśleṣa* (phoneme-pun) and the others are included, as appropriate, within either *sabhaṅga* or *abhaṅga* *śleṣa* beyond the *padaśleṣa*. As for the author of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, however, he states:
"When multiple meanings are expressed by means of *śliṣṭa* (coalescent) words, it is desired as *śleṣa*;
[this occurs] through phonemes (*varṇa*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), genders (*liṅga*), two bases (*prakṛti*), or even two words (*pada*)."

Having thus defined the eightfold *śleṣa* (punning) through the variations of case-endings, numbers, and languages, and so forth, he further classifies it as threefold: with word-break (*sabhanga*), without word-break (*abhaṅga*), and consisting of both.

Thus, having again divided [the śleṣa] into three types, he stated: "These three varieties are to be understood as occurring, as applicable, within the eight aforementioned varieties. Consequently, according to the view of the *Kāvyadarpaṇa* and other such works, even though examples such as "bearing the luster of a blue lotus" (*bibhrannīlotpalarucim*) and "possessing" (*dadhat*) constitute non-ambiguous śleṣa (*abhaṅgaśleṣa*), their status as illustrations of gender-śleṣa (*liṅgaśleṣa*) remains entirely unrestricted. However, according to the view of the *Alaṅkārakaustubha*, because its own definition does not apply in the manner explained above, its example of gender-śleṣa—beginning with "of excellent arms" (*pravaradoḥ*)—is indeed incorrect. Nevertheless, this following example will serve as an illustration even according to that school's view: [Example: *“The Lord of the Gods, who bears the splendor of the moon, who possesses the brilliance of the sun, and who holds the earth, is victorious.”* In this instance, the words *induśobhām*, *arkarociḥ*, and *urvīdharam* are each capable of being interpreted in two ways based on their respective genders; thus, they are examples of gender-śleṣa. Furthermore, in the verse beginning with “the one who has a beautiful face” (*sundarānanā*), the word *sundarānanā* is a feminine noun, while *sundarānanaḥ* is a masculine noun; since both are possible through the application of the suffix *aṇ*, this is an example of gender-śleṣa. Similarly, in the verse beginning with “the one who has a beautiful body” (*sundarāṅgī*), the word *sundarāṅgī* is feminine, while *sundarāṅgaḥ* is masculine; since both are possible through the application of the suffix *ac*, this too is an example of gender-śleṣa. Likewise, in the verse beginning with “the one who has a beautiful form” (*sundarākṛtiḥ*), the word *sundarākṛtiḥ* is feminine, while *sundarākṛtiḥ* is masculine; since both are possible through the application of the suffix *ktin*, this also is an example of gender-śleṣa. You are the one who brings joy to the entire world, you are the remover of inauspiciousness, and you alone are the creator of well-being; O Hari, having placed my supreme mind upon you, the most delightful Supreme Self, here I offer my highest devotion.

Here too, there is a *śleṣa* (punning connection) between the two Śrīs (Lakṣmī and Śrī). "Ātmanīnā" means that which is highly beneficial (*bhṛśam hitā*) for the Self (*ātmane*), that is, the Supreme Self (*paramātmane*). Its vocative is "he ātmanīne! The suffix *kha* is applied in the sense of "beneficial" according to the rule *ātman-viśvajana-* etc. There is the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ātmādhvānau khe*. O Rame! You are the one who gladdens the entire world, thus you are "akhilajagadānandī"; you are the remover of inauspiciousness, thus you are "aśubhahārī"; and you alone bring about auspiciousness, thus you are "śubhakārī."

In all these cases, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇi 'ṭiḍhḍhāṇañ*. Here, having placed your mind upon you—upon this [deity] (*asyām*)—I remove (*harāmi*) the subsequent sin (*enaḥ*), that is, the transgression occurring after the act of total surrender (*bharanyāsa*). According to Amara, "sin" (*enah*) is synonymous with "impurity," "evil," and "transgression. The sense is that since previous sins have already been destroyed and future sins do not adhere, I take them away. This is the first person singular of the present tense (*laṭ*) in the ātmanepada for the root *hṛ* (to take).

In the interpretation according to the Lord (Bhagavat), the word division is: *ātmani ine manorame parame naḥ*. O Hare! You are called such because you intensely cause joy (*ānandayati*) to the entire world; you are the remover of the inauspicious (*aśubha-hārī*). You alone are the performer of the auspicious (*śubha-kārī*). By these two epithets, [the text] shows that you cast away inauspiciousness and extend a continuous stream of auspiciousness.
"That which, by mere remembrance, bestows upon men the state of Brahman—that is the supreme blessing (*maṅgala*)."

Thus the meaning of the authoritative proof has been summarized. Everywhere, according to the rule *supyajātau* [Pāṇini 3.2.78], the suffix *ṇini* is applied. O *ine* (O Lord), who are captivating to the mind with auspicious qualities such as beauty and good character, and who are delightful; in you—this very one, the supreme Self, the innermost Self of all—we, "us," should place (*nyasyāḥ*). The meaning is: "You should make us those whose burden is placed in you. This is the second person singular present middle voice of the root *as* belonging to the *divādi* class, preceded by the prefix *ni*.

In this instance, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the feminine and masculine genders in the three qualifiers beginning with "jagadānandī" (delighting the world), because they are heard in an identical form. Although the sequence of phonemes differs due to one being formed with a *ṅī*-suffix (*ānandī*) and the other with a *ṇini*-suffix (*ānandin*), the two meanings are understood through the recollection of such words; thus, they conform to the general definition of *śleṣa*. Furthermore, in the phrase "nyasya hare," there is a *śleṣa* between the case-ending (*sup*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). It should also be noted that in "ātmanīne manorame paramenaḥ," there is a *pada-śleṣa* (word-pun). Although the sequence of phonemes differs due to one being formed with a *ṅī*-suffix (*ānandī*) and the other with a *ṇini*-suffix (*ānandin*), the two meanings are understood through the recollection of such words; thus, they conform to the general definition of *śleṣa*. Furthermore, in the phrase "nyasya hare," there is a *śleṣa* between the case-ending (*sup*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). May the Greatly Auspicious Mother of the World, who favors the virtuous, who protects all those who have abandoned worldly attachments, and who is highly honored by the king of the gods, shine forth for me. 888.

Here too, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *bhagavatī* (the Blessed One) and *lakṣmī* (fortune). She is the "protector" (*pātā*), meaning the guardian, of the party of the virtuous; and she is also described as one who has "partiality for the virtuous" (*sādhujanapakṣapātā*). Furthermore, she is the "savior" (*trātā*), the protector, of the crow (*vāyasa*)—the son of Indra—who was abandoned by all, according to the manner stated in the passage, "He was abandoned by his father," and thus neglected by the entire world. And she is one by whom such a crow was saved. This is well-known from the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*.

The Mother of the worlds is the creator and progenitor by means of three steps. The King of the Gods (surarāṭ) is the sovereign lord of the deities. The word *bahu* is a separate term that connects with the subsequent [words]. The Measurer (mānetā) is the illustrious Leader (Śrīnāyaka). Alternatively, the entire phrase beginning with *surarāṭ* is a compound: "she who is reached (i.e., endowed) with the great honor and excessive worship of Surarāja (Indra). The suffix *kta* is used here for the root *iṇ*. Thus, the meaning is "she who is honored by him. This is well-known in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas.

He who possesses "sumahatī śrīḥ"—that is, great and highly venerable fortune (śrī), Lakṣmī, or prosperity—is so described. This is an epithet of the very one who is addressed as "māneta. Alternatively, *sumahaḥ* may mean "one of beautiful luster" (*śobhanatejāḥ*). Or, there may be a word-break after *sumaha*, with the suffix *-i* added, meaning "one of beautiful festivals" (*śobhanotsava*). May that Śrī, Lakṣmī, manifest and shine forth for me. Here, because the masculine and feminine genders are the object of a single utterance, there is a "śleṣa of gender" (*liṅgaśleṣa*).

It should be noted that this is a "sabhaṅga" (broken) type of pun, because the two meanings are understood through the recollection of words with different phonetic sequences (*anupūrvī*), such as "partiality toward virtuous people" (*sādhujanapakṣapātṛtva*) versus "the state of being partiality itself toward virtuous people" (*sādhujanapakṣapātatva*).
Linguistic Pun (*bhāṣāśleṣa*):
Linguistic pun occurs through the unification of various languages that have different meanings.
(81) When there is a conjunction (*śleṣa*) of various languages possessing different meanings, it is linguistic pun.

I praise Him whose arms are equal [in length], whose innate essence is the nectar of compassion, whose luster is straight, who has dispelled delusion, who is the abode of Lakṣmī, and who dwells upon the mountain Mahendra. 889.

In this context, the Sanskrit language is devoted to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), while the Prakrit language is devoted to Lakṣmī. For instance, in the case of the Blessed One: *bāhāsamaṃ* means "unequaled by arms," that is, by *bāhābhiḥ* (arms), meaning he possesses four extraordinary arms, peerless in their skill at protecting the entire world. *Sahajasampariṇāhidayārasaṃ* refers to him whose innate (*sahaja*) and expansive (*sampariṇāhī*) essence of compassion (*dayārasaḥ*) is naturally perfected. *Saralabhāsaṃ* refers to him whose radiance (*bhāḥ*) is straightforward (*saralā*) and noble (*udārā*).

I praise the abode of Kamalā (Śrīnivāsa), whose neck is beautiful—meaning auspicious due to being marked with three lines—and who is called "Tamo-han" because he destroys darkness, which is ignorance; [the suffix] *ḍa* is applied to the root *han* according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well. Furthermore, he is "Hara," so called because he seizes or withdraws [the world], and thus "Ahi-hara" is one who destroys serpents, the ender of the nāgas; [the meaning is] that he dwells within him, having Garuḍa as his vehicle. I laud him, the dwelling place of Lakṣmī.

In the case of Lakṣmī, *bāhāsamaṃ* means "that which pacifies suffering. It is called *śamā* because it pacifies (*śamayati*), with the suffix *pacādyac*. Thus, it is that which pacifies *bādhā*, meaning the affliction of the world. By the rule "khaghadhathabhāṃ haḥ," the letter *dh* in the word *bādhā* is replaced by *h*. By the rule "śossal," the letter *ś* in the word *śama* is replaced by *s*. By the rule "svarasya bindvami," the vowel *ā* in the word *samā* is shortened. The same applies in subsequent instances. *Sahajasaṃ* means "possessing innate glory" (*yaśasā sahitāṃ*), according to the rule "tena saha."

By the rule *ityādinā*, because the application of *av* in the compound *avopasarjanasya* is optional, there is an absence of the substitution of *sa*. By the rule *āderjaḥ*, the *ya* of the word *yaśas* becomes *ja*. By the rule *antyahalo’śradudī*, the final *s* is elided. By the rule *snamadāmaśironabhonari*, although the word *yaśas* is masculine, it takes the feminine gender in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The short vowel is as before. [The compound means] "one whose essence of compassion is expansive," that is, one whose essence of great pity is vast.

In the rule *prāyo luk kaga-caja-tadapayavām*, because of the inclusion of the word *prāyaḥ* (generally), there is no elision (*luk*) of the letter *y* in the word *dayā*. Since it has been stated that "in a compound, even a difference in words is accepted with respect to the case-endings of the sentence," as in the case of *sudoha* and so forth, there is no elision of the letter *d* in the word *dayāśa*. [The term] *saralabhāsaṃ* means *saralabhāṣām*, i.e., "of noble speech. By the rule *śossaḷ*, the sibilant *ṣ* becomes *s*.

In the compound *bhāsam*, because it consists of separate words as before, the letter *bha* is at the beginning; therefore, by the rule *“khaghathadhabhāṃ haḥ”* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), there is no substitution of *ha*. This is because the term *“akhoḥ”* (not after *kha*) is understood to carry over from the previous context. Even when intending the word to be a single unit (*aikapadya*), the substitution of *ha* does not occur due to the continued application of the term *“prāyaḥ”* (generally), as seen in examples such as *paṭṭaṇabhavaḥ*. The vowel is short, as previously stated. The entire phrase *sugalntamoham* is a single compound word. In *sugalantamohāṃ* and *sugalanta*, the substitution of *nta* for the present participial suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* occurs according to the rule *“śatṛśānacoḥ”* (Pāṇini 7.1.78).

Then, by the word *moha*, there is a *pañcamī-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose delusion has completely dissolved. The sense is: "the remover of all diversity. [The form] *ahrīhare* is for *ahidhare*; the word *sthitām* (situated) is to be supplied [as the object]. Because the compound is intended to be treated as a single word, the letter *dh* is understood to be non-initial, and thus the substitution of *h* [for *dh*] occurs according to the rule *khaghathadha* etc. *Santam* means peaceful, that is to say, serene. *Tam tām* refers to her who dwells in the lotus (*kamalāvāsam padmāvāsām*). I praise her.

Because *uḍva* and so forth belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended categories), there is no substitution of *l* here. In this case, there is a "blend of languages" (*bhāṣāśleṣa*) because the Sanskrit and Prākṛta languages share the same phonetic utterance. In the same way, blends of other languages such as Śaurasenī should also be inferred.
The "fusion of case-endings" (vibhaktiśleṣa) is said to occur when there is a fusion of nominal suffixes (sup) and verbal suffixes (tiṅ).

If there is a pun (śleṣa) consisting solely of nominal suffixes, solely of verbal suffixes, or of a combination of both nominal and verbal suffixes, it is called "vibhakti-śleṣa" (the pun of inflectional endings).
Just as the vast, ever-blissful, and exceedingly great lights cling to the summit of the king of serpents' mountain, so too do the worlds cling there. 890.

Here too, there is a *śleṣa* (punning connection) between the Blessed One and Lakṣmī. For instance: those whose *gāya*—meaning fame (*kīrti*)—is *uru*, that is, vast; and furthermore, those whose [nature] is *san*, meaning possessing bliss (*ānanda*). These are *bhūyāṃsi*, meaning exceedingly many. And here, "manyness" refers to extensiveness rather than a specific numerical quantity.

Since the word *bahu* is observed to be used not only for number—as in the rule "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*)—but also for the vastness that is the counter-correlative of smallness—as in "whether little or much" (*alpaṃ vā bahu vā yasya*)—the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *bahu* [denotes] numbers such as three and so forth, and also in the sense of 'vast,' like its primary meaning. Here, "vastness" (*vaipulya*) refers both to qualities and to essential nature. Thus, the meaning is: "possessing infinite auspicious qualities and being all-pervading. Consequently, the Lord is superimposed upon those great lights in that very capacity.

They cling to and remain upon the summit of the crest of the serpent’s mountain. Intending to state the reason for this, he says: "They protect (avanti) the worlds (jaganti). This is the third-person plural present indicative form of the roots *lag* (to cling) and *av* (to protect).

On one side, the worlds that cling to the summit of the mountain of serpents (Śeṣa) exist as protectors, guarding [the earth]. "Many" is the stated meaning. "Great, great lights" is the accusative plural. The meaning is: the splendor (śrī) determined as being such in its true nature. "I would sing extensively"—that is, I would sing more than enough; the meaning is: I would perform the chanting of his fame. And furthermore, after the singing, "I would always rejoice"—that is, I would find delight at all times.

In both instances, the third person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*) is used in the sense of a request. Here, in the phrase "vilaganti" and so forth, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the nominal suffix and the verbal suffix.
Just as you have never, even in the past, rejected anyone who has sought refuge at your lotus feet, O Acyuta, so it is likewise now regarding my own forest; what cause for doubt could there be? (891)

"O Acyuta!"—the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is that one does not fall away (*na cyavati*) from the vow of protecting those who have sought refuge; this is the vocative case. And this [epithet] serves as an embellishment for the intended meaning of the present context: the sense is that [He protects] even someone who has gone for refuge at His lotus feet, even if that person be lowly by birth, conduct, or other such means. "Even previously"—that is, even in the past—"You did not reject him. From the root *as* (to throw) preceded by the prefix *nis*, in the *luṅ* tense, second person singular (*sip*), with the substitution of *aṅ* for *cl*, and the addition of the augment *thuk* according to the rule *asyatesthuk*.

The sense is this: even now, regarding the matter of intoxication and the matter of protecting me, he is not "without hope" (*nirāstha*)—that is, not indifferent or devoid of expectation—but rather he is indeed full of expectation. *Nirāstha* means one from whom hope (*āsthā*) has departed; *nanirāstha* means not so. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *āsthā* is used in the senses of support, standing, effort, expectation, and a woman. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and the nominal case-ending (*sup*).

May she whose eyes are like lotuses, who dwells within the lake of the minds of the virtuous, and who possesses priceless beauty—she who is a flood of cooling compassion—be ever present for me, who am scorched by worldly existence. 892.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) regarding the Blessed Lord (*Śrī-Śrīpati*) in the nominative and vocative cases. In the sense of *Śrī* (the Goddess), the word *sumanohṛt* is analyzed as a separate compound meaning "extremely captivating"; alternatively, it may be taken as a collective epithet for the lotus (*sarasīruha*). She dwells in the lotus (*sarasīruhe nivāsabhāk*). She possesses priceless beauty (*anarghaśrīḥ*), meaning divine splendor. And she is *sarvadā*, meaning "giving everything"—that is, the bestower of all desired objects. Such is the lotus-eyed *Śrī*; here one should recall the description: "her eyes are as broad as lotus petals."

"Śiśirakṛpāsāraḥ" means "one whose essence is cool compassion. The ablative case is used here due to the elision of the suffix *lyap* (meaning "having attained"). Thus, the sense is: "having attained the state of being the essence of cool compassion. The doubling of the second *sa* is according to the rule "anaci ca," for the sake of a different meaning [of the word]. "Bhavataḥ saṃsāreṇa" [is explained as follows]: the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all cases. The meaning is: "may it be present toward me who am tormented by worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)."

In the case of Śrīpati (Viṣṇu), however, the meaning is that [the Goddess] dwells in the lotus-lake of the hearts of the wise (sumanasām) and is to be meditated upon by the virtuous. This word ending in the vocative case is an epithet of "O Lotus-eyed One" (abjalocana). The same applies hereafter. "Anargha-śrī" is a vocative addressing Him whose fortune (śrī) is priceless—that is, Lakṣmī.

"O Lotus-eyed One! O Blessed One! O Puṇḍarīkākṣa! The word "bhavataḥ" (of you) is to be separated as "bhūyān" (very great); thus, "O Lord, may your exceedingly abundant, cooling essence of compassion always—constantly—be present for me, who am scorched and overwhelmed by the miseries of the self and so forth; that is to say, may it spread. Here, a pun (padaśleṣa) on the words should also be observed.
Or alternatively:

Constantly compassionate toward her devotees, granting fearlessness to the gods, and having utterly conquered the ocean, she—indeed, the sustainer of all beings—out of affection protected this entire world. (893)

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) regarding the earth and Śrī in the first and third [lines]. She is called "the giver of the desired goal (*arthadā*) to her devotees" because she bestows the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) that are sought after by her devotees; alternatively, in the other sense, she is "that which belongs to the devotees" (*bhaktārthā*), according to the rule: "A compound with *artha* is obligatory, and it takes the gender of the substantive. She is thus described as one whose compassion (*dayā*) is such. The word "constantly" (*satatam*) means "toward the gods" (*sureṣu*).

In such expressions as "giving to a non-Brahmin is equal [to giving to a Brahmin]," the locative case is used because the recipient (saṃpradāna) itself is intended to be expressed as the locus (adhikaraṇa). She is so described because she has bestowed her splendor—that is, her radiance—upon them; in the alternative sense, she is so described because she has granted fearlessness to the gods. She is "born of the ocean" (udadhijā), meaning born from the Ocean of Milk; in the alternative sense, she is so described because she possesses an excellent (ut) and abundant (adhi) victory (jaya). She is the nurse (dhātrī) and progenitor of all beings, that is, the mother of the world; the meaning is "by Śrī."

This entire world was protected from the fear of *saṃsāra* by him; the *liṭ* (perfect tense) is used for the object (*karman*). The ablative case is employed according to the rule *bhītrārthānām*. Alternatively, there is a word-split: *sarvabhūtadhātrī ādarataḥ*. *Sarvabhūtadhātrī* refers to the Earth, as Amara states: "The Earth is the supporter of all beings (*bhūtadhātrī*) and is girdled by the ocean (*abdhimekhalā*). From *ādarataḥ*, meaning "out of respect," this entire world was protected (*tatre*); the *liṭ* is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) of the root *trā*. Here, one should also understand that there is a *padaśleṣa* (phonetic pun) in the phrase *sarvabhūtadhātryādarataḥ*.

May the side-glances of the Goddess who dwells in the lotus— which bestow security, sustain the bound, nourish steadfastness, and steal away the names of all evils— grant me prosperity, for they are like her very lotus-dwelling.

Here, because the side-glances are specified as being "similar to those of the one who dwells in the lotus," it should be understood that words such as *kṣemakṛtaḥ* (bestowing welfare) and so forth are qualifiers of both her [glances] and [the lotuses] without any grammatical modification (*avipariṇāma*). Therefore, it should be noted that there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the genitive and nominative cases, as well as between the singular and plural numbers.

May those whose feet are established in the abode of the Lord of the Serpents’ Hill— the trees that never wither even in the forest of delusion, the protectors of all prosperity— sport within our hearts.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the locative case in the sense of the Lord (*bhagavat*) and the nominative case in the sense of His feet. For instance: "In the matter of satisfying those who bow—that is, those who prostrate—the *asvapnataru* (the tree that never sleeps), the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (*suradruma*)," meaning, in Him who is such a bestower of all desires. In the alternative sense, however, it means: "in the protection (*avana*) of those who bow, [there are] two who are exceedingly 'not sleeping' (*asvapna-tarau*), i.e., exceedingly vigilant. This is the nominative dual. The same applies to what follows.

May our hearts sport within that Supreme Brahman—the primordial cause of the universe, the first of all worlds—whose abode is the Mountain of the Serpents (Śrīśailam), which is the ground (or support) for all prosperity (or the protector of all). [The term] *amlānau* means those in whom there is no *mlāni*, that is, no loss of joy; in the other sense, it means "not withered," i.e., free from exhaustion. [The term] *avanau* means the ground or foundation of all riches; in the other sense, it means "protectors. [The compound] *phaṇigiridhāmani* refers to that whose dwelling place is the Mountain of the Serpents. May our minds take delight therein.

The meaning is: "May [He] be attached. This is the first person singular of the imperative (loṭ) in the ātmanepada (taṅ) from the root *hṛ* preceded by the prefix *anu*. Alternatively, the word is a compound: *phaṇigiridhāmaniviṣṭapādau*. The meaning is: "the two feet of Him who is situated (*niviṣṭa*)—that is, established—on that abode (*dhāma*), namely the place called Phaṇigiri; [those] feet (*pādau*) are His two feet (*caraṇau*)."

"Anu" in *naḥ hṛdayaṃ cittam anu* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "anu in the sense of a mark (*lakṣaṇa*)," and thus the second case ending is applied to the word *hṛdaya* by the rule "the second case is used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. [The phrase means] "let them sport" (*viharantām*). This is the second person dual of the imperative (*loṭ*) for the root *hṛ*, which is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. By the rule "for *tas*, *thas*, *tham*, and *mip*, there are the substitutes *tām*, *tām*, *tam*, and *ām*," the substitute *tām* is applied to *tas*. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the singular and dual endings—the vowels *i* and *u*, and the consonants *i* and *a*.
Just as these two [arms] of mine—long, renowned, most praiseworthy, exceedingly well-nourished, and ever captivating to the heart—remain, they extend indifference toward all faults. (896)

Regarding the phrase "in him who is thus described as having very great renown," this refers to the side of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). Alternatively, regarding the side of his two arms, it means "those two which are renowned in such a way that they are exceedingly long," or "those two which are renowned as being exceedingly long. The same applies to what follows. "In him who possesses surpassing excellence" (*atipraśasti*) means one whose praise is preeminent; in the alternative case, it means "exceedingly praiseworthy. "In him who is characterized by extreme fullness" means one whose nourishment is complete; in the alternative case, it means "possessing fullness in an extreme degree."

May my mind, acting as the agent, always remain—that is, settle—upon the Blessed One described above, who displays indifference toward faults, meaning a state of detachment from defects. [The form "āstām" is the first person singular of the imperative (loṭ) of the root *ās* in the sense of "sitting. Alternatively, the word may be read as a compound: *cetoharau*. In this case, the analysis of the phrase is: "may the two arms of this [Blessed One] always remain as servants (*dāsyaṃ*). According to Amara, "arm" (*doḥ*) is synonymous with "forearm" (*bhuja*), "upper arm" (*bāhu*), and "thigh" (*praveṣṭa*). Thus, it refers to the two arms of the Blessed One under discussion.

May those two who spread my servitude—that is, my state of being a subordinate—be forever captivating to your hearts, O you two who steal the mind! (The form *stām* is the second person dual present imperative of the root *as*, with the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*). Here, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) between the locative and nominative cases, as well as between their singular and dual numbers. In the phrase *sadāstām*, there is a word-pun (*pada-śleṣa*), as well as a pun on the verbal suffix, the case-ending, and the number.

Just as one who honors and serves a virtuous person—always esteemed for their auspicious qualities, a locus of fortune, possessing a mass of profound luster, renowned, wise, and charming—indeed becomes [like them]. 897.

In this verse, regarding the two subjects, Śrī and Śrīnivāsa, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the vocative and locative case endings respectively. To illustrate: in the sense of Śrī (the Goddess), the syntactic division (*cheda*) is as follows: "O Lakṣmī, who art ever honored by the wise (*sumanas*), whose greatness consists of auspicious qualities (*śubhaguṇamahite*), O thou who art indeed intelligent (*medhāvati*) and charming (*manohare*), [I] resort to thy feet (*pade*)."

"O you whose mind is attentive (ādṛta-sumanāḥ)!"—this is the vocative of that [word] formed from "ādṛtāḥ sumanasaḥ budhāḥ yayā sā ādṛtasumanāḥ. O Great One (mahi! of auspicious qualities! O Abode (nivāsabhūmi)! "O you who possess an abundance (bhūmā) of intense (ghana) splendor (ruci)!"—this is the vocative of that [word]. The optional feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied here according to the rule "ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām. "O Renowned One (yaśasvini)!"—the vocative is formed as before. "O Intelligent One (medhāvatī)"—this is the vocative of that [word] meaning "she who possesses intelligence (medhā)."
O Manoharā! O charming one! O venerable lady! O Mother! Or rather: O Lakṣmī! I always serve—that is, I worship—your feet.

In the case of the Lord’s side (the Vaiṣṇava interpretation), however, the word division is as follows: *ādṛtasumanasseve śubhaguṇamahite sadā api lakṣmipade nanu me dhāvati manaḥ hare bhavati*. O Hari! O Blessed One! My mind indeed runs toward You—who are served by those with honored minds (gods), who are glorified by auspicious qualities, and who are the abode (pada) of Lakṣmī; that is to say, the dwelling place of Śrī. This is the meaning.

Because the word *lakṣmī* ends in the suffix *ī*, there is an optional shortening (*hrasva*) in the compound according to the rule *iko hrasvo’ṅyo gālavasya*, as in the example *lakṣmaṇaḥ* meaning "endowed with fortune. [The phrase] *ghanasyāmbudasya rucibhūmā yasya* refers to him who possesses an abundance of luster like that of a dense cloud. [The term] *yaśasvin* means "possessing fame," in accordance with the expression *tasya nāma mahadyaśaḥ*. Here, the suffix *ini* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), either in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*) or praise (*praśaṃsā*). My mind—that is, my consciousness—runs toward you, the one who exists; it proceeds [toward you].
In this context, word-pun (*padaśleṣa*) and other such figures should also be observed.

May your minds be fixed upon You—the Lord of the worlds, the beloved of Lakṣmī, the bestower of boons, the radiant one, the most charming, the auspicious, the one free from worldly existence, and the one honored by the heart of the Lotus-born Brahmā. (898)

Here too, as before, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the vocative and locative cases. To explain: in the case of *lakṣmī* (Goddess Lakṣmī), the word division is: "O *varadevi* (bestower of boons), may the mind (*manaḥ*) become delightful (*bhāvati*); [may it] be in You, who are auspicious (*śubhe*) and free from worldly existence (*bhavarahite*). O Sovereign! O possessor of majesty! She is called *lakṣmīkāminī* because she desires the prosperity (*lakṣmī*) of the worlds; this is her vocative. The meaning is: one who longs for the granting of sovereignty to the worlds. She is called *bhāvatī* because she possesses luster (*bhās*); this is her vocative. The meaning is: she is radiant.

O charming and captivating one! O auspicious and beautiful one! O you who are free from worldly existence and distressed by births caused by karma! "Jātam" refers to a multitude of lotuses, according to the *Viśva* lexicon which states, "‘Jātam’ is used for both a multitude and a person. In its heart—that is, in the center, specifically within the pericarp (*karṇikā*)—she resides. She is honored and worshipped, for the *Śruti* says, "She who dwells in the lotus, she who has a lotus as her rim. O Varadevi! "Varadevī" means she who is both excellent (*varā*) and a goddess (*devī*); this is the vocative form, meaning the divine queen of the gods.

Regarding the phrase "devo kṛtābhiṣekāyām," Amara [states that the word *deva* is used here]. "Your mind" is the agent; "of mine" is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). "May it be" (*bhavatāt*) means "may it abide. This is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *bhū*. By the rule "tuhyostātaṅāśiṣyanyatarasyām," the suffix *tātaṅ* is substituted for *ta* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). The meaning is: "May it remain fixed upon you alone."

The word division is as follows: *bhagavat-pakṣe varade vibhau atimanojñe bhavatāt manaḥ tu ayi śubhebhavarahite*. [This means: "O auspicious one, may your mind take refuge in Him who is the Lord of the worlds, the Sovereign, the Giver of Boons, the All-pervading, the Exceedingly Beautiful, and the Benefactor of the Auspicious Elephant. He is the Lord (*īśvara*) of the worlds; He is the Giver of Boons (*varada*), bestowing what is desired; He is the All-pervading (*vibhu*); He is Exceedingly Beautiful (*atimanojña*). Regarding "Auspicious" (*śubha*), it is because of the saying: "And the most auspicious among all auspicious things. Furthermore, He is "the Benefactor of the Auspicious Elephant" (*śubhebhavarahita*), meaning He is one who acts for the welfare of the lordly elephant (*gajendra*). Thus it is said.

Alternatively: "O mind! O heart! May you become [fixed] upon Him alone—the Lord of Śrī, who is auspicious (śubhaḥ), meaning the bringer of the welfare consisting of the supreme beatitude (niḥśreyasa); who is the 'bestower of boons' (varaḥ) to the elephant (ibhasya)—that is to say, the granting of boons; who is beneficial (hitaḥ) to that [elephant], or [resides] therein; who is honored (mahitaḥ) with the heart (hṛdā)—that is, by the mind—of the lotus-born (padmajātaḥ), namely Brahmā. The word *tu* is used for emphasis. The meaning is: "May you become attached to the Blessed Lord alone. The form *bhavatāt* is the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *bhū*, with the substitution *tāt* for *hi* in the sense of a benediction (*āśiṣi*).

In this instance, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the feminine and masculine genders; in *varadevi-bhāva-timanojñe* and so forth, there is a pun on the words (*pada-śleṣa*); and in *bhavatāt*, it should be understood that there is a pun on the person (*puruṣa-śleṣa*).

"Just as I long for the abundance of the beauty of the dark luster of the petals of the *kuvalaya* lotus, [so do I long for] the abundance of the radiance of the side-glances of the Blessed One, whose greatness is supreme and whose bestowal of the most excellent qualities and sovereignty is boundless. (899) In this verse, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the accusative case ending in relation to Lakṣmī’s side-glances and the ablative case ending in relation to the Blessed One. There is also a *śleṣa* between their plural and singular number endings. To explain: *kuvalayadalāsitimnaḥ* refers to those things whose blackness (*asitimā*) is indeed the very blackness of the *kuvalaya* petal.

I long for the abundance of light—the exceeding brilliance—of the side-glances (apāṅga) of Śrī, which are overflowing with boundless generosity in bestowing that sovereignty which is most excellent (praguṇatama), meaning exceedingly straight (ṛju), even more than that of the Blessed One Śrīnivāsa, whose majesty is loftier and whose opulence is surpassing. [Amara states: "Ṛju, ajihma, and praguṇa" mean straight. The sense is: "May the splendors of Lakṣmī’s side-glances flow forth upon me. This is the intended meaning.

In this context, the words beginning with *kuvalayadalāsitimnaḥ* (as dark as the petals of a blue lotus) are adjectives qualifying *bhagavataḥ* (of the Blessed One), ending in the fifth case singular. Their meaning is "dark like the petal of a blue water-lily. *Apāṅgasya* means "of the side-glance"; *rucibhūmeḥ* means "from that which is an abundance of splendor," thus signifying "possessing beauty equal to that of the bodiless god of love (*anaṅga*). *Uccamahimnaḥ* means "of unsurpassed greatness" or "of boundless bestowal of the most excellent sovereignty"—the meaning is exactly as stated.

"I desire"—that is, I long for—"the riches of Śrī, beginning from the state of liberation up to sovereign power, from the Blessed One, Śrīnivāsa, who has been described in the aforementioned manner. Herein lies a pun (*śleṣa*): in the word "bhagavataḥ," there is a play between the ablative singular and the genitive singular; and in the word "śriyaḥ," there is a play between the genitive singular and the accusative plural.

May I attain the lineage of those like me who possess the splendor of abundant giving, who bear the beauty of profound and unsurpassed compassion, and who uphold the radiance of the lotus. May it be a succession that protects the Fortune of the world.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the second and sixth case endings regarding "the illustrious one" (*śrī*) and "her glance" (*tatkaṭākṣa*). To explain: [the word] *anuttānām* means "not shallow," that is, "deep. As Amarasimha states: "The words *nimna*, *gabhīra*, and *gambhīra* mean deep; *uttāna* is the opposite of that. Since it is said [in grammar] that these words take all three genders up to the limit of "unfathomable" (*āgādha*), they possess gender according to the object they qualify. In the alternative sense, however, it is the genitive plural: "of those who have been driven away (*nuttānām*)" by intense compassion (*ghanakaruṇayā*). The same applies in the subsequent instances as well.

Regarding the statement from the *Amarakośa*: "The words *nutta*, *nunnā*, *asta*, *niṣṭhyūta*, *viddha*, *kṣipta*, and *īrita* are synonyms," [the following applies]: because of the grammatical rule *nudavidondītrāghrāhībhyo'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.56), which prescribes an optional substitution of *n* for the *t* of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) after the root *nud*, there is no substitution of *n* for the *t* of the suffix nor for the preceding *d*; rather, there is the substitution of *c* (known as *cartva*). The word division is *bhaje yaśobhābhṛtām*. [This means] "I worship those who are filled (*bhṛtām*), that is, full (*pūrṇām*), with fame (*yaśas*) and splendor (*bhā*). In this instance, the absence of the required placement of the shorter term first in a *dvandva* compound due to the word *bhā* being short is not considered a fault.

This is because the rule "samudrābhrāddhaḥ, lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ" and others, by their inclusion [in the grammatical system], indicates that this particular section is non-eternal (anitya). Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "those supported (bhṛtā) by the manifestation (bhā) of fame (yaśasaḥ). In the alternative sense, there is a word-break as "bhajeyāma. [The term] "śobhābhṛtaḥ" means those possessing beauty (śobhām bibhrati). [The phrase] "subahudām" refers to her who bestows very abundant giving (vitaraṇam). In the alternative sense, "subahudāḥ" refers to those who give very much; the suffix "ka" is applied according to the rule "āto'nupasarge."

"Abode" (dhāma) means a place; thus, the meaning is "her who is held by him [Viṣṇu], whose abode is the lotus" (kamalālayām). In the alternative sense, it refers to those who possess (dharanti) the radiance (dhāma) of lotuses (sarasīruhāṇām)—the suffix *kvip* being added to the root *dhṛ*. I worship (bhaje), that is, I serve (seve), the supreme (param), that is, exceedingly (atimātram) and highest (parām), Goddess Śrī, the protectress (avitrīm) of those like me (mādṛśām), that is, of those such as myself. This is in the present tense (*laṭ*). In the alternative sense, "Śrī" means prosperity (*saṃpad*). It is the protectress (*avitrīm*) of that, using the suffix *tṛn* after the root *avi*. Because of the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule "na loka... (*Pāṇini 2.3.69*), the accusative case is used for the object.

May I serve—that is, worship—the lineage (rekhā) of those glances (kaṭākṣāḥ), which are the illusory splendors (māyāḥ śriyaḥ) of her eyes; this is the optative sense (*liṅ*). Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the two case endings mentioned—singular and plural—and between the singular and plural numbers. Furthermore, one should note the word-pun (*pada-śleṣa*) in the phrases "may I serve" (*bhajeya śobhā*) and "the lineage" (*paraṃparām*) and so forth.

Salutations forever to my deity, the bearer of the lotus, who destroys misfortune, who knows all things, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree for the multitude of those who bow before him, and who possesses a fame as radiant as the lotus. 901.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the dative case (*caturthī*) in reference to the Blessed One and the locative case (*saptamī*) in reference to Śrī. To explain: "the destroyer of sins" (*duritabhit*) means "to him who destroys sins" (*duritabhide*). The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc. In the alternative sense, "that which breaks" (*bhidaṃ*) is formed with the suffix *ka* according to the rule *igupadhajñā-* etc.; [the word refers to] that [lotus]. The same applies in what follows. "To the knower of all" (*sarvavid*): he who knows or finds everything is the "knower of all" (*sarvavit*); [this is used] because of the Vedic scripture, "He who knows all."

In the [primary] sense, "to the Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*); [in the secondary sense], "to the Kalpa-tree" (*kalpabhūruṭ*), which is a wish-granting tree for the multitude of suppliants seeking their desired objects—the meaning being "to the bestower of sought-after things. In the [secondary] sense, "to that which grows on the Kalpa-land" (*kalpabhūmiruha*). To Him who bears the renown of Lakṣmī (*kamalāprakhyātibhṛt*)—the meaning being "to Him whose very nature is defined by Śrī. As it is said: "Hrī and Lakṣmī are Your two wives; [salutation] to Viṣṇu of beautiful form.
"The entire world, both moving and unmoving, rests upon His side-glance;
that Goddess stands upon His chest like the radiance of fire."

"He is indeed the Lord of all, the glorious one, an ocean of auspicious qualities"—such scriptural and Puranic statements are to be considered here. In the alternative [allegorical] sense, "filled" means full because of its renown as a *kamala* (lotus); "to him who holds the *abja*" (the conch), meaning he holds the conch (*abja*)—in the other sense, the meaning is "held by the lotus" (*padma*), according to the scripture beginning with "seated upon the lotus. To my deity, in the form of the deity Mahālakṣmī, let there always be salutation (*namaḥ*). In the alternative sense, this consists of two words: *daiva* and *te*.

O my destiny! O you who are the very form of my good fortune! O Blessed One! Let there be salutation (*namaḥ*) unto You. (The dative case is used here according to the rule beginning with *namas-svasti*). Here, a word-play (*padaśleṣa*) is also to be observed. Or as in another example: "To the Source of all worlds, to such a Sovereign, to the one who grants life to the glory of the King of Gods, to the Compassionate One, to the Honored One—I indeed offer myself. (902)

Here too, as before, there is *śleṣa* (punning double entendre). O King of the Gods! O Lord of the Devas! O Śrījīvana!—that is, O you who are the very life (*jīvana*) of Śrī (Lakṣmī), or alternatively, O Śrīnivāsa, meaning "O you whose abode is Śrī. To the source (*prabhu*) of all worlds, that is, to the sovereign lord; and to the pervasive one (*vibhu*). The sense is: to Him whose essential nature (*svarūpa*), character (*svabhāva*), and majesty (*vibhava*) are beyond the reach of speech and mind. The word *tattādṛk* has the same meaning as the word *tādṛk*.

Just as the word *tattulya* has the same meaning as the word *tulya*, or alternatively, he is so called because he possesses that which is like that; thus, the meaning is "to one who is incomparable" (*asadṛśāya*). To the compassionate one (*dayālave*), that is, to one possessed of pity (*kṛpāśāline*)—the suffix *āluc* is applied here in the sense of the agent according to the rule *aspṛhigṛhi* etc.—we would offer ourselves to you (*te tubhyam*). "Our own" (*svam*) means the self that has become ours, in the manner described by the statement: "Ownership (*svatvam*) has arisen in the self, while lordship (*svāmitvam*) resides in Brahman. We would offer our very selves. This is the third person plural of the optative (*liṅ*) from the root *arpayati* preceded by the prefix *sam*.

In this context, "the source of all worlds" means the one who is the cause of the universe. Regarding that which has been so described: "surarājaśrījīvanadayālave" is a single compound word. It refers to Him in whom there is a "lava"—a trace or fraction—of "dayā," compassion, and who is the "jīvanaḥ," the one who gives life to the "surarājaśrī," the sovereignty of the king of gods (Indra). This is well known from the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas. In "mahite," meaning worshipful or venerable; in "tattādṛśe vibhave," meaning in such a manifestation or power; that is to say, in the Blessed Śrī Mahālakṣmī.

In the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, Lakṣmī is indeed designated as a manifestation (*vibhūti*) by the statement: "He made her his supreme abode upon His chest. The particle *nanu* is used here for emphasis; the meaning is "in Lakṣmī alone. I offer myself (*svam* = *ātmānam*). This is the first person singular present indicative of the root *arpayati* preceded by the prefix *sam*. Here, the surrender of the Self by the Lord and His consort is expressed. Or, for example: "O You whose eyes are vast and auspicious, who are the snare that cuts the bonds of worldly existence (*bhava*), please offer Your own Self to Your husband, the supporter of all moving and non-moving beings. (903)

Here too, as before, there is a pun (*śleṣa*). In the sense of the Blessed One: to him who is so described—that is, to the cutter (*lavitā*), from the root *lūñ* with the suffix *tṛc*, of the bond (*pāśa*) consisting of worldly existence (*bhava*) for those devotees who resort to him; to the leader (*netā*), from the root *ṇīñ* with the suffix *tṛc*, of vast, abundant, auspicious, and supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*); to the husband (*pati*), the lord of Śrī, the mother of all the worlds and the sustainer of all moving and unmoving beings; to the high-souled Rāghava, the refuge of all the world, I offer myself—*nivedaye*—I surrender my very self.
"Announce me immediately as Vibhīṣaṇa, who has arrived."

In this context, according to the rule "that which one intends through an action is also the recipient (saṃpradāna)," the word *pati* takes the fourth case (*caturthī*) because it bears the designation of the recipient. In the interpretation of Śrī, [the phrase refers to] that which is a *lavitra*—meaning a sickle or reaper—for the bond consisting of worldly existence (*bhava-maya-pāśa*) for those who worship her. The suffix *itra* is applied to the root *lū* by the rule "artilūdhūsūkhanasahacara itraḥ"; thus, *lavitram* means "a sickle" (*dātram*), according to Amara. The meaning is "in the cutter. [The Lord is] he whose eyes are large and auspicious; [and he is] of the Earth, the sustainer of all moving and non-moving beings (*nikhila-carācara-dhātrī*).

Alternatively, "nikhilāḥ" means complete; "carācarāḥ" means moving and stationary beings (the animate and the inanimate). Of such a "dhātryāḥ," that is, the earth—"vipulā gahvarī dhātrī," according to Amarasimha—[I] offer myself as an "apatye. Here, the word division is "apatye" [as a separate term]. "Apatye" means in the daughter. According to Amarasimha: "Sutaḥ" and "putraḥ" [are masculine]; "amī" (these following), however, all say "duhitaram" (daughter); "apatyam" and "tokam" apply equally to both. Thus, the meaning is: in the Blessed One, the daughter of Janaka, I offer my own self.

In the verse, "One should offer oneself to Viṣṇu of stainless splendor," the locative case is used after the word *apatya* (offspring) because the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Here, both word-play (*pada-śleṣa*) and gender-play (*liṅga-śleṣa*) are also to be observed.
Just as when the folded palms of those of noble intellect fall upon Sundarī— the foremost of beautiful women and the supreme deity of the fair-browed— those palms bring about all prosperity for her.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the sixth and seventh case endings (*ṣaṣṭhī* and *saptamī*), as well as between their plural and singular forms. [The term] "among the foremost of beautiful women" (*sundarīṇām agraṇyām*) means among those who are preeminent; [the term] "among those of noble intellect" (*udāradhiyām*) means among those of great wisdom or generous mind; [the term] "among the supreme deity, the Blessed One" (*paradaivatasya*) refers to the Goddess Lakṣmī, the woman with lovely brows. In all instances, the substitution of *ām* for the genitive ending (*ṅi*) occurs according to the rule "ṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ. The meaning is that they fall [upon her] regarding the subject of glory, arising through a competitive spirit of "I first, I first" (*ahamahamikayā*).

The meaning is: "of those [women] distinguished by such qualifiers as 'the foremost among the beautiful' (*sundaryagraṇyām*) and so forth. By the use of the word *tāsām* ("of them"), it is indicated that the words previously shown in the locative singular are here to be understood in the genitive plural. For instance: *sundarīṇām agraṇyām*, meaning "among the foremost of the beautiful"; since the stem does not end in *an*, there is no insertion of *nuṭ* before the suffix *ām*. And: *udāradhiyām*, meaning "of those of noble intellect."

Furthermore, "those other deities" refers to gods such as the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and others; their "women with beautiful brows" are the goddesses—alternatively, "those other deities and women with beautiful brows. According to Amara’s lexicon, *bṛndāraka* means "deities. This refers to Sarasvatī, Rudrāṇī, Indrāṇī, and so forth—the beautiful-toothed wives of the gods. In both cases, because the designation *nadī* (feminine noun ending in long ī or ū) is optional by the rule *vāmi*, the *nuṭ* augment does not apply to the genitive plural suffix *ām*. Thus, the construction is: "producing all prosperity for them."
If there is similarity between two verbal roots (prakṛti) brought about by unconnected suffixes (pratyaya), that is *prakṛtiśleṣa* (root-pun);
it is of two kinds, depending on whether the suffixes are nominal endings (*sup*) or verbal endings (*tiṅ*).

If the similarity between two bases (*prakṛti*) of different forms is produced by unjoined suffixes (*pratyaya*), that is *prakṛti-śleṣa* (the punning of bases). The dual number is indicative of the plural as well. And that [pun] is of two kinds: depending on nominal suffixes (*sup-pratyaya*) and depending on verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-pratyaya*). The term "unjoined" (*aśliṣṭa*) is an adjective qualifying the suffix, intended to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *pratyaya-śleṣa* (the punning of suffixes); for in the case of the punning of suffixes, that very [type of pun] will indeed occur.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"That man who, through the grace of Hari—or even through the wrath of another deity—attains prosperity, shall become a destroyer of the great calamities of the multitude of lords of merit. (905)

That man who attains growth through the grace of Hari is virtuous, meritorious, praiseworthy, and lauded by all the worlds; he is called *mahāvyasanarut* because he wards off great calamities and misfortunes—the term being derived from the root *rudh* with the *kvip* suffix, followed by the substitution of *jaś* and *cartva*. He shall be free from the stain of adversity, like Vibhīṣaṇa and others—this is the sense. It is indeed a marvel that even one who attains growth through the grace of another deity would likewise become such a person as described.

In reality, however, this entire word is *sukṛtīśastomahet* (one who destroys the assembly of the lords of the virtuous). "Lords of the virtuous" (*sukṛtīśāḥ*) refers to those foremost among the meritorious; [the term] means "one who destroys (*hanti*) their assembly (*stomaṃ vyūham*)," hence *sukṛtīśastomahā*. The suffix *vic* is applied to the root *han* by the rule "it is seen after other roots as well. It is not the suffix *kvip*, because in the rule "after *brahman*, *bhruṇa*, and *vṛtra*, [there is] *kvip*," one must rely upon a fourfold restriction.

By this, such usages as "You are indeed a matricide," "You are indeed a patricide," "The world-renowned slayer of the enemies of the gods," and "That man who does not cross the ocean of existence is a slayer of his own self" are explained. He is so described because he weeps—that is, sheds tears—due to vices (*vyasana*) such as hunting, gambling, and sleeping by day, which are said to arise from desire (*kāma*); and due to the eight faults arising from anger (*krodha*), such as backbiting, violence, and malice, which have been mentioned. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *rud* in the sense of shedding tears, and there is the substitution of *c* for *r*.

His heart would become agitated by the multitude of calamities described above—meaning he would be like Rāvaṇa and others. According to Amarasimha, "vyasana" refers to misfortune, downfall, or a vice born of passion or anger. Here, there is a *prakṛtiśleṣa* (root-śleṣa), as the similarity between *rudhi* and *udyi* is caused by the suffix *kvip*. There is also a *padaśleṣa* (word-śleṣa) in the word *sukṛtī* and so forth. Or, for example: "He who is foremost in the assembly of the virtuous and exerts himself in the mastery of many scriptures conquers his enemies; for he is a great sage who has brought about the destruction of the fame of the enemy-demons through the cultivation of auspiciousness. (906)

Here, a learned devotee of the Blessed One is the subject under discussion (*prastuta*), while a hero is the non-subject (*aprastuta*); there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the two. The word *agresarayut* means "one who is joined with those who are foremost" (*agresarāḥ*) in the assembly (*samitau*) of virtuous (*sādhu*) scholars (*viduṣām*). It is derived from the root *yu* (meaning "to mix") belonging to the *adādi* class, with the suffix *kvip* and the augment *tuk*. Thus, the meaning is "possessing the company of the virtuous. In the other sense, it means "properly (*sādhu*) in battle (*samitau*)," for the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *samiti* may refer to combat (*sāṃparāya*), an assembly (*sabhā*), or a gathering (*saṅgama*)."

"Those who are leaders, with them he fights"—thus [is the compound formed]. From the root *yudh* (to fight), the suffix *kvip* is applied; then the substitution of *jaś* (the dental *t*) and *cartva* (the retroflex *ṭ*) occur. "He knows many scriptures"—thus [is the compound formed]. From the root *vid* (to know), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc.; then *cartva* occurs. Alternatively, a collection of weapons is a *śastra*; he pierces (*vidhyati*) with that great *śastra*. From the root *vyadh* (to pierce), the suffix *kvip* is applied, followed by the substitutions of *jaś* and *cartva*. He conquers—that is, overcomes—the enemies, namely the constant adversaries such as desire (*kāma*) and so forth; alternatively, he conquers his foes.

He is a man of great wisdom, great learning, and exceeding fortitude. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The term *dhīra* may be used in three senses: a learned man, one who acts according to his own will, and one endowed with fortitude. He is thus described as one by whom auspiciousness and welfare have been established; he is one who praises the fame of the enemy of the Rākṣasas—that is, the glory of the foe of the Daityas—and is therefore the author of a composition concerning the divine fame of the Lord, which is the auspiciousness of the world. The sense is that he is like Parāśara, Vyāsa, and others. [The form is derived from] the root *stu* (to praise) with the suffix *kvip*, followed by the augment *tuk*.

He is so described because he has arranged a beautiful protection (*rakṣā*)—meaning a protection of auspicious things (*śubha*) or auspicious protection itself—for his own side; the meaning is that he specifically brings welfare to the world. This is a separate word (*bhinnaṃ padam*). He is so called because he pierces (*tudati*) the fame of his enemies; the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *tud*. [The verse] "may he be" (*bhavet*) follows. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between verbal roots of similar form when combined with the prefix *su-* and the word *yaśas-* as an upapada—namely, the roots *yu* and *yudh*, *vid* and *vyadh*, and *stu* and *tud*—when reduced to their basic forms (*prakṛti*) by the application of *kvip*. Furthermore, in the second half of the verse, there is also a *pada-śleṣa* (coalescence of words).

O Lord of the Mountain of Serpents, it is a marvel that for both those who face you and those who turn away from you, a great pain arises— such is the case for one seeking liberation and for one seeking worldly existence.

"Facing you" (*tvadabhimukha*) and "turning away from you" (*tvadvimukha*); he is so called because he "releases existence," that is, he releases *bhava*, which is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). [This is formed] from the root *muc* with the suffix *kvip*, and the substitution of *k* for *c* according to the rule *coḥ kuḥ*. Alternatively, he is so called because he is "deluded by existence" (*bhava*) or "in existence" (*bhave*). [This is formed] from the root *muh* with the suffix *kvip*; the optional substitution of *gh* for *h* according to the rule *vā druhamuhaṣṇuhaṣṇihām*, followed by the substitutions of *jaś* and *cart*. In both of these cases, there is "great *ruk*"—that is, *ruca*, meaning luster or radiance. According to Amara, "prabhā, rug, and ruci" are synonyms. The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ruc* in the sense of luster.

In this context, *ruk* means disease (*roga*); according to Amarasimha, "the feminine forms are *ruk*, *ruj*, and *rujā*. The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ruj*. In both cases, the rules for *jaśtva* and *cartva* apply. Here, there is a homogeneity (*sārūpya*) between the roots *muc* and *muhy* when preceded by the word *bhava*, and between the roots *ruc* and *ruj* when used alone; thus, this is a *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic pun on the verbal roots).

O Lord, we declare that you alone—and none other than you—cut the bonds of the fetters of existence; yet at the end, the wise one who knows the nature of the various elements understands your true intention.

"O Lord! We declare you, as well as others such as the Four-faced One (Brahmā), to be the 'shatterer of the bonds of the fetters of worldly existence' (*bhavapāśabandhamuḍi*). The underlying sense is that we are speakers of various types of puns (*śleṣa*). As for that intention—the purpose behind employing such words in both cases—it is, at the conclusion during the moment of final determination, beyond doubt in many ways, that is, in numerous manners."

One who knows *prakṛti*—that is, the Supreme Brahman which is the cause of the world, as well as the root *prakṛti* which is the source of the bondage of worldly existence—is called a *prakṛtijña*. Regarding the word *prakṛti*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The term *prakṛti* may denote the equilibrium of the *guṇas*, ministers and the like, inherent nature, the womb, a sign, or the citizens. Here, *yoni* means the cause.
