The word *liṅga* means a sign (*cihna*). Just as in the passage beginning with "the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which has been described by Me," the term *prakṛti* is used for the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), so too in passages such as "Vāsudeva is the supreme *prakṛti*" and "and *prakṛti*, because there is no contradiction with the promise and the illustrations," the word *prakṛti* is employed even for the cause of the universe. Alternatively, he is so called because he knows the *prakṛti*—that is, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*)—of both you and others. The sense is that knowing that cutting the bonds of worldly existence (*bhavapāśa*) is your own nature, whereas being deluded by the bonds of worldly existence is the nature of others.

Alternatively, "many" (aneka) means numerous; those who are the "progenitors" (dhātavaḥ)—the four-faced Brahmās residing within their respective cosmic eggs—are His "nature" (prakṛti), meaning the cause. This is established by such scriptural texts as, "He who created Brahmā in the beginning. The word *dhātu* ends in *-u*, being derived from the root *dhā* with the Uṇādi suffix *tun* according to the rule *sitanigamimasisicyavidhāñkruśibhyastun*. Vyāsārya himself has demonstrated this very derivation in the passage, "By the grace of the Progenitor (dhātu), [one realizes] the majesty of the Self."

In the phrase *pakṣe ante bhavapāśabandhamuṭi*, "at the end" (*ante*) refers to the conclusion [of the verse]. Therein reside several verbal roots—namely, *muṭ* in the sense of "thrusting and crushing," *muṣ* in the sense of "stealing," and *muh* in the sense of "bewilderment"—which are respectively listed in the *tudādi*, *kryādi*, and *divādi* groups. One who knows those forms—that is, the verbal bases (*prakṛti*) which serve as the bases for the *kvip* suffix—is such [a person]. Thus, the wise man (*budhaḥ*), who knows the reality of both the transcendent and the immanent, as well as the grammarian, understands this.

The meaning is that he knows the intention behind the pun (*śleṣa*) on these two words. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "he releases" (*muṭati*) or "he steals" (*muṣṇāti*) the bond of the fetters of existence (*bhavapāśabandha*), the word ending in the *kvip* suffix refers to the Blessed One. In the analysis "he is deluded" (*muhyati*) by the bond of the fetters of existence, the word formed with the *kvip* suffix refers to one other than the Blessed One. Here, there is a pun between them. In this context, the similarity (*sārūpya*) among the roots *muṭ*, *muṣ*, and *muh* occurs when the *kvip* suffix is applied. For *muṭi* and *muṣ*, the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stop) and *cartva* (the retroflex stop) apply.

However, for *muh*, it should be understood that because the optional substitution of *gh* by the rule *vā drahamuhaḥ* does not apply here, the substitution of *ḍha* by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* takes place, followed by the substitutions of *jaś* and *cartva*.
Just as You,

O Acyuta, spontaneously take delight in the multitude of Your devotees through Your affection, so too should one know this regarding the removal of sins and the attainment of yoga and kṣema, for You possess the knowledge of the various specific elements of all things.

O Acyuta! You are *vimṛḍ*, so called because you especially gladden (*mṛḍati*) by your very own nature (*svataḥ svabhāvāt*); the meaning is that your essential nature is unlimited bliss (*aparicchinna-sukha-svarūpa*), as is heard in such passages as, "Prāṇa is Brahman, Kaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ is Brahman; that which is indeed Kaṃ is Khaṃ, and that which is Khaṃ is Kaṃ. Likewise, [the term applies] to the multitude of devotees (*bhakta-tati*) and their relations—this also connects with what follows. You are *vimṛḍ* because you especially endure (*viśeṣeṇa mṛṣyati*) or forgive (*kṣamate*) offenses (*āgasām*), that is, transgressions.

The meaning is that He is patient with great offenses. Furthermore, He is the *vimṛṭ*—one who specifically wipes away (*viśeṣeṇa mārṣṭi*) and purifies the sins and the sufferings belonging to His devotees; the meaning is that He is the one who completely eliminates all calamities. Moreover, *yogāḥ* are the attainment of what is unattainable, and *kṣemāḥ* are the preservation of what has been attained; He is their *vimṛṭ*, meaning He reflects upon them, the sense being that He is the one who deliberates [on their welfare].
As it is said: "For those people who worship Me with undivided thought, for those who are ever-devoted, I provide their *yoga-kṣema* (acquisition and preservation)."
Thus it is from the song. However, this entire collection of the Blessed One’s qualities has been stated as something that "should be heard in many ways, from many sources.
A wise person should extract the essence from all scriptures—whether small or great—just as a bee gathers nectar from flowers.

In the manner thus described, in many ways; the word "tu" (but) serves to emphasize the distinction. Only one who knows the true essence of the meaning of the scriptures (*śāstrārthatattvavit*) should know—that is, understand—it, and no other.
He who lacks his own wisdom and possesses only great erudition does not know the meaning of the scriptures, just as a ladle cannot perceive the flavors of soups and curries.

The sense is that one of such a coarse intellect as has been described [cannot grasp this]. Only one who knows those many specific verbal roots (*dhātu*) would understand this meaning; no other, namely one who is not a grammarian (*aśābdika*), could—this is the sense to be supplied. Here, in sequence: *mṛḍ* (to be happy) belongs to the Taudādika class; *mṛṣ* (to endure) belongs to the Daivādika class; *mṛj* (to cleanse) belongs to the Adādika class; and *mṛś* (to touch) belongs to the Taudādika class. When these four roots are preceded by the prefix *vi-* and take the suffix *kvip*, they become identical in form.

It should be understood that in the previous example, there is a single uniform form for all three [roots]. Here, from *mṛḍ* with the prefix *vi-* and the suffix *kvip*, after the change of *ṛ* to *ṣ* (*cartva*), and from *mṛś* by changing the dental *s* to the retroflex *ḍ* (*jaśtva*) and then to *ṣ* (*cartva*), as well as from *mṛj* and *mṛś* by applying the rule "vraśca" etc. to change the *j* to *ṣ*, then to *ḍ* (*jaśtva*), and finally to *ṣ* (*cartva*), the form *vimṛḍ* is identical in all cases.

Thus has the first type of *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic punning on verbal roots), which depends upon nominal suffixes (*sup*), been described. The second type, which depends upon verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), is as follows:

O lotus-eyed one, alas, you grant the fruit of both these [actions] without restraint: that which Ajāmila and others called upon you by name—Nārāyaṇa and so forth—out of compulsion or force, and that which the sacrificers, such as Uparicara Vasu and others, offered through ritual observances. (910) He who, like Ajāmila and others, called upon you by name—such as Nārāyaṇa and so forth—out of compulsion or force, has used the root *hveñ* in the sense of "to call" or "to compete," belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa; the form *juhāva* is derived from this root in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). By the rule *abhyastasya ca*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *hveñ* before it undergoes reduplication, followed by doubling.
And he who is the sacrificer, such as Uparicara Vasu and others, [did so] out of ritual observance.

The meaning is: by the process described in the passage, "But those who have reached the culmination of speech, purified by various refinements (*saṃskāra*), they indeed are the pure Bhāgavatas, whose sole sacrifice is Vāsudeva," [the Lord] offered [oblations] to you in the sacrifices (*adhvareṣu*)—this is the construction. "He offered" (*juhāva*) means he gave oblation (*havis*) directed toward you. This is derived from the root *hu* (meaning "to give" and "to eat") belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class, in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). And here, "giving" (*dāna*) implies the act of casting [into the fire]. They say that this [casting] is understood by its very nature as being performed upon a Vedic receptacle (*ādhāra*) and involving sacrificial material (*havis*).
Here, since the verbal roots *hvayati* and *juhoti* maintain a uniform form before the *liṭ* suffix, this is a "śleṣa" (paronomasia) of the root with respect to the *tiṅ* suffix.
Or rather, how great indeed must be her fortune, she who bore you, the abode of the universe, in her womb; and from whom you, O Śauri, the progenitor of the world, drank milk like an infant.

"O Abode of the Universe!"—this address is intended to illuminate the marvelous nature of her fitness for bearing the one who is about to be described. The sense is: "She who is Devakī. [The Lord] placed you in her womb (*garbhe adhāt*), that is, she bore you (*dadhāra*); this is from the root *dhā* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. The meaning is: how immeasurable is her fortune? The word *iva* is used as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*). Furthermore, [the Lord is called] the "Creator of the worlds" (*jagatāṃ savitā*), the progenitor; this too is intended to manifest the wonder of the drinking of the breast-milk that is about to be described.

The meaning is: "of her," that is, Yaśodā; "like an infant," like a common suckling child; "who drank" (adhāt) the breast-milk—how great indeed must be the fortune of her! This is the construction. [In the verb *adhāt*,] the root *dheṭ* means "to drink"; the suffix *luṅ* is used; and by the rule *vibhāṣā ghrādheṭśācchāsaḥ*, there is an optional elision (*luk*) of the *sic* augment. Here, there is a formal identity between the roots *dhā* and *dheṭ*.
Just as his compassion for all the serpents who support the earth chooses their fame, so too does he utterly crush his enemies and their armies here on earth.

The compassion of the wearer of the serpent-king (*uragadhara*) makes all those who are humble (*vinata*) excellent (*vara*), that is, it chooses them as the best; the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the word *vara*. It also makes the fame and glory of these humble ones vast (*uru*), that is, it expands it; when the suffix *ṇā* is applied to the word *uru*, the substitution of *vara* occurs according to the rule beginning with "priyasthira" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 6.4.157). He states the reason for this in the passage beginning with "it crushes" (*kṣodayati*). For, because this divine compassion makes the enemies of these humble ones mean (*kṣudra*) and wretched, it crushes them.

From the word *kṣudra* (small), by applying the rule for the state of being like that which ends in *iṣṭhan*, there is the elision of the *yaṇ* and subsequent letters according to the rule "asthūladūra... etc., as well as the *guṇa* substitution of the preceding vowel. The term *kṣodayati* means he completely pulverizes (*niḥśeṣam*) the armies belonging to him—that is, those connected with the enemy who has been humbled. From the word *kṣoda* (powder), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied; the meaning is "he grinds into powder. According to Amara, "in the sense of powder, [the word] is *kṣoda*. Here, because the words *varoru* (fair-thighed) and *kṣudra*, and *kṣoda* and *kṣoda*—all ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*—are identical in form when followed by the third-person singular ending *tip*, there is a *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic pun on the verbal roots).

O Beloved of Lokeśvara! That mere fragment of your sidelong glance, thick with the essence of compassion, whatever person it takes as its object, makes that person a *bṛndāraka*—a preeminent leader—in the entire world, and [augments] his splendors. O Beloved of Lokeśvara! Your fragment of a sidelong glance, dense with the essence of compassion, whatever man it takes as its object—that is, brings within its range—makes that man a *bṛndāraka*, meaning a chief or leader, among all people in the world.

From the word *bṛndāraka*, by applying the suffix *ṇi* with the status of *iṣṭhavan* (as if it were the superlative suffix), there is the substitution of *bṛnda* for that [word] according to the rule "priyasthira... and so forth; the meaning is that he makes [the world] the support for all. Amara states: "The two words *bṛndāraka* and *rūpin* mean 'foremost'. He "brindāyati" his glories—that is, he makes them into *bṛndas*, he collects them into masses; the meaning is that he brings them together into that very [place]. From the word *bṛnda*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "tatkaroti. Here, there is a formal identity between the two words *bṛndāraka* and *bṛnda* when they take the causative suffix (*ṇijanta*).

In the first two examples, there is uniformity between the bases (*prakṛti*) which consist of pure verbal roots; however, in the subsequent two, one should understand the difference between the bases characterized as causative (*ṇyanta*) and nominal roots (*nāmadhātu*).
O Acyuta, that a man who eats with devotion the remainder of what you have eaten—being sinless—is carried even by the *ātivāhika* deities headed by Agni; this indeed is a marvel! (914)

"O Acyuta! That person by whom your sinless remnant (anaghaṃ tvadbhuktaśeṣaṃ) is eaten—that is, consumed—is indeed 'eaten' even by the *ātivāhika* deities such as those of the *arciḥ* path; this is truly a marvel. But the truth is rather this: by the power of tasting the grace of the remnants offered to the Lord, a person is honored even by the *ātivāhika* deities of the *arciḥ* path, let alone by others. This is the intended meaning: "Having eaten the sinless remnant of the oblation offered to the Lord, and having cast off all sins, one undoubtedly attains liberation (*mokṣa*)."

Thus, the meaning of the authoritative scriptural evidence of the Blessed One is to be investigated here. Regarding the first sense, the suffix *yak* is applied to the root *bhakṣ* in the passive voice (*karman*) with the present tense marker (*laṭ*). Regarding the second sense, the suffix *syapratyaya* is applied to the root *bhaj* with the future tense marker (*lṛṭ*); then, by the rule "acoḥ kuḥ," there is the substitution of *k* for the *c*, and by the rule "iṇkoḥ," there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* that is a portion of *syapratyaya*. Here, there is a similarity (*sārupyam*) between the roots *bhakṣ* and *bhaj* produced by the suffixes *yak* and *syapratyaya*.

Although, in the formulation of a rule regarding suffixes (*pratyaya*), "being the base" (*prakṛtitva*) consists in being the object of designation (*uddeśyatva*), and thus *bhakṣi* and *bhajyi* do not possess the same form because they are bases as defined by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), nevertheless, it must be maintained that they do possess the same form as bases since they both occur prior to the suffix *tiṅ*, provided one accepts that "being a base" consists in invariably occurring prior to the suffix. Alternatively, the phrase "the blending of the base" (*prakṛtiśleṣa*) means "the blending of the stem" (*aṅgaśleṣa*).

This being the case, the inclusion of such examples as well is entirely unrestricted; for since "vakṣyasi" and "anayoḥ" possess the status of *aṅga* (subordinate element) as defined by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), they share the same formal character. Indeed, the definition of *aṅga* is: "That which is the basis for the rule prescribing a suffix is the *aṅga* with respect to that suffix."
A combination (*saṅkara*) of the two aforementioned types of *prakṛti-śleṣa* is also possible, as in the following example:
"O Enemy of Naraka, when you were seen by the best of yogis, I placed my soul in you with a gaze moistened by compassion; now, bearing your name in my mouth, I am no longer in hell. (915)

In the manner stated in the verse, "That which is to be seen by the best of yogis who perceive the subtle is seen by those perceivers of the subtle with a most excellent and subtle intellect," [the Lord] is worthy of being seen (*dṛśye*). [The suffix] *kyap* is applied here according to the rule *ṝdupadhāt*. With my self (*ātmā*) placed within You—my self being entrusted to You—I become beloved by You, the agent, through Your compassionate gaze as the instrument; or rather, *dayārdradṛśā* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound serving as an adjective for "by You" (*tvayā*), and the construction is joined by repeating the word *dṛśye*. The meaning is: "I am desired [by You]."

This is the first person singular present indicative (*laṭ*) in the passive voice (*yak*) derived from the root *dṛś* (to see). "Bearing your name in the mouth" means uttering your name; that is to say, [I shall not be cast into hell]. Regarding the phrase "bearing in the mouth," there is a word-break as *na āsye* (not in the mouth) in the alternative sense of "in hell" (*niraya*). The particle *purā* is an indeclinable used to indicate certainty. The construction is *purā na āsye*. The meaning is: "By certainty, I shall not be cast away. This is the first person singular present indicative in the passive voice derived from the root *as* (to throw), preceded by the prefix *ā*, in the sense of casting away.

And this present tense suffix (*laṭ*) occurs here in the sense of the future due to its connection with the particles *surā* and *aśabda*, according to the grammatical rule: "The present tense is used after the particles *yāvat* and *purā*" (*yāvatpurānipātayorlaṭ*). Here, there is a combination (*śleṣa*) of the verbal bases (*prakṛti*) ending in *kyap* and *ṇyat* respectively—namely, the bases *dṛśya-* and *āsya-*—along with their respective case endings (*sup*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), such as *ṅi* and *iṭ*. Thus, these two are intermingled. Although the verbal root (*dhātu*) is identical in both cases, the establishment of the verbal base pun (*prakṛtiśleṣa*) proceeds by taking into account the distinction created by the difference in suffixes.

In the *Amara-sudhā*, [the word] *āsya* is derived thus: "That by which syllables (*varṇa*) are cast forth (*asyante*), or that in which a morsel (*grāsa*) is cast forth, is the *āsya*. This is based on the root *asu* in the sense of "casting" (*kṣepaṇe*), with the suffix *ṇyat* according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Alternatively, it is explained in the same work: "It flows (*āsyandate*) or trickles out due to its acidity, hence it is *āsya*. This is based on the root *syandū* in the sense of "flowing" (*prasravaṇe*), with the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule *anyebhyo'pi dṛśyate*. In this latter case, the difference in the verbal roots clearly results in a difference in the base forms (*prakṛti*).

It should be understood that here there is not only a pun on the base forms alone, but also a pun on the suffixes (*pratyaya*); such is the specific excellence of the poetic figure (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*).
The punning of the base (prakṛtiśleṣa) does not depend solely on nominal and verbal suffixes; rather, it can also occur in dependence upon the bases of secondary derivatives (taddhita).

O Lord, by Your compassion, may he who has taken refuge in You become more renowned and his prosperity likewise increase; but may he who is hostile toward You become even more wretched and his multitude of calamities even greater.

O Lord! A person who has taken refuge in You shall, through Your compassion (*ghṛṇā*) and grace (*kṛpā*), become *prathīyān*—one who possesses *prathā*, which means renown or fame consisting of the manifestation of one's virtues; that is, one who is exceedingly renowned (*atiśayena prathāvān*). [The formation is as follows: from the word *prathā*, with the suffix *matup* and then the comparative suffix *īyasun*, the *matup* is elided by the rule "vinmatoḥ. Furthermore, His glory—the glory of one who has taken refuge in the Blessed One—is also *prathīyān*, meaning exceedingly vast (*atiśayena pṛthuḥ*), that is, extremely extensive.

From the word *pṛthu* with the suffix *īyasun*, the substitution of *ra* for the *ṛ*-vowel occurs according to the rule "ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ. However, the phrase "by your disgust" (*tvatpratikūlastu tava ghṛṇayā*) is also connected here. According to Amara, "ghṛṇe" means "disgust" (*jugupsā*) and "compassion" (*karuṇā*). The meaning is: "by your disgust that [he] is unworthy," that is, by the contempt originating from you. "Sādhīyān" means "accompanied by mental distress" (*ādhi*); "sādhīyān" is that which is exceedingly *sādhi*, meaning one who possesses unsurpassed mental anguish. [This state] would come to pass.

For him who is opposed to you, even a multitude of calamities is *sādhīyaḥ*—meaning exceedingly (*atiśayena*), very much (*bāḍha*), or extremely firm (*atimātra-dṛḍha*). From the word *bāḍha*, when the suffix *īyasun* is added, the substitution *sādha* occurs according to the rule "antikabāḍhayornedasādhau. Amara states: "gāḍha, bāḍha, and dṛḍha [are synonyms for firm]. Here, there is a uniformity (*aikarūpyam*) between the base forms of *prathāvat* and *pṛthu* on one hand, and *sādhi* and *bāḍha* on the other, when followed by the same secondary suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*).

A pun involving both the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and the nominal derivative suffix (*taddhita*), along with their respective bases and suffixes, is also possible. For example: "O Śrī Śāradā, how can you desire that which is difficult to obtain—immortality from the Great Bliss? "Do not be ashamed, my dear; how many people here have not been made immortal by Him? (917) In this verse, there is a pun on the word *amṛtam*. When taken with the verbal root *mṛ* ("to die") and the suffix *kta*, it means "immortality. When taken with the root *mṛj* ("to wipe/cleanse") and the suffix *kta*, it means "something wiped away" or "removed. Thus, the pun operates through both the verb and its derivative forms.

"One who possesses *agha* (evil/suffering) is *aghī*; the suffix *-in* is used here in the sense of a constant connection (*nityayoga*), meaning one who is eternally miserable. [As Amara states: 'The word *agha* refers to evil, suffering, and calamity. From the Great Bliss—that is, from the limitless bliss described in the passage, 'That is the one bliss of Brahman'—how could I hope for or expect the nectar of liberation, which is difficult to attain even from the Blessed Lord, the Lord of Śrī? The implication is that it would be like a dog hoping for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) fit for the gods."

In the word *etai*, the substitution of *ai* for the final *e* of the first person imperative (*loṭ*) is applied. Thus, *aṅga*!—this is an address to someone else or to oneself. *Mā trapīṣṭhāḥ*: "do not be excessively ashamed" (*trapūṣ* means "to be ashamed"). In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the augment *iṭ* is optional because the root ends in *ū*. Due to its conjunction with *māṅ*, the negative particle, the augment *aṭ* is absent. To the objection, "How can one such as I not feel shame at being commanded by one such as You?", he replies with the words beginning with *iha*. The construction is: "In this world (*iha*), how many people have been excessively ashamed before that Blessed Lord (*tena śrīśena*)?"

*Trapiṣṭhāḥ* means people who are excessively *tṛpra*. Mādhava states that *tṛpra* means suffering (*duḥkha*), and here the word refers to one who possesses that [suffering]. The meaning is: "those whose suffering is even greater than yours. From the word *tṛpra*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added in the sense of superlative degree; by the rule *priyasthira-* etc., *tṛpra* is replaced by *trapī*. [The sense is: "How can you feel shame for promising liberation when, in truth, so many have already been led to the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*)? This is the underlying thought.

In this case, there is a uniformity between the verbal root *trap* and the nominal base *tṛpra*, respectively, when joined with the suffix *iḍā* (in the form *iḍāśliṣṭa*), the personal ending *thās*, and the secondary suffix *iṣṭhan*; it should be understood that there is likewise a uniformity between the two suffixes themselves.

Now, as for the pun on suffixes (*pratyayaśleṣa*): if there is identity of form among many streams of roots and suffixes through their being joined with [identical] suffixes, this is called a pun on suffixes.

That wherein a similarity is observed among several combinations of base (prakṛti) and suffix (pratyaya), caused by the coalescence of their respective suffixes, is this "coalescence of suffixes" (pratyayaśleṣa). These two definitions—of the coalescence of base and suffix—are described here in accordance with Rudraṭa. In reality, however, it is as follows: "If there is a coalescence of two bases, that is 'coalescence of base' (prakṛtiśleṣa);
if there is a coalescence of two suffixes, it is desired as 'coalescence of suffix' (pratyayaśleṣa)."

This much alone is sufficient for the definition [of *vācya*], since it follows the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other authorities. The author of the *Kāvyapradīpa* maintains that because the variety of case-endings (*vibhakti*) serves as a cause of distinction, the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is employed separately to refer to those [suffixes] other than [case-endings]. For example: "Where the lover of Fortune (Viṣṇu) appears as one who forgives my great offense, and where his immeasurable protection from the affliction of egoism shines forth extensively—by him, my desired goal shall likewise be attained. (918)

The Lord is the lover of Śrī; by this, the presence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is expressed. He is the "forgiver" (*kṣamitā*), the one who will endure my transgression (*madāgaḥ*); this is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) from the root *kṣam*. The augment *iṭ* is optional because the root begins with *ū*. He states the reason for this in the phrase "wherein": the construction is "wherein," that is, in whom—the beloved of Śrī—there is "extensive forgiveness. One who forgives is "forgiving" (*kṣamī*). The suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied to the root *kṣam* according to the rule *śamityaṣṭābhyo ghinuṇ*; the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies here by the rule *nodāttopadeśasya*.

The state of that [forgiveness] is "forgivingness" (*kṣamitā*), which shines forth as the endurance of great offenses. Now he states its effect: "My series of torments" (*tāpāliḥ*)—the succession of internal and other sufferings—"is calmed" (*śamitā*); it will be pacified. This is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) of the root *śam*. The meaning is: since my offense has been forgiven by the Blessed One, the affliction of my threefold suffering will surely perish. Not only this much; likewise, "by him"—that is, by him [the Lord], "by me."

*Abhimatā* means desired; *śamitā* means that which pacifies (*śāmyati*), thus it is a *śamī*. As before, the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied, and there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. Its state is *śamitā*—the state of being peaceful (*śāntatā*), as heard in the scripture "peaceful and self-controlled. The sense is that this is conducive to the worship of the Blessed One. *Āpsyate* means will obtain. Here, in the pair *kṣamitā* and *śamitā*, there is a "fusion of suffixes" (*pratyayaśleṣa*), because the similarity between the combination of stem and suffix in each case is caused by the phonetic identity with the suffix *tāl*.

Just as the Blessed One was grasped by my heart, so too were all my senses rendered incapable of grasping their wicked objects; thus, by me, who am blessed, even the suffering of wandering through the forest of existence has been transformed. The Blessed One was "grasped" (agrāhi) by my heart—that is, by my mind; this is the ellipsis. The meaning is that he was apprehended or meditated upon. This is the *luṅ* (aorist) passive form of the root *grah* with the *ciṇ* suffix. Furthermore, "all my senses," such as the eyes and so forth, acting as the agent, became "incapable of grasping" (*agrāhi*) their wicked objects; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object. The ellipsis is that they became non-apprehending.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *grah* in the sense of the agent according to the rule *anandigrahipracchi...*. For this very reason, I, the fortunate one who has achieved my purpose, have "become" (*abhāvi*). The form *abhāvi* is derived from the root *bhū* in the sense of a state (*bhāve*) using the *luṅ* (aorist) with the *ciṇ* affix; thus, even the suffering of wandering through the forest of existence (*bhava-kāntāra*) for me has "become non-existent" (*abhāvi*), meaning it will not exist. The meaning is that henceforth it shall not occur again. The suffix *ini* is added to the root *bhū* in the sense of the future according to the rule *bhaviṣyati-gamyādayaḥ*, and by the rule *bhuvaśca*; furthermore, it is treated as *ṇit*. This is because the term *ṇit* is understood from the preceding rule *āṅiṇit*. Thereafter, a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is formed.
In this case, the form *agrāhi* is derived from both roots, *a-bhū* and *a-bhavi*, as there is uniformity between the two suffixes, *ciṇ* and *ṇini*.

Just as you were the beginning of the worlds, so too is your greatness beyond even words that have no beginning; you existed on the mountain of the serpent-king, and having taken refuge in you, I too have become Bhavānī, O Hari.

O Hari! You are the beginning of the worlds; as stated in the scriptural passage "from which indeed these [worlds arise]," you were the cause. This is the second person singular aorist (luṅ) of the root *bhū*. Your majesty, however, was beyond even words that have no beginning—beyond the scope of speech—as per the Śruti: "from which words turn back. The negative particle (*nañ*) is compounded with the word *bhū*. The sense is that you alone are the one who has become the cause of the universe. On the mountain of the serpent (Śeṣācala), you were born; the meaning is that you manifested in the form of an image for the sake of protecting the world.

This is the second person singular imperfect (*laṅ*) of the root *bhū*. The sense is: "having taken refuge in You, even though my heart acts like a deer in the mirage of the desert of sense-objects, [I am so]. *Abhavaḥ* means "one who is free from rebirth. *Bhavāni* is in the imperative (*loṭ*) used for a request; the meaning is "I hope that you may become [thus]. Here, in both instances—*abhūḥ* and *abhavaḥ*—there is a formal identity between the suffixes *sip* and *sup*.

Just as the touch of a subtle form causes distress to those standing face-to-face with their teachers, so too does it cause me distress from afar; O Mother, may Hari quickly remove all my sins and make me dear to Him.

"O Mother! You have spread me out (*atanoḥ*) before the Teachers; this is the second person singular imperfect (*laṅ*) of the root *tan*. This word *atanoḥ* is repeated: 'May the affliction of Kāma (*atanoḥ*) be far from me (*me*). The sense is that by being in the presence of the Teachers, lust and other passions do not touch me. May you remove (*apanudeḥ*) all my evil, both past and future sin; this is the second person singular optative (*liṅ*) of the root *hṛ* used in the sense of possibility."

The phrase "of that Hari" (*māṃ tasya hareḥ*) is to be understood as recurring here. You should extend—that is, make—[this person] dear to Lord Hari, who is the object of His affection in the manner stated [in the Gītā]: "And he is dear to Me. The suffix *liṅ* in the root *tan* (to extend) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). I consider it certain that you, who grant the teacher’s favor, will indeed make him an eternal servant of the Lord in the supreme ether (*parame vyoman*), preceded by the removal and destruction of his future and past sins.
Has that Lord, who even while I was in the womb provided for my sustenance,
now fallen asleep or has he returned to ordain the remainder of my life?
The intended meaning is "according to this rule. In this context, there is a formal identity between the suffixes *sip* and *ṅasi* in the expression "atanoḥ hareḥ" (of the bodiless Hari).

O ocean of compassion, for one who has taken refuge in you, there is no falling; rather, even that [fall] is [prevented] by you. Thus, may your two feet [protect] me—what else remains for me to request? 922.

O ocean of compassion! For one who has taken refuge in you, there is no "falling"—that is, no downward descent (the word *pāta* being formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an action). Rather, even that very fall is protected by you (the word *pāta* being formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the object). By this, both the warding off of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable are expressed. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "The word *pāta* [means] 'protected' as well as 'falling'. To the question, "What does this gain for you in the case of such an extraordinary benefit for the one who has sought refuge?", he says: *tvad-* (your...). [The sense is: Your two feet [are mine]; the thought is, "Am I not also one who has sought refuge in you?"

"Thus [it is that] two protect from falling. This is the *laṭ* (present tense) first person dual of the root *pāt* ("to fall"). The word "thus" (*evam*) indicates a gesture of demonstration. The sense is: "While you alone protect those who have taken refuge [in you], you two, my feet, protect me; thus, by comparison with him, I alone obtain the pre-eminence. The meaning is: "What else is there for me to pray for, other than protection consisting of the warding off of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable? For everything that is worth praying for is included herein."

In this instance, since the suffixes *ktvā* (a *kṛt* suffix) and *ktas* (a *kta* suffix) following a noun-ending (*subanta*), as well as the suffixes following a verbal ending (*tiṅanta*), are identical in form for the second and third meanings, this is a case of "suffix-pun" (*pratyayaśleṣa*) that is intermingled with the primary "word-pun" (*padaśleṣa*); thus, it differs from previous examples.
Now, as for the pun on words (*vacanaśleṣa*):
that would be a pun on words if words are joined together.
The meaning is that if the case endings (*vibhakti*) of either nouns (*sub*) or verbs (*tiṅ*) are joined together, it is called "punning of number" (*vacanaśleṣa*).
For example: "May Lakṣmī—who sports in the heart of Hari, who strikes down calamities, who nourishes prosperities, and who shines—restrain my restlessness at her feet. (123)

In this context, for the two forms *khelantī* and *dīvyantī*, the augment *num* is obligatory before the feminine suffixes *śī* and *nadyoḥ* by the rule *śapchyanoḥ nityam*. However, in the case of *tudatī*, there is no *num*, because its application is optional according to the rule *ācchīnadyoḥ num*. The meaning is "let her obstruct" (*rundhā*) and "let them obstruct" (*niruddhāni karotu kurutām*). The form *rundhā* is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*) in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) derived from the root *rudhir* (meaning "to cover") with the sense of obstruction. In the alternative case, it is the second person dual of the imperative in the active voice (*parasmaipada*) derived from that same root.

Here, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) between the singular and dual numbers in the nominal forms beginning with "khelantī" and the verbal form "rundhāmi"; furthermore, a pun on gender (*liṅgaśleṣa*) is also to be observed here.

May those who possess exceedingly great and self-originated splendor, whose majestic forms inspire awe, whose minds are ever fixed on supreme beauty, and who are the soul of all, bestow the highest glory.

Here there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on Śrī Paravāsudeva and the incarnations in manifest form (*arcāvatāra*) residing in divine places such as Śrī Veṅkaṭācala. In the first sense, he is so called because his *mahaḥ*—that is, his majesty or splendor—is very great (*sumahat*). He is one whose worship (*māna*) has been performed in many ways (*bahudhā*) by the Self-born Creator (*svayaṃbhuvā vedhasā*). He is so called because he possesses both the exalted *arcā*—the incarnations in manifest form located at Śrī Veṅkaṭācala and other sites—and the *vibhava*—the incarnations such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others—or else, it refers to that by which these are possessed.

One whose mind is "suśrīka" (possessing beautiful prosperity) is one in whom the mind is constantly possessed of auspicious *śrī* (fortune or Lakṣmī). According to the statement, "The mind of this Goddess is established in Him, and His [mind] is established in Her," the meaning is that his mind is incessantly longing for Lakṣmī. May the Supreme One, the Soul (*ātman*) of all who enters within and governs, namely Para-Vāsudeva, bestow (*saṃdadhatām*) upon us (*naḥ*) prosperity (*śriyam*), which is abundance in every respect.
This is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*) derived from the root *dhā* (to hold/support) belonging to the *bhūvādika* class.

In the second alternative, however, these qualifiers end in the plural number, in accordance with the substantive *vibhavāḥ* (manifestations). They are those for whom there is a "sumahān mahaḥ"—that is, a very great festival, such as the Nityotsava (eternal festival) and Pakṣotsava (fortnightly festival), and so forth. Amara states: *maha uddhava utsavaḥ*. This word *mahaḥ* ends in a short vowel. The term *svayam* means by oneself, that is, without being prompted by another. They are so described because they have established (*kṛta*) many abodes (*dhāmani*), such as Veṅkaṭācala and other locations, upon the earth (*bhuvi*).

Those whose *arcās*—meaning worshipful objects or images—are *ūrjitāḥ*, that is, powerful or majestic, are so described. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *arcā* refers to both worship and an image. They are *suśrīkamanāḥ*, meaning those who desire or are beloved by Śrī (Lakṣmī); that is, they are exceedingly desirable to Lakṣmī or are exceedingly beautiful. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *kamanaḥ* means a lover, desire, handsome, or the Aśoka tree. They are the *ātmanas*—the very selves, manifestations, origins, or lords—of all things, both sentient and insentient; the meaning is that they are the Lords of the Universe (*jagadīśvarāḥ*).

The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of worship in those various divine places. [The term] *saṃdadhatām* means "constantly bestowing the supreme glory, the most excellent prosperity. This is the third person plural imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *dhā*, belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class. Here, in the phrase *sumahāmahāḥ*, there is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the nominative singular and plural endings; and in *saṃdadhatām*, there is a *śleṣa* between the nominative singular and plural endings within the finite verb (*tiṅanta*). However, it should be understood that in *svayaṃbhūkṛta* and so forth, there is a *pada-śleṣa* (word-level pun).
In the word *paraśriyam*, since it is a compound (*samasta*), the doubling of the letter *śa* is optional according to the rule *anaci ca*.

O descendant of Raghu, even if someone is treated as an enemy by you but is nevertheless placed before you even once, he shall become the enjoyer of your abundant and flavorful possessions, or at least the recipient of your life-sustaining domain. (926)

O Raghunandana! That man who—even but once—is placed before you (puraskriyate), meaning honored, respected, or (in the alternative sense) attacked; for Amara states: "The word *puraskṛta* means honored, an enemy, attacked, or placed in front"—that very person, of the kind described, [conquers] those things which have four corners (*aśrayakoṭi*), such as women, wealth, and so forth; for Amara states: "Women, protectable objects, and wealth are the corners."

This word is established as an *ajanta* (ending in a vowel) through the rule *‘suprātasuśva’* etc., within the context of a *bahuvrīhi* compound; that is to say, [it refers to] those existing at the four ends of the quarters. It is a "region" (*viṣaya*)—a land—that bestows life-force (*prāṇada*), meaning it grants power, to the "bearers of essence," namely the kings (*rasābhṛt*). According to Amara, "region" (*deśa*) and "territory" (*viṣaya*) are synonyms. The particle *vā* is displaced in its position; its meaning is "he will surely enjoy" or "he will certainly protect" (*alaṃ bhoktā vā bhokṣyaty eva pālayiṣyaty eva*). The root *bhuja* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "eating. From this root, the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) is formed.
According to the *Viśva*, the indeclinable *vā* may signify "option" (*vikalpa*), "comparison" (*upamā*), or "certainty" (*evārtha*).

Elsewhere, that man, attacked by enmity, is an "unskilled eater of *śrāṇā*"; this is the word division (*cheda*). "Unskilled" (*acatura*) means incompetent. "Not nourished" (*nabhṛtā*) means not nourished by flavor (*rasa*), thus "flavorless" (*rasābhṛtā*); the meaning is "lacking taste. "*Śrāṇā*" refers to barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), according to Amara’s lexicon: "*yavāgūruṣṇikā śrāṇā*. "Eater" (*bhoktā*) means one who consumes; it is the agentive form derived from the root *bhuj*. Precisely because of this, due to the prohibition in the rule *na lokāvyaya-niṣṭhā-khal-artha-tṛṇām*, there is no genitive case for the object in the word *śrāṇā*, but rather only the accusative. "Life-giving" (*prāṇadam*) means that which cuts off life, i.e., a destroyer of breath.
The term *prāṇa* refers to the internal wind within the body, to the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*),
to life-span, to the vital faculties, to the essence of beings, to the sacred syllable *praṇava*, and to the vital organ of poetry.

Thus ends the *Ratnamālā*. This refers to "poison" (*viṣa*) as an object that does not actually exist; one must not forget the identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its referent. That [poison] is the enjoyer [of the situation]. Your opponent, being in distress, lives somewhere or other on the consumption of poor food; or, unwilling to live in such a manner, he drinks poison. But he does not exert his prowess in your presence—this is the intended meaning.

In this verse, in the phrase *caturaśrāṇāṃ rasābhṛtām*, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) between the genitive plural and the accusative singular, which is intermingled with a word-pun (*pada-śleṣa*). In the word *bhoktā*, there is a pun between a nominal stem ending in a case suffix and a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). In the word *ayam*, there is both a word-pun intermingled with others and a pun between the nominative and accusative case endings.

Just as for those who worship the All-Knowing One, his mind is superior due to its excellent qualities and so forth— He whose power is unimpeded, whose nature is great, and who destroys even the most persistent evils.

Here there is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the words *bhagavat* and *bhāgavat*. To explain: he who knows (*vid*) is called *vidaḥ*; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhala-kṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). He who knows everything is *sarvavidaḥ*, i.e., *sarvavit*, as the Vedic scripture states: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (*yassarvajñassarvavit*). He possesses excellent qualities and so forth (*suguṇādimān*): "excellent qualities" (*suguṇāḥ*) refers to auspicious attributes such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and the like; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), his essential nature (*svarūpa*), forms (*rūpa*), and other attributes are included. He is so described because these belong to him. The possessive suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of eternal connection (*nityayoga*) or excellence (*atiśāyana*).

And that light is unobstructed, and He possesses it; He is endowed with divine radiance capable of eclipsing the sun and other luminaries, as stated in the passage beginning, "The sun does not shine there. The reason for this is that He possesses great intrinsic nature (*mahāsvabhāva*); His nature is transcendent and self-luminous, for His manifestation is not dependent on anything else, unlike that of the sun and similar sources. Alternatively, *bhāḥ* means power (*prabhāva*), according to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *bhāḥ* [is used] in the sense of power and brilliance. Thus, the meaning is that He possesses great majesty.

The word *nudaḥ* means "one who pushes away" (*nudati iti nudaḥ*), with the suffix *ka* added according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*. It refers to one who dispels evil that has a miserable end; the meaning is that he shakes off both past and future sins. The word *varīyān* means "exceedingly vast" (*atiśayena uruḥ*). From the word *uru*, the suffix *īyasun* is applied, and by the rule beginning with "priya-sthira," etc., the substitution of *vara* for *uru* occurs. *Yadu-varīyān* means the Lord who is the most excellent in the Yadu clan—the ornament of the Yadu lineage—may He occupy our mind; the meaning is that He may dwell within our hearts.

The word division is *pakṣe bhaja tān naḥ*. O our mind (*naḥ* = *asmākam cetaḥ*); O mind! *Sarvavidaḥ* means those who know everything; [it is derived from] *sarvam vidanti iti sarvavidaḥ*, with the suffix *kvip* after the root *vid*. The meaning is "the omniscient ones."

"Excellent qualities" (*suguṇāḥ*) refers to those who possess great virtues such as the "eight qualities of the self" mentioned by Gautama and others—namely, compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of fatigue, auspiciousness, generosity, and absence of longing. Among them, the "first" or "foremost" ones are so designated; here the suffix *ḍimac* is applied according to the rule *agrādipaścāḍḍimuc* in the sense of "originating from. They are those whose power is unimpeded and who possess uncurtailed majesty.

Those whose nature is great are so described; those who dispel endless misfortune (*duranta-durita*) are likewise described—[the suffix] *kvip* is added to the root *nud*. Those well-known ones belonging to the best of the Yadus are "Yaduvarīyās. Because the class beginning with *gaha* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *cha* is applied. This means "the Bhāgavatas. [The word] "bhaja" means "serve. It is the second person singular present imperative of the root *bhaj* (which is *parasmaipadin*). In the preceding case, it is the third person singular present imperative.

In examples such as *suguṇādimān*, there is a blend of word-play (*padaśleṣa*) involving both singular and plural numbers. The same applies to the blending of the nominative (*prathamā*) and accusative (*dvitīyā*) case endings. In cases such as *yaduvarīyān*, however, there is a blend of number and case ending just as before; the distinction here, however, is that there is a blend between the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) ending in the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *īyasun* and its base (*paramaprakṛti*), which consists of the words *uru* and *vara*.
Just as you,

O Śauri, being most senior, warded off the calamities for the people of Vraja, so too, being even more venerable, did you dispel the great evils resulting from the uprooting of Kāliya from the Yamunā.

O Śauri! "Varṣīyān" means the eldest or the most ancient; the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who is exceedingly old. From the word *vṛddha*, when the suffix *īyasun* is added, the substitution of *varṣa-* occurs according to the rule beginning with "priyasthira-. You, O Śauri, restrained—meaning you held back—the calamities, that is, the afflictions of the people of Vraja, the multitude of Nanda’s cowherd folk, which were caused by excessive rain during the occasion of the Govardhana sacrifice by the enraged Indra (*Vṛddhaśravas*). This is the sense. You suppressed those disasters.

Moreover, "garīyān" means exceedingly venerable, the teacher even of teachers—that is, the Primordial Preceptor (Prathamācārya), as stated in the passage: "Thou art his worshipful and most venerable Guru. This is also supported by the reading of the *Sahasranāma*: "Guru, Gurutama. [O Lord], because of the uprooting—meaning the expulsion—from Kālīya, the serpent of that name, Thou art more venerable than the poison (*gara*) belonging to Kālindī, the Yamunā; the suffix *cha* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *gaha*. Likewise, in the word "varṣīyān," [Thou art] one who has shaken off—meaning dispelled—the faults.
Here, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between the nominative singular and the accusative plural; everything else is to be understood as in the case of the verse beginning with *yaduvarīyān*.
O Murāri, your neck, eyes, and nails may indeed attain comparison with the lotus; yet when the entire world is in peril, your compassion, your two eyes, and your four arms [alone] do so. 929.

O Mukunda! Your neck attains (*gāte*), goes to, reaches—meaning it achieves—the likeness of a lotus and the equality of a conch shell. Your two eyes attain (*gāte*) the likeness of a lotus, that is, they achieve similarity with a lotus. And your nails attain (*gāte*) the likeness of a lotus, that is, they achieve the common quality of the moon. From the root *gāṅ* in the sense of "going," belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, the forms are respectively the third person singular, dual, and plural of the present tense (*laṭ*). In the plural form, the substitution of *at* for *jha* occurs according to the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*.

Your compassion protects the entire world through a mutual exchange of functions (*karmavyatihāra*). *Karmavyatihāra* means the reciprocal interchange of actions; the meaning is that Your two eyes provide protection suited for the function of the arms. Thus, Your two eyes provide protection suited for the function of compassionate arms, while Your four arms provide protection suited for the function of compassionate vision.

From the root *pat* preceded by the prefix *vyati*, the Ātmanepada affix is applied according to the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*; thus, there are the first-person singular, dual, and plural forms of the present tense (*laṭ*) in sequence. Here, the form is identical across all three numbers—whether it is *gāte*, *vyatigāte*, or *vyatipāte*—and this constitutes a *vacanaśleṣa* (pun on number). The distinction is that this is a pure instance [of *śleṣa*], not a mixed one as in the previous example.

The author of the *Alaṅkāra-kaustubha* states: "Among these eight types of *śleṣa*, that which appears to be included within another should be intended as being distinct from it. It should be understood that these varieties of *śleṣa* occur, as appropriate, even in the previously illustrated examples of *śleṣa* involving the contextual (*prakṛta*) and non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), and so forth. Thus, the eightfold *sabhaṅga-śleṣa* has been defined. An example of *abhaṅga-śleṣa* is found in my own *Nṛsiṃha-vilāsa*:

May that great Puruṣa, Hari, who bestows the glory of immortality upon the virtuous and who has increased the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), bring joy—He whose splendor is like the orb of the charming moon and who resides within the mouth. 930.

In this verse, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) regarding both Śrī Hayagrīva and Nṛsiṃha, who are the very subjects under discussion as being worthy of praise. [He is] "bestowing" (*prayacchan*)—the present participle is used here in the sense of cause (*hetu*), according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*—"the glory of immortality" (*amṛtaśriyam*) for the virtuous; that is to say, the *Trayī* (the three Vedas). For the Śruti states: "The Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas—that indeed is the immortal glory of the virtuous. By means of this bestowal (*pradānena*), [he is so described].

He by whom Hiraṇyagarbha—that is, Brahmā—was nourished and strengthened; the meaning is that he is the one who restored the four-faced one to life by recovering and returning the Vedas stolen by Madhu and Kaiṭabha. This is according to the Śruti: "He who first created Brahmā and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him. In this regard, the narrative of the Hayagrīva incarnation found in the Mokṣadharma section should be consulted.

In one sense, he is one by whom the womb—the belly—of Hiraṇya (Hiraṇyakaśipu) has been thoroughly severed; in another sense, he is one who bestows the glory of immortality—the wealth of liberation—upon the virtuous knowers of Brahman, and is thus pre-eminently increased. His abode is like the orb of the charming moon; in the other sense, his splendor is like the light of the orb of the charming moon, for it is said that the divine form of Nṛsiṃha is white, as in the verse: "I worship Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, white as the moon."

May that great Hari, who is both a horse and a lion, be for your delight! Herein, because it encompasses multiple meanings understood through the recollection of words possessing identical phonetic sequences—without depending on a mutually distinct word-break (pada-bhaṅga)—this is *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (unbroken paronomasia).

Regarding this, some say that between these two types of *śleṣa*—the *sabhaṅga* (with word-break) and the *abhaṅga* (without word-break)—in examples such as "sarvadomādhavaḥ," where there is a connection between the two words "sarvadaḥ" and "sarvadā" according to the analogy of lac and wood (*jatukāṣṭhanyāya*), the *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* is a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) because it resides in the word (*śabdavṛttitvāt*). However, in the case of *abhaṅgaśleṣa*, since there is no division of words in words such as *abja* or *kamala*, there is no connection between two distinct words; thus, because residing in the word is untenable, and because two meanings are connected by being denoted (*vācyatayā*) within a single word, this is an ornament of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*) according to the analogy of two fruits on a single stalk (*ekavṛntagataphaladvayanyāya*). This is what they claim.

Others, however, maintain that both *sabhaṅga* (with word-splitting) and *abhaṅga* (without word-splitting) *śleṣa* (punning) are indeed verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*), because they follow the presence and absence of the words themselves. It is not appropriate to claim that *sabhaṅga-śleṣa* is a verbal figure because it rests upon the words, while *abhaṅga-śleṣa* is a semantic figure (*arthaśleṣa*) because it rests upon the meaning; for in this case too, the distinction is established through the very same method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as is the case with defects such as harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) or qualities such as density (*gāḍhatva*), and figures like alliteration (*anuprāsa*). To postulate some other distinct regulating factor would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor should it be argued that, because even *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (unbroken pun) follows the presence and absence of the word (*śabdānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyitayā*), it would be a *śabda-śleṣa* (verbal pun), thereby rendering *artha-śleṣa* (semantic pun) devoid of its own scope. For example: "With a little he attains elevation; with a little he goes to a low state.

Oh, how similar is the nature of the scale-beam and of the wicked man! In this instance, although the words are the same, the application differs according to the two meanings. Thus, *artha-śleṣa* retains its distinct domain.

In such cases, as in "where even with a slight elevation," and so forth, the status of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is not destroyed even when there is a change of words; for they have declared that in those very instances, the sovereignty of the category of *arthaśleṣa* (semantic paronomasia) prevails.

The author of the *Kuvalayānanda*, however, maintains that both [types of *śleṣa*] are figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*). This is his underlying intention: this *śleṣa*, though twofold—distinguished as "with word-break" (*sabhanga*) and "without word-break" (*abhaṅga*)—is indeed a figure of sense alone; for it is appropriate that its status as a figure of sense follows from its nature of conveying multiple meanings. Furthermore, the relationship of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) alone is the determinant of those respective figures, just as is the case with worldly ornaments.

For a worldly ornament, such as a bracelet or an anklet, residing on the hand or foot, is designated specifically as an ornament of the hand or foot. This same principle applies to the ornaments found in poetry as well. Nor should it be argued that this [particular ornament] is a verbal ornament because it follows the presence and absence of the word; for if that were the case, it would follow that all ornaments are verbal ornaments, since they all likewise follow the presence and absence of the word.

Nor is it correct—as asserted by the author of the *Sarvasva* and others—that non-ambiguous *śleṣa* (paronomasia) belongs to the category of semantic figures (*arthālaṅkāra*) because it rests on two meanings supported by a single word according to the maxim of "two fruits on a single stalk," whereas ambiguous *śleṣa* belongs to the category of verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*) because it consists of the fusion of two distinct words according to the maxim of "lac and wood. This is so because, under the view that "the word differs with the difference in meaning"—a position reinforced by the reasoning that "it is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings"—even in the case of non-ambiguous *śleṣa*, a difference in words is as unavoidable as it is in the case of ambiguous *śleṣa*.

Since the *śleṣa* (punning) of words alone is easily established, both of the following two views are incorrect: that both are verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*), or that the *sabhaga* (with word-break) is a verbal ornament while the *abhaṅga* (without word-break) is a semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*). Therefore, it is more appropriate that both are indeed semantic ornaments.

Others, however, say: because both depend upon the meaning for their aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), both are semantic ornaments; whereas alliteration (*anuprāsa*), *yamaka*, and so forth do not depend upon the meaning for their charm, and thus they are not semantic ornaments, but rather verbal ornaments due to the diversity of sound.

Jagannātha, following the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, states: "Śleṣa (paronomasia) is the presentation of multiple meanings by means of a single word. That is twofold: by way of presenting multiple attributes and by way of presenting a single attribute. The first [type] is twofold: by way of the manifestation of multiple words and by way of the manifestation of a single word; thus, Śleṣa is threefold. Among these, they say the first is *sabhaṅga* (with word-splitting) and the second is *abhaṅga* (without word-splitting). The third, however, is *śuddha* (pure)."

Thus, although this [śleṣa] is threefold, it is further divided into three types based on whether it relies solely on the contextual (prakṛta), solely on the non-contextual (aprakṛta), or on both the contextual and the non-contextual. In the first and second varieties, there is freedom of choice regarding whether the substantive (viśeṣya) is itself a *śliṣṭa* (punning) word. However, in the third variety, the punning quality must belong to the expressive word for the attribute (viśeṣaṇa) alone, and not to the expressive word for the substantive; for if the latter were also punning, there would be a total disappearance of *dhvani* rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*). Even when only the attribute is punning, the *śleṣa* occurs only when both the contextual and non-contextual subjects (*dharmin*) are explicitly mentioned.

"But when only the subject under discussion (*prakṛtadharmimātra*) is taken up, it is the province of *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation). Thus, where there is a single [instance of] multiple meanings having only the subject under discussion as their qualificand, that is the first [type]. Similarly, where there is [multiple meaning] beginning with 'the non-contextual' (*aprakṛta*), etc., that is the second. Where there is a qualifier of multiple meanings having both the separately mentioned contextual and non-contextual subjects as their qualificands, that is the third. And the final definition is 'being one or another of these'. So he said. Following his opinion, a mere indication is illustrated; therein, the first, which has only the contextual as its object and involves a *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* (pun with word-splitting), is as follows:
May that Viṣvaksena, whose hand—playing with the existence of the auspiciously beautiful Lakṣmī—does not require any external support, pacify all obstacles. 931.

The hand of that Blessed One possesses a state of trembling, a state of being tremulous; yet, through that non-trembling—through that lack of agitation—he protects the world while it is in a state of auspicious well-being (*subhavya-jagatkṣema*). Regarding the attainment of this state, the root *bhū* (in the sense of "attainment") takes the suffix *ghañ* according to the rule *'abhū prāptāv ātmanepadī'* from the *ādhṛṣīya* group. Thus, he plays (*dīvyan*) and protects the world.

In one sense, he is the Lord Viṣvaksena, the commander of the Blessed One’s army; his hand—which possesses a most auspicious and exceedingly beautiful luster—protects the world by playing with the *vetra* (staff) through its existence, its stability, or its excellence, according to the saying: "Upon the vibration of the tip of this staff, this entire universe is established. In another sense, he is one for whom there is respect (*ādaraṇa*) for Śeṣācala, the mountain of Śeṣa. In the alternative sense, he is one for whom there is respect that is "unyielding" (*ahārya*) toward Śeṣa, the Infinite One—that is, a respect that cannot be removed by others.

The sense is that, because He too is eternally established as his very own self, there is an uninterrupted love for Him. That Viṣvaksena is the Blessed Lord; according to Amara, "Viṣvaksena is the four-armed one. In the alternative sense, [he refers to] the General of the Blessed One's army. May he pacify obstacles—that is, impediments to the accomplishment of knowledge and hindrances to worldly welfare. For both [the Lord and the General] are declared to be objects of worship for the purpose of quelling obstacles by the two verses beginning with "clad in white garments" and "whose [vehicle is] the elephant."

In this instance, since both the Blessed Lord and Viṣvaksena are equally topical, this is a *sabhanga* (equivocal) type of paronomasia; it relies solely on what is topical by means of a single word (*śruti*) manifesting two terms (*padadvaya*), thereby conveying multiple meanings through the presentation of distinct attributes.
This [type of pun] is also possible even when the two objects to be qualified are not connected, as in:

"May the leader of the Bhṛgus, the leader of the Raghus, or the leader of the Yadus—[he who is] intent on repeatedly routing the gods, and who has severed the arms of his enemies with his arrows—be my protector. (932)

"He causes to melt," thus he is *drāvaṇa*; "the melting of the sun" (*raveḥ drāvaṇaḥ*) is *ravidrāvaṇa*. By means of his manifold splendor—that is, his brilliance—he melts [everything] with his own radiance, just as fire melts a mass of gold; this is the meaning. The sense is that he possesses great majesty (*mahāpratāpa*). As it is said in the *Matsya-purāṇa* and other Purāṇas: "He who, with his thousand arms, whose skin is hardened by the striking of bowstrings, shines like the autumnal sun with its thousand rays."
Thus,
this glorious King Kārtavīrya Arjuna, possessing a thousand hands, surpassed even the Thousand-rayed Sun by means of his great splendor.

And thus: "one who is such an adversary" (*para*)—according to the *Viśva* lexicon, "the supreme enemy of both the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the individual self (*apara*)," which here refers by implication to Kārtavīrya. His arrows are those that take away the lives of enemies (*asuhṛt-prāṇāpahārin*); these are the "enemies' arrows" (*asuhṛdbāṇāḥ*). This qualification is stated with reference to the verse: "He who discharged five hundred arrows with a single impulse. Alternatively, it may mean "those consisting primarily of the arrows of enemies."

The one who cuts through—that is, severs—the expanse or multitude of those arms numbering a thousand is Bhṛgunetā, the descendant of Bhṛgu, Rāma. In the other sense, he is the leader of the Raghus, the Blessed Lord Rāghava, who cuts through the expanse of those twenty arms which belong to Rāvaṇa—those arms in which there are arrows that take away the life-breaths (asuhṛt) of his enemies. [Note: *amara-vit* is derived from the root *vyadh* with the suffix *kvip*, meaning "one who pierces the immortals" in one sense, and "one who takes away the life (*asu*) of others" in the other.]

"Except for the leader of the Yadus, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—who is supremely intent on various ways of routing and driving far away the immortals, the gods; who is the one who has leaped across the expanse of the arms of that enemy Bāṇa, the son of Bali—he shall be my protector and savior. Here, because three incarnations of the Blessed Lord are introduced, there is a *prakṛtaśleṣa* (contextual pun) with broken word-division (*sabhaṅga*), wherein the subjects (*viśeṣya*) are not themselves joined by the pun.
This very second [type], consisting of non-interruption, is as follows:
let the divine ancient jewel shine forth, its glory celebrated throughout a Manvantara, singing the deeds of its ancestors and being expert in the composition of creation and re-creation. (933)

That which possesses the manifestations (*vibhava*) renowned throughout the *manvantaras*—referring to those such as the Horse-headed (*Hayaśiras*) and others mentioned in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* and other texts as "the *manvantara*-incarnations of Viṣṇu"—and elsewhere, whose glory is celebrated through descriptions of the *manvantaras*. That which is born in the lineage (*vaṃśa*), meaning the bamboo flute (*veṇu*), [the suffix] *yat* being applied according to the rule for words beginning with *diś*; thus, it means "born in the lineage" (*vaṃśya*), signifying the bamboo tube. By that [flute], he has performed singing; thus it is so described, meaning he is one who delights in the essence of flute-playing.

In this section, that in which the deeds and conduct of the descendants of the Solar and Lunar dynasties, such as kings and others, are sung and proclaimed— where the past participle is placed after the noun because the term *āhitāgni* belongs to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*— is the Sarga (Creation).

Creation is said to be the manifestation of the subtle elements, the senses, and their objects, arising from the Great Principle (*mahat*) through the agitation of the unmanifest qualities, resulting in the threefold ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
Thus is the collective creation (samaṣṭisṛṣṭi) as described in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata. Re-creation (pratisarga) consists of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of these beings favored by the Puruṣa.
This emission (visarga) is a collection, from seed to seed, comprising all that is moving and unmoving.

That which has been thus defined—the creation of the diverse manifestations of the moving and non-moving world, consisting of the aggregate of Mahat and the other principles, and known by the synonym *visarga* (emission)—in the "composition" (*racane*) or execution thereof, [the Lord] is "skilled" (*niṣṇātam*), meaning proficient. In the alternative sense, [it refers to] the Supreme Brahman, determined as such in its true essence; it is a divine (*divyam*), non-material (*aprākṛtam*), beautiful, and ancient (*purāṇam*, eternal) jewel, skilled in the description of both primary creation (*sarga*) and secondary dissolution (*pratisarga*). Elsewhere, however, the definition of a Purāṇa consists of five characteristics: primary creation (*sarga*), secondary dissolution (*pratisarga*), genealogies (*vaṃśa*), the periods of the Manvantaras (*manvantarāṇi*), and the history of the dynasties (*vaṃśyānucaritam*).

Thus, having described the *Śrīmad-Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa*—the best of Purāṇas possessing the five characteristics mentioned above—it is called a "jewel among Purāṇas" (*purāṇaratna*) because of the statement: "He fashioned that very jewel of a Purāṇa. May it shine, may it blaze! Here, in the passage beginning with "manvantara," there is *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (unbroken pun) with a shared substantive (*śliṣṭaviśeṣyaka*), since multiple meanings are conveyed by means of the appearance of the single word "one" (*eka*) while setting forth multiple attributes.
An example of the *abhaṅga* (unbroken) type when the two qualifiers (*viśeṣya*) are not connected [with the same word] is as follows:

"May that Supreme Brahman, or its Consort, grant us immeasurable prosperity—He who has a pair of hands adorned with lotuses, and whose abode is born from the ocean of milk; She who possesses a slender form and is the source of the ocean of milk. (934)

It is "honored by lotuses" (añcitaṃ kamalaiḥ), meaning worshipped with them, and even more praiseworthy than that; it is "possessed of a pair of hands joined by two lotuses" (kamalābhyāṃ añcitaṃ karayugalaṃ yasya). It is "having its abode and residence arising from the jar and the ocean" (kalaśapayorāśisaṃbhavaṃ), meaning its place of dwelling is there, and its source of birth (saṃbhavasthānaṃ) or birthplace is the jar and the ocean. In this instance, there is a lack of phonetic fusion (aśliṣṭatā) between the two qualifiers.

The third type is the pure (*śuddha*) [śleṣa], which has as its object only the subject at hand (*prakṛta*). For example: "May the ancient sage Nārāyaṇa himself—whose fame is celebrated in the *Mahābhārata* and who possesses the luster of the most radiant monsoon clouds—bestow upon us faultless vision. (935) This [verse] concerns both the Lord Kṛṣṇa and Dvaipāyana; it is "pure" because it conveys multiple meanings by means of a single common attribute (*eka-dharma-puraskāreṇa*). They say that this very [type] is "semantic punning" (*artha-śleṣa*).

The fame renowned through the composition known as the *Mahābhārata*, the dark-blue hue of a monsoon cloud, and the state of being Nārāyaṇa himself—these attributes are identical in form in both cases. Here, the meaning of the authoritative source, “Know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa,” is intended. This is a pure *śliṣṭaviśeṣyaka* (paranomasia with a shared substantive).
This very same [type of simile] is one where the substantive is not connected [to the comparison], being connected only with the attribute, as follows:

"May that ancient jewel, which captivates the heart of Hari, and which is a jewel among brides—possessing a luster that surpasses the sun rising from the belly of the ocean-king, the lord of jars—protect me. (936)

The epithet "possessing a splendor that surpasses the noble" (*aryamātiśāyiruci*) is an attribute of Lakṣmī, based on the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "Born from austerity, he is of the color of the sun."
Thus, these three divisions have been demonstrated as having only the primary subject matter as their scope.
An example of one whose subject matter is not the primary topic (*aprakṛtaviṣaya*):
"O Blessed One, by your power, the sun—whose heat is unrestrained, whose rays flash like flames, who bestows splendor upon the world, and who destroys darkness—has shone forth. (937)

O Blessed One! He is so described because his rays (hetayaḥ) are flashing or shining forth (visphurantyaḥ) during the summer day (ūṣmāhaḥ)—the day of the hot season—unrestrainedly (niraṅkuśaṃ), according to the rule "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac. Regarding the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in the word *visphuranti*, the rule "sphurati-sphulatyor-nir-nivi-vibhyaḥ" prescribes this change optionally; therefore, in this case, since the root *sphurat-* follows the prefix *vi-*, the *s* is not changed to *ṣ*.

According to the *Ratnamālā*, "ūṣmāṇaḥ" refers to the vapors of summer heat, and "hetiḥ" refers to a flame, a weapon, or a ray. Elsewhere, "niraṅkuśoṣmā" is treated as a separate word, meaning "unrestrained heat" or "unimpeded warmth. Regarding "haviṣā," it means with clarified butter (*ājya*); as Amara states, "ghṛtam, ājyam, haviḥ. He is one whose blazing flames (*heti*) are flickering. He is so called because he produces that splendor (*śrī*)—both radiance and prosperity—which causes the world to flourish, shine, and rejoice, thus being "world-delighting" (*jagadullāsinī*).

The Sun’s quality of illuminating the world is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, Fire’s capacity to bestow prosperity is well-known from the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, as in: "O Jātavedas, bring to me the golden Lakṣmī who is radiant with the moon," and "One desiring fortune should seek it from the consumer of oblations. The term "dispeller of darkness" (*dhvāntadhvaṃsī*) carries the same meaning in both cases. Regarding "Citrabhānu": according to Amarasimha, both the Sun and Fire are called "Citrabhānu" (*sūryavahnī citrabhānū*). By your splendor (*ojas*), he was driven away (*niradhāvi*), that is, utterly dispelled. This is derived from the root *dhāv* preceded by the prefix *niṣ*, in the *luṅ* tense, with the *ciṇ* affix in the passive voice.

In this verse, there is *sabhaṅga-śleṣa* (pun with word-splitting) in the first half, *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (pun without word-splitting) in the third quarter, and in the phrase *dhvāntadhvaṃsī*, there is a pure *śleṣa* based on a non-contextual subject where the substantive is shared (*śliṣṭaviśeṣyaka*).

Just as the rain-cloud—possessing a form radiant with a full, shimmering lightning-flash, manifesting great power through the winds, and bringing showers that nourish the world—was surpassed in splendor by you. (938)

O Blessed One! He is so described because his luster (*bhā*) and complexion (*chavi*) are complete and undiminished. His form is radiant with his own *dambholi*—the thunderbolt weapon. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), his form is radiant like a bee (*ali*) amidst the water (*ambu*) that is full (*saṃpūrṇa*), filled (*pūrita*), and shining (*bhāsvat*); the meaning is that he is as dark-hued as such a bee. Or else, he is one whose water (*ambu*) is shining (*bhāsvat*) in its entirety (*saṃpūrṇa*); therefore, he is said to have the radiant luster of a bee, as explained above.

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of two qualifying words (*viśeṣaṇobhayapada*). In one sense, he is "one of great manifestation" (*mahāsphūrti*) among the Maruts, the gods—that is, one who is exceedingly radiant; in the other sense, he is "one of great manifestation" by means of the Marut, the wind—that is, one who possesses extreme radiance or, in other words, excessive movement. [The root] *sphur* [is used] in the sense of "moving," from which the suffix *ktin* is applied to form the abstract noun. "The rain that nourishes the world"—this has the same meaning in both senses, because in both cases it is stated that they bestow rain, as in: "May Parjanya rain for us according to our desire; what Indra rains... Thus, both are said to be givers of rain.

*Parjanya* refers to Indra and the thundering cloud; as Amarasimha states: "The two *parjanyas* are the god Indra and the raining cloud. This [epithet] also, like his previous qualifiers, serves to indicate his connection with the rainy season (*prāvṛṣeṇyatva*). He was "surpassed" (*paryabhāvi*)—that is, overcome—by your fortune (*śrī*), meaning your prosperity, and by your splendor (*tviṣ*). Here, within these three qualifiers, there is respectively *śleṣa* (pun) that involves word-splitting (*sabhaṅga*), *śleṣa* without word-splitting (*abhaṅga*), and pure *śleṣa*; these concern only the non-contextual (the clouds/Indra), having a shared subject (*śliṣṭaviśeṣyaka*).
An example where the two non-contextual subjects are not connected [to the common attribute] is as follows:
"The sky, though blue like a circle of water-lilies and clouds, is surpassed by the splendor of Hari; it is stainless and bestows joy upon the deer sporting within the clouds. (939)

Of the river Hrādinī; in the alternative sense, of the lightning Hrādinī—Amara states: "Taṭinī, hrādinī, and dhunī [mean river]; hrādinyau [means] thunderbolt and lightning. [The compound] *sāraṅgollāsadāyirasadam* means that which gives (*dadāti*) the nectar (*rasa*) which provides joy (*ullāsada*) to the *sāraṅgas*, i.e., the bees (*bhṛṅga*). Amara states: "*Sāraṅga* [means] the *cātaka* bird and the bee. In the alternative sense, *sāraṅga* refers to the *cātaka* birds. *Ullāsadāyi* is a separate word. The division of the compound is: *rasat* (shining) and *amalam* (pure).

The meaning is that [the sky] flows, roars, is stainless, and is unclouded—extremely smooth. The blue water-lily (*kuvalaya*), the *indīvara*, and the circle of clouds are surpassed by the splendor of Hari. Here, in the first quarter-verse there is no word-play (*abhaṅga*), while in the second there is word-play (*sabhaṅga*). In the word "blue" (*nīla*), there is pure *śleṣa* (paronomasia) with an unjoined substantive.
An example concerning both the relevant (prakṛta) and the irrelevant (aprakṛta) subject matter is as follows:

"Śauri (Viṣṇu), possessing the beauty of a charming great lotus, having a dark luster, and being like a supreme conch shell born with the jasmine flower, shines like Kubera (Dhanada), having obtained the pure Vṛṣagiri (the bull-like mountain) from the celestial river (Gaṅgā). (940) In one sense, he is "one who possesses Śrī (Lakṣmī)," who is "charming" (hṛdyā) because she resides on his chest, and who has "great lotuses" (mahāpadmā) because two large, worshipful lotuses are held in her hands. In the other sense, he is "one who possesses the wealth of the treasure called Mahāpadma," which is "charming" (hṛdyā) because it is dear to the heart, and who has the "beauty of a great lotus" (mahāpadma-śrī). He is thus described accordingly.

He whose delight (*ruci*) is in the blue, and whose desire (*abhilāṣa*) is for the treasure named Nīla; he who possesses the excellent (*vara*) conch Pāñcajanya, which is born with the *kunda* flower and is as white as it, being like that flower—thus he is described. In the alternative sense, he is one who possesses the two treasures named Vara and Śaṅkha, which are co-existent with the *kunda* treasure and remain together with it.

He who is attained by that best of mountains, the Lord of the Mountain (Girīśa)—who is called Vṛṣa because he is pure (*vimala*), having removed the impurities of the world—or rather, he who is the "Attainer" (*āpta*) by means of him; or, in another sense, he whose bull (*vṛṣa*) is as pure and bright as Gaṅgā, the river of the sky (*viyaddhunī*); and he for whom Girīśa—that is, Rudra—is an "attained one" (*āpta*), meaning a trusted friend (*pratyayita*). As Amara states: "Āpta and pratyayita are synonyms. Thus, the meaning is "the friend of Tryambaka."

The Blessed One, Śrīnivāsa, shines and glows like Kubera, the giver of wealth. Here, because the primary subject (the Blessed One) and the secondary subject (Kubera) are not based on word-puns (*aśliṣṭa*), while the adjectives are based on puns (*śliṣṭa*), this constitutes the third variety [of *Śleṣa*]. However, this is intermingled with a simile (*upamā*).

Furthermore, if one were to compose a metaphor by reading "the Lord Dhanada sports" and thereby making even the non-contextual element (*aprakṛtāṃśa*) subject to *śleṣa* (paronomasia), even then the *śleṣa* remains unimpaired because the contextual substantive (*viśeṣya*), Śauri [Viṣṇu], is not itself paronomastic. Nor should it be mistaken that this is *samāsokti* (condensed expression), because here the non-contextual substratum (*dharmī*) is also directly denoted by the word.
