However, where only the non-contextual behavior (*vyavahāra*) is supported by the power of the word, while the non-contextual substratum is not, there *samāsokti* is desired.

In this regard, it is considered that this figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) mostly occupies the domain of another figure of speech. In such cases, does it act as a sublater (*bādhaka*), or is there a state of commingling (*saṃkīrṇatva*), or rather is it itself the sublated (*bādhyatva*)? On this point, Udbhaṭa and others say: "That which is commenced when another has already taken effect is the sublater of that [other]. By this principle, since this [figure] is commenced precisely within the domain of another figure of speech, it sublates that other figure; furthermore, there is no distinct domain for it [of its own].

Where there is scope for one [figure] to exist without subverting the other, such is the case: *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) prevails when both subjects are either non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) or contextual (*prakṛta*), whereas *dīpaka* (The Illuminator) occurs when the subjects are both contextual and non-contextual. Furthermore, *upamā* (Simile) and other figures are permitted by that [latter]. And:
"O King, you alone are the protector; you are the sufficient support of the quarters;
you are the ground of the breezes from the chowries; therefore, you are the embodiment of the three worlds."

Regarding the statement in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* beginning with these words, it should be said that this is the intended subject matter, because here the metaphor (*rūpaka*) alone is clearly manifest. This is because the nature of consisting of the three worlds cannot be easily established without the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of identity upon the meanings such as "the netherworld" (*pātāla*) presented through paronomasia (*śleṣa*). If so, how then is there the cognition of a simile (*upamā*) in such cases as: "This king, bearing the abundance of rivers, is like the ocean"? Or how is there the cognition of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) when the word "kimu" is substituted for the word "yathā" in that very same verse?

If it is argued that [the term] "another" (apara) implies "of the metaphor" (rūpakasya), we say no; for here there is merely the appearance (pratibhāna) of similes and the like, but not their actual existence. Indeed, even though silver-ness is perceived in mother-of-pearl due to its whiteness, it does not exist in reality. Therefore, *śleṣa* alone—which is the cause for the emergence of the appearance of similes and so forth—is the ornament (*alaṃkāra*) in all its own domains.

Others do not accept this, for instance, regarding the statement "by which [the suffix] is not applied when [the condition] has not been reached," and so forth; consider the following verse by another author: "May that Lord of the Gods be victorious, who established his abode on Vṛṣācala (the Bull Mountain), he by whom the venerable Goddess Śrī—who always possesses a streak of enemies (or: who always bears a line of friends) within her heart—is eternally placed here. In this verse, [if the rule were as stated, the suffix *ṅasi* would not apply to *vṛṣa* because the condition of proximity to *acala* has not been met]. However, the suffix *ṅasi* is indeed applied [to form *vṛṣāt*], and thus the aforementioned objection is untenable. Furthermore, in the case of the expression *sarvadomādhavaḥ*, the suffix *ṅasi* is applied to *sarvadaḥ* [to form *sarvadāt*], and thus the objection is invalid. Moreover, in the case of the expression *yenāgaṅgāmadīdharat*, the suffix *ṅasi* is applied to *yena* [to form *yenāt*], and thus the objection is invalid. Therefore, the objection is not sound. Furthermore, in the case of the expression *yenāgaṅgāmadīdharat*, the suffix *ṅasi* is applied to *agaṅgām* [to form *agaṅgāt*], and thus the objection is invalid. Consequently, the objection is not sound. Furthermore, in the case of the expression *yenāgaṅgāmadīdharat*, the suffix *ṅasi* is applied to *agaṅgām* [to form *agaṅgāt*], and thus the objection is invalid. In the verse of ours cited previously, what figure of speech is there other than *śleṣa* (punning)? It is certainly not *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), because the two subjects (*viśeṣya*) are not mentioned separately, and because there is no suggestion of a comparison (*aupamya*). For that [figure] finds its footing only when the two subjects—whether both contextual or both non-contextual—are mentioned separately, and when there is a necessary perception of similarity. Indeed, it is not intended here to establish a similarity between Hari and Hara, or between the Lord and Indra.

Furthermore, in this case, nothing other than the presentation of two meanings through a single phonetic form (*ekaśruti*) gives rise to any aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), such that we might admit another figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). Indeed, the presentation of two meanings through a single phonetic form is *śleṣa* (paronomasia) itself. And thus, since *śleṣa* has its own scope, it is not logical for it to be an exception (*apavādaka*) to other figures of speech.

For this very reason, the statement that figures such as simile (*upamā*) are mere flashes of intuition (*pratibhāna-mātra*) is also inconsistent; for there is no obstacle to a simile existing even when the common property is a word alone, just as it occurs with qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth. Therefore, regarding the verse "This city has now become entirely resonant, like the orb of the moon," the traditionalists maintain that it is indeed a simile despite the similarity consisting of words alone. As Rudraṭa stated:
"Clearly, these two—simile and accumulation (*samuccaya*)—are ornaments of meaning (*artha-alaṃkāra*);
however, they are possible here too by relying on a commonality that consists of words alone."

Thus, even in the case of other figures of speech within the domain of *śleṣa* (punning), their existence is only ultimate (*pāramārthikī*), not merely apparent (*prātibhāsikī*). On the contrary, it is more appropriate to say that *śleṣa* itself is a mere appearance; for since the entire domain of the *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile) is occupied by the three types of *śleṣa*, there is no room [for the simile] to exist, and it is therefore proper that this [simile], having its own scope already preempted, should be sublated. In examples such as "honored in battle (*samarārcita*) yet honored by the gods (*amarārcita*"), *śleṣa* is nothing more than a mere appearance, like the double moon seen by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*).

However, it cannot be considered a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) because its life-force—the second meaning—does not remain established. It is quite clear that while even a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of contradiction (*virodha*) constitutes a figure of speech, this is not the case for *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Therefore, in such instances, the figure of speech is the contradiction itself, which is produced by the spark of *śleṣa*; it is not *śleṣa* produced by the spark of contradiction. Thus:
"O jewel among pearls of a noble lineage, O swan of the learned mind!
Your fame is not small, O King; you are great, whereas the poet is not transparently pure in his verses."

In this case, in the first half-verse, there is only *rūpaka* (metaphor) produced by the suggestion (*pratibhā*) of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), and not *śleṣa* produced by the suggestion of *rūpaka*. In the second half-verse, the *vyatireka* (contrast) is likewise. Furthermore, when each [figure] is presented in its own specific form, no figure whatsoever lacks applicability within the domain of *śleṣa*.

If it is argued that [śleṣa] is established as a distinct figure of speech, then, by considering the general nature of sublation, there would result the sublation of everything that applies to its own domain; consequently, both *śliṣṭaparaṃparitarūpaka* (metaphor with double entendre) and *śliṣṭasamāsokti* (metaphorical compound expression) would be utterly eliminated. Therefore, śleṣa cannot function as an exception [to other figures], but rather constitutes a case of "intermixture" (*saṃkīrṇatva*).

Others, however, maintain that figures of speech (alaṃkāras) receive their respective designations primarily because they produce aesthetic charm (camatkāra); yet, when they function as auxiliaries to something else, they relinquish those names. For example, in the verse, “The face of the deer-eyed woman shone upon the earth, just as the orb of the moon shines in the expanse of the sky,” the connection of a single attribute between the subject at hand and the subject not at hand receives the name *dīpaka* (the illuminator). But in the verse, “The face of the slender maiden shines like the moon in the sky,” it relinquishes that name.

For this very reason it is said: "Designations are made on the basis of predominance. And thus, since *śleṣa* (paronomasia) exists here merely as an embellishment for other figures of speech, how could it—like one staying in another's house—be capable of bearing the designation of the figure *śleṣa* itself? Therefore, some have even said that it is virtually sublated (*bādhyaprāya*).

And this very simile, though independent, exists in various places as a supporter of all other ornaments, bringing ever-new beauty to Sarasvatī; it is to be discerned by connoisseurs in diverse examples.

Furthermore, this should be noted: where both the contextual and non-contextual subjects (*viśeṣya*) are conveyed by means of a single word with double meaning (*śliṣṭapada*), that is the province of *dhvani*, according to the ancients. For instance, in the example of *śleṣa* involving both the contextual and non-contextual, such as "He has ascended the mountain peak" (*asāvudayamārūḍhaḥ*), *śleṣa* is not considered an *alaṃkāra*; for that [figure] only manifests when two meanings possess an equal status through the operation of direct denotation (*abhidhā*).

Therefore, in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) regarding both the contextual (*prakṛta*) and the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), since there is an absence of factors such as context that restrict denotation (*abhidhā*), the word functions equally toward both meanings; thus, it is the figure of speech *śleṣa*. Here, however, because its [denotative] power is restricted to the contextual meaning by context and other factors, its extension is blunted with respect to the non-contextual meaning; consequently, the word conveys that meaning through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*). Thus, this is *dhvani* where the suggested sense is equal to the resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
The trunk of that noble-souled elephant, whose body was difficult to assail, which rose high from a broad lineage, and which had mastered the art of gathering arrows,
was always made beautiful by the sprinkling of the ichor-fluid as it moved with leaping strides to ward off enemies.

In this context, while a certain king is being described—whereby, through the operation of *abhidhā* (denotation) supported by the context, the word-meaning "the hand of a king" is first perceived verbally as one who is auspicious in nature (*bhadra-ātman*), born of a noble lineage (*viśāla-kula*), possessed of many gathered arrows (*aneka-śara-saṃgraha-śālin*), and a repeller of adversaries (*pratyarthi-nivāraka*)—thereafter, by the power of the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) of words such as *bhadra*, the meaning of "the trunk of a superior elephant" is understood: one of the *bhadra* breed, with a high back-bone (*viśāla-pṛṣṭha-asthi-samunnati*) and covered by bees (*bhramara-parīta*).

Thus, the cognition of the non-contextual meaning, such as the elephant and so forth, is established by experience. And that [cognition] does not arise through the function of denotation (*abhidhā*), because that function is restricted by context and other factors. Therefore, the cognition of that [meaning] occurs through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*); consequently, since the non-contextual meaning is suggested, teachers such as Mammaṭa and others maintain that this is a "suggested dhvani" based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) wherein the suggested element is a simile (*upamā*) arising from resonance (*anuraṇana*).

The intention of those [ancient scholars] who maintain that "the ancients desire *dhvani* based on word-power (*śabdaśaktimūla*) in this example of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the relevant and the irrelevant, because—by means of the *dīkṣita*s [the commentators], through the context and so forth, and in order to avoid the sentence having an incoherent meaning when it results in expressing either the relevant matter or the irrelevant matter—an analogy (*upamā*) of the relevant matter is suggested" is as follows: [they hold this] regarding the figure of speech such as analogy, which is rooted in the expression of both the relevant and the irrelevant.

This is intended to mean that [the secondary meaning] is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), but not that the non-contextual meaning itself is exclusively what is suggested; for even a non-contextual meaning, if it is conveyed by the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*), necessarily possesses the status of being the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*) and thus does not depend on suggestion (*vyakti*). Although the contextual meaning first becomes manifest instantly through the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), and only subsequently does the non-contextual meaning flash forth—preceded by the awakening of various other powers directed toward those respective objects through the force of the mutual proximity of words such as "king" (*rāja*) and "tax" (*kara*), which denote the king, the wealth to be seized, and so forth.

"It does not follow from this that [the second meaning] is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). For when something is conveyed by power (*śakti*), there is no dependence on suggestion whatsoever. If it is argued that [the second meaning] flashes forth only after the expression of the primary sense has been completed, then let it be a 'hidden pun' (*gūḍhaśleṣa*) if you wish; for hidden puns exist elsewhere as well. Having said this, they cited the verse beginning with "This [person] is exceedingly old" (*ayamatijaraṭhāḥ*) as an example of a hidden pun.

For this is their intention: it should not be doubted why there is no status as *vyaṅgya* (the suggested) because, once a verbal cognition regarding the primary subject matter has been produced through the context and the grasping of the intended meaning of that subject, a subsequent cognition of the non-primary subject matter arises. Even though the non-primary subject matter flashes forth later through the awakening of another power (*śakti*) directed toward that specific object, it does not possess the status of *vyaṅgya*. For what is perceived subsequently is called "obscure *śleṣa*" (*gūḍhaśleṣa*).

Others, however, argue that since context and other factors act as obstacles to the capacity of denotation (*abhidhā*) to express a non-contextual object, even in a case where denotation does not transfer to a second meaning, if there should be the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of a word capable of effecting such transfer, then the power of denotation—which was previously obstructed by context and the like—is revived once its suppression has been countered. Consequently, the manifestation of the non-contextual meaning occurs through that [revived] denotation; thus, this is not the province of *dhvani*. Therefore, the manifestation of the non-contextual meaning here occurs through denotation itself, and is not considered *dhvani*. As it is said: "Just as the word 'garment' is connected to the sense of 'dwelling' through the proximity of the word 'place,' so too is the word 'moon' connected to the sense of 'face' through the proximity of the word 'lotus. Thus, because the non-contextual meaning is understood through the power of denotation, this is not an instance of *dhvani*. Furthermore, in cases where the primary meaning is incompatible with the context, such as in the verse beginning "The moon rises," the manifestation of the non-contextual meaning is achieved through the power of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), and therefore it is the province of *dhvani*. However, in the aforementioned example, since the connection between the two meanings is established through the power of denotation, it is not *dhvani*. This is because the capacity of denotation is not entirely destroyed; rather, it is merely suppressed by the obstruction of context and other factors, and is subsequently restored by the presence of a word capable of transferring the meaning. Since the non-contextual meaning is grasped through this restored denotation, it does not fall within the scope of *dhvani*. "Here, the lotus-lake, smiling joyfully, longs for her beloved, the abode of Ramā"—hearing this report and desiring Padmāvatī, Hari rejoiced. (941)

This is indeed a statement expressing the following meaning: having observed a lotus pond in full bloom at dawn, someone said to another that the divine Śrīnivāsa—who was enamored with the princess of Ākāśarāja named Padminī and was pondering how their union might come about—heard this as a source of eternal bliss.

In this context, although these words—such as *sahasitā* (well-blossomed), *padminī* (a lotus plant), and *svasya priyam* (her own beloved)—are restricted in their denotation by the specific context and other factors to mean that "the lotus creeper desires the dwelling or residence of Ramā (Lakṣmī)," nevertheless, when the second meaning is about to be unfolded, they are revived by the word *upaśruti*. This is because the word *upaśruti*, while signifying "hearing," also carries the secondary sense of "desire" (*abhilāṣa*). Thus, the word *upaśruti* brings back to life the meanings previously suppressed.

In this context, the second meaning—that the lotus-like Padmāvatī, daughter of King Ākāśa, who is here smiling gently and laughing softly, desires the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa, the abode of Ramā, as her own beloved and lover, wishing "May he become my lover"—is conveyed by words whose denotative power (*abhidhā*) has been restricted by contextual factors and the like. Having set out upon the path of suggestion (*dhvani*), it is then seized by the neck by means of the term *upaśruti* (an eavesdropper), and thus brought back under the operation of denotation (*abhidhā*).

They say: "When it has become expressible (*vācya*), it falls within the scope of the figure of speech *śleṣa* (punning); but elsewhere, in the absence of such a revival of the denotative function (*abhidhā*), it occupies the path of *arthāntaradhvani* (suggestion of another meaning)."

This is also a distinct domain of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), as it is not confounded with other figures of speech. Nor should there be any suspicion of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) here; for in this statement, the account of the lotus-pond (*kamalinī*) is itself the subject at hand, and thus there is no case of the unmentioned being understood through the mentioned. Furthermore, one should not argue that this must be *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), since the unmentioned is understood through the mentioned; for the term *padminī*, which serves as the substantive, is itself paronomastic, and thus that figure does not apply.

Nor should it be argued that this is *dīpaka* (the illuminator) because of the connection of a single attribute between the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*). For there is no intention on the part of some neutral speaker to express the identity of attributes between the relevant and the irrelevant; furthermore, the two subjects—the relevant and the irrelevant—are not presented separately. That [figure of speech] arises only when those two are presented separately. Nor is it *gūḍhokti* (obscure speech), since here there is no intention to speak of one thing under the guise of another. Therefore, this is a distinct province of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone; such is the direction [of the argument].
A detailed treatment, however, is to be found in the treatises of the ancients.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the Lake of the Figure of Speech *Śleṣa* (Pun), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description).

First, *Samāsokti* (Speech by Synecdoche) was defined based on the similarity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the subject at hand. Following that, figures such as *Parikara* (the Ornament), which rely upon those qualifiers, were defined. Now, however, *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* is being described as the opposite of that.
Where there is a description of the irrelevant that serves as an indicator of the relevant subject at hand, this poetic figure is called Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description). || 85 ||

Where the description of an irrelevant matter (aprastuta-vṛttānta) brings about the understanding of a relevant matter (prastuta-vṛttānta), that is called Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description). The distinction from Samāsokti (Concise Expression), however, is that in the latter there is the cognition of the irrelevant through the relevant. Furthermore, "praśaṃsana" here means mere description and not praise; otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (avyāpti) in cases such as: "There are many holes within, and many thorns without."

When the effect, the cause, the pervaded, the pervader, or the similar is intended, but another [related thing] is mentioned instead—this very [figure of speech], namely Parikara, thus becomes fivefold. (86)

The comprehension of the subject at hand (*prastuta*) through the description of an irrelevant occurrence (*aprastutavṛttānta*) occurs when there is a connection. This connection may be that of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), the relation between the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), or similarity (*sārūpya*). In the case of words ending in the locative case, the term "in the subject at hand" (*prastute*) is understood to apply [to each]. "Speech about another" (*anyagīḥ*) is *tadanyokti*. Thus, when the effect is the subject at hand, [there is a reference] to the cause; when the cause is the subject at hand, [there is a reference] to the effect; and the terms "the pervaded" (*vyāpya*) and "the pervader" (*vyāpaka*) signify the particular and the general respectively.

There are four varieties: the statement of a general when a particular is introduced, and the statement of a particular when a general is introduced. The fifth variety occurs when the similar is presented in relation to the similar. As they say: "When the effect, the cause, the general, or the particular is introduced, the mention of something else that is different from it—[or] when the equal is mentioned in relation to the equal—is fivefold."
Thus [it is said]. In that regard, an expression of the cause when the effect is under discussion is as follows:

"The lotus-creepers, having had all their wealth taken away by Fate for the sake of the face of the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), are now called 'tāmarasa' (red lotuses) by those of most noble intellect. (942)

Therefore, they say that this very row of lotuses possesses *arasatām*—that is to say, tastelessness, lack of sapidity, or worthlessness; in another sense, it possesses *tāmarasatām*, the state of being a lotus (*tāmarasa*). The rest is clear.

Here, by means of the cause—the extraction of the essential essence for the purpose of creating the divine lotus-face of Śrīnivāsa, which is conceived as being present within the rows of lotuses—the extraordinary excellence of superhuman beauty, fragrance, delicacy, and so forth, residing in the divine lotus-face of Śrīnivāsa (the subject of description), is perceived as its effect. Thus, this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on a cause, conjoined with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).

Just as the Creator, desiring to fashion mountains from the wind-eaters (serpents), dug out all the mountains to extract their essence, it is certain that those [mountains] were actually the dwelling-caves of the infinite gods.

Here, by means of the implied removal of the essential portion of the subject matter—the creation of Śeṣādri—through its being conceived as residing in all mountains generally (though not specifically intended), there is perceived a certain greatness of the Śeṣādri-resident that transcends all principal mountain ranges (*kulācala*). "Those whose caves are excavated by gods and deities" refers to those with infinite and boundless caverns; according to Amara, *devakhātabila* means "caves. Some hold that the words *devakhāta* and *bila* are used separately to denote caves, while others maintain that this compound word *devakhātabila* as a whole denotes them. As for example:

O Mother, having taken the entire essence of the luster of lightning flashes, the Creator fashioned your body; it was for this reason that poets thereafter declared, "Lightning flashes are but momentary radiance. (944)

The actual state of affairs is that those whose brilliance lasts for only a moment—meaning they possess very little light and have lost their luster immediately thereafter—are yet described as "shining intensely" (viśeṣeṇa dyotamānāḥ). This is a case of [ironic] hyperbole.

O jewel of the serpent-mountain, since the Creator has thus stripped you of your essence to create your divine form, it is certain that every single sapphire is thoroughly aware of its own worthlessness in comparison.

In this case as well, one should recognize an *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on a causal connection. *Asāratā* means "lack of essence" or worthlessness; however, the actual state of affairs is that *asāratā* is exceedingly beautiful (*sutaraṃ asāratā*), for *asāratā* is a name for *masāra*. We have already stated previously that "the word *masāra* may refer to sapphire (*indranīla*)."
The statement of the effect when the cause has been introduced is as follows:

"At first, she was brought by the gods with a beautiful face; even her leadership [of the seasons] was [due to them]; later, out of fear and generosity, the fragrant one (Spring) went forth, and finally, she reached the very end."

O Blessed One! At first, Surabhi—the wish-fulfilling cow—was "Sumukhī" (fair-faced), possessing a pleasant countenance rooted in the joy produced by hearing the excellence of her own speech as described by ordinary people, prior to hearing of Your great magnanimity. In the alternative sense, regarding the word *surabhi* itself: it is "Sumukhī," meaning that which has the syllable *su-* (meaning "excellent" or "golden") as its primary opening (*mukham*), for the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *mukha* denotes the principal, a beginning, the mouth, and also an exit."

For that very reason—namely, her having a beautiful countenance—she was brought forward, made to precede [the others], or honored by the wise gods who recognize merit. Alternatively, the word *tatpura* is a compound; it means "immediately after that gold" (*tasya suvarṇasya puraḥ*). She was brought to possess the state of being accompanied by the letter *ra* (i.e., the word *sarā*, "with *ra*"). Afterwards, due to your own magnanimity, O Śrīnivāsa.

The sense is that [the Earth] is so celebrated by such Vedic passages as "He who is the giver of self, the giver of strength," and by such Puranic statements as "Who else is more magnanimous than He? She is "terrified" (bhītā) out of fear of the possibility that her own renown for magnanimity might be eclipsed; in the alternative [punning] sense, she is "terrified" (bhītā)—meaning joined with the letter *bhi*—after the letter *ra* (repha), that is, following the letter *ra*, due to her magnanimity (*audāryāt*), which implies being unrestrained (*nirargalatvāt*). Thus, she is "joined" (*itā*) with the syllable *bhi*.

Therefore, because she perceived danger at the end, she was released; the meaning is that she went away, having been dismissed by the gods with the thought, "We should not entertain such a terrified woman. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), she reached the *visarga* (the *visarjanīya* sound) at the end—that is, at the end of the word expressing her own name—since the word "Surabhi" ends in that manner. Thus it is said.

Here, by means of an irrelevant matter—the effect such as the fear of Surabhi—which is rendered probable through propriety (*aucitya*), the extraordinary greatness of the majesty of Śrīnivāsa’s magnanimity, which is the cause of that effect and is not shared by others, is made known. Thus, this is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on an effect, conjoined with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
O Enemy of Mura, I consider this multitude of stars to be a collection of pure egg-masses produced by the swan of Your fame as it dwells in heaven. (947)

"Peśīnivahaṃ aṇḍanikaraṃ"—according to Amarasimha, "the term *peśīkośa* [denotes] an egg when deprived of its two [shells]. Here, by the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the unmentioned multitude of stars is a mass of fetal sacs (*peśīnivaha*) produced by the swan of the Lord’s fame, one perceives that the extraordinary excellence of the whiteness of that fame—the cause of this—is supermundane. Or as in another example:
"By the outburst of light from the pregnant crest-jewel of the Lord of the Serpent Hill (Śrī Śeṣa), these vast masses of rain-clouds have been born as full-grown calves in heaven. (948)

By the sprout—the burgeoning growth—of the Blessed One’s radiance and splendor, [the clouds] are like pregnant women (*antarvatnī*); regarding *dyau*, Amara states: "The word *dyau* (in the dual *dyāvau*) denotes heaven and two women, as well as a cloud. The rest is clear. Here too, through the poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) that the masses of rain-clouds—which are not the subject under discussion—are pregnant with children born of the sky impregnated by the sprout of the Blessed One’s bodily luster, the supreme excellence of the blackness of the sprout of the Blessed One’s bodily luster, which serves as the cause for that [conceit], is made manifest. This is a blend of *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), while the previous [verse] was a blend of *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Or as it is said:
"The spreading droplets of light from the lotus-feet of Śrī, as she emerged from the ocean, were gathered together by the impact of one wave against another and took on the form of coral. (949)

At this time of descent, the splendor of the lotus-feet of Śrī Mahālakṣmī, which had spread across the ocean, was gathered together by the force of mutual wave-splashing—like minute particles of sand, foam, and spray—and through these coral creepers, which are perceived as the effects, the supreme abundance of the crimson hue of the causal splendor of those lotus-feet is manifested, surpassing all others.
Or for example:

"O Śauri, by Your majesty two most minute sparks have burst forth; one is the sun in the sky, while the other is the submarine fire in the waters of the ocean. (950) Here, through the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) that the two unmentioned subjects—the sun and the submarine fire—are sparks produced as effects of the Lord’s majesty, it is understood that the majesty of the Lord—their respective material cause—is possessed of a brilliance surpassing thousands of millions of rays and the submarine fire.
In this instance, the majesty is understood to be a great fire.
O Blessed One, within the water of Your auspicious fame, which fills the vessel of the cosmic egg, the stars sport like bubbles and the moonlight froths like foam. (951)

Here, by means of the poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) that the stars and moonlight—which are not the subject at hand—are the bubbles and foam produced from the milk of the Blessed One’s fame, the unsurpassed excellence of the extreme clarity of the Blessed One’s fame, which is the subject at hand, is perceived.
O Lord of the Bull-mountain, just as the moon, having somehow been deprived of its excellent luster by your fame and falling headlong downward, attains the state of being the body of the night.

O Lord of the Vṛṣa-mountain! By this [statement], his distinction from the well-known moon is understood. The Lord of the Night (the moon), whose excellent color—his whiteness—is surpassed by your fame (*tvadyaśasā*), has been made to fall away; that is to say, he has been rendered pale. By describing how his color has been displaced by your fame—a description that suggests his defeat by a eunuch—the fact that his suffering is exceedingly unbearable is illuminated.

For this very reason, the expression "falling headlong" (adhaśśirāḥ) is used because he is seen in an inverted state at the moment the moon faces the mountain of setting; the meaning is that it occurs with great effort and difficulty due to the exertion required to travel such a distance. As the *Utpalamālā* states: "The word *katham* and others likewise [denote] effort, gravity, and intensity. He attains the existence of his body (*śarīrabhāvitvam*).

The meaning is that although the abandonment of the body was inevitable according to the saying, “When the honor of the virtuous has faded,” he did not do so, but instead sustained his body by resorting to the second alternative, namely, “or departing to a distant land. In this context, the compound is a *bahuvrīhi* containing another *bahuvrīhi*: the word *vibhāvarīśa* (the lord of the night, i.e., the moon), having its head (*ardhaśśirāḥ*) falling—that is, moving in reverse order—causes the letter *va* to fall away (*cyāvitaḥ*), and thus the letter *ra* (*ravarṇaḥ*) remains. Thus it is described.

The meaning is that the letter *va* has been displaced and the letter *ra* has been brought to that very position. It acquires the sequence [of letters] such as "śarīrabhāvī," which signifies being present in the body; this is to be understood because the word *vibhāvarīśa* is produced in that manner according to the method already demonstrated. However, one must not forget the identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its meaning. Here, the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), *vibhāvarīśa*, is unmentioned (*aprastuta*), whereas the object of comparison (*upameya*), the glory of the Blessed One, is the subject at hand (*prastuta*).

And thus, by means of the effect—extreme lack of luster—which is not the subject at hand (aprastuta) but is manifested through the force of the possibility that [the moon] has lost its excellent complexion and so forth due to having gone to the Lord of Night (the moon), the very subject at hand (prastuta)—the extraordinary purity inherent in fame—is perceived. Here, the relation between cause and effect is of the nature of the "prompted" (prayojya) and the "prompter" (prayojaka). In this same manner, it should be understood as appropriate in subsequent instances within this section.

Just as a mass of coral in the ocean, having assumed a distorted facial expression due to the luster of the lips of the Lord of the Earth who bears the hooded serpents, remains perpetually submerged even without its mouth.

*Mukhabhaṅga* means humiliation; it is a common worldly expression meaning "without even a face. The sense is that he is truly unable to show his face. In the alternative [punning] sense, *vinā* refers to the syllable *vi*, and the coral cluster (*vidruma-nivaha*) is characterized by a "face" (*mukha*), meaning the principal letter *vi*. This is based on the identity between the signified and the signifier.

Here, the unintended effect of the multitude of coral trees—consisting in their taking refuge in the ocean—which is being imagined as being brought about by the contraction of the face resulting from the luster of the Lord’s lower lip, serves to indicate its cause: the excellence of the redness of the jewel-like lower lip of Śrīnivāsa, which is the intended subject. Thus, this too is indeed an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on an effect.

O moon-faced one, the honey-dust, which was first celebrated for its abundance of sweetness, became mere dust when shaken off by the nectar of your lips, due to the overwhelming superiority of that first ground.

O you with a face like the moon that slays Madhu! O beloved of the Blessed One! This [fact] reveals the skill of your lips in shaking off the honey-dust: before the shaking-off performed by the nectar of your lips, the honey-dust—famous for its abundance of sweetness (*madhurima-bhūman*) due to its extreme sweetness—became mere dust (*dhūlī*), separated and scattered because it was overwhelmed by the excellence of the sweetness of your lip-nectar.

The meaning is: "it has become devoid of essence" (nissārā). In the alternative sense, *prathamabhūḥ* means that which exists at the beginning (*ādau vidyamānaḥ*), namely the letter *ma* (the *mavarṇa*). Through its displacement (*vidhuratayā*), the word *madhūlī* is produced as *dhūlī*; the point is that the word *madhūlī* is formed in that way by the removal of the letter *ma*. Here, through the described effect—the transformation of the non-contextual *madhūlī* (honey-bees) into *dhūlī* (dust)—there is the comprehension of the excellence and transcendence of the world, which is the cause of that effect: the sweetness of the nectar of the lower lip of the Mother of the World, who is the contextual subject.

Here too, the relationship between cause and effect consists precisely in the nature of the relationship between the prompted and the prompter; its intermingling with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is just as before.

O Mother of the World, having fully experienced the poison of being surpassed by the playful grace of Your gait, even the intoxicated royal swan displayed his impotence; this was indeed quite fitting. O Mother of the World! Even though the royal swan was intoxicated—that is, drunk—the sense is that it had been previously surpassed by the playful grace of Your gait. He was "surpassed" (*avamata*) by the playful grace of Your gait. By this indication of being defeated by a woman, his extreme inferiority is suggested.

For this very reason, having consumed (sevitvā) poison (*viṣa*), venom (*garala*), and water (*jala*) to the full extent (*alam*—meaning sufficiently), or in the alternative sense, having consumed them in such a way that the letter *ṣa* had fallen away—that is, making the word division *alam* as *laṃ*—and having attained (*sevya*) the letter *la*, he indeed manifested true manliness (*sādhu*), and not merely some kind of impotence (*klībatva*) or eunuchhood (*ṣaṇḍatva*). For anyone who considers himself a man, when defeated by others, recovers his breath and exerts his prowess once more to retaliate.

Yet he does not despair out of impotence (*klībatā*). The sense is: "How could this man, defeated by a woman, not manifest his impotence after drinking poison? In the alternative (punning) sense, the word *kṣība* (intoxicated), by the removal of the letter *ṣa* and the insertion of the letter *la* in its very place, reveals its form as *klība* (impotent). Here, through the non-contextual effect—the swan’s being surpassed in the grace of his gait and play—which is being imagined, there arises the perception of the cause of that effect: the excellence of the beauty of the graceful gait and play of the contextual [heroine], Śrī.
Just as the fish, terrified by the theft of the beauty of your eyes, O Mother of the World, found their lives only after becoming skillful at changing the color of their faces. 956.

O Mother of the World! The *śakula* fish, having committed the theft—that is, having stolen—the beauty of Your eyes, became terrified and frightened; consequently, their facial color was altered or reversed. The sense is that by smearing themselves with charcoal powder, ashes, and the like, they changed the color of their faces so that others could not recognize them as they were before. Therefore, they have become clever rather than negligent.

The sense is: what other skill could there be than even employing such a means in times of distress? Not finding their livelihood—that is, not finding the sustenance of life—they were those whose facial color (mukha-varṇa) had its syllables (śa-ku) transposed or read in reverse order. There is a superimposition of a plural number pertaining to the meaning onto the word itself. Having become *kuśalāḥ*—the meaning being that by reversing the first two syllables of the word *śakulāḥ*, the form *kuśalāḥ* is produced. Thus, they did not find "life," which is to say, water.

"In that [state], they are submerged" means to that extent. Here, by means of the unmentioned action of stealing and so forth belonging to the śakula fish, there is the cognition of the cause of that action—the abundance of the beauty of the eyes and other qualities of Lakṣmī, which is the subject at hand.
O Mother, having been defeated by your eyes, the Wind-god, upon losing his sight, became a companion to the Wind; for if he had not resorted to the Wind, how could he have lived? 957.

O Mother! The deer (hariṇa) is "vātāyu" (wind-lived); and the word *vātāyu* itself, having been surpassed by your eyes—precisely because of that disappearance from sight, that is, due to the loss of its loveliness—became a "friend of the wind" (*vāyusakha*). The sense is that it became invisible like the wind. Alternatively, [the compound] is analyzed as: "having attained invisibility due to the departure of visibility," using the ablative case (*pañcamī*) with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*. Having become a "friend of the wind," it means it fled with a speed equal to the wind.

Alternatively, "dṛśya" means perceptible; from the "gamana" (departure) or attainment of that heat (*tāpa*), having become the "friend of the wind" (*vāyusakha*)—that is to say, having become like fire consisting of heat. In the case of the word-play (*śabdapakṣe*), "dṛśya" refers to the phoneme *tā*; from its "apagamāt" (disappearance), he becomes the "friend of the wind. This means he is joined with the two phonemes *vā* and *yu* alone. Having become so, he "ānīt" (breathed)—meaning he attained existence elsewhere. There is also a word-break as "sa vā āyuḥ sthitiḥ. That "vātāyuḥ" (wind-life); here the particle *vā* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.

According to Amara, "syuḥ... evaṃ tu punar vai vā" are words expressing certainty (*avadhāraṇavācakāḥ*). [The phrase] means: if there were not even the duration of life, or rather, the remainder of life, would he live? Indeed, he would not live at all. The sense is that because the duration of life is so difficult to remove, he lived even after having encountered such a defeat. In the case of the word-play (*śabdapakṣe*), however: if that word *vātāyu*—meaning either the "state of the wind" (*vāyusthiti*) or the sequence of syllables "vā," "yu"—did not exist, would it [the word] live? Indeed, it would not live.

The sense is that even when the collection of phonemes forming the word "vāyuḥ" (wind)—such as the letter *tā*—is elided, the persistence of the very nature of the word becomes impossible. Here, through the non-contextual effect of the defeat of wind and so forth, which is merely imagined, there is perceived the excellence of the beauty of the eyes of the Mother of the World, who is the actual cause of that [defeat].

O Hari, although you remain in heaven having taken by theft the wealth of others, and although you are free from sin and equal to the gods, you are nonetheless unrestrained, like a tree that withers its own roots.

O hare! Even the celestial tree, the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), though situated in heaven—the divine realm established by its own inherent nature—has acquired such vast magnanimity only by stealing, that is, through theft, your wealth of generosity. The sense is: "Without the theft of your wealth of generosity, how could this tree possess even so much nobility? The word *adāntaḥ* means one who has not been punished for his offenses by any king; it is a conventional form derived from the root *dam* (to tame) ending in the suffix *-kta*, according to the rule *vā dānta*.

The *Amara-kośa* states: "The *dānta* is one who has been tamed; *dama* is the punishment for violence. He was born somewhere on earth as such a person—one whose sin was difficult to digest (*durjara*) yet indestructible (*nirjara*). Regarding the state of being punished by kings, [the *Manusmṛti* says]:
"Having committed sins, men who have been punished by kings become stainless and go to heaven, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds."

By this recollection, there would be the state of having one's sins purified. The sense is that, because he was not of such a nature [to suffer], his sin became "nirjara" (dissolved) somewhere. In the alternative [punning] sense, the word *nirjarapādapa* (the celestial tree) is "adānta," meaning it does not have the letter *da* at its end or in its middle; thus, being devoid of the letter *da* in the middle, it results in the form *nirjarapāpa*.

Here, by means of the effect—the attainment of the sin of theft—which is attributed to the tree of Nirjarā (the Jina) though it is not the subject at hand, the excellence of the greatness of the Lord’s speech, which is the cause of that effect, is understood as being indeed the actual subject. Or, for example: "O Abode of Lakṣmī! Having her pride shattered by listening to the excellence of Your speech, she abandoned her tranquility; then, becoming pale-faced and agitated, she became powerless. (959)

O Kamalālaye! *Śabalā* refers both to the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmagavī*) and to the word *śabalā* itself. She is so described because her pride—that mental exaltation of thinking "I am a great benefactor"—has been quelled by hearing the discourses of another. For this very reason, she is "releasing *śam*"—that is, abandoning the happiness born of the knowledge of one's own excellence; in the other sense, she is "releasing the letter *śa*. (The root *muc* is svarita-accented.)

For this very reason, her face became discolored and lusterless; alternatively, the word *śabalā* (variegated), having become *vi-*—that is, one whose initial syllable is the phoneme *vi*—became *vibalā*, meaning weak. The sense is that she became powerless due to the destruction of her enthusiasm (*utsāha*), for there is no strength other than enthusiasm, as it is said: "There is no strength superior to enthusiasm. Alternatively, the word *śabalā*, by the removal of the letter *śa* and the substitution of a modification in its place, resulted in the form *vibalā*. This is the meaning.

Here, while the great magnanimity of the Blessed Śrī is the subject introduced for description, the pacification of the pride of the celestial cows and other such effects—which, though not the immediate subject, are rendered probable through propriety—are described.

And this is not an effect of a [physical] object, as in the previous examples beginning with "In the beginning, by the gods... as you sported in heaven," but rather, like the effect of beholding her [Śrī's] hair-tresses in the verse "Seeing that mass of hair, the yaks would loosen their fondness for their tails," it is the effect of hearing of her magnanimity.

Just as the essence of milk becomes the essence of milk, and the plantain becomes nectar, so too does the silk-cotton fruit become like nectar; yet even these would be rendered sapless if the speech of the beloved of the Lord of the Mountain of Double-Tongued-Ones (the Lord Śiva) did not reach the path of one's hearing. The "essence of milk" (*dugdharsa*) means the essence of milk (*kṣīrarasa*). It is so called because its *rasa*—its sweetness—is drawn out (*recita*) after being filled with milk (*prapūrta*). *Mocā* refers to the plantain fruit (*kadalīphala*). Alternatively, it may mean the silk-cotton fruit (*śālmalīphala*), the sense being that it is as sapless as that. In both cases, the suffix *aṇ* is elided according to the rule *phale luk*. The analysis of the compound is: "the fruit of the *mocā* tree is *mocā*."

‘*Kadalī*, *śālmali*, and *mocā*’—thus says the *Ratnamālā*. *Sudhā* means nectar (*amṛta*), or the powder used for plastering, or the latex of the *snuhī* plant; the sense is that [the speech] is as pungent as those. Amara states: ‘*Sudhā* is plaster, nectar, or *snuhī*. The rest is clear. Here, through the effect consisting of the disparagement of the flavors of milk and so forth, the excellence of the sweetness of the speech of the Goddess of the Universe—the cause of that—is understood. And here, the relation of cause and effect exists between two cognitions. Therefore, there is no flaw even if the quality of tastelessness and so forth—which is perceived as residing in the flavor of milk and the like—is not actually produced from the flavor of her speech in its own nature.

"Just as the object (artha) possesses a basis in its being an effect, so too, even though the cognition (buddhi) is an effect, its status as having a basis in an effect is not lost. Such examples of *kāryanibandhanāprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise based on an effect) have been cited by the ancients, and thus we too shall cite them. In reality, however, there is no fault even if it exceeds that [standard]. For it cannot be restricted that in *aprastutapraśaṃsā* there are only five types of relationship between the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*); for that [figure] is seen even in other types of relationships—so say the Dīkṣitas.
O Lord of the mountain-clans who dwell in caves, O Moon among mountains, I perceive heaven and earth as the two vast pearl-oyster shells for the pearl of your divine fame.

For here, by means of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the two unrelated bases, heaven and earth, are the shell of the pearl of the Lord’s fame, the greatness and other qualities of the related subject—the pearl of the Lord’s fame which is contained within them—are perceived. Nor is there a relationship such as cause and effect between a pearl-oyster and a pearl; rather, there is only the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). Likewise, other relationships such as coexistence (*sahāvasthāna*) must also be resorted to, as for example: [Example omitted per instructions]

In a certain part of the sky, particles of dust from the Kaustubha gem—scraped away by the touch of Viṣṇu’s chest against the whetstone—are carried along by the wind known as Bhāsvat and shine brightly.

The "stain" (*kalaṅka*) of the Kaustubha gem consists of the mud, moss, and other impurities adhering to it at the time of its birth from the ocean; these are "collected," meaning they have been gathered together. Here, the relationship between the particles of the stain and the Kaustubha is one of coexistence. In this passage, the luminosity of the sun is concealed, and by superimposing the state of being "particles of the stain collected by the wind" (*nabhasvat*) upon it—an irrelevant (aprastuta) attribute—the infinite solar brilliance of the relevant (prastuta) Kaustubha gem, which coexists with that [sun], is made known.

Just as particles of dust clinging to Sītā’s body, which had risen from the surface of the earth, were carried by the waters of her consecration into the ocean and, having increased in volume, attained the state of jewels; || 963 ||
Here, in the first half [of the verse],
she is described as having arisen, having burst through the earth in the field scarred by the plowshare,
strewn with the auspicious dust of the furrows resembling the pollen of lotuses.

Thus the meaning stated is made known once again. "By the waters of consecration" means by the auspicious consecratory waters belonging to the time of descent; the sense is that they were led to the ocean by way of the Gaṅgā and other rivers. "Swollen" means they have become distended like chickpeas and the like placed in water; this is the sense. The rest is clear.

Here too, as in the previous example, the connection between Sītā’s body and the particles of dust is one of coexistence alone. Because the particles of dust are imagined to be jewels, the boundlessness of the excellence of the beauty of the divine and auspicious form of Sītā and others, which coexists with them, is perceived.

Regarding this very verse, there is an alternative reading: *laṅkāgatabhūmisutātanulagnakṣoṇireṇukaṇanikarāḥ*. In that case, according to the description "lying on the ground with her limbs pale," there is a connection between the divine and auspicious body of the blessed Sītā and the dust of the earth during her stay in Laṅkā. By the phrase "with the waters of consecration" (*abhiṣekajalaiḥ*), the auspicious bathing (*maṅgalasnāna*) occurring immediately after the slaying of Rāvaṇa—specifically mentioned in the line "then Sītā, having bathed her head"—is intended. The rest is identical to the previous version.
Or for example:
"O Mother, daughter of the ocean, this moon is merely a remnant of your face, since it always bears the splendor of your smile in its entirety and not otherwise. (964)

O Daughter of the Ocean! O Mother! The moon, the bearer of white luster, has become a *śeṣa* (remnant/subordinate) to your face—having attained the state of being a subordinate as defined by the rule, "A *śeṣa* is that which exists for the sake of another. Since this moon is such a *śeṣa* to her [your face], he carries, in its entirety and without deficiency, the splendor of her service—that is, the excellence of *dāsya* (servitude), which consists of performing all duties appropriate to every place and time, in the manner described by the words, "I shall do everything."

Not otherwise—that is, not by way of deficiency. For this reason, [the moon] always bears the splendor (*lakṣmī*)—the beauty—of your face, or rather the fortune of the face, only in its entirety, and not otherwise. The sense is that the likeness to that [face] belongs only to the full moon, and not to one that is deficient. Here, through the excellence of the sovereignty of the loveliness of the primary subject—the glorious face—which is suggested by its relation to the moon (the non-primary subject) as its complement, the preeminence of the moon's own beauty is perceived.
In this case, there is no relationship such as cause and effect between the moon of the venerable face; rather, it is a relationship of the subordinate and the principal.

Thus, having relied upon the analogy and the object of comparison, the two types of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on a relationship of cause and effect as imagined by the poet have been shown. It is also seen elsewhere, as for example: "O Blessed One, one who has placed his burden upon Your feet is truly the best of beings; yet, without being inferior to You, he is nevertheless described as being the very best of beings. (165)

O Blessed One! that best of the virtuous, the foremost among those who have sought refuge, having placed his burden upon Your feet, does not become distressed or tormented by *bhava*—that is, by *saṃsāra*—in the interval between the performance of means and the attainment of the fruit. Because of the intensity of his suffering, even the maintenance of the body commenced by past karma becomes undesirable; for its definition is: "He who grieves even while the body commenced by past karma remains is called one who is distressed (*ārta*). Then, intending to speak of the *dṛpta-prapanna* (the haughty seeker of refuge), he says: "Now (*atha*)..."

Alternatively, having become such a surrendered soul (prapanna), even if he is deficient due to the internal persistence of a portion of his *prārabdha* karma, he is nevertheless described by the wise as being truly excellent and foremost among those who have taken refuge (*prapannāgragaṇya*). He is not, however, disregarded as one who has not surrendered; for the definition of a "proud" (*dṛpta*) surrenderer is: "He whose grief is directed toward the acquisition of another body is called proud."

Alternatively, the best of men is one who has placed his burden upon your feet; [the word] *antara* is used here in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), according to both Amara and Medinī, who state: "The word *antara* [is used in the senses of] space, limit, enclosure, disappearance, distinction, and for the sake of that. The author of the *Ṭīkāsarvasva* and others observe that the word *antara* is seen in the sense of "for the sake of that" in examples such as "rice for the sake of the boiled rice" (*odanāntara-staṇḍula*).

"He becomes inferior to you" means that he is less than you, the Supreme Self, the principal (śeṣin), because of his inherent nature as a subordinate (śeṣatā) characterized by subservience to another, as stated in the rule "the subordinate exists for the sake of another. The word *atha* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), according to the *Medinī* lexicon which states: "'atha' and 'atho' may occur in the sense of doubt, [but also] in the sense of entirety, commencement, and conjunction. Thus, although he is inferior to you in the manner described, he is nevertheless described as being "most excellent" (*sattama*) and not as being inferior. "If you have a desire for your own life" means: if you have a longing for your own existence.
Always remember your own servitude to Hari, His sovereignty, and your true nature.

The meaning is that it has been stated that the knowledge of the relationship between the individual self (pratyagātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) as the entirety and its possessor (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva) alone is the cause of existence.

In this context, the compound *saduttama* is formed by the rule *sup-supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), meaning "that which exists (*bhavaḥ*) in the middle (*antareṇa*) [of the word] *sattama*. It does not become deficient (*ūnaḥ*)—that is, lacking—by the letter *du* (*du-varṇa*). This is because the sound of the letter *du* is heard within that word. The sense is: even if, at some point or another, it were to become deficient by the letter *du*, it is still described as being precisely *sattama*, the word *sattama* itself; for when the letter *du* is removed from the word *saduttama*, it is produced in that very form (*sattama*).

Here, by means of the description—which is not the primary subject—of the distress caused by the worldly suffering of those who have sought refuge, the excellence of the greatness of taking refuge at the lotus feet of the Blessed One, which is the cause of that [distress], is made known. In this case, there is no causal relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison invented by the poet; rather, it is natural.

Just as the Lord of the Day (the Sun) may appear like the Lord of the Poor (Venus) due to a difference in the perception of Lakṣmī (light), and yet the Lord of the Day actually possesses the nature of the Lord of the Poor—what room for doubt is there in this matter? 966.

By virtue of a particular glance from Lakṣmī—that is, by virtue of the connection with her sidelong look—the Lord of the Poor (Dīneśa), though formerly a sovereign of the destitute, shall shine like the Lord of Day (Dineśa), like the thousand-rayed sun. Moreover, furthermore, even the Lord of Day (Dineśa), the radiant sun, by virtue of a particular glance from Lakṣmī—that is, by virtue of the absence of her sidelong look—attains the state of being the Lord of the Poor. What is the use of doubt here? What is the point of uncertainty?

In this alternative view, O Lakṣmī! even the word *dīneśa* (the Lord of the wretched), by virtue of a change in perception—namely, through seeing the vowel *i* as the vowel *ī*—would appear like the word *dineśa* (the Lord of the Day). It would shine forth as the word *dineśa*. The particle *iva* is used here for poetic embellishment (*vākyālaṃkāra*). The meaning is that when the vowel *i* is perceived as the vowel *ī*, the word *dīneśa* assumes the form of the word *dineśa*.

Here, by means of the effect—the attainment of the state of being the lord of the wretched (*dīneśatva*) and the lord of the day (*dineśatva*)—which is unmentioned (*aprastuta*), the unrestrained power of its causes, namely the presence and absence of Lakṣmī’s sidelong glance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which are themselves the subject at hand (*prastuta*), is understood. Here too, as in the previous example, the relationship is one of cause and effect.
O Mother of the World, if even one who is a cowherd is rejected by you, he will become a mere golaka; since he is excluded from the four castes, what doubt can there be in this matter? (967)

O Mother of the World! Even if a man were Indra, the protector of heaven, another guardian of the quarters, a king, or even the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), if he were rejected and cast aside by you, he would become a *golaka*—one born of a widow as defined by the rule "a *golaka* is [the son] born when the husband is dead"—and would be abandoned and excluded by the fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*). What doubt is there in this? None at all; such is the meaning.

If, in this context, the word *gopālaka* is deprived of its final syllable *pā*—that is, if it is made to consist of four syllables (*catur-varṇa*)—then by virtue of that state of being four-syllabled (*cāturvarṇya*), it would become nothing but a *golaka*. For the word *gopālaka*, consisting of four syllables, would become three-syllabled upon the removal of the syllable *pā*.

Here, from the non-contextual effect—the attainment of a miserable state by the cowherd—which serves as the object of a poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*), there is understood the contextual cause: the unrestrained power of the punishment meted out by the Mother of the World.

"How is it that these people, though possessing nothing, possess dwellings as magnificent as the splendor of gold? Could this be the Mountain of Serpents (Śeṣaśaila), and have they come here desiring to behold it? || 968 ||

In this context, when those who were destitute had gone toward the Mountain of the Serpent (Śeṣācala) and beheld there, within dwellings that resembled mere rags, an infinite wealth manifested by the side-glance of Śrīnivāsa, they were questioned by someone as to the cause of it; yet, instead of stating the cause—which was the grace of the Lord—they replied that they had gone to the Mountain of the Serpent desiring to see Him. Thus, this too is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on a cause; enough of this long digression. Let us return to our subject.
An expression of a particular when a general category has been introduced is as follows:
"The tree, yielding fruit in the form of shade, brings ease to the world; but as for the *śākoṭaka*, even crows, owls, and the like would not desire it. (969)

In this regard, while the general statement—that toward Śrīnivāsa, only one such as you, a treasury of virtues like great magnanimity, is sought by those desiring their own desired fruits, whereas one devoid even of a trace of virtue is shunned by all—is intended to be made, a specific instance has been mentioned instead to convey that meaning; thus, this is *viśeṣanibandhanā* (the figure based on a particular).

Just as for those who take refuge in the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), there would be no failure to obtain even the slightest desired object—knowing this, why should a wise person resort to other trees born from the earth? (970)

In this context as well, since it is known that one who takes refuge in a great benefactor equal to Śrīnivāsa will never fail to attain their desired object, why would a wise person resort to others who are stingy? While a general statement was intended, a specific instance has been mentioned instead to facilitate that understanding; "trees born of the earth" means men dwelling upon the ground. Or, for example: "O Mother of the World, due to the pride of his sovereignty over the celestial realm, Nahuṣa became a non-sleeping serpent (ajagara) with a long body (ahrasvākāra), having become so when your grace was absent. (971)

O Mother of the World! When your grace was absent, Nahuṣa—due to the mental agitation caused by the majesty of his sovereignty over the three heavens—became one for whom there was no "jāgarā" (vigilance); that is to say, having become unwatchful regarding the prevention of future calamities, he remained thus. Consequently, he became one whose "ākāra" (form) was "ahrasva" (not short), meaning one of massive body. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *hrasva* applies to the meanings 'small' and 'dwarf'."

The meaning is that he was born as an *ajagara*, a specific kind of serpent, due to the sage’s curse; or alternatively, the construction may be "he was born" (i.e., remained) as such. In this regard, the Indian legend of Nahuṣa should be recalled. In the alternative [grammatical] sense, the word *ajāgara* becomes *jāta* when there is an *ā*-vowel associated with the letter *ja*. The suffix *tasi* is used here in all its case-terminations. That which has a short *a*-vowel (*hrasva*) is so described; thus, having been brought to the *a*-vowel in place of the *ā*-vowel, it remains as *ajagara*, resulting in the form *ajagara*—this further meaning is also full of poetic charm.

Here, regarding Śrī, it is stated that when the flow of your grace becomes feeble, even a great person falls into a miserable state; thus, while the general principle is the subject to be expressed, a specific instance has been mentioned.

O Rāghava, had the son of Vinatā not obeyed your command out of pride for his sovereignty, he— though possessed of great power— would indeed have been a mere man, fallen from his station here and there.

O Raghava! If Sugriva, the son of the Wind-god—whose mind was uplifted by the acquisition of his kingdom—had not carried out your command regarding the search for Sita and other matters exactly as promised, even though he was *sanayaḥ* (possessed of statesmanship) and *nītimān* (observant of policy), he would have fallen from his kingdom and become *nanayaḥ* (devoid of statesmanship), being utterly bereft of policy. The compound is formed with the negative particle *na*; the sense is that he would have been considered simply "unprincipled" (*anītimān*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that he has fallen away from this world and that world; for there is a traditional teaching (smṛti) stating: "Indeed, one who does not repay a favor done for him falls away from both worlds. Or else, the meaning is that he has fallen away from wealth and dharma; for it is said in the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "O dear one, for one who does not repay a favor, there is a great loss of dharma, as well as a loss of wealth and friendship. Or again, "fallen here and there" is a common expression meaning that he has fallen into improper and censurable places.

It would have been so. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The particle *api*, though displaced in the sequence, expresses censure (*garhāyām*). The meaning is as follows: if, in one instance, the word *inatanayaḥ*—which consists of the letters *na*, *ka* (represented by *n*), and *ya* (*yakāreṇa*)—were to fall away from the *i*-vowel (*itaḥ*) and the *ta*-vowel (*tataḥ*) and become disjoined, it would result in the form *nanaya*. Here, although the general principle to be stated is that even one born of a noble family (*mahākulīnaḥ*) would fall from both worlds if he were to transgress the teaching of the Blessed One, this specific case has been mentioned instead.

In the examples shown above, there is generally indeed a mixture with *śleṣa* (paronomasia). However, as for the mixture with other figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*), it should be inferred by the intelligent according to the possibility in each respective case.
Just as Arjuna, having obtained you as his guide at the forefront of the Kuru battle, became invincible and possessed of exceeding splendor, O destroyer of Kaṃsa, so too [did others]. || 973 ||

O destroyer of Kaṃsa! Arjuna, having obtained you as his restrainer, charioteer, and leader, surpassed the Lord of Heaven, Indra, becoming one who transcends the lords of heaven (*atidyupati*). On the field of battle, remaining undefeated and unsubdued by enemies, he thus became one of exceeding splendor (*atidyuti*) and immense brilliance. In the alternative sense, the word *atidyupati* does not shine (*na rājitaḥ*) by means of the letter *pa*; thus, while being "unconquered" (*aparājita*), it results in the form *atidyuti*.

Here, while the general subject matter under discussion is that "a person who has obtained the Blessed One as a guide becomes victorious everywhere and radiant," there is instead the expression of a specific instance not under discussion.

Just as the thunderbolt was wielded by the enemy of Bala during the great battle for the abduction of Pārijāta— when the reeds were like lotuses and the conflict was vast— it has been moved by you only as easily as a blade of kuśa grass.

O Blessed One, the sun to the lotus that is the very lineage of the Yadu king named Śūra! This address is intended to highlight Your supreme majesty. Furthermore, in the great battle for the seizing of the Pārijāta tree, the thunderbolt (*vajra*) wielded by Balaripu (Indra) was shaken, displaced from its position, and rendered powerless—this is the meaning.

By the rule "the root *cal* [becomes short] before *kampane*," there is an absence of *mittva* (as in examples such as *śīlaṃ cālayati*), and consequently, there is an absence of the short vowel caused by that *mittva*. The meaning is: "he wove only *kuśa* grass," that is, he made it consist primarily of grass. In the alternative reading, the word division is *alitam*. That which lacks *li*—that is, the letter *l* (*livarṇa*)—is *ali*; that which has been made *ali* is *alita*. From the word *ali*, by adding the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "making it so" (*tatkaroti*), the past passive participle suffix *kta* is applied in the objective sense. The elision of the causative suffix *ṇi* occurs by the rule "before a *seṭ* past passive participle suffix."

Alternatively, *li* has arisen in this [word], thus it is *lita*; that which is not *lita* is *alita*, meaning "devoid of the letter *li*. By the rule *ata iñ* and *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. [The word] *kuśam* itself was stretched out (*atāni*). The meaning is that the word *kuliśa* (thunderbolt) was produced as *kuśa* by the removal of the letter *li*. Here, while the general subject matter is that even the great weapons raised with fury against the Lord are rendered as worthless as straw, the specific instance described is the shattering of the towering pride of Indra’s raised thunderbolt. As in another example: *...* (Example verse omitted per instructions) ...In this way, a general statement is expressed through a particular instance. This is the figure of speech known as *Paryāyokta* (Periphrasis). (Note: The provided text contains a commentary on a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), specifically *Paryāyokta*, where a general truth is conveyed through a specific illustration.)

O Mother, having understood from your words that her own sin was like honey, she became possessed of merit; for if that sin were not thus led away, it would surely have become essential—what doubt could there be in this?

O Mother! *Sāragham* honey is that which is made by bees (*saraghābhiḥ*). In the sense of "made by that," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *asaṃjñāyām*; thus, Amara states, "A bee is a *madhumakṣikā*. By your word, [he] understood himself to be *avaram*, meaning inferior or lowly; in another sense, it means one from whom the letter *ra* (*raḥ*) has been shaken off (*avadhūtaḥ*), i.e., deprived of the letter *r*. The elision of the word *dhūta* occurs according to the rule *prādibhyo dhātujasya*. Having understood this, he became *sāgham*, meaning existing together with suffering (*agham*).

The meaning is that he became distressed upon realizing his own inferiority in comparison to the Śrīvacana (the word of Śrī). According to Amara, "agha" refers to sin, suffering, or calamity. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), the word *sāragham* becomes *sāgham* by the removal of the letter *ra*. However, if he were not to attain [it] in the manner described—that is, if he were not to reach it—then it would surely remain *sāram*, meaning excellent or full of essence; the sense is that it would not be tasteless (*nīrasa*). In this case, the word is divided as *gham*.

In the same way, if the word *sāra* were to be derived from the syllable *gha* (as in *gha-varṇa*), then upon the removal of the syllable *gha*, it would result in the word *sāra* itself; this is the intended meaning. Here, while one ought to speak of the sweetness of the Blessed One’s speech as being superior to all things in general, the statement regarding its specific quality of being more flavorful than honey is made.
When a specific subject is introduced, a general statement [is made] as follows:

"Those who know the secrets of action, knowledge, and worship, and who have themselves attained their goal—they, whose sole wealth is poverty, how can such people exist without [your] compassion? (976) The construction is: "How do they become those who have attained their goal? Here, while a specific point—that "I am destitute and must be revived by you alone, standing in the place of other means"—is introduced, a general statement beginning with "those whose sole wealth is poverty" is expressed. Thus, this is *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Irrelevant) based on a general principle.

Just as the Great Being alone is the one to be approached by men seeking their highest good, so too, whatever little may be desired cannot be obtained from others who are destitute and intent on deception.

In this context, although it is specifically to be stated that Śrīnivāsa alone—and not other limited deities—is to be served even by those people who desire all human goals (puruṣārtha), one should understand that a general statement has been made instead as a means of establishing that specific point.

Or rather, how could the virtuous, the omniscient, the lords, and the auspicious ones not have made the moon-like nails of your feet—the crest-jewel of the Lord of Mountains, the sovereign of the hooded serpents—their own crowns? 978.

In this context, although a specific statement ought to have been made—namely, that by bearing the moon-like nails of your feet upon his head, the Blessed Śrīnivāsa will attain even greater omniscience than mine—the author employs a general expression instead.

Or rather, O Lord, you are exceedingly cool with compassion, as if out of shame bestowed by the rays of the moon; for this very reason, though you are of excellent character (*suśīla*), you are not cold (*aśīta*) toward those who seek refuge, and you provide a beautiful netherworld (*sutala*). 979.

O Blessed One! You are exceedingly cool through compassion—that mercy characterized by the desire to dispel the suffering of others regardless of one's own interest—which itself was rendered even more chilling by her who bestowed shame upon the rays of the moon. For this very reason, you are also "suśīla": one whose conduct (śīla) is beautiful; the word "api" (also) serves as a conjunction, meaning that you possess such excellent character.

*Sauśīlya* (gentleness) is defined as the nature of maintaining an unbroken intimacy even with the dull-witted. This is well-known from the accounts of Guha, the Śabara woman, and the cowherds in the incarnations of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. Since gentleness could never manifest in the absence of the coolness of compassion (*dayā-śiśiratā*), the statement regarding their relationship as cause and effect is made. For this very reason, He is "un-cool" (*aśīta*)—meaning untiring—in the protection (*avane*) of those who have taken refuge; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *śīta* is neuter in the sense of the quality of cold, and masculine/feminine in the senses of 'cool' and 'lazy'."

Alternatively, the particle *api* indicates a contradiction. Thus, there is an apparent contradiction in saying that he is "of excellent character" (*suśīla*) due to the coolness of his compassion, yet is "not cool" (*aśīta*)—that is, not cold—but rather "hot" (*uṣṇa*). The resolution of this contradiction is simply that he is "unwearied" (*analasa*). Furthermore, he is "sutala": he is well-established (*sutala*), for the root *tala* means "to stand firm," and the suffix *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). The meaning is that he is firmly established in being ever-vigilant in protecting those who have sought refuge. Alternatively, he is "sutala" because his foundation (*tala*) is beautiful; thus, you are one whose very nature is auspicious.

The sense is that you possess a virtuous nature precisely because of your vigilance in protecting those who depend upon you. According to Amara, the word *tala* refers to the lower part or the surface, and is not feminine. In this context, the word *suśītala* (very cool), by the mere absence of the letter *ta*, becomes *suśīla* (of good character). Furthermore, that same word, when not cool—that is, when it has departed from the syllable *śī*—becomes *aśīta*; thus, by the mere absence of the syllable *śī*, it becomes *sutala*. Here, while a specific statement was required—namely, that you are established in vigilance specifically for my protection—a general statement has been made instead.
When a similar subject is introduced, the mention of something similar is as follows:

"O cloud, while you are blowing, purifying, and pouring down rain, and are moving directly toward me, this swelling of distress caused by the young *cātaka* bird shall not remain with you for long. (980) Here, the narration of the story of the young *cātaka* bird—which is similar in nature—concludes in the matter of consoling the seeker (*prapanna*), namely that when the Lord has turned His face toward one who is full of compassion, who is ever-virtuous, and who is dependent on Him, your distress shall not endure for long. Thus, this is "Praise of the Irrelevant" (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) based on similarity (*sārūpya*).

O Lord of the Mountain, the King of Serpents, how many jewels, bearing various names, are there not in every direction? Yet, do they ever attain the status of the *cintāmaṇi*, that wish-fulfilling gem? 981.

Here, the disparagement of jewels other than the *cintāmaṇi* culminates in the disparagement of those who grant limited results—namely, the various deities other than the Blessed One—who are themselves the subject of censure; thus, this too is based solely on similarity (*sārūpya*).
This [type of simile] is also seen with punning adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇā*), as for example:

"Pierced by swarms of arrows, yet possessing uplifted pride and abounding in most formidable courage; a hero leading the way in battle, he of great renown attains the state of being the Abode of Fortune (*Śrīnivāsa*). (982)

Here, through the use of punning adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇaiḥ*), the praise of an unmentioned heroic man—which is the intended subject (*stavyatvena*)—culminates in the praise of Śeṣādri, who is the actual subject (*prastuta*) and shares the same characteristics as that hero. The substantive *śūra* (hero) is not itself punned here. He is "pierced" (*anuviddha*) by hosts of *pattriṇaḥ*—meaning arrows on the one hand and birds on the other—and is "followed" (*anubaddha*).
