He is "elevated" (*ucchrita*): in one sense his pride (*mānaḥ*, defined as the loftiness of mind), and in the other his stature (*mānaḥ*, defined as measurement). [The word *māna* thus carries two meanings: "pride" and "measure"].

According to the *Medinī* lexicon, "klība" refers to a measure such as a *prastha*. He is one whose strength (*sattva*) or power (*bala*) surpasses Bhīma (Bhīmasena) or Rudra; thus he is "Atibhīma. In the alternative sense, he is so called because in him there are "Atibhīma-sattvas"—extremely fierce creatures such as tigers and other beasts. He is the "Agrasara" (foremost leader) in battle (*saṃkhye*). In the alternative sense, he is the "Agrasara" (leader) in "Saṃkhyā," meaning the calculation of the great mountains.

A hero, a brave man; and that which is both beautiful and extensive is "suprathana"—a praiseworthy battle. It becomes the abode, the dwelling place, of its splendor, that is, its fortune of victory. Alternatively, he is so called because his fame is beautiful and extensive; the meaning is that he attains the state of being one in whom the Lord Śrīnivāsa resides.
Just as you, O lotus, by the grace of Hari, surely always attain the blossoming of your face; for, having obtained the aesthetic essence (*rasa*), you experience infinite fragrance.

O lotus! By the grammatical rule "the word *padma* may be used in the masculine," you possess the masculine gender. You are successful and blessed, because by the grace (*prasāda*)—that is, the light and the favor—of Hari (the Sun) and the Blessed Lord, you always attain the blossoming of your face. Having obtained the nectar (*rasa*), you experience infinite and immeasurable fragrance (*āmoda*).

The meaning is that, in accordance with the manner stated in the Śruti—“Bliss, indeed, is the essence; for having obtained this very essence, one becomes blissful”—you find the bliss of the Supreme Brahman, which is of the nature of bliss, as it is being cultivated through a sequence of hundredfold increases. Here too, by means of punning adjectives, the praise of the lotus (padma), though not the primary subject, culminates in the praise of the knower of Brahman who possesses a form similar to it; the substantive "lotus" (padma) itself is not a pun.
Or for example:

"O *mākanda* tree, you are blessed; through your devotion to Mādhava, you possess a noble reputation for your abundance of fragrance. Furthermore, you quickly fashion even your most passionate sprout into one that truly knows the essence of greenness. (984) O *mākanda*, O mango tree, you are blessed. He explains this very blessedness with the words "through devotion to Mādhava": through the attachment (*saktyā*) of Mādhava—the Spring (*vasanta*)—you are "well-regarded" (*sumataḥ*), meaning by means of your flowers (*sumaiḥ*). The suffix *-tas* here functions as a substitute for all case endings (*sārvavibhaktikas-tasi*).

In the month of Mādhava, he whose mind is well-disposed through devotion to the Blessed One is thus described; that is to say, he is a follower of the established doctrines of those proficient in the Upanishads (*trayyanta*). Alternatively, there is a word-break as *sumate* in the phrase *sumata-āmodam*. O *sumate*—O one of great wisdom!—this is an epithet of the mango tree (*mākanda*). You attain, or reach, the abundance of fragrance, which is to say, an excess of bliss.

Even a sprout (*pallava*), though possessing an intense redness and being exceedingly passionate, soon attains the state of being green—the quality of *harita* (greenness)—as expressed by the suffix *kvip* from the root *vid*. And you bring this about; for it is well known that a leaf is red in its stage as a sprout and turns green in its stage as a mature leaf. The distinction is that a fresh leaf is a sprout (*kisalaya*), while a youthful leaf is a leaf (*patra*). Elsewhere, he is not merely fortunate himself.

But [the author] says "atirāgiṇam" (one who is excessively passionate) to show that you cause even those who are dependent on you and devoid of dispassion to live. "One who knows the *tattva* of Hari"—that is, one who knows the reality (*tattva*) of Hari, which is his true nature (*yāthātmya*), or the authoritative reality in the form of Hari; or the *tattva* named Hari, namely the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). [The suffix] *kvip* is used after the root *vid*. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *tattva* refers to one's own nature and the Supreme Self. Thus, it means "one who knows Brahman. And you cause such a person to flourish.

Here, the praise of the mango tree (*ākandataru*), which is not the primary subject, culminates in the praise of the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) who sustains those dependent upon him, who is the actual subject at hand. In this instance, the word *mākanda*, serving as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), is non-ambiguous (*aśliṣṭa*).

In verses of this kind, even when there are punned adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇa*), it is indeed *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) alone; it is not the case that *samāsokti* (speech of compression) acts as its subordinate support, because *samāsokti*, having a form that is the very opposite of this figure, cannot serve as a support for it. As for the claim made in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* that *samāsokti* supports this [figure], that is incorrect; for if the suggested narrative (*pratīyamānavṛttānta*) is itself the subject at hand (*prastuta*), then *samāsokti*—which would be the supporter—cannot even arise, since that [figure] is admitted only when the subject at hand is the expressed meaning (*vācya*).

If, however, the subject matter were irrelevant, then the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) itself would not exist, because that figure is accepted only when the narrative of the irrelevant subject is the expressed meaning (*vācyatā*). Therefore, with the intention that *samāsokti* (condensed expression) consists merely of a second meaning suggested by punning adjectives, its description [in other texts] must be reconciled in some way or another. And this [figure] is called *aprastutapraśaṃsā* based on similarity; in this case, the expressed meaning sometimes remains in a state of neutrality toward the implied meaning.

In some cases, it requires an implied distinction in order to attain compatibility with its own inherent qualification; and in some cases, even that which is implied possesses identity with the expressed meaning in certain respects, while the expressed meaning, in turn, requires identity with the implied meaning in certain respects.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Can a cat, even if it has approached with great difficulty the lofty peak of a mountain, ever be able to smell the scent of a fierce tiger? (985)

In this context, the story of the cat under discussion leads to the following conclusion: even if those of meager intellect who fancy themselves wise were to obstinately declare that this very [cat] is the Supreme Brahman—the cause of the universe as propounded in the Upanishads (the "heads" of the three Vedas)—such a claim regarding another deity remains utterly remote from even a scent of equality with the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Brahman, whose great majesty is proclaimed by thousands of voices throughout the Upanishads through attributes such as being the cause of all and the unconditioned Lord of all. Thus the matter concludes.

In this case, since the meanings that constitute the expressed sense are possible in the context of the cat, the comprehension of the expressed meaning occurs precisely without superimposing the meanings that have been established as implied.
The second example is as follows:
"O bee, endure this confinement within the bud of the lotus for just a few moments; here the sun, the destroyer of the lotus petals, scatters his mass of rays like a lion. (986)

Here, by means of the non-contextual account of consoling the bee trapped within the interior of a lotus bud, there is understood the contextual account of consoling those who have taken refuge at the lotus feet of the Lord—a corresponding narrative wherein it is suggested that one should endure this bondage of worldly existence for only a very short time, as the glances of the Lord are now close to extending toward you.

Just as a small pool, having been dried up by the heat of the sun, becomes indeed fit for austerity upon reaching [the rain], so too, O fish, abandon your dejection; a line of clouds is rising up before you.

Here, by means of the narrative of consoling a fish—which is not the subject at hand—the meaning understood is one of consolation toward a wretched person distressed by dwelling in the midst of a family excessively corrupted by poverty: "Do not grieve; prosperity is near for you."
Just as a monkey might constantly say, "I too am a weaver with threads," what loss could there be for a weaver who produces cloth fit for the gods? 988.

*Markaṭaka* refers to the insect named *ūrṇānābha*; as Amara states: "The female spider (*lūtā*), the weaver (*tantuvāya*), *ūrṇānābha*, and *markaṭaka* are synonyms. You weave cloth during your life; for the verbal root is *veñ* (to weave). [He is] the weaver (*vāta*) of the silk cloth worthy of the gods; the suffix *tṛc* is added to the root *veñ*. This is a compound formed with a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Here, the censure of the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) and the praise of the weaver (*kuvinda*), which are not the immediate subject, ultimately resolve upon two figures who are their counterparts in the context of what is being praised or censured: on the one hand, the bad poet (*kukavi*) who composes a few verses that are unrefined, lacking in skill, and irrelevant to the subject; and on the other, the sovereign of the circle of poets (*kavikulasārvabhauma*) who is capable of composing beautiful and auspicious poetry adorned with the Lord’s excellent qualities. This [figure] is a particular kind of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*), as it is intermingled with the *avajñā* (disdain) ornament to be discussed below.
Just as you do not wither under the rays of the sun, nor do you thrill even at the beams of the moon, you are a stone of insurmountable hardness; enough with the detailed account of your conduct!

Here, by means of the irrelevant account of the stone, the story of the foremost of fools—the relevant subject—is made known through its similarity; for he, though scorched by many worldly afflictions, remains unheated because his mind does not melt due to repeatedly hearing the nectar of the Lord’s stories and other such practices, and thus he is worthy of censure.
Just as you possess the fragrance of the Puṣkalaka region, wherever you may be born, even the Lotus-eyed One nourishes that abundant fragrance within his heart.

*Puṣkalakasīmā* means the "boundary of the *puṣkalaka*. A *puṣkalaka* is a specific kind of musk deer, which they call the "musk-cat" (*gandhamārjāra*). *Sīmā* refers to the scrotum; as Medinī states: "Now, *puṣkalaka* [is used] for the musk deer," and "*sīmā* [is used] for a jar, a boundary, a field, and also for the scrotum, in the feminine. Because of the prohibition [of the suffix *ṅīp*] by the rule "after *manas*," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* characterized by a final *n* does not apply. *Gandhas* of that [scrotum] refers to a specific fragrant substance produced therein; this is its vocative.

Even though the referent is a single entity, this word is always plural in form—like *dārāḥ* (wives) or *gṛhāḥ* (houses)—according to the grammatical rule: "The word *gandha* is recorded as meaning fragrance, sulphur, a trace, and pride; that same word is also traditionally held to denote a substance when used in the plural or in the masculine."

Here, by means of the irrelevant narrative concerning the fragrance of the Puṣkalaka boundary, the relevant narrative is made known: that even those born of lowly lineage, if they are sentient beings enriched with auspicious qualities such as knowledge of reality, dispassion, and devotion, become eternally pleasing like excellent jewels by virtue of being recipients of the grace of the Blessed Lord Śrī Śrīnivāsa. Thus, the relevant matter is conveyed through its similarity to the other.
Or rather, trees such as the mango give but a small amount of fruit; what need have we for them? O most noble Mandāra tree, you are surely a giver of more than one’s desires. 991.

Here, the disregard for mango and other trees, as well as the praise of the *mandāra*, ultimately culminates in the disregard for the other deities—who are the subjects under discussion by virtue of being unworthy of honor—and in the praise of the Lord Śrīnivāsa, who is the subject under discussion by virtue of being worthy of praise and who shares the same nature as those [trees].

In the first three examples, since bees, fish, weavers, and worms are animals, and in the subsequent three examples, since stones, fragrant substances, and *mandāra* flowers are insentient, they are incapable of being addressed; therefore, the comprehension of the expressed meaning occurs only through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) that is implied, which requires their identity with the [respective] subjects.
Or as it is said:
"O bee, listen to my words; do not feel dejected because of your impure color, for you have become successful by being brought back to life through taking refuge in the lotus of Śrīnivāsa. (992)

One who is of impure complexion, blue in color, or of unclean appearance is a Śūdra. He is endowed with glory (*śrī*) by taking refuge in that lotus-foot which is the abode of *Śrī*, that is, the Great Lakṣmī; he is *Śrīnivāsa* (the Abode of Glory) through such refuge, as well as through taking refuge in both Padmā and Lakṣmī.

In this case, the qualification [“blue”] is employed as the cause for removing the bee’s distress; however, that is not possible. For blueness is not a defect in the bee, nor is being restored to life by taking refuge in the lotus a merit, such that it could serve to dispel its distress through praise. Therefore, the identity between the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the implied meaning (*pratīyamāna*) must be required both in the qualified portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) and the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*). The distinction is that in the former case [the *dhvani* of *rasa*, etc. it was required in one part, whereas here it is required in its entirety.

O Cātaka bird, you are indeed very great; do not fall into despondency on account of being called a "small bird" (stokaka). Seeking nectar, you take refuge in Hari alone—who else among the twice-born is greater than you?

*Stokakaḥ*: "Very small"; the suffix *kan* is added to the word *stoka* in the sense of "small. Alternatively, *stokakaḥ* means "one who cries out with a small sound," referring to the *cātaka* bird; as Amara states: "The *stokaka* and the *cātaka* are synonyms. "Seeking nectar" means seeking water, that is, being thirsty. In the alternative sense, it means "seeking the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). "A twice-born (*dvija*)" refers to a bird and a Brahmin. "Who is superior?"—meaning none at all. "To Hari, Maghavan, and the Blessed One"—that is, to Viṣṇu, Indra, and the Lord [Śiva] respectively. [The answer is: "Who is superior? No one."

In this case, the qualifying attribute (viśeṣaṇa) employed as the cause for warding off the Cātaka bird’s dejection is not possible [in its literal sense]. For being a *stokaka* (a small bird) is not the cause of the Cātaka’s dejection, nor is taking refuge with Indra out of a desire for the first drop of water a cause for excellence; such that dejection might be warded off by praising it. Therefore, according to the manner described above, a state of identity between the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the implied meaning (*pratīyamāna*) is required for both the substantive and the qualifying portions.
Or for example:

"O swan (*marāla*), you are eternally pure and most skillful in distinguishing between poison and nectar; yet you resort to both right and left wings, and thus you have been brought low by fate. (994) O swan, O *haṃsa*, you are eternally pure (*śuci*)—that is, bright white. In the secondary sense, according to the saying "he who is pure in purpose is truly pure," it means you are free from the intent to steal the property of others and so forth. You are [thus].

Regarding "poison and nectar" (*viṣāmṛtayoh*) and "water and milk": according to the *Medinī* lexicon, "poison" (*viṣa*) refers to both a venomous substance and water; "nectar" (*amṛta*) refers to the remains of a sacrifice, ambrosia, water, and clarified butter. "Discrimination" (*viveke*) means in the act of separating. In the alternative sense, the words "poison" and "nectar" function through metaphorical usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) to signify the unreal and the real respectively. One who is "more skillful" (*nipuṇataraḥ*) in their discrimination—that is, in the thorough investigation of them. Regarding "right and left" (*dakṣiṇavāmau*), these mean the right and the left, as well as the upright and the adverse; according to the *Medinī*, "right" (*dakṣiṇa*) applies to one born on the right side, to the upright, and to that which follows the will.

"‘Vāma’ refers to that which is contrary to what is beautiful on the left side of a bride; thus says the *Ratnamālā*. You take refuge in two wings, two feathers, and two established doctrines (*siddhānta*); therefore, you have been cast down by Fate (Brahmā) and by Destiny (the Divine), made inferior by being turned into a vehicle—or, in the other sense, you are despised by all or have fallen into hell.

Here, through the account of the irrelevant [story of the] ruddy goose (*rāla*), there is intended to be expressed a reproach, preceded by the praise of his qualities, directed at a certain self-important scholar who possesses many branches of learning and accepts both the doctrine of the Lord and its opposite as equal."

In this case, since praise based on purity and so forth, or blame based on taking recourse to the right or left wings, is impossible in respect to the unmentioned swan (*marāla*), the identity of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) with the suggested meaning (*dyotyartha*)—in the manner shown—must be required both in the aspect of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and in the aspect of the attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Just as these banyan trees, though their branches are matted and their fruit is sapless, are nonetheless red with passion for that fruit; alas, they are frequented by those who fall [into them] with hymns of praise longing for such fruit. 995.

These banyan trees (*vaṭa*)—the *nyagrodha* trees—are suggested to be desirous of fruit in the manner about to be described. Though they possess branches (*śākhin*), are matted with roots (*jaṭāla*), and are even provided with aerial roots (*śiphānvita*), they become red (*rakta*) in their own fruit, which is sapless and devoid of juice. For such a quality of those fruits is well known. In the alternative sense, "those possessing branches" refers to students of the Vedic portions, and "matted ones" means ascetics endowed with matted hair (*jaṭā*).

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: “*Śākha* refers to a branch, a wing, an arm, a portion of the Vedas, or a part of a tree”; and “*Jaṭā* refers to hair clinging [to the head] or a root. They are attached—that is, deeply engrossed—in that which is sapless (*nīrasa*), namely, in trivial pleasure (*tucchānanda*) consisting of fruits such as cattle, sons, heaven, and other such worldly ends. They are frequented by swarms—that is, multitudes—of those very birds who desire such fruits, and likewise by crowds of people falling downward; alas (*bata*)! what sorrow this evokes when one contemplates such impropriety.

In this instance, the qualifying attributes employed as the grounds for praising and subsequently censuring the *nyagrodha* trees are impossible [in their literal sense]. For neither "being a tree" nor "having matted roots" is a ground for praise, nor is "having red-colored, sapless fruit" or "being frequented by birds attached to such fruit" a ground for censure, such that they would be censured following praise for those very qualities. Therefore, as before, the expressed meaning requires an identity with the suggested meaning to be established between the portions of the subject and its qualifiers.
The third [type of simile] is as follows:
"Alas, why do you fish take refuge in shallow and trivial ponds, where the waves rise repeatedly due to the presence of exceedingly powerful enemies in the form of favorable, abundant currents? (996)

On the shore (*kūle*), on the bank (*tīre*), those who possess many (*bhūrayaḥ*) or numerous (*bahulāḥ*) fishermen (*dāśāḥ*, *kaivartāḥ*). In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), they are called *bhūridāśāḥ* because they give (*dāśanti*) abundant (*bhūri*) wealth or gold (*vastu*, *suvarṇa*) to their dependents (*anukūlānām svāśritānām*); [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the root *dāśṛ* (to give) in the sense of the object. By the splendor (*bhāsā*) or power (*prabhāvena*) of Atibala, the wind; for Amara states, "Atibala is the shaker," and Medinī states, "The word *bhās* is feminine and denotes power or a ray."

[He saw] those whose waves—meaning the surging ripples—are constantly rising and spreading upon the water; [and] elsewhere, those whose enemies—the Daityas and others—have repeatedly suffered defeat, meaning their state of excessive power (*balabhāva*) has been utterly shattered. The rest is clear.

Here, by means of the censure of the shallow lake and the fish residing within it—which are not the primary subject—there is intended to be conveyed the censure of the minor deities other than the Blessed Lord and their worshippers, who are the actual subjects at hand. In that regard, while lack of depth and shallowness serve as the causes for the impropriety of resorting to both the expressed and the implied [lake and deity], this is not the case for having many favorable fishermen, being exceedingly strong, and having waves frequently rising against the enemy.

Since the quality of being a generous giver of favorable things is not a defect when applied to the suggested sense of a minor deity, but rather a merit, identity with the expressed *kāśāra* (lake) is required in that respect. Furthermore, regarding the aspect of being repeatedly broken by the exceedingly powerful state of the enemy, there is identity with the suggested minor deity in the case of lakes; for the state of having waves produced by water caused by the power of the wind is not unfavorable to leaving the lake, but rather favorable to taking refuge in it.
O brother bee, why do you wander through the forests and resort to this *ketakī*, which follows the wind, is renowned for its beauty, and is full of thorns? 997.

Followed by wind-eating serpents and sages, she is resorted to [by those seeking worldly gain]; yet, compared to the supreme deity (paradevatā), she is renowned throughout the world as being of exceedingly meager majesty—meaning her wealth and prosperity are utterly deficient and inferior due to the splendor and abundance of flowers and sacrificial offerings (sūnā-prasūna-śrī). Here, it is implied that for any person to worship a minor deity other than the supreme deity is fruitless for you.

In this context, the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) presented as the reason for the impropriety of worshiping both the expressed object (the *ketakī* flower) and the implied object (the minor deity) is impossible [as a reason]. This is because being "famous for its beauty" (*sūnaśriyātivikhyātatvam*) is not a defect in the case of the *ketakī*; rather, it is a merit, since the abundance of blossoms is conducive to its being worshipped. Regarding that aspect [of the flower], identity with a minor deity must be presupposed; and regarding the minor deity, identity with the *ketakī* must be presupposed, because the fact of being resorted to by ascetics is not conducive to their abandoning [such a flower].
This is because it conforms to the worship of that [deity]. Thus, it should be understood that the meaning of the sentence is established by relying on mutual identity (*tādātmya*).

This third variety of Aprastutapraśaṃsā based on similarity has been presented here in accordance with the *Rasagaṅgādhara*. However, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other works, this Aprastutapraśaṃsā based on similarity is said to be threefold: in some cases, it occurs merely through the non-superimposition of the suggested meaning upon the expressed meaning; in some cases, through the superimposition of the suggested meaning; and in some cases, through both superimposition and non-superimposition according to different parts [of the meaning]. Thus, its threefold nature is described.
In that regard, there is no difference in the first two types, but in the third type, there is some difference. Here is an illustration of that.

First, she was sleepless in her own state; then she quickly attained the quality of patience (*kṣānti*); then she assumed a dark form (*kṛṣṇa-rūpa*) and became dense with juice in her fruit—how great is this fortune! 998.

That well-known grape is *mṛdvīkā*. First, at the beginning, in its own place—that is, in its own denotative word—it is *anidrā*, meaning that it does not have the phoneme *drā* absent from it; this is a compound with the negative particle *na*, as in "motionless like a lotus in a windless place" (*nivātapadmastimitena*). The meaning is that it is initially accompanied by the phoneme *drā*. The feminine gender, which resides in the object, is superimposed upon the word. That whose final [phoneme] is the phoneme *kṣā* (the letter *kṣa* with the vowel *ā*) is [the word]; this is used in the neuter gender for the sake of general reference.

The state of that [tree] is "possessing patience" (*kṣāntimatva*); according to the rule *anaci ca*, there is a doubling of the letter *t*. Thus, the meaning is that its latter half is joined with the syllable *kṣā*. Furthermore, in its fruit, it attains entirely the form of Kṛṣṇa—that is, the state of being black-colored—because it becomes such at the stage of the fruit's ripening. And it is "dense with sap," meaning thick with juice. In the alternative sense (the metaphorical interpretation), it stands upon its own ground (*svapade*), which refers to its own protection and its own resolve; for Amara states: "The word *pada* is used in the senses of resolve, protection, place, mark, foot, and object."

The sense is: [they were intent] on their own preservation and on the practice of the means for that purpose. "Sleepless" (anidrāḥ) means vigilant; therefore, they possess patience (*kṣāntimat*). Patience is the state of being patient (*titikṣutva*), according to the manner described in the passage, "He is calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, and patient. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for concentration (*samāhitatva*) and other qualities. By this, the completion of the practice of the means is stated. Now, regarding the fruit: in the state of fruition, having attained the form of Kṛṣṇa—that is, similarity of nature with the Lord—they have obtained the fruit corresponding to the practice of the means. This is the meaning.

It is dense with juice and thickened by the bliss of experiencing the fullness of Brahman. The sense is this: how great is its fortune—this fortune is beyond the reach of words. Here, in the case of the grape, the initial qualities of sleeplessness and patience are to be understood as the grounds for praise in their own right; they do not require the superimposition (adhyāropa) of a realized knower of Brahman upon those parts to serve as the cause of that praise.
As for the fruit, the attainment of the form of Kṛṣṇa and its density of rasa are themselves the grounds for praise; thus, there is no superimposition upon those parts.
O parrot, what indeed do you achieve by being slightly alarmed at the touch of the palmyra tree, which has fruit that is sweet upon first appearance yet pithless, difficult to grasp, and harsh? (999)

O parrot! [I am one] by whom fruits have been taken—fruits that are sweet at first sight but ultimately tasteless, moreover difficult to grasp and hard to obtain; and even when grasped, they are harsh and rigid, causing distress in the state of experience. This is because [the tree] is slightly agitated—that is, trembling—by the wind through mere touch, due to its rough leaves. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), it refers to one who is terrified even by a slight touch—that is, by giving away even a very small amount—meaning one who is excessively greedy.

The suffix *śānac* is derived from the root *vijī*, belonging to the Taudādika class, meaning "to tremble with fear. This root is generally preceded by the prefix *ut*. The sense is: "What indeed can you accomplish with a palm tree (*tāla*)? No purpose whatsoever of yours will be fulfilled by it. Here, the irrelevant (aprastuta) advice directed toward a parrot culminates in the case of a certain person who, out of disregard for the Blessed Lord, is intent on serving minor deities or greedy kings.

In that context, since the palm tree’s quality of yielding fruit that is sweet upon impact and so forth is itself the very cause for reproach, it is not necessary to superimpose the qualities of a greedy petty deity or a king upon that aspect of the tree as something being manifested. However, regarding the fact that it trembles at even a slight touch, such a superimposition is necessary; for while a mere movement caused by the wind or similar factors is not a cause for reproach, in this specific case, there is superimposition in one respect and its absence in another.
Just as you,

though pierced through and possessing holes, are foremost in stringing together the virtues of others, so too, O cluster of gems, because you possess a noble leader (or are devoted to Śrī Nāyaka), you alone are pleasing to those of beautiful vision (or to virtuous women).

O multitude of gems! Although you are irregular, though you are excessively round, though you have holes, and though you are hollow, you are called "the one who resorts to the Śrīnāyaka"—that is, he who resorts to the central gem of a necklace (śrīnāyaka), for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *nāyaka* refers to a leader, the best, a necklace, and also the central gem. When there is the weaving, the arrangement, and the stitching together of that supreme (*para*) quality—the sense being the thread or gold—you become the foremost (*agra*), the best (*śreṣṭha*), the moving (*sara*) necklace (*hāra*).

Therefore, for that very reason, you are dear to beautiful women, residing within their hearts; [this is derived from the word *hṛdaya* with the suffix *yat* in the sense of "being in," according to the rule *aśarīrāvayavācca*. Although you are spherical and possess a hollow interior, being strung upon an excellent thread and fashioned with a central gem, you have attained the state of a necklace and dwell within the hearts of deer-eyed women, and not otherwise—this is the intended meaning.

In this context, "ativṛtta" means one who has transgressed, that is, one of wicked conduct; for this very reason, he is also "sarandhra," meaning possessed of faults—according to the *Medinī* lexicon, "randhra" refers to both a defect and a hole. Because the illustrious Lord (*śrīnāyaka*), the Abode of Fortune (*śrīnivāsa*), honors such a person, the term signifies one who possesses devotion to Him.

You are the foremost—the first—among those who string together the auspicious qualities of that very Supreme Self, such as omniscience, the power of true resolve, amiability, and so forth; that is, you are the one who composes treatises concerning Him. Therefore, you are indeed dear to the hearts of the wise, for [the suffix] *yat* is used in the sense of "dear to the heart" (*hṛdayasya priyaḥ*).

Here, the entire meaning of the Gītā passage is summarized: by the first quarter-verse, the sense of "Even if he be of very evil conduct"; by the second and third quarters, the sense of "He who worships Me with undivided devotion"; and by the fourth quarter, the sense of "He is indeed to be regarded as virtuous, for he has rightly resolved."

In this case, the fact that the cluster of jewels has been worn out and possesses holes is not a defect; on the contrary, it is because their extreme roundness and the presence of these holes are conducive to being fashioned into a necklace. Therefore, regarding that aspect, one must rely upon the superimposition (adhyāropa) of a particular man. However, it should be understood that such superimposition does not apply to [the necklace's] possession of the status of a noble hero, its eagerness to grasp the virtues of others, or its being pleasing to the hearts of those with good vision.

Thus, the *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) has been defined in accordance with the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other such works. However, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, having defined *aprastutapraśaṃsā* as "that [figure] wherein the contextual (*prastuta*) activity is praised by means of a non-contextual (*aprastuta*) activity through any one of the types to be described, such as similarity (*sādṛśya*) and so forth," and having demonstrated its five varieties beginning with "the first is that in which the contextual is understood through its own likeness to the non-contextual," etc., [proceeds as follows].

Having elaborated upon its examples, [the author] concludes: "Thus, this *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) has been defined in five ways according to the tradition of the ancients. In reality, however, the first variety of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* admits of numerous forms. That variety is said to exist where the intended (*prastuta*) is understood through a denoted subject that is entirely unintended (*atyantāprastuta*). Likewise, there is another form where both narrative events are intended in a particular context."

As in the section on water-sports, when a bee, a lotus-pond, and others were present before them, and the hero was standing nearby, deeply enamored of his own heroine, a certain female friend of the heroine spoke these words:
"O bee, though it is dark, you have a face full of passion; though it speaks much, it is blooming; and though it is fickle, it is full of nectar—how is it that you do not abandon the lotus-pond?"

If it is asked: "In this verse, how can there be *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description)? For since the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is itself the subject at hand (*prastuta*), it does not fall under the definition of that figure," we say no. For by the term *aprastuta*, what is intended is a meaning other than that which constitutes the primary object of the speaker's intention (*mukhyatātparya*). And since that [other meaning] may be either entirely irrelevant to the context (*atyantāprastuta*) or relevant (*prastuta*), there is no fault whatsoever. Nor should it be argued that this would result in all instances of *dhvani* being reduced to *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.

Therefore, it should be understood that the qualification "in some manner such as similarity (*sādṛśya*) and so forth" has been included in the definition [of *samāsokti*]. By this, the claim made in the *Kuvalayānanda* and other works—that when two things are both contextual (*prastuta*), there is a distinct figure of speech named *prastutāṅkura*—is to be disregarded. For if one were to postulate a separate figure of speech based merely on a slight difference [from an existing one], there would follow the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of figures of speech, since the varieties of verbal expression are endless; this has been stated repeatedly.

This, however, must be understood: when that which is entirely irrelevant is the expressed meaning (*vācya*), the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*) is forcibly drawn in by the denotative function (*abhidhā*) because it does not terminate there; thus, its status as *dhvani* (suggestion) is beyond dispute. But when both [the relevant and the irrelevant] are relevant, its status as *dhvani* is even more indisputable. Thus, there are two varieties based on similarity. As for the four varieties based on the relation of cause and effect or general and particular, these are indeed subdivisions of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion), because they serve as the means for *dhvani* only insofar as they consist of mere insinuation (*āgūraṇa*) entirely devoid of even a trace of contact with denotation (*abhidhā*) and the other functions.
Now the birds have reached the sky on all sides, and the bees take refuge in the flowers of the mango trees;
the lake is shrinking, and alas, to what state indeed shall the wretched fish resort?

In this case, when the narrative concerning a king who has perished and the men who depend solely upon him is the subject at hand, it is indisputably *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). However, when both the narrative of the lake and the narrative of the king are the subjects at hand, then too, according to the direction previously stated, it is that same [figure]. But when the narrative of the lake alone is the subject at hand, then in this verse, where the narrative of the king constitutes a subordinate suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), [it is *dhvani*].

What is the ornament [employed here]? It is certainly not *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because it is the subject at hand itself that is being praised. Nor is it *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), because the equality of adjectives—which is the very life-breath of that figure and is accepted by all rhetoricians—is absent here. Furthermore, one should not claim that there is a variety of *samāsokti* based on pure similarity alone, just as there is a variety based on the equality of adjectives; for if they were considered a single ornament without being connected by a common attribute (*ekadharmālīḍhatva*), it would follow that all figures of speech would be one and the same. Moreover, those who establish the system have not stated that this constitutes a sub-variety of *samāsokti*.

If it is argued that for this very reason, authors such as the author of the *Alaṃkārasarvasva* have demonstrated that the basis of similarity lies in resorting to a different compound while strictly preserving the identity of the words expressing the qualifiers—and not by neglecting them—it is replied: the figure of speech here is indeed *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description). Its meaning is not "the praise of the non-contextual" (*aprastutasya praśaṃsā*), but rather "by means of the non-contextual" (*aprastutena*). And that [praise], by implication, belongs precisely to the contextual subject.

And thus, where the expressed or the suggested—whether non-contextual (aprastuta)—is praised by means of the contextual (prastuta) through one of the various modes such as similarity, that is "Aprastutapraśaṃsā" (Praise of the Non-contextual); therein too, it is indeed Aprastutapraśaṃsā. But it is not the case that the suggested alone [is praised] while the expressed is not. Thus he declared.

And thus, even in cases such as "purā yatra srotaḥ" (where formerly there was a stream), there is a praise of the contextual subject—the forest—characterized by the reversal of the density and sparseness of trees and the like; this is achieved through a non-contextual, expressed meaning, namely a village, city, or similar location inhabited by families where there has been a reversal of prosperity and adversity regarding wealth, lineage, and so forth. Therefore, his intention is that in such instances as well, it is indeed Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Non-contextual).

The author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, however, stated: "Regarding the fivefold division of types mentioned here—namely, those based on the relation of general and particular, cause and effect, and similarity—when both the general and the particular, or the cause and the effect, are expressed as the literal meaning (*vācya*), then there is the manifestation of *arthāntaranyāsa*. When two things based on similarity are expressed as the literal meaning, it is *dṛṣṭānta*. But when the non-contextual (*aprastuta*) is expressed as the literal meaning and the contextual (*prastuta*) is understood by implication, in every such case, the conclusion is that it is *aprastutapraśaṃsā*."

In this view, however, in examples such as "Where formerly there was a stream," since that which is under discussion (the *prastuta*) alone is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and that which is not under discussion (*aprastuta*) is the implied meaning (*gamya*), it is indeed *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation). Enough with this prolixity.

Furthermore, having stated, "This [figure] is also seen by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*)," he cited the example: "Blessed indeed are the winds in the forest. In accordance with that, here is the following example: "Blessed are those who, being devoted to none other than the lords of the mountain where serpents dwell, even the trees on earth worship them with their own flowers—blessed indeed! (1001)

In this context, from the irrelevant statement "They are venerable; they are fortunate," and so forth, it is understood through contrast (*vaidharmya*) that even those sentient beings who possess human birth are unworthy of honor and unfortunate if they do not worship Śrīnivāsa. However, Mammaṭa and others maintain that in the verse "Fortunate indeed are the winds in the forest," since one's own censure is perceived through the praise of the winds, *vyājastuti* (disguised praise) alone is appropriate. It should be noted that, according to that view, this verse cited by us would also deserve to be an example of *vyājastuti*.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Indirect Praise (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Sprout of the Contextual (*prastutāṅkura*):
when the contextual is suggested by means of the contextual, that is the *prastutāṅkura*.

Where another intended subject (*prastuta*) is illuminated by the description of the present subject (*varṇyamāna*), there is the figure of speech named *Prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the present). Thus, it is established that the description of the present subject which manifests another principal present subject is the *Prastutāṅkura* figure. Because the present subject acts as the manifester, it is called "a sprout" (*aṅkura*) based on the etymology "like a sprout"; therefore, this name is literal (*anvartha*).
O mountain slope, at this moment, having embraced this cloud adorned with peacock feathers, you perceive nothing; yet how long will this exceedingly fickle one remain even upon you? (1002)

In this context, during the occasion of wandering in the forest in the rainy season, a certain gopī who had been previously deceived by him speaks thus, addressing a mountain slope; for she has disregarded other women due to her overwhelming passion for the bliss of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s embrace—this constitutes the relevance of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that because addressing one who should not be addressed makes the expressed meaning impossible, the expressed meaning here must be something entirely irrelevant, mentioned merely to illuminate a relevant similar object; for in instances such as, "O Karṇikāra tree, you have seen her; we, O bee, are ruined by our search for the truth; you indeed are successful," we observe even the addressing of one who should not be addressed due to mental distraction and the like, making it difficult to claim that such an act is utterly impossible.

Thus, by means of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*)—which consists of a reproach regarding the work on the mountain slope—the very context of the speaker’s reproach toward her is illuminated: "Why do you, out of a sense of self-importance, embrace this extremely fickle son of Nanda and disregard other women, or for how long will he remain devoted even to you? In this case, within the implied meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*), the word *ghana* (dense) conveys the sense of "shallow" through the figure of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (contrary indication).

Regarding the phrase *udbarhibarham*: in the literal sense (*vācyārtha*), it means "one by whom the peacock feathers have been raised up" or "unfurled"; in the suggested sense (*pratīyamāna*), it means "one who has donned a crest of peacock plumes. The statement "you know nothing at all" is metaphorical (*aupacārika*) in the literal sense of the mountain slope due to its being covered by thick clouds; however, in the suggested sense of the heroine, the intention is that she knows nothing because of her overwhelming state of bliss (*ānanda-pāravaśya*). In the literal sense, "excessive and flickering lightning" refers to the lightning itself; in the suggested sense, however, it means "one whose nature is exceedingly fickle."

Just as the multitude of trees, by taking refuge at your feet, attain a high position of great prosperity, so too does Fortune attend you with her followers; O Lord of the Ahirāja mountain, who else is greater than you?

O Ahiśaila! Your foothills are the peripheral mountains; you are that upon which they rest—both as your feet and as your refuge. You are the lofty abode and birthplace of the flocks of birds (*vīnām*) and of the groups of Brahmins who study the branches (*śākhā*) of the trees (*śākhinām*), for they have built their nests there. Furthermore, you are the seat of exalted prosperity, your plateaus (*sānūni*) having attained the splendor (*śrī*) of mountain ridges (*prasthān*).

Elsewhere, that Śrī, renowned as the Mother of the World and so forth, follows [you], being devoted to you in the manner described by the saying, "She followed you like a shadow. Who else could be greater—that is, more vast—than you who are such? In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the meaning is: who else is more venerable than the Lord of Śrī, the possessor of great majesty? Here, through the narrative of the serpent-mountain (the present subject), the very narrative of Śrīnivāsa (the intended subject) is illuminated.

Both the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) meanings are equally relevant as they are both intended to be cultivated. Nor should one suspect a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the relevant and the irrelevant here, for such a figure is manifested only when the substantive (*viśeṣya*) itself is paronomastic; and in this case, the substantive is not paronomastic.

"Look, friend! Just as he longs to touch the cloud-covered mountain of Indra, so too does he desire to remove it"—hearing these words from her husband during the rainy season, Śrī lowered her face. 1004.

The wind is "that which touches" (*sparśanaḥ*), and it is also understood as "the agent of touching. Here, through the contextual narrative of the rain-wind acting as the agent that removes the clouds—which is the occasion for longing—the very contextual narrative of the Lord sporting with the Goddess during the rainy season, characterized by His longing to remove the bodice from His beloved’s breasts, is made known. The fact that the expressed meaning is contextual is clear from the statement, "O friend, look at the rainy season! Furthermore, the revelation of another contextual matter is disclosed by the poet himself in the second half of the verse through the phrase, "with her face bowed upon hearing her husband's words."

"O cloud, you mock the stability of the earth by embracing the flickering lightning; yet, from the perspective of the clouds, the earth appears far away and unstable"—speaking thus, she was fully embraced by Śauri.

O cloud! Embraced by the flickering lightning, you bear a dense creeper of capriciousness—the rainbow-creeper. The implication is that the stable earth is far from you, because of your abiding in the sky. In the alternative sense (of the metaphor), you are embraced by Śrī (Fortune), who is *capalā*—meaning fickle-natured; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *capalā* refers to Kamalā (Lakṣmī), lightning, a wanton woman, and long pepper. Therefore, you are one whose fickleness (*cāpalya*) is intense (*ghana*).

The meaning is that the Earth-goddess—yourself, being of such a nature as this—is of a firm and unswerving character, yet you have cast her far away into the category of those to be neglected. The implication is: how could steadfast affection possibly exist in one like you, who are fickle and embraced by instability?

Here, by means of the speech addressed to the rain-cloud (*ghanāghana*) during the monsoon—which, while being introduced, establishes the height of Lakṣmī’s affection for you alone—it is illuminated that you have neglected me; thus, the very subject at hand, Śrīnivāsa, is the object of this contextual lamentation. In this verse, the fact that the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is the contextual subject is made perfectly clear by the vocative address "O Cloud. Furthermore, the illumination of another contextual subject is made explicit by the poet himself in the second half of the verse.
"Just as a peahen, even when her beloved is right beside her, sees only the fresh rain-cloud,"— when this was said during the rainy season in the forest, a cowherd girl cast her gaze away from Kṛṣṇa.

When this was spoken by someone—this is the ellipsis—the cowherd woman (gopī), the wife of a cowherd, withdrew her own gaze from Kṛṣṇa. [The form *avāñcicat* is derived from the root *añc* preceded by *ava*, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the *luṅ* tense, third person singular. Here, on the occasion of the cowherds' forest excursion during the rainy season, by means of a statement made by someone regarding a peahen—which pertains to the subject at hand—the very situation of a cowherd lady who, disregarding even her own beloved, gazes with passion only upon the Son of Nanda (Kṛṣṇa) is illuminated as the actual matter under discussion.

The expression "in the forest ground during the rainy season" makes it understood that the literal meaning (vācyārtha) is the subject at hand. Furthermore, the revelation of another related subject—namely, [the eyes] casting a downward glance toward Kṛṣṇa—is explicitly disclosed by the poet himself. In this case, compared to the two previous examples, the disclosure by the poet of the suggested meaning is even more evident.

In this regard, according to the view of Locanākāra, there is *anyāpadeśa-dhvani* (suggestion through the mention of another) in the first two examples. For he states that there is *anyāpadeśa-dhvani* in the two examples of *prastutāṅkura* (the suggestion of a relevant matter), namely: "O bee, while the *mālatī* is present, why [linger] on the thorny *ketakī*? O bee, divert your wandering mind toward other flower-vines which can endure being trampled. Why do you pointlessly torment the young, pollen-less bud of the new *navamālikā* out of season? Thus he asserts the presence of *anyāpadeśa-dhvani* in these two examples of *prastutāṅkura*.

For instance: "In *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), since the expressed meaning is irrelevant, it is not to be described; thus, when the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) has not reached its conclusion there, the manifestation of the relevant meaning through that [expressed meaning] is a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). But here, because the expressed meaning is relevant, once the denotative function has reached its conclusion therein, the manifestation of the intended meaning by the power of the beauty of the sense is nothing other than *dhvani* (suggestion)."

The point is this: in *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is not fit for description and thus lies outside the scope of the poet’s creative effort (*kavisaṃrambha*), the limit of that effort is restricted solely to the contextual matter (*prastutavṛttānta*). Since the finality of the intended purpose (*tātparyaparyavasāna*) rests upon the comprehension of that suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) alone, the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) does not reach its conclusion; therefore, there can be no occurrence of *dhvani*. Although the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* might otherwise be possible in such cases, it is not possible in the two examples shown here.

Since the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) is the primary subject at hand, the poet’s creative effort (kavisaṃrambha) rests therein; thus, the function of denotation (abhidhā) terminates at that very point. Consequently, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha), having gained its scope through the power of the beauty of the subject matter, manifests by transcending the level of the expressed. Therefore, in this case, it is appropriate to regard it as *anyāpadeśa-dhvani* (suggestion where the literal sense serves as a pretext).

"In reality, however, this is merely an *alaṃkāra* (ornament) and not *dhvani* (suggestion)," so it has been established in the *Citramīmāṃsā*; thus say the Dīkṣitas in the *Kuvalayānanda*. This is the intended meaning: in *samāsokti* (condensed expression), since the described event (*vṛttānta*) is the subject at hand (*prastuta*), the primary denotation (*abhidhā*) terminates there; yet, although the unmentioned event is understood through the power of the similarity of adjectives, because it brings beauty to the expressed meaning by means of the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) that is at hand, it does not constitute *dhvani*. Or, as in: [text follows]

In the figure *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), that which is suggested—being perceived through a relationship such as the general-particular relation—is not included within *dhvani*, because it serves merely as an embellishment (*upaskāraka*) for the expressed subject matter. Likewise here, although the expressed object is the reproach of the bee, and the denotative function (*abhidhā*) has reached its conclusion, the reproach of the beloved—which is suggested through similarity—is nonetheless the very focus of the poet’s creative intent (*kavisaṃrambha*). Since both are equal in this regard and possess primacy, it is appropriate that this be classified as *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion) characterized by "equal prominence" (*samaprādhānya*).

Furthermore, the established doctrine is that *dhvani* occurs only when there is a desire to emphasize the prominence of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) over the expressed meaning (*vācya*). Now, in this case, the suggested meaning does not possess such prominence; for if it did, it would follow that it was unintended (*avivakṣitatva*), which would render it impossible to include it within the category of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*). Therefore, since the *dhvani* of "indirect reference" (*anyāpadeśa*) is inappropriate in the two examples cited, the "germ of the relevant matter" (*prastutāṅkura*) alone is suitable.
As for the third, fourth, and fifth examples, however, no one disputes their status as figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*). For it has been said by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*: [text follows]
Even when a suggested meaning is implied by the power of the word and its sense, if it is further developed by the poet through his own statement,
that is another distinct figure of speech belonging to Dhvani.

Thus, these are examples based on similarity (*sādṛśya*). Examples based on other types of relations (*saṃbandha*) may also be cited by somehow relying on the fact that the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) are both relevant to the context; of those, a mere indication is given here:
"O Blessed One, that poet of noble intellect who praises you with even a single mouth shall be honored by the gods as if he had four, five, or six mouths. (1007)

In this context, just as Brahma-hood, Śiva-hood, and Skanda-hood [are the subjects], the four, five, and six-faced forms—which are the expressed meanings of the cited sentences—are also to be described as being subordinate to them by virtue of their being the glory of the praise of the venerable Śrīnivāsa; thus, through that medium, the entirety of Brahma-hood, Śiva-hood, and Skanda-hood is understood. Therefore, this is the "Emergence of the Subject" (prastutāṅkura) based on the relationship between part and whole.

Or rather, those pearls, resembling bubbles arisen from the midst of the nectar-ocean of the beauty of the Blessed One’s face, shone as they were attached to his forehead ornament (*lalāṭikā*). [1008] The analysis of the compound is *budbudanibhāḥ* (resembling bubbles) and *yāḥ* (which). A forehead ornament is called *lalāṭikā*; according to the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* ("located there"), the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *karṇalalāṭātkanalaṃkāre* ("after *karṇa* and *lalāṭa*, the suffix *kan* is used when referring to an ornament").

Here, because the pearl-ornaments on the forehead of the Blessed One—which are introduced as the subject of description—are conceived as bubbles upon the ocean of the nectar of the beauty of His face, the boundless abundance of that facial beauty, which serves as their cause, is perceived. That [beauty] too is indeed introduced as the subject of description. In this case, the relationship between the abundance of facial beauty and the pearls conceived as its bubbles is either one of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) or one of material cause and effect (*prakṛtivikṛtibhāva*).
Or rather: Surely the overflowing tide of the ocean of the beauty of Śrī’s body has drunk the sky, flowing excessively on all sides around the island of the divine form of Hari.

Here, by means of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that Pītāmbara—who is introduced as the subject of description—is an overflowing surge from the ocean of the beauty of Lakṣmī’s divine form, there is illuminated the abundance of that beauty which cannot be contained within his divine body, serving as the cause for the overflow of that lake which is heavy with its full waters. In this case as well, the relationship between the abundance of beauty and Pītāmbara—who has attained identity with that overflow—is precisely one of part and whole (*ekadeśya-ekadeśa-bhāva*).

Just as in my own *Prapannānanda-stava*, I surely meditate upon the pearl [of the goddess's breath] which has been spat out by the great king of fish that are her eyes, as they sport in the lake of the luster of her face, and which now rests lodged within the cavity of her nostrils. (1010)

Here, the abundance of beauty and other qualities appropriate to the divine eye—which has attained identity with the fish as a means of producing the pearl of the nose (the subject under description)—is suggested. That [abundance] is also indeed the subject under description. Here, the relation is that of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*). Likewise, the limitless abundance of the splendor of the face—which has been made identical to a lake as a means for the sporting of the great king of fish that is the eye—is illuminated. That too is indeed the subject under description.
Here, the relation is that of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).

O Moon-like Lion among Men, just as the intellect of your devotees is all-consuming, their fame likewise washes away the very shores of the quarters, and the rows of their houses scrape the clouds. 1011.

Here, in order to manifest the supramundane nature of the Blessed One, his great magnanimity—as well as his deeds and the excellence of his devotees, their learning, and so forth—is intended to be described; thus, his great magnanimity is understood by means of these [qualities]. This is therefore the *prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the subject at hand), based on the relationship of cause and effect.
Where the cognition of the cause is also expressed by means of the effect within a verse, that is not this ornament; rather, it is simply inference (anumāna).
Just as necklaces [adorn] the necks of men, so do wives with most beautiful faces [adorn] their sides; likewise, delicate youths speak of such magnificent sights as Lakṣmī herself.

The word *mahodārāḥ* (most noble) is an adjective qualifying *lakṣmīdṛśām* (of those possessing the beauty of Lakṣmī), which is in the accusative case. This [word] is the object (*karman*), while *hārāḥ* (necklaces) and so forth are the agents (*kartṛ*). Here, by means of the effect—the abundance of pearl necklaces and the like—the cause, namely "those possessing the beauty of Lakṣmī," is understood; this is expressed through the figure of speech called *anumāna* (inference), wherein the literal meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*). This particular ornament is the invention of Dīkṣita.

All earlier authorities, however, subsumed it within *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) based on similarity alone; thus, we have previously stated that it is included within *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.
Thus ends the thirty-first lake, "The Sprout of the Subject at Hand," in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the lake of "Indirect Expression" (*paryāyokta*):
"Indirect expression occurs when that which is intended to be said is expressed by means of another figure."

The meaning is that "another mode" (*bhaṅgyantara*) refers to a different manner of expression (*anyabhāṅgī*) other than the specific form in which the intended object is expressed. It is stated in the *Rasagaṅgādhara*: "Paryāyokta is the presentation of an intended object by means of another mode. Its significance is this: when an object that is obtainable through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) in a certain form is presented through denotation (*abhidhā*) in a form even more beautiful than that, it is *paryāyokta*.

Nor should it be argued that this [beauty] belongs exclusively to the sound (dhvani), for in that case there would be a distinction between the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya). Thus, the conclusion is reached that *paryāyokta* occurs when a suggested object is expressed by a word through another form that is even more beautiful than the form of its being suggested; therefore, since the suggested form lacks beauty relative to the expressed form, it does not fall within the domain of *dhvani*. This is the general direction. The distinction is that in *paryāyokta*, the expressed is primary, whereas in *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, it is the suggested that is primary.

This is a name whose meaning corresponds to its etymology (*anvarthanāmadheya*), based on the derivation: "that in which the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is stated by way of synonym (*paryāyeṇa*) or through a different mode of expression (*bhaṅgyantareṇa*)."
May that man who composed the commentary on the Sūtra of Pārāśarya (Vyāsa) and also of Pāṇini—whose dwelling was such that it could not be taken away—delight my mind. 1013.
Now begins the ocean of Paryāyokta (Indirect Expression):
Paryāyokta occurs when that which is intended to be expressed is stated by means of another mode of expression.

The meaning is that "another mode" (*bhaṅgyantaram*) refers to a different manner of expression than the specific form in which the intended object was meant to be conveyed. In the *Rasagaṅgādhara* as well, it is stated: "Paryāyokta is the presentation of an intended object by means of another mode. Its significance is this: when an object obtainable through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) in one form is presented by denotation (*abhidhā*) in a form even more beautiful than that, it is *paryāyokta*.

Nor should it be argued that this [beauty] belongs exclusively to the sound (dhvani), because in that case there would be a distinction between the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya). Thus, the conclusion is reached that *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) occurs when a suggested object is denoted by a word through another form that is even more beautiful than the form of its being suggested; therefore, since the suggested form lacks beauty in comparison to the expressed form, it does not fall within the domain of *dhvani*. This is the general direction. The distinction is that in *paryāyokta*, the expressed is primary, whereas in *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), it is the implied that is primary.

This is a name whose meaning corresponds to its etymology (*anvarthanāmadheya*), based on the analysis: "that in which the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is stated by way of synonym (*paryāyeṇa*) or through a different mode of expression (*bhaṅgyantareṇa*)."
May that man who composed the commentary on the Sūtra of Pārāśarya and also of Pāṇini—which, like their monasteries, is not to be taken away—delight my mind. 1013.

Pārāśarya is Vedavyāsa. According to traditional scripture (āgama), the venerable Rāmānujācārya, the commentator on his [Vedavyāsa’s] Sūtras, and the venerable Patañjali, the commentator on Pāṇini’s Sūtras, are both incarnations of Śeṣa. Here, the status of Śeṣa belonging to the mountain where Śrīnivāsa sports is suggested; that very point is stated by way of a different turn of expression. The state of being suggested occurs through the mode of being Śeṣa.

It should be understood that the expressed meaning (*vācya*)—namely, that the mountain is the place of the Lord’s pastimes by virtue of being the site where the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtras* of Pāṇini and the son of Parāśara [Patañjali] resided—is more beautiful than the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). Nor should it be argued that it is contradictory for the suggested meaning itself to be the denoted object; for we do not claim that it is denoted in the same manner as it is suggested—that is, in its aspect as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*). Rather, we maintain that it is denoted in the form of being the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtras* of Pāṇini and the son of Parāśara; thus, there is no contradiction.
May that Supreme Person remove the inauspiciousness of the world— He by whom both he who eats the wind (the yogi) and he who eats him (the eater of the yogi) alike become his bed and his vehicle.

Furthermore, the phrase "and he who eats him" is stated with the intention of referring to one who eats snakes of that same species. Here, the Lord’s bed and vehicle are designated in a form even more beautiful than the suggested forms of being the infinite [ocean] and Garuḍa, by means of the expressions "he who eats the wind" and so forth. Alternatively, the Lord—who is to be understood through his own unique nature—is expressed in this very way through another form, such as being the eater of the wind and the like.
Or rather,
he by whom even the three castes are purified while studying the positions of the vehicle, the banner, and the right eye— this one is my protector.

In this context, the fact that the Lord’s vehicle and banner possess the form of Vainateya (Garuḍa), and that the abodes of His right eye possess the form of the Sun, is suggested; yet, because these are perceived through a form even more beautiful than that, they are described by way of another artifice as being of the nature of the Vedas. Furthermore, the quality of "being studied" attributed to the four—the vehicle and so forth—is figurative, based on their consisting of the three Vedas (*trayī*), according to such scriptural statements as, "He is the fair-winged Garuḍa," and "This very triple knowledge shines."

Alternatively, it should be understood that even here, the Blessed One alone is the object of comprehension in his own unique form; he is simply designated by way of another figurative expression, such as having the three Vedas as his vehicle and so forth.
May that hero protect you— he who, having removed the agitation caused by the embrace of a thousand arms, became for the wives of Bali’s sons a source of auspicious hope and instruction.

Here, Lord Vāsudeva is suggested by virtue of being the one who severed the multitude of arms of the demon Bāṇāsura; yet he is expressed through another poetic turn—one even more beautiful than that—by way of being the object of the auspicious benedictions bestowed by the demon's wife, who was delighted by his great service in the form of relieving her from the pressure of the embrace of a thousand arms.
May that weapon, by which he was deprived of his prowess and which removed the fatigue of Kārtavīrya as he bore the burden of his many hundreds of arms, be victorious in the world! (1017)

In this instance, the intended meaning—the Lord’s act of severing the thousand arms of Kārtavīryārjuna—is not expressed directly as such; rather, it is conveyed through the form of removing the exhaustion caused by bearing the weight of those arms. Alternatively, the Blessed Lord Daśarathi, who is accessible through His own unique nature, is expressed by way of a different turn of phrase as one who removes the fatigue from the burden of Kārtavīrya’s arms and who seizes away the splendor of his axe-wielder.

Nor should it be argued that *paryāyokta* ought to be defined by taking as its basis only the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) consisting of "the state of being the conqueror of the wielder of the axe who cut off the arms of Kārtavīrya," and not by taking as its basis the state of being the son of Daśaratha (Dāśarathi-hood) which is obtained through the power of the epithets; for the aforementioned suggested meaning—consisting of the state of being the conqueror of the wielder of the axe—is merely a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for establishing the expressed meaning. Therefore, since the intended suggested meaning, namely Dāśarathi-hood, is the primary element (*pradhāna*), it is proper to describe the figure by taking that very [primary] meaning as its basis.

At the end of this very verse, if one removes the word *jagati* from the phrase *sa vijayatāṃ jagati* and reads it instead as *rāma*, then in the expression *namaḥ rāhustrīkucanaiṣphalyakāriṇe haraye* (Salutation to Hari, who renders the breasts of Rāhu’s wife fruitless), the intended suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—just as [in the previous case] the cutting off of Rāhu’s head—is precisely his victory over Kārtavīrya by wielding the axe that severed his arms. It should be understood that it is by taking up this very [suggested sense] that the figure is appropriately termed *paryāyokta*.

For this very reason, the statement in the *Kuvalayānanda*—"In the verse, 'Salutations to him by whom the breasts of Rāhu’s wife were rendered useless,' the Lord Vāsudeva is suggested in his own unique form, while being expressed in another form as the cause of the uselessness of Rāhu’s wife's breasts"—is consistent [with our view]. As for the claim that "the cognition of him in the form of the Lord is unsuitable as the subject matter of *paryāyokta* because it is obtainable through the force of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa-maryādā-labhya-tvena*)," that is charming only when left unexamined.

For in *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), there is no specific excellence of charm (*vicchitti*) produced by the beauty of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), by which its lack of beauty might be established; rather, [the charm] arises solely from the expression through a different turn of phrase (*bhaṅgyantara*). Indeed, the suggested meaning is generally seen to be less beautiful precisely because of that expression through a different turn of phrase—as, for example, when "one should come here" is intended as the suggested sense, yet it is expressed as "this place should be adorned" or "it should be made fruitful," and so forth. Therefore, the objection regarding its lack of beauty is entirely irrelevant; enough of this prolixity.
The same should be understood regarding the examples previously shown, such as "he who eats the wind."
May that wondrous splendor of His, whose single eye dwelling in heaven illuminates the entire world by day, while His other [eye] does so incessantly by night, grant me well-being. (1018)

In this instance, the Lord’s state of having the sun and moon as His eyes is understood, yet it is expressed in a more beautiful manner through a different approach: "May He protect us—He by whom even he who devours those two during the lunar phases, though his head has been severed, is himself protected; and may He protect us—He by whom that place where the gods roam day and night is beautified by those two. (1019)

The sense is: "in which [space]," meaning in the sky (*vyoman*). The gods (*tridaśāḥ*) move there, because they are sky-dwellers; and that sky as well. "Day and night" (*divāniśam*); the accusative case is used here to denote continuous connection. The sense is: "those two," namely the Sun and the Moon. They "adorn" it, meaning they embellish it respectively. And those two, the Sun and the Moon, whom Rāhu—this is the sense—swallows during the lunar nodes (*parvasu*). May that Blessed One, by whom even he was deprived of his head, protect us. Here, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and so forth are suggested (*vyaṅgya*), though expressed through a different form. And this is intermingled with the *ekāvalī* (single-string) ornament to be described later.
May that couple sport for us— the woman who holds a lotus in her hand to signify its name in reverse order, and the man who holds it in his heart within his own heart.

The purpose of this statement is to express the opposite; it signifies "possessing a mind that is contrary" (saramatām), which is to say, having a mind characterized by the name "Tāmarasa" (the lotus) in reverse order. Here, the suggested meanings (vyaṅgya)—namely, her being Lakṣmī and his being Nārāyaṇa—are expressed through an indirect manner.
May that deity protect me— she whose form they describe as being like the splendor of water-laden clouds, yet whose very nature is the opposite of what that description implies.

May that Goddess protect me—She whose splendor the Vedas and other scriptures describe as "dark as a rain-cloud" (*jaladasarasām*, meaning dark like a water-bearing cloud). Her form (*rūpam*)—where *rūpa* refers to inherent nature or color, according to the *Ratnamālā* lexicon—is expressed by the term "viparītatadabhidheyam," which means it is denoted by the phrase "Sārasadalajaṃ" (born from lotus petals) used in reverse order; that is to say, it is produced from lotus petals or equal to them, in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "She who has the color of a lotus" (*padmavarṇām*).

For this very reason, it is an instance of *padārthavṛttinidarśanā* (illustration based on the function of word-meanings). May that Goddess protect me. Here, the Lord Śrīnivāsa and the Goddess Śrī are suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and expressed through a different mode (*bhaṅgyantareṇa*) as the beautiful luster of a rain-cloud and the form of a lotus petal, respectively.

May He who created the elements protect [us]— He from whom the first element arose, and immediately after that the second from His feet, the third from His mouth, the fourth from His breath, and the fifth from His navel.

Here, earth, water, fire, air, and ether are stated as the manifested [elements] by way of another method. Here, the Gaṅgā is intended to be spoken of as the second element. In this regard, the following authorities should be considered: "From his feet came the earth; from Viṣṇu’s feet the Gaṅgā was born; from his mouth Indra and Agni; from his breath the wind was born; from his navel the intermediate space arose. And this is a conflation of the *ratnāvalī* and *kāvyaliṅga* figures of speech to be discussed hereafter.
Or rather, let that god play at dice as he pleases—he to whom the ocean gave both his ornament and his wife; for that very ocean became the girdle or even the garment of his beloved.

This refers to the aforementioned ocean. It became, by its very nature, the girdle (*sārasana*) or the garment (*vasana*)—meaning a silken cloth (*aṃśuka*)—of that very deity’s beloved, his consort; for the *Śruti* states: "The goddess Earth, the wife of Viṣṇu, the daughter of Mādhava, the beloved of Mādhava. The sense is that this is well-known in both ways, as in: "The supporter of beings, girt by the ocean," and "Like the ocean-clad earth, whose womb contains treasures."

In this instance, the state of being adorned with the Kaustubha gem, the status of being the Lord of Śrī, and the status of being the beloved of the earth are suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*). This is a case of commingling (*saṃkīrṇa*) with figures such as *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing).

In this ornament (*alaṃkāra*), the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is subordinate to the expressed meaning (*vācyapara*), whereas in *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), the expressed meaning is subordinate to the suggested meaning. Therefore, the followers of the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* maintain that this ornament is a variety of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion) where the suggestion serves as a factor for the establishment of the expressed meaning. Jagannātha and others, however, state that this ornament is threefold: in some cases, when the effect is understood through the expressed cause; in some cases, when the cause is understood through the effect; and in some cases, when there is a mutual indifference between the two, involving merely a relationship between related entities.
In that context, regarding the inference of an effect from a cause as the expressed meaning, it is as follows:
"O friend of Ramā, those who offer peerless flowers at your feet sow seeds of auspiciousness at their own feet according to their will."

"In *tvadīye* means in your feet, or in the feet of your devotees (*bhāgavatas*). In *svapade* means in one's own place, or in one's own established purpose, or in one's own reality. Here, by the cause of sowing the seed, the effect in the form of prosperity is understood."
When the cause is inferred from its effect, as for example:
"O Lotus-eyed One, whatever worlds your devotee desires, those very worlds arise for him instantly through mere volition, O Lord. (1025)

These worlds; here, the meaning of the scriptural passage, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition (saṃkalpa) the fathers arise for him," has been considered. Here, from the effect—namely, the creation of worlds at will by the devotees of the Lord—the liberation-sovereignty (muktaiśvarya) described in such passages as "He becomes his own ruler" (sa svarāḍ bhavati) is understood as its cause.
Wandering through the forest regions, he who simultaneously caused the thousand-eyed Indra and the thousand-rayed sun to shed tears of both grief and joy— he is this man worthy of service.

Here, by means of the expressed effects—the weeping and the beautiful form of Sutrāman (Indra) and Aryaman respectively—the causes consisting of the daughter’s misfortune and the daughter’s prosperity are understood. This differs from the previous example in that it is a mixture with the figure of *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence), which will be discussed hereafter.
When there is a cognition of one relative by means of another relative who is indifferent to both of them.
May he, whose left and right eyes cause the clusters of blue and great blue lotuses to bloom—being cool and yet not cold—quell this fever and this dullness. 1027.

May this very one pacify the fever—the internal heat and the like—and the dullness, which is coldness and ignorance. Here, by means of the expressed qualities of the cool and extremely cool left and right eyes that cause the blooming of the blue and great blue lotuses, neither the effect nor the cause is conveyed; rather, it is solely through their accompaniment that the state of having the moon and sun as eyes is understood.
