For here, the relationship between the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) is merely one of coexistence, not one consisting of the nature of cause and effect; likewise, in the previously shown examples such as "He whose pleasure is to be carried away," the relationship should be understood accordingly. This [figure] is a combination of *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence) and *parikara* (accessory). Some, however, call this *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) when a present effect makes a present cause cognizable.

These [figures] do not admit of being separate ornaments from *prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the contextual). However, Dīkṣita and others maintain that in such cases it is indeed *prastutāṅkura* alone; this is clear from the *Kuvalayānanda* and other works.
If one's own desired object, or that of another, is accomplished by means of a charming pretext,
the wise know that as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).

Based on the etymological derivation "that in which something is stated by way of a synonym (paryāya) or under a pretext (vyāja)," this too is called *paryāyokta* (periphrasis). Furthermore, this particular variety is the discovery of Dīkṣita himself. It should be understood that the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is "the state of being either one of those two varieties."
Among these, the first is as follows:
"The cloud thunders, lightning flashes; avoid going outside, O timid one! May Śauri be victorious, who, while thus suddenly warding off his clever [lover], embraced the Goddess of Fortune. (1028)

In this passage, under the guise of displaying fears such as the thundering of clouds, the Blessed One has composed a means for achieving his own desired end, which takes the form of an embrace with Lakṣmī.

"Or as [in the verse]: 'The curls have been disheveled by the wind, the tilaka mark has been blurred; I shall restore them. May Hari, who kisses the face of Śrī with a joyful heart, thinking 'this is that very [tilaka],' be victorious! (1029). Here, under the pretext of straightening the disheveled curls and so forth, the very accomplishment of his own desire—namely, the kissing of the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Ocean by the one clad in yellow garments—is revealed.
The second example is as follows:
Out of a desire to gather flowers, Lakṣmī enters a rugged grove; her friend, the moon-bearing mountain (Himavat), says to her, "Go with me, for I am weary. (1030)

In the word *apacāya*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied according to the rule *hastādāne cerasteye* (Pāṇini 3.3.40). There is also a form of the word *mahi* ending in a short vowel, based on the instruction of Vācaspati: *vīciḥ paṅkirmahiḥ kelir ityādyā hrasvadīrghayoḥ*. Here, under the pretext of urging Lakṣmī—who had entered the bower-thicket while distracted by gathering flowers—to provide assistance, the Lord’s desire for her enjoyment was accomplished by a female friend who stood apart under the pretext of being fatigued; thus, the accomplishment of another's desired object (*pareṣṭasādhana*) is depicted.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the Chapter on Paryāyokta (Indirect Expression), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Vyājastuti (Praise by Disguise):
"If censure is manifested through praise, or praise through censure..."
In that regard, the wise call the figure of speech named "Praise in Disguise" (vyājastuti) an ornament.

Where praise, even when being expressed, has its nature sublated by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and results in censure, there is one form of "Praise in Disguise" (*vyājastuti*), following the principle that it is praise in the form of a pretense because of its unreality. Where, likewise, censure being conveyed by words has its form sublated as before and results in praise, that is the second form of "Praise in Disguise.
Now, the ocean of "Praise in Disguise":
"If censure is manifested through praise, or if praise [is manifested] through censure."
In that regard, the wise have declared the ornament named "feigned praise" (vyājastuti).

Where praise, even when being expressed, has its nature sublated by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and results in censure, there is one type of *vyājastuti* (disguised praise), following the understanding that it is "praise in the form of a disguise" because of its unreality. Where, moreover, censure being conveyed through words has its form sublated as before and results in praise, that is the second type of *vyājastuti*. [The term is so called] because of "praise by way of a disguise," namely, by means of censure.

Thus, it should be understood that both types constitute the literal meaning (*śabdārtha*) through two etymological derivations (*yogārtha*), namely, the *karmadhāraya* and the *tṛtīyā-tatpuruṣa* compounds respectively.
First, an example:
"O fortunate one, you dwell at home, skillfully providing for the pleasure of your children and wife; you never undergo the ruinous toil of serving the Lord of the Serpents or the Mountain. (1031)

In this context, the praise "you are blessed," which is merely a deceptive form directed at some worldly person, being contradicted by reality, results in an implied censure regarding that person's lack of service to Śrīnivāsa.
The second [type] is as follows:

"O Lord of Ramā! Who else besides you would feel such loathing? Who else besides me would be so shameless? Who else could constantly endure sin? And who else, even when constantly patient, could act in that manner? (1032)

In that case, even though the offense has been repeatedly forgiven, the word "offense" (agham) is persistently attached again and again. Who would commit such an offense (agham = aparādham)? Therefore, the sense is: "I am shameless, while you are full of self-reproach. Here, the censure expressed by "who is full of self-reproach? being sublated, results ultimately in praise: that the abundance of forgiveness belonging to the Friend of Ramā is peerless.

In this case, a single object, having initially been the subject of either praise or censure through one particular aspect, becomes the subject of censure or praise through another aspect by the power of the context and other factors; therein, whatever portion is sublated results in a different form, while the remaining portions persist according to their own nature—this is what should be understood. And this [figure] may be mixed with other figures, as for example:
Though Lakṣmī is dear to your heart, you embrace the peerless and supreme Tulasī as your forest garland around your neck; you are the Lord of All—what more can we say? (1033)

"Incomparable" means not corresponding to her own [status] in terms of character, age, conduct, and so forth; the literal meaning, however, is "matchless. "Another" means belonging to another and superior. You are the Lord of All; according to the saying, "Lords show the way to purity, but they do not take up a soiled path," it is fitting for you, the Lord of All, to set forth on the right path, and not to proceed yourself upon an evil path—this is the intended meaning.

The actual state of affairs, however, is as follows: according to the principle stated in the verse, "Let it remain that the Vaijayantī garland on the chest of the Lord of Raṅga, along with Tulasī, the lotus, and the Kaustubha gem, speaks most eloquently of His universal sovereignty," You are the sovereign of the entire universe by virtue of Your chest being adorned with Tulasī, the Vaijayantī, and Lakṣmī. Here, through the figure of speech *samāsokti* (synecdoche), there arises the perception of the Lord’s engagement in the behavior characteristic of a *pallavika* (a type of low-born servant); based upon this, the censure ultimately results in praise.

O Śauri, although one of Your hands is full of fear while the other is full of majesty, people call You the "Bestower of Fearlessness" (Abhayaprada); for indeed, fame is easily attained by those of virtuous deeds.

[He is] with respect, with fear, and with apprehension. "Sādhvasī" means one who possesses *sādhvasa* (trembling/dread); the state of being so is *sādhvasitā*. [The Lord is] "rich" (*āḍhya*) in that quality. Here, the censure of the Blessed One—though nourished by the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth)—ultimately results in praise, because he bears a retinue of divine weapons such as the conch and the Nandaka sword, which are solely intent on destroying the wicked, and thus he is the pre-eminent leader in bestowing fearlessness upon all the worlds. As in the following example:
O Blessed Bhārgava, how indeed do they say that your weapon is without rival? For when you grasped your axe in battle, it was as if the enemies possessed no other axe at all.

When you took up the axe (*paraśu*) in battle, it was by your enemy alone—*dviṣatā* being a singular form denoting the entire class—that another axe, *apareṇa* meaning "by another," namely *paraśvadha*, came into being (*abhāvi*). How then can they say that your weapon has no rival? The sense is that your enemy himself became the supreme axe (*para-paraśvadha*). In the alternative sense, *dviṣatā* means "by the enemy" (*vairiṇā*), and *apareṇa* means "by [the word] *paraśu* with the letter *r* removed," i.e., by the word *paśu*; thus, [your enemy] became a beast (*paśu*).

The sense is that as soon as you take up your axe (*paraśvadha*), every enemy becomes a mere beast (*paśu*), falling within the range of slaughter like an animal. Alternatively, it means by another [weapon], namely a *paraśu*—where the syllables *pa* and *ra* are absent—and thus by a dog (*śuna*); the sense is that it was easily struck down like a puppy. Here, the apparent censure in the form of a reproach regarding the unrivaled nature of Lord Bhārgava’s axe results in a praise for its effortless shattering of the entire host of enemies;
this is an instance of *śleṣottambhitā* (praise supported by paronomasia).

Just as one fortunate woman takes her child’s breast-milk with affection, while another takes it with the intent to kill, O Healthy One, you grant the same fruit to both; who is capable of explaining the distinction between them? (1036)

In this regard, by means of the censure— "You are devoid of discernment because you grant equal results due to the absence of distinction between the categories of the pleasant and the unpleasant for the Blessed One"— it is said:
"O dear one, how can there be talk of friend or foe toward Govinda, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the World, who consists of the world and whose self is all beings?"
I am equal toward all beings; I am the refuge and the friend of all.

In the manner thus described, praise is understood through the state of being a friend to all. This [praise] is further nourished by a specific form of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), characterized by the aforementioned equality of conduct toward both the beneficial and the harmful. Likewise, in the verse cited in the section on *tulyayogitā*, "And of Caidya and others who were cursing," this *vyājastuti* (ironical praise) is also to be observed.

And this *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) occurs only when the praise and censure with which a particular subject is initially introduced result in its censure and praise respectively; for it is the established doctrine of the ancient rhetoricians that it should not extend to the case where the censure or praise of one thing results in the censure or praise of another.

Regarding *vyājastuti* (ironical praise), the commentators, intending to show that it is fivefold, have illustrated it accordingly: there are two types when praise and blame are understood as having the same object through either blame or praise; two types when they are understood as having different objects; and one type when the praise of one thing brings about the manifestation of the praise of another. Thus, they have presented it as being of five kinds.

The intended meaning is as follows: in the definition, "Vyājastuti is the manifestation (*vyakti*) of praise or blame through blame or praise," the term *nindāstutibhyām* (through blame and praise) and the term *stutinindayoḥ* (of praise and blame) do not intend a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). Thus, the sense is that *vyājastuti* is the manifestation of praise through blame, or of blame through praise, or of praise through praise. This is because of the etymological derivations: for the first [type], it is "praise by means of a pretext" (*vyājena stutiḥ*), and for the latter two, it is "praise in the form of a pretext" (*vyājarūpā stutiḥ*).

For this very reason, since there is no conformity with the meaning of the words in "feigned praise" (*vyājastuti*), it has been stated that "feigned censure" (*vyājanindā*) is a distinct figure of speech, wherein censure is manifested through censure. Thus, in the first two types [of *vyājastuti*], there are four varieties, as each is twofold based on whether the praise and censure share the same object or have different objects. The other type, however, which consists of praise with a different object, is only one; thus, there are five varieties in total. It should be understood that the definition common to all of them is: being either praise or censure that culminates in the other (praise or censure), while being distinct from feigned censure (*vyājanindā*).
In that very view, the verse defining [the figure] is as follows:
"Praise through censure, or censure through praise, which share a single object;
or praise whose suggested meaning has a different object—this is *vyājastuti* (disguised praise)."

The meaning is that there are five types of *vyājastuti* (disguised praise): four types arise when praise suggests censure, or when censure suggests praise—whether the objects of the two are different or identical; and one type arises when praise suggests praise whose object is different from that of the expressed praise. Thus, it is fivefold.
When the subject matter differs, censure is manifested through praise, as in:
"Blessed are these birds, deer, wild trees, and serpents who dwell upon the mountain purified by the placement of Mādhava’s feet; they are truly worthy of honor. (1037)

Here, through the praise of the blessedness of the birds and other creatures dwelling in the forest of the king of beasts, the lack of blessedness—characterized as blame—in those who do not belong to that class is suggested.
Daṇḍin maintains that this very *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) is not based on the relation of cause and effect;
as he says:
"Indirect praise (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) occurs when there is a laudation in the absence of the primary subject."
The deer live happily in the forests, not serving others.
With objects easily obtained without effort, such as grass and sprouts of darbha,
this very mode of life of the deer is praised here, even though it is irrelevant to the present context.
By that high-minded one, who was weary of the affliction of serving a king.

"In reality, however, it is more appropriate to say that this is *vyājastuti* (feigned praise), because there is a specific distinction from *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) in that censure is manifested through praise. Otherwise, even in well-known examples of *vyājastuti*, since the praise and censure of the subject at hand are understood through the censure and praise of the non-subject, one might as well claim that every instance of *vyājastuti* is merely *aprastutapraśaṃsā*."—thus [state] the Dīkṣitas.

Others, however, maintain that in well-known instances such as "O messenger, what discernment do you have? Well done! Again, well done!", since praise and censure share a single attribute (*ekadharmatva*), *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) is impossible there; consequently, because *vyājastuti* (disguised praise) possesses a sovereign distinct domain, *aprastutapraśaṃsā* will not simply be subsumed under *vyājastuti*.

For if one were to admit *aprastutapraśaṃsā* even when the subject matter (*dharmi*) is the contextual (*prastuta*), then the admission of *lalitā* as a separate ornament (*alaṃkāra*) within that very same domain would be contradicted. Thus they say.
When the subject matter is distinct, praise is manifested through censure, as in:

"What need is there for other wretched gods, who are devoid of Lakṣmī and incapable of bestowing the nectar of immortality—those whose worlds are measured by only three steps, while our feet purify the entire earth?"
In this instance, the praise of Śrīnivāsa is manifested through the censure of other deities.
Regarding the manifestation of praise through censure or censure through praise, examples have already been shown when they share the same subject matter.
The manifestation of praise for one through the praise of another is as follows:
"O Acyuta, in what field, for how many days, or of what name did he perform penance, that this bee now finds a lotus equal to your feet without ceasing? (1039)
In this context, through the praise of Milinda, there is expressed an excellence of fortune consisting of the beauty, tenderness, and delectability of the lotus feet of the Blessed One.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Chapter on Disguised Praise (vyājastuti), in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.
Now, the lake of indirect censure (*vyājanindā*):
Indirect censure occurs when censure is suggested by means of what appears to be praise. (91)

Where the censure of one person is manifested through the censure of another, that is *vyājanindā* (disguised censure), based on the etymological derivation: "censure under the pretext (*vyāja*) of censuring something else."

O lotus-eyed one, how shameful is this, this foremost doltishness, this vast wickedness far exceeding speech and mind—that I should look upon the faces of those who have turned their backs on you! (1040)
Here, by means of the self-reproach arising from observing those who have turned their faces away from Śrīnivāsa, the reproach of such a person as being the most sinful is suggested.

Just as you yield a fruit that is sweet at first but bitter in its ripening and pungent in taste, you, O palāśa tree, are to be resorted to by those who have risen high; you are not for one such as I, O tāla tree.

"Sweet at first" means sweet upon impact; this refers to the idea that "like the juice of a palm fruit, it is sweet at first but bitter and unpleasant in its transformation. It is [frequented] by *uccair-bhūta* (high-born) beings—specifically gods—and by *palāśas* (carnivorous creatures). Alternatively, it is to be resorted to by *palāśas* (leaves) born (*bhūta*) in the high regions above. The underlying sense is: "for one like me who seeks divine fruit. The construction is: "it is not to be resorted to."

In this statement of one who has taken refuge in the Blessed One, the censure of other deities—who yield only insignificant fruits—is suggested by means of the censure of the palmyra tree. This ornament, too, is indeed the invention of Dīkṣita alone.

Now, one might ask: "How can this 'disguised praise' (*vyājastuti*), which has not been mentioned by any previous rhetorician, be accepted as a figure of speech? It is replied: because it stands as a counterpart to the fifth variety of *vyājastuti*—namely, "the manifestation of the praise of one thing through the praise of another"—it possesses an identical logical structure. Furthermore, just as with praise, even in the case of censure, since it possesses a specific distinctness from *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, it cannot be subsumed under that; and since there is no conformity of meaning in *vyājastuti* [with other figures], it cannot be subsumed there either. Therefore, it is appropriate to accept its status as a separate figure of speech, for it is fitting to acknowledge what was not stated by the ancients when it is logically consistent.

If it is argued: "In cases where the praise of one thing is perceived through the praise of another, or the censure of one through the censure of another, if we admit the figures *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) and *vyājaniṃdā* (feigned censure), then the figure *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) should not be mentioned in examples consisting of praise and censure; for those too could be subsumed under *vyājastuti* and *vyājaniṃdā*," it is replied: In a case where, from a narrative concerning an irrelevant subject (*aprastuta*) in the form of praise or censure, a corresponding narrative concerning the relevant subject (*prastuta*) is perceived—as in the verse beginning "There are many internal flaws..."—[the figure is *aprastutapraśaṃsā*].

In such cases, since *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on similarity has found its scope there, it cannot be prevented from occurring here as well. Furthermore, if *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) and *vyājaniṃdā* (feigned censure)—in which the praise of one thing results in the praise of another, or the censure of one results in the censure of another—are also possible, let them certainly occur; however, this [figure of speech] must not be abandoned.

Although, in the verse cited immediately above—"sweet at first, bitter in its ripening"—the censure of other deities who grant inferior fruits is implied through the censure of the palmyra tree, and thus there is also *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description) based on similarity (*sārūpya*), nevertheless, since that very [figure] is rooted in "disguised censure" (*vyājanindā*), it is also unavoidable there as the first [figure] to present itself. And so, this *aprastutapraśaṃsā* being enlivened by *vyājanindā* produces an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
O mud, you who possess an uncontrollable pride, prance as you will; what fault is there in you? He who regards you as equal to musk is indeed a despicable forest buffalo.

Here, by means of the censure of the forest buffalo and the censure of the mud rooted therein, there is perceived the censure of a certain most foolish person—who is known to be equal to a great knower of Brahman—and of a certain ignorant fellow who fancies himself a scholar; thus, this is Aprastutapraśaṃsā based on similarity (sārūpya), specifically in the form of "disguised censure" (vyājanindā) rooted in "disguised censure. This constitutes a specific distinction from the previous [type]. In the same way, Aprastutapraśaṃsā is also seen in the form of "disguised praise" (vyājastuti) rooted in "disguised praise."

O Peacock, is it not true that the garland of clouds—which spread for you that plumage worthy of being the crest-ornament for the son of Nanda—is itself worthy of praise? What need have you for further praise through your dancing?

*Tatāna* means he spread out or expanded. *Stutyā* means worthy of praise. *Ānandena nṛtya* means perform a dance with joy; this is the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *nṛt*. The sense is: "Perform your dancing at will; what purpose do you have for the praise of those like us? Alternatively, the sense is: "What purpose do we have for your praise—that is, for a hymn addressed to you—when the *kādambinī* (the cloud-bank), which bestows excellence even upon you, is already manifest?"

The statement, "What is the use of praising you? also serves to produce an excess of joy; thus, it ultimately results in praise itself. Here, through the praise of the unmentioned garland of clouds and the praise of the peacock rooted therein, there is understood the praise of the crest-jewel of great donors—the Great Lakṣmī—who possesses the majesty suitable for the worship of the Blessed One obtained through her glance, as well as the praise of her devotee. Therefore, this is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on similarity (*sārūpya*), which takes the form of a "disguised praise" (*vyājastuti*) rooted in another "disguised praise."
Or rather,
consider the Creator, who, out of manifold delight, fashioned you, O young cakora bird, as one whose sole sustenance among all the twice-born is the nectar-essence of the moon's rays.

Here, the praise of the Creator, which was not the primary subject, and the resulting praise of the Cakora bird, ultimately culminate in the praise of the Teacher—the supremely compassionate and great devotee of the Lord—whose very life consists solely in the experience of serving the lotus feet of the Blessed One obtained through His grace, as well as that of his disciple.

Bukkapaṭṭana Veṅkaṭācārya, however, maintains that there are exactly three varieties each for both "disguised praise" (vyājastuti) and "disguised censure" (vyājaniṃdā). Thus, it is stated in his *Alaṃkāra-kaustubha*:
"Where praise is perceived—whether by means of praise or even by means of censure—we recognize there the figure of speech known as 'disguised praise' (vyājastuti)."

The threefold nature of *vyājastuti* (ironical praise) consists of: praising one thing by means of praising another, praising that very thing by means of censuring it, and praising one thing by means of censuring another.
Whether through praise or even through censure, wherever censure is perceived, we recognize there the poetic figure of "Censure by Disguise" (vyājanindā).

Praise as a means of censure (*stutyā nindā*) is of two kinds: censure through the praise of that very person, and censure through the praise of another. Censure as a means of censure (*nindayā nindā*), however, is of only one kind. Having thus demonstrated the threefold nature of "disguised censure" (*vyājastuti*) along with its respective examples, [the author] notes: "Although in the *Kuvalayānanda* it is accepted that even the manifestation of censure through praise is indeed 'disguised praise,' and thus five varieties of *vyājastuti* are stated; nevertheless, in cases where censure is manifested, 'disguised censure' alone is appropriate, whereas in the manifestation of praise..."

"Having accepted *vyājastuti* (ironical praise), it is more appropriate to adopt only these [two] varieties; for, according to the logic of the 'even and uneven' (*samaviṣama*), it is necessary that mutually opposing figures occupy distinct domains—this is what we have stated otherwise, as has been demonstrated."
Thus ends the thirty-third string of gems, the "Indirect Censure" (*vyājanindā*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on the figure of speech *Ākṣepa* (Paralipsis).
That is *Ākṣepa* which is the negation of one's own statement upon reflection.
The figure of speech *Ākṣepa* consists of the negation of a stated matter preceded by a thorough consideration of it.

O Lord of the multitude of serpents, protect me who have sought refuge, fallen as I am on the path of worldly existence; I am blessed that my burden has been placed upon you—what else could I hope for? (1045)

In this context, having reflected upon the futility of seeking self-protection by placing the entire burden of one's self upon the Blessed One, the negation is indicated by the words "Or rather" (*athavā*) and so forth.

Or rather, since the life of the Moon, whose luster has been eclipsed by the radiance of your face, is now in peril, may he somehow survive through the grace of the Lord of the World (Viṣṇu). Or else, may he somehow survive through the grace of Śiva, the cool-rayed one. 1046.

*Jaivātṛka* means long-lived (*dīrghāyuḥ*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *jaivātṛka* applies to a man [who is long-lived]; it applies to the moon and to one who is emaciated, and in three genders [it denotes] long life. Here, because the cool-rayed moon has its luster dispelled by the radiance from the face of the Blessed One, there arises a possibility of doubt regarding his life, in accordance with the saying: "When the honor of the virtuous has faded, there is either death or departure to a distant land. By the power of the semantic pun (*arthaśleṣa*) inherent in the word *jaivātṛka*, the poet describes the denial [of the moon's existence] after considering its longevity.
This quality of being interwoven with a pun (*śleṣasaṃkīrṇatva*) constitutes a distinct aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) compared to the previous instance.

Or rather, O King, how could you have carried off that maiden from the ocean, who was known for her tawny hue? For she was forbidden by the scriptures; yet where do injunctions and prohibitions apply to one's own will?

"O Lord! The state of being *piṅgalā* is *piṅgalatā*; here, the masculine form is applied according to the rule *‘tvatalorguṇavacanasya’*. She was *śrutāṃ*, meaning heard of or renowned—by which is meant she is famous in the sacred scriptures (*śruti*) as 'the golden-garlanded Piṅgalā'; this is the intended sense. How did you marry the daughter of the ocean? Why this objection? To this he replies: *sā hi* (for she...). That girl of *piṅgala* complexion is prohibited by the scriptures:
'One should not marry a tawny (*kapilā*) girl, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is *piṅgalā*.'"

Thus, [the practice] is prohibited by the *smṛtis* of Manu and others regarding marriage. The particle *hi* is used either as a causal marker or to indicate what is well-known. He provides the resolution himself with the words "or else" (*athavā*). Alternatively, in the case of one who acts according to their own will (*svairasya*), that is, one who is unrestrained (*niravagrahasya*), the meaning is "of one whose independence is beyond questioning," following the statement: "They say that independence is divine and not to be questioned. The sense is: where are injunctions and prohibitions applicable? Not in one place, because of being unrestrained; nor in the other, because of being subject to no *karma*. This is the intended meaning.

In this case, it should be understood that there is a distinction from the previous instance as well: the prohibition of the objection—which is rooted in a consideration of the scriptural injunction forbidding marriage with a girl of a tawny complexion—is established by way of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) through the reflection upon her own free will.

Or rather: "I bow slightly to you, O jewel among those who bear the five weapons; do not be fickle. Or else, since you are mobile from beginning to end, you are indeed mobile even in the middle—so what is the use of further praise? (1048)

"O bearer of the five weapons and the jewel! 'I honor you,' 'I worship you,' 'I bow to you'—such is the worldly expression. 'For a little while' means for a short time. 'Do not be fickle'—the sense is: abandon fickleness and become steady. Alternatively, 'fickle at the beginning and end' means being fickle throughout the beginning and the end, or fickle from start to finish; the sense is that you are always of a restless nature. You [are now] in the middle—for the sake of accomplishing my desire, such is the sense."

"Even though you have been propitiated with prayers so that you, though graceful (*añcitā*), might not be fickle (*cañcalā*), you remain indeed moving, indeed fickle. What can be accomplished by this discourse—a mere string of useless words? The meaning is: nothing at all. The sense is that because one's inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is difficult to overcome, my prayer is simply ineffective. In the alternative [poetic] sense, the word *cañcalā* has the feminine gender of its referent superimposed upon the word itself. It is described as such because its first and last letters are *ca* and *lā*. (That is, it begins with *ca* and ends with *lā*.)

"In the middle" means that which has the group of letters *añci* absent; she is so described because even though [the word] is formed, the particle *api* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). She is "fickle" (*calā*) because she possesses the two letters *ca* and *lā*; the suffix *ac* is added in the sense of possession according to the *arśa-ādi* class. The meaning is that if the group of letters *añci* situated in the middle were elided from the word *cañcalā*, it would result in the form *calā* alone. Here, having perceived the futility of the request "May you not be fickle" upon reflecting on her inherent nature, a prohibition is made. [Commentary: In this case, the prohibition is made after considering the uselessness of the requested matter by reflecting on her very nature. O Blessed One, by your grace, even the fine silk garment that had been presented to the princess of Pañcāla turned into a mass of chaff for the Kurus; for indeed, it was as if their very destiny were written upon it.

O Blessed One! By Your grace, it was manifested—that is, having come forth and remained present at the moment Duḥśāsana stripped away her garment. For what reason did even the *dukūla* silk garment of the Princess of Pañcāla become for the Kurus, Duryodhana and the others, like a *kukūla*—that is, like a pit strewn with spikes or like a fire of chaff? Even that most enchanting *dukūla*, produced by the overflowing grace of the Blessed One, became for them a site of downfall or a cause of burning; this is the sense of the wonder.

"Kukūla refers to a pit strewn with spikes, but not to a fire of chaff," says Amara. "The word *kukūla* is neuter when it denotes a large pit filled with sharp iron spikes and the like, constructed near a fortress to prevent the movement of the enemy army; however, it is masculine when it means a fire of chaff," says the author of the *Ṭīkāsarvasva*. Alternatively, "that writing" refers to the writing on the foreheads of those Kurus; for it is indeed so. The particle *hi* is used here for emphasis.

The sense is that even the perception of an object which is the very cause of the world’s joy as being a cause of its destruction follows the lines of fate inscribed upon the forehead by the laws corresponding to one's past actions; therefore, there is nothing here to be wondered at. In the alternative (pakṣa) sense: the word *dukūla*—that which has no *duḥ* (the letter *d*), i.e., *adu*; it stands forth (*prādu*) with excellence (*prakarkṣeṇa*) because it is devoid of the letter *du*. From where [does this arise]? From the "bad letter" (*kuvarṇa*), meaning from the position of the letter *du* having been assigned [there instead]. This is the sense.

Just as in the injunction, “One should not say *girā* with *girā*; having made [the word] *airam*, one should chant,” the word *irā* which is prescribed after prohibiting the word *girā* occurs precisely in the place of the word *girā*, so too here it should be understood that the *ku*-vowel (*kuvarṇa*), being prescribed after prohibiting the *du*-vowel (*durvarṇa*), occurs in that very same place. This point has already been stated previously. It reached the state of *kukūla*, that is, the state of the word *kukūla*.

The *tallipi* (the "bad-script") consists of the arrangement of incorrect phonemes preceded by the removal of the letter *du*. It is a script that conveys the aforementioned sequence; for instance, the meaning is that through a particular rearrangement of syllables, the word *dukūla* became the word *kukūla*. Here, the negation of the matter—which had been made an object of doubt as to how the divine *dukūla* (fine silk garment) manifested through the grace of the Blessed One could have become a *kukūla* (chaff-fire) with respect to Suyodhana and others—is achieved by reflecting on the true nature of that script.
This [figure] is embellished by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction), *padārthavṛtti-nidarśanā* (illustration based on the literal sense of words), and other such devices.

Or rather, how could the radiance of the sun possibly prevail here against the expansion of your own light? Or else, if linguistic derivation (*vyākṛti*) is the authority, then that [derivation] is unestablished regarding the object of the suffix *ābhīya*. (1050)

O Blessed One! In this world, when there is the expansion of the *ābhā*—that is, the splendor—of those belonging to you (*bhavadīyānām*), meaning your devotees (*bhāgavatānām*), what indeed could be the expansion of the sun’s *ābhā*, or what state could it possibly reach? We do not know; such is the sense. Alternatively, *abhīyam* is derived from *ābhā* with the suffix *cha* according to the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*.

It follows that in relation to the effect belonging to the splendor of Bhagavān—the effect consisting of its expansion—that effect belonging to the splendor of the sun—the effect consisting of its expansion—would be unestablished, unaccomplished, and virtually non-existent. The sense is that the expansion of the sun’s splendor would not be able to raise its head before the expansion of the splendor of Bhagavān.

The meaning is that when an operation prescribed under the governing rule *ābhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22) within the scope of the *ābhīya* section, or an operation established according to the Śabdanaya, is to be performed upon a common locus (*samānāśraye*), that *ābhīya* operation—prescribed by the aforementioned governing rule—is considered *asiddha* (non-existent), because of the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22).

The meaning is this: just as in the case of *edhi* from the root *as*, when the *ābhīya* operation of changing *hi* to *dhi*—according to the rule *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ*—is to be performed, the *ābhīya* operation of *etva* (the change to *e*) effected by the rule *ghvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca* is treated as *asiddha* (non-existent). And just as in the case of *āsīt*, when the *ābhīya* augment *āṭ* is to be applied according to the rule *āḍajādīnām*, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) according to the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* is treated as *asiddha*.

Furthermore, "having a common substratum" (samānāśrayatva) means having a common locus (samānādhikaraṇatva) in one place, because both the splendor of the Lord's portion (bhāgavata-bhānu-tejas) and [the other] exist right here in this world. Elsewhere, it should be understood as having a substratum that is neither deficient nor excessive compared to the collection of causes related to the scripture, which would otherwise be unestablished.

In this verse, regarding the doubt as to what state the radiance of the sun might reach when the radiance of the Lord’s splendor is spreading—wherein the grammatical technicality (paribhāṣā) that an operation pertaining to the Ābhīya group is treated as non-existent when an Ābhīya operation is to be performed upon a common substratum—is utilized through the identification based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (punning), the prohibition [of the sun's light] is described by means of the phrase "or rather" (*athavā*) and so forth. This is an instance of the ornament of *pramāṇa* (proof/authority) intermingled with other figures.

O Lord, those whose wealth was diminished, those who were bowed down, and those who were full of doubt have all been restored by you; O Knower of All, is this not fitting? Or rather, has it been sung by you that "I am equal to you"? (1051)

Those whose wealth has been diminished (*apacita*), honored (*pūjita*), or cut away (*vilūna*)—the prefix *apa-* being used with the root *ci* (to gather) in both senses. Thus, the *Ratnamālā* states: "In the feminine, *apacitiḥ* means honor, atonement, destruction, or expenditure. Here, by means of the support of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the phrase "those whose wealth has been diminished," the doubt regarding the Lord—which was raised—is refuted by reflecting upon His equanimity based on His own words: "I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear.
This [refutation] is further nourished by figures such as *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), *viśeṣa* (distinction), and *pramāṇa* (corroboration).

O Ornament of Lakṣmī (Kamalālalāmaka), just as those who perceive what is adverse [perceive] what is favorable, you maintain an equal attitude toward all; alas, such is your imperishable nature! [Kamalālalāmaka: He for whom Lakṣmī (kamalā) is the ornament (lalāma) is Kamalālalāmaka. The suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule "śeṣādvibhāṣā. The meaning is Śrīnivāsa. *Note:* This verse plays on the paradoxical nature of the Divine: while ordinary beings perceive opposites (the favorable and the adverse), the Lord remains equanimous toward all, regardless of their qualities. The term *akṣara-svabhāva* refers both to his immutable nature and, by wordplay (*śleṣa*), to his name *Akṣara*. The commentary explains that *kamalālalāmaka* is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) ending in *kap*, signifying the Abode of Śrī.

The vocative form of that [name] is: "O Kamalālalāmaka! Regarding you, even for those like Vidura, Akrūra, and others—who possess eyes that are favorable and whose sole essence is favorability—as well as for those like Śiśupāla, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and others—who perceive with hostility and whose sole nature is hostility—you bestow, that is, grant, an equal goal, a common *puruṣārtha*. The exclamation "batā" expresses either sorrow or wonder born from such a consideration of your distribution [of fruits]. In the other sense (the word-play), "Kamalālalāmaka" is a vocative address directed at that very person [Śrī Kṛṣṇa].

The meaning is that you reveal the same intended object (*abhidheya*) whether to those who see [the verse] in direct order (*anuloma*) or even to those who see it in reverse order (*pratiloma*). According to Amarasimha, "object" (*artha*) refers to the denotation, wealth, thing, purpose, or cessation. The point is that because the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) remains identical in both direct and reverse orders, the phrase *kamalālalāmaka* expresses the same meaning. The exclamation *bata* expresses either joy or wonder born from the contemplation of such a nature of words. The word *vā* has the sense of "or else" (*athavā*).

Your nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed your innate disposition (*nisarga*), meaning that you are imperishable (*akṣara*)—that is to say, unshakable by any other means. The sense is that this is because you yourself have sung [in the Gītā], "He is equal toward the parties of friend and foe. In the alternative [punning] sense, *akṣarasvabhāva* refers to the nature of the syllables of the word *kamalālalāmaka* belonging to you (the poet). According to the rule *anaci ca*, there is a doubling of the letter *s*. Thus, the very form of the letters is exactly so.

The sense is that since the forward and reverse readings are identical in their sequence, their capacity to reveal the same meaning is not cause for wonder. Here, by the phrase "of those with adverse views" (*pratikūladṛśām*), the negation of the suggested meaning—namely, that "their nature as syllables is thus"—is indicated. This [verse] is embellished by the figures of speech *śleṣa* (paranomasia) and a specific variety of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism).

"How is it that you, though raining down torrents of water from the finest clouds, have dried up the ocean? Or rather, O son of Daśaratha, you yourself were indeed a great archer! O son of Daśaratha! [The term] *ghanavaraśaradhārāvarṣī* means "one who possesses the rain (*varṣa*) of the streams of water (*śaradhārā*) from the best of clouds (*ghanavara*). The suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). In the alternative sense (referring to Rāma), it means "one who rains down a continuous succession of arrows," using the suffix *ṇini*.

Drying has come upon him; he is one in whom the ocean or lake has been dried up. In another sense, he is one by whom the ocean—the sea—has been brought to desiccation (*śoṣa*); here the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense from the causative root *śuṣ*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *abdhi* refers to both the ocean and a lake. How were you? This is a marvel! The meaning is: how is it that you have become a dried-up lake even while possessing the pouring down of torrents from clouds? Or else, you were a great desert (*mahādhanvan*), a vast arid region.

It is no wonder that you are a dried-up lake even while the clouds are pouring down torrents of rain; the sense is that this is due to the inherent nature of the desert (*marudeśa*). He whose bow is great is thus described as one with a "stoutly raised bow" (*uddaṇḍakodaṇḍa*); such is the actual state of affairs. The suffix *anaṅ* is applied at the end of the compound according to the rule *dhanuṣaśca*. Alternatively, it may mean "he whose *dhanvan* (bow or desert) is great. As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *dhanvan* refers to a desert (*marudeśa*)—it is masculine—or to a bow and dry land, in which case it is neuter. [Rāma says: "O son of Sumitrā, bring my bow and arrows that resemble venomous serpents."

The sense is that, according to the manner expressed in the words "I shall dry up the ocean," it is not at all surprising that you—the foremost of great heroes, with your fierce bow raised high—should dry up the ocean by raining down a continuous succession of arrows.

Here, by depending upon a superimposition of non-difference based on the *śleṣa* (pun) of two meanings—clouds and water, or dense arrows and so forth—as conveyed by the words *ghana*, *śara*, etc., there arises the doubt: "How can it be a dried-up lake even while possessing the state of raining down streams of water? This doubt is resolved through a reflection on its true nature, characterized as being a region of great winds (*mahāmāruta-deśatva*), which is produced by relying on a superimposition of non-difference based on the *śleṣa* of two meanings—great desert and great bow—as conveyed by the word *mahādhanvan*. This [figure] is a blend of *vibhāvanā* and *viśeṣokti*.

Or rather, how could your state of being a tree (avanatvam) possibly belong to Hari, who is adorned with the beautiful, auspicious, and glorious creepers of the Surabhi cow? Or perhaps it would be so, if you were the destroyer of the entire multitude of Palāśa trees. 1054.

O friend! In the fragrant season of spring, there are certain creepers (*latā*) which are thus described as being endowed with auspicious beauty (*śrī*) consisting of an abundance of flowers and the like; by these [creepers] he is honored (*añcita*), that is, joined. In the alternative sense, *surabhi* means charming, and *śubha-śrī-latā* refers to one who possesses such auspicious beauty; from the word *śrīla*, the suffix *lac* is added in the sense of possession according to the rule for words beginning with *sidhma* (Pāṇini 5.2.97)—as Amara states: "One who has *lakṣmī* is *lakṣmaṇa* or *śrīla*. The state of being so is *śrīlatā*; by that he is honored, meaning he is worshipped by the world due to his being distinguished by such splendor.

How could there be for you the state of being a forest (*vana*), which is the absence of the state of not being a forest (*avana*)? The sense is that since the state of being a forest necessarily follows from being endowed with abundant creepers (*samṛddhalatānvitatva*). However, the actual state of affairs is this: "avana" means one who protects (*avati*); its state is the quality of being a protector of the world (*jagadrakṣakatva*). Or rather (*yadi vā*), you are the destroyer of the multitude of all those who possess leaves (*palāśin*)—that is, trees (*viṭapin*)—and those who consume flesh (*kravyād*), for they eat the leaf (*pala*). That destruction of the leaf-eaters would be the cause of your state of being a protector (*avana*) in this context.

The sense is that the very fact of being the uprooter of all young trees (*taru*) would be the reason for the absence of "forest-ness" (*vana-tva*). In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), the sense is that the very fact of being the uprooter of all night-stalkers (*niśicara*, i.e., demons) is the cause for the protection of the world (*jagadavana*). Here too, as in the previous example, the objection and its refutation are based solely upon the exploitation of *śleṣa* (punning double entendre).

Others have declared that *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is a negation which, being contradicted, implies some particular detail; they say its scope consists of what is yet to be said or what has already been said.

A negation that, being sublated, results in another meaning and implies some particularity, is "like a negation" (*niṣedha-iva*), that is to say, a semblance of negation (*niṣedhābhāsa*). The author of the *Alaṃkārasarvasva* and others call this "suggestion" (*ākṣepa*). For this very reason, it is defined in the *Kuvalayānanda*: "Some wise men consider suggestion to be a semblance of negation. This [suggestion] is of two kinds: that which has a subject yet to be stated (*vakṣyamāṇa-viṣaya*) and that which has a subject already stated (*ukta-viṣaya*).

In that regard, if a prohibition is stated after first introducing a general description, then it pertains to what is yet to be said (*vakṣyamāṇaviṣaya*). When the result is the perception of a specific quality—namely, the impossibility of being described—it pertains to what has already been said (*uktaviṣaya*). This [type of] *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is also twofold: in some cases through the negation of the mere thing itself, and in others through the negation of the narration of the thing. However, that which pertains to what is yet to be said consists solely of the negation of the narration of the thing. Examples are given in reverse order: [Example of *uktaviṣaya*: "O friend, tell me this much: is he well? But do not ask about his health.
