Listen, I shall relate to you a tiny fragment of my tale of despair: O Lord, when you are untouched by compassion, what indeed remains to be said? (1055)

In this context, regarding the speech of a certain person weary of the world addressed to the Blessed One, having begun in a general manner with the words, "Hear my discourse on despondency," the statement, "O Lord, what indeed could there be to be said? constitutes an *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) concerning the subject matter about to be described; it results in the perception of the impossibility of speaking because it is difficult to express due to the surging of extreme exhaustion caused by the negation of what ought to be told. This *ākṣepa* consists in the negation of the narration of the actual fact.

O Lord, you may suffer here like a forest fire, or like a deer struck by lightning upon the mountain peak of the king of beasts; enough, enough with this talk before those who are speechless and devoid of respect.

The sense is this: even for those who show no respect through speech, it is useless to recount one's own wretchedness before them; for you too are "one to whom words and respect are not due" (*avākyanādara*), as has been heard in scripture. In this regard, the scriptural passage from the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā—"He has absorbed all this, he to whom words and respect are not due"—should be reflected upon. "One to whom respect is not due" (*anādara*) means being devoid of the need for deference because all desires have been attained, and thus there is nothing remaining to be honored.

For this very reason, the meaning of the Śruti passage, "Therefore, being *avākī* (speechless), having treated the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass as mere straw due to the perfection of his sovereignty, he remains in silent repose," is as follows: *vāka* means speech; by the rule *cajoḥ kughiṇṇyatoḥ*, the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *g*) occurs for the root *vac* when followed by the suffix *ghañ*. One who does not possess such *vāka* is *avākī*.

In this passage, regarding the speech of a certain afflicted person directed toward the Blessed One, after stating one part of the matter—"I suffer here like a deer in a forest fire"—the remainder of what was to be said is negated by the phrase "enough, enough. Thus, the futility of further speaking is made perfectly clear by Your very nature; therefore, this is an *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) concerning the stated subject, characterized by the prohibition of further narration of facts, which serves to manifest a specific distinction.

Thus, in this case of implication (ākṣepa), four factors are required: the intended meaning, its negation, the impossibility of that negation, and the communication of a specific [positive] sense. Therefore, it is neither a prohibition of what is enjoined, nor an injunction of what is prohibited; rather, there is an implication of an injunction by means of a prohibition. They say that because the prohibition is unreal, the sentence culminates in an injunction.
The author of the *Kāvyadarpaṇa* maintains that in some cases, a negation is observed of that which is actually being stated. An example of this is as follows:

when one ought to command, "Protect me," the statement made is, "It is not proper for you to be the one who commands; you yourself must protect the wretched—what is the use of a request? This constitutes indifference (*audāsya*). (1057)

"Do that which you desire; how can I release you?"—this is deceit. "Even while protecting the entire world, why do you not protect me?"—this is an insult. "Indeed, even a decrepit elephant was dearer to you than I"—this is reproach. O Infinite One, what indeed can those dull-witted as they are in discerning faults say before You? (1058–1059)
"O Bhūman!"—this is an address to the Blessed One. This specific group of two verses is called a *yugma*; a *viśeṣaka* consists of three stanzas;
a *kālapaka* consists of four; and that which exceeds this is known as a *kulaka*.

This is according to the definition [of *ākṣepa*]. Here, the negation expressed by "it is not proper for you, the one who commands," regarding that which is being said such as "protect me" (*pāhi*), implies a specific point: "In every way, we, who are most innocent and have entrusted our burden to you, ought not to be neglected by you."
An implied denial (*ākṣepa*) consisting of the negation of a stated subject is as follows:
"I am not omniscient; you are a friend to all—what need is there for me to say more? Whether one is wretched or not wretched, those like you bestow compassion regardless of the occasion. (1060)

"O Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) is an address to the Blessed Lord. Here, the denial by the poet—the singer—that "I am not a poet" is logically untenable; thus, while resting upon the speaker’s truthfulness by avoiding descriptions of impossible matters through hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) and the like, it implies the specific point through a general statement: "This wretched person should not be neglected by you, who are the friend of all and omniscient. In this instance, there is a negation of the entity that is the form of a poet.
Or for example:

"Surely he who does not find joy in your virtues, Ānanda, is certainly no human being; and truly, he who does not always rejoice in those [virtues] of Hari, O Lord, is not a human being. Here, the negation—that he is "not a human being"—is logically untenable with respect to a human who neither finds joy in the Lord’s virtues nor rejoices in them; thus, it successively implies the specific qualities of being like a *piśāca* (demon) and being like a deity, respectively.
Or as it is said:
"O Śauri, I do not speak flattery; the groups of women of Your human servants, standing upon the tops of jeweled palaces, take up the moon's mark to serve as collyrium for their eyes. (1062)

In this passage, within the speech of the praising poet, the prohibition of "flattery" (*cāṭu*) in the first quarter—being sublated by the prohibition of "falsehood"—results in the manifestation of a specific quality: the truthfulness of the meaning contained in the remaining three quarters. This truthfulness is established through the bold poetic assertion (*kavi-prauḍhokti*) of the poet. Since the *Tattvabodhinī* lists *cāṭu* among the indeclinables (*avyaya*), the word *cāṭu* is an indeclinable; alternatively, it may be neuter, as the lexicon states: "The word *caṭu* is not feminine; it is *caṭuḥ*. As in the following example:
O Govinda, O delight of Nanda, O handsome one, I do not venture to look upon you; let those women whom you divert with your playful sports see you as they please.

"Let those women see [him] according to their own will and as they desire. In the fourth quarter, the word division is *svaiḥ rantā yāḥ*. The construction is: "O playful one (*rantā*), let those women whom you delight with your own sports (*vihṛtaiḥ*)—the suffix *kta* here denotes the state of being—see him.

Here, in the speech of a certain cowherd woman who is beholding the Blessed One, the Son of Nanda, the prohibition against her own enthusiasm for seeing Him is logically inconsistent; this inconsistency reveals her wretchedness, as if she were saying to another heroine, "Are you not attached to me? What can I do?"

Just as there is a semblance of prohibition (*niṣedhābhāsa*), a semblance of injunction (*vidhyābhāsa*) is also accepted as *ākṣepa* (paralipsis). The meaning is that because the logic is the same, when a prohibition is implied by an untrue injunction, it is another form of *ākṣepa*. They say that four factors are required here: an undesirable object, its injunction, the semblance-nature of that injunction, and the communication of a specific quality residing in the object.
If you utterly neglect me when I have, by chance, come upon the path of truth, how will you ever again unite this one who has strayed onto a wrong path with what is beneficial? This is what I fear.

The meaning is: "If you now neglect me—who have come near the path of the righteous by virtue of some accidental merit—then by all means (bāḍham) neglect me in that very same way. Here, *bāḍham* is an indeclinable used in the sense of agreement. Furthermore, in this context, the request for neglect directed toward the Supreme Person by a certain devotee of the Lord is logically inconsistent; thus, appearing as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), it actually leads to the understanding of a prohibition. The injunction "neglect" (*upekṣasva*) is explicit.

The prohibition "do not neglect me" is concealed by the display of fear, namely: "If you were to do so, you would have to exert great effort to turn me—who, once again under the influence of karma, has set out upon an evil path—toward what is appropriate and beneficial. For this very reason, the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* defined this variety as: "Another type of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) occurs when the injunction is explicit and the prohibition is concealed."
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the Section on Paraleipsis (Ākṣepasara), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now, the figures of speech rooted in contradiction:
therein, the figure of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"Contradiction is the appearance of contradiction even when there is no actual contradiction."
Through its own relationship and its relationship with others, birth and the other [marks] become tenfold.

Although there is no contradiction in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that figure in which a contradiction appears on the surface is the ornament of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*). Contradiction is of two kinds: established (*prarūḍha*) and unestablished (*aprarūḍha*). Establishment is the state of not being overcome by a subverting cognition (*bādhabuddhi*); its opposite is non-establishment. Of these, the first is the province of a defect (*doṣa*), while the second is the province of the ornament. For this very reason, it is called "semblance of contradiction" (*virodhābhāsa*): it is an *ābhāsa* because it "shines forth slightly" (*ā īṣad bhāsate*), and it is both a contradiction and an *ābhāsa*.

This means that although it is perceived at the very outset, it is immediately set aside by a cognition of non-contradiction arising all at once. Even there, the figure of speech *virodhālaṃkāra* (apparent contradiction) is an appearance of contradiction untouched by cognitions of cause and effect and so forth; however, when touched by such cognitions, it becomes the figures of speech such as *vibhāvanā* (peculiar causation), which will be discussed later. And this [apparent contradiction] arises from the connection of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*) with themselves and with others.

Thus, ten varieties are established: genus with genus, quality, action, and substance; quality with quality, action, and substance; action with action and substance; and substance with substance alone. As it has been said:
"Genus may be in opposition to four—genus and so forth; quality to three;
action to two; and substance only to substance. These are the ten."

Thus [it is said]. The contradiction between a universal (*jāti*) and a quality (*guṇa*) has not been stated separately, because the contradiction of a universal with a quality is already included therein. This should be understood similarly in what follows. Furthermore, "action" (*kriyā*) here should be noted as being neither the pure *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as held by the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), nor the form of motion (*spanda*) as held by the Logicians (*naiyāyika*), but rather a specific activity denoted by various verbal roots (*dhātu*). In that regard, an example of the contradiction of a universal with a universal is as follows: "O Enemy of Naraka! O Supreme Self! Since your abode possesses delightful palaces, lakes of extreme serenity, and likewise assemblies, surely your hells must be [equally] hells [of bliss]. (1065)

Here, there is a contradiction between the class of celestial vehicles (*vimāna*) and so forth and the class of hell-beings. Although this contradiction between the two classes appears immediately before us, it is resolved by reflection upon the statement to be cited later: that, from the perspective of the Lord’s abode, they are excessively contemptible and thus equal to hell.
Here [in heaven], there are delightful celestial vehicles that move at will, as well as assembly halls, various pleasure gardens, O King, and lotus-pools with pure waters.
"These indeed, O dear one, are the hells [relative] to the state of the Supreme Self"—
this is the meaning of the authoritative passage from the Mahābhārata that has been considered.

O Lord, for those whose hearts are cooled by meditation upon you, the rays of the moon, the breezes from the sandalwood mountains laden with camphor, and even the sun itself become more scorching than the sun. (1066)
Here, there is a contradiction between the genus of camphor and so forth and the quality of extreme heat.
Just as a lamp made of camphor pieces, being consecrated by the act of lustration (nīrājana), quickly cools the lotus-eyes of men—O Veṅkaṭanātha, so does this [work] cool your lotus-eyes. 1067.

Here, there is a contradiction between the universal property (*jāti*) of being a lamp and the action of cooling the eyes. An example of a universal property (*jāti*) in opposition to a substance (*dravya*) is as follows:

"The son of Daśaratha, an archer who split even the ten directions with his twangings, became like the fire at the end of an eon for the moon-faced women dwelling in the city of the Ten-faced one. (1068)
Here, there is a contradiction between the universal (jāti) of the nature of fire and the substance (dravya) characterized as the son of Daśaratha.

This [type of contradiction] may also be based on paronomasia (śleṣa). Among those, an example of the contradiction of a genus (jāti) with genus, quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and substance (dravya) is as follows:

"The mountain of the Lord of Śrī possesses vast essence; its body is delightful with tender creepers. Yet it rises into the sky by its greatness—this being named 'Ananta' (the Infinite)—is indeed a great marvel! (1069)

The pleasure-mountain of Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of Śrī, is the *vihārācala* (mountain of sport). Here, there is an apparent contradiction (*virodha*) based on genus (*jāti*), as it is both a mountain (*adri*) and a large being (*pṛthula-sattva*). The resolution (*parihāra*) is that it is a mountain where large beings (*sattva* = living creatures) reside; or alternatively, that it is one whose luminosity (*lasattva* = *lasat-tvam*, from the root *las*, "to shine") is vast. There is an apparent contradiction based on quality (*guṇa*), as it is both soft (*mṛdu*) and yet possesses a beautiful body (*abhirāma-tanu*). The resolution is that its beautiful body is formed by those soft creepers (*latā*).

There is a contradiction with the action expressed as "it flies to heaven" by virtue of its "greatness," "magnitude," or "weight"; the resolution is that it "surpasses even heaven" by virtue of its "power. This mountain is described as having "Ananta" (the Infinite) as its name, which refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Since "space-ness" is not a universal (*jāti*) because it exists in only a single individual, there is a contradiction with that substance (*dravya*) insofar as the universal of "mountain-ness" cannot have that [space] as its locus; the phrase "named Śeṣa" indicates the absence of that [contradiction].
Or for example:

"O Lord of the World, your vehicle, the sun (*pataṅga*), though swift (*āśuga*), possesses the fragrance of blooming blue lotuses (*unnidrakuvalayāmoda*); this friend of the night-lilies (*kumudasuhṛd*) is endowed with the most exalted splendor. (1070) Here, the term *pataṅga* as "your vehicle" refers to the sun (*bhānumat*), while *āśuga* refers to the wind (*māruta*); thus, there is a contradiction between two classes (*jāti*). This is resolved by the fact that *pataṅga* also means "bird" (*vihaṅga*) and *āśuga* means "one who moves swiftly. The phrase *unnidrakuvalayāmoda* presents a contradiction through its qualities (*guṇa*), as it implies the fragrance of blue water-lilies (*kuvalaya*), whereas the sun brings joy to the entire earth (*prakāśitapṛthvīmaṇḍalapramoda*). This is resolved by the fact that *unnidrakuvalayāmoda* can mean "that which brings delight to the blossoming earth."

"By whom the splendor of darknesses was uplifted and raised"—this constitutes a contradiction with the act of uplifting. This is resolved by interpreting it as "one by whom excellent prosperity has been increased. Regarding the moon, which is the friend of the night-lotuses (*kumuda*), since being a friend of the lotuses resides in only a single individual, it is not a universal (*jāti*); thus, this is a term denoting a substance (*dravya*). Consequently, there is a contradiction consisting in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*) of the universal "solar-ness" (*sūryatva*) in that [moon]. Solar-ness is a universal because it resides in twelve individual solar entities.

He is "well-composed" (samāhita) because he is averse to those whose joy is contemptible—that is, those who desire objects that ought to be abandoned—or because he is an adversary to them; or alternatively, he is so called because he takes away the life-breaths of those such as the Daityas and Dānavas, whose joy (mut) is contemptible and sinful. Herein lies the distinction: in both cases [of the previous examples], there is a pun (*śliṣṭatva*) involving two opposing meanings, whereas in the former case, it involves only one.
Thus, the contradiction of birth with the four factors, beginning with birth itself, has been explained.
Now, an example of the opposition between one quality and another:
"O Lord of Veṅkaṭagiri, when you look upon them, the courtyards—which were dusty due to a lack of sweeping and difficult for the poor to enter—become muddy with streams of your charity. (1071)

Here, the contradiction between the quality of being covered in dust and the quality of being muddy is resolved by a difference in time, since the latter becomes possible through the power of the Lord’s sidelong glance.
Or, for example:

"As Indra gazed upon the foremost of the Raghus, who held the arrow that uprooted the faces of Bālin and Daśānana, his mind became turbid and then clear. (1072) "Nidhyāyataḥ" means "gazing. Here, there is a contradiction between the two qualities of turbidity and clarity; this is resolved by the distinction of the causes, namely, the killing of his own son Bālin and the killing of Daśānana, who was an enemy of himself.
An example of the contradiction between a quality and an action:
"O Lord, for those who burn all around you and for those who listen to your deeds, their hearts—though filled with rising and intense joy—alas, grow faint. (1073)

Here, there is a contradiction between the quality of "the state of being agitated by intense, surging bliss" and the action of "becoming slackened"; the resolution is that [the senses] become such that no other objects of knowledge remain.
May those great ones on earth, who have entrusted their hearts to You, be ever victorious—those virtuous ones from whom, O lotus-eyed Lord, even a mere atom given away becomes as Mount Meru. (1074)
Here, there is an apparent contradiction between the quality of atomicity and the substance in the form of Mount Meru; the resolution is that even a small object can bestow a great fruit.

Or rather, let there be salutation to those virtuous ones who, having placed that Supreme Brahman within their hearts, fashioned the atom with most firm qualities, making it utterly motionless by its own attributes. (1075)

Here, there is an apparent contradiction between the quality of atomicity and the substance that is the Supreme Brahman, which is characterized by unsurpassed greatness, as stated in such passages as, "He is greater than the earth, He is greater than the intermediate space. The resolution is that this atomicity is for the purpose of meditation upon the Supreme Brahman—who is heard of as greater than everything—by way of its being established within the limitation of the heart-abode. Thus it is revealed in scripture: "This is my Self within the heart, subtler than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet."

The distinction here is that in the previous case there was a contradiction between a quality and a substance, whereas here it is between a substance and a quality. The construction is as follows: "making [it] motionless by means of the strongest qualities—meaning ropes—and by means of qualities suitable for meditation, thereby binding and firmly establishing it, they made that Brahman minute. Regarding the word *niṣpanda*, there is no substitution of *ṣ* because the root *spad* is not taught with an initial *ṣ*. Thus Vāmana says: "In the word *niṣpanda*, the substitution of *ṣ* is to be questioned, as no grammatical rule [for it] is observed."
And this has been examined by us in detail in the *Haṃsasandeśarasāsvādinī* at the verse beginning with "nyastaniṣpandadṛṣṭiḥ."
The opposition of a quality to another quality, to an action, or to substances, based on *śleṣa* (punning), is as follows:
"Though soft, you possess a wondrous form; though innocent, you extend the welfare of the world; though exceedingly fickle, you are the sustainer—O Rame, this conduct of yours is marvelous. (1076)

"O Rāme! You are soft with tender limbs"—this is a contradiction (*virodha*) between the quality [of softness] and the term "wonderful embodiment" (*adbhutā mūrtiḥ*), since an "embodiment" implies hardness. The resolution (*parihāra*) is that she possesses a heart soft with compassion, which can be easily resorted to even by those who have committed offenses, and that she possesses a transcendent, divine form; for Amara states: "The word *mūrti* refers to both hardness and the body. "You are charming and ignorant"—this is a contradiction between the quality [of ignorance] and the action "you extend the welfare of the world," because one who is ignorant lacks the capacity to perform such deeds.

The resolution [of the apparent contradiction] is that "mugdhā" means "sundarī" (beautiful), as the *Viśvakośa* states: "mugdha is used for beautiful and deluded. Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the quality "extremely fickle" (*aticañcalā*) and the substance "the nurse (*dhātrī*) or ground (*bhūmi*)" [of all qualities], because she is immovable (*acalā*). The resolution is that "aticañcalā" means one who has transcended the flickering lightning-streaks due to her excellence of luster, and she is the Mother of the worlds (*jagatām mātā*). The *Medinīkośa* states: "dhātrī refers to a mother, the *āmalakī* tree, the earth, and a foster-mother. As in the following example:

O Blessed One, though you are clad in yellow garments, it is a marvel that you are nonetheless delightful with a green hue; for by your own radiance you illuminate the entire world, and yet you are the Lord of all beings.

"He whose rays (aṃśavaḥ) are yellow (pītāḥ)—that is, he who wears yellow garments (pītāṃśukaḥ)"—this presents a contradiction with the quality of being "delightful by virtue of its green (harita) color. The resolution is that "Hari" refers to the state of being yellow (haritā), and thus he is delightful by that [state]. "You clarify (viśadayasi) the entire world with your own radiance (rucyā)," which presents a contradiction with the action of making something "white (dhavala). The resolution is that "you clarify" means you purify it through your own affection (nijarucyā) directed toward it.

The term *bhūteśaḥ* (Lord of Beings) as *rudraḥ* (Rudra) involves a contradiction with the substance (*dravya*), because Rudra possesses a dark-colored body and thus cannot logically possess a yellow color. However, there is no contradiction in taking it to mean "Lord of all beings," based on the Vedic scripture: "He is the Lord of Beings, He is the Protector of Beings. Here, the contradiction of a single quality—namely, the quality of wearing yellow garments—is stated in relation to other qualities, actions, and substances. One should understand that this differs from the previous case, where each of several distinct qualities, such as softness and so forth, was individually shown to be in contradiction with other qualities and so on. This is the distinction to be noted.
Thus, the contradiction of a quality with three things—namely, another quality and so forth—has been demonstrated.
Furthermore, O Mukunda, just as you sever with your discus the great heads of the enemies falling before you in battle by means of your action, so too do you bestow supreme bliss upon them.

In this case, there is a contradiction between the act of cutting and the act of delighting; for you bestow the experience of unsurpassed self-bliss in liberation, and thus [the former] is absent. Or, as in another example: "O lotus-eyed one, you who grant all desired objects are difficult to attain even through manifold austerities; yet you make those who bow before you happy, and indeed, you make them suffer. (1079)

Here, there is a contradiction between the two actions of making happy and making unhappy. Their absence [is established] by the presence of the two delimiters mentioned in the first half of the verse, corresponding respectively [to each action]. In both instances—“you make happy” (*sukhākaroṣi*) and “you make unhappy” (*duḥkhākaroṣi*)—the suffix *ḍāc* is applied according to the rule: “*ḍāc* is used after *sukha* and *priya* in the sense of compliance (*ānulomya*), and after *duḥkha* in the sense of opposition (*prātilomya*).”

Just as Bhīṣma was deeply moved upon seeing the slayer of Kaṃsa—even though he was intent on killing him—when the Lord held the Sudarśana discus in his hand with impetuous force and was thus difficult even for the gods to behold. (1080)

Regarding the term *sudarśana*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "it is seen well" (*suṣṭhu dṛśyate*). Here, the suffix *yuc* is applied as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *khal*, according to the rule: "In common speech (*bhāṣā*), the suffix *yuc* is prescribed after the roots *śas*, *yudh*, *dṛś*, *dhṛṣ*, and *mṛṣ*. However, regarding the term *durdarśa*, the word *darśa* means "seeing" (*darśanam*), derived from the root *dṛś* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). The analysis is: "that for which seeing is difficult" (*duṣkaraḥ darśo yasya*). It does not mean "it is seen with difficulty" (*duḥkhena dṛśyate*). If it were the latter, the form would have to be *durdarśana*, according to the aforementioned Vārttika.

Nor can the formation be justified by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), because the suffix *yuc*—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule—is itself optional; for its prohibition is established by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "In the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and words having the sense of *khala*, there is no application of the rule of optional forms. Therefore, it is proper that the formation be justified solely through the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the manner described above. In this very same way, Vedic and Smṛti passages such as "that which is difficult to see," "this form is very difficult to see," and "difficult to see [is he] whose ornament is the crescent moon," as well as modern usages, are to be explained.

Here, there is a contradiction between the acts of desiring to kill and pleasing by the sight [of the enemy]. In the word *anvarakta*, the suffix *laṅ* is used after the root *rañj* preceded by the prefix *anu*. An example of contradiction between an action and a substance is as follows: "The light clinging to the very high peaks of the mountains that fill the bellies of the winds, though it has dispelled the turbidity [of the atmosphere], spreads a far greater degree of sootiness among the enemies. (1081)
Here, there is a contradiction between the action of assuming impurity and the substance consisting of the form of the Blessed One, which is superposed as being [identical with] light.
Just as when the loud,

bursting sounds from the snapping of the formidable bow of the great dancer [Rāvaṇa] by the boy-scion of Raghu caused even Phālākṣa to tremble, the sky to split apart, and the moon to fall to the earth.

Here, the contradiction between actions such as trembling and substances such as Phālākṣa is resolved through the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) regarding the excessive roar produced by the breaking of the bow of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva).
Thus, the contradiction of action with both action and substance has been demonstrated.
The opposition of one substance by another is as follows:

while your fame was spreading, constantly illuminating the entire world with extreme clarity, O Lord whose crest is the mountain of the king of serpents, Mount Kailāsa, the golden mountain, became [pale]. (1083)

Here, there is a contradiction between the substance in the form of the Golden Mountain and the substance in the form of Kailāsa; this is resolved by the praise of the excellence of the whiteness of his fame.
Through paronomasia (*śleṣa*), there is a contradiction between an action and both an action and a substance, as well as between a substance and a substance, as follows:

"O ocean of virtues, though you feel compassion for all beings and enter into them, you cast off pity; O Lord, though you create desire, you are indeed the Supreme Brahma—alas, O Blessed One! (1084) [In this verse, "compassion" (*ghṛṇā*) is contradicted by the action of "casting it off," while "desire" (*kāma*) is contradicted by both the action of "creating" and the substance "Brahma."]

Here, there is an apparent contradiction between the action of "entering into the interior of all beings" preceded by compassion and the action expressed as "you abandon *ghṛṇā* (loathing). The resolution is that you abandon *ghṛṇā*—meaning loathing arising from an excess of affection (*vātsalya*)—because you perceive [the body] merely as an object of experience, despite its existence within a wretched physical frame. Furthermore, there is an apparent contradiction between the action of "creating *kāma*, i.e., the god of love," and the substance "Lord" (*īśa*). The resolution is that you are the "Lord of the past and the future" who grants all desired objects to those who have taken refuge in you. In this regard, it is said: "The Person, the size of a thumb, stands in the middle of the self."
He is the lord of the past and the future; he does not shrink away from that.

Thus the meaning of the scripture has been considered. Furthermore, there is an apparent contradiction between the two substances in the statement, "Śarva is indeed Brahmā, the four-faced one. The resolution is that Brahman is the Supreme Brahman, which is infinitely and unsurpassably great (bṛhat) both by its essential nature and by its attributes.

Thus, the various types of contradiction have been demonstrated in accordance with the views of the predecessors. In this definition, the phrase "of genus and so forth" (*jātyādīnām*) intends to refer to properties (*dharma*) in general, as it is intended to be an inclusive indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, they say that this includes cases such as: "He who, though indeed a child, is the Ancient Person; though of pure form, resembles a dark cloud; though a benefactor of the world, acts as its destroyer; though a savior from fire, is a savior from serpents," and so on—in which there is the absence of a delimited attribute (*sakhaṇḍopādhi*) or an absence itself.

In reality, because distinctions such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are unpleasing [as figures of speech], and because they are rooted in either purity (*śuddhatva*) or punning (*śleṣa*), this [figure] is of only two kinds. For this very reason, Kuvalayānanda states that the general definition is simply this: "When there is an appearance of contradiction, it is desired as 'apparent contradiction' (*virodhābhāsa*). Consequently, all the verses that will be demonstrated by him will be examples of apparent contradiction alone. For example:

Though his feet are set upon the earth, he has established his station in heaven; though he dwells in the Draviḍa country, he is accompanied by Kaliṅga; though he is the moon, he is a blossomed hundred-petaled lotus—this is Śeṣagirirāja. 1085.

"Having set foot on the earth" (*bhuvi bhūmau kṛtapadaḥ*) yet "having set foot in heaven" (*divi nabhasi kṛtapadaḥ*)—this is a contradiction. It is resolved by [the fact that] he has made his nest among the *divi* birds, also known as blue jays (*cāṣa*). "Going to the Draviḍa country" (*dramiḍadeśagaḥ*) yet "accompanied by Kaliṅga" (*sakaliṅgaḥ*, i.e., together with the Kaliṅga country)—this is a contradiction. It is resolved by [the fact that] he is accompanied by the bird also known as the *dhūmyāṭa*. "The moon" (*śaśadharaḥ*) yet "by whom the hundred-petaled lotuses" (*śatapatrāṇi*) or water-lilies (*kuśeśayāni*) have been caused to bloom—this is a contradiction.

It is explained as being the dwelling place of a specific deer called the *śaśa* (hare) and as having caused the delight of a specific bird called the *dārvāghāṭa*. Regarding this, Amara states: "Now, the *caṣa* is the *kikīdivi*; then there are the *kaliṅga*, *bhṛṅga*, and *dhūmyāṭa*; and then the *śatapatraka* is the *dārvāghāṭa*."

This very one, who has become the Śeṣa-mountain by bearing upon his head the Puruṣa who shines with the hoods [of serpents], now, accompanied by the serpent Hira, bears what wonder upon his own crest? (1086)

He who exists—meaning is established—in the *Mahābhāṣya*, the speech of Patañjali (the Serpent) descended as Śeṣa; he who is the root *bhrāj* (to shine), beginning with *phaṇ* and others, present in the group of roots (*dhātugaṇa*) starting with *phaṇ*; and who is "most abundant" (*puru*)—meaning exceedingly frequent—upon the head, that is, in the final letter *ja*; and who is eternal, in such a way as not to be sublated by anything else.

*Ṣam*: It maintains or bears the sound *ṣ*, which is prescribed by the rule *vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrājacchaśāṃ ṣaḥ* as the substitute for the final letter [of the preceding root] followed by *ṭ*. The mention of *rājī*—accompanied by the suffix *ik*—is intended to indicate that this [root] is associated with *rāji*, namely the verbal root *rājṛ* meaning "to shine," because this [root] is also listed in the *phaṇādi* group. This very same root is what is referred to as *ṭu bhrājṛ* meaning "to shine. [The term *mūrdhani*] means "in the final letter."

The substitution of a *ka*-class consonant (*kavarga*) prescribed by the rule *ku coḥ kuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.30]—the word *hi* is used for emphasis, meaning "that very [substitution]"—is "strange" (*vicitram*) in the sense that he "bears" it (*dhatte*). This is because, in the case of the root *bhrāj* belonging to the *phaṇādi* group, the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *kutva* (the substitution of *k*). The point is that possessing the *kavarga* substitution is contradictory, just as in the case of the root *bhrājṛ* mentioned in the statement *ejṛ bhrējṛ bhrājṛ dīptau*. As it is stated in the *Kaumudī* treatise: "In the rule for *ṣatva*, due to association with *rājṛ*, only the *phaṇādi* root *ṭu bhrājṛ dīptau* is taken."

As for the claim that "only *kutva* [the substitution of *k* for *j*] applies to the root *bhrājṛ* in the sense of 'shining' according to the rule *ejṛ-bhrejr̥-bhrājṛ dīptau*," the resolution is as follows: the word *phaṇāḥ* means "hoods"; by the word *ādi* ("and so forth"), there is the inclusion of "tongues," "crest-jewels," and so on. That which shines (*bhrājata*) with those things of which hoods (*phaṇāḥ*) and others are the beginning is called *phaṇādibhrāṭ*. This is derived from the root *ṭu-bhrājṛ* (in the sense of "shining") with the suffix *kvip*, preceded by the words *phaṇādi*. By the rule *vraśca* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], the *j* becomes *ṣ*; by the rule of *jaśtva* [8.4.53], it becomes *ḍ*; and by the rule of *cartva* [8.4.41], it becomes *ṭ*. The meaning is: "that which is the king of serpents (*phaṇirāja*)."

Having become Śeṣagiri, having attained the state of the Śeṣa mountain, he bears upon his head—that is, on his own summit—the Supreme Person, the Highest Puruṣa, Śrīnivāsa. This very one is "Ahirājisahacarita"; this is a compound word meaning "accompanied by Ahirāji. Accompanied by Ahi-rāji (the king of serpents), that is, joined with the row of hooded serpents in Pātāla, because he is the sovereign over them; he supports *ku*—the earth (*ku* means the earth, according to Amara’s lexicon)—upon his head, that is, within the circle of hoods.

The essential meaning is this: he who supports Śrīnivāsa, who rests upon the form of the Residual Mountain (Śeṣācala), and bears Him upon his own head—he alone is the King of Serpents (Phaṇirāja) who carries the entire surface of the earth upon the crown of his head.

The host of servants at the lotus-feet of Your Majesty, though residing on the mountain of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), shines forth possessing the fourfold excellence (*caturbhadra*)—this is truly marvelous! Though they are beyond numbering (*saṃkhyātiga*), they are *bhadrās* (auspicious ones or a specific breed of elephant). For according to the traditional teaching: "Elephants are to be known as threefold: the *manda*, the *bhadra*, and the *mṛga*. Alternatively, the meaning is that they possess innumerable blessings (*asaṃkhyātam-aṅgala*). 1087. The host of servants at the lotus-feet of Your Majesty, though residing on the mountain of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), shines forth possessing the fourfold excellence (*caturbhadra*)—this is truly marvelous! Though they are beyond numbering (*saṃkhyātiga*), they are *bhadrās* (auspicious ones or a specific breed of elephant). For according to the traditional teaching: "Elephants are to be known as threefold: the *manda*, the *bhadra*, and the *mṛga*. Alternatively, the meaning is that they possess innumerable blessings (*asaṃkhyātam-aṅgala*).

"Caturbhadraḥ" (the fourfold auspicious one) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing an emphasis (*avadhāraṇagarbha*), meaning "one who has exactly four auspicious things" or "one whose [four] are auspicious," just like the term "abbhakṣaḥ" (one who subsists on water). This is what constitutes the poetic figure *sphurita*. However, the resolution is as follows: "caturbhadram" refers to the powerful fourfold auspiciousness consisting of *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa*. As stated by Amarasiṃha: "The *trivarga* consists of *dharma*, *kāma*, and *artha*; the *caturvarga* includes those plus *mokṣa*; when these are accompanied by power (*bala*), they constitute the *caturbhadra*."
They say that the analysis of the compound is either "that in which there are four excellent auspicious things," or "the collection of the four auspicious things. Others, however, say:
"Wealth accompanied by generosity, knowledge free from pride, valor endowed with patience, and enjoyment devoid of attachment—this fourfold auspiciousness is difficult to find."

Thus they say. This is clear from the commentary on the verse "caturbhadrataras tvayā" (you are fourfold more auspicious), which is heard in every chapter of the *Bhāratīya-ṣoḍaśarājaka*. [The term] "caturbhadrabhāk" means "one who possesses the four auspicious things. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *bhadra* refers to Śiva, the francolin partridge (*khañjarīṭa*), a bull, and the *kadambaka* tree; as a masculine noun it denotes a specific breed of elephant, and as a neuter it signifies auspiciousness and the *mustā* grass."
O moon of the Raghu dynasty, alas, at the very moment you were about to string your bow, you caused the glory of the earth, along with its enmity, to be removed from your hand! 1088.

O Lord of the Raghu dynasty! "When you, the *āropayitṛ* (the one who causes to ascend), are the *ropa* (the arrow)"—this is the apparent contradiction (*virodha*). [The term] *ropa* is derived from the root *ruh* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the agentive suffix *tṛc*. According to Amara: "The words *patrī*, *ropa*, and *iṣu* all mean 'arrow'. The word should be split as *āropayitā*. The resolution (*parihāra*) is that it means "one who makes [the bow] *adhijya*" (strung). At that very moment of stringing the bow, "he is called the *cāpayitṛ* (the one who makes into a bow) because he makes the *ropa* (the arrow) into a *cāpa* (a bow)"—this is the contradiction. [In this case], after the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to the root *ruh*, the substitution of *p* for *r* occurs according to the rule: "In the case of *ruh*, *p* is substituted for *r* optionally" (*ruhaḥ po’nyatarasyām*). Thus, at the time of stringing the bow, he is so called because he transforms the arrow into a bow.

The word *āpayitā* is to be split as *ca* (and) *āpayitā*. At that very moment, the "attainer" (*āpayitā*)—meaning the one who brings the bow near and places the arrow upon it—[acted]. [The phrase] *purāsanpraśastaveṣā* refers to the Earth-born Śrī, Lakṣmī, who had descended in the form of Sītā; you took her by the hand and married her. In the alternative sense, *sadveṣāḥ* means those possessed of hatred, the enemies; their *kṣiti* is the earth belonging to them, and the *śrī* (prosperity) born therein—you placed that in your hand, meaning you brought it under your control. In the other case, the meaning is that you subdued them.

Facing you, Fortune shall be both turned away and not turned away; she shall partake of gold and yet partake of the forest. Although there is a distinction between these two states, it is a marvel that they are nonetheless non-different.

O Śrī! One who is *abhimukha* (facing you) shall be a possessor of gold (*hiraṇyabhāk*), that is, a possessor of great wealth characterized by gold; but one who is *anabhimukha* (not facing you) shall be a possessor of the forest (*araṇyabhāk*), meaning he shall enter the forest, having fallen from his sovereignty. Thus, although there is indeed a distinction—a difference between these two—in the manner described, [the word] *yadyapi* is used here in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), according to Keśava. Nevertheless, there is non-difference (*abheda*) alone; this is the contradiction (*virodha*). The word *hyabheda* is a compound (*samasta-pada*).

The resolution is that the distinction arises solely from the letters *hi* and *ava*. The sense is that in the two words *hiraṇyabhāk* and *araṇyabhāk*, the difference lies only in the letters *hi* and *a*, since the remaining sequences are identical. This contradiction, based on the identity between word and meaning, is expressed through *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

O moon-faced Mukunda, he who does not find freedom from the bondage of Dāmodara surely causes everyone to marvel when he finds freedom from all worldly joy (or "freedom from the belly," *sadāmodarahitatām*). 1090.

"O Moon-faced Mukunda! He who does not find 'dāmodara-hitatām' (the state of being beneficial to Dāmodara)—here the word is split as *dāmodara-hitatām*—that very person, finding 'dāmoha-rahitatām' (freedom from the delusion of worldly bonds), causes everyone to marvel; thus there is an apparent contradiction (*virodha*). The resolution, however, is that the entire phrase beginning with 'sadāmoda' is a single compound. The sense is this: *san* means excellent; *āmoda* is bliss born from experiencing the auspicious qualities of the Lord. Thus, it means 'finding freedom from that [bliss]'"—no, rather, it means "finding freedom from the absence of such bliss. (That is, he finds the presence of that bliss.)

Then the great bull among the Asuras, having attained a state of supreme delusion with an exceedingly loud cry, met his end before Acyuta while men looked on; yet for them, there was a true liberation.

*Asuramahokṣaḥ* means "the Asura who is a great bull," that is to say, the bull-demon (*vṛṣabhāsura*). This compound follows the pattern of *mahārājadaśaratha*. He has resorted to an excessive (*param*) delusion (*moha*), according to the rule *dvitīyā śrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.24). The sense is that he did not realize that his desire to kill the Lord—who is the delight of Nanda—was itself the cause of his own ruin.

Therefore, having approached with a very loud voice while all people were looking on—while everyone was watching—even though he was devoid of a beautiful liberation (sumokṣa) from Acyuta, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, who was the cause of his own death, he nevertheless attained a beautiful liberation (sumokṣa) beforehand; such is the apparent contradiction.

The resolution is as follows: *asumokṣa* means one who releases (*mokṣayate*) or abandons the vital breaths (*asu*); thus he was one whose liberation (*mokṣa*) or release was excellent (*su*), hence *sumokṣa*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied to the object of the root *muc*, which is listed in the *dhātuvṛtti* among the *curādika* (tenth class) roots with the meaning "to bring to an end" (*avasāne*). Here, "end" (*avasāna*) means casting off (*kṣepa*). Hemacandra states: "The word *mokṣa* [is used] in the sense of supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*), a particular tree, release, and death."

In this context, "atyuccaiḥ" means exceedingly high, that is to say, extremely great because it consists of a collection of many syllables. "Asuramahokṣaḥ" refers to the word *asuramahokṣa*. "Svaraḥ" means well-sounded (*suṣṭhu araḥ*), being devoid of the letter *ra* (*repharahitaḥ*). Then, immediately after that, there is the division: "sa ahaśritaḥ. Here, "maḥ" is the singular ablative case.

Immediately after the letter *ma*, being devoid of the vowel *a* (the syllable *aho*)—that is, being separated from both the vowel and the consonant—it became, for the sake of the beholding men, "asumokṣaḥ"; the sense is that it appeared in the form of the word *asumokṣa*. At the beginning, prior to that, from *acyuta*, there was the word *cyuta* (formed with a past passive participle suffix in the sense of the action), meaning the loss of the vowel *a*; and there was also *sumokṣa*, the word *sumokṣa*, appearing in that manner. This is the intended meaning.

The word *asuramahokṣa* (the great bull among the Asuras), when separated by the letter *ra* from the vowel *a* and the consonant *h*—that is, from the two syllables *ah*—becomes *asumokṣa*; subsequently, being deprived of its initial vowel *a*, it appears as *sumokṣa*. This is the established meaning. This is a case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) blending the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*).
O Moon among mountains, it is a marvel that you have looked with favor upon two men who possess the fortune of stability, yet have disregarded two others who enjoy the lack of such stability. (1092)

*Śvasthiti* means that which has its existence for tomorrow; that is to say, existing tomorrow, or persisting for a long time. *Bhāgya* refers to sovereignty arising from the ripening of auspicious karma; in another sense, it refers to the condition or state of dogs—that is, *bhāgya* in the form of poverty arising from the ripening of inauspicious karma. As Amara states: "Bhāgya is karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious. Upon attaining that [poverty], there is nevertheless the contradiction expressed by the phrase "those who enjoy the fortune of non-existence tomorrow" (*aśvasthitibhāgyajuṣau*).

The "state" (*sthiti*) of horses is their standing or condition; such is the fortune consisting of the sovereignty of horse-riding, which is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical expression) for the sovereignty of elephants and so forth. In the alternative sense, "horse" (*aśva*) means that there is no standing (*sthiti*), implying it is of extremely short duration. One who "enjoys such fortune" (*bhāgyaṃ juṣete*)—meaning one favored by Your glance—obtains the sovereignty of the fourfold army to be experienced for a long time; whereas one neglected by You experiences misfortune in the form of taking refuge with lowly creatures such as dogs, and even that lasts for only a very short time. This is the essential meaning.

Alas! This lofty summit of the king of serpents’ mountain, which was previously renowned for its state as Nīlalohita (Śiva) the Skull-bearer, now attains both a fierce majesty and a non-fierce gentleness. [Commentary: "Lofty" (*udagram*) means elevated. "This" (*adaḥ*) refers to *idam*. It is the "summit" (*agram*) of the "king of serpents’ mountain" (*phaṇirājagireḥ*). "Nīlalohita" is Śiva, and he is the "Skull-bearer" (*kapālī*); his "state" (*bhāvaḥ*) is "renowned" (*prakhyātaḥ*), and that is the "state of being Nīlalohita the Skull-bearer" (*nīlalohitakapālibhāvaḥ*). For that reason—alternatively, in the other sense, there are "renowned rows" (*pālayaḥ*) of "blue" (*nīla*) sapphire gems and "red" (*lohita*) ruby gems.

In that [place] where there is that which is renowned as the blue-and-red skull-bearer (Śiva), by virtue of its existence—that is, its essential nature—the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule "lohitān maṇau" (Pāṇini 5.4.30). Amarasimha states: "The red jewel is *lohitaka*, the ruby (*padmarāga*). The construction is "sphurat" (shining); the meaning is "manifesting. For this very reason, there is the state of being fierce (*ugratva*), which is to say the state of being Rudra and his likeness. Thus, the apparent contradiction is: "he attains both fierceness and non-fierceness" (*anugratām*); the resolution is: "he attains non-fierceness, that is, gentleness (*saumyatām*)."

In one sense, the word *udagram*—meaning "supreme" (*agram*) or "exalted" (*udagram*)—is a compound word; when it is not illuminated by the letter *da*, it attains the state of being *ugra*, meaning it becomes the word *ugra*. This constitutes a contradiction, for [if it were *ugra*], it would lack the two syllables [of *udagram*]. The resolution is as follows: [the term] *anugratām* refers to the state of that which has the collection of letters *gra* following after [the initial *uda-*]; thus, it means the state of being *anu-gra-gram*. This is because the aforementioned letters are present within the word *ugra*.

O Lord, ocean of noble qualities, you always lead a person who is already beset by calamities to further calamities; alas, even one who has not yet resorted to your feet, you consign forever to the shelter of misfortune.

"You cause [him] to be attached to his own feet (*padalagna*) yet not attached to his own feet (*apadalagna*)," this is a contradiction. The resolution is: "always (*sadā*) not attached to calamity (*āpadalagna*)," meaning not dependent on misfortune. Furthermore, "you cause [him] to be always not resting on his feet (*padānāśrita*), unattached to his own steps, yet resting on his feet (*padāśrita*), devoted to his own steps"—this is a contradiction. The resolution is: "always resting on calamity (*āpadāśrita*)," meaning possessed of adversity. "Though you are the leader of Śeṣācala (the serpent-king), you are the leader of the sinless and the immovable; moreover, O Blessed One, though your form is radiant, it is indeed devoid of radiance. (1095)

"There is no contradiction in saying 'you are not the leader of Śeṣācala' [if taken literally], for it is resolved by the meaning 'the leader of the entire (aśeṣā) immovable (acalā) earth. There is a contradiction in saying 'you do not possess a radiant form,' for it is refuted by the sense that 'you possess a form as radiant as the sun (avi-bhānu). The rest is easy to understand."

Though he is as radiant as Mount Meru, he does not shine like Mount Nameru; though he is a mountain for the king of beasts (the lion), he is a mountain for the deer; though he is rich with the dense chanting of the *japa* mantra, he is indeed devoid of *japa*—this is a marvel! 1096.
It is radiant with *nameru* trees, which are trees that provide shade; and it is purifying even for the unborn Brahmā—this is the resolution of the apparent contradiction.

Though cool, he is not cold; though pure, he is black; though smooth, he is indeed not subtle; and though fragrant, he is devoid of scent—such is the one who dwells upon the summit of the king of mountains, which possesses two tongues [fire and water]. 1097.

"Śiśiraḥ" (cool) yet "aśītakaḥ" (not cool)—this is a contradiction, for "aśītakaḥ" means one devoid of cold. The analysis of the compound is: "one for whom cold (śītam), that is, the quality of coldness, does not exist. The suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule "śeṣādvibhāṣā. He is "dayāśītalaḥ" (cool with compassion) yet "analasaḥ" (not lazy); this is resolved by the rule "śītoṣṇābhyāṃ kāriṇi," whereby the suffix *kan* is added to the word "śīta" in the sense of "one who acts [in that manner]. Amara states: "ālasyaḥ, śītakaḥ, alasaḥ, anuṣṇaḥ" (lazy, cool, idle, not warm). Furthermore, "śuciḥ" (pure) yet "asitaḥ" (black)—this is a contradiction, for "asitaḥ" means not white.

He is pure (*śuci*), with evil dispelled (*apahatapāpman*); for that very reason, he is "not black" (*asita*) and "unbound" (*abaddha*), meaning free from the bondage of karma; thus he is composed (*samāhita*). Regarding the word *sinoti*, which means "to bind," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object. Although he is smooth (*ślakṣṇa*) and lean (*kṛśa*), he is "not subtle" (*asūkṣma*) and "not thin" (*akṛśa*); this constitutes an apparent contradiction (*virodha*). This is resolved by taking *ślakṣṇa* to mean "sweet-spoken," *asūkṣma* to mean "not deceitful," or understanding it as "great" (*mahān*).

"Ślakṣṇa means soft, thin, or slender; ślakṣṇa also means one who speaks kindly," according to the *Amara-kośa*. "Sūkṣma refers to deceit, the inner self (adhyātma), or the atom (aṇu); as a tri-lingual adjective, it means small or minute," according to the *Medinī-kośa*. There is an apparent contradiction in describing him as both "fragrant" (*surabhi*)—meaning possessing a sweet scent—and yet "devoid of fragrance" (*gandhaśūnya*), meaning lacking the quality of scent. This is resolved by the fact that "manohara" (charming) and "anavalepa" (free from pride/arrogance) are used here. According to the *Viśva-kośa*, starting from "surabhi refers to the campaka flower" up to "it also means fragrant and charming"; and "gandha refers to sulphur, fragrance, a trace, relation, and pride."

O King of the Unblinking Eye (the Sun), though you are imperturbable and powerful, you do not afflict those who are weak; it is a marvel, O Soul of All, that you cut through the entire web of virtues of the wise fishers.

O Soul of All! You are the king of the *animiṣas* (gods), yet you are the king of fish (*matsyarāja*) who is neither fickle nor a fish—this is the apparent contradiction (*virodha*). You are the sovereign of the gods (*devādhirāja*), yet your character is unwavering (*acañcalaśīla*)—this is the resolution (*avirodha*). [As Amara states: "The two *animiṣas* are the gods and fish. [And Medinī, beginning with] "Fickle (*capala*) refers to mercury and a fish," continues with "it is also used for the loquacious, the tremulous, and the moving. Furthermore, although you are powerful (*prabala*), you do not oppress the weak, tiny fish (*śakulārbhaka*)—this is the contradiction. For it is the very nature of the fish species that the strong should oppress the weak.

The sense is: "because of the absence of that. The resolution is: as the Lord of all, you are more powerful than everything; thus, you do not oppress those who are weaker than yourself, such as the four-faced Brahmā and others. "Sudhīvarāḥ" means excellent fishermen (*sudhī-vara*); the contradiction lies in the statement that you cut the net of qualities (*guṇa-jāla*) made of thread belonging to those mature fishermen. [In reality,] there is no such contradiction, for you sever the bond of *prakṛti* belonging to the best of the wise (*sudhī-vara*). Thus, the absence of that [contradiction] is established.

O hero of the Raghus! In the fire of the prowess of your arms, you formerly caused Virādha to flourish (*edhayase*)—that is, you made him like fuel (*edham*) or wood (*idhmam*)—yet you did not cause him to thrive (*naidhayase*); this is the apparent contradiction. [The resolution is as follows: Regarding the word *purā*, according to the rule *puri luṅ cāsme*, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the past; thus, "you caused Virādha to flourish" means you caused him to grow. However, the resolution through a shift in interpretation is: "you did not cause him to flourish," but rather you consumed him in the fire of the prowess of your arms. You nourish (*āśayase*) [the virtuous] and destroy (*nāśayase*) the flesh-eaters and those with donkey-like faces, O hero of the Raghus! O hero of the Raghus! You nourish Virādha in the fire of the prowess of your arms—you made him like fuel or wood—but you do not cause him to thrive; rather, you consumed him in the fire of the prowess of your arms. This is the resolution through a distinction in the application of the meaning.

"By them"—meaning by those flesh-eating, meat-consuming night-stalkers such as the *kaṅka* (herons) and jackals; the verb "you cause to eat" (*āśayase*) from the previous verse is to be supplied here as well. Thus, there is a contradiction: "you do not cause [them] to eat" (*na āśayase*), meaning you do not cause them to consume [the food]. Yet, "you cause the leaders of the donkeys"—namely Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and others—"to perish" (*nāśayase*), meaning you destroy them. Then follows the resolution: "you cause [them] to be eaten by the flesh-eaters," as explained previously.

By the rule "gatibuddhipratyavasāna" and others, the carnivorous beings (*kravyād*), who are the agents (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative sense of the root *aś* (to eat), become the objects (*karman*) in the causative sense (*ṇau*). As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *kravyād* may refer to a demon (*rakṣas*) in the masculine, while in other genders it refers to meat-eaters. The distinction here is that the contradiction is demonstrated by two homophonous verbal forms (*tiṅanta-śabda*).

O son of Daśaratha, you who protect the worlds with a compassionate mind—do you not protect [us]? Having been consecrated, O king of men, that majesty of yours shone forth, causing this wonder. (1100)

"O son of Daśaratha! You, being compassionate-minded, protect and guard the worlds (*jaganti rakṣasi pālayasi*); [yet you do not protect], which is a contradiction. The resolution, however, is that the singular number in *rakṣasi* is intended to signify the class (*jāti*). Thus, the construction is with the remote negative particle (*nañ*) as "not being compassionate-minded toward the *rākṣasa* species" (*rākṣasajātau na dayamānamanāḥ*). This is similar to the usage in the verse: "Not making vocal sounds through excessive weight, nor vocal sounds stained by the cessation of flowers," where one says "not cessation" (*na virāmam*) [meaning "without cessation"].

The meaning is that he was practicing cruelty, according to the expression "he formed a cruel intent toward a crow. Regarding the phrase "protecting the worlds": the implication is that if your mind were compassionate toward the race of *rākṣasas*, how could there be protection of the world? "He, your lordship," who is thus the destroyer of the *rākṣasa* clan, having received his consecration (*kṛtābhiṣeka*) at Sāketa—that is, having attained the royal coronation—shone (*rarāja*), meaning he blazed forth. This constitutes a *virodha* (paradox), as it says "he did not shine" (*na rarāja*).

A "king of men" (*nararāja*) is one who is the king (*rājā*) of men (*narāṇām*); the resolution of this is the vocative address "O King of Men" (*he narendra*). This contradiction is based on a pun (*śleṣa*) between words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) and nominal suffixes (*subanta*), and thus it differs from the previous type.
Thus has the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (apparent contradiction), based on *śleṣa* (paronomasia), been elaborated.
This very Pure One moves as it does not move; it is far away and likewise it is near. It is within and without this world simultaneously—that is the wondrous Supreme Brahman.
In this regard:
it moves, and it does not move; it is far, and it is near;
it is within all this, and it is outside of all this.

Thus the meaning of the scripture has been considered. For instance, that is the Supreme Brahman. The word "simultaneously" (yugapat) applies everywhere: "It moves and it does not move; It trembles and It does not tremble"—this is the contradiction. "It is known as if very swift, yet in reality It does not tremble"—this is the resolution, because it is consistent with the preceding mantra: "The One, unmoving, is swifter than the mind. "That Brahman is far away and likewise near"—this is the contradiction.

"This designation of being far and near belongs to the All-pervading One itself, depending on the nature of the person—whether demonic or divine"—this is the resolution. And the venerable Śaunaka said:
For those who have turned their backs on Govinda and whose minds are attached to sense objects,
that supreme Brahman remains far, far away.
For those men whose minds are absorbed in Govinda through the state of being identical with Him,
and who have renounced sense objects, that [state] should be understood as being present in their very presence.

Thus [it is said]. That Brahman exists simultaneously both within and without this world; hence there is an apparent contradiction, because in the world one does not observe people situated inside a house to be outside at that very same time. The resolution, however, is that such a possibility exists due to its all-pervasiveness. Likewise, it is heard in the Taittirīyaka: "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that, both within and without. That Brahman is "wondrous," meaning it is of a marvelous nature.

This is a pure *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction) that is slightly infused with the scent of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). The Veda itself is intended to demonstrate the path of such ornaments; therefore, the very meaning expressed in the Veda has been composed here [as an example].

This is what must be understood here: where the particle *api* indicates contradiction (*virodha*), in that case the contradiction is verbal (*śābda*); elsewhere, however, it is logical (*ārtha*). This is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) of the ancient authorities. In this regard, although the verbal nature of the contradiction does not consist in its being an object of the cognition produced by words—since nothing other than the relation between the qualifier and the qualified ever appears in a verbal cognition—it is nevertheless so designated.

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as "the three are also non-three," since the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) serves as the relation when the negative particle is construed with the meaning of the subsequent word, and since that very [counter-correlativity] constitutes the meaning of the term "contradiction" (*virodha*), its manifestation occurs precisely as a relation. This is because such an account does not apply to cases like "even while asleep, he is awake. Nor can it be argued that even there, through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the cognition is "the sleeper is non-different from one who possesses wakefulness which is contradictory to sleepiness"; for this is contrary to experience. Thus, the aforementioned systematic arrangement remains untenable.

Regarding this, they say: in examples of contradiction such as "Even while asleep, he is awake; here even the three are not three," when two properties—such as being asleep and being awake—are first presented by two words, the contradiction residing in them is also recalled through the cognition of their relationship, aided by the presence of the word "api" (even).

Immediately thereafter, because the causal complex for obstructing cognition is more powerful, the thought "these two properties are contradictory" arises—either mentally or through verbal expression. Due to this obstruction, the cognition of non-difference between the sleeping and waking states does not arise; consequently, the comprehension of syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) occurs by taking up the second meaning manifested by the second power (*śakti*), but not the contradictory meaning. As for the ancient masters (*prāñcaḥ*), they hold that although the cognition of contradiction—which has its roots loosened—subsides, it nevertheless serves as a cause of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) by virtue of being the domain of the poet’s creative intent (*kavi-saṃrambha*).

The moderns, however, maintain that without the manifestation of two meanings, even the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*) cannot occur; therein, one meaning is the arouser of the contradiction, while the second is the object of the comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*). This is true; however, regarding the second meaning which is the object of the comprehension of the syntactic connection, even though it is different from the arouser of the contradiction, it appears as non-different through the superimposition of non-difference based on *śleṣa* (punning homophony).

And thus, although there is a comprehension of the connection by taking the second meaning—which is not contradictory—the contradiction itself approaches the mind as another cognition, like one who has fainted and is now breathing, because the contradictory meaning that was its own locus has not ceased entirely. For this very reason, it is said to be "wonderful" (*camatkārī*). Indeed, that which has ceased entirely is not capable of producing wonder; nor does anything become an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) without generating wonder. Therefore, the root of the cognition of contradiction is not at all weakened.

Nor do they say that there is an absolute cessation [of the world]. Now, one might object: "In the employment of particles such as *api*, a verbal contradiction appears; therefore, [your position] remains inconsistent. If this is argued on the grounds that in the system of the Grammarians (*śābdika*), particles (*nipāta*) are not admitted to possess denotative power (*śakti*), we reply: no. For established indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) and established suggestion (*nirūḍhadyotanā*) are equal in rank to denotative power itself.
Now, the figure of speech *virodha* (contradiction) cannot be intended to exist between two universals (*jāti*) or between two substances (*dravya*).
O Lord, when the splendor of your magnanimity shone forth, even the celestial tree became mere grass;
and in the brilliance of your majesty, Mount Kailāsa appeared as if it were a mountain of gold.

In my own verse beginning with "kusumāni śarāś... and in another's verse beginning with "candro bāḍabo duḥkhite hṛdi," there is only the manifestation of *rūpaka* (metaphor) based on superimposition (*āropa*). If contradiction were asserted even when superimposition exists, then why would that same [contradiction] not be asserted in the case of "the face is the moon"?

Nor should it be argued that, because the entirety of the domain of *rūpaka* (metaphor) is pervaded by contradiction (*virodha*), the latter—having found scope in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—acts as an exception (*apavāda*) to *rūpaka* within its own domain, resulting in the latter’s loss of subject matter; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the very *virodha* you desire not being established in such instances as: "The celestial tree is a blade of grass, Mount Kailāsa is Mount Meru, the arrows are flowers, the bracelets of lotus-stalks are heaps of forest fires, the moon is the submarine fire, and the river on Śiva’s crest is the Yamunā. This is true.

For in this collection of ornaments (*alaṃkārasamudaya*), it is beyond dispute that whichever figure among them ascends to the path of aesthetic wonder (*sahṛdayacamatkṛti*) for the connoisseur, that alone is the ornament in that context. Thus, although there is a contradiction in metaphors (*rūpaka*) such as "The face is the moon," nevertheless, that contradiction is not what is intended to be conveyed there. Rather, for the purpose of perceiving all the qualities residing in the moon—such as its power to produce delight—in the face, the non-difference from the moon itself is the intended meaning; therefore, that alone is the source of aesthetic charm, and not the contradiction.

On the contrary, even if a contradiction exists, because it is not conducive to the intended meaning, it is as good as non-existent and thus does not constitute a figure of speech; for mere existence is of no consequence. In instances such as "The celestial tree is grass, the flowers are arrows," since what is intended to be expressed is the extreme wonder of the Lord’s magnanimity and the condition of the woman separated from her lover, the implied contradiction—though internalized—shines forth in accordance with that intention, and thus it is indeed a figure of speech.

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of *rūpaka* (metaphor), contradiction (*virodha*)—though not intended as such—might fail to be an *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure); whereas in the case of actual contradiction, such as in "The celestial tree is grass; the flowers are arrows," since identity must necessarily be intended for the manifestation of contradiction, it would follow that this is a case of *rūpaka*. This objection cannot stand, because the definition of *rūpaka* must include the condition of being unaccompanied by the intention of contradiction.

Alternatively, since non-difference (*abheda*)—which is employed here for the purpose of manifesting contradiction—is devoid of aesthetic charm (*acamatkāritva*), its status as the figure of speech *rūpaka* is inappropriate, because aesthetic charm alone is the very life-force (*jīvātu*) of an ornament (*alaṃkāra*). This is the direction [of the argument]; the detailed treatment, however, is found elsewhere.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Contradiction (*virodha*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Peculiar Causation (*vibhāvanā*):
"Peculiar Causation is the production of an effect even in the absence of its cause. (98)
The meaning is that *vibhāvanā* (the "manifestation") is the production of an effect as presented through its co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the absence of its cause. As it has been said:
"Even when there is a negation of the action, the manifestation of the result is *vibhāvanā*.

Here, by the word "action" (*kriyā*), the cause is intended. In this case, although a contradiction appears on the surface when the production of an effect is described as co-occurring with the absence of its cause, that contradiction is resolved by the postulation of another cause.

O jewel of the serpent mountain, alas! While people are merely gazing upon it, you bind and drag away their mental net—which is exceedingly restless toward sense objects even without a physical net. (1103)

For here, although the net is the cause of binding and dragging, even when binding and dragging are presented as occurring despite its absence, they ultimately result—though seemingly contradictory at first glance—in being caused by the beauty of the Lord’s divine form.

Now, in this case, the production of a particular effect is what is being demonstrated; yet the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of that which is understood to be its cause is not perceived. And as for that whose causal absence is perceived, the production of that effect has certainly not been demonstrated. Furthermore, what is intended here is the binding and pulling [of the object]—that is, its stabilization and subjugation—and not the grasping of a tether.

If it is argued that the "net" (*jāla*) is not the cause for the Lord’s acts of making [beings] immobile and subjugating them through the mental net, but rather for the binding and capturing of fish, deer, and so forth—this is not so; for the primary meanings of "binding" and "attracting" are *nahan* (tying) and *grahaṇa* (seizing), whereas the secondary meanings are making immobile and subjugating.

When the concealment of difference has been achieved through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on the similarity between those two—the secondary and the primary—the net, which is the cause for catching fish, deer, and so forth, becomes the cause for immobilizing and subjugating [the object]. And in the absence of that [concealment], there is no fault here, because of the presentation of immobilization and subjugation as being identified with the effect.

And thus, in this alaṃkāra, throughout all its varieties, the figure of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—consisting primarily of the identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) [of two things]—remains as its vitalizing principle. Consequently, there occurs a final resolution by taking up one limb of two similar objects—which are effectively unified like a single mass of milk-rice (*pāyasa*)—through a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the absence of a cause related to the other limb.

And therein, the causal factor (*kāryāṃśa*) exists solely as that which is sublated by its opposite, namely the absence of the cause (*kāraṇābhāva*), and not as the sublater; for the causal factor is imagined (*kalpita*), whereas the absence of the cause is established by its very nature (*svabhāvasiddha*). For this very reason, the causal factor culminates in another form. And for this same reason, it differs from the figure of speech "Contradiction" (*virodhālaṃkāra*), which consists of two opposing factors of equal strength. Thus it has been said: "In the figure of 'Vibhāvanā', the emergence of the effect appears as being sublated by the negation of the cause; in 'Virodha', however, there is a mutual sublation."

Thus they say. In this very illustrative verse, when the first half is read as "Indeed, the mind is exceedingly restless even without a net; alas, it is a net of [unblinking] eyes," *rūpaka* (poetic identification/metaphor) stands as the vitalizing element (*anuprāṇayitṛ*) of this ornament (*alaṃkāra*). For this very reason, the statement in the *Rasagaṅgādharagrantha*—"In *vibhāvanā*, the mere cognition of a superimposed identity alone is the vitalizer; and that is sometimes by means of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), and sometimes by means of *rūpaka*"—is also consistent.

Therefore, it should be noted that it was previously stated in this very context that, for the most part, we maintain that the *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consisting of the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāna*) exists as the vitalizing principle (*anuprāṇaka*).
This *vibhāvanā* (poetic figure of "causation without a cause") is of two kinds: that with a stated cause and that with an unstated cause. Of these, the first is as follows:
"O Lord, for the daughter of the ocean who constantly embraces you—your body as radiant as a blue lotus—the dark hue [previously] on her breast was due to the application of musk."

For here, the application of musk-paste is the cause for the dark-blue hue of the Ocean’s daughter’s breasts; yet, even in its absence, the blueness being described—though seemingly contradictory—is resolved as being caused by the Lord’s embrace. Since the Lord’s embrace is mentioned, this is an instance of [the figure] *upāttanimitta* (where the cause is explicitly stated). The second type, however, has already been illustrated by the example "even without a net," because the beauty of the Lord’s divine form—which is the cause for drawing in the net of the mind and the eyes—is not mentioned there. Or, for example: [Example omitted in source] In this case, the cause—the excellence of the Lord’s beauty—is not mentioned. Thus, it is an instance of *anupāttanimitta* (where the cause is not explicitly stated).
