Placing you—who are eternally free from collyrium—into her other eye, which is like the mountain of collyrium, Lakṣmī shines forth with eyes that are dark and tender, even though she herself is devoid of collyrium. 1105.

The ontological reality is that [the eye] is not collyrium, nor is it non-collyrium, but is distinct from collyrium, being free from the taint of karma; for the Śruti declares, "It is partless and stainless" (*niṣkalaṃ nirañjanam*). While *nirañjanā* means "devoid of collyrium for the eyes," its ontological reality is "devoid of the taint of karma. Here, although she possesses dark eyes even without collyrium, the cause—namely, her natural state—is expressed by the phrase "and she is this dark-eyed one" (*taṃ ceyam asitekṣaṇā*). Since that cause is not explicitly stated [as the reason for the darkness], this is a case of *vibhāvanā* (poetic fancy) where the cause is left unstated.
The second [type of] vibhāvanā is considered to be the production of an effect even when there is an incompleteness of causes.

The meaning is that "demonstration" refers to the production of an effect even when there is an absence of completeness among the causes—that is, when there is a deficiency in either the property delimiting causality (*hetutāvacchedakadharma*) or the relation delimiting causality (*hetutāvacchedakasambandha*).
In that regard, regarding the lack of dharma:
O lotus-eyed one, my heart is even harder than a ball of black iron; yet it is a marvel that you melt it with the cool, spreading glances from the ocean of your pitcher-like breasts. (1106)

In this instance, regarding the goal of softening a heart that is extremely hard, the deficiency of the glances' emission consists in their lack of sharpness and other such qualities. Regarding the deficiency of connection (*saṃbandhavaikalya*), as in: "O jewel on the head of the serpent-king (Śeṣa), the pollen of the lotus-feet of Your Majesty, though not touching the eyes of Your devotees, alas, causes them to well up with tears! (1107)

"Bāṣpāyate" means it causes tears to flow. Here, the deficiency in the completeness of the dust—which is the cause for the emission of tears—consists in the lack of contact with the form [of the eyes].

According to Daṇḍin, however, this is *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation). For, in the first example, the extraordinary greatness (*mahāmahimatva*) of the Lord’s glances is conveyed, while in the second example, that of His foot-dust is conveyed; such is his definition.
When there is an observation of the deficiency of qualities, genus, actions, and so forth,
for the very purpose of indicating a specific excellence, that is intended as *viśeṣokti* (the figure of speech of "peculiar assertion").

Thus [ends the verse]. The meaning of the *kārikā* is as follows: for the purpose of showing or making known the excellence of power and so forth belonging to a particular subject under discussion, the "display of deficiency"—that is, the presentation of the lack of qualities, genera, actions, and by the word "etcetera," substances—which demonstrates their uselessness for the accomplishment of the effect, is the figure of speech named *viśeṣokti*. However, following Dīkṣita, we have shown that even the deficiency of sharpness and so forth constitutes a case of *vibhāvanā*, as it takes the form of the absence of a specific cause.
The third is *vibhāvanā*:
the third [type] is *vibhāvanā*, which is the production of an effect even when there is an obstacle.

That by which something is obstructed is an obstruction (*pratibandha*), and that which causes obstruction is an obstructer (*pratibandhaka*). When the effect arises despite the presence of an obstructer, this is the third type of *vibhāvanā*.

O Wielder of the Discus, it is wonderful that those who possess the splendor of the indeclinables shine forth as virtuous beings, even though they do not fall [into lower realms] because they have taken refuge in you, the beginning of all, and do not function as non-sentient entities.

O Cakradhara! Because certain words—namely, those beginning with *ca* (and so forth)—which belong to the group starting with *uccaiḥ* (high) and *cādi* (the *ca*-group), do not have the function of denoting non-substance (*asattvavṛtti*), meaning they do not denote non-substances, but rather denote substances (*dravyavācin*); therefore, they are not *nipātas*, being devoid of the technical designation *nipāta*. The point is that since the rule "those beginning with *ca* [are *nipātas*] when not denoting substance" prescribes the designation *nipāta* only for those *ca*-words that signify non-substance, that designation does not apply to those which denote substances.

This is indeed logical. But this is marvelous: that those who are called "possessors of imperishable fortune," meaning they possess imperishable glory (avyaya-śrī) or imperishable state (avyaya-bhāva), should shine forth as such. The sense is that it is truly a wonder that they possess imperishability when there is not even the designation of "particle" (nipāta)—which is the very cause for being called "imperishable. For the authors of the Sūtras prescribe the designation "imperishable" for particles by the rule: *svarādinipātamavyayam*.

The resolution [of the compound] is as follows: "uccādim" means the beginning (ādim) among the high (ucceṣu)—that is, among those who have ascended to exalted positions such as the Four-faced One (Brahmā), or the beginning of the high ones. Alternatively, through the power of the identity between the word and its meaning, it is understood as "the wheel (cakra) and so forth," by virtue of the vocative address "O Cakradhara" (O Wielder of the Discus). Having taken refuge in You, those knowers of Brahman, whose nature is goodness (sattva), do not become "non-sattva-natured" (asattvavṛttayaḥ); that is, they do not become such, but rather remain indeed of a sattvic nature.

By means of two negations, the possibility of its existing as a non-entity is excluded. As Vāmana said: "When a negation that was possible is itself negated, there are two negations. [Thus: "The Puruṣa is indeed the great Lord; he is the impeller of sattva."

The meaning is that, according to the manner stated above, those who take refuge in You, the impeller of the quality of *sattva*, become exclusively *sāttvika*. For this very reason, they are "not fallen" (*anipātāḥ*), meaning they do not undergo the fall characterized by the intermediate or downward paths of the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* types; rather, as it is said, "Those established in *sattva* go upward," they possess the highest destination. And for this same reason, they are "possessors of imperishable glory" (*avyayalakṣmībhājaḥ*), meaning they enjoy eternal sovereignty in the form of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

"They shine" means they blaze by virtue of their eternally uncontracted knowledge. Here, even though there exists an obstacle in the form of not being a particle (*nipāta*), the production of the effect in the form of being an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is described; thus, the definition is consistent. This [verse] is embellished by the figure of speech *samā* (simile), which is enlivened by hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) rooted in the identification [of two things] based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (punning).

Just as even those who dwell in dense moonstones are overcome by heat when they are far removed from the consecration of the compassion of the great serpent-king who bears the burden of the earth, so too do afflictions overwhelm men.

Here, despite the presence of the obstructing condition consisting of the state of being situated within a dense mass of extremely cold moonstones, there occurs the production of the effect characterized by the suppression caused by heat. This is an instance mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Just as when the serpent-king, his head raised high, moves through the sky-path named Vinatānandana upon his own crest, he experiences great delight; oh, how wonderful! (1110)

Regarding the phrase "vinatānandane": it refers to him whose name is "the delighter of Vinatā. Alternatively, *vaihāyasa* means a multitude of birds (*vihāyas*); the suffix *añ* is applied here according to the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ* to form a collective noun. *Tasya rāṭ* means the king of those; thus, the meaning is Garuḍa, the king of birds.

"Vaihāyasa" means those who exist in the supreme sky or atmosphere, such as Ananta, Garuḍa, and others—both the eternally liberated (*nityamukta*) and the liberated (*mukta*). Their king is the Lord Śrīnivāsa, the sovereign of all gods; "in him" means upon his own head, that is, on the upper part, or the summit portion. While he moves there, the best of the mountain-dwelling serpents—that is, the serpent Śeṣa—is the actual state of affairs. "With uplifted head" means with raised hoods.

On its side, the mountain with its lofty peaks experiences great exultation—an immeasurable bliss—and a radiance through its festivals (*mahas*). Here, despite the presence of an obstacle in the form of the movement of Garuḍa above it, the production of the effect—namely, the possession of great exultation through the raising of its hoods by the preeminent serpent—is described. The identification based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as before.
Or rather,
O Blessed One, even though one has always been brought to this state of extreme and noble passion, for those who do not turn toward you, the great burning heat of existence brings about utter defeat.

O Blessed One! [He wards off] people who are not facing You. The word *saḥ* (he) is to be split as *dāhāritamaḥ*; this term *saḥ* connects with what follows later. *Dāhāritamaḥ* means "the greatest enemy of burning" (*atiśayena ariḥ aritamaḥ*), that is to say, one who is an extreme adversary or an obstacle. Even when there is attachment—meaning even upon contact—with a gem that is exceedingly (*atimātram*) or excessively (*atyartham*) noble (*udāraḥ*, i.e., great), [he wards them off].

That very great burning heat produced by fire, which is renowned for its extreme sharpness and arises from purity (śuci), is overcome—that is, surpassed. Ah! The sense is that the emergence of the effect, namely the production of burning, is astonishing even when there exists the presence of a jewel that obstructs burning. However, the resolution [of the pun] is as follows: *sadā* means "always"; *hāritam* means "captivating," for Amara states, "the words *valgu*, *vāma*, and *hāri* denote the beautiful. Thus, it is always captivating.

Even when there is excessive joy and intense delight in the embrace and clinging of beautiful women, the burning heat of that existence—the cycle of worldly rebirth (*saṃsāra*) which is exceedingly impure and unholy—prevails. The meaning is this: the heat of *saṃsāra* overcomes those people who, though enjoying the embrace of most lovely women, have turned their faces away from the Lord. Or as it is said: "When the great-bodied serpent-king stands upon the forest ground before one's very eyes, alas, men flee far away in extreme terror of the dense forest and its creatures. (1112)

On the forest ground, which possesses great extent and a body with a massive hood—meaning, on that serpent-mountain Śeṣādri, whose wings have a vast expansion and fullness; this is the reality. "When situated in the region before his eyes" means when he was seen while remaining very close by. The implication is: for the sake of serving Śrīnivāsa, for the pilgrims who had come from a very great distance.

The most terrible and exceedingly fierce terror caused by the creatures of the dense forest of existence—the fear produced by predatory beings among those living entities born within that thicket—flee far away and run off. Aha! When a great-bodied, large-hooded, and mighty venomous serpent is seen right before one on the ground of the great forest, the fear of the predatory forest creatures vanishes; the sense is that this is a marvel, because the very sight of it is the cause of such great fear.

The resolution, however, is profound and difficult: that which is *bhava*, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), from that arises what is born of the profound existence; the word *tu* is used for emphasis and connects with the subsequent clause. *Sādhvasaṃ* means fear; it indeed flows far away. For travelers, by the mere description of Śeṣādri, the fear produced by *saṃsāra* is cast off. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *gahana* [denotes] both forest and suffering."

In the word *bhavajantu*, the letter *na* is an optional *parasavarṇa* (homorganic substitute) for the *anusvāra*, according to the rule *vā padāntasya*. Here, despite the presence of the obstacle consisting in the sight of great beasts of prey (*mahāvyāla*), the accomplishment of the travelers’ goal—namely, their removal from the fear of wild and cruel forest creatures—is described as being animated by a metaphorical identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
The fourth is the "elimination" (vibhāvanā); the fourth elimination would be the production of an effect from a non-cause.
The production of an effect from what is not a cause—that is, from something distinct from a cause—is the fourth *vibhāvanā*.
Dispelling the darkness of doubt as to whether he protects me or not, the Lord of the Mountain emits the moonlight of his row of teeth from his serpent-like tongue.

Here, since the production of moonlight from the row of teeth—which is distinct from the cause of [actual] moonlight—is described, there is conformity with the definition [of *utprekṣā*]. The resolution is that the smile, made smooth by the rays of the teeth, is identified (*adhyavasita*) as being moonlight itself.

Just as Śrī quickly embraces the Blessed One, covering the Kaustubha gem with her palm, she becomes one whose face is bent down by the flashes of lightning that leak from the hollows between her fingers.

Here, the radiance of the Kaustubha gem, covered by the palm of the hand, is perceived as being like lightning because it flickers as it slips through the openings between the fingers at every moment; thus, the birth of lightning from the Kaustubha—distinct from its usual cause—is described.

Just as from the Mountain of Gold (Kanakāhārya)—which is another name for Śeṣādri, as we have stated more than once—there arose thousands of mountains with magnificent peaks of brass (ārakūṭa) that were unremovable; and from those [brass mountains] arose the date-palm trees, which bear exceedingly wonderful and excellent fruit. From "Kanakāhārya" [meaning] the Golden Mountain, [arose] thousands of mountains with "udārakūṭāḥ"—that is, those whose peaks (kūṭa) are made of excellent brass (ārakūṭa), meaning bell-metal (pittala). As Amara states: "Rīti is feminine, and ārakūṭa is masculine. Thousands of such unremovable mountains arose.

In this context, "ahāryāḥ" means incapable of being taken away by anyone; "udārāḥ" means great; and "kūṭāḥ" refers to peaks. Thus, from those "arakūṭāhāryebhyaḥ"—meaning from those [peaks] that cannot be taken away—and from those "udāraśṛṅgebhyaḥ," thousands of "kharjūranagāḥ" have arisen, meaning silver mountains, or as the phrase suggests, "kharjūra" trees have arisen. Regarding the word "kharjūra," the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *kharjūra* applies to silver and a threshing floor (*khala*); it is masculine for a scorpion and neuter or masculine for two types of trees. And the *Amara-kośa* states: "The words *naga* and *aga* denote both mountains and trees."

The meaning is that those [trees] produce copper, which is the most excellent (*variṣṭha*) among dates, horses, and copper. The verb *phal* (to bear fruit) is also used with an object, as seen in such usage as: "by the rays of the sun, beautiful like parrots, bearing the fiery luster produced by the touch of the hot-rayed one. In the alternative sense, they bear fruit in such a way as to be most excellent (*variṣṭha*), meaning they display fruits that are exceedingly large (*uru*) or best (*vara*). [The lexicon states: "The word *variṣṭha* refers to black pepper; it is neuter when meaning copper, masculine when meaning the *tittiri* bird, and used in three genders when meaning 'excellent' (*vara*) or 'great' (*uru*)."

Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. Here, the effect—namely, their production—is described as arising from causes such as the Mountain of Gold (*Kanakācala*) and the Mountain of Brass (*Pittalācala*), which are actually the Mountain of Silver (*Rajatācala*) and so forth; therefore, this too is a case of *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit of causelessness). Its distinction from the preceding [type] consists in its being mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia), its being mixed with the *mālādīpaka* (chain-illumination) to be described later, and its possessing the form of a series (*mālārūpatva*).
Just as the branches that have grown forth without restraint from the udumbara trees on the high Nāgadharā mountain, so too has the fruit of Hārīti emerged from them.

From the high Nāgadharā mountain, the Sīsa (lead) peak, the *udumbara* trees—meaning copper trees—have emerged without restraint; this constitutes the apparent contradiction (*virodha*). The resolution (*parihāra*) is that from the mountain of serpents (*uragācala*), trees known by the alternative name *jantuphala* have grown. Regarding the term *nāga*, it begins with: "In the neuter, *nāga* refers to mercury, lead, and a particular musical instrument," and continues: "*Nāga* [is used] for a serpent, an elephant, a person of cruel conduct, and a cloud. Furthermore, "*Udumbara* refers to the threshold, a species of tree, and also a cluster of trees."

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *tāmra* is masculine when referring to a type of leprosy, but neuter when referring to copper. From those *tāmra* trees, *ayaśśākhāḥ*—meaning branches of iron (*ayas*)—arose; yet these were *prāyaśśākhāḥ*, meaning excellent branches made of the finest metal (*prāya* = *śreṣṭha*). This constitutes the apparent contradiction (*virodha*). The resolution (*parihāra*) is that *prāya* means "abundantly," so branches were produced in great abundance. From these branches, *rītiphalaṃ*—the fruit of bell-metal (*pittala*)—emerged.

"Hā" is used in the sense of wonder (*āścarya*). "Hārī" means that which is charming in its manner, or that which shines forth through its charm; as Amara states: "Avalgu, vāma, hārī, and śāli [are synonyms]," and "The word *iti* is used for cause, context, manner, and so forth, as well as for completion. Medinī states: "*Iti* is used for cause and manifestation. The resolution is that the fruit has arisen. Here too, everything is exactly as in the previous example. The distinction, however, is the intermingling with the *ekāvalī* (single-string) ornament.
Or rather, this is a most extraordinary marvel: that from the foot of the Lord, who is as generous with light as a forest of crimson lotuses, the Gaṅgā arose to purify the world.

The Gaṅgā was born from the foot—meaning the ray and the foot—of the divine Sun (Bhānu), who is a generous donor of the luster of the forest of red lotuses; in the other sense, she was born from the foot of the divine, radiant, and glorious Lord (Bhagavān). Here, the effect—the birth of the Gaṅgā—is described as having arisen from the Sun’s foot even though it was not her cause. Her distinction from previous examples lies in her being blended with the poetic figure of *hetu* (poetic causation) which is about to be discussed.
The fifth [type of] *vibhāvanā* is when the production of an effect occurs from something contradictory; that is the fifth *vibhāvanā*. For example:
A certain lion among gods, tossing up the weight of the joy of the female elephants belonging to the mountain-king, the lord of the Kumbhīnasas, alas, wiped away the fear of the elephant.

"Nirjara" means ageless, and he is also a "siṃha" (lion); in another sense, this refers to Śrīnivāsa, the best of gods. "Kumbhinī" refers to a female elephant or the earth, according to Amara’s lexicon: "Gaurī, Ilā, Kumbhinī, and Kṣamā [are synonyms for the earth]. "Ullāsabhāram" means an abundance of radiance or an excess of joy. Here, because the ageless lion—who is the opposite of the one who causes the kumbhinī to exult—produces the effect of removing that exultation and dispelling the fear caused by it, the definition of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is followed.
Just as a lion cub delights a multitude of elephants and mountains, it too, alas, terrifies rutting elephants by its very roars alone.

The "Nāgāvanībhṛt" (the mountain that supports serpents) refers to the king of elephants; however, the actual state of affairs is that it is Śeṣādri (the Mountain of Śeṣa). It loudly delights the multitude of lion cubs (*kesarikiśoraka-nikāya*). That multitude of lion cubs, too, by their very roars, [overcomes] the elephants (*kariṇaḥ*)—specifically those that are "split," meaning intoxicated (*prabhinnān mattān*); for Amara states in his list of synonyms for specific types of elephants: "‘Prabhinna,’ ‘garjita,’ and ‘matta’ [are used for an elephant]. The true reality, however, is that they are [actually] torn apart (*vidāritān*).

Here, two *vibhāvanās* (causes of effect appearing without their usual causes) are described, conjoined with the *ekāvalī* (string-of-pearls) figure to be mentioned later: first, the act of pleasing the lion cub is depicted as arising from the king of elephants—which is contrary to what would please it—by means of his drying up the elephant's rut; and second, the act of producing that very rut is depicted as arising from the collection of lion cubs—which is contrary to what would produce it. The specific distinction is that these are supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), just as in the previous case.

Just as a pearl necklace, though its straightness has vanished and it is possessed of dense flickering lustre, attains great nobility through the scattering of gems, O Acyuta, so does Your ornament [of grace]. (1120)

The sense is that he was "disappeared" (*antarhita*), meaning hidden or not manifest anywhere. He is thus described as one whose virtues were "straight" (*sarala-guṇa*), that is, noble qualities. In the alternative sense (the pun), he is one in whose interior (*antaḥ*)—within the hollow space—there was fixed (*hita*), threaded, a "straight" (*sarala*) cord (*guṇa*), namely a thread of gold or the like, because it was straight due to being knotless. As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *sarala* refers to the Padmaka tree; it is masculine, and when meaning 'noble' or 'crooked,' it is used in three genders. Furthermore, he was possessed of an exceedingly intense greed (*lobha*).

In this context, "ghanatarala" refers to one whose necklace has a "tarala"—a central gem—as its "ghana" (thick or prominent part); thus, "tarala" means the central gem of a necklace, according to Amara. [The pearl necklace] is "bhānvita," meaning endowed with luster; for this very reason, it is called "muktāhāra," which literally means "one who has abandoned food. The implication is that, due to extreme miserliness, he does not even fill his own belly. Indeed, the definition of a miser (*kadarya*) is recorded as follows: "He who, out of greed, causes suffering to himself, to his religious duties, to his children and wife, and to his parents and brothers—he is known as a miser."

Thus: in the [literal] sense, a "muktāhāra" is known as an ornament—an adornment consisting of a string of pearls—and a certain man greedy for such an ornament is suggested. From the "scattering of wealth" (*vasu-vikiraṇa*), that is, from the free distribution of riches (*vasu* = wealth), he becomes exceedingly generous (*atyudāra*)—both a great donor and highly venerable; according to Amara, "the word *udāra* denotes a giver and something great. He attains that state.

Here, [the figure] is described through a superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) based on a common substratum (*śleṣa*), wherein the accomplishment of that effect [is attributed] to a greedy person who is the opposite of magnanimity (*audārya*). Its distinction from the previous example lies in its being embellished by *samāsokti* (speech of brevity). For example:
"O friend, he who eats only what remains after being eaten by Hari truly eats auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). But he who eats something else entirely—how strange!—he too eats auspiciousness."

This verse is in the form of an instruction addressed by someone to another. *Aṅga* is an indeclinable used for addressing; according to the grammatical rule, "pyāṭ, phāṭ, aṅga, he, hai, bhoḥ [are used for addressing]. O dear one, O virtuous man! that person who eats only what remains after Hari has eaten—that is, the sacrificial offering (*havis*) left over after being offered to the Lord—enjoys auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), which extends from the removal of all sins up to the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Therefore, one should oneself regularly partake of what has been eaten by the Lord.
"For the destruction of all evils and for the perfect attainment of liberation.
Thus it is said: "Those who have been adorned by you with garlands, perfumes, garments, ornaments, and unguents;
those servants who eat your remnants—they cross over your Māyā."

This is the sense, based on such statements from the *Śrīmatpārameśvarasaṃhitā*, the *Śrībhāgavata*, and other sources: that man who eats food that has not been offered to the Lord—whether it be something not offered at all, or something offered to a deity other than the Lord—he too, O dear one! O virtuous one! eats auspiciousness; he becomes a partaker of welfare according to the manner described, which is indeed a marvel. For the consumption of food and other items not offered to the Lord is prohibited in the *Bharadvājasaṃhitā* and other texts, as in: "One should not consume what has not been offered. Furthermore: "If even once a Brāhmaṇa, for whom knowledge is difficult to attain, eats [such food]..."
"He who consumes the floral offerings (nirmālya) of Śaṅkara and other [deities] shall certainly become an outcaste (caṇḍāla);
for thousands of millions of kalpas he is cooked by the fires of hell. So too is the best of the twice-born who eats the floral offerings of Rudra and the other celestial dwellers. Thus it is said.
That which is offered to Viṣṇu is declared pure and fit to be eaten by sages;
having eaten that which has been offered to another, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Furthermore, since the *Padma*, *Brahma*, and other Purāṇas record that consuming food offered to deities other than the Blessed Lord is indeed a cause for sin (*pratyavāya*), the statement that eating such food brings about auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is truly astonishing; this is the intended sense. The resolution [of the objection] is as follows: the word *aṅgamaṅgalam* is a compound. It refers to that which is "maṅgala" (auspicious) in the sense that it lacks (*avidyamāna*) the sequence of syllables beginning with "ṅga. Thus, "maṅgala" means "mala," which signifies sin (*pāpa*). He "eats" (*bhuṅkte*) it.

"Malas" (impurity) refers to sin, excrement, and dregs—so says Amara. Furthermore, one must not forget the identity between word and meaning. Those who eat food offered to the Lord, who subsist on the remnants of sacrifice, being virtuous, are liberated from all sins.

By the process thus described, one becomes a partaker of auspiciousness preceded by liberation from all sins. On the other hand, the other person becomes a mere vessel of evil and a mere eater of sin; the essential meaning is that he becomes solely a consumer of sin, according to the manner stated in Śruti and Smṛti: "Those sinful ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin. Here, the accomplishment of the effect—namely, being a consumer of that [sinful food]—is stated as resulting from eating food such as unoffered rice, which is the opposite of being a consumer of auspiciousness.
This [verse] is preceded by the samālaṅkāra (simile) mentioned in the first half; however, the distinct difference in aesthetic charm from the previous example is quite evident.

In this regard, the following should be noted: in the definition, the phrase "from the contradictory" (viruddhāt) means "because of the non-coexistence with the effect. Thus, here, because the effect consisting in being the enjoyer of auspiciousness and the cause consisting in eating food not offered to the Lord do not coexist in a single locus in the form of a person, there is spatial contradiction (daiśiko virodhaḥ). In the same way, spatial contradiction alone is to be seen in all three previously illustrated examples, such as "the mountain that is the lord of the serpents" and so forth.

Just as the one of great splendor, with his own hands, by means of arrows as sharp as the love for Hari that he had discharged, immediately rendered his opponents—though they were already trembling intensely—utterly paralyzed with dullness. 1122.

Hari is the Lord Sun. With his own rays—meaning his beams—and with his two hands, which are intertwined, joined, and united, and for that very reason sharpened, he [afflicts] those who are excessively trembling due to coldness and mental confusion caused by a lack of resolve, respectively, by means of swift-moving winds and arrows. The rest is clear. Here, the attainment of that [trembling] by the Sun is stated despite its opposition to trembling caused by coldness. The specific point is that there is a temporal contradiction (*kālika-virodha*), because the rays of the Sun and trembling caused by coldness cannot coexist at the same time.

Just as the moon, though naturally the lord of the virtuous and possessing the beauty that causes the blue lily to bloom, does not delight those who dwell in lotuses during the day due to the intense heat; so too is this [the case]. 1123.

This moon, the lord of the stars and of the virtuous, who is by nature the maker of nectar and possesses cool rays—this is the sense—is, despite its beauty that causes the expansion of its own lineage and age, perfuming (rendering fragrant) the assembly, that is, the multitude of lotuses, during the day with its great heat, its exceedingly scorching splendor, which is its own light. "Sadaḥ" refers to an assembly or a gathering of women and neuter things, according to Amara. Alas! This is a marvel. Such is the meaning.

The actual state of things is such: he is one for whom there is *śrī*—meaning *lakṣmī*, splendor, or prosperity—which, being inherently existent for those who know Brahman, acts as a moon (*amṛtakara*) bestowing the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), causing the blue lotuses to bloom, and granting joy to the circle of the earth; he is thus described. This Lord (*nātha*), the sovereign of the worlds, is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). He is called *atimahoṣṇaśrī*: one whose *śrī* (prosperity) is exceedingly great and hot (*uṣṇa*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *uṣṇa* refers to the summer season (*grīṣma*); it is masculine when meaning 'clever' (*dakṣa*), and has other genders when meaning 'hot' (*aśīta*). Thus, by this description, he is like the day (*divā*) or heaven (*svarga*). [Medinīkośa: "The word *uṣṇa* is masculine in the sense of summer, clever, and 'not cold'; it takes other genders accordingly."]

Regarding the word *dakṣa*, Amara states: "It means clever, skillful, dexterous, and quick. Those who sit upon the *puṣkara* (lotus) are called *puṣkarasadaḥ*; the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *sad*. Regarding those celestial dwellers (*dyusadaḥ*), i.e., the gods, Medinī states: "*Puṣkara* [means] the sky, water, and lotus. It causes them to rejoice (*āmodayate*) or gladden; Medinī states: "*Āmoda* [means] fragrance and joy. The meaning is that by bringing about the state of possessing exceedingly abundant prosperity for heaven, he causes the gods to experience bliss.

Here, by virtue of its removing the fragrance of the assembly of lotuses, the accomplishment of the effect—which is the removal of the fragrance of the assembly of lotuses—is attributed to the moon, which is the opposite of that [lotus]. Since the moon and the fragrance of the lotuses cannot coexist at the same time, this constitutes a temporal contradiction (*kālika-virodha*).
If the arising of the cause is described as occurring after the effect, it is the sixth figure, Vibhāvanā (the Poetic Concealment).

In the expression "from the effect" (*kāryāt*), the meaning of the ablative case is causality (*hetutva*) and not immediate succession (*ānantarya*) or the like; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of the reversal of the temporal sequence between cause and effect.

It is truly a marvel that even the ocean of compassion for the humble, which arose from the mountain of the lord of serpents (Śeṣa) out of his own glory, becomes an ocean of wonder when one beholds it. 1124.

Here, since the birth of the ocean—the cause—is described by means of Lakṣmī and the Moon, who are its effects, this is the figure of speech *vibhāvanā*. By resorting to a comparative compound (*upamita-samāsa*) in the phrases "like an ocean of compassion" and "like an ocean of wonder," the contradiction—that great compassion and great wonder are produced—is resolved.
"Is the moon born from the mind?"—indeed, she spoke these words never before heard; yet it was no wonder that the moon’s mind became so gracious toward the Lord of the Auspicious Bull (Śiva). 1125.

The Veda, whose speech is from time immemorial, says: "The moon was born from the mind. [This creates a] contradiction: that the mind of Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Mountain (Girīśa)—who possesses an auspicious bull (vṛṣa) as his mount—became clear from the moon (vidhu) which serves as the crest-ornament (mauli) upon his head. [However, there is no contradiction: He is the auspicious Lord of the Bull-mountain (Vṛṣagiri), that is, Śeṣagiri; from the moon (vidhu) which is his crest-ornament (mauli), and which is the cause (hetu) for the Lord, my mind—and so forth—became clear, its impurities removed by the sight of the Blessed One and other such means.

The resolution of that [objection] is through a different interpretation of the construction: "It was born" (*ajanīti*). Here too, the production of the mind—the cause—from the moon—the effect—is described; the distinction from the previous case is the description of a reversal of the well-known causal relationship established by the Śruti.
"Just as the sun was born from the eye of the Blessed One," so says the *Puruṣasūkta*; "the clear vision of Hari, the treasury of splendor, has been born within me"—this is my wonder. (1126)

The *Pauruṣa-sūkta* states, "From the eye the sun was born. [The poet says: "It is a marvel to me that the clear and serene gaze of the Lord Hari, the abode of splendor, was born as the sun, the treasury of light"—this constitutes the apparent contradiction (*virodha*). However, the resolution through a shift in interpretation is as follows: from Hari, the Lord Śrīnivāsa, who is a treasury of splendor (*dhāmanidhi*)—meaning a treasury of radiance (*tejonidhi*)—my "gaze" (*dṛṣṭi*), meaning knowledge (according to Amara: "the word *dṛṣṭi* denotes knowledge, the eye, and seeing"), has become clear and stainless. Thus is the resolution.
Here too, the arising of the cause—the divine eye—is described from the effect, the sun.
Just as it is heard in the Puruṣasūkta that "Indra and Agni were born from the mouth," oh, the face of the victorious and pure Blessed One has now appeared before my very eyes! 1127.

"In his mouth Indra and Agni" is heard in the *Puruṣasūkta*. [The prima facie view is: "The face of the Lord—of the victorious (jiṣṇu) Indra and of the pure (śuci) Agni—appeared (*prādurabhūt*) or was born (*ajāyata*) before my very eyes; oh, what a contradiction! The resolution, however, is as follows: the face of the Lord—who is victorious (*jiṣṇu*), meaning ever-conquering—and who is pure (*śuci*), meaning whose sins have been destroyed—appeared (*prādurabhūt*) before me, that is, it became manifest (*āvirbhūtam*) to my direct perception (*pratyakṣam*). Here too, the manifestation of the cause—the Lord's face—is stated [to occur] from the effects, namely Indra and Agni.
The rest is just as before.
Just as we have learned from the scriptures that the Gaṅgā became stainless upon reaching Viṣṇu’s foot, it is a marvel that Viṣṇu’s foot itself appeared stainless upon reaching the Gaṅgā. (1128)

"We have heard from the presence of Gaṅgā that the stainless Viṣṇupada, the foot of the Blessed One, has manifested and been born"—this constitutes the contradiction. "On account of Gaṅgā, Viṣṇupada—the intermediate space (antarikṣa)—being stainless, has manifested and become visible"—this is the resolution. For the birth of a cause from its effect is indeed manifest.

These six varieties have been defined by the authors of the *Kuvalayānanda*; however, among the earlier authorities, only the first variety was defined here, and not the other five. It is understood that these five varieties are indeed the original inventions of Dīkṣita.

The author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* and others, however, maintain that "the distinction between the first type [of non-apprehension] and the second type is indeed difficult to establish; for in the case of 'the production of an effect even in the absence of its cause,' what is intended is the absence of the cause as delimited by its causal determinant (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) and having a counter-positive delimited by that same causal determinant. This intention is simpler than the acceptance of a different type [of non-apprehension]. Likewise, an obstacle is also simply the absence of a cause."

Because the absence of an impediment (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is a cause [of cognition], even this third distinction is not distinct. In the fourth distinction as well, the absence of a cause is implied; for when it is said, "This is the sound of a lute from a conch," there is an understanding that it occurs even without a lute, and thus there is no difference. Therefore, since the other modes are subsumed within the first mode, the claim that there are six types is indeed untenable.

If, however, there is a persistent insistence that the statement in the *Kuvalayānanda* must be justified by some means, then it should be justified as follows: First, the general definition of *vibhāvanā* is "the production of an effect even in the absence of its cause. This, moreover, is twofold: verbal (*śābdī*) and implied (*ārthī*). The verbal variety is threefold.

The threefold [classification] of absence (*abhāva*) is as follows: first, that which is preceded by the statement of an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a causal individuality distinct from an obstructer (*pratibandhaka*); second, that which is preceded by the statement of a deficiency (*vaikalya*), wherein the absence of the effect occurs even when the causal individuality is present, being caused by a deficiency in the possession of a specific delimitation (*avacchinnatva*); and that [deficiency] consists of either the property that delimits causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakadharma*) or, in some cases, the relation that delimits causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakasambandha*); and third, that which is preceded by the statement of an obstructer. Thus, the implied (*ārthī*) [classification] is also threefold.

The production of the subject matter at hand occurs either from another effect belonging to the same class as the subject matter, or from an effect contrary to the subject matter, or from its own cause. For they say that this very point is what is expressed by the statement, "the birth of an effect from a non-cause," and so forth.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on Vibhāvanā (Peculiar Causation), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Viśeṣokti (Peculiar Allegation):
Viśeṣokti occurs when the effect does not arise even though the cause is fully present.

The figure of speech called *viśeṣokti* consists in the non-production of an effect even when the collection of causes is present. In this case, the apparent contradiction is resolved by the thought that some other well-known cause is lacking.
Just as I have bathed at sacred fords, studied extensively, mastered the scriptures, and performed a multitude of good deeds—alas, what has become of this undisciplined consciousness of mine? (1129)

"Consciousness is indeed volition"—this means that it is the intellect (*buddhi*). "Alas, what has happened?"—this expresses an excess of despondency. Here, although there is a convergence of many causes for the purification of the mind—which serves as the primary cause for the knowledge of Brahman, such as bathing at sacred fords and so forth, according to the scriptural injunction: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting"—the description of the non-arising of the effect, namely the purification of the mind, constitutes the figure of speech known as *viśeṣokti* (poetic exception).

In this context, an obstacle consisting in the absence of the Lord’s benevolence, the maturation of accidental merit, and so forth, is perceived. This [obstacle] is one whose cause has not been stated, because the obstacle that causes the non-arising of mental purity has not been mentioned.
Just as someone, though having heard much, does not know you, O Nārāyaṇa, to be the supreme reality; or as one who has plunged into milk does not perceive its flavor, like a wooden ladle—alas! (1130)

In this case, although the cause in the form of extensive learning (*bahuśrutatva*) is present, the non-arising of the effect in the form of knowledge—that Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme reality, as heard in the scripture "The supreme reality is Nārāyaṇa"—is described.
"O King, you do not possess knowledge; my knowledge does not diminish.
Deprived of knowledge, you dwell in darkness and do not recognize Keśava."

In the manner thus described, an obstacle consisting of being devoid of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), being overwhelmed by darkness (*tamas*), and so forth, is perceived; therefore, this [obstacle] is also one whose cause has not been stated, because no obstacle caused by ignorance of the aforementioned Supreme Reality (*paratattva*) has been mentioned.

One who has "plunged and stirred" the *pāyasa*—that is, the supreme food—is so described. Yet, the *dāruhastaka* is a specific object made of wood, shaped like a hand, which serves as a tool for stirring and serving *pāyasa*, soup, and the like. As Amarasimha states: "The *dāruhastaka* is a wooden ladle (*taṇḍūra*). In this context:
He who lacks innate wisdom but possesses only great learning does not understand the meaning of the scriptures, just as a ladle cannot taste the flavors of the soup.

Thus, the meaning of the passage from the *Śrīmadbhārata* is reaffirmed. Its distinction from the previous example, however, lies in its being mixed with a simile (*upamā*). An example of [the figure] based on the aforementioned cause (*uktanimitta*) is as follows: "Even if penances have been performed, they do not purify a sinful man who is averse to Nārāyaṇa, just as sacred fords (*tīrtha*) do not purify a vessel that has held liquor. (1131)

In this case, although the causes characterized by the performance of various kinds of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) are present, the effect consisting of purification does not arise. This is due to the aforementioned cause; for a specific obstacle to the cause of impurity—namely, being averse to Nārāyaṇa—is present here. As it is said: "O King of Kings, expiatory rites performed by one who is averse to Nārāyaṇa do not purify him, just as rivers do not cleanse a vessel that once held liquor."
Thus, the meaning of the verse from the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam is made known through recognition.
Or as it is said:
"Alas! Even while the full moon shines within the utterly pure sky, the intellect of the most deluded does not abandon its darkened impurity. (1132)

By these two qualifiers, "pure" and "full," are summarized the qualities of being the opposite of all that is to be discarded and being a mine of infinite auspicious attributes, as proclaimed in the Dahara-vidyā in the passage beginning, "This Self is free from evil. [The term] "within" refers to Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, who is established in the space within the lotus of the heart situated inside the body known as the city of Brahman, as taught in the Dahara-vidyā: "Within this [city] is a small inner space; within that small space is the ether."

By this method of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the abundance of indicative marks (*liṅgabhūyastva*), it is indicated that Nārāyaṇa alone is the object of worship in all supreme vidyās. Furthermore, even while [the world] is manifest, the statement "this world of Brahman is indeed once-for-all illumined" expresses that the manifestation of the nature of Brahman appears as unobscured; by the suffix *cānaś* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), it is indicated that this manifestation is not adventitious.

The meaning of the scriptural passage from that context—“Just as those who do not know the field might pass over and over a hidden treasure of gold and not find it, even so all these creatures, though they go to this world of Brahman day after day, do not find it, for they are veiled by untruth” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2)—is kept in mind here for those who are most deluded and covered by ignorance. The meaning of the word *pratyūḍhāḥ* is that they have been led away from their true nature, brought into a different state, or, in other words, veiled.

The *tāmasī* intellect is dark; it does not abandon its impurity, which is the defilement of worldly suffering. Elsewhere, [it is said that] when the moon—pure, stainless, full, and possessing all its digits—is in the sky, that is, in the midst of the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*), the locative case is used because the word *antaḥ* is included in the *śauṇḍādi* group, expressing the intention that the whole (the sky) is the locus. A detailed discussion of this has been provided by us in the *Rasāsvādinī*.

"Even while the moon is shining (*vilasamāne*), the 'dark night' (*tamasvinī*)—understood here as the intellect (*buddhi*) abounding in darkness (*tamaḥ*)—does not abandon its 'staininess' (*mālinya*), that is, its soiled state caused by the gloom. Here, although the cause—the shining of the moon—is present, the non-arising of the effect—the abandonment of staininess—is described. This too, like the previous example, possesses a stated cause, because the phrase "dark night" provides the obstructing factor for the non-abandonment of staininess. The distinction is that the former was pure and embellished by simile (*upamā*), whereas this one is intermingled with paronomasia (*śleṣa*) and other figures.

Or rather, the lord of the night (the moon), though overcome by the claws of a lion (or a monkey) and lacking the brilliance of patience and other virtues, became indeed dull-witted when licked by the rays of his own feet; for he was truly one whose color had not diminished. 1133.

Although defeated by the nails of the Blessed Lord Hari, the Moon, the lord of the night, was not touched by shame or mental anguish in his heart—that is to say, he remained free from shame and free from distress. Therefore, characterized by forbearance—the endurance of such defeat—he remained with his color unimpaired; indeed, his luster was complete. The word *hi* is used for emphasis. He became radiant in the sky (*dyu*), as Amara states: "The words *dyu* and *div* both mean heaven. He shone brightly.

Regarding this, he states another reason with the word "sa" (he): "He," namely the Moon, is indeed "jaḍaḥ," that is, truly a fool. The sense is that fools generally do not despond even when suffering humiliation from others; rather, being devoid of discrimination, they even rejoice.

In this context, the word "kṣapādhyakṣa" (the lord of the night) is a single compound term meaning "one who shines with patience and other virtues. Alternatively, it means "one who shines with the two *kṣa*s"—that is, one who shines by means of the two *kṣa* sounds located at the end and the beginning, i.e., the final and initial portions. Here, within his own heart—that is, within the interior of the word "kṣapādhyakṣa"—it became "pādhyalīḍha," meaning it was embraced by the cluster of syllables "pādhyā"; thus, it remained with its letters unimpaired, with every syllable complete.

The sense is that not even a single syllable has been omitted. Here, although the cause—being overwhelmed by Hari’s nails—is present, the non-arising of shame and so forth is described. Because the obstacle to the arising of shame and so forth, namely "insentience" (*jaḍa*), is mentioned as the cause, this is an instance of the aforementioned type [of *hetu*]. Its distinction from the previous example lies in its being embellished by a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) based on the identity between the word and its meaning.
O beautiful lady of Mukunda, her vision is as full of essence as a lake; even by adverse speech, it does not undergo even a trace of agitation, for such indeed is its nature.

O Mukunda-sundarī! Your eye—delightful as a *sārasa* crane and beautiful as a lotus—does not experience even a trace of distortion or a slight perturbation, even by adverse speech or words that are contrary to its own nature. For you, whose heart is profoundly noble and deep, your gaze is naturally and eternally lovely; it never undergoes change due to the slightest adverse word that might cause agitation. Rather, the sense is that it remains exactly as it is. He states the reason for its remaining so with the words "of her" (*tasyāḥ*).

For indeed, because the sequence—the manner—of that vision is of such a kind, being of that very nature, it remains entirely unaltered even when a cause for agitation exists; therefore, this is a *viśeṣokti* (a figure of speech expressing an effect despite the absence of its usual causes). This too has the aforementioned subject matter, since the phrase "for her sequence is of such a kind" introduces the obstructing factor that prevents the arising of any modification. In this regard, the word *sārasasarasā* does not undergo even a trace of modification when read in reverse order.

The femininity inherent in the meaning of the word *sārasasarasā* is superimposed upon the word itself; such is the nature of the sequence (*paripāṭī*, i.e., *ānupūrvī*). Even when read in reverse order, it possesses a manifestation characterized by the presence of syllables very similar to those in the forward order; this demonstration of another aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) constitutes its distinction from the previous example.
Some maintain that there is a third [cause] characterized by an inconceivable motive, and they cite as an example:
"That flower-armed god alone conquers the three worlds;
though his body was destroyed by Śambhu, his power was not taken away."

Thus [they argue]: in the case of *anuktanimittā* (the unmentioned cause), the cause is perceived when it is being reflected upon in its specific defining form (*nimittatāvacchedakarūpeṇa*). But here, it is not so; rather, it occurs in the form "there will be some cause. This, they maintain, is the distinction between *anuktanimittā* and *acintyanimittā* (the inconceivable cause). Others, however, hold that "conceivability" is not a qualification of the cause in *anuktanimittā*, because that would entail the fault of postulating an unnecessary complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*) by assuming a further distinction.

However, they say: "That [type of non-existence] in which neither of the two kinds of causes—namely, being thinkable nor being unthinkable—is mentioned is 'one whose cause is unmentioned. Therefore, that which has an unthinkable cause does not deserve to be a separate category from that whose cause is unmentioned."
The sign consisting of what is to be contemplated has already been explained above.

O Lord of inconceivable signs, since you, the powerful one, remain awake in order to completely eliminate all that is evil, why does the wicked man who hates your majesty still persist even today, O Blessed One? (1135)

Here, although there is a convergence of the causal totality consisting of the Lord’s wakefulness—a form of great power most capable of destroying evil deeds—there is nonetheless a description of the non-arising of the effect, which is the total eradication of the wicked people who hate His majesty; thus, this is the figure of speech known as *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation). That [non-arising] must have some underlying cause for its persistence, yet it is truly inconceivable, because it lies beyond the scope of ordinary cognition.

O Mother, just as the preeminent serpent-king is perpetually nourished by you with your gracious gaze, it is a marvel that his vision remains unerring even when directed toward those who are crooked, for it is not corrupted by passion.

"O Mother! By you—who are *prasannā* (clear, pure, or gracious), *surayā* (with wine, or by the goddess Surā), and *svacchayā* (transparent or contented)—there is satisfaction; such is the actual state of affairs. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *prasannā* applies to the goddess Surā, to a woman, and in the three genders to the transparent and the contented. And according to Amara, in the synonyms for wine: "*gandhottamā*, *prasannerā* [are synonyms for *surā*]. "Always *suhitaḥ*" means satisfied or satiated; in the other sense, it means one who acts for the welfare of the entire world through the excellent protection (*sutarāṃ hita-rakṣaṇena*) of others.
Hṛṣīkeśa, together with Lakṣmī, who is the very embodiment of compassion,
is celebrated as the protector in all philosophical systems and even in the Vedāntas.

Thus, because it is stated that the protection of the world is achieved through sacred literature (*sāhitya*) alone, he does not stumble due to *mada*—that is, a mental derangement. Alternatively, the word *namadaskhalitaḥ* is a single compound term: he is "unfaltering toward those who bow," meaning he is free from deviation in his vow to protect those who have sought refuge. Furthermore, his gaze is not corrupted by *rāga*—the redness caused by intoxication; in another sense, it is not defiled by faults such as envy.

Here, although the full presence of the causes—namely, constant serenity and a state of being well-satisfied—is established, there is the description of the non-arising of effects such as pride and faltering; thus, this is the figure of speech known as *viśeṣokti*. That what the cause for the non-arising of such effects might be is truly inconceivable, because it lies beyond the scope of ordinary cognition. This instance is distinguished from the previous example by its being reinforced through *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Or rather: "Is it not so that the Lord of the Day (the Sun) has become the Lord of Monkeys (Sugrīva) for the sake of serving you? O Hero of the Raghus, although there is a difference in form between these two, alas, their essential identity was indeed grasped! (1137)

O Raghuvīra! Is it not so that the Sun, the lord of the day, has manifested as Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, to perform service and attend upon you? This is according to the Vedic scripture: "The self indeed bears the name of son. Although there is a difference in form between these two—the lord of the day and the lord of monkeys—that difference was not perceived by people (the word *janaiḥ* being understood). Ah, what a wonder! Here, despite the presence of the complete causal conditions for perceiving the difference in form, the description of its non-perception constitutes the figure of speech *Viśeṣokti* (Specific Statement), caused by an inconceivable motive.

The actual state of affairs regarding these two words, *vāsarādhipa* and *vānarādhipa*, is that no difference is perceived between them except through the letters *sa* and *na*; no other phonemes contribute to the distinction. This alone constitutes the specific difference from the previous example.

In this regard, it should be noted that where the absence of the cause and the absence of the effect are presented through direct statement (*śruti*) as qualified by their respective delimiters (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), there the figures of speech *vibhāvanā* and *viśeṣokti* are verbal (*śābda*); otherwise, they are extrinsic (*ārtha*).

O Slayer of Madhu, it is a marvel that for those who incessantly drink the nectar of your deeds, which are as sweet as honey, their thirst increases at every moment despite its form remaining unimpaired. For in the world, lack of proximity is the cause of thirst; yet in the absence of such [lack], even when there is proximity, an intensification of thirst has been depicted. Likewise, proximity is the cause of satiety; yet even when that exists, the absence of satiety has been made known.

However, since the non-existence of the effect due to the non-existence of the cause is not presented by the word through the relation of the qualified and the qualifier (vaiśiṣṭya) with the delimitor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) in the manner previously shown, this very fact constitutes the blending (*saṃkara*) of the figures *vibhāvanā* and *viśeṣokti*. Bearing precisely this point in mind, Mammaṭabhaṭṭa, after citing the verse beginning with "yaḥ kaumāraharaḥ," stated that no distinct figure of speech is clearly manifest here.

Vāmana, however, defined it as follows: "When one assumes a reduction of [only] one quality [of the object of superimposition], while maintaining the firmness of the identity, it is *viśeṣokti* (peculiar assertion). And he provided the example: "Gambling, indeed, is for a man a kingdom without a throne. For here, gambling is superimposed upon kingship by way of identity. Now, how could gambling—which is devoid of a throne—support an identity with a kingship that possesses a throne? Thus, in order to refute the argument that would uproot the superimposition, the absence of a throne is likewise assumed in the superimposed object, namely, the kingship.

Therefore, this is indeed a *rūpaka* (metaphor) with a firm superimposition, not a *viśeṣokti* (poetic omission). Likewise, even in Puranic verses such as "Brahmā was not four-faced," it is specifically a variety of *rūpaka*. Similarly, even when there is the conceptualization of an excellence of qualities (*guṇādhikyakalpanā*), it is also specifically a variety of *rūpaka*, as in "Dharma incarnate on earth was Kārtavīrya," and so forth. Thus, those who define the figure *viśeṣālaṅkāra* as "the strengthening of similarity through the conceptualization of the loss or increase of one quality" are also refuted.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the Section on Peculiar Allegation (Viśeṣokti), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the thirty-eighth section, the Section on Impossibility (Asambhava):
"The statement of the impossibility of the accomplishment of an object is Impossibility (Asambhava)."
The poetic figure named *asaṃbhava* (the impossible) consists in the description of the impossibility of accomplishing some particular task. For example:
"When the daughter of Drupada was thus insulted by rogues in the assembly of the Kurus, who could have known, O Blessed One, that Your compassion would protect her in such a manner? (1139)
O Hari, who by means of Vāmana—whose purpose was fulfilled by covering the earth with only three steps—did you conquer the three worlds? By whom indeed was this known? (1140)
Just as [one might say] "always," O Lord of the Darvīkara Mountain, my heart has been placed in you; yet you take that very same heart away from me, O God—I do not know why you are such as this.

In these three examples, the impossibility of the accomplishment of the objects—the protection of Pāñcālī, the conquest of the three worlds, and the abduction of the heart—is revealed by phrases such as "who knows? and so forth; thus, there is conformity with the definition [of the *asambhava* figure]. Or again, for example:
"O cloud, hide the sun so that the young cowherd boy may suffer no heat in the forest; thus I pray. But who would know that he is drinking up the forest fire? (1142)

This is the speech of Yaśodā. "O Cloud" is an address to the rain-cloud. Here, by the phrase "who indeed could know," the impossibility of the realization of the matter—that the cowherd youth [Kṛṣṇa] has drunk the forest fire—is revealed.

"Just as one might give away the existence of auspicious states, O Lord of Ramā, so these have taken refuge [in You]; yet, O Hari, we do not know how You could take away their very existence of auspicious states. (1143)

*Śubha* (auspiciousness), *kalyāṇa* (well-being), *bhās* (splendor), *dīpti* (radiance), *vibhava* (prosperity), and *aiśvarya* (sovereignty)—these form a dvandva compound: *śubhabhāvibhavāḥ*. In the second half of the verse, regarding the resolution of the apparent contradiction, the vocative *he śubhe* is used. *Bhāvibhavān* means "those who are to be born in future lives. Here, the very impossibility of the accomplishment of the object—namely, the removal of auspiciousness and future births—is revealed by the phrase "we do not know [this] of Hari."

"O Hare, Lord of Ramā"—this [verse] is distinguished from previous examples by its being a confluence of the *parikarāṅkura* (the "germ of the preparatory figure"), *śleṣa* (punning), and the *viṣama-viśeṣa* (the specific type of incongruity), consisting in the placement of a substantive (*viśeṣya*) that contains within it the intention of both bestowing and taking away prosperity.

This ornament is indeed the invention of Dīkṣita; it was not observed by the ancients. However, in the three examples shown in that work—beginning with "the earth measured by three feet" (*caraṇatrayamitadharaṇī*) and so forth—even though there ought to be the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction), because the contradiction is evident through the actions such as the traversing of the three worlds by the substances belonging to Vāmana and the others.

For this very reason, authors such as the author of the *Alaṃkārasarvasva* have cited the verse “*ayaṃ vārāmeko nilaya iti ratnākara iti*” (‘He is the sole abode of waters, he is the mine of jewels’)—which serves as an example of *asaṃbhava* (impossibility) in the *Kuvalayānanda*—as an illustration of the contradiction between substance and action (*dravyakriyāvirodha*). However, in the final example, “*śubhabhāvibhavāndadyāḥ*,” there ought to be a variety of the figure *viṣama* (incongruity) yet to be described, because it describes the failure to attain a desired object despite an effort toward it, and the acquisition of an undesired object.

Nevertheless, in the initial verse, "In the assembly of the Kurus, the daughter of Drupada," since neither such a contradiction nor any other poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is possible, the figure of *asaṃbhava* (the impossible), defined by the aforementioned characteristics, must necessarily be admitted due to its possession of a specific charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*). Since the presence of that same specific charm—characterized by the description of the impossibility of accomplishing the intended meaning—is witnessed solely by the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) even in the second and subsequent examples, that very figure is the predominant one; therefore, by that alone...

The designation is appropriate according to the maxim that "designations occur by way of predominance"; however, the other [factor] remains subordinate as its auxiliary—this should be understood by the wise.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Impossible (*asaṃbhava*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Inconsistency (*asaṅgati*):
"Inconsistency is the contradiction between cause and effect when they reside in different loci."
The wise declare that this ornament is described as *asaṅgati* (incongruity).
The figure of speech named *asaṃgati* (incongruity) consists of the apparent lack of common locus between cause and effect, which manifests at first glance as being contradictory.

"As long as the stream of your sidelong glances is poised to flow forth, so long do the afflictions of those who bow before you spontaneously dissolve away, O Śrīvatsāṅka. Here, because the cause—characterized by the readiness for the stream of sidelong glances to flow—and the effect—the dissolution of afflictions—are located in different substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the phrase "contrary" (*viruddha*) and so forth is employed to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And in this case, since that [cause] acts as the instigator of the effect precisely while residing in a different location, there is no room for contradiction. For example: * *yāvatkaṭākṣadhārā...* (As cited above). * *yāvad dūraṃ prasarati vitatajyotiḥprasaro 'ruṇasya / tāvad dūraṃ vrajati rajanī tamasā saha nitarām // 1 //* "As far as the expansive beam of light from the dawn-red sun extends, so far does the night depart completely along with the darkness. Here, the cause is the expansion of the sun's rays, and the effect is the departure of the night; these two reside in different substrata. However, because they are related as cause and effect, there is no contradiction. * *yāvad dūraṃ prasarati vitatajyotiḥprasaro 'ruṇasya / tāvad dūraṃ vrajati rajanī tamasā saha nitarām // 2 //* "As far as the expansive beam of light from the dawn-red sun extends, so far does the night depart completely along with the darkness. Here, the cause is the expansion of the sun's rays, and the effect is the departure of the night; these two reside in different substrata. However, because they are related as cause and effect, there is no contradiction. * *yāvad dūraṃ prasarati vitatajyotiḥprasaro 'ruṇasya / tāvad dūraṃ vrajati rajanī tamasā saha nitarām // 3 //* "As far as the expansive beam of light from the dawn-red sun extends, so far does the night depart completely along with the darkness.
