Therefore, having attained a state of "lack of *lasattā*"—where *lasattā* is the existence or presence of the letter *la*, so "lack of *lasattā*" (*alasattā*) means the absence of the presence of the letter *la*—it became simply the word *gauḥ* (cow), namely *g-au-ḥ*.

The sense is that it is established in that manner by the removal of the letter *la* according to the method stated above. Here too, as before, there is the non-attainment of the desired and the attainment of the undesired.

O Mother, as if out of curiosity to compare themselves with your body, the creepers approached you; but being repelled by the disparity in their color compared to your complexion, they became *tilaka* marks and departed for the forest regions. 1195.

O Mother! The *latās* and *latikās*—the former with the suffix *kan* added in the sense of "smallness"—reveal the extreme delicacy of creepers. Having approached out of curiosity to compare themselves with your body, they were surpassed by your form; thus, due to the "reversal of the complexion of their faces" (*mukhavarṇaviparyāsāt*), meaning the loss of facial luster characterized by defeat.

In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), because of the reversal—that is, the inversion—of the initial syllables *la* and *ti* of the words *mukha* (face) and *varṇa* (complexion), they became *tilakāḥ*, a specific kind of tree (as Amara states: "the *tilaka* is the *kṣuraka*"). By this, the loss of even that delicacy which remained in the state of a creeper (*latā*) is indicated. In the alternative sense, the intention is that the word *latikā* is thus transformed into *tilakāḥ* according to the aforementioned method. The meaning is that they went to the forest regions, unable to show their faces to anyone, and hid themselves somewhere within the depths of the thicket.
Everything else is as explained previously.

Just as Śiva, whose radiant splendor was shaken by the dance of the son of Hari (Kṛṣṇa), and who, shaking his heads in anger, approached and stood before him, was once again cast down by him; so too [is this man]. (1196)

The *svaru* is the thunderbolt; the sense is that it desires to conquer the *Nandaka*. Its splendor was shaken by the *Nandaka*—the sword of the Lord Hari bearing that name—and for this reason, he shook his own head; this is an expression of the manifestation of his wrath. Then, at that very moment, though he stood facing him at the front line out of anger, the intent being for a duel, he was once again humbled and surpassed by that *Nandaka*.

The sense is that in every way he did not conquer, but rather was defeated and went into exile. In the alternative interpretation (pakṣe), "svaruḥ" refers to the word *svaru*, meaning the head—that is, the portion situated at the top. "Vidhūnvan" means casting off or abandoning the collection of phonemes consisting of the syllable *sva*. Regarding the phrase "abhavatsaṃmukhaḥ," the word division is "abhavat tsammukhe. In the alternative word-division "abhavat sammukhe," there is a doubling of the letter *t* according to the rule *anaci ca*.

The meaning is as follows: although the *tsaru* (the hilt) exists by reaching—that is, being situated at the *mukha* (the tip)—which is a collection of phonemes having the form *tsaṃ-tsaṃ*, and although it remains there as the *tsaru*, yet when the phoneme *sva* (the letter *s*) located at the beginning (*mukha*) of the word *svaru* is elided and the phoneme *tsa* is placed in its very place, the word *tsaru* is produced. By that [sword] Nandaka, [the other sword] was surpassed; the sense is that this occurs because the *muṣṭi* (the grip) is situated below the blade of the sword. Amara states: "The word *tsaru* refers to the grip of a sword and similar weapons."

In this instance, the attainment of the desired—namely, the forms *svaru*, *nandaka*, *jaya*, and *iṣṭa*—as well as the acquisition of a formidable undesirable object in the form of being cast down (*adhaḥkṛta-svarūpa-utkaṭa*), are both composed through *śleṣa* (punning). In such cases, the power of the identity between word and meaning must not be forgotten.

Just as a cluster of blossoms, desiring to rival the likeness of Lakṣmī’s breasts, became a crane (baka) [as it withered], so indeed do the attainment of the desired and the encounter with the undesired fall to the lot of those who possess a body. 1197.

A cluster of flowers (*stabaka*), consisting of a bunch of excellent blossoms, desiring to attain equality with the *kokā*—the female ruddy goose—of Lakṣmī’s (Śrī’s) breasts, which are themselves like male ruddy geese (*cakra-vāka*), became a *baka*, a crane. According to Amara: "The terms *nutta*, *nunna*, *asta*, *niṣṭhyūta*, *viddha*, *kṣipta*, and *īrita* are synonymous. The sense is that although it strove to achieve similarity with the *kokā* of the breasts of the one possessing supreme beauty, it was cast down and became a lowly bird called a *kahva* (crane), rather than becoming equal to the *kokā* of her breasts.

Furthermore, the word *baka* (crane) is understood here as *śivamallī*, a specific type of flowering tree belonging to the *pāśupata* class, which was abandoned by Lakṣmī; this is also the sense conveyed. Amara states: "The *śivamallī*, the *pāśupata*, the *ekāṣṭhīla*, the *baka*, and the *vasu* [are synonyms]. And Medinī states: "'Baka' may refer to the *bakapuṣpa* flower, the *kahva* plant, the god Śrīda (Viṣṇu), and a demon. The implication is that for one rejected by Lakṣmī, entry into the *pāśupata* doctrine is entirely appropriate. In the alternative sense, the word *stabaka* (cluster of blossoms)—being *astaḥ* (without the letter *sta*)—became *baka*.

*Bhāga* means *bhāgadheya* (fortune/lot). According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *bhāga* is said to mean form (*rūpa*) and wealth (*artha*), while *bhāgadheya* refers to a portion (*ekadeśa*) and fortune. There is also the usage: "One who possesses a share (*bhāgin*) enjoys happiness. *Sūnabhāgī* means one whose *bhāga* (portion) is *sūna* (excessively deficient); that is, one whose fortune is extremely low. In the alternative sense, *bhāgī* means "one who partakes" (*bhajati*). By the rule "saṃpṛcānurudha... etc., the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied to the root *bhaj*, and by the rule "cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ," the change to *k* occurs.

"He is a partaker of flowers" (*puṣpabhāj*) means he is a recipient of flowers; the rest is easy to understand. Here too, as before, there is both the non-attainment of the desired and the acquisition of the undesired. The distinction, however, lies in its being a mixture of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Or, for example:
"O Mādhava, wishing to steal your reputation, the cloud, having fallen from its own nature in their midst and adopted the behavior of a crane, was not restrained even by a word. (1198)

O Mādhava! The cloud (*balāhaka*), which carries water (*vārivāhaka*), desires to steal away your color; for this very reason, it has fallen away from its own color even in the middle—that is, in the midst of itself. In another sense, it has fallen away from its two constituent letters, *lā* and *ha*, in the middle. Or rather, it is one from whom the two letters *lā* and *ha* have been lost. A twice-born man who lives like a heron—looking downward, deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends, treacherous, and falsely humble—is said to follow the "heron-vow" (*bakavrata*).

The meaning is that he adopts the "heron's way" (*bakavṛtti*) in the manner described; or else, it means remaining silent like a heron due to not obtaining what he desires; or rather, it refers to becoming a bird named *kaha*. In the alternative sense (of the word-play), the word *balāhaka* attains the status of the letters *ba* and *ka* alone, once the letters *la* and *ha* have been removed—this is the intended sense.

The meaning is that he was not honored even by word; according to the principle stated, "One should not honor those who are irrational and act like herons (bakavṛtti) even with mere words," he was not honored even by speech alone. Alternatively, the sense is that because a heron is an animal, he did not even attain human speech. Here, it is described not merely that Balāhaka failed to obtain his desired goal—the removal of the Lord’s complexion—but rather that he experienced increasingly severe misfortunes, such as the loss of his own caste and so forth.

Or, for example: "Did the Kulācala mountain, desiring equality with the breasts of Śrī and having become determined, become a potter—by fashioning even jars that resemble them—attain his desired goal? (1199)

The Kulācala (the Mountain Range), having become "niścita" (fixed/decided), became a *kulāla* (potter); that is, he was deprived of his *kartari* (instrumental agency). In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), the word *kulācala* becomes *niścaḥ*—that from which the letter *ca* has departed—and having been made *niścita*, it became *kulāla*. Here too, following the non-attainment of the desired object (similarity to the breasts of Śrī), there is the acquisition of an undesired state for the Kulācala, namely, being a potter.

O Lord of the Bull-peak mountain, alas! Just as a certain elephant, considering the excellence of your gait to be easily attainable, became your rival, attained the state of a moth (*śalabhatva*) through the blow of a whip; [O Lord of the Elephant-peak mountain! Regarding "whip" (*kaśā*), Amara states: "A *kaśā* is the whip used for striking horses and other animals. From the "blow" (*ābhighātāt*). In the alternative sense: by the letter *śa*, there is a "striking," that is, an elision (*vilopana*). This is a compound according to the rule "the instrument is expressed by the past passive participle" (*sādhanaṃ kṛtā*). It means: from the "striking" (*ābhighātaḥ*)—that is, the removal—of the letter *ka* (the letter *kavaṇa*), namely, by removing the letter *ka* and substituting the letter *śa*. Thus, the word *kalabha* ("young elephant") becomes *śalabha* ("moth"). The meaning is: having thought the majesty of your gait easy to emulate, the elephant, through the blow of the whip, became a moth. O Lord of the Bull-peak! Similarly, in the case of the mountain: a certain [elephant], thinking the majesty of your gait easily attainable, became your rival, and through the "striking" (elision) of the letter *ka* by the letter *śa*, he attained the state of a moth. O Lord of the Elephant-peak! Alas! [He was destroyed. (Note: The commentary explains a *śleṣa* (punning) *parihāra* (resolution). The verse plays on the words *kalabha* (elephant), *gati-vibhavam* (majesty of gait), *kaśā-abhighātāt* (from the blow of a whip), and *śalabhatvam* (state of a moth). In the second interpretation, these same words are re-read: *kalabha* becomes *śalabha* through the substitution of *ka* with *śa*.)
The young elephant attains the state of a locust; the word "kalabha" attains the state of the word "śalabha."

O Consort of the Lord of the Serpent Hill, O Mother of the World, how else could the *śirīṣa* flower, which desires to steal away the exquisite delicacy of your body, have become like chaff before you? 1201.

*Haraṇeccham*: that which has a desire for seizing (*haraṇe icchā yasya tat*). *Śirīṣam*: a flower that is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *śirīṣa* tree; its neuter gender follows the rule "all [words] ending in a consonant are neuter when denoting a fruit or flower" (*dvihīnaṃ prasave sarvam*). *Kaśya*: that which deserves a whip (*kaśām arhati*); the suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of "deserving" according to the rule "from *daṇḍa* and others, *ya*" (*daṇḍādibhyo yaḥ*). This means sharpness corresponding to the stroke of a whip. Regarding such a stroke, Amara states: "*Kaśya* means one who deserves a whip. In the alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), it refers to the striking of the letter *śi* by the letter *ka*; that is, by the insertion of the letter *ka* in place of the letter *śi*.

"Become like dried cow-dung" means having become exceedingly harsh, like dry *gomaya*; in this context, the word *karīṣa* is used, as Amara states: "For that which is dried is *karīṣa*, not feminine. Here, one should note that instead of the attainment of the desired object—namely, the Śirīṣa flower’s acquisition of the beauty and tenderness of the body—there has occurred, on the contrary, the attainment of an undesirable state: a hardness that is the opposite of its natural inherent tenderness.

O Lord of the serpent-mountains! Just as the body of the sun, desiring to seize the brilliance of your golden celestial chariot (*tapanīya-vimāna*), was from the very beginning rendered powerless—indeed, it became like a mere *karīra* (creeper-stump)—so too is this [the case for others]. O Lord of the serpent-mountains (*sarīsṛpa-girīndra*)! The "body" (*śarīra*) of Tapanas, the Sun—the word *śarīra* being used here literally—desiring to take (*āditsu*) the splendor of your golden (*tapanīya*) celestial chariot, having merely formed the wish to seize it, was from the very beginning (*āditaḥ*) rendered powerless (*aśakatayā*). The word *śaka* is derived from the root *śak* with the suffix *pacādyac*, meaning "one who is able. Then, through the formation of a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) and the addition of the suffix *tal*, we arrive at *aśaka*, meaning "incapable. Thus, it was incapable from the start. 1202. Just as the body of the sun, wishing to seize the luster of your golden celestial chariot, was indeed from the very beginning rendered powerless, O Lord of the serpent-mountains, it became like a mere *karīra*. (Note: The term *karīra* refers to the young shoot of a bamboo or a thorny shrub; here it serves as a metaphor for something that has become withered or insignificant.)

In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), "aśa" means that which lacks the phoneme *śa* (*avidyamāna-śa-varṇa*). That which has a *ka* (*kakāra*) in such a position—its state is "thatness" (*tattā*); by this, the meaning is that through the elision of *śa*, the *ka* is obtained right there. It was like a *karīra* (a bamboo sprout), that is, it became dark blue; the sense is that it became devoid of luster. In the alternative sense, the meaning is that the word "karīra" was formed. According to Amara, "the word *karīra* denotes a bamboo sprout [and is not feminine].

Here, the Sun’s body experienced the non-attainment of its desired object—in the form of the desire to seize the splendor of Śrīnivāsa’s golden celestial chariot—and the occurrence of an undesired state, namely, becoming a *karīra*.

Just as a saw, though moving inwardly without opposition in order to reach your breast, attains a supreme state of emergence only to become, in the end, a mere crooked cut; so too does he who seeks you. 1203.

Having supplied the word *śrīḥ* (O Śrī) as an address, [the meaning is: "The cakravāka bird (*cakraḥ kokaḥ*), for the sake of attaining your breasts—that is, to obtain the birth of your breasts—though he worships (*bhajan*) some god or the Sun (*bhānum*) within his heart (*antaḥ*) who grants him pleasure—" according to Amara’s lexicon, which states: "The word *kaḥ* is used for the wind, Brahmā, and the sun; it is masculine. The construction is "even while worshipping," which means "even while practicing devotion. "Attaining contrariety" (*vailomyam*) means "hairiness" (*vilomatvam*); this refers to the state of being hairless (*aromaśatvam*), which is worthy of the beautiful breasts described in the phrase "and in the case of a woman, her breasts are hairless. The particle *api* ("even") is to be supplied here as well.

The sense is that even upon attaining only that much, having become a *krakaca*—that is, a saw (*karapatra*)—he obtained birth as a saw due to his hairlessness. Immediately thereafter, having attained another birth (*udbhava*; Amara states: "birth, origin, and arising are synonyms"), meaning that although he had already obtained birth as a saw through his lack of body hair, he attained yet another birth for the sake of accomplishing his desired object; the sense is that he became merely one with crooked teeth (*vakrakaca*), that is, one with curly hair (*vakrakeśa*), and did not obtain the birth of breasts.

The analysis of the compound is: "he who is both crooked (vakra) and hair (kaca). In another sense, the word *cakra*, having reached (*āpya*) the end—that is, the middle—while assuming (*bhajan*) even the letter *ka* through reverse order (*vailomya*, i.e., being composed of letters in inverted sequence), results in the form *krakaca*. Then, having reached (*etya*) the letter *va*, which is even more (*param*) than the letter *kra* at the beginning—that is, appearing with an exceeding (*atiśayita*) radiance (*udbhava*), meaning shining with manifest splendor—it results in the form *vakrakaca*. This is the meaning.

Just as a certain bird, free from blemish, appeared before you desiring to be your vehicle, O Lord whose mount is the king of birds, it then, by virtue of its transformation, became a sparrow at every moment.

O Lord whose vehicle is the king of birds! This [statement] serves as an embellishment for the intended meaning under discussion. It contains a reason (*hetugarbha*): because of the reason that he is "spotless" (*vikalaṅka*), no bird whatsoever—even the Sun, who is denoted by the word *ka*—is spotless. Alternatively, the construction may be: "What bird is spotless? The sense is that it is a marvel that even such a being fails to achieve the desired object of his intention. According to Amara: "The word *ka* refers to the wind, Brahmā, and the sun (in the masculine)."

"Any bird" (ko'pi khagaḥ) means some bird whose name is unknown; this sense should also be supplied as an embellishment (*upaskārya*). According to Amara, "khaga" refers to arrows, the sun, or birds. The meaning is that you desire the state of being his vehicle (*vāhatva*), that is, the status of being the king of birds (*khagendra*). "Desirous" (*īpsuḥ*) means wishing to obtain it; the sense is that while the desire is under one's own control, the attainment of the fruit is not. At first (*agre*), he was a sheep (*aviḥ*) or a mouse. In reality, however, "avi" refers to that which is denoted by the word *avi*, or your abode (*bhavana*) consisting of splendor (*tejas*).

The sense is that [the word] belongs to you because it is situated within that maṇḍala. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *aviḥ* refers to a mountain, the sun, a ram, a mouse, and a blanket; it also means a wall, a house, and light; as for the feminine form, it refers to a woman in her menses and the earth. Regarding the phrase "in a mouse and a blanket," the author of the *Daśaṭīkāsarvasva* and others, in their commentary on the verse from the *Amarakośa*—"*avi*, *yaśas*, mountain, ram, and sun"—explain that it means "in a mouse (*ākhu*) and in a blanket (*kambala*). In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), at the beginning (*agre*), *aviḥ* means "devoid of modification" (*vikāraśūnya*), that is, having abandoned its altered color (*tyaktavivarṇa*). It became so.

Then, immediately thereafter, at every moment, by virtue of transformation—that is, by virtue of attaining successive distinct modifications—[the syllables] *ka* and *la* (in the sense of the Kali age) were followed by the word *anukalam*. According to the rule "the indeclinable [is compounded with a word denoting time]" (*avyayaṃ vibhakti*), this forms an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "subsequent. By virtue of the transformation (*vikṛti*)—meaning the action (*kṛti*) or placement (*nyasana*) of the vowel-less letter *vi* (from the prefix *vi*)—he became the bird known as the *kalaviṅka*, the sparrow.

The word *vikalaṅka*, according to the method described, results in the form *kalaviṅka* through the removal of the initial syllable and the insertion of a vowel after the letters *ka* and *la*. This is the distilled meaning. Here, it should be observed that the bird *vikalaṅka* not only fails to attain its most desired state as the vehicle of the Lord, but moreover undergoes the acquisition of intense misfortunes such as being turned into a mouse; this is sustained by the identification [of the two meanings] based on *śleṣa* (punning homophony), which rests upon the identity between word and meaning.

O Mother, although safflower has been cast aside as it seeks to obtain your preference— having lost its golden luster— it might nevertheless overcome you with its breast, were it to abandon its weakness and assume manhood.

O Mother! [It was] saffron, or safflower, or gold. In this context, the word *kusumbha* is explained by the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *kusumbha* refers to gold, safflower (*mahārajana*), and a water-pot. They say that *mahārajana* is the saffron flower. [The moon], desiring your luster—your radiance—and thus being cast down, i.e., surpassed by your light, and consequently having its excellence destroyed; that is, its beautiful own color (*su-varṇa*)—the syllable 'su' and its own hue—having been ruined, it became so described.

Then, after attaining such a state, let the jar (kalaśa) or the elephant's frontal globe (karikumbha) abandon its impotence, lack of boldness, and neuter gender, and instead assume manhood (*puṃstva*) or virility; that is to say, let it become masculine. The sense is that by eliding the syllable *su*, the word "kumbha" is produced as a masculine noun. For the word *kumbha* is indeed taught as masculine in the rule: "The two *kumbhas* are a pot and the head of an elephant. Nevertheless, the word *tava* ("of you") is understood to carry over [from the previous verse].

The sense is: "by means of your breast," which is inherently male (puṃstva). The intention behind the singular number is that since the victory can be accomplished by one alone, there is no need to prepare with both. It would be "conquered" (jīyeta), meaning it would be overcome; for here the root *ji* has the sense of "overpowering," and thus it takes an object. As stated by Bhartṛhari: "The root *ji* [is used] in the senses of 'victory' and 'overpowering';
in the first sense it is intransitive, while in the second sense, the attainment of excellence, it is transitive."

Thus, in this case, it is not merely that Kusumbha fails to obtain his own desired object; rather, even in the process of assuming another form, an unavoidable acquisition of something undesirable is depicted.

Just as this moon, whose syllables are destroyed at the beginning and end because it cannot attain the likeness of Your face which is desired, has perished; so too, O Mother, the moon, though possessing the essence of ripeness (*pākarasa*), has brought about destruction even while finding the supreme field (*kṣetra*). 1206.

O Mother! This is the night-maker, the moon; and there is also the word *kṣapākara*. Because of the failure to attain that desired likeness of your face, it has become *kṣara*—wasted—extending from beginning to end, from head to foot, or from birth until death. And it is also *kṣara*, wasted, at its two ends: on the first day of the bright fortnight (*pratipad*) and on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).

In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), that which has *kṣa* (the letter *kṣa*) and *ra* (the letter *r*) at its beginning and end is so described; *paraṃ* means another, and *kṣetraṃ* means the body or the supreme seat of the perfected ones (*siddha-sthāna*). As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *kṣetra* [is used] for the body, a field, a place of the perfected, and the three powers. The meaning is: even while perceiving some particular field of the Lord's manifestation. In the alternative sense, the words *kṣe traṃ* are separate; the construction is *kṣe paraṃ traṃ*.

The meaning is that while remaining in the letter *kṣa*, he attained the collection of three letters beginning with *tra* at the position of the letter *kṣa*. Being "shameful" (*trapākaraḥ*), he was indeed dependent on modesty; being a cook (*māhanasikaḥ*), he was beneficial through the taste of his cooking, providing nourishment for those who eat—this is the sense. Thus he lived (*prāṇīt*).

The meaning is that although "trapākara" was established as "pākara"—where, despite the addition of the phoneme *kṣa*, it underwent a change into another phoneme—it nevertheless attained its existence within the sequence of syllables (*varṇānupūrvī*) as the unaltered form "pākara. Here too, as before, there is the attainment of the undesirable and the failure to attain the desired.

Just as a female Bhilla woman, though possessed of great pride (*asuramā*), having lost most of her skin-color (*lopitabhūyovarṇā*) while longing for the highest caste through a smile originating from the mouth of Hari, became fragrant with jasmine garlands (*surabhimallī*); so too was she [the goddess]. (1207)

*Surabhimallī* refers to the *mallikā* flower associated with spring (*vasanta*). By mentioning its connection to *surabhi* (fragrant/delicious), the excellence of the *mallikā*'s color, fragrance, and so forth is conveyed. *Surabhi* means "delightful"; *mallī* refers to a specific class of women devoted to the practice of wrestling (*mallānām khuralī-khelana-parā jātiviśeṣāḥ*), and it should also be understood as meaning "a woman of that class. Alternatively, one may consider the word *surabhimallī* itself [as a compound]. There is an identity between these two meanings. Furthermore, she is endowed with *ramā*, which is beautiful; or alternatively, she is endowed with the *mā* (glory) of the *surāḥ* (gods).

By the word "api" (even), it is understood that [the natural color] was insufficient for that much. "From the smile born from the mouth of Hari, the Blessed One"—that is to say, even from the color of that smile. By the qualification "born from the mouth," the fact that the smile possesses the color of a Brahmin is understood. "Desiring the highest color"—the word "by him" is to be supplied, meaning "by that smile. She is so described because her abundant natural color had been erased by it. For this very reason, she is called *suramā*: one who "delights well" (*suṣṭhu ramate*) in the Asura, with the suffix *pacādyac*.

Therefore, it is a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning "devoid of joy. She was a *bhillī*, a Kirāti; the sense is that she was of a birth even lower than that of a *mallajātī*. In both instances, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for designating a caste (*jāti*). In the alternative [interpretation], she is one "whose many syllables (*varṇa*) have been erased"—just as in expressions such as "one whose smoke has mostly vanished" (*chinnabhūyiṣṭhadhūmā*), the sense is "one whose syllables remain only in small measure. He shows precisely those erased syllables in the word "asuramā."

Because she was devoid of the three syllables "su-ra-me," she became known as "Bhillī. The sense is that when the sequence of syllables "su-ra-me" is elided from the word *surabhimallī*, only the two syllables "Bhillī" remain. Here, the failure to obtain the desired object—namely, a complexion even more beautiful than the smile on the Lord’s face—and the acquisition of an undesired consequence—the loss of her own natural color—are brought to fulfillment through the sovereign power of *abhedādhyavasāya* (identification based on non-difference), which rests upon the foundation of *śleṣa* (punning) that relies on the identity between word and meaning.

O Acyuta, just as an elephant desiring to reach your path might, out of fear of punishment, assume the form of a monkey by taking on another shape while still near you, and subsequently become a mere monkey; so too [is the case for those who seek your state]. (1208)

O Acyuta! The elephant (vāraṇa)—the word *vāraṇa* itself—desiring your path through theft, is for that very reason *aṇaka*, meaning contemptible; as Amara states: "kheṭa, garhya, and aṇaka are synonyms. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), being devoid of the letter *ṇa*, it is *sanna*, meaning fallen apart, precisely between the desire and the theft; the suffix *kta* is used in the active sense from the root *sad* meaning "to fall apart," and by the rule "radābhyām," the *t* of the past participle suffix and the preceding *d* both become *n*.

In one sense: after the removal of the internal *ṇ* (in the word *vānara*), the remaining syllables are *vā-ra*. Being situated between these two letters (*varṇa-dvitaya-madhye-sat*), that which has a *na* (*nakāra*)—namely, the form *vana*—attained the state of a monkey (*vānaratām*), meaning the state of a leaping creature (*plavaga-tām*) and the status of the word "monkey" (*vānara-śabda-tām*). Thereafter, by attaining an even lower form than that—that is, by attaining the form from which the *r* has departed (*apara-rūpasya*)—meaning through the expulsion of the *repha*, it became merely *vāna*, that is, utterly dried up (*śuṣka*). In the other sense: after the removal of the *ṇ* within the word *vānara*, what remains is *vā-ra*. That which has a *na* situated between those two letters becomes *vana*. Thus, it attained the state of a monkey (*vānaratām*). Subsequently, by attaining a form even lower than that—meaning by the removal of the *repha*—it became merely *vāna*, that is, completely withered.

Hemacandra states: "The word *vāna* [is used] in the sense of a dry fruit, sewing, going, and a mat. In this case, the word *vāna* has occurred. Here, the elephant's failure to obtain the desired object—namely, the theft of the Lord’s gait—and his acquisition of undesirable results such as being tied up with ropes (*aṇaka*) are depicted.
Or as it is said:
"O Blessed One clad in blue garments, one who desires to attain the supreme form of your robe, though disciplining himself, has become a great mass of forest at the edge [of the world]. (1209)

O Lord Nīlāmbara Balabhadra! [As Amara states: "Nīlāmbara is Rohiṇeya. He is a mass of forest and an ocean; the word *vanarāśi* also [conveys this]. Desiring to attain that which is supreme (*param*)—the likeness of your garment’s blue form (*celākāra*), meaning its blue color—he was thus disciplining himself, training his own self for the sake of becoming fit to assume that very form.

In one sense, while making the forest a heap (*rāśi*)—that is, while removing the letter *na* [from *vana*] so that it becomes "heap" (*rāśi*)—it became, at the end or in conclusion, a *varāśi*, a coarse cloth; for Amara states, "a *varāśi* is a thick garment. In another sense, the meaning is that it resulted in the word *varāśi*. Here, the failure to obtain the desired object—the divine silk garment in the form of Lord Balabhadra—and the acquisition of the undesired object—a coarse cloth—are described with respect to the forest-heap.
O Infinite One,
if the ocean were to strive to attain the state of being a mere fragment like the earth, it would remain but a vast heap [of water] due to the diminution of its primordial form.

O Infinite One! O Blessed One who has transcended the threefold limitations! Just as the ocean is a mass of water for the earth which is limited, so too for You—who are Yourself unlimited—even the state of being *aṃśuka* (a fine garment) belongs to You; that is, You possess the nature of a subtle cloth. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *aṃśuka* may refer to a smooth garment, or to clothing in general, or to an upper garment (*uttarīya*)."

The sense is that if one strives to obtain [something], then due to the diminution—that is, the contraction—of even the initial form, the primary nature itself, the result would be merely a coarse cloth (*varāśi*), and not a fine, most praiseworthy, divine garment. The linguistic fact is that the word *vārāśi* is derived as *varāśi* because of the shortening of the initial vowel (*ā*). Here too, as before, the distinction is the same mixture of the impossible and the probable (*saṃbhāvanā*). As for example:

O Acyuta, the full moon, desiring to gradually subdue your face—which is the birthplace of the twice-born (brāhmaṇas) and has bestowed upon it the sovereignty of the king of the twice-born (the moon)—alas, that impure-souled one has resorted to the luster of non-brāhmaṇas (or the lack of splendor). 1211.

O Acyuta! The full moon bestowed the status of king upon the twice-born (Brāhmaṇas) out of pride, thinking, "I am the king of the Brāhmaṇas," according to the Vedic revelation: "Soma alone is our king, so say the Brāhmaṇa subjects. [He also bestowed it] upon the source of the twice-born—the place of origin for Brāhmaṇas—according to the Vedic revelation: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth."

Desiring to bring even your face under his control—that is, to place it within his own power—he gradually became one of defiled soul; by such a resolve, he became a most sinful man, and the factual state of affairs was that his body lost its luster through the waning of its digits during the dark fortnight. The meaning is this: for the sake of proclaiming his own status as a Brahmin-king, he set out to subjugate the face of the Lord—the source of his own birth—which belongs to one who is not a Brahmin (i.e., a Śūdra), and thus he himself attained the state of being a non-Brahmin.

In this context, "he lived by the light of the sun" (aveḥ bhānoḥ tejaḥ upājīvīt) means he accepted it as his means of subsistence. This is because the connection of the moon with the sun and its being endowed with the light granted by the sun is well-known from the Vedas and other sources. As the astronomers say: "The rays of the sun, concentrated in the moon which consists of water, dispel the nocturnal darkness. Here too, the failure to obtain what is desired and the acquisition of what is undesired are evident.

O Mother, just as the swan was defeated by your fame, so too the full moon, though possessing a smile-like luster, somehow became like a prisoner at the end, remaining with her head cast down in a dark cell.

"O Mother! The swan (*marālikā*) desires equality with your fame—this is the underlying sense. Having been surpassed by your fame, she thus becomes *amāliḥ*—a companion (*āli*) of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) [according to Amara: *āliḥ sakhī*]. That is to say, she becomes soiled (*malinā*). In the alternative interpretation, the word division is *amā-āliḥ*; the meaning is that she is devoid of the letters 'ma' and 'li'. Then, somehow, with great effort; in the alternative interpretation, this means through the hardship of abandoning the letters 'ma' and 'li'."

The word *rākā* refers to the full-moon night (*pūrṇaniśākara-pūrṇimā*), meaning that it has attained clarity. The expression *marālikā* (swan) results in the form *rākā* by dropping the letters *ma*, *ka*, and *li*. The two words "by you" (*tava*) and "conquered" (*vijitā*) are to be supplied to both [the preceding and following clauses]. Having been conquered by the luster of your smile—the radiance of the gentle laugh produced by seeing her in that state—she, in the final stage of the conclusion, remains with her head cast down (*avāṅmūrdhā*), even while staying in confinement (*kārāsthitā*), that is, in a prison cell.

The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. The sense is that she attained only the aforementioned wretched state, and not her desired goal. In the alternative (secondary) sense, the word-form *avaśiṣṭā rākā* results in *kāra* when reversed; this is the meaning. Here, the failure of the female swan (*marālikā*) to obtain the desired similarity with the luster of Śrī’s fame and smile, and the attainment of undesirable qualities such as soiledness (*mālinya*), rest upon a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) based on the identity between the word and its meaning.
Or rather,

O playful consort of the Lord of the Golden Mountain, having attained the loss of his own plumage due to the splendor of your mass of hair, the lord of peacocks becomes an object of reproach, assuming the state of a mere monkey-king.

O Consort of the Lord of the Golden Mountain (*kanakagirīśavilāsinī*)! "Golden Mountain" refers to Veṅkaṭādri. "Lord of Peacocks" (*kalāpīśaḥ*) refers to the most excellent of peacocks; the sense is that he desires to attain the splendor of the mass of your hair. Therefore, having incurred the loss—the falling away—of his own plumage (*kalāpa*) due to the very cause of the splendor of your tresses, he becomes an object of reproach. The sense is that, disregarding his own inferiority while desiring to rival the mass of Ramā’s hair, he becomes censurable by the world after suffering the loss of his own feathers.

The sense is that one who attains the state of a lord of monkeys (*kapīśatām*)—that is, the status of being the best among monkeys—becomes excessively fickle like a monkey when his mind is agitated by the failure to obtain what he desires and the arrival of what is undesirable. In another sense, the word *kalāpīśa* (lord of peacocks), having undergone the loss (*apacyutim*) of its own letter *la*, becomes blameworthy (*vacanīyaḥ*) and results in the form *kapīśa* (lord of monkeys). This is the meaning.
O Acyuta, as the moon’s digit was eclipsed by the luster of Your plowshare, it became turbid; having lost its former appearance, it attained a complexion that was even more deficient than its own.

O Acyuta! The meaning is that the digit of the moon (vidhukalā) desires to emulate the beauty of your forehead. It was eclipsed—that is, surpassed—by the splendor of your brow (tvatphālarucā); consequently, being "vikalā," having reached a state of deficiency in its parts, it failed to attain even some semblance of color or form (varṇa). Not only this, but having lost its former shape and its previous natural hue, it then became turbid and opaque; for Amara states: "kaluṣa, anaccha, and āvila mean turbid."

In this context, we have stated more than once that the specific word-form *vidhukalā* is a superimposition of the feminine gender onto a meaning [originally] residing in the word. [The compound] *dhvastadhūḥ* means "she whose *dhu-* has been destroyed" (*astaḥ*, i.e., *nirastaḥ*); thus, it means "having the syllable *dhu-* cast out. Having become *vikalā* (from *vikaleti*), she has not even attained the syllable *ka*—that is to say, she is "devoid of the letter *k*."

The word *āgatapūrvākārā* means: she whose first (*pūrva*) form (*ākāra*), namely the phoneme *ā*, had previously (*pūrva*) arrived—that is, appeared—before all other letters; being such, she became turbid (*āvilā*). The word *vidhukalā* results from the elision of the letter *dh*, becoming *vikalā*; then, with the elision of the letter *k* and the subsequent attainment of the vowel *ā* at the beginning, it becomes *avilā*. This is the derived meaning. Here too, the attainment of the desired and the encounter with the undesired are clear. As in the following example:

O Mother, sugarcane juice, though constantly shaken by the taste of your speech and always possessing the nature of a non-existent thing, attained at the end a certain state as "ikṣuraka" (a type of grass), yet it was not enjoyed even by bees. || 1215 ||

O Mother! That sugarcane juice, world-renowned for its sweetness—meaning the liquor made from mangoes (rasālāsava)—desires even greater excellence than the essence of your speech. Thus, though it has been utterly surpassed by the essence of your speech and consequently assumes the state of a slave or servant, the *ikṣuraka* (a specific type of small thorny shrub) remains merely that, even while worshipping Brahmā at the end; it does not become superior to the essence of your speech. For this very reason, it is [the object] of those who drink honey—the drinkers of *śīdhu* liquor, that is, the bees.

Even though he was fit to be enjoyed, he did not exist; *āsa* is an indeclinable (avyaya) that resembles a verbal form (tiṅanta). The sense is based on the saying: "One devoted to honey does not look at the thorny *ikṣuraka*. In the other sense, the word *ikṣurasa* always bears the state of being devoid of the letter *s* (*asatām*), meaning its *sakāra* has been destroyed. At the end, in the conclusion, even by taking (*bhajan*) the letter *ka*, it results in the word *ikṣuraka*. Here, the failure to obtain what is desired and the acquisition of what is undesired for the sugarcane juice are quite evident.

O Mother, just as the lute (vallakī) is shaken by its own sound, so too do your words attain the state of being sung by the Kīras; having reached the state of a creeping vine (vallarī), they have become surpassed by your exquisite delicacy.

"O Mother!"—the sense is that the lute (*vallakī*) desires to equal your voice. Having been shaken by your voice—that is, by the sound of your throat—it goes, indeed it goes, into the state of a *kīrī* (a female parrot) or a *śukī* (a female maina) in order to weigh your words; it has attained the state of a *vallarī* (a flowering creeper). The meaning is that at the very moment it attained the state of a *kīrī*, it became a *vallarī*. Furthermore, it was utterly surpassed by your delicacy, that is, your exquisite tenderness.

In this alternative interpretation, the word *vallakī* undergoes a transformation into *kīrī*; that is to say, the phoneme *kī* becomes the phoneme *rī*, meaning the removal of the *kī* sound and the insertion of the *rī* sound. Thus, it results in the form *vallarī*. Here, one should observe both the failure of the lute (*vallakī*) to obtain what it desired and the attainment of a succession of undesirable things.
Or for example:
"O Nārāyaṇa, by your glories, even Airāvata has his face and color shattered; licked by shame, he wanders at the edge of the forest, having attained the state of a pigeon. (1217)

He whose facial complexion, the luster of his face, and primary color were shattered is described as such; for this very reason, he was overwhelmed by *trapā* (shame). In the alternative reading (*pakṣe*), the word division is *atra-pāvalīḍhaḥ*; here, in place of the shattered facial complexion, there is *pāvalīḍhaḥ*, meaning endowed with the color *pā* (the color of a pigeon), that is, a pigeon-like smoky hue. In the alternative sense, it means the state of having the word "pārāvata" [as its name]. The rest is clear.
Here too, the failure to obtain the desired object and the attainment of the undesired are described regarding Airāvata, who sought equality with the Lord’s fame.
Or rather,

O Śrīparibṛṭha, the ocean, having lost its quality of being drinkable and desiring to attain your profundity, was shaken and, in its calamity, attained the state of worthlessness by becoming a mere well.

O Śrīparibṛḍha! The ocean Akūpāra, desiring Your profundity—and for that very reason shaken by You (the word "by You" being understood)—has thus lost its original form, that is, its nature consisting of profundity and so forth. Alternatively, it has lost its own original pleasing appearance. Consequently, having fallen into a state of worthlessness, powerlessness, and tastelessness, it has become merely a well; that is to say, it has attained a dimension equal to that of a well.

And he attained such a form; the sense is that he became shallow. In the alternative [allegorical] sense, the word *akūpāra* has lost its initial first letter ‘a’, being thus described as having its first phoneme, the letter ‘a’, [removed]. To exclude the possibility of it being the second ‘a’, the term ‘initial’ (*ādya*) is used. It reached a state of worthlessness (*asāratām*); ‘ā’ and ‘ra’ are called *ārau*, and that which exists together with them is *sāra*. That which is not *sāra* is *asāra*; the state of being so is *asāratā*. This means the condition of being devoid of the consonants in the form of the letters ‘a’ and ‘ra’.

Having fallen into a well, he attained a form described as merely "kūpa. This means that by the disappearance of the initial vowel *ā*, and of the subsequent vowel *ā* and the consonant *r*, only the two syllables remaining as "kūpa" were left; such was the form he acquired. Here too, as before, the incongruity should be understood.

Just as the Lord of the Sun (the Sun-god), desiring both your thighs for his own hands, was rendered deficient by you; even so, let the Lord of the Moon (the Moon-god) also be made equal [in beauty] to one of your feet—what would that matter? (1219)

O Blessed One! The lord of the Kali age, the king of elephants, desiring to place his trunk upon Your thighs—therefore, by You, he was made *vikala* (deprived of luster), or, because of the non-distinction between the letters *ra* and *la*, *vikara* (one whose trunk is impaired). Following that, let there be the *bhādhīśa*: either the thousand-rayed sun (*bhānām adhīśaḥ*), where this word *bhā* ends in *ā* meaning "rays," or the moon, the lord of the stars (*bhānām adhīśaḥ*). Then the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is repeated.

Therefore, even by speaking thus, could anything be equal to your foot—either by its gait or by its nails? The sense is that even if it were the sun, it would not be equal to your foot due to its redness (or lack of grace), and even if it were the moon, it would not be equal to your nail due to its whiteness (or lack of luster). In another sense, the word *kalabhādhīśa* (Lord of the Moon), when deprived of the letters *ka* and *la*, results in the word *bhādhīśa* (Lord of Light). This is a *viṣama* (uneven) figure as before. Or as in this example: "O Master, since she has fled because her heart was shaken by the flavor of your words, and now dwells within her own mind, that grape—though soft—would surely become nothing but clay; what doubt is there? (1220)

O Master! That *mṛdvīkā*—the grapevine (as Amara states: *mṛdvīkā gostanī drākṣā*)—desiring the essence of Your speech, having departed far away because her heart was shaken by the nectar of Your words, became possessed of a dejected mind (*avasattimat*), that is, her heart became despondent; she would surely become nothing but earth (*mṛttikā*), assuming the very form of clay.

The sense is that she would thus become sapless (nīrasā). In the alternative interpretation, there is a word-break as *dhutatvād vyapayātā*; in the first word-break, *dhutatvāt vyapayātā*, the doubling of the letter *da* occurs according to the rule *anaci ca*. In the phrase *yā vasattimatsvāntā*, there is a word-break as *yā avasat ttimatsvāntā*. The specific word-form *yā mṛdvīkā* has departed from (*dvyapayātā*) the syllable *dvī*; or, it is that from which the syllable *dvī* has departed (*apayāta*).

The meaning is "having cast away the two-fold color. *Ttimān* means that which possesses the letter *ti* composed of a doubling; she who has such [a *tti*] within herself—that is, within her interior—is so described. Thus being, she *avasat*, meaning she dwelt. In this interpretation, regarding the form *avasattimad*, one should observe that although there are three *ta*-letters, the second *ta* is elided by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe*, so that in both meanings there remains a state of having two *ta*-letters. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *anta* is not feminine; it denotes certainty, destruction, essential nature, the front, proximity, and the interior."

It would become mere clay; the meaning is that it would result in "clay" according to the manner described. In this case, the grape not only fails to obtain the fruit of the word *śrī* (fortune), but rather incurs the attainment of an intense undesirable state in the form of being clay. Or, for example:

"Having ascended to heaven, Nahuṣa desired to obtain the fame of being the 'Lord of Śacī'; then, cursed and deprived of his fame, he became one who was turned away from fortune (*śrī*) and lost his desire for fame. (1221)

Nahuṣa, well-known as having ascended to heaven—meaning he had attained the station of Indra—was one whose desire was for the title "Lord of Śacī. Immediately following such a resolve, due to his turning away from Śrī (Lakṣmī), he was cursed by a sage (as is understood from the context). Deprived of his fame and destitute of splendor, his greed for that [title] turned him into a python (*ajagara*). Although it is said: "Now, *gonasa*... [the term refers to this].

According to the rule "tilipsassyāt," the word *tilipsa* denotes specifically a particular great serpent called the *gonasa*, and does not denote the *ajagara* (boa constrictor), as per the rule "both *śayu* and *vāhasa* [denote] the *ajagara*. Nevertheless, it should be noted that, despite some slight difference between these two—the *gonasa* and the *ajagara*—their identity is established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*), just as is the case with the *grāha* and the *nakra*. Some read the word *tilipsa* as *tilatsa*.

We have, however, demonstrated this particular poetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) by following the more common reading *tilipsa*. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *til* meaning "to move" (*gatau*), one who "moves" (*telati*) is *tiliḥ*; according to the rule *ikkṛṣyādibhyaḥ*, the suffix *ik* is added, resulting in *tili*, which refers to a moving object. One who "devours" (*psāti*) or eats that is a *tilipsaḥ*. The root *psā* meaning "to eat" belongs to the *adādi* class; from it, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto'nupasarge*. Alternatively, from the root *til* meaning "to moisten" (*snehane*) belonging to the *tudādi* class, *tilana* (moistening) is *tiliḥ*; one who devours by means of that is thus called *tilipsaḥ*. This is merely a demonstration of the meaning in some way or another.

In this case, one should not be overly insistent on the etymological meaning of the parts, as this is a conventional (rūḍha) word. Here, the attainment of an undesirable state—namely, becoming a python—following the failure to obtain the desired object, characterized by Nahuṣa’s acquisition of the fame of being the husband of Śacī, is described. In the alternative sense, the word *abhikhyātilipsa* means that when the sequence of syllables (*abhikhyā*) is removed, what remains is *tilipsa*. Or, for example:

"O Kṛṣṇa! Alas, some wicked bird, desiring to become dark-blue (*mecakī-bubhūṣu*) by stealing away your many splendors, attained a state of blackness (*peca-katām*), yet ended up with a pure white garment (*viśada-aṃśukatām*). (1222)

"O Kṛṣṇa! Indeed, this [bird]—meaning some bird who has attained or reached a clear and distinct state of being a parrot (*śukatām*) as a supplement to the meaning about to be spoken—desires to become exceedingly dark (*mecakībubhūṣuḥ*), so that it may become very black; the intention is that because its own green color is not intensely dark, it wishes to become extremely black. Alternatively, it is one whose rays (*aṃśavaḥ*) are clear (*viśadāḥ*); [the suffix] *kap* indicates the meaning 'one who possesses,' thus meaning one of pale-white color."

"Having attained that state" means having reached it; "some bird" implies a swan (*haṃsa*). "Desiring to become dark-blue" (*mecakībubhūṣuḥ*) means wishing to turn black. The suffix *cvi* is used here in the sense of becoming something that was not previously so. In the alternative interpretation, "dark-blue" (*mecaka*) refers to the eye-spots (*candraka*), and one who possesses these is a peacock (*mayūra*). The *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *mecaka* denotes the eye-spot of a peacock, and in the masculine, the dark-blue color; when associated with that [color], it is used like an adjective; in the neuter, it refers to collyrium and darkness. The *Ratnamālā* also says: "'Mecaka' refers to an eye-spot, darkness, and the blue color (masculine); in the three genders, it denotes that which possesses these."

"From the stealing"—that is, on account of the theft—of the "splendor," meaning the deep blue-black luster, of your abode; being thus a sinner, a perpetrator of sin (as Amara states: "Now, in the masculine, [the word] *pāpa* refers to substance, sin, merit, happiness, and so forth"), he attained the state of a *pecaka*, that is, an owl—"Alas! expressing lamentation.

In reality, however, the word *khaga* (bird), desiring in many ways to become *mecaka* (dark-colored)—that is, wishing to be the word *mecaka*—becomes a sinner (*pāpa*) by the slight removal of the mere consonant *m* (i.e., the *maḥ* becoming *paṃ*). Having thus become such a sinner, it attains the state of a *pecaka* (a rhinoceros or a kind of bird); the meaning is that the word *mecaka*, wishing to become [something else] in the manner described, became the word *pecaka*.

In this instance, for Śuka or Haṃsa, upon attaining the state of a peacock, there is not only the failure to obtain that [original form], but rather the acquisition of an intense undesirable state in the form of being a woodpecker (*pecaka*). And this is brought to fulfillment through an excellence of non-difference based on *śleṣa* (punning conjunction), which has acquired its majesty through the power of the identity between word and meaning. In these examples, it should generally be observed that they are rooted in simile (*upamā*), contain the essence of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), and are supported by *śleṣa*.

Thus, the unsuitability of the nature of birth as being associated with both the non-attainment of the desired and the attainment of the undesired has been shown in general. This very [unsuitability], when combined with the previously mentioned threefold division of the undesired and the previously mentioned fourfold division of the non-attainment of the desired, becomes twelvefold. Among these, first, the twofold division consisting of the non-attainment of objects that are means to one's own happiness and the attainment of objects that are means to suffering has been illustrated.

O Jewel of the Bull-Hill (Śrīśaila), just as the sun, wishing to abandon its flickering nature, attained the state of being the central gem in your necklace—yet even having attained it, it did not cast off that [flickering]; alas, it remained terrified therein! 1223.

The sun is understood as the "jewel of the heavenly world" (*svarlokaratna*). Its "tremulousness" (*taralatva*) may mean its own fickleness, its state of moving about (*ṣidgatva*), or its brilliance; for such is the actual state of things. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *tarala* is used in the sense of 'fickle,' 'moving about,' and also 'brilliant,' and it possesses all three genders. Desirous of departing (*vijihāsuḥ*), even after attaining the status of the central gem of your necklace, it did not abandon—that is, it did not relinquish—that tremulousness; the meaning is that it once again fell into a state of trembling.

The factual state of affairs is that, by being situated in the middle of the necklace, it acquired the name "tarala" (the central gem); however, the meaning is that it "attained" (*avāpsīt*) the flaw of a gem called "trāsa" (trembling) there, or else it "shone" (*bibhāya*) there. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "trāsa" refers to both fear and a flaw in a gem. In the alternative interpretation, the word division is "tatra āsa. There, meaning in the middle of the necklace; "āsa" means it shone. [This is from] the root *as* in the sense of "shining," in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

Here, through the effort to remove the object that is the cause of suffering—namely, the flickering nature of the sun—the non-removal of that [suffering] and the acquisition of another means of suffering in the form of terror are depicted. This very same phenomenon is designated elsewhere as "the failure to obtain a desired object despite an effort for the sake of avoiding misfortune and obtaining it, and the attainment of another undesirable thing," based on a superimposition (adhyavasāya) supported by the foundation of paronomasia (śleṣa).

The failure to achieve one's desired object—which consists in bringing about the means of suffering for another—and the consequent attainment of the means of suffering for oneself: both of these occur, as in the case of a certain cruel woman who, desiring to harm you, O enemy of Kaṃsa, ornament of men, failed to obtain her goal through the giving of breast milk and instead suffered great injury herself. (1224)
Here, by the phrase "that very [power]," the absence of bringing about what is undesirable to the Blessed One is shown.
Or for example:

"O Raghava, the locusts that were the lords of the night-stalkers' armies, though they exerted themselves to extinguish the lamp of your majesty, found their own extinction to be easily attained. (1225)

"For the extinguishing and the pacifying. Extinguishing (*nirvāpaṇa*), pacifying (*śamana*), and ending (*nidhana*) are synonyms; Amara states: "Extinguishing is the act of causing to die (*saṃjñapana*). Here, because the lords of the night-stalkers' forces have undertaken an effort toward a desired end—namely, the extinguishing of the fire of Raghu’s majesty—their goal is not attained; on the contrary, they themselves encounter that which is undesirable. This is an instance [of *viṣama-alaṃkāra*] intermingled with *rūpaka*.
O Son of Nanda, it was as if the world’s kinsman, desiring to bind you with her virtues, exerted herself in vain; yet she has now been bound by your own virtues, and thus she moves but slowly.

"To bind you with qualities"—that is, with ropes; from the root *bandh* (to bind), the suffix *tumun* is applied. There is a conjunction of the letters *na*, *da*, and *dha*. "With your qualities" means with ropes, and also with auspicious qualities such as good character (*sauśīlya*) and so forth. Here, Yaśodā not only fails to achieve her desired object—namely, the binding of her own son—but rather obtains an undesired result for herself: being bound by those very qualities. And the undesirability of this binding is established through the superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) of identity based on the pun (*śleṣa*) between the two meanings conveyed by the word *guṇa*. As in the following example:

Desiring to surpass your form, the Creator fashioned a cloud with a split face; out of anger, he released it, and thus, having its face shattered, it became known as the *mūta* (the broken-faced one).

The Creator Brahmā, desiring to overcome—that is, wishing to surpass—your complexion of glossy dark-blue (snigdha-śyāmaliman), made the cloud's face distorted with anger; the sense is that he struck it firmly on the face. This is a popular proverbial expression. He "bound" (mumuve) it; from the root *mūṅ* meaning "to bind," in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Therefore, this cloud has its face broken, meaning that by being struck down, it is unable to show its face to others.

*Mūtaḥ* means precisely "bound. The suffix *kta* is applied to the verbal root *mṛṅ* (to bind) in the sense of the object (*karman*). Amara states: "That which is bound and tied up is called *mūta*. The actual state of affairs is that the word *jīmūta* becomes *mūta* when its primary syllable *jī* is elided. Here, through the exertion toward a desired object characterized by the means of suffering—namely, the suppression of the Lord's form—not only does Jīmūta fail to obtain it, but the attainment of the means of suffering, such as facial contortions and the like, is also described; thus, the definition [of the figure *vibhāvanā*] is consistent.
Or, for example:

"The ruddy goose (koka), having its supreme quality severed by the blow from the victorious breasts of the Goddess of Fortune, assumed a certain form and, becoming a crow (kāka), became an ill omen (ariṣṭa). (1228)

*Koka* refers to the *cakravāka* bird; the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *kuk* (meaning "to take") by the rule for *laghūpadha* (*guṇa*), resulting in *koka*. Regarding the "conquest" (*jaya*)—that is, the overcoming—of Śrī’s breasts: "overcoming" (*abhibhava*) means making something inferior, a function conducive to producing suffering inherent in another. He was "prepared" (*sannaddha*) or ready for that. For this very reason, he was "completely cut down" (*abhivilūna*) by them—that is, his excellence (*agrya*) or preeminence, such as beauty and so forth, as well as his mountain-like prowess (*parākrama*), were severed in every respect. The suffix *kap* is added according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*.

It is also understood that he had his excellent bowstring cut. By the word "only" (*eva*), the difficulty of regaining the quality that has been discarded is illuminated. Therefore, assuming a certain most pitiable form or appearance—that is, becoming a crow (*kāka*) or a raven (*vāyasa*)—he became *ariṣṭa*. [The term] *ariṣṭa* means one who possesses *ariṣṭa*, which is inauspiciousness or a sign of death; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. However, the essential truth is that he became what is denoted by the word *ariṣṭa*. [As the lexicon states: "Ariṣṭa refers to the inauspicious, copper, garlic, and the maternity chamber."

"Nor does this [word] exist in the signs of death, nor in the *kāka* (crow), nor in *phenila* and *nimba*," according to the *Ratnamālā*. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), *koka* refers to the word *koka*. "That which has the foremost quality" (*agryaguṇaḥ*) means that whose quality (*guṇa*)—so called because it occurs at the beginning (*agre*) within itself—is the vowel *o*; thus it is "that which has the foremost quality. "That in which the letter *ka* is cut off" (*vilūna-ko*) is a *bahuvrīhi* containing another *bahuvrīhi*. The meaning is simply that the letter *ka* has been removed. From that, [the remaining part is] *kam*, the letter *ka*.

The construction is "even the letter *ā*. The meaning is that while worshipping [the Goddess], the letter *ko* undergoes a transformation into the letter *kā*. For this very reason, becoming a *kāka* (crow), it is established as *ariṣṭa*, which signifies a crow. One must not forget the identity between the signified and the signifier.

Here, because the kokila (cuckoo) exerts effort toward attaining its desired object—which is characterized by the means of suffering in the form of being eclipsed by the breasts of Śrī—it is shown that there is not merely a failure to attain that object, but rather the attainment of an undesirable state culminating in the status of a crow; thus both aspects are demonstrated.

If the lunar spot, out of the pride of its power, seeks to conquer the tilaka-mark upon your face, then, being utterly defeated, that spot will become a crow and abandon its "mad-ambala" (its dark, powerful nature).

The word "splendor" (śrīḥ) is understood here by implication. "Madabalam" is a collective dvandva compound meaning "intoxication and strength. If the spot on the moon were to leap up—that is, fly upward—in order to conquer or surpass the tilaka on your face due to its excessive pride in its dark luster and the power of its support, then, being defeated by that tilaka, it would abandon its intoxication, pride, strength, and power, and become like a *kaṅka*, a specific kind of vulture.

The sense is this: just as a vulture, greedy for meat, failing to consider whether that [meat] is difficult or easy to obtain, suddenly swoops down and, being struck by stronger birds from the sky, flees far away—so too is this "kalaṅka" (stain/disgrace). In the alternative interpretation, the word division is *madamba laṃ ca*. O *madamba* (my mother)! The word *kalaṅkaḥ* (the term "kalaṅka") [takes] *laṃ*, meaning the letter *l*; the word *ca* (and) is placed out of its natural order (*bhinnakrama*) and is connected with the word *kaṅka*.

The meaning is that he will become *kaṅka* (a heron), as if he were *ujjhan* (one who abandons). Alternatively, the particle *ca* has the sense of "but" (*tu*), and is connected with *ujjhan*; thus the meaning is: "But [he], abandoning [it], will become a *kaṅka*. Here too, because of the effort toward a desired object—namely, the eclipsing of the beauty-mark on Śrī’s face by the *kalaṅka* (stain)—there is the failure to attain that, and the attainment of a prominent undesired state in the form of becoming a *kaṅka*. This is composed in the form of a future possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) based upon a hyperbole (*atiśaya*) rooted in paronomasia (*śleṣa*).

Or rather, O Lord, just as the gambling hall (masāra), desiring to conquer Your splendor, approached You with its first defeat; though it subsequently attained great wealth, it ultimately met with dispersion, having been defeated by Your two eyes. 1230.

O Lord, that famous *masāra*—the sapphire (*indranīla*)—is cited in the lexicon *Bhūṣaṇa* in the entries "masāra indranīle syāt" and "masāragalvarkamukhaḥ. Desiring your victory—that is, your overcoming—it seeks its first defeat, its very initial humiliation. In the alternative sense, the word *masāra* [is analyzed as follows]: in the phrase "saprathamabhaṅgam," the division is "sa-prathamabhaṅgam. O "Sapratha" (O you of wide fame), this is a vocative qualifying the word "Lord" (*nātha*).

"Saprathaḥ" means that which exists together with "prathā," or renown; this is its vocative form. Having undergone the elision of the letter *m* (i.e., dropping the *m* of "mabhaṅgam"), immediately thereafter—in the initial portion—the sense is that he has attained "vibhavam," meaning power or majesty, which serves as the instrument for victory. In the alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), even after attaining the "bhavam"—the existence—of the syllable "vi," the particle "api" indicates that such power is of no consequence. In this context, "api" is used as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).

The meaning is that not only was the letter *ma* elided, but it also underwent a transformation (*vikāra*) right there. "Fishiness" (*visāratām*) means the state of being a fish (*mīnatām*), according to Amara’s lexicon: “*visāra* and *śakulī* [both mean fish]"; it is also understood as "insubstantiality" or "weakness. In the alternative sense (the pun), it means that the word *visāra* was actually formed. He was conquered by your two eyes, your two organs of sight; here too, as before, both meanings apply.
Or rather:

O Lord, when you were victorious, the female crane was somehow cast from the lead by your horse Śabalāśva; even though she has now regained her luster, she remains merely a crane and can never be a conqueror.

O Lord! Śabalā, the wish-fulfilling cow, was abandoned at the very outset—meaning her hope was cast off—at the yoke, that is, at the beginning, regarding the matter of Your victory and the overcoming of those who act against You through her gift, her generosity, and her instrumentality. Then, even if she somehow attained *kāntimatvam*—where *kānti* means desire (or, as Medinī states, "splendor and desire"), thus meaning the longing for the subject of Your victory—or even if she attained *dyutimatvam* (radiance)—she remains nothing but a crane (*balākā*), like one with a lotus-stalk in its beak (*bisakaṇṭhikā*).

But [your opponent] is not your conqueror; likewise, she does not fly away anywhere, nor is she able to overcome you—this is the meaning. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the word-form *śabalā* is "abandoned at the front" (*dhuri ujjhitā*), that is, deprived of the letter *śa*. Then, regarding "possessing beauty" (*kāntimatva*): *kā* is the final letter of which it consists, thus it is *kāntima*; the state of being that (*bhāva*) refers to the doubling of the letter *ta* according to the rule *anaci ca*. The neuter gender is used in the general sense, as in the example "the fulfillment of the purpose of autumn" (*śaradaḥ kṛtārthatā*).

Even though she has reached the end, being composed of the letter *ka*, she becomes merely a *balākā* (crane), and not the word *jetrī* (conqueror); such is the meaning. Here too, everything is exactly as before. Or, for example:

"O Blessed One Balabhadra, desiring the glory of victory over Your garment, the cloud (*balāhaka*) in the middle [of the sky] acted like a crane (*baka*) through the impetuosity of pulling the plow (*hala*) in reverse. (1232)

O Blessed Balabhadra! This [epithet] is for the purpose of highlighting your blue garments. *Balāhaka* means "cloud" or "water-bearer," used here to highlight the excellence of your deep blue hue. Desiring to surpass—that is, to overcome—the splendor of your garment, at this very moment, in the midst of this [encounter], the plow (*halam*) was cast all around; the sense is that it was thrown by you with the impetuosity of its own pulling.

The crane (*baka*), having become pale like a crane due to the mental anguish rooted in the failure to achieve the desires of others and the attainment of his own undesirable ends—anguish which overcomes its natural blackness—did not, however, attain a superior excellence of lovely blackness through the splendor of victory over your garment; such is the sense. Alternatively, it means that he became intent on meditation (*dhyāna*) like a crane.

In this context, the word *balāhaka*—by the forceful drawing out (*karṣaṇa-rabhasena*), that is, the displacement, of the two letters *ha* and *lā* which are reversed (*paryasta*) or transposed within its middle; or rather, by the forceful drawing out of the letters *ha* and *lā* such that they become reversed—the letter *ha*, which was at the end, being moved after the letter *lā*, which was originally first—it becomes the meter *baka*, meaning the form *baka* is produced.

O Mother, as if out of curiosity to conquer the pair of your eyes, the deer approached; having been repelled by them, it suffered injury here and attained a state of emaciation on the mountain of the Lord of Birds.

The word *hariṇa* means a deer; here, it refers to harm or loss (*kṣati*). In the alternative sense, "by *ina*" means by the letter *i*; "with *hakṣati*" means the removal of the letter *ha*. The compound is formed with a genitive of general relation. Having approached—that is, having attained the letter *i* in place of the letter *ha*—it reached the state of *iriṇa*, meaning emptiness or the loss of its own form. In the alternative sense, it became the word *iriṇa*. As Amara states in his list of words ending in *ṇa* among various meanings: "Now, *viṣāṇa* may mean [a horn] in three genders... *iriṇa* is a void, a saline wasteland."

And the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *iriṇa* means a saline wasteland or a void. Here, for the deer, there is the attainment of the undesired and the non-attainment of the desired, in the form of being subjected to the harm of another.
O Acyuta, if sandalwood, desiring to surpass you— who are the essence of all fragrances— by its own scent, I think it would either have to become the slayer of Cakra (Viṣṇu) or else simply weep.

The term *sarvagandha* means "possessing all fragrances," as heard in the passage, "He who is all-action, all-desire, and all-fragrance. Because of the negation of ordinary fragrances and so forth in the passage beginning with "soundless and touchless," the meaning is that He possesses all auspicious qualities—extraordinary, unique to Himself, eternally faultless, unsurpassed, constituting His very objects of enjoyment. The implication is: "How can such a You be compared to sandalwood, which is merely a substrate for ordinary and limited fragrance?"

If Saurabha, desiring victory, were to effect a "bhidā"—meaning a piercing or breaking—by means of his Sudarśana discus (the compound *bhidā-sādhana* meaning "that which effects breaking"), he would surely go to his destruction through the letter *k* [of the word *cakreṇa*], which acts as a "bhidā" (a refutation) of the letter *kre*. Then, after reaching such a state, he would merely "krandana" (wailing), that is, simply weeping; or, in another sense, he would become the very word "krandana. Here, the attainment of the desired and the attainment of the undesired regarding the sandalwood are constructed through the mode of poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*).
Or rather:

When the lotus, having been struck by those two [the sun and moon] who desired honor on earth through the victory of the luster of your hands, became face-down before them—its beauty diminished and its color faded—it became the Mother [the Earth]. 1235.

O Mother! [The lotus] has "much loss" (*bahuhāni*) at the beginning—that is, in its initial state. It is "one whose disrepute has arisen" (*uditāvarṇa*), meaning it possesses the blame or scandal that "it has been defeated"; as Amara states: "Disparagement, reviling, censure, and defamation are synonymous with *avarṇa*. Alternatively, it may mean "having disrepute arisen due to much loss. In the other sense (the wordplay), the division is *bahu-hā*. At the front—the frontal part—it is "much cut down" (*nyudita*), meaning it is split (*dita*) by the cluster of syllables *nyu-ṇa-nyu*, or rather, destroyed.

The word *tādṛśam* means "of such a kind. *Avarṇa* refers to that which has no color (*akāra*). Thus, *nyuditāvarṇa* means "one whose color has been removed"; according to Amara, *dita*, *chita*, and *vṛkṇa* all mean "cut. It became *nyubja*, meaning broken by disease; this form is correct due to the grammatical rule of *nipātana* stating "the words *bhujam* and *nyubjam* are used for the hand and affliction, respectively. According to Amara, *nyubja* means "bent by disease. The actual state of affairs is that the lotus-foot became bent. *Hā* expresses grief. The rest is clear.
Just as the sun, desiring to conceal your disc with its own radiance, approached you, it was seized by your splendor; stripped of its rays and deprived of its garland, it was destroyed by him.

By that great splendor, the brilliance of the discus, he was "niraṃśukaḥ," meaning his garment was stripped away, or alternatively, his rays were shed. In the other sense, the great demon named Mālī—whose name is composed of the word *aṃśu* (ray) and *mālī*—became "aṃśumāli," meaning that by the removal of the word *aṃśu*, only "Mālī" remained. The rest is clear.

Just as a *mālūra* fruit, desiring to surpass the breasts of beautiful women and wishing to be called by their name, was instructed by a scribe to write "māphalam" (a worthless fruit), so too did it become designated as such. 1237.

Having desired—that is, having looked toward—the fruit of the *mālūra* (bilva) tree as a means to conquer the beauty of Śrī’s breasts, [the tree] was immediately (*aram*) cut down by those two breasts; that is, it was severed right after [the desire arose], not with delay—meaning it was utterly defeated. The sense is that the *māphala* (the "fruit of the mā" tree) has failed to achieve its intended purpose; for, according to the maxim "as long as one lives, one sees auspicious things," the tree, being incapable of accomplishing its own desired end, now harbors despair, thinking, "How can I possibly remain alive?"

It was fleeing in all directions out of fear of its adversaries; [the form] *abhidhāvat* is derived from the root *dhāv* preceded by the prefix *abhi*, in the present participle (*śatṛ*). Likewise, due to its *lipi*—that is, by the power of the lines on the forehead which indicate such karmic fruits—it was reduced to nothing but breath, and thus became "blameworthy" (*vācya*), meaning devoid of vigor and contemptible. Regarding the word *vācya*, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *vācya* is used in the sense of the censurable, the inferior, and that which is fit to be spoken."

In this context, the word *mālūraphala* (the wood-apple fruit) undergoes a transformation: following the desire to surpass the breasts of Lakṣmī, it is "cut" (*lūna*)—meaning deprived of the letter *la* (*lūvarṇena nyūna*)—and being thus "devoid of the letter *ra*" (*ara*, i.e., lacking the phoneme *ra*), it remains as *māphala* when written according to its constituent letters. This is what is meant by "remaining well" (*suśiṣṭa*, i.e., properly remaining). It then "runs toward" (*abhidhāvat*) its primary function; for "denotation" (*abhidhā*) is defined as "the primary operation residing in a word, which is the cause of the cognition of the object directly denoted by the convention. As the definition states: "The primary operation residing in the word, which is the cause of the cognition of the denotable meaning, is called *abhidhā*."

The word "tathoktam" (so-called) means that which possesses this [quality], formed with the suffix *matup*. It was "vācyam," meaning it became something that ought to be spoken; the sense is that it became fit for conventional usage by virtue of possessing the power to have the object in the form of a *śrīphala* as its referent.

Alternatively, the very object in the form of the *mālūra* fruit was written by means of the phonemes (*varṇa*) residing in its own expressive word; thus, according to the aforementioned method, by the removal of the phoneme *lū*, it became "suśiṣṭa," meaning properly remaining. Being "abhidhāvat"—that is, possessing the designation *māphala*—it became fit to be spoken as its own denotable object (*vācya*), meaning it became suitable for linguistic usage without ever abandoning its own designated referent. *Māphala* means the *śrīphala* (bilva) fruit.

And [the word] *bilva* signifies the fruit of the *mā* tree; this is because of the Vedic revelation: “The *vanaspati* is your tree, namely the *bilva*” (Śruti). Furthermore, it should be understood from the *Vāmanapurāṇa* cited in the commentary of Vidyāraṇya: “The *bilva* was in the hand of Lakṣmī,” and from the statement in the *Bhārgavatantra* cited in the commentary of Pṛthvīdhara: “She of slender waist, leaning against the tree, held the *bilva* produced from her own hand. The term *phalaḥ* is derived from the root *phal* with the suffix *pacādyac*, meaning that which bears fruit or comes into fruition.

*Māphala*: The word *māphala* refers to the *bilva* fruit because it is produced from the hand of Lakṣmī (*mā*). Its derivative product is *māphala*. Alternatively, it is a *madhyamapadalopa* (elided middle term) compound like *śākapārthiva*, meaning "one whose fruits (*phala*) bestow grace (*mā*)"—that is, one who grants prosperity (*śrī*). This is because of the scriptural statement, "May his fruits dispel internal obstacles through austerity and external misfortune (*alakṣmī*)," which indicates that the fruit bestows prosperity. Thus, the meaning is "one whose fruit bestows grace."

Therefore, the elision of the suffix *vikāra* for the sake of the fruit [is applied]. It should be understood that the word *māphala*—like the word *śrīphala* found in the lexicon which states, "The *bilva* is called *śāṇḍilya*, *śailṛṣa*, *mālūra*, and *śrīphala* as well"—denotes the *bilva* tree; and likewise, words such as *lakṣmīpati* denote the Lord of Lakṣmī, just as the word *śrīpati* found in the lexicon which states, "*Śrīpati* is *Puruṣottama*," denotes *Puruṣottama*. Here, the attainment of the undesired and the non-attainment of the desired (in the form of bringing about misfortune to others) are attributed to the *mālūra* fruit.

Just as the wood-apple (*mālūra*) was prepared by the two breasts of the Lord’s consort to overcome it, so too, from the blow of those very breasts, the lotus-root (*śālūka*)—already wounded and having resorted to water—became [a mere remnant]. (1238)

O Hariṇī! A *mālūra* is the fruit that is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *mālūra* tree; the suffix *luk* is applied by the rule *vaikārikāṇo luk*, and the sense is that it is neuter. It is "prepared" (*sannaddha*) for the "overpowering" (*abhibhavana*), that is, the eclipsing, of your two breasts; therefore, [it is as if] cut down (*chāta*)—the past passive participle *kta* is used in the sense of the object—from a single initial blow (*abhighāta*), that is, a strike, from those two [men], namely your two breasts; [this is derived] from the root *cho* in the sense of "cutting," with the suffix *kta* in the passive sense.
