By the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*, there is the substitution of *ā* for *e*; "cut down" is *chāta*, according to Amara.

Alternatively, there is a word-break as *śātam*. *Śātam* means "thinned," "emaciated"; the sense is that it has been made lean. [This is derived from] the root *śo* in the sense of "making thin," with the suffix *kta* and the substitution of *ā* for *o* as before. For this very reason, it is "that which has resorted to water" (*śritanīrakaṃ*), meaning that by which water has been resorted to; in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. The sense is that it was submerged in the water out of fear of further blows. Regarding *śalūkaṃ*: Amara states, beginning with "The *kahlāra* is indeed the *saugandhika*," that "the bulb (*kanda*) of these is the *śālūka*."

It is called *śalya* because it pierces (*śalyate*) or moves (*śalati*), derived from the roots *śala* in the sense of "moving" or "covering," with the suffix *ūkaṇ* according to the rule "from *śali* and *maṇḍi*, [the suffix] *ūkaṇ*. This is clear in the *Sudhā* commentary. Alternatively, the word *mālūra* is so called because, having undergone the destruction (*dhvaṃsana*) of its initial first letter, the syllable *mā*, it constantly moves toward (*atati*) the form *śā* or *śākāra*; thus it is described as such, derived from the root *ata* in the sense of "continuous movement," with the suffix *aṇ* in the objective sense (*karmaṇyaṇ*).

The meaning is as follows: that by which the letter *ra* has been expelled from "śritanīrakam" (resting in water) is "nīraḥ"; and that which has taken refuge in the letter *ka* [after the removal of *ra*] is likewise called "nīra-ka". Furthermore, when the letter *śa* takes the place of *mā* and the letter *ka* takes the place of *ra*, the form "śālūkam" (lotus root) is produced. In this context, there is the non-attainment of the desired object—namely, the mango fruit's surpassing the breasts of the Goddess—and the attainment of an undesired state, namely, its transformation into a lotus root due to being struck and so forth.

Just as a camel, out of pride in its gait, approaches you while being shaken by the wind from your mouth, it remains only at the front; though it has become a mere sheep, it does not yet honor the battle. 1239.

O Blessed One! The elephant, advancing toward you for the purpose of an attack out of pride in his gait—an arrogance born from the depth of his stride—was shaken by the whirlwind of your mouth. Regarding the phrase "by yours" (*asya tava*): he was shaken by the very force of the whirlwind of your mouth, that is, by the abundance of the breath and hissing from your mouth. A *vātyā* is a collection of winds; the suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of a collective according to the rule *pāśādibhyo yaḥ*. Its feminine gender is established by the grammatical injunction *tal bṛnde yenikaḍyactrāḥ*.

By this, his defeat by a woman is illuminated. For this very reason, immediately thereafter, having ascended into the sky—meaning, being fixed somewhere in the heavens—he was born as a *uraṇa*, a ram; that is to say, he underwent birth as a ram, or rather, he became devoid of prowess like one. It may also be understood that he entered the sign of Aries (*meṣarāśi*) in the sky. Therefore, this elephant or ram even today does not place battle before him—that is, he does not honor combat—out of fear of defeat; such is the sense.

In the word *vāraṇa* (elephant), the syllable *vā* is the primary constituent; however, when it is "shaken off" (*atyādhūta*), meaning cast aside, and the vowel *u* (*u-varṇa*) is placed before or immediately after it, the form *uraṇa* is produced. This [new form] even now does not place the cluster of sounds *ra-ṇa* (the letter *ra* and the letter *ṇa*) at the beginning, but rather bears them only at the end. The sense is that in both the words *vāraṇa* and *uraṇa*, the sound-cluster *ra-ṇa* is not seen at the beginning, but is seen only at the end.

In this case, there is for Vāraṇa both the non-attainment of the desired object—characterized by the infliction of an adverse result consisting in the reduction of his progress toward the Blessed One—and the attainment of an undesired object in the form of being a ram.
Or as it is said:
Having approached out of curiosity to surpass your face, that moon was cast away midway; yet, becoming a night-maker, he provided protection against the cold wind. (1240)

O Mother! That moon, renowned for bestowing joy upon the world, came out of curiosity to surpass your face, but was repelled midway by your curls—that is, by your *cūrṇakuntalas* (fine, curly locks). The sense is that for such a being, direct opposition to your face makes the defeat of it quite easy. In the alternative sense, the word *niśākara* (moon) has its *ka* (the letter *k*) "repelled" (*nirasta*) within the interval—that is, from among its constituent letters—meaning the letter *k* has been removed.

"Becoming a *niśāra*—that is, becoming a cloak for warding off the cold wind" (Amara states: "The word *niśāra* occurs in the sense of a cloak for warding off the cold wind"). In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), the meaning is that he becomes the word *niśāra*. The implication is: "Have you become a servant for the purpose of warding off the cold wind for yourself or for another? He performed this. Herein lies both the non-attainment of the defeat of Śrī’s face by the Moon, and the attainment of an undesirable state, namely being a *niśāra* (a servant). As in the following example:
O Blessed One, as the moon approached you face-to-face to conquer your fame, it indeed became filled with apprehension midway, its luster fading due to your teaching.

O Blessed One! The moon, out of curiosity, was approaching face-to-face to conquer and achieve victory over Your fame; in the alternative sense (pakṣe), it was reaching the letter *sa*, which is the first among all letters and constitutes its face (*mukha*). Then, without delay, at that very moment—meaning in the interim—in the alternative sense, in the middle part, it was punished by You with a lesson corresponding to its transgression; in the alternative sense, the letter *śā* was expelled from it.

With his complexion faded, his luster drained away, and his syllables cast out, he became filled with apprehension and pierced on the left side. In the alternative sense, the word *śaśāṅka* (the moon), by placing the letter *sa* at the beginning and by the loss of the letter *śa* in the middle, results in the form *saśaṅka* (apprehensive). This is the meaning.

O Blessed One, as if desiring to conquer Your nails, the moon—struck by these [nails] on its surface and ultimately losing its own essence (visarga)—became distressed and survived only by taking refuge in the Fish (the Fish-bannered God). 1242.

O Blessed One! The moon (Indu), desiring to conquer Your nails, engaged in this "talātali" battle—so called because they struck one another palm-to-palm (*talaistalaiḥ*) with those very nails. In that struggle, having been struck and wounded until finally reaching the point of death, he was spared by Your compassion and released far away; such is the sense. Therefore, being exceedingly distressed and tormented, he lived on merely by taking refuge in *Ina* (the Sun)—that is, by relying upon an obscure lord.

Alternatively, the construction is: "Having resorted to no lord whatsoever, the living being merely sustained its breath. The sense is that it performed only the maintenance of life, but was not able to overcome them. In the other [punning] sense, the word *indu* (moon), moving toward the *visarga* (the *visarjanīya* letter) at the end—without abandoning the *visarga*, yet merely "distressed" (*dūnaḥ*), meaning having become deficient in the letter *du*—resorted to the phonetic cluster *in* (*ina*) and "sustained its breath," which is to say, it obtained its own existence as a word-form. Everything else is as explained previously.

O Blessed One, just as the ancient sun, having been surpassed by Your new splendor, became dimmed and was cast down from the sky, so too did Pradyotana, bowing before Your weapon, fall with his head cast downward.

O Blessed One! The sense is that the sun (*bhānu*), known as *Pradyotana*, desires to conquer your splendor. He is [to be] praised by a "new" one—that is, by a youth; this is the actual state of affairs. The suffix *-ya* is applied according to the rule *aco yat*. He has been surpassed and eclipsed by your majesty (*mahaḥ*), your brilliance (*tejaḥ*); for this very reason, he is fallen from the sky (*dyo*)—that is, from the atmosphere or from heaven. The cause for this is that he is "himself ancient" (*svayaṃpratana*). *Pratana* means old or worn out. The suffix *ṭyu* is applied according to the rule *naśca purāṇe prāt*.

According to Amara, "purāṇa," "pratana," "pratna," "purātana," and "cirantana" all mean ancient. The sense is: how could he, who is himself old, not be overwhelmed by your youthful splendor as he vies with it? Due to the blow inflicted by your brilliance—that is, from the strike caused by your luster—he became *avākśiras*, meaning with his head cast downward; that is to say, he bowed down, his head bent and broken by that blow, and sought refuge.

In one sense, the word *pradyotana*—being "deprived of *dyo*" (meaning the syllable *dyo* has been elided from it)—becomes *pratana*, which results in *pratama*. Then, through the elision of the cluster of syllables beginning with *pra* (the prefix), meaning "having reached that," [it becomes *nata*]. The ablative case is used here in the sense of "omission" (*lyablope*). Being "downward-headed," that is to say, being reversed, it became *nata*; thus, it resulted in the form *nata*.

The word *pratana* results from the inversion of the two syllables *ta-na*, which remain after the elision of the prefix; this is the established meaning. Here, the Lord’s desire to overcome Pradyota is understood through the force of the contextual association (*samabhivyāhāra*), while the attainment of the undesirable is quite evident. The rest has been explained.
O Mother, just as a piece of sugarcane, overwhelmed by the flavor of your words, became garlic and the like; having then become a piece of liver, it subsequently became food for carnivorous beasts.

O Mother! A piece of sugarcane, a piece of *rasāla* (mango), or a piece of mango fruit—each of these, in comparison to the flavor of your speech, becomes like garlic and the like; that is, surpassed by the flavor of your words. It becomes the foremost (*ādya*) among things such as garlic (*rasonaka*), or rather, it becomes a foodstuff consisting of garlic. As Amara states: "Garlic (*laśuna*), *gṛñjana*, *ariṣṭa*, *mahākanda*, and *rasonaka* [are synonyms]."

The sense is this: although it was initially perceived as sweet in its general nature, through a lack of reflection on its true essence, it became overwhelmed by the flavor of the most sweet words of Śrī [the Goddess], and thus, being cast aside by them, it turned foul-smelling. Not only this much; thereafter, having become a *kālakhaṇḍa*—a piece of flesh known as the liver (according to Amara: "Both *kālakhaṇḍa* and *yakṛt* are the same")—it became food for *kravyādas*, meaning raw-flesh-eaters such as birds or Rākṣasas.

"Kravyād refers to both a flesh-eater (māṃsāśin) and a Rākṣasa," according to the *Ratnamālā*. The sense is that these [beings] became their object of consumption, but not those who know the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). In the alternative sense, the word *rasālakhaṇḍam* means "garlic" (*rasona*), being devoid of the letter 'r' and the vowel 'ā'. That which has the letter 'ka' as its first [syllable] means it is composed of the letter 'ka' at the beginning. The compound is a descriptive determinative (*viśeṣaṇobhayapada-samāsa*) consisting of the two qualifiers *rasona* and *kādyam*. Having become thus, it results in the form *kālakhaṇḍam*.

In this case, for one who desires to savor the essence of the *Śrīvacana*—a section of the *Rasāla*—there is the failure to obtain it and the attainment of undesirable results such as being like garlic (*rasonaka*).

Just as Vaiśvānara, being struck by that rivaling vigor of yours, was then cast down; emitting heat and abandoning his food, he attained the state of a monkey and became truly a "vāna" (one who has abandoned).

O Blessed One! He is Vaiśvānara, the fire; there is an identity between him and the word "Vaiśvānara. He is so described because he vies with your *ojas*, that is, your majesty. Struck—that is, assailed—by him, he fell immediately thereafter. The particle *vai* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), according to the statement of Amara, "It should be thus, *tu*, *punaḥ*, *vai*, *eva*," which was read by Subhūti as "*punaḥ* and *vai*. This is clear in the *Sudhā* commentary. The meaning is: he simply fell down.

In the case of the word *vaibhraṣṭa*, it is a compound (*samasta-pada*). The meaning is "one who has undergone the loss of the phoneme *vai*. *Vyūṣmā* means "devoid of heat," that is, one whose majesty has been extinguished; in the alternative sense, it means "one from whom the letter *śa* has departed," because the letter *śa* is designated as an *ūṣman* (aspirate/fricative) according to the rule: "The letters *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are *ūṣmans*. Having attained the state of a monkey (*vānaratām etya*), the sense is that he became as extremely fickle as a monkey due to a heart bewildered by a lack of discernment.

In one sense, the meaning is that when the *sa*, *sva-ra* (vowel), and *vyañjana* (consonant) are removed from *pakṣe vai iti*, and the solitary *vyañjana* *ś* is also removed, what remains is *vānara*. The underlying sense is that he was performing a *prāyopaveśa* (fast unto death) out of grief rooted in his defeat, while abandoning all food and drink. In the other sense, the word is split as *hā* + *āhāram*. Abandoning the letter *ra* (*repha*), the word *vānaḥ*—meaning "dry" (*śuṣka*)—indicates that he somehow sustained his life-breaths even while being parched. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *vāna* refers to something dry or a dried fruit."

The *Hemacandra* lexicon states: "The root *vān* [is used] in the sense of drying fruit, drying, sewing, going, and a mat. From the roots *pai*, *o*, or *vai* in the sense of "drying," the suffix *kta* is applied according to rules such as "the suffixes beginning with *kta* [are added] after roots meaning 'going' or 'transitive action. By the rule "also after roots ending in *o*," its [the *kta*-suffix's] *t* becomes *n*. By the rule "for *e* and *ai* at the time of instruction, when followed by a suffix other than one beginning with *ś*," there is *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel). In the alternative case where the *r* is also elided, what remains is *va-na*; having thus been brought (*ānīta*), the sense is that it attained existence merely by that much. Herein lie the failure to obtain the desired and the attainment of the undesired for Vaiśvānara.

O Mother, by your pair of breasts, the lotus bud has been deprived of its beginning and end; furthermore, even the stainless mirror has been cast down by your two cheeks through the attainment of the essence of both its beginning and end.

O Mother! A lotus bud—that is, a lotus calyx—is soft and solitary; this is the sense. By your pair of breasts, which are exceedingly hard, mutually supportive, and existing as a couple—this is the sense—it has been "distressed" (vikalita), meaning rendered deficient, deprived of its full power and so forth, and surpassed by competing with them; this is the sense. This applies "at the beginning and the end," meaning at both the start and the conclusion, in every respect; this is the sense. It has been made "distressed" (vikala), rendered devoid of its totality of strength and the like, and cast down by them in their rivalry.

Immediately thereafter, the meaning is as follows: "possessing strength that is essential from beginning to end" (ādyantasāra) refers to one whose essence is such; the state of being that is "essentiality from beginning to end" (ādyantasāratā); by the attainment (āptyā) of that—that is, by the acquisition of the possession of power and so forth in every respect—he desires to act against you. Furthermore, the sense is that although he is like a stainless mirror, he has nonetheless attained birth as a spotless looking-glass (nirmalādarśa).

The sense is that what has been shaken from your two cheeks and cast far away—even though it was possessed of substance—is utterly defeated by these two which are more substantial; for one who competes with two superior entities, there can only be total humiliation. In another sense, the word *kamalamukula* (lotus bud) has had its initial and final syllables (*ka* and *la*) displaced or removed; the meaning is that it has been made to undergo the loss of the letter *ka* at the beginning and the letter *la* at the end, respectively.

Now, by attaining the state of being *sāra* (essential) through the presence of *a* and *ra* at the beginning and end: *ara* means that which exists together with *a* and *ra*; the state of being that is *sāratā*, and by the attainment of that. The meaning is: through the connection of the letter *a* at the beginning and the letter *ra* at the end. "Becoming a stainless mirror" (*amalamukura*) means that the word *amalamukura* comes into being. In this case, for the lotus bud, there is not only the non-attainment of the desired object—namely, the attainment of the form of the two breasts of Śrī—but also the attainment of the undesired, such as being torn apart and so forth.

Thus, for that very [lotus], even in another birth as a stainless moon, there is not only the failure to obtain the desired object in the form of surpassing the beautiful cheeks, but rather the attainment of an undesirable result in the form of being shaken by those two. This should be understood in all cases.
Or as it were:

O you who desire your own victory, the saffron (ghusṛṇa), surpassed by the luster of your lower lip, has abandoned its own color; having become like a wood-worm (ghuṇa), it has settled and hidden within some hollow in a piece of wood.

O Mother! *Ghusṛṇam* means saffron, specifically that which is produced in Kashmir (*kāśmīrajam*). [The moon] desires its own victory—that is, it seeks to overcome you as its object by means of itself. For this very reason, it is surpassed (*parāstam*)—that is, disregarded—by the luster of your lower lip; consequently, it is "fallen" (*srastam*), meaning ruined and rendered lusterless, even from its own color (*svavarṇataḥ*), that is, even from its own natural beauty. In the alternative sense (the pun), the word *ghusṛṇam* [is analyzed as follows]: according to the rule for the suffix *tasi* following words beginning with *sva-*, the term *svavarṇataḥ* means "among its own constituent letters. Thus, [the word *ghusṛṇam*] is surpassed among its own phonemes.

"Srasta" means that the phoneme *sṛ* has fallen away (*asta*) or been cast out (*nirasta*); thus it is so described. When "sṛ-asta" stands, the substitution of *yaṇ* (i.e., *ṛ* becoming *u*) occurs; the meaning is that the letter *sṛ* has been expelled. Having attained the state of a woodworm (*ghuṇatām*), or in another sense, the state of the word "woodworm" (*ghuṇaśabdatām*), it has fallen from its own dwelling within the wood into some other region of space, and even there, into some cavity or some corner. It should be supplied [in the commentary] that "within the wood" means within another piece of timber, and "even there" means in some hole; for it is well known that woodworms reside within the interior of cavities in wood. "Līnam" means having reached dissolution (*layam*).

Just as, O Mother of the World, even aśoka wood—though situated in the midst of agaru and its form throbbing with redness when permeated by your fragrance—became *aguru-guru* (heavy with weight) while being *aguru-guru* (not heavy/superior), so too did the world become [weighty]. O Mother of the World (*jagajjanani*)! *Agaru* is a well-known specific fragrant substance fit for kings; as Amarasimha states: "Vaṃśaka, agaru, rājārha, lohaja, krimijaja, and aṅgaka. This word is also masculine, as Śrī Harṣa says in the *Dvirūpakośa*: "It is both *agaru* and *aguru*. (Note: The verse plays on the double meanings of *agaru* [aśoka tree] and *aguru* [the fragrant resin], and the compound *aguru-guru*, which can mean "not heavy" or "heavy with weight," depending on the context.)

Hemacandra also states in the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*: "The word *aguru* [is used] for that which is not heavy (*agaru*) and for the *śiṃśupā* tree. Vopālita and others likewise hold this view. Furthermore, there is the usage: "the fragrance of *aguru* cut by the cold. It is understood that [he] desired to surpass the illustrious Parimala. Even though situated in the midst of trees or mountains—by this, one may understand that he dwelt having taken refuge in a desert-fort (*dhanvadurga*), an earth-fort (*mahīdurga*), a water-fort (*abdurga*), a forest-fort (*vārkṣadurga*), a human-fort (*nṛdurga*), or a mountain-fort (*giridurga*).
With every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for, by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.

By the manner stated thus, his status as one stationed in a fortress is suggested. By "your fragrance" (tvatparimalena)—that is, by the scent of your limbs—his status as a heroic man is understood, in accordance with the meaning to be expressed hereafter. The truth is that he is "pierced" (viddhaḥ), wounded by weapons and the like, and thus repelled. For this very reason, he is described as "one whose form quivers with ulcers" (arubhiḥ sphurantīmūrtiḥ); "wound" (aru) is synonymous with "scar" (īrma) and "boil" (vraṇa), according to Amara.

In this context, *agaru* refers to the word *agaru*. It is called *agamadhyastha* because its middle is not the letter *ga* (the syllable *ga*). Nevertheless, it is described as having a "throbbing form" (*arusphuranmūrti*), meaning its essential nature is manifested by the letters *a* and *ru*; the sense is that even when the letter *ga* is removed, only the two syllables *aru* remain.

Then, "madhyasthagu" means one whose *sthagu*—a specific protruding and deformed part of the body emerging from the chest—is situated in the middle, that is, in the center of the body. This is explained in exactly this way in the *Śrīrāmāyaṇabhūṣaṇa* regarding the passage: "This *sthagu* of yours is long. The sense is that, due to being excessively pierced, it is a deformed specific bone that is broken and swollen within. For this very reason, he is *aguru*, meaning devoid of weight (or dignity). In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), it refers to one who has the letter *gu* (the phoneme *g*) situated in the middle.

The remaining word *aru* (wound), by the insertion of the syllable *gu* in the middle, becomes *aguru* (not heavy); this is the meaning. *Aruraguḥ* is a compound word (*samasta-pada*). It means one for whom the *gauḥ* (the earth) was not present due to wounds (*aru*)—that is, one who was so called because of his wounds. According to the rule *go-striyoḥ*, there is a shortening [of the vowel], and thus the substitution of *iK* for *eC*. The sense is that, being distracted by the pain of his wounds, he became one whose discrimination of the directions was lost—in the manner described in the passage "the directions vanish from me"—or one whose verbal communication was destroyed, or one whose range of vision was obstructed.

According to Amara: "The word *go* [is used] in the sense of heaven, cattle, speech, Indra, the quarters, the eye, the sun, the earth, and water; it is feminine when referring to the object of sight, and masculine when referring to a male. The poet’s intention in employing both the word *parimala*, which is always masculine, and the word *agaru*, which is optionally masculine, is this: that a man who possesses only occasional prowess, yet vies with a man of constant manliness, will surely meet such a miserable fate as he was disregarded by the latter.

In this context, "aru" means that which is devoid of the letter *ru*; "agu" means it became [the word] "agu. The underlying meaning is as follows: first, the form "agu" was established; then, with the elision of the letter *ga*, it became "aru"; then, by placing the letter *gu* between the letters *a* and *ru*, it became "aguru"; and finally, with the elision of the letter *ru*, this word emerged as "agu. This is the distilled meaning.

Or again, O beloved of Śrī, suppose a parrot, desiring to conquer the splendor of your body, were driven away by her; with its vowels and consonants transposed, could it possibly attain that same state as "karī" (an elephant)? 1249.

O Beloved of Śrī! This parrot (*kīra*—as Amara states, "the *kīra* and the *śuka* are synonymous") desires to conquer the splendor of your body. This statement—that the parrot seeks to surpass the Lord’s bodily luster—is based on the poetic convention (*kavisamaya*) that establishes an identity between the green and the dark-blue colors. Thus it is said in the *Alaṃkāraśekhara*:
"Between the lotus and the moon; between Kṛṣṇa and Hari; between the elephant and the serpent;
and between the yellow and the red, as in the cases of gold and the flames of fire."
In the case of the moon, the hare and the deer; in the case of the banner of Kāma, the sea-monster and the fish; and among the Dānavas, Asuras, and Daityas—identity alone is intended.

Thus, for this very reason, the expression "constructed of parrots, women, and sapphires" and so forth is justified. For this same reason, by being "shaken off" by that body of yours or by its luster, the state of being defeated by a woman is illuminated.

With the vowels and consonants reversed—where the vowel is the sound produced from the throat and the consonant is the mark such as green color or the parts like the beak and wings—he is thus described; the sense is that since it is difficult to conquer the splendor of the Lord’s body, which is his own adversary, in this form, he abandons his former shape out of a desire for another form. "Let him be a *karī*"; let him indeed become an elephant (*gaja*). Let him abandon the state of being a parrot (*kīra*) of small stature and become an elephant with massive limbs.

Even by that much, would she find—that is, could she possibly attain—your gait, the stability of your body, or the stability of your own delight? That gait is "that-gait"; she [would seek] it in that manner. And how could she obtain your profound and noble movement? She could not obtain it at all. The sense is this: for the gait and other qualities of the Lord’s divine form—which is peerless like the deep blue throat of a peacock—cannot be easily acquired merely by assuming a dark complexion, a stout physique, and so forth, which are devoid of true beauty (*lāvaṇya*).

In the alternative case, the word *kīra* has its vowels and consonants transposed. That is to say, it is that whose "vowels"—the vowel *ī* and the vowel *a*—are transposed; such is the meaning of the term, which is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*. The sense is that there is a transposition only of the vowels in the form of *ī* and *a*, and not of the consonants in the form of *k* and *r*. This being so, the intention is that the word *kīra* should result in the form *karī*.

In this context, by the word *kīra*, only the base form (*prakṛti*) is intended, and not the form qualified by the nominal suffix (*sup-pratyaya*). For both Viśva and Hemacandra state: "The term *svara* refers to the vowels beginning with *a*, as well as to the intermediate sounds (*madhyama* etc.)"; and "The term *vyañjana* refers to a beard, a mark, a seasoning, a limb, and the consonants beginning with *ka*. Here, Kīra does not merely achieve victory over the luster of the Lord’s body; rather, he also incurs the undesirable consequence of losing his own previously established luster.
Or rather, O Rāghava, desiring to diminish your proficiency in aiming and your skill of hand, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa himself became broken-faced and rendered helpless by you in his first battle. (1250)

*Kṛtamukhatām* means having a praised face; the underlying reality (*vastusthiti*) is skillfulness (*kuśalatvam*). Amarasimha states: "A *vaijñānika*, a *kṛtamukha*, a *kṛtī*, and a *kuśala* are synonyms. *Kṛtahastatām* means possessing a praised hand; the essential point is having a hand trained through the practice of shooting arrows. Amarasimha states: "*Kṛtahasta* refers to one who is adept in application. *Bhagnamukhaḥ* means one who has undergone a breaking of the face; the underlying reality, however, is being defeated (*parābhūta*).

*Vihastaḥ* means one whose hands are agitated and who is bewildered; as Amara states: "The words *vihasta* and *vyākula* are synonyms. The rest is clear. Here, there is the failure to attain the desired object—namely, the infliction of an undesirable result upon the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) characterized by the loosening of his grip caused by his mouth being covered by Rāghava—and the attainment of such an undesirable result for himself.

Just as the Lord of the Night-stalkers [Rāvaṇa] himself became desisted in his effort to abduct the daughter of the Lord of Mithilā [Sītā], so too, O jewel of the Solar dynasty, has he become desisted in his effort against you.

To cause the daughter of the Lord of Mithilā to cease [her grief], to make you separated from Rāma, and to ordain that Rāma be deprived of his wife—[the Creator] himself became one who has ceased, one separated from his wife (Rāmā), and one not separated from his wife (Rāmā). In reality, however, he was born as one whose own end (virāma) had come; the rest is clear. Here too, everything is to be understood as before.
Just as the Goddess of Fortune,
though she shook her jar on all sides in an attempt to surpass your breasts, became merely a fragment even after appearing before them in the form of the *vaiśasa* vessel.

O Śrī! The *kalaśa* (water-pot)—according to Amara, "the word *kalaśa* occurs in three genders," though here the sense is that it is singular—has been surpassed by your two breasts, which are male (in gender). Therefore, shaking off its tranquility (*śama*), that is, becoming enraged; elsewhere, the word *kalaśa*, shaking off—that is, discarding—the letter *śa* located at its end (*antataḥ*), having come forward and standing before your breasts for the sake of a duel (as implied by the context).

"Vaiśasam" means slaughter, a killing performed by a wicked person; having reached or undergone such violence, [the word] "vai" is a separate word referring to the front or face portion. Having become "śasaṅgatam," that is, joined with the letter *śa*, it became simply "śakalam," meaning merely a fragment or a severed piece. In the alternative sense, the meaning is that the word "śakalam" itself was thus produced.

Just as, O Rame, even a pure twice-born man of beautiful speech, if disregarded by your word, becomes sluggish and dejected; and a Cārvāka, though initially well-treated, ends up utterly alienated in the end. (1253)

He is *rame* (the one who delights). He is *śuciḥ* (pure), *viśadaḥ* (clear), a *dvijaḥ* (twice-born) bird, meaning a *haṃsa* (swan); by implication, he is understood as a pure Brahmin (*vipra*). He is *cāruvākaḥ*, one whose speech (*vāk*) is beautiful; that is, his words are pleasant to hear and captivating due to their conformity with the scriptures. Regarding the word *vāk*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *vac* in the sense of the action itself, resulting in the substitution of *k* for *c* according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*. Even though he is such [a being], he is [further characterized] by your *vacasā*—by your speech; this is also understood to mean by the scripture consisting of the *Lakṣmītantra* and other such works.
"Disregarded by him" means competing with and thus held in contempt by him. Furthermore, there is a similarity between the warbling of women and the calls of swans:
"By their warblings, the flocks of pure-winged birds [swans] have had their voices equaled through the sweetness of the Mādhavī [jasmine] flowers."

Thus it is established in such cases. For this very reason, *alasadūna* is a *viśeṣaṇobhayapada-karmadhāraya* compound meaning "lazy" (*alasa*) and "unwilling or incapable of retaliation" (*pratikartumapaṭu*), as well as "distressed" (*dūna*) and "tormented" (*paritapta*). Consequently, he is "dragged away" (*kṛṣṭa*) or "expelled" (*niṣkāsita*) to a very distant place by those virtuous Brahmins (*sādhavo ye viprāḥ*); or rather, he is "far removed from the virtuous" (*sādhūnāṃ satāṃ viprakṛṣṭaḥ*), meaning situated at a distance. As Amara states: "The word *viprakṛṣṭaka* means *dūra* (far). The sense is that he has been cast out.

It is the established fact that "sādhu" means excellent or superior among birds such as the *vīṇā* (lute-bird). A *cārvāka* is one who adheres to the Cārvāka doctrine; the sense is that his words are not to be accepted. As it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"One should avoid all those deceptive words spoken by the Arhat, the Cārvākas, and those recited by the Buddha and others."

Thus [it is said]. "Bhavati" is in the vocative case; "O lady! means "O venerable one. Regarding the phrase *alasadūna*, the analysis is *alasa-t* and *ūnaḥ*. The word *cāruvāka* is "deficient" (*ūna*)—meaning lacking the letter *u*—and thus becoming *cārvāka*, it is joined with *alasa-t*. This is the formation from the root *las* (to shine/play) in the *laṅ* tense. Alternatively, due to the non-distinction between *ra* and *la*, *alasa-t* means *arasa-t*: it produced a meaningless sound like that of a cloud, that is, it cried out. This is derived from the root *ras* (to sound) belonging to the *bhūvādika* class in the *laṅ* tense.

In this context, it should be understood that for the stainless twice-born one who desires to surpass the words of Śrī, there is not merely the failure to attain them; rather, by treating them with contempt, he incurs undesirable consequences such as indolence and deficiency. This attainment of excellence is secured through the singular beauty of an *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) based on the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) of the word and its meaning, supported by the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Or for example: "O Mother, alas, the plantain tree, which vied with your thighs, was struck down by a foot; yet, having become a bud (kalikā), it then grew old through your fingernails, and finally became dark (kālikā) with its tresses. (1254)

"O Mother! The plantain tree (*kadalikā*) is the *rambhā* (the celestial nymph Rambhā). The sense is that she was a woman alone; in the alternative sense, it is the phonetic form of the word *kadalikā*. She vied with your two thighs—Amara states, 'The word *sakthi* is neuter, while *ūru* is masculine'—thus she was one who rivaled your thighs. *Spardhā* means emulation, and that consists of the desire to overcome another. For this very reason, she was struck by your foot—the word 'by you' being understood. In the alternative sense, the word division is *apadā*."

The meaning is that, being struck, she became "apada," which is to say she was deprived of the letter *da*. Now, being a "kalikā"—that is, having the form of a bud—she desires to achieve vengeance by discarding some object of yours through the assumption of another form; this is the underlying sense. In the alternative [grammatical] sense, the word-form *kadalikā* is produced as *kalikā* by the removal of the letter *da*. (Amara states: "Kalikā and koraka are masculine"). She was struck—that is, defeated—by your "nakharas," i.e., by your nails.

Then the mature, fully grown, and bold Kālikā, having become a mass of clouds—meaning she attained birth as such—was struck down, or surpassed, by your locks of hair; it is understood that even though Kālikā is Goddess Durgā, she was so overcome. Hemacandra states: "Kālikā refers to a type of Yoginī, a flaw in gold and other metals, a mass of clouds, wine, Gaurī, and a fresh rain-cloud."

In this context, the word *kalikā*—the specific manifestation of the word-form—is designated as "vṛddha" (grown/expanded) after its initial vowel has undergone *vṛddhi* substitution; thus, by the rule "that [word] whose first among its vowels is *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*," it becomes *kālikā*. This is the meaning. Here, the failure to attain the desired object—namely, the complete subjugation of Lakṣmī’s thighs and other limbs by the plantain tree (*kadalikā*)—as well as the attainment of a succession of undesirable consequences such as being kicked by her feet, are both depicted.
Or rather, O Rāma, may the sun, by gradually abandoning its nature as the adversary, the beginning, and the end, become your son; yet even that would be like a plantain tree being split apart.

He rāme! *Kadalikā* means *rambhā*. The sense is: "of you, whose complexion is celebrated in the Vedas as 'golden-hued' (*hiraṇyavarṇaḥ*) and 'sun-hued' (*ādityavarṇaḥ*). For the sake of conquering—that is, for the subjugation of—your body, that which is "adverse" (*pratikūlam*), meaning opposed to the victory over the body of the sun-like splendor desired by [the speaker], and which extends from beginning to end (*ādyantam*), that is, from head to foot (*āpādamastakam*), is the state of being like a crow (*kākarūpatvam*), meaning a color equal to a crow's, or a dark-blue color as unyielding as charcoal; this is the sense.

The meaning is that in the two opposing sides, which are inverted, the first and last letters—the initial and final phonemes—assume the form of the word *kāka* (crow); specifically, the final letter takes the form of *kā* and the initial letter takes the form of *ka*. Through the power of the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*), the status of the plantain tree (*kadalikā*) as a *kāka* is established. The benediction, "May she, being *jahatī* (abandoning), gradually in the course of time become the sun (*savitā*), the maker of light (*bhāskara*) itself," is intended as a mockery.

In the alternative case, [the word] occurs sequentially with the first and last phonemes, but not as before by reversing the order of the last and first; thus it is said to "exist together" with the two phonemes *vi* and *tā*. The meaning is that it is joined with the phoneme *vi* at the beginning and the phoneme *tā* at the end in due order. Even so, it would still be "split apart" (*vidalitā*) or shattered, because its desired form is not established—this is the sense. The point is that the specific word-form *kadalikā*, through the reversal of phonemes according to the stated method, would result in the form *vidalitā*.
Here too, both points are clear.
O Lord, just as the lord of the night-stalkers is intent on showing contempt for you, alas, O Blessed One, he has indeed met with that very contempt through his own efforts, being himself bodiless.

O Blessed One! The lord of the night-stalkers (Rāvaṇa) was intent on performing an act of contempt and defeat toward you. Through effort and exertion, you rendered that very lord of the night-stalkers—who had arrived at [your] contempt—devoid of body (atanoḥ). "Bat" expresses wonder. Elsewhere, there is a word-division as *avadhī raṇam*. [He rendered him] devoid of a not-insignificant body (*atalpāt*). The masculine form is applied according to the rule: "In the case of words used in the masculine in the third case and following, the neuter takes the masculine form when it is of the same stem."

The construction is as follows: "Because of *yatanāt* (from effort), [the word] *yatana* is derived from the root *yat* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of abstract state (*bhāve*); he killed that very one who had approached the *raṇaṃ* (battle). Although even in the case of the primary meaning according to the literal hearing of the words, there indeed occurs the non-attainment of the desired and the attainment of the undesired, it should be understood that the presentation of the second meaning is for the sake of an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) consisting in the attainment of an intense undesired result. Or, for example:

"Those who desire victory say that the lotus of Hari’s eye became lame when struck by the foot of the serpent-mountain king; they call that [lotus] 'kañja' because it was deprived of the skill of movement (*uccāraṇa-pāṭava*). (1257)

"Struck by the foot" means beaten; "conquered" means defeated. "Lame" (khañja) refers to one whose gait is obstructed. For the verbal root is *khaji* in the sense of "deficiency of movement. Amara states: "A lame person is called *khoḍa* or *khañja*. The distinction here is that this [verse] is headed by *apahnuti* (concealment). In reality, however, it is more appropriate to regard this as an example of *apahnuti* alone, because it is that very figure which produces the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) here through its predominance. We have stated more than once that designations are made according to what is predominant.
This should be inferred accordingly in other examples as well.
O Lord of Śrī, O jewel of the Vṛṣabha mountain, those heretics who were intent on assailing Your abode through their own prowess have been cast out by Your remnants and have become impotent.
O Lord of Vṛṣādri! O Śrīpati! Those who, deluded by ignorance, declare another deity to be supreme—other than Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe—they indeed are remembered as heretics (pāṣaṇḍins).

These are the characteristics described in such passages. According to Amara, "pāṣaṇḍas" refers to those who bear all [heretical] marks. "Pauruṣāt" means from prowess, that is to say, from resolute intent; as the Medinī lexicon states: "pauruṣa may refer to the state of a man, to his action, or to his splendor. "Dhāma" refers to your abode situated on Vṛṣādri (Śrīparvata), as well as the divine form of your image installed therein; according to Amara, "dhāma" can mean a house, the body, luster, or power. "Ākramitum" means to bring under one's own control; "baddhāsthāḥ" means having made a formal pledge or vow.

They were heretics (*pāṣaṇḍāḥ*). They were cast out—that is, rejected—by Your remnants, namely Your servants, the Bhāgavatas who are incarnations of Śeṣa, specifically the venerable sage Rāmānuja; this is the intended meaning. The plural number is used for honor. Being thus cast out, they became like eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍāḥ*), that is, as if impotent and devoid of manliness. In the alternative sense, the word *pāṣaṇḍāḥ* (heretics) becomes *ṣaṇḍāḥ* when the letter *pā* is removed, resulting in the meaning "eunuchs"; this is also a source of poetic charm.

In this matter, certain heretics, disputing with a king who—being distressed by the assault of adversaries and possessing only the wealth of devotion—had offered him a conch and discus for his protection, sought to bring that Lord in the form of a divine image under their own control, asserting, "This is none other than Subrahmaṇya. By means of their own power, they entered through a gap in the wall of the Lord’s temple from the side of the Śeṣa-form and caused that Lord in the form of the image to accept the conch and discus.

It is recorded in tradition that these [heresies] were refuted by the authors of the Śrībhāṣya; herein, the heretics fail to achieve their desired end—which consists in the attainment of an adverse result characterized by the invasion of Your abode—and they instead incur an undesired result in the form of impotence.
Desiring to report that poem of Viśvatomukha given by Śauri, alas, I could not remember it due to the anxiety caused by the many examples I had cited.

Thus, both the attainment of what is undesirable—which consists of bringing about the means of suffering for another—and the attainment of what is undesirable for oneself—which consists of the means of suffering—are shown. Furthermore, there is the non-cessation of that [means of happiness] due to one's exertion toward a desired object—which consists of the removal of the means of happiness for another—and the attainment of the means of suffering for oneself; as in the case of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), who, desiring to deprive his wife of her happiness by making his daughter Vipulā suffer, instead caused his own beloved to suffer when he was struck by the arrow of the best of the Raghus. || 1259 ||

The form *vyadhita* is the *luṅ* (aorist) in the active voice (*kartari*) from the root *vadh*, preceded by the prefix *vi-*, which is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); it means "he did" (*akārṣīt*). Here, Rāvaṇa did not effect the deprivation of the Lord’s consort Vaidehī of the happiness of her husband—which was what he intended to do—but rather brought that very [deprivation] about for his own beloved. Although it is not proper to count this separately because the cessation of the means of happiness is essentially of the nature of a cause of suffering, nevertheless, just as there is happiness when the causes of suffering cease, so too, since suffering arises from specific causes even when the means of happiness cease, its separate mention is appropriate; this is how it should be understood.
Just as the sister of the Yātudhānas, having prepared herself to tear apart the best of the Raghus by swallowing Vaidehī, was herself torn asunder at her nose and ears and rendered deformed. 1260.

"To tear apart" (*vidāram*) means to cause a split, that is, to separate from one's husband; it also means to rend or to cleave. In the compound *nāsākarṇe*, the singular form is used because it refers to parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*). Here, Śūrpaṇakhā was intent on securing for herself the means of her own misery by seizing Vaidehī, who was the means of happiness for the Lord, the son of Daśaratha; however, she did not merely fail to obtain her goal, but instead attained an undesirable result for herself in the form of the tearing away of her own ears and nose. This instance is supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia). The previous example was a pure case [of *viṣama*].
Or, for example:
O Nṛhari, Hiraṇyakaśipu, who strove to repel the devotion to You manifested by Prahlāda, was himself repelled by You.

"*Nirasanāya* means for the sake of rejection (*pratipakṣepāya*). *Nirasana* implies rejection (*pratikṣepa*) and killing (*vadha*); as Medinī states: 'The word *nirasana* is used in the sense of killing and rejection. In this context, Hiraṇyakaśipu did not ordain the "rejection" of that devotion to the Lord—which was the means for Prahlāda’s unsurpassed happiness—but rather, he himself encountered "rejection" (death). This too is inherently pregnant with *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Furthermore, the presence of the figure of speech *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is equally present throughout. As in the following example: [Example omitted per instructions]

Unable to endure your excellent state and desiring to steal it from your feet, the lord of elephants, having approached, lost even his own existence despite his muttering of prayers, due to the failure of his own course.

O Blessed One! The lord of elephants (the king) [is] at your two feet—that is, at your own feet; it may also be understood as referring to two Brahmins who have studied the Vedic branches (*śākhā*). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *caraṇa* is not feminine; it refers to a follower of a Vedic school (*bahvṛca*), a root, a lineage, and also a foot. [He seeks] *sadgati*: excellent knowledge—that is, the wisdom which serves as the means for attaining the highest world. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "'Gati' is feminine; it refers to a path, a state, knowledge, a journey, and a means. However, the essential meaning is "an auspicious departure. He was unable to endure this.

By the prohibition of the genitive case in the phrase "na loke" and so forth, the accusative case is used for the object. For this very reason, *taccucorayiṣuḥ* means "desiring to seize your feet. *Etya* means having approached, that is, having become directed toward him; *bhraṃśam etya* means having reached a fall or ruin due to the loss of his own knowledge and his own departure (*svagataiḥ*). The ablative case is used here by eliding the suffix *lyap*. Even though he was *japataḥ* (reciting), [he fell] despite the study of the Vedas which removes the fault of theft—according to Amara, "recitation (*japa*) may be Vedic study (*svādhyāya*)."

He did not attain his own existence—the persistence of his own essential nature, or his being, or his preeminence, or his excellence; for Amara states: "The word *sat* [is used] in the senses of true, good, existent, excellent, and venerable. In the alternative sense, the word *gajapati* (lord of elephants), having suffered the loss of its initial and final syllables (*ga* and *ti*) due to the failure of its own movement, did not attain its own existence—that is, the persistence of its own verbal form as the word *gajapati*—even with the two remaining syllables in the middle while being recited.

In this instance, the lord of elephants did not obtain the desired object—the attainment of a good rebirth (*sadgati*), which is the means for supreme bliss at the feet of the Blessed One—but instead attained only the undesired object, namely the loss of his own status. It should be noted that this [instance] is sustained by the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on the pun (*śleṣa*) between the two meanings conveyed by words such as "feet" (*caraṇa*). An example of the failure to obtain a purely desired object is as follows: "O Sun of the Raghu dynasty, Bharata, unable to turn you back from the forest you had reached by virtue of the two boons granted to Kaikeyī and the word of Daśaratha, has now returned. (1263)
In this passage, only Bharata’s failure to attain his desired object—namely, the return of his elder brother Rāmabhadra from his forest exile—is recorded.

Just as the multitude of conscious beings, seeking refuge in the Lord who is intensely possessed of the qualities of Śrī, in order to cast off their own deluded qualities, themselves become thoroughly possessed of those very same deluded qualities—this is indeed a marvel! (1264)

The term *mūḍhaguṇa* means "the quality of delusion"; thus, the word should be split as *saḥ mūḍhaguṇaḥ*. The apparent contradiction is that this man, while seeking refuge, is [described as] possessing the quality of delusion (*mūḍhaguṇa*). The resolution is that he is one whose *guṇāḥ*—meaning "qualities" or "strings"—are *samūḍhāḥ*, i.e., gathered together; namely, the "eight great qualities" mentioned in the saying, "Eight qualities adorn a man. Thus, the meaning is that he becomes endowed with highly precious qualities. The *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *samūḍha* is used in the sense of 'gathered' (*puñjita*) and 'bent' (*bhugna*)."

In this case, for a group of sentient beings desiring to eliminate the quality of delusion, there is merely the non-attainment of that [quality], but not the perception of any other undesirable state. The distinction is that the former is pure, whereas this is mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Or as it is said: "O Viṣṇu, even the cloud, having clung to Your feet yet failed to reach them—being a mere likeness of Your body—became faceless; for how can that which is merely a delusion be fruitful, even if desired? (1265) O Viṣṇu! The sense is that Your feet—that is, Your lotus-feet—are the bestowers of all fruits corresponding to whatever is desired. In the alternative sense, "Viṣṇu's foot" means the sky (*antarikṣa*). It is precisely with the intention of conveying this meaning that the vocative "O Viṣṇu" is used.

The cloud (*abhraṃ vārivāhaḥ*)—meaning your body, which is comparable to you and equal to your divine form; the sense is that it could not even serve as a slight comparison for your body. It became "faceless" (*amukham*). This is a common worldly expression: the meaning is that due to the failure to obtain what was desired, out of shame, no one was able to lift their face and show it. As for the literal state of affairs, "faceless" (*amukham*) means having the letter 'a' at the beginning of the word "face" (*mukha*), because the word *abhra* begins with the letter 'a'.

For instance, how could the desired or sought-after goal of one who is deluded, whose mind is unstable, and who is agitated by the violent gusts of the wind—even if he takes refuge at the foot of Viṣṇu—ever bear fruit? The point is that since concentration is not achieved for a mind situated on the stages of "distracted" (*kṣipta*) or "extremely distracted" (*vikṣipta*), there is no accomplishment of yoga itself; and how then could the fruit to be attained through it be realized? Furthermore, even the non-deluded is indeed "deluded," because of the identity between word and meaning (*tādātmya*).

Here, as before, the mere failure to obtain the desired object—consisting in the cloud’s similarity to the divine form of the Lord—is mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia). The same applies in subsequent cases as well. It should be noted, however, that if it is intended that "facing downwards" constitutes an undesirable outcome, then this must be considered an illustration of a specific variety of *viṣama* (the Uneven), namely that which consists in the attainment of the undesired following the failure to obtain the desired.
Or, for example:

At first, the Indra-jewel, in order to obtain your luster, donned the armor of threads; yet, O Lord, though it reached that state, being incapable [of the task], it abandoned them and remained merely the Indra-jewel. (1266)

O Lord! The sapphire (*indranīla-ratna*), the jewel of Indra, at first attained the *tanta*—meaning it was bound with the protective thread (*pratisara-sūtra*)—in order to obtain your luster; the reality is that it even underwent the stringing of gold and other threads. The actual state of affairs is that it attained the letter *ta*, the binding (*saṃnāha*), and the connection with the letter *tu*.

"Because of incapacity," meaning because of the inability to accomplish what is intended and desired; "having loosened and cast off this armor, which was bound with joy"—here the word *saṃnāha* (armor) is to be construed with *muktvā* (having released). The particle *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). It is also understood that although he had reached such an [exalted] state of armor, due to his incapacity, he simply abandoned that very kind of armor, which was characterized by such effort.

In the other sense (the verbal pun), having abandoned that letter *ta* as well as the letters *tu* and *tva*, the "jewel of Indra" (*śakra-maṇi*) remained exactly as before as an "emerald" (*indranīla-ratna*). The meaning is that it did not, however, obtain your luster. In the other sense, the word *śatakratu-maṇi*, by the method explained, results in the form *śakra-maṇi* upon the removal of the letters *ta* and *tu*. Here, there is merely the failure of the jewel of Indra to obtain its desired object; this is a blend with the figure of speech known as *pūrvarūpa* (reversion to the original form), which will be discussed later.
Or, for example:

"O friend of Hari, the essence of the mango tree, though its head is surpassed by [the excellence of] your speech which has descended in the form of nectar, it would not obtain that [nectar]; it would remain merely the essence of the mango. (1267)

The meaning is that the essence of *rasāla*—whether sugarcane juice or mango juice—might indeed be *rāsalasāra*, but it shall not descend [into my heart] as the nectar of your words. The truth is that even when the word *rasālasāra* is read in reverse order (*vilomatayā*), its form remains identical. The rest is easy to understand. Here, there is merely the non-attainment of a desired object for the *rasālasāra*; this too is embellished by the *pūrvarūpa* (premonitory symptom) which will be described later.

O lotus-eyed young woman, since your two youthful breasts are like coconuts celebrated for their excellence in pairs, the stalk between them must have been merely the two syllables of the word *nālika* (coconut). 1268.

O lotus-eyed young woman! And this [fruit] which is about to be mentioned serves as an embellishment for the youthfulness of your breasts. The sense is that the coconut (*nārikela*) fruit is inherently neuter (*klība*). As for the phrase "famous for *dvaṃdva*," the actual state of affairs is that they are renowned as a pair; the analysis of the compound is *dvaṃdva* (pair) + *prathitau* (renowned). According to Amarasimha, "the word *dvaṃdva* refers to both conflict and a pair. The sense is that your two youthful breasts are two males (*pumāṃsau*).

The sense is that the one desiring victory had merely formed a wish for conquest by failing to consider the relative strength and weakness of his own and the enemy's forces. "In the middle" means between the desire for the goal and the attainment of it; "wasting away" means undergoing decay. The reason for this is given as "falling from youth": *vayaścyut* means one who falls (*cyavate*) from youth (*vayas*), which here refers to the state of being young; from the root *cyu* (to fall) belonging to the *bhvādi* class, the suffix *kvip* is applied with the augment *tuk*. Thus, it means "old. The construction is either "it was indeed incapable" (*nālam eva*), meaning powerless, or "it was not sufficient" (*alam na āsīt*), meaning it lacked the capacity.

The sense is: how could he—who is himself a eunuch, aged, emaciated, and alone—be able to conquer two who are arrogant in battle, in their prime, and supported by their youth? Even the phrase *nālamātrāvaśiṣṭam* (only the stalk remaining) suggests this. In the alternative [punning] sense, the word *nārikela* (coconut) has two syllables dropped from its middle; thus it is a compound word where "two syllables" (*akṣaradvaya*) "drip out" (*ścyotati*). The term *ścyutiḥ* is derived from the root *ścyut* (meaning "to flow") belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, with the suffix *kvip*.

This [verb *sravati*] is intransitive only when its agent is a liquid substance, like the verb *sravati* itself. Here, however, it is transitive because its agent is a non-liquid substance. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound may be "that which trickles from two syllables" (*akṣaradvayāt ścyotati*). The meaning is "fallen from two letters. It was simply "not enough" (*nālam*). The meaning is that the word *nārikela* (coconut) remained as "not enough" (*nālam*) alone, deprived of the two letters "ri" and "ke. In this case, there is merely the failure to obtain what is desired.

However, if one intends to convey that the desired object results in an undesirable consequence for another, this should be understood as an example of the variety of this figure that will be discussed later.

"O Mother! It is truly marvelous that those people who, having crossed the Vaitaraṇī river, desire to behold Hari, you never show them Hari after they have crossed the Vaitaraṇī. (1269) O Mother! "Those people of yours" refers to your devotees. The particle *vai* indicates well-known fact. "Having crossed the Vaitaraṇī" means having reached the transcendence of the sun; the sense is that it involves piercing through the solar orb. "Desire to behold Hari" refers to Vāsudeva; the form *didṛkṣante* is derived from the root *dṛś* with the desiderative suffix *saN*, following the rule *jñā-śru-smṛ-śāṃ san*.

"O Hari, you do not show yourself even once to those people who have crossed beyond the Vaitaraṇī; this is truly strange. [The word] *vaitaraṇyatīteḥ* is a compound (*samasta-pada*). The resolution (*parihāra*) is: "Because they have crossed beyond the Vaitaraṇī—the river at the gate of Yama's city—you do not show yourself to Yama. The verb *dṛś* (to see) is transitive with two objects according to the rule *dṛśeśca*. Here, by means of punning (*śleṣa*), the mere failure to obtain what is desired is shown for the illustrious devotees.

Just as one who, relying upon the infinite state, shines even with his head downward—that too I delight in; for your splendor shall remain as it was before, yet a birth that seeks the light of your feet does not partake of the radiance of the sun.

The radiance of the sun (*bhānubhā*), which is the splendor of the sun, having taken refuge in the state of the infinite—the feet of the Blessed One and the station of the intermediate space—let it perform austerity, let it practice penance, and let it undergo heat. It shall remain exactly as it was before; it shall indeed be the radiance of the sun alone. It does not, however, undergo birth through the nature of the splendor of your feet. Even when its syllables are reversed, the word *bhānubhā* remains *bhānubhā* itself and does not assume any other sequence.

In this verse, the mere failure to obtain her [the Goddess's] feet—even through penance performed with head downwards by Bhanubhāyā, who desired birth as the very luster of Lakṣmī’s feet—is described; it is a blend of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *pūrvavastūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a prior fact).
Or for example:

"O Mother of All, surely Kālikā (the goddess Kālī), desiring to obtain birth from your tresses—were she even to stand with her head downwards, she would still remain only Kālikā and not a *kabarī* (tress). [Amara states: "The word *kālikā* refers to a bank of clouds. Here too, there is merely the non-attainment of the desired object by Kālikā, which is intermingled with the possibility of her retaining her prior form.

O lotus, you do not realize that by leaping up with the thought, "May I become worthy of dwelling upon a lotus in a lotus pond," you have obtained only what is undesirable; for this very reason, O water-born one, you suffer this humiliation of being born from mud. 1272.

O Lotus! You leap up, thinking, "May I become worthy of that state—of abiding within the lotus-hand, the hand-lotus, of Padmā, Lakṣmī. By means of that very lotus-hand of Śrī, you do not perceive your own humiliation. In the phrase "tava paribhūtim," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule "ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi," and not in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). The rest is clear.
Or for example:

"O Cloud, you who desire to serve the Lord of Ramā, why do you ascend the plateau of the bull-like mountain? For he indeed takes away your splendor; indeed, one whose heart is dull does not perceive the impending calamity. (1273)

O Cloud! O Jīmūta! [O you who] bestow the upper plateau (adhi-tyakām) of the bull-like mountain—“the ground above is called adhi-tyakā,” according to Amara; [you who are] jaḍa-hṛt, meaning one whose heart is rigid, or, by the non-distinction between *la* and *ḍa*, one whose water is held within the interior, or one who takes water from the ocean—the rest is clear in its meaning.

In these two examples, there is indeed, respectively, the attainment of desired objects in the form of the suitability for the lotus and the cloud to abide upon the lotus-hand of Lakṣmī and the fortune of serving Śrīnivāsa; however, there is also the acquisition of intense undesirable results in the form of being insulted by them and the abduction of Lakṣmī. Thus, this is the *viṣama* (incongruity) figure consisting of the attainment of purely undesirable results. Or, as in another example: "O Rāma, the lotus, its luster eclipsed by the brilliance of your eyes, having attained masculinity and approached you to deceive you, is now struck down by you. (1274)

"O Rāma! [The address] 'he' is used to indicate that the matter about to be described was performed by his incarnation. The sense is that *kamala* (lotus) is *nalina*, and is neuter (*klība*). The sense is that it was [struck] by the luster of your eyes as if by a woman. Then, having its radiance crushed, it attained masculinity (*puṃstvam*), that is, manhood or the masculine gender; the sense is that, for the sake of counteracting that, the lotus became a illusory deer (*māyāmṛga*). According to Amara, 'the word *kamala* may also refer to a deer. It was struck down in the past—meaning it was slain."

In the phrase "puri luṅacāsme," the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the past sense due to its connection with the word *purā* (formerly). The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "hanteratpūrvasya. The rest is clear. Here, while there is indeed the attainment of the desired object for the lotus in the form of deceiving Śrī Rāma, there is also the attainment of an intense undesired object in the form of being struck down; thus, this too is of the nature of the attainment of a purely undesired object.
Or for example:

"O fickle one! Is it not true that you, who were once like a companion to the thunderbolt and always desired to attain glory, have taken refuge in the midst of riches? Yet, though you possess the splendor of your desires, there shall be an absence of that very splendor for you here. (1275)

Regarding *aśaninām*: the suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) to denote abundance or constant connection with the thunderbolt (*aśani*). *Sahabhūḥ* means "born together," that is, "one who has been born along with them. The vocative form is *he aśanisahabhūḥ*. Alternatively, it may mean "the companion of the thunderbolt (*aśani*, i.e., the *vajra*)," so called because lightning and the thunderbolt coexist in the same place. The particle *nanu* is used as a gentle address; indeed, O fickle *saudāmanī*! This is said to indicate her fickleness.

Desiring eternal and unshakable prosperity (*śrī*), you have taken refuge in the very midst of, and clung to the interval between, various fortunes (*śrī*) and the divine Lakṣmī; thus, you possess the prosperity you desire. However, in this midst of fortune, there will be a lack of food for you—a scarcity of sustenance. Not being satisfied with merely that which accompanies the rice of your meal, and seeking a glory superior to that, you shall indeed obtain it, but you will also encounter a great misfortune in the form of a lack of food. As it is said: * *tvaṃ nityaśriyam acañcalāṃ lakṣmīm īpsuḥ satī śriyaḥ saṃpadāṃ bhagavatyā lakṣmyāśca madhyam antaram avalagnaṃ ca śritā satī yathepsitaśrīśca bhavasi; parantu te tavātra śrīmadhye 'śanābhāvaḥ syād āhāradaurlabhyaṃ bhavet.* * *aśanaśālisahabhūtvaṃ tāvanmātreṇāparituṣyantī tato 'tiśayitāṃ śriyam apekṣamāṇā tāṃ labhase eva, parantv aśanābhāvarūpa-mahāniṣṭaṃ ca lapsyase iti bhāvaḥ.* * *yathocyate...* (As it is said... (Note: The final phrase "yathocyate" indicates that a verse follows, but as no specific verse was provided in the source text, the translation concludes with the explanation of the preceding prose.)
One should acquire wealth only so much as is required to fill one's belly;
he who considers more than that to be his own deserves punishment as a thief.

Thus it is said. And the term *śanisahabhūḥ* (co-existent with Saturn) is also obtained; that is to say, she who stands together with Saturn is "afflicted by Saturn" (*śanipīḍitā*). The sense is that even if one somehow obtains what is desired from her who is thus afflicted by Saturn, the acquisition of the undesired is difficult to avoid. In the alternative [poetic] interpretation, the word division is *yathepsita-śrī-raśanā-bhāvaḥ*. By the rule *ro ri*, there is the elision of the *repha*. Then *te* means "of you," and *raśanābhāvaḥ* means "the state of being a girdle. The sense is that because of your constant possession of beauty (*śrīmattā*), since beauty resides in the middle part [of the body], you will surely possess the state of a girdle.
"Likewise, *saptakī* is a girdle," according to Amara; here too, as before, there is the attainment of nothing but the undesirable.

Just as the lotus appeared in the form of your hand to dispel the torment caused by the trunk of an elephant, O beloved of the lotus-eyed one, it likewise experienced the torment caused by the hand of Hari (Viṣṇu) in this case as well.

The "squeezing by the hand" (*karapīḍana*) of Hari—the lion—and the Blessed One; in one sense, *karapīḍana* means the crushing of the trunk, while in the other sense it means the grasping of the hand (marriage). That [lotus] is the *aravinda*. Here too, even in the case of the birth of the lotus (*aravindajanman*), although there is the attainment of the desired object in the form of the removal of the elephant's trunk-squeeze, there is also the acquisition of an undesired object in the form of being squeezed by the hand of Hari. Thus, this too is indeed the "attainment of the purely undesired. It should be understood that through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), even that which is most desired is rendered undesirable. As in the following example:
O Lord of All, desiring that you might become like me through an enemy king, alas, the moon has indeed become a messenger, accompanied by the day, as soon as it came within your sight.

O All-pervading Lord! Desiring that you—who are the sovereign emperor of the entire world—should be "sadṛk" (equal) to me, [the moon] is joined by the sun’s friend; in the alternative sense, [you are] joined by the king, the moon, and by me. Here, the meaning of the third case (*mayā*) is non-difference (*abheda*). Thus, the sense is: "possessing two eyes that are non-different from me and accompanied by the sun. Being one who desires this—*icchun*—it is grammatically correct due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *icchu* from *vindu*. [The implied object of desire is] you, the supreme ruler of the entire universe.

The meaning is that he was "seen" (dṛggataḥ) simply by having come within the range of vision. Accompanied by his own friends and many lords (inānvitaḥ), he became your very messenger (dūta eva), the bearer of your message. The sense is this: at the time of not seeing you, considering himself to be a great king and wishing to make even you—the Lord of all worlds—resemble himself, he approached; yet, by the mere sight of you, he abandoned his pride and obtained the role of your messenger along with the lords of his own faction.

Accompanied by Ina (the Sun), he came into your sight—that is, he reached the very range of your vision. The implication is that this was because he had heard of the subordination of both the Moon and the Sun to him. Not only this; he became his messenger as well. The sense is that, according to the scriptural statement, "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable One, the Sun and the Moon stand held in their places," he did not transgress his command.

In one sense, the word *indu* (moon) is "joined" (*anvita*) with the collection of letters *inā-iṃn*, and it is "bound" (*ūta*)—meaning "yoked"—with the letter *du*. This is because the word *in* possesses such a nature; this is the intended meaning. Here, for the moon who desires to obtain similarity [to the word *sadṛk*], there is indeed the attainment of that desired object through the power of identifying [the two] as non-different, based on the pun (*śleṣa*) between the two meanings: the word *sadṛk* itself and its referent, "one who has a similar appearance.

Nevertheless, since there is also the perception of an undesirable state, namely being a "messenger" (*dūta*), this too is merely the attainment of something undesirable. As in the following example: [The moon, though desiring to become like the sun, becomes a messenger of the sun. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The commentary explains a poetic figure where the moon, wishing to be like the sun (*sūrya*), becomes a *dūta* [messenger] of the sun, resulting in the paradoxical attainment of an undesirable status despite the initial desire for a desirable similarity.)

In one place, the crows, striving to become friends with your braid of hair, were not at all disagreeable; even when they came between you and her, they remained exactly as they were despite the intervention.

"O Śrī!"—this is understood through the force of the context. "Kālikās" refers to clouds (*kādambinīs*); as Amara states, "the word *kālikā* is also used for a mass of clouds. In this case, the feminine gender and plural number, which belong to the meaning, are superimposed upon the word itself. "In some place, anywhere at all, being non-adverse," meaning they are devoid of hostility; for friendship cannot be established where there is hostility—this is the sense. In the alternative sense (of the word *kālikā*), the meaning is that they maintain their beauty even when reversed.

The actual state of affairs is that [the crows] were striving for friendship, amity, and equality with your braid of hair. Being *satyaḥ* (truthful) and *yatamānāḥ* (striving), they attained the state of being *āntarālitām*—that is, *āntaryaḥ* (intermediate) and *ālayaḥ* (dwelling-places)—which refers to the condition of being intimate friends (*antaraṅga-sakhitvam*). As Amara states: "Āli, sakhī, and vayasyā all mean a female friend. Even so, they remained as *kākāḥ*, meaning crows, even in the event of reversal—that is, even at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*).

In that very way, they were indeed *kākāḥ* (crows), but not in a fitting sense. In the alternative interpretation, the construction is: "having reached *alitam*—that is, the absence (*śūnyatā*) of the letter *li*—in the middle (*antarā*), even the *kākāḥ* [become *alika*]. Thus, they were indeed *kākāḥ*. Furthermore, even in the reverse order (*vilomatve*), they remained *kākāḥ* alone and did not possess any other sequence.

In this case, although there is the attainment of the desired state of friendship with Śrī Kālikā—based on the power of the identification (adhyavasāya) of two meanings conveyed by the word *antarālika* through paronomasia (*śleṣa*)—there is also the occurrence of the acquisition of an undesired state in the form of a crow (*kāka*). This too is the "uneven" (*viṣama*) figure consisting of the attainment of something solely undesirable, by virtue of the power of paronomasia.
The failure to obtain what is desired, characterized by the avoidance of the undesired, is as follows:
"O Blessed One, pearls were produced here from your teeth with the thought, 'Let us dwell here without fear'; yet even these have now been seized by great terror. (1279)

"Released" (muktāḥ) means pearls; "fearless" (atrāsāḥ) means being devoid of fear, or elsewhere, being free from the defects of gems—according to the *Viśvakośa*, "trāsa" refers to both fear and the defect of a gem. "We dwell here"—having been born in this manner within your mouth in the form of teeth (*radātmanā*), these very pearls are now "seized by great terror" (*mahābhayena*) even in your mouth; yet, in reality, they are possessed of great fearlessness (*abhayā*). This is the actual state of affairs.

Just as we take refuge in you, thinking, "You will lead us across this existence beset by calamities," so do you expand that very same existence in its manifold variety; O Sun of the Bull-Mountain! 1280.

In the first example here, the attainment of a desired object—characterized by the avoidance of an undesirable state—is shown in the form of fear, which is grasped through a *śleṣa* (pun) on two meanings conveyed by the word "muktānām" (of those who are liberated). In the second example, through the power of a *śleṣa* rooted in the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*)—where "vipadā" means "the world (*bhava*) accompanied by calamity (*āpad*)" in one sense, and "vibhava" (prosperity) meaning "the world (*bhava*) accompanied by the word 'vi'" in the other—the non-attainment of a desired object, which consists in the failure to avoid the undesirable, is revealed.

Just as those men who worship you in order to avoid being the source of enemies, arrows, maces, and swords—for them, you ultimately bestow at all times the very state of being the source of enemies, arrows, maces, and swords. (1281)

*Arayaḥ* refers to desires (*kāma*) and the like; *daraḥ* is fear caused by them; *gadaḥ* is the disease caused by them. To avoid being a "mine" (*ākara*)—that is, a locus—for these, [the Lord acts]. The same applies to the second half of the verse as well. In reality, however, the meaning of "being a mine of enemies, fear, and diseases" is that he holds the discus, conch, and mace in his hands. The intended sense is that he possesses the same form as the Blessed One (*bhagavatsārūpya*). Here too, the attainment of the desired object—which consists in the avoidance of the misfortune characterized by being a mine of enemies, fear, and diseases—is composed through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Just as the moon, out of hatred for the luster of your face, attained the state of being food for dogs and, desiring to dispel that [stigma], remained with its head bowed even while in the lotus [of the sky], yet did not abandon its whiteness; so too [does he remain]. 1282.

O Blessed One! The moon, the possessor of bright rays, having attained the state of being a dog—meaning the state of being eaten by dogs, or being at the head of dogs—or alternatively, the state of being a dog-cooker (an outcaste), meaning one for whom a dog is the primary food—due to his hatred for the splendor of Your face; for it is said:
"He who hates the Lord Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, the master of the worlds, is born among dog-cookers after a thousand births as a dog."

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*). The sense is that this is but a small fruit for one who harbors hatred toward the lotus-face of the Blessed One. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), *śvādya* means "that which has a dog as its first [thing]"—that is, the state of being food for dogs (*śvādyatva*). Due to the identity between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakayostādātmyāt*), having attained that state of being food for dogs, he desired to dispel it (*vyapanunutsuḥ*: wishing to remove it). At *puṣkara*, a specific sacred ford (*tīrtha*) of that name, and in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), he remained with his head cast downward (*adharitaśirāḥ*: having his head turned down), even while performing such penance; this is the sense.

This statement is made because, at the moment of setting, the orb of the moon appears with its head downward in the sky; in the secondary sense, it means that although he stood in a contrary (viloma) manner, he did not abandon his nature as a dog (*śvādya*). Just as before, he remained a leader among dogs or a devourer of dogs (*śvabhakṣakī*), and did not obtain what he desired. The point is that even visiting holy pilgrimage sites does not purify those who hate the Blessed One.
As it is said: "Those who hate the Great-Souled One and do not remember Keśava—there is no [auspicious] destination for them in holy pilgrimage sites, nor even for those who associate with them."

Thus, from the *Mahābhārata*. In this context, even though the word *śubhrāṃśu* (the moon) is recited in reverse order, it remains *śubhrāṃśu* itself and does not abandon its status as "one whose parts are bright" (*suvarṇādyatva*). Herein lies the non-attainment of the desired object, which consists in the avoidance of what is undesirable for the moon.
Just as the moon,
thinking "I have been touched on all sides by a dog," became utterly bewildered, so too did it become even more so when it fell headlong into the infinite ocean to remove that stain.
