The moon (Śubhrāṃśu) is extremely deluded—possessing the state of delusion—thinking, "I have been touched and stroked on all sides, everywhere, and on both sides by Śuna, by Śunaka, and by Śuvarṇa. In the alternative sense, it refers to that which has the cluster of syllables *bhra* and *bhr* at its end and middle.

In order to remove that—that is, to dispel his delusion that he had been touched by a dog on all sides—he remained exactly as before in the infinite Lord and in the intermediate space; even though falling headlong, he remained standing in a reversed manner, and indeed remained merely deluded. In one sense, he became the Moon (Śubhrāṃśu) himself, and not otherwise. Here, as previously, the Moon fails to attain his desired object.

Just as the moon, though composed of rays, does not abandon its white luster even when its position becomes exhausted at the beginning and end [of the month] because it has not attained the splendor of your face— nor did the white-rayed moon abandon that luster even while falling headlong downward.

O Blessed One! The moon—possessing white rays and white beams—at the beginning of the month and at the end of the month; this is stated with the intention of referring to the full moon at both the start and conclusion of the month. Furthermore, it is "composed of those rays" (*tanmaya*), using the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of abundance. Having failed to attain the splendor of your face, it reached a state of exhaustion—a state of weariness, meaning a state of languor. Then, even as it fell headlong downward, it did not abandon that state of exhaustion; it did not relinquish its languid condition.

In this context, the word *śuklāṃśu* (moon) is "sutarām" (exceedingly) or "atitarām" (most exceedingly) *śumaya*—meaning abundant in the letter *śu*—at both the beginning and the end, because the letter *śu* alone remains manifest at the start and the conclusion; this is the intended meaning. Even though it is "adhaśśiraḥ" (head-downwards), that is to say, situated in reverse order, it did not abandon its internal position or existence as the syllable-group *klā* in the middle; for even in its inversion, it remains in that very state. Here too, everything is exactly as explained previously.

Just as you are praised by a complete poet, whereas the poet of another is indeed a deficient poet; so too, even if he were to bow his head in homage, this one would remain a deficient poet and not a complete poet.

"Sakalakavi" means a complete poet, that is to say, a great poet (mahākavi); "vikalakavi" means a minor poet. In this context, for the minor poet, there is the failure to obtain the desired object, which consists of the avoidance of his own misfortune.

Just as the light of the sun, its power struck down by your splendor, undergoes a loss of luster, yet that light would not be so if it were to revolve counter-clockwise as before; so too it is with those possessing your own energy.

O Blessed One! Bhānubhāḥ (the one with the splendor of the sun) possesses a radiant luster. It is understood by implication that she desires equality with Your brilliance. When struck by Your splendor—that is, when subjected to the impact caused by Your majesty—she becomes one who experiences the breaking of her knees; "jānubhaṅgabhāk" means she undergoes the crushing or fracture of the kneecaps (the joints of the thighs). Thus, the meaning is that she is one whose knees are broken. For this very reason, she is "abhāḥ," one who does not shine. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *bhās* (to shine). She is "bhābhāḥ," one whose radiance (*bhā*) has become non-radiant (*abhā*) due to fear (*bhayāt*).

In the analysis of the compound as *na bhāti* ("does not shine"), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *bhā*. It ends in an *ā*, like the word *viśvapā*. In either case, the meaning is "not shining with radiance. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as *bhā iva ā īṣad bhāsate* ("shines slightly like a star"); or as *bhā-bhāḥ*, where *bhā* means "great light" at first, and after the bending of the knee (*jānu-bhaṅga*), there is "very little light" (*alpatara-prakāśa*). In this alternative view, the phonetic form is *bhānubhā*; the phrase is split as *tvattejo'bhihataujāḥ* (whose vigor is struck down by your splendor) and *bhaṅgam*.

She whose vitality (*ojas*), strength (*bala*), support (*avaṣṭambha*), or power (*prabhāva*) has been struck down by your splendor is so described; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *ojas* denotes brilliance, support, as well as power and strength. Having thus undergone a loss of the syllable *nu* (becoming *bhābhāḥ*), she—though being *bhābhāḥ*—is now established as *bhābhā*. The sense is that even though she was previously humiliated in the manner described at the beginning, she remains so.

Having first avoided what is undesirable, if she were to become either hostile or favorable toward your splendor in order to attain equality with it—according to the *Medinī* lexicon, which states, "The word *prasavya* may have the gender of its referent when meaning 'hostile' or 'favorable'"—even then, it would remain exactly as before; it would merely be a semblance of light (*bhābhā*), possessing no radiance or having very little light.

However, the meaning is as follows: [the compound] *tvadojobhāḥ* would not be formed in the sense of "shining like your splendor" (*na tu tvadoja iva bhāti*), because the word-form *bhānubhāḥ*—which is established as *bhā-bhā* in one alternative—whether read forward (*anuloma*), backward (*pratiloma*), or in a circular manner (*prasavya*), would result only in *bhā-bhā*, and not in the sequence *tvadojobhā*. Furthermore, by the phrase "if it were to be read in a circular manner" (*yadi punaḥ prasavyā syāt*), it is understood that even if there were a reversal following the exclusion of *bhānubhāsaḥ*, the state remains exactly as it was previously.

The same applies to the case of sound, form, and meaning, because the words *bhānubhāsa* and *bhābhāsa* possess identical forms in both their direct (*anuloma*) and inverse (*pratiloma*) states. Here, the mere non-attainment of the desired object—namely, the removal of the unwanted state consisting of the mass of light (*bhābhāra*) obtained by *bhānubhāsa*—is present. This is distinguished from the previous case because it is assisted by the previously mentioned variety of "unequal" (*viṣama*) [poetic figure], characterized by the attainment of the undesirable (such as the breaking of her knees) following the failure to obtain the desired object, which was the similarity to the Lord's splendor. Thus, there is a distinction compared to the former instance.

O God of gods! The king of elephants, desiring to attain a gait equal to yours (*tvadgamana*), failed to reach it; instead, having attained the state of being "jarājata" (grown old), even with his head cast down, he did not thereafter abandon that state of being "jarājata. O God of gods! The king of elephants desired to attain a gait equal to yours—meaning a movement like your own—but without reaching that gait of yours, or rather, because he did not go [to you] (*tad-agatvāt*), O Lord (*deva*), he became "aga" (one who does not go). Having thus become "jarājata" (old/grown), even though his head was cast down, he did not thereafter abandon that condition of being "jarājata. (Note: *Jarājata* is a compound of *jarā* [old age] and *ājata* [born]; *aga* is derived from *na gacchati* [does not go].)

*Tadaga* means "that mountain"; *tadagatvam* is the state of being that [mountain]. The meaning is: precisely because of not reaching you (*tvadgamana-aprāpteḥ*). *Jarājatvam* refers to the state of being an old goat (*jarānvita-chāgatvam*); alternatively, *jaraḥ* is derived from the root *jṛ* with the suffix *pacādyac*, meaning "one who grows old," and he is an *aja* (goat), thus an "old goat. *Tattvam* signifies identity with that, namely, the lack of capacity for the beauty of movement. In the alternative sense, the word *gajarāja* (king of elephants) becomes *jarāja*—meaning the word-form *jarāja*—because of *agatvāt*, i.e., due to the absence of the letter *ga*. Thus, it means having attained the state of being the word *jarāja*.

"Then, even with his head downwards"—this is a common worldly saying. In this context, even though he attained the opposite state (becoming a horse), he did not abandon his "jarājatva" (the state of being a king of elephants) in either case; he remained simply "jarāja. The sense is that he did not escape that condition. Here, the primary subject presented is merely the failure to attain the desired object—namely, the avoidance of the undesirable state of becoming a jarāja (an old man)—which was the elephant-king's lot. However, the specific variety of *viṣama* (the incongruous), characterized by the attainment of the undesirable state of being a jarāja preceded by the failure to attain the desired object of equality with the Lord’s departure, is mentioned as a subordinate element. Everything else is exactly as in the previous example.

Just as the moon was shaken by your fame and reached its own friend, the sun; and that [sun] too, being shaken by your splendor, abandoned him [the moon]; yet this [moon], though not abandoned, has fallen into a state of distress.

O Blessed One! The moon (Indu), shaken by Your fame, sought out some king (Ina) as his own friend (suhṛd)—the sense being that it was for the sake of avoiding its own misfortune. In the alternative sense, "Ina" refers to the Sun (Bhānu), and its friendship with Him is well-known in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra). It "sought" (āpa): having lost its digits, it approached the solar orb at the new moon (darśa) in order to increase them—this is the meaning.

That king, that very Bhānu (the Sun), too, being shaken—specifically agitated—by your splendor in the manner described as "a thousand suns in the sky," abandoned this moon, which had become a cause of ill omen even for himself; he cast him off. The sense is that the separation of the moon from the solar disc at the beginning of the bright fortnight is indeed well known.

"Abandoned by that king *Ina* (the Sun) and abandoned by *Indu* (the Moon)—having been cast off with the thought, 'This one is the cause of his own misfortune'—this *Indu* fell into a miserable state (*dusthitimān*), a state of wretchedness. In reality, however, the word *indu* was "abandoned by the collection of letters *ina* and *in*" and thus "possessed of the state of the collection of letters *dur*" (meaning it became the word *durdur*). Here, the distinction is that not only did the Moon fail to obtain the desired object—which would have been the avoidance of his own calamity—but he also brought about calamity for his own refuge.
Just as I strive to utterly abandon this most terrible, essence-less, and shoreless saṃsāra, O Supreme Person, why do You not extend Your respectful compassion? (1289)

"I am striving; I am exerting myself. This is the first person singular of the present tense (*laṭ*) in the active voice (*kartari*) from the root *udyuj*, belonging to the *raudhādika* class, preceded by the prefix *ut*. Here, there is merely the non-attainment of the desired object—characterized by the avoidance of the misfortune that is worldly existence—for one who is afflicted and has taken refuge in the Lord. This is a pure example [of the figure of speech]. The distinction, however, is that previous examples were intermingled with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other such figures.
The failure to attain a desired object resulting in the attainment of something undesirable is as follows:
seeing Bhīṣma rushing forward with great impetuosity to kill you, O Bhīṣma, while you held his discus, Arjuna blocked him; and seeing that alliance with his kinsmen, he rejoiced. (1290)

He saw Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, who was as terrible as he appeared, rushing forward with his discus raised in order to kill him; and Bhīṣma, seeing that his own vow—to ensure that the Blessed One would take up arms despite having promised not to do so—had become meaningful and fruitful through the Blessed One’s actual taking of the discus, rejoiced. Herein, the Blessed One’s failure to achieve his desired end—which consisted of inflicting an undesirable result upon Bhīṣma in the form of killing him—is recorded.

In this very context, one should observe with a subtle vision that Bhīṣma’s attainment of the means for happiness—namely, the fulfillment of his own vow—and the removal of the misfortune consisting of the means for suffering—namely, his death—are both recorded; and likewise, the Lord’s attainment of the misfortune consisting of the means for suffering—namely, the breaking of His own vow—is also recorded.
O Mother,
even Hanumān, who strove to slay the multitude of night-stalking demonesses, had his desire thwarted when he came upon the path of your most compassionate words.

The female night-stalkers (niśicaravadhvaḥ) have one eye, one ear, and so forth; the sense is that the time has come for you to comfort them after the slaying of Rāvaṇa, in order to destroy their entire multitude. As it is said by Hanumān in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa: "If you indeed permit me, I wish to slay all these Rākṣasīs by whom you were previously threatened."

And so forth: "O monkey, for those words of yours that are most compassionate, or for sins, or for merits, or for those deserving of death—the noble one should act with compassion; for there is no one who does not commit an offense."

The meaning of such statements is clear. Here too, Hanumān experiences the non-attainment of his desired object, which consists in inflicting an undesirable result upon the Rākṣasa woman—namely, her slaughter.

Whosoever may attain that station which is yours—endowed with splendor, possessing the wealth of Śrī, firm in intellect, and radiant—who indeed could prevail against that station, even if they were to exert every effort? (The word "O Blessed One" is understood from the context. "Your own" means your devotee; "possessing the wealth of Śrī" means one whose majesty is equal to that of Dhanada (Kubera); "firm in intellect" means one of great intelligence. By these two terms, the fullness of both material prosperity and the power of eloquence is expressed.

Therefore, being ablaze and possessing exceeding splendor, whatever state—whether pertaining to this world, the next, or liberation—one might reach or attain, who indeed could prevail against that state or the place acquired therein, even if one were to exert effort toward its subversion or destruction? The sense is: no one at all. Alternatively, the construction may be: "Who could prevail? meaning even Brahmā himself; the sense is that even he would certainly not be able to do so.

But in the other case, regarding your [verse] beginning with "yat padaṃ śrīdaśrīḥ" and so forth—what person, even if they exerted effort to reverse that word (to read it in reverse order), would be able to succeed? For even when recited in reverse with great effort, the original sequence remains intact. Here, the failure of an ordinary person to achieve their desired object—which consists in inflicting an undesirable result upon another by reversing the words established by a devotee of the Lord—is described. This is an instance mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia); however, in the previous example, it was pure.
O son of Daśaratha, had you not rendered that exceedingly terrifying prowess of yours devoid of its heat, then even the host of night-stalkers would have remained utterly formidable.

O son of Daśaratha! If the race of night-stalkers (Rākṣasas), which is exceedingly terrifying and most cruel, had desired to make your majesty—that from which the heat, warmth, and cruelty have departed—such [as it is now], then even so, that majesty of yours would have remained exceedingly formidable; the sense is that it would have become truly terrifying because its heat could not be dispelled. (Note: The conditional *lṛṅ* is used here in the sense of the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*) following the desiderative form of the root *kṛ*.)

The meaning is also striking: had he intended to produce the word *atibhīṣma* (extremely terrifying) in its alternative form [by removing the *ṣ*], deprived of the sibilant (*ūṣman*) in the form of the letter *ṣ*, he would have produced it simply as *atibhīma*. Here, the failure to obtain the desired result—namely, the cooling of the host of night-stalkers by the heat of the Lord’s majesty—is shown through the form of a poetic possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). Thus, eight sub-varieties of the third type of the "Uneven" (*viṣama*) have been demonstrated. Other varieties may also be illustrated in this same manner; however, I desist for fear of exceeding the limits of this work.

The author of the *Kuvalayānanda* maintains that even in a case where one person, commissioned by another for the sake of accomplishing the latter's desired end, disregards the employer's wish and achieves only his own, there too the figure is indeed *viṣama* (the "uneven") because it consists in the non-attainment of the desired object. For example:
"Thinking, 'What shall I do now that she has vanished there? Rādhā, though she had sent her beloved away with this thought, 'This is my cleverness,' did so with agitation. (1294)

With the confidence that "this is mine," my mind—meaning, until the arrival of my beloved, the son of Nanda—is sent by me with agitation (which implies seeing him from nearby). Since the word *dhī* is feminine, the metaphorical role of a female messenger (*dūtī*) is understood therein. That mind is indeed absorbed in that beloved alone, according to the maxim: "Every sentence is restrictive" (*sarvaṃ vākyaṃ sāvadhāraṇam*).

The sense is that, because it is difficult for others to grasp separately, it has attained oneness by being merged right there. [In the root *lī*] meaning "to adhere," the suffix *kta* is used in the active sense (*kartari*). Alternatively, the sense is that she has been transformed into that very form. The word *nāma* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). The meaning is "I think she is hidden" (*nilīnā*), or perhaps in a sense of reproach (*kutsane*). The implication is: "Fie upon her! She who was sent by me with the conviction that she was not unfaithful toward her lover, yet is now sporting right there. Amara states: "The word *nāma* is used in the senses of making manifest, possibility, anger, approach, and reproach."

"What shall I do? What shall I perform?"—thus Radha thought. Here, disregarding the desire of Radha who was the one to be enjoined, [the speaker] has accomplished only his own wish. This is the figure of speech *viṣama* (incongruity), intermingled with *samāsokti* (speech of brevity). An example of when there is first the attainment of a desired object, followed by its non-attainment, is as follows:

"When you go to the vicinity of the mountain, for a mere moment the moon—deprived of its spot by the luster of the crystal rocks on its slopes and thus resembling your face—then becomes as it was before. (1295)

But after passing beyond the vicinity of your mountain, it becomes as it was before; because of the great distance, the moon possesses its dark spot as clearly as before. Here, for one who desires the moon’s spotlessness through its resemblance to the face of Lord Veṅkaṭanātha, there is the attainment of that desired state for only a moment upon reaching the vicinity of Veṅkaṭagiri, but not for all time; thus, this is the non-attainment of the desired object following its temporary attainment.
In some cases, even when the desired object is not attained, there occurs a particular kind of interruption based on the delusion that it has been attained. For example:
"Thinking, 'The fresh butter has come,' upon seeing a young cloud nearby, a certain cowherd girl, filled with delusion, hurriedly strove to catch it. (1216)

In this instance, the delusion of attaining what was desired is shown to belong to a certain cowherd girl with beautiful eyes who, though failing to obtain her wish, was awaiting the opportunity to bind the young Krishna, who delighted in stealing butter.
Where, due to the non-attainment of the whole, there is only the attainment of a single part thereof, even in that case there is indeed the non-attainment of that [whole]. For example:

O lotus-eyed one! The *milinda* (bee), desiring to attain your splendor—that is, to become your abode or to possess a complexion like yours—abandoned its own limited radiance; yet, though it now shines with immeasurable beauty, it remains merely an *alinda* (a porch). [In the alternative sense: O lotus-eyed one! The word *milinda*, desiring to attain your splendor—that is, the state of being your abode or having a luster equal to yours—therefore abandons its own "limited radiance," which consists of the presence of the letter *mi* or the syllable *mi*. Thus, even while shining with immeasurable glory, it becomes merely an *alinda* [the word *alinda*]. 1297.

In the word *mita*, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). Regarding the *visarga*, there is an optional elision according to the rule: “The elision of *visarga* before a *khara* or a *śari* should be stated. Thus, the meaning is “even while abandoning (*tyajan*)”—that is, relinquishing—the connection with the letter *m*. [The word] *amitaśriyā* means by abundant splendor or by prosperity; the doubling of the letter *śa* occurs according to the rule “*anaci ca*” (Pāṇini 8.4.47). In the alternative reading, the word division is *aṃ itaḥ śriyā*.

Having acquired the letter *a* (the syllable *aṃ*) from this [word], though shimmering with splendor and manifesting through the excellence of its meaningful form, it became merely an *alinda*—that is, a vestibule outside the door. The sense is that it did not become your entire domain. According to Amara: "The words *praghāṇa*, *praghaṇa*, and *alinda* refer to the outer chamber of a door. In the alternative sense, the meaning is that having acquired the letter *a* in place of the letter *mi*, it became the word *alinda* itself.

In this context, just as in the injunction "One should not say 'girā girā'; having substituted 'irā', one should chant," the word *irā* which is prescribed after the prohibition of the word *girā* occurs in the very place of the word *girā*, so too here, the vowel *a* (*avarṇa*) which is prescribed after the prohibition of the vowel *i* (*mikarṇa*) occurs in the very place of the vowel *i*.

For this very reason, the statement in the *Tattvabodhinī* and other works—that the suffix *śyan*, being prescribed after the prohibition of *yak* in the rule "After the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*, for the Easterners, there is *śyan* and the Parasmaipada," occurs in the very place of that [prohibited *yak*]—is consistent. Here, it should be understood that because Milinda failed to obtain the divine abode of the Blessed One, which was his desired goal, even the attainment of the *ālinda* (veranda), which is but a part of it, constitutes the non-attainment of the desired object (*iṣṭānavāpti*).

Where the attainment of some indifferent object that is not desired is described as being preceded by the non-attainment of what is wished for, even there it is merely the non-attainment of the desired. For example:

O Lord of Śrī! That *ghanasāra* (camphor), though renowned for its coolness, fragrance, and other qualities, became known as "the dust of the feet of Śrī" (*śrīpādareṇu*), having become the river at Your feet—the Gaṅgā—by assuming the name and splendor of that river. (Notes: *Ghanasāra* refers to camphor; according to Amarasimha, "Now, *karpūra* is neuter, while *ghanasāra* is [also masculine]. Regarding the term *abhikhyā*, Amarasimha states: "The word *abhikhyā* denotes both name and beauty.")

For the sake of attaining that [state], he remained with his head downward—meaning, bowing his head at your feet—even though he was already "anagha" (sinless) by virtue of the "rasa" (water). By this, it is shown that he attained the status of being known as the river flowing from the Lord's feet. The actual state of affairs is that the word *ghanasāra* (camphor), when read in reverse order, results in the form *rasānagha*. One must not forget the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthayostādātmyam*). He became one whose name was the "dust" (*reṇu*) of the "glorious feet" (*śrīpāda*), that is, the dust of the feet of Lakṣmī.

The essential point is this: even if one somehow managed to achieve the state of a purifying *tīrtha* in order to obtain the designation "the river of the Lord’s feet," if that were not attained, let it be so; or even if the designation "the river of the Lord’s feet" (*śrīpādasarit*) did not exist, on the contrary, the name "the dust of the Lord’s feet" (*śrīpādareṇu*) existed. The truth is that on Śrī Veṅkaṭādri, the camphor-dust offered to the divine form of the Lord is conventionally referred to as "the dust of the Lord’s feet."

In this case, for Ghanasāra, the mere failure to obtain the desired object known as the dust of the Lord’s feet is intended; however, the state of being the dust of the venerable feet is not an intensely undesirable thing, such that this verse would serve as an example of the first variety of the third type of *viṣama* (the incongruous). Rather, it should be understood that [the former] is simply unattained.

O Consort of the Daughter of the Ocean, just as the atasi flower, desiring the excellence of your splendor, fell from its balance-scale upon attaining equality with it, so too was the auspicious tulasī plant, having attained the state of being tulasī, beloved to you. 1299.

O Lord of the Daughter of the Ocean! *Atasī* refers to the flower of the linseed plant (*kṣumākusuma*), according to Amara’s lexicon: “*Atasī* may be *umā* or *kṣumā*. The suffix *aṇ* has been elided in accordance with the rule “*puṣpamūleṣu bahulam*” (Pāṇini 4.3.166). The phrase “even of your *lakṣmī*” means even of your radiance; alternatively, the sense that it refers even to the Goddess Śrī herself should be supplied as an embellishment.

She who possessed the desire for preeminence—that is, for being most highly praised—having fallen from that desired state and reached a decline, became blessed simply by attaining equality with you through the acquisition of the *tulā* (the balance-scale). The sense is that even when one's supreme desire is not attained, one is fulfilled by that much alone. By becoming *tulasī*—that is, by attaining the state of being *tulasī* (the word *kyap* is used in the sense of "state" according to the rule *bhuvo bhāve*)—she indeed became dear to your heart, residing in your heart and beloved by it.

In one sense, the word-form *atasī* is "fallen from those two," meaning it is devoid of the letter *a* and the letter *ta*. Regarding the doubling of the *ca* in the term *taccyutā*, we have stated more than once that, for the sake of conforming to another meaning, the optional doubling of the *ca* by the rule *anaci ca* must be accepted. Through its attainment of equality—that is, by the sequential substitution of the letters *tu* and *la* in place of the letters *a* and *ta*—having become *tulasī*, it attained the status of the word *tulasī* and became charming.

In this context, for Atasī, who desired even the excellence of the Blessed Lakṣmī, the state of being Tulasī was merely undesired and not intensely disliked; therefore, by not obtaining that [Tulasī-state], there is simply the non-attainment of her sole desired object.
Or rather,

O Lord, even if the Goddess of Speech were to hang her head in shame, desiring to bear the full burden of the splendor of the river that is your feet, it would be only the banks of that river which could support her.

O Lord! Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, desiring to bear the state of being the bearer of the entire burden—the quality of carrying all loads—of the Gaṅgā that is the river of your feet, would even have her head turned downwards; yet she would still remain on the very bank of that river of your feet.

The sense is that even with great effort, it would possess a luster similar to its bank, but not a luster equal to it. In the alternative sense, the word-form "Bhāratī" (the Goddess of Speech), if reversed, results in "Tīrabhā" (one who has a bank); this is the meaning. Here too, for Bhāratī—who desires the splendor of the river that is the Lord’s feet—the attainment of the brilliance of that bank is something unintended; yet, as it is not of the nature of an intense aversion, it is merely the non-attainment of a desired object (*kevaleṣṭānavāpti*). As in another example:
O Mother, desiring the beauty of your cheeks, the ketakī flower abandons its own color; and becoming a peacock, it attains the supreme splendor of the mass of your hair. (1301)

Having abandoned her own color—that well-known, supramundane fair complexion—and in the alternative sense, having abandoned that very syllable "ta" which constitutes her own denotative word [ketakī], she became a *kekī* (peacock); in the alternative sense, the word for her denotative object, *ketakī*, results in the form *kekī* through the removal of the letter *ta*. This is due to the power of the identity between the signified and the signifier. She [then] assumed the beauty of the mass of curls—the splendor of the tresses; the rest is clear.

In this case, although the Ketakī flower fails to obtain the beauty of Śrī’s desired mass of hair, because that [beauty] is not undesirable to her, there is merely the non-attainment of the luster of Lakṣmī’s cheeks which she herself desires; thus, it is like "the non-attainment of a desired object" (*kevaleṣṭānavāpti*). In the definition, regarding the phrase "attainment of the undesirable" (*aniṣṭāvāpti*), the negative particle (*nañ*) compounded with the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*) has the sense of contradiction (negation of identity), as in "non-god" (*asura*), "unrighteousness" (*adharma*), or "inauspiciousness" (*aśubha*), and not the sense of being different from it, as in "non-human" (*amānuṣa*) or "non-horse" (*anaśva*). By this, it is established that the "undesirable" (*aniṣṭa*) is of the nature of misfortune (*anartha*).

And thus, the secret is this: it is only the attainment of such an undesirable [result] that constitutes the "uneven" (viṣama), and not the case of any neutral person who is merely distinct from the desired; for this is evident from the observation of many previous examples.

Even in a case where the attainment of the undesirable or the non-attainment of the desired is understood solely through the power of *śleṣa* (punning) and not in reality, there too the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous) certainly occurs. For example:
"O Lotus-eyed One, alas, for those who worship you, the Lord of the world, thinking 'May we never suffer defeat anywhere,' it is you yourself who brings about their attainment of defeat! (1302)

"O lotus-eyed one! There is a contradiction [in the following]: 'Those who worship you so that they may never suffer defeat anywhere—do you, on the contrary, bring about their attainment of defeat? [Resolution: *Para* means supreme (*śreṣṭhā*). *Abhava* refers to the absence of worldly existence (*bhava*); this is either an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning 'the non-existence of existence' (*arthābhāve'vyayībhāvaḥ*), or a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning 'that which is not existence' (*na bhavaḥ abhavaḥ*). The attainment of that (*abhavaprāptiḥ*) means the attainment of the highest good (*niḥśreyasaprāptiḥ*). Alternatively, "O *para*" is an address to the Blessed One. The attainment of *abhava* has the same meaning as stated above; thus is the resolution. In this regard:
[He worships] the Lord of the Universe, the Unborn God, the Sovereign of the World, the Imperishable."
Those who worship the lotus-eyed one do not suffer defeat.

Thus the meaning of the verse has been considered. Here, the attainment of defeat is expressed through *śleṣa* (paronomasia) as either the attainment of the undesirable or the non-attainment of the desirable; it is not established as a literal fact.

Just as the Kaumudikī crane, desiring the moon’s disc and failing to obtain it, becomes joyless and follows after the birds that bear its name; so too, O Lord, [the world] becomes devoid of joy and pursues those who speak of You.

O Lord, O Blessed One! Desiring to attain equality with your mace Kaumodakī and your discus Sudarśana, she is therefore *avāgrā*—that is, bent down. According to Amara, the term *avāgra* means "bent down" (*avanatānata*). The sense is that she has approached them in humility for the sake of obtaining that equality. Consequently, she is *vimodā*, meaning her joy has vanished. Alternatively, the construction may be joined as *tadalābhe 'vāgrā*: because she did not obtain that [equality], she is bent down; the meaning is that her head is bowed due to the contraction caused by failing to achieve it.

In reality, this expression is used because it is observed that the Kaumodakī mace is held by the Lord’s left hand with its tip indeed pointing downwards. *Kaukī* is derived from *koka* (the ruddy goose) with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *tasyedam*, and then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. Alternatively, regarding the specific word-form *Kaumodakī*: when the two syllables *mo-da* are removed, it becomes *kaukī*; such is the meaning. That bird (*khaga*) whose name (*abhidhā*) is that of the discus (*tasya cakrasya*) is so described; the meaning is the *cakravāka* bird.

Just as it is taught that "the *koka*, the *cakra*, and the *cakravāka* are those named after the parts of a chariot (*rathāṅga*)," he attained a connection—that is, a state of association—with that [name], meaning he attained the status of a *kaukī*. Here, the attainment of the undesirable state of being a *kaukī* by the *Kaumodakī* occurs through wordplay (*śleṣa*) alone, and not in reality.
Just as you serve the feet of Hari to dry up the former mud entirely, so too, O friend, new fame shall arise from it; yet you do not realize this again.

"O friend!"—this is an address directed toward some particular companion. "In its entirety," meaning without remainder, you "devote yourself to," that is, you meditate upon with affection and serve, the "foot"—meaning both the foot and the ray—of Hari, the Blessed One, and of the Sun, in order to dry up, eliminate, and parch all former mire, that is, past sin and ancient mud.

Therefore, from devotion to that [Brahman], fame arises; in the manner stated in such scriptural passages as "I become the glory (*yaśas*) of the Brahmins," the Supreme Brahman—which is the means to glory—will arise, meaning it will be attained by those practicing meditation whose form is identical to direct perception. Furthermore, it does not pass away (*na vyeti*), meaning it does not undergo decay or perish. Alternatively, "fame" refers to the renown of being a knower of Brahman; this will arise, meaning it will be born, and furthermore, it does not pass away, meaning it does not diminish.

On the other hand, you do not realize that a new and fresh fame—mud—will arise once again. Here, through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), it is depicted that for one who worships the foot of Hari in order to dry up all previous mire, even though the attainment of that [drying] occurs, there is the acquisition of an undesirable result in the form of unprecedented mud.

"Just as the moon, though making every effort with the thought, 'I am weary from wandering incessantly through existence, yet I am not deluded; may I always remain somewhere in the station of Hari,' finds its desire fulfilled only during the rainy season—O Hari! 'I am constantly exhausted by wandering (caṅkramaṇa) in existence (bhava), that is, by the cycle of saṃsāra, or by the delusion that the body is the self'—this is an expression of world-weariness (nirveda).

Therefore, being 'undeluded' (abhrānta)—meaning free from constant wandering or free from the delusion that the body is the self—may I always (satatam) dwell (syām) in some place (kvacana) within the station of Hari (haripade), that is, in the temple of the Blessed One."
One should dwell in the temple of Viṣṇu performing even the slightest act;
one should dwell in the temple of Viṣṇu even without performing any act at all.

Such is the sense derived from the teaching of the Blessed One. Thus, although he exerted himself, the Moon obtained his desired object—the aforementioned wish—only during the *prāvṛṣ* (the rainy season) and not at other times. The meaning is that the Moon alone attained a state of wandering within the station of Viṣṇu (the sky) during the rainy season specifically, and not in autumn or other seasons.

But the actual state of affairs is this: he is eternally existent, yet constantly born; weary from his circumambulation of Mount Meru, he has ceased wandering in the sky at the feet of Hari and now finds his station within a cloud in the atmosphere. Here, by the power of *śleṣa* (punning) alone, there is the attainment of some desired object at a particular time, but not the attainment of all desires at all times.

Thus, although the attainment of the undesirable and the non-attainment of the desirable have been demonstrated primarily through the power of the identification based on *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the examples previously shown, they are now presented again with further analysis for the sake of clarifying the understanding of beginners who seek instruction.

Thus, among all these varieties which contain within them a relation of conjunction characterized by the nature of the produced and the producer, it should be understood that there is no conformity between cause and effect: in some cases, because of the presence of qualities that are dissimilar; and in other cases, because the intended cause—by producing its desired effect—results instead in the non-attainment of the desired and the attainment of the undesired, thereby lacking conformity with the effect. Consequently, the general definition [of causality] does not apply. This is how it should be considered.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, on the figure of speech Viṣama (the Uneven), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now, the section on the figure of speech *Samālaṅkāra*: they know that as *Sama* (the Equal) wherein a fitting conjunction is described.

The description of a union between two things that are mutually appropriate is the figure *samālaṃkāra* (the Equal). Here too, "union" (*saṃsarga*)—whether characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or by production (*utpatti*) and so forth—is the definition common to all its varieties. Within that, the appropriateness of a union characterized by conjunction and the like is twofold: it may culminate in praise or it may culminate in censure. This is the first variety of *sama*, which is the opposite of *viṣama* (the Unequal).
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Śrīśaila is surely your proper place; you are indeed Śrīnivāsa. It is fitting that you bestow upon those who have sought refuge the gift of prosperity along with bliss. (1306)

O Hari, just as you cause the world to flourish with your own splendors for Sarasvatī, the foremost of the wise, I consider your fortune to be like that of a night-lotus; thus, it is only fitting that you are called Vidhu (the Moon).

"O foremost of the wise, best among the thirty gods!"—the analysis of the compound is *agrasara*, meaning "one who moves in front. The suffix *ṭa* is applied according to the rule *puro'grato'greṣu sarteḥ*. Just as in examples such as *yūdhaṃ tadagrasaragarvitakṛṣṇasāram* ("a herd of proud black antelopes moving at its head"), there is no mandatory substitution of the vowel *e* for the word *agra* due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

O Hari! By your glances—whether as side-long looks or as the specific volitions expressed in the thought "May I become many"—you naturally, by your very essence, cause the world (the singular number being used to denote the class) to flourish, that is, you expand it through the process of creation. Of such a one as you, whose prosperity consists in being the Lord of all worlds, by what people could it be disregarded or held in contempt? The sense is: by no one at all. In the alternative [Vaiṣṇava] interpretation, the division of the words is: *vibudhāgrasarasvataḥ*.

O foremost of the wise, O best of gods! [The Amarakośa states: *aparārthya*, *agra*, *prāgrasara*, *prāgrya*, *agrya*, *agrīya*, *agriya*]. With your *ālokas*—that is, with lights, meaning your own rays—you cause the world of the ocean, the waters of the Sarasvatī, to swell. Your splendor (*śrī*) is esteemed by the night-lotuses (*kairavas*), being dear to the white water-lilies. Therefore, I consider it entirely fitting that you are the Moon (*vidhu*). Yet, the truth is that you are the Blessed Lord (*bhagavān*).

O Lord of Kamalā, just as you wear a girdle at your waist even amidst many ornaments, so too is this [girdle] appropriately situated in the middle; for it is not disfigured even when addressed with words of opposition.

Because of this reason, even when addressed with contrary words—that is, speech opposed to her own wishes—this lady is not "vikṛtā," meaning she is of unaltered nature; the sense is that, by virtue of having a vision fixed solely on justice (*nyāya*), she does not undergo any mental transformation even when confronted with speech contradicting her own desires. The "impartiality" (*madhyasthatā*) of such a woman refers to the state of standing in the middle, in what is right and just; we have stated more than once that in cases such as "the fulfillment of the purpose of autumn" (*śaradaḥ kṛtārthatā*), the neuter gender is used for the abstract quality (*sāmānya*).

The meaning is "abiding on the path of justice. Amara states: "Madhya is used in the sense of 'just' (*nyāyya*). And the *Ratnamālā* states: "'Madhya' is not feminine; it means 'middle,' 'just,' 'opportunity,' and 'waist' (*avalagna*). In this context, the word *kāñcikā* (girdle) remains unchanged in its phonetic sequence even when read in reverse order—this is the meaning. The factual state of affairs is that for this girdle, being situated at the waist—that is, being fastened to the *avalagna*—is appropriate. The intended sense is that it is the sole ornament of her waist.
O Blessed One, although your eye and the lotus differ in color, they are identical in form from beginning to end; since neither is ever disagreeable in the middle, their friendship is indeed fitting.

O Blessed One! Your eye and the lotus are identical in form at the beginning and end—that is, at the root and the outer corner, or the first and last parts—because both possess a reddish hue. They are also identical in syllable, because the first and last syllables of these two words are composed of the letter *na*. Yet, in the middle—that is, in their central portions—they differ in color, possessing mutually distinct hues; for the meaning is that the pupil in the center of the eye is dark blue, whereas the pericarp of the lotus is golden-yellow.

In the case of the *pakṣa* (the phoneme *ya*), the meaning is simply the middle syllable (*madhyamākṣara*) which is distinct from the others (*li*). "Always non-opposing" (*sadā'py apratikūlam*) means free from mutual opposition; the sense is that the presence of some slight opposing property is of no consequence because of the possession of many non-contradictory properties. In the case of the word (*śabda-pakṣa*), the sense is that it is "always non-opposing" both in its direct order (*ānulomya*) and even in its reverse order (*prātilomya*). "Non-opposing" (*apratikūla*) means possessing an unaltered sequence (*anupūrvī*).

Therefore, the friendship between these two lotus-eyes is indeed appropriate; the sense is that even though there is some difference in their attributes, their similarity is fitting because of the existence of a great many common characteristics. Furthermore, in this context, if by the phrase "your eye" one intends the Lord’s eye which is like the sun, even then these qualifiers are equally applicable to both. For instance, the quality of having an identical form from beginning to end applies to both, as they are both of a reddish (aruṇa) hue.

The sun possesses a variegated color in its center because it is reddish even in the middle; likewise, the lotus has a yellowish-brown (piśaṅga) color in its center according to the description given. Furthermore, both are eternally non-adverse to one another, as their mutual favorability is renowned in both worldly experience and the Vedas. Therefore, friendship between the sun and the lotus is indeed appropriate. The rest is the same [as previously explained]. Or, for example: "Moreover, since camphor (ghanasāra) is by nature full of fragrance (rasānagha), this [friendship] is indeed fitting. O Acyuta, for you who are free from all faults (rasānagha), this is a worthy ornament (lalāma) for the camphor. (1310)

Indeed, O Acyuta! Since even toward a person whose disposition (bhāva) or nature (svabhāva) is perverse (prasavya)—that is, contrary—your affection (rasa) is stainless (anagha), meaning your love is faultless; or rather, the analysis of the compound may be "one whose stainlessness consists of rasa. By the word "even" (api), it is indicated that the quality of having stainless affection toward one of a favorable nature is established by the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so).

In reality, however, the word *ghanasāra* results in the form *rasānagha* when it signifies opposition; this is the meaning. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The term *prasavya* applies to both the left (*savya*) and to that which is contrary (*pratikūla*). Therefore, this *ghanasāra*—meaning one whose essence (*sāra*) is dense (*ghana*) or strength—is such that even in its state of being *prasavya*, this [word] is to be supplied here. The sense is: as if toward a person of favorable nature, so too toward an object of adverse nature.

*Rasānaghaḥ* means possessing faultless affection; the sense is that for this Greatly Noble One (*mahodāra*), there exists no distinction between the categories of "favorable" and "unfavorable" regarding the object of His love. Alternatively, *rasa* refers to the mine of infinite auspicious qualities characterized by bliss, and *anagha* means the opposite of everything that is to be abandoned. The sense is that whether a sentient being is favorable or unfavorable, no difference whatsoever arises in His natural state of possessing both these characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) due to that favorability or unfavorability.

"O lady with a divine countenance, it is fitting that you bear a *puṇḍra* (sandalwood mark) upon such a forehead (*lalāma*) as yours; for there is a perfect correspondence between the two, both being characterized by their essence of camphor (*ghanasāra*) and their stainless nature (*anaghātva*). [Amara states: 'The word *lalāma* is used for a tail, a forehead-mark (*puṇḍra*), a horse, an ornament, preeminence, and a banner. Indeed, it is well known that the forehead-slate of the Lord Śrīnivāsa is graced by a camphor *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*. Or, for example: Just as your face is radiant with the splendor of the moon and likewise fragrant, so too is it indeed fitting that it serves as the *lalāma* (forehead-mark) for the moon on the peak of the serpent-mountain (Śeṣācala). (1311)

"By the name of Candra"—that is, by the name *candra*; "brilliant," according to the rule that "camphor (*ghanasāra*) is designated as *candra*. In the alternative sense, it means "resplendent with a beauty resembling the moon. Likewise, "fragrant" (*surabhi*), meaning sweet-smelling; in the alternative sense, "charming," for the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *surabhi* is recorded as denoting both fragrance and the charming, like a term applicable to its referent. Alternatively, the word may be read as the compound *tathāsurabhi*, meaning "possessing a world-transcending fragrance."

The status of that camphor as the "forehead-ornament" (lalāma) of your face—meaning its role as a decorative mark (puṇḍra) or an ornament—is the subject already mentioned. Herein, in the first example, there is a description of the association between Śrīnivāsa and the granting of fortune (śrīpradāna), which are mutually corresponding; in the second, between the state of being the cause of light for oneself and the state of increasing the world; in the third, between the states of being situated at the center of Kāñcī; in the fourth, between the lotus-eye and friendship; and in the fifth and sixth examples, between the camphor and the forehead-ornament of the face of Śrīnivāsa.
This constitutes the description of their conjunction.
Just as one who,

internally contemplating Your auspicious refuge— resplendent upon the mountain that is the king of serpents— becomes here and now that very auspicious refuge through the principle of "the nature of the sacrifice," so too have I become free from association with the bee.

O you who shine like a mountain of cobras and bulls! Contemplating—that is, meditating upon—within myself that auspicious refuge of yours, your divine and auspicious form which serves as the object of meditation, I [attain this] by the principle of *tat-kratu* (the nature of one's resolve), according to the scriptural teaching: "As is a person’s resolve in this world, so does he become after departing from here. Here, *kratu* means worship (*upāsanā*). This occurs right here, and not after departing from this life; such is the sense of "this wonder. [The term] *repha* means censurable sin (*agha*).

In passages such as "and because of serving that which is censured," sin (*agha*) is stated to be censurable. He who has no association (*saṃsarga*)—that is, no connection (*saṃbandha*)—is "one devoid of association with *repha*. Thus, being one whose refuge is auspicious (*śubhāśraya*), I became one whose form is auspicious (*maṅgalavigraha*). In the alternative sense, the word *śubhāśraya*, when deprived of association with the letter *ra* (*arephasaṃsargaḥ*), results in the form *śubhāśayaḥ* (one whose intention is auspicious). This is based on the identity between word and meaning. As Amara states: "The term *repha* refers to the sound *ra*; when used as a masculine noun it denotes the letter *ra*, but as an adjective it signifies something contemptible."

The essential meaning is this: "By meditating upon Your divine and auspicious form, all my sins have been dispelled and my disposition has become virtuous. According to the Viśvakośa: "The word *āśaya* may mean intention (*abhiprāya*), as well as the mind (*mānasa*) and a receptacle (*ādhāra*). Here, there is a description of two corresponding things: the meditation upon the auspicious refuge and the attainment of the state of having that same auspicious refuge.

Just as both the delighter of Vinatā and the one skilled in supporting the earth are equally expert in bearing the world, so too is a certain friendship between these two lords of birds and serpents appropriate, despite their difference in form.

Both of these lords of birds and serpents are equally skilled in gladdening Vinatā and the virtuous; they are both renowned for their excellence in carrying Viśvaṃbhara (the Earth) and Viśvaṃbharā (the Goddess). [The suffix *caṇap* is used here according to the rule *tena vittaḥ*. That is to say, there is no difference whatsoever between these two, Garuḍa and Ananta.

Therefore, friendship between these two is appropriate, because both possess identical characteristics; this is the intended meaning. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the word *patagādhipapannagādhipa* is a compound (*samasta-pada*). The distinction lies solely in the two instances of the letter *na* containing the letter *ta*; for the letters *pa*, *ga*, and so forth are identical in both cases—this is the intended meaning. Herein lies the appropriateness of the mutual friendship between the Lord of Birds (*pataga-adhipa*) and the Lord of Serpents (*pannaga-adhipa*). As in the following example:
O Blessed One, those Vaiṣṇavas who remain with unchanging dispositions even during times of upheaval—by them alone are such ascetics served as they take refuge at Your feet.

O Blessed One! Even at a time of reversal—that is, even during a period of adversity and extreme distress—those Vaiṣṇavas who remain with unaltered dispositions, that is, with their very nature as subservient to the Lord exactly as it is (the suffix *kta* here denotes state), those Vaiṣṇavas of such a kind, whose nature remains unchanged even in times of reversal, have taken refuge at Your feet; or rather, they have taken refuge in Your state, meaning Your emblem, the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*).

This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti): "The triple-staff is indeed the mark of Viṣṇu. The meaning is that those who have taken refuge [in him] are the triple-staffed ascetics (tridaṇḍins). The sense is that self-controlled ascetics (yatayas) are to be served, and not those who are otherwise. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), even at the time of the reversal of syllables, the Vaiṣṇavas remain unchanged in their nature; the sense is that even when this specific word "vaiṣṇavaiḥ" is recited in reverse order, it remains exactly as it was.

The meaning is that such ascetics (*yatayaḥ*), described in the manner stated, [would remain] even in the opposite of this state, remaining exactly as they were before. There is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the plurality residing in the sense onto the word. Here, there is a fitting association with Vaiṣṇavas, triple-staffed ascetics (*tridaṇḍin*), or surrendered ascetics (*prapanna-yatis*).

Just as the Blessed Lord is the presiding deity (adhibhū) over the worlds, so too are you Śrī; this is indeed fitting, for generally, even when divided between the masculine and the feminine, they possess a single uniform nature.

O Śrī! You are the Lord (Bhagavān), the sovereign ruler (adhibhūḥ) and supreme lord (adhīśvara) of the worlds, for it is heard in scripture: "He is the Lord of all," "The Lord of the universe," and so forth. Amara states: "Adhibhū means a leader or guide. You too are the sovereign ruler and supreme lady (adhīśvarī) of the worlds, according to such scriptural passages as: "The Goddess who rules, the sovereign mistress of the world; the mistress of this universe, the wife of Viṣṇu. Thus, this state of being the supreme lords of both of you is perfectly suited. He states the reason for both being sovereign rulers with the words beginning "prāyeṇa" (generally), because even though they are distinct—the male group (pauṃsne) and the female group (straiṇe)—[they are united].
Among gods, animals, and humans, O Maitreya, the Blessed One Hari bears male names, while Lakṣmī bears female names; beyond these two of us, nothing else exists.
Whosoever possesses the male form, he is Viṣṇu; this is the certainty.
Whosoever, however, possesses the female form, there Lakṣmī is established.

Thus, according to the method stated in the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and other Purāṇas, although we have divided ourselves through a particular mutual desire, we remain identical in form and possess a unity of nature characterized by the pervasion of the universe and so forth;
for as the world is pervaded by me in my own essence and by my very nature,
so too is all this pervaded by her, who is likewise the sovereign controller.
"I pervade her, and likewise she pervades me, the Lord"— as stated in the Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā and other texts. By the use of the word "generally" (prāyeṇa),
hear this distinction between me and her, O Lord of the Army (Seneśa):
She is the sovereign mistress of all, my beloved, who has become the very essence of my life.

And by the statement, "I am the Lord of that world and of this world, as proclaimed in the Vedas," it is indicated that there exists some degree of distinction [between the two]. Therefore, the status of being the *adhibhū* (the presiding deity over beings) is entirely appropriate for both of you. In this context, both words beginning with *adhibhū*—namely *adhipumān* and *adhistri*—are derived from the roots *pumān* (man/masculinity) and *strī* (woman/femininity). According to the rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau bhavanāt*, which prescribes the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* for meanings ranging from "offspring" (*apatya*) up to "being" (*bhavana*), the suffix *snañ* is applied after the word *pumān* and the suffix *nañ* after the word *strī* to denote a collection or an abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus, they signify the collective nature of masculinity and femininity.

The phrase "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) means "when the case-endings beginning with *su* follow," which is understood according to the established rules of grammar (*śabdaśāstra-maryādā*). The sense is that these two words—one masculine and one feminine—possess "generally" (*bhūmnā*) a uniform form, as such uniformity is observed in them. The word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) is used because, in the case of the feminine gender, other forms are also prescribed when the case-endings *ṅi* and *ām* follow. Therefore, there is a correspondence between both the masculine and feminine words denoting "the over-lord of the earth" (*adhibhū*).
Or rather: O Primordial God, if we could know that supreme being who manifests within the heart through merit, then it would be appropriate to say that this being manifests within the heart.

O Ādideva! O Blessed One, the cause of the entire universe! By this, the following is recalled: "The Ādideva, the mighty-armed Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord. From a particular merit (sukṛta)—which is distinguished by the divisions of intentional, incidental, occasional, and consequential—if the supreme, most excellent *sattva*, the quality of purity (*sattvaguṇa*), should manifest in the heart—that is, in the mind—then the sense is that if, through the attainment of the quality of purity rooted in the purity of food, there should arise purification of the mind (*cittaśuddhi*).

Then we would rightly know—that is, we would understand—it to be fitting that You, who are renowned as the cause and controller of the entire universe, become manifest within the heart (the mind); or rather, that You become the object of meditation in the form of *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant remembrance), which has the same nature as direct perception, being one who partakes in that manifestation which is dear to the heart (*hṛdya*). This is the first person plural of the optative (*liṅ*) of the root *vid*.

Here, the shadow of the meaning of the Vedic scripture—“When food is pure, the mind becomes pure; when the mind is pure, mindfulness becomes firm”—is recollected. In this context, there is a description of the purity of the mind and the manifestation of the Lord, which correspond to one another.
O Hari, for those who remember you at dawn— the crest-jewel of the Vṛṣa clan— and who possess the self of Acyuta, it is only fitting that they attain both auspiciousness and purity.

"O hare!"—this address is intended to accord with the recollection of Hari at dawn that is about to be described. For it is said: "As you rise, think of Hari. By this very word, his auspiciousness—which is conducive to attaining the excellence (bhadra) to be described—is also illuminated. "For those in whose hearts dwells the Blessed Lord Hari, the abode of auspiciousness, there is constant celebration, constant prosperity, and constant auspiciousness."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. O Acyuta! By this, His purifying nature is indicated as being conducive to the accomplishment of the purity that is about to be described. As it is said:
"Even one deeply addicted to great sin, by meditating for even a moment on Acyuta, becomes a great ascetic again, the purifier of those who purify the assembly."

Thus: at dawn, at the break of day, for those self-possessed ones—the wise—who remember you, the crest-jewel of the Vṛṣa clan (Śiva) and the crown of Śeṣādri (the serpent-hill), that state of auspiciousness (*bhadra*) which is attained through the remembrance of you, Hari, who is described as the abode of blessings, is indeed fitting. Furthermore, that state of purity (*uccha*) and cleanliness (*śuddhi*) which is attained through the remembrance of you, Acyuta, who is described as the most purifying, and the resulting sanctity (*pavitratva*) that is obtained, is likewise entirely appropriate.

The word *cukṣa* is derived from the root *cukṣ* (meaning "to purify") with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). Regarding the term *bhadra*, the *Medinīkośa* begins by stating, "Bhadra [is used] in the sense of auspicious (*śiva*), the khañjarīṭa bird, a bull (*vṛṣabha*), and a cluster (*kadambaka*)," and continues, "In the neuter, it refers to Maṅgala and musta grass," and finally, "*Cukṣa* likewise [refers to] song, purity (*śuci*), skill (*dakṣa*), as well as constant repetition and that which is pleasing. In the alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), for those who remember You—the crest-jewel of the Vṛṣa lineage, the ornament of the Vṛṣabha clan—that which is to be attained, namely *bhadratva* (auspiciousness) and *vṛṣabhatva* (bullhood), is appropriate. The word division is: *ca*, *ukṣatvam*. (And [there is] the state of being a bull.)

The meaning is that even this attainment of the state of a bull (*ukṣatva*) is appropriate; the sense is that for those who remember the ornament of the Vṛṣabha lineage, this fruit is entirely fitting. Herein lies the correspondence between the remembrance of the crest-jewel of the Vṛṣa clan and the attainment of auspiciousness and so forth.

Just as it is fitting that this cloud (payodhara) should thunder, for it is one whose splendor is unfailing (acyuta-śobhana), which moves through the sky (nabhas-ga), which increases in volume through contact with the wind (sparśana-tas), and which is exceedingly lofty; indeed, it is a "cloud-bearer" (payodhara). [Note: *Acyu-ta* = unfailing; *śobhana* = splendid; *nabhas* = sky; *ga* = moving; *sparśana* = wind/contact; *sphātimān* = possessing expansion/increase. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *karmadhāraya* compound where both members are adjectives (*viśeṣaṇobhayapada-karmadhāraya*): one whose splendor is unfailing (*acyuta-śobha*) and which moves in the sky (*nabhas-ga*). Or, it may mean that which moves through the sky whose splendor is unfailing (*acyuta-śobham nabhas tad-gacchati*). It possesses expansion through contact with the wind (*māruta*). Thus, it is rightly called a "cloud-bearer" (*payodhara*). 1318.

In the word *sparśanataḥ*, because the letter *s* is a *kharpara* (a consonant not followed by a vowel), the elision of the final *visarga* of the word *nabhoga* is to be desired, even when there is a different meaning, for the sake of phonetic similarity (*śabdasārūpya*). The same applies to the word *śrīstanati*. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows]: *acyuta* refers to the Blessed Lord; that which possesses beautiful enjoyment (*bhoga*) is thus described. The term *sparśana* means "touching" or "contemplation" (*avamarśa*). From that [comes] *tataḥ*; here the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).

Alternatively, during that occasion of beautiful enjoyment of pleasures, he becomes "sphātimān"—meaning swollen—due to the touch or contact [of her]. According to Amara, "sphāti" means growth. He is thus described as one whose splendor (*śrī*) is exceedingly elevated. It is fitting that the king of clouds (*ghanāghanarāṭ*), the rain-bearing cloud of the monsoon, should thunder or roar; for indeed, this "payodhara" (cloud/breast) is full of water. In the other sense (the metaphorical), it is fitting that he who is exceedingly elevated should "śrīstanati," meaning he acts like the breast of Śrī (Lakṣmī).

For indeed, this cloud is full of milk; here, there is a correspondence between the king of the thick clouds—who performs the action of being like breasts as determined by the identification with the distinct roar expressed by the word "thundering"—and the [actual] breasts. This is a figure mixed with simile (upamā).
O Purifier, that a man has failed to obtain the hardship of serving your lotus feet is indeed a hardship ordained by the gods; for this [failure] is indicated by divine tribulation. 1319.

O Purifier! O Blessed One, whose nature is pure according to the saying, "You alone are the purifier of all beings, O delight of the Raghus"! You are the performer of service—that is, the one who practices devotion—to Your lotus feet. [The term] *śramalabdha* means "one who has attained the fruit of labor"; here, as in the case of the expression *tribhuvanavidhātuḥ*, there is a compound with a possessive genitive (*śaiṣika-ṣaṣṭhī*) joined with a word ending in the suffix *-tṛ*. The meaning is: one who possesses the exertion of attending upon the lotus feet of the Blessed One.

"A human being, serving among the ranks of rogues who make their living by gambling, obtains labor; this is appropriate"—this is the apparent contradiction, as it is suggested by the tone (*kāku*) that it is "not appropriate. However, the resolution is through the division of the words: *sevana-kṛcchram-alabdhaḥ*. Among the ranks—that is, the rows—of rogues who make their living by gambling (*devanakṛtām akṣadevinām dhūrtānām*), he has not obtained (*alabdhaḥ*) the labor (*kṛcchram*) of service (*sevanasya*). [The word *sevana* is derived from the root *ṣivu* (to sew) with the suffix *lyuṭ*; *kṛcchra* means suffering or hardship; *alabdhaḥ* is formed from the root *labh* with the suffix *tṛn*.]

He shall not experience the suffering caused by being drawn into the midst of a gang of rogues; for the sense is that such faults do not arise in one who is skillful in serving the lotus-feet of the Blessed One. Here, the avoidance of association with rogue people, brought about by service to the feet of the Blessed One, is appropriate. The specific feature is the blending of the figures of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction) and *yamaka* (chiasmus).

Just as Your divine form was constantly beheld by those [sages] on the mountain Adhityagiri, so too do these [beings] here and in the hereafter bear that very same form which is ever beheld; this is indeed fitting.

O Lord! Those people by whom Your form was perceived—that is, directly realized—on Mount Adhyagiri, those very people always maintain that form of Yours perceived here and in the hereafter. The sense is that this is appropriate because there is no discrepancy between the means and the fruit. In reality, however, the meaning is that they maintain a form perceived here in this world—that is, made manifest and established as sovereign—thereby becoming kings.

The *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *adhyakṣa* may refer to an appointed official (*adhikṛta-puṃs*), or, like its primary meaning, to that which is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, in the phrase "the form ever overseen in the supreme state" (*paratra ca paramapade'pi sadādhyakṣitaṃ rūpam*), the division is *sat-adhyakṣitam*. The term *sat* means "excellent," being endowed with auspicious qualities such as the possession of true desires (*satyakāmatva*). The word *akṣitam* means "unimpaired" or "undecaying" (*akṣīṇa*), derived from the root *kṣi* (to perish) in the passive sense with the suffix *kta*, meaning not diminished by mental affliction (*ādhi*) caused by hunger and other such needs. They bear that natural form described in passages such as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*). As for example: * *adhyakṣo'dhikṛte puṃsi syāt pratyakṣe'bhidheyavat* — *Medinī*. * *paratra ca paramapade'pi sadādhyakṣitaṃ rūpam sat ādhyakṣitam iti cchedaḥ*. * *sat praśastaṃ satyakāmatvādiśubhaguṇavat*. * *ādhinā manovyathayā aśanāyādihetukayā akṣitaṃ akṣīṇaṃ 'kṣi kṣaye' karmaṇi ktaḥ*. * *rūpam 'apahatapāpmā' ityādyuktaṃ svābhāvikaṃ rūpaṃ dadhati*. * *yathāvā*... [as follows].
O Blessed One, since your mind maintains equanimity toward all beings as equal, it regards even that which is hostile toward you with nothing but friendliness. (1321)

O Blessed One! According to the manner expressed in the words, “O Lord of All, the refuge of all, the friend of all; I am equal toward all beings,” your heart—the conscious mind—being devoted to you, that is, possessing affection for you as the friend of all, maintains equanimity and an equal vision toward everything. This is a poetic attribution (*āropa*) of the qualities of a conscious being—such as those mentioned in the phrases “equal toward the parties of friend and foe” and “peaceful and tranquil toward all beings”—to your own heart.

If your mind, which is hostile toward all your friends, should become hostile toward you, it indeed attains a state of opposition—that is, a state of inequality—precisely by being opposed to universal equanimity (*sarvasamatā*). In this context, the phrase "attaining hostility toward him" (referring to *samatā*) also nourishes an extraordinary aesthetic charm; for the word *tāmasa* (dark/obstructive) is the reverse (*pratiloma*) of the word *sama-tā* (equanimity), and its state is "darkness" (*tāmasatā*). Thus, the meaning is that it attains a state of darkness.

Here, there is a fitting conjunction of the attainment of universal equanimity and the passion directed toward one who possesses that universal equanimity on the one hand, and the attainment of a state of darkness (tāmasatva) which is contrary to those two on the other. The specific distinction lies in its structural form as a *mālā* (garland-like series) and its being infused with the figure of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).

All these examples are mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other figures; this, however, is a pure example: "O Omniscient One, you protect the ignorant; O Ocean of the nectar of compassion, you protect me who am pitiable; O Kinsman of the distressed, you protect the wretched—if you do so, O Lotus-eyed One, it is indeed worthy of you. (1322)
All this [praise] culminates equally in mere flattery. As for that which culminates in censure, it is as follows:

"It is fitting that the pursuit of insatiable sense-objects belongs to me, the crest-jewel of the wicked; for even dogs, donkeys, jackals, and the like do not fail to turn away from what is to be abandoned. (1323)
Or as it is said:
"O Lord, has not the cool moon indeed stolen away the pure splendor of your smile? Alas, being devoid of virtuous conduct, it has assumed a nature of darkness; that is only fitting. (1324)

"O Lord! O Blessed One! The cool-rayed moon (Śītalamahas) has stolen away the splendor of your radiant smile and your blossoming prosperity; this is understood. Alas!—this is said in lamentation. Devoid of *śīla* (good conduct), that cool-rayed one has assumed the nature of darkness (*tamassvabhāva*), the nature of the quality of *tamas*. This is fitting; the sense is that it is entirely appropriate for one who steals the splendor of your smile and is devoid of virtuous conduct to be of a dark nature."

The actual state of affairs is that he bore (*babhāra*) that which is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of darkness (*tamas*), namely the total absence of gloom (*timira*). In the alternative sense, the word *śītalamahaḥ*—devoid of the three syllables *hā-śī-la*—bore its own nature, that is, its own existence (*svasattā*), by means of the collection of syllables *tama*. The meaning is that when the collection of syllables *hā-śī-la* is removed, only that much [the word *tamaḥ*] remains. Here, there is a correspondence between the seizing of another’s property and the bearing of the nature of darkness, which culminates in censure.

Just as Milinda, having stolen the gold from your hair, has fallen from his former status—alas, this bee indeed attained the state of a Pulinda, even though he had taken refuge with the foremost of men. The word "O Śrī" is understood through the force of the context. "Milinda" refers both to the bee (*bhramara*) and to the name Milinda; there is an identity between the two. The sense is that the "jātarūpa" (gold) of your "kaca" (hair)—that is, the hair which serves as an ornament—or alternatively, "kaca" is so called because it "shines" (*kaca* in the sense of *dīptau*, with the suffix *pacādyac*). Thus, by stealing the gold of your hair, Milinda has fallen from his original color and rank. For this very bee has indeed become a forest-dweller (*pulinda*), despite having sought shelter with the supreme person. (Note: The commentary explains the pun on *milinda*: the bee is dark-colored due to its blackness, while the king Milinda was likely of fairer complexion; thus, by "stealing" the golden hair-ornaments, the bee has lost its former "color" and become like a dark-skinned forest tribesman.)

"Jātarūpa" means gold of ten colors (*daśavarṇasuvarṇa*). "Kacajāta" refers to that which is produced from hair (*śiroruhaja*), specifically the color blue (*nīlarūpa*); this is the actual state of affairs, because of its theft. Having fallen from the first color—that is, from the Brāhmaṇa caste, and from the first syllable "mi"—he is one who, although having resorted to those elder-born men, the males (the Brāhmaṇas)—this is a compound with a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "even though he has resorted to them. In reality, however, the sense is that he is the "elder-born" (*agraja*)—the first [syllable] in place of the syllable "mi."

"Resorting to the collection of phonemes in the form of *puṃ-puṃ*": the word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The meaning is that not only was the letter *mi* lost at the beginning, but he also resorted to the phoneme *pu*. He attained the state of a *pulinda*, which is a specific tribe of barbarians (*mleccha*); as Amara states: "The varieties [of barbarians] are the Kirātas, Śabaras, and Pulindas—these are the tribes of barbarians. In the alternative sense (the pun), he also attained the status of the word *pulinda*. The author then conjoins another cause for his attainment of this *pulinda*-state with the word *eṣa*.

For indeed, since this Milinda is a *madhupa*—a drinker of intoxicants—it is only fitting that he should attain the state of a *pulinda*; such is the intended meaning. The truth, however, is that he is a "licker of nectar" (*makaranda-lih*). Here, the correspondence between his theft of the gold of his tresses and so forth, and his attainment of the status of a *pulinda*, results ultimately in censure.

O Lord, just as even that which is born from Your mouth—the lotus—has become turbid within due to its hatred for Your feet, and thus became inferior; for one such as this, even the status of an outcaste is fitting.

O Lord, although the lotus (*jalaja*) born from Your own mouth possesses the color of Brahmā (*brahmavarṇa*), the factual state is that it is accompanied by the syllable *ja* in its "mouth-part" (the prefix), due to the identity between word and meaning. Because of the non-difference between *la* and *ḍa*, the term *jalaja* is also perceived as *jaḍaja* ("born of the dull-witted"). Through hatred for Your feet, it attains turbidity—that is, impurity—within the mind; alternatively, the phrase may be split as "not turbid within" (*antarā avilatām*).

That in which the letter *la* has departed is *vila*; that which is not *vila* is *avila*. The state of being so is *avilatā*; [the phrase] "having attained that *avilatā*" means the absence of the letter *la* in the middle. Having approached the one born of the lowest caste—the Śūdra class—as Amara states, "The Vṛṣalas are those born of the lowest [caste],"—in the alternative sense, that which has the final *ja*, the letter *ja*, at its end is thus described. He says "of such a one" (*īdṛkṣasya*) to show that this is not its only result; the meaning is: "of one who hates your feet."

The state of being an outcaste (*antyajatva*) and even being a *caṇḍāla* is entirely appropriate. The underlying sense is based on the statement: "One who constantly hates Viṣṇu should be known as one whose seed is base (*antyaretas*). In the alternative sense (the word-play), the meaning is: "the state of having its final letter as *ja*" (*antyajatvam*), referring to the word *jalaja* (lotus), since its last letter is indeed the letter *ja*. This is because, in this context, the words *jaghanyaja* (born from the lowest part) and *antyaja* (last-born) possess identical meanings.
Here, the connection between the hatred of the title "Lord" (*bhagavatpada*) and such states as being born from the lowest part results in censure.

O best of the Raghus, it was indeed fitting that Airāvaṇa, having attained the state of being "devoid of enemies" (arahita) through your supreme glories, became known as Rāvaṇa—this being the very opposite of your enemy. 1327.

O best of the Raghus! Airāvaṇa, the elephant Airāvata, having encountered and attained hostility (*ahitatvam*)—that is, opposition—due to the whiteness of your pre-eminent and most excellent glories, attained the state of being Rāvaṇa. In the alternative sense, the word *airāvaṇa* is a compound consisting of *agrairahitatvam*. Having attained the state of being devoid of the first letter *ai*, it attained the state of being *rāvaṇa*; that is to say, it was thus formed.

This is fitting for this Airāvata, who is hostile toward you—that is, who possesses hatred directed at your very substance. Herein lies the correspondence between Raghuvara’s [Rāma’s] acquisition of the state of Rāvaṇa (the one who roars with hatred) and his hatred for the fame of the best of the Raghus. Or, for example:

"O Jewel of the Mountain of Serpents (Śeṣa), that which is a hell (niraya) regarding you is obtained by him; for he who hates you is certainly a hell (naraka) himself—this is indeed appropriate. (1328)

That which is *niraya* regarding you—meaning one who has departed from *niraya*; according to Amara, “*niraya* is a fate (*vidhi*) that brings misfortune (*ayaḥ śubhāvahaḥ*). The compound is formed by the rule “*nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā*” (compounds beginning with *nir-* take the fifth case when meaning ‘departed from,’ etc.). The sense is: he is devoid of the auspicious rite (*śubhāvahavidhi*) consisting of your worship, which is enjoined as a necessary duty by the statement, “There is no Vedic act more meritorious than the propitiation of Viṣṇu. By that [deprivation], *niraya*—that is, hell—is attained. That hell is a *kutsita-nara* (a contemptible man); the suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of contempt (*kutsāyām*).

"One who hates you"—here the suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), and by the rule "na loka" (Pāṇini 2.3.69), the genitive case is prohibited. For this man, hell (*naraka*)—that is, the abyss (*niraya*)—is "fixed," meaning it will certainly come to pass. Here, there is a correspondence between the lack of service to the Blessed One and the attainment of hell, as well as between the hatred for Him and the reaching of that infernal state. The distinction here is that this is of the form of a "garland" (*mālā*). However, its ultimate purpose is censure, just as in the previous examples. Among these illustrations, the first is mixed with a simile (*dṛṣṭānta*), while the others are mixed with puns (*śleṣa*) and other figures; this is the distinction.
The second [type of] similarity is that which consists in the resemblance of the effect to its cause.

The similarity (*sārūpya*) of the effect with its cause is also the ornament of "Equalization" (*samālaṃkāra*).
