Here, there is a correspondence (*anurūpya*) regarding the connection characterized by origination. And that [correspondence] is twofold: through the production of an effect possessing qualities identical to those of the cause, and through the production of qualities corresponding to the nature of the object with which [the cause] was in contact. This is the counterpart to the second type of "Incongruity" (*viṣama*).
Among these, the first is as follows:

"O Lord of the Hill of Serpents, the Gaṅgā, having attained union with the Sun (or: having become the wife of Sūrya), is enriched with lines of wheels, lotuses, and fish; this is fitting for her who has arisen from Your feet. (1329)

Regarding the term *gaṅgā*, it is so called because she has performed (*kṛta*) an embrace (*śleṣa*), that is, a union (*saṃsarga*), with the Kālindī, who is born of the Sun (*sūryabhavā*). Regarding the side of the Blessed One’s feet (*bhagavaccaraṇapakṣe*), however, it should be construed as: by whom the non-existence of bondage (*abhavāśleṣa*)—the absence of connection to worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)—has been brought about for the wise (*sūrīṇām*, i.e., the learned). She is enriched (*āḍhyā*) by the lines (*rekhā*) or rows (*paṅkti*) of *cakrāḥ* (ruddy geese), *abjāni* (lotuses), and *matsyāḥ* (fishes).

In the other case [the feet], she is enriched by the lines in the form of the discus (*cakra*, the Sudarśana), the conch (*abja*, the Śaṅkha), the lotus (*abja*, or alternatively the lotus itself), and the fish (*matsya*).

Just as the daughter of the ocean-king, the profound abode of Śrī and your beloved, appropriately bestows upon the virtuous the wealth consisting of elephants, horses, cows, jewels, and the like. (1330)

Elephants, horses, cows, and jewels—namely Airāvata, Uccaiḥśravas, the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), and the thought-gem (Cintāmaṇi)—elsewhere refer only to actual elephants and so forth. When the gods (sumanas) flee, [the earth] trembles. Here, in these two examples, the similarity between the effects—the Gaṅgā and Lakṣmī—and their causes—the two oceans that are the Lord’s feet—is accomplished through a superimposition of non-difference based on paronomasia (śleṣa). In both cases, the correspondence of the relation of "origination" (utpatti-lakṣaṇa-saṃsarga) is stated by means of the production of an effect from a cause possessing qualities identical to its own. As for example: [The text continues with further examples.]
The ocean gave birth to you and to poison, both of which have brought the world to a swoon; for now, this world has indeed become full of poison, having grown from the offspring of Sagara.

The *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *śrī* [denotes] dressing, beauty, prosperity, and straight trees; [it also denotes] speech, Lakṣmī, cloves, poison, and the *bilva* fruit. The ocean (*jaladhi*) brought forth you—who are designated by the word *śrī*, which is a synonym for poison—as well as poison (*viṣa*), also known as *garala*. By both of these—by you and by poison—the world was rendered unconscious, deluded, and deprived of its senses. In the case of the *śrī* [meaning Lakṣmī], the literal meaning is that [the world] was pervaded by you and by Viṣṇu, according to the manner stated in the verse: "O Mother, [the world is pervaded] by you and by Viṣṇu."

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The term *saṃmūrchana* denotes pervasion, as well as height and delusion. This production of such objects by the ocean is now appropriate. For [the word] is to be split as *sa garajātasamvṛddhaḥ*; the construction is *so 'yam*. That aforementioned ocean has been nourished (*saṃvardhita*) by a mass of poison (*garajāta*), meaning it consists of poison and abounds in venom. Therefore, the sense is that the production of things denoted by the word *śrī*, which is another name for poison, from this ocean is fitting.

In reality, however, *sagareti* is a single, inseparable word. It means "increased by those born of Sagara," that is, by the sons of Sagara; [the ocean is] "consisting of poison" (*viṣamaya*), which signifies "consisting of water" (*jalamaya*). Here too, there is a similarity between the cause (the ocean) and the two effects (Śrī and poison), a majesty attained through *śleṣa* (paronomasia). The distinction is this: while the two previous examples culminate in praise, this one culminates in censure.
Thus, just as in the first variety of *samālaṃkāra*, it should be understood that here too a twofold division occurs, characterized by its culmination in either praise or censure.

In the second type of "Equal Radiance" (*samaprabheda*), the second example is as follows: "The crest-ornament fashioned from camphor powder upon your lotus-like face, so enchanting, dispels my fever and bestows fragrance; this is indeed fitting. (1332)
*Kamalāmanoharā* is a vocative address. The word *lalāma*, ending in the letter *n*, is neuter in gender, according to the grammatical rule: "Both *lalāmaṃ* and *lalāma* [are used]."

That the heart of the Lord of the Añjana Mountain—smoothened by the spreading luster of the Kaustubha gem and deeply reddened by the lac-dye from Kamalā’s feet—delights my mind, is indeed fitting. 1333.

It delights, reddens, and gladdens. In the first example cited here, there is a correspondence between the contact with the cool, fragrant, and thick sandalwood tilaka-mark upon the Blessed One’s face and the two effects produced: the dispelling of heat and the arising of fragrance. In the subsequent example, there is a correspondence between the contact with the luster of the Kaustubha gem and other ornaments upon the Blessed One’s chest and the effect produced, which is the delighting of the mind.

O daughter of the nectar-ocean, it is only fitting that you— who were born together with the Hālāhala poison and who entered the hearts of both the serpent-king and the Lord of Mountains— should always be carried by him whom you serve.

The actual state of affairs is that [the mountain] is the heart, the interior, and the chest of the Lord of the Earth who is like a serpent, the sovereign king of serpents, the Lord of Śeṣācala; yet it serves him, drinks from him, and worships him; it faints and swoons, attaining a mental agitation rooted in his sovereignty. The rest is clear. The distinction from the two previous examples is as before: those two culminated in praise, whereas this one culminates in censure.

Thus, the summary is as follows: in the three examples of the first variety of the second type of *samaviśeṣa* (such as "embraced by one born of the sun" and so forth), there is a conformity of the effect to the nature of its cause; whereas in the three examples of the second variety (such as "the powder of camphor" and so forth), there is a conformity to the connection with adventitious factors such as camphor.
Whatever effort is extended for the sake of accomplishing a desired goal, and which is equal to the third [alternative], its accomplishment without anything undesirable is called "equal" (sama).

The meaning is that *samālaṃkāra* (the figure of Equalization) consists in the correspondence between the effort exerted for the sake of attaining some desired object and the resulting attainment of that very object, occurring without the occurrence of anything undesired. However, when there is the attainment of another, more intense desired object, that will be called *praharṣaṇa* (Joy). This third type of *sama* is the opposite even of the threefold *viṣama* (Incongruity) summarized as "the attainment of the undesired despite an effort toward a desired object," because here there is the attainment of the desired and no occurrence of the undesired.

Just as one who has served the moon at night, though it is dark, may continue to serve it incessantly even by day, so too, having attained the nature of divine vision through you, one rejoices while experiencing their desired object.

He rejoices incessantly—even in the absence of night; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of the absence of the object [of the word *niśā*]. That moon is Śrīnivāsa, the Moon; such is the truth. To serve that [moon], he resorts to the blue lotus (*indīvara*) at night; the meaning is that because night is the time for the practice of yoga, he worships the moon then. His being the essence of your divine vision—meaning his being the form of your beautiful eyes, or his being the essence of uncontracted knowledge regarding you—is understood to be his perfectly pure nature.

Having attained its desired object—the cherished goal consisting of the constant attendance upon the moon—it experiences that very object. Herein, even during a state when night is absent, because the blue lotus achieves its fulfillment through a cause characterized by worship performed at night for the sake of obtaining the desired object defined as attendance upon the moon, there is a correspondence characterized by *sasaṃsarga* (conjunction) due to the arising of that [fulfillment] without any undesirable consequence.

O Mother, just as the lotus, though constantly longing for the glory of being grasped by the hand of Hari, attained that very thing only after performing penance in the waters facing Hari, so too did it obtain birth from Your hand.

[The verse] conveys the glory of being grasped by the hand of Hari, the excellence of being taken by the hand of the Lord, and the intensity of contact with the rays of the sun; it brings [the lotus] toward the Lord and toward the sun. That very same thing—the glory of being constantly grasped by the hand of Hari—is shown here as well: for the sake of attaining the desired object characterized by the perpetual grasping of Hari’s hand, the attainment of that [glory] is demonstrated for the lotus, which was performing penance facing Hari, even without any undesirable circumstance in another birth.

O Mother, it is fitting that the jar of nectar, which exists in your breasts, is called "Sukala" (one who possesses beautiful digits), for it is capable of giving various enjoyments according to one's wealth, while itself remaining full of manifold desires even as it enjoys them. || 1337 ||

O Mother! He who, though possessing a jar of nectar—a vessel of immortality (and by the word *sudhākalaśa*, even when there is *vibhava*, meaning on the occasion of sovereign power)—is one whose manifold hopes and extended cravings (*āyatatarṣṇā*) persist to give enjoyments to the Lord of the World, the Blessed One, or even to enjoy them himself; [in the alternative sense] he is one whose various forms of fear (*vidhāśas*) have departed (*vigata-dhā-kāra-śaka*).

Born from your breasts, he became *sukala*—one who possesses both renunciation and enjoyment in accordance with his desires (according to Amara: *sukala* means "a donor and an enjoyer"). The actual fact is that by the removal of the letter *dhā*, the word *sukala* was produced. Here, the nectar-jar (*sudhākalaśa*) attains its desired object without any undesirable consequence. Or as another example:

Desiring birth from your breasts, the Kulācala mountain remained engaged in penance, enduring cold and heat; by fondling itself [as if it were] your lotus-like breasts, it attained the state of being a *kucata* (breast). (1338)

O Kamalā! This Kulācala (the mountain of your lineage) stands performing penance (*tapas*) because it desires to be born from your breasts; that is, it is engaged in ascetic practice—implying, in one sense, the month of Māgha and the winter season, and in another, standing firm during the heat of summer (*tapa*), remaining motionless or situated in the sunlight. For a Kulācala does not become unstable due to the passage of time.

Therefore, having endured cold, wind, and heat—enduring the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) according to the method described in such passages as "in summer becoming one who performs the five-fire penance (*pañcatapas*), and in the rains a sage [who endures] the downpour"—he is, in the alternative sense, naturally enduring cold and the like; for a mountain does not tremble from cold or wind, nor does it wither from heat. He states the fruit of his asceticism (*tapas*) with the word "kucatām" (may they be crushed).

"Lālayan" means delighting or sporting with one's own self, the inner self, the Blessed Lord; from the root *laḍ* (to sport), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is applied according to the rule "lakṣaṇahetvoḥ". Here, "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the result. The meaning is: for the sake of pleasing his own inner self. In that context, "kucatām agāt" means he descended into the state of being breasts. In the alternative sense, the word *kulācala* is to be split as *kamale alālayan*.

"Alālayan" means making one's own self—that is, one's own form—"alāla. "Alāla" refers to that which has no "lā" (the letter *la*) or "la" (the letter *la*); thus, performing in such a way—making it devoid of the two syllables "lā" and "la"—it attained the state of being "kuca," that is, the word "kuca. The sense is that according to the stated method, when the letters *lā* and *la* are absent, only "kuca" remains. Herein, the Kulācala mountain achieves its desired object without any undesirable consequence.

Just as one who, desiring to become the mere remnant of the fruit of Śrī’s breasts, renounces the enjoyment of dry meat, yet does not abandon for his own sake the pure *mālūra* fruit when it remains as a remnant of the *mā* fruit—[the *mālūra* being the *bilva* fruit, according to Amara: "The *bilva*, *śāṇḍilya*, *śailūṣa*, *mālūra*, and *śrīphala* are synonyms"].

The two breasts of Śrī are indeed the fruits; their state of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) consists in their being of the nature of that which is to be accepted (*upādeya-svarūpatva*) through the desire to achieve excellence over them. The "enjoyment" (*vallūra*)—meaning consumption—is the eating of dried meat (*śuṣka-māṃsa*). As Amara states: "That which is roasted and dried is *vallūra*; it has three genders. The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the action (*bhāve*) to the root *bhuj*, resulting in the substitution of *ku* for the *j* according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*. Hemacandra states: "Bhoga [is used] in the senses of kingdom, maintenance of a courtesan, happiness, wealth, the body of a serpent, its hood, protection, and consumption."

He was a renouncer, characterized by the abandonment of all forbidden foods, such as dried meat (*vallūra*); the sense is that without purity of food, there can be no arising of purity of being (*sattva*). Therefore, he was pure, faultless, or holy. Consequently, he became the "remnant" (*śeṣa*) of the fruits of *māyā*—that is, of the two breasts, which are metaphorically determined to be the very fruit of *māyā* (or *śrī*, Fortune)—meaning he became their residual essence and the source of their excellence, thereby attaining the status of being the desired remnant for himself.

The meaning is that it never abandons its own purpose (*svartha*), its own human goal (*svakīya-puruṣārtha*); rather, being eternally subordinate (*nityaśeṣa*), it experiences service to Him. In the alternative sense (the word-play), the term is *mālūraphalam*. Here, there is identity between the word and its meaning. It is "desirous of attaining the status of being subordinate to the fruit of Śrī’s breasts" (*śrīkucaphalaśeṣatvaprepsāvat*). The analysis of the compound is: "one who has abandoned the enjoyment of the *lū* sounds. Being characterized by the aforementioned desire, it is "one who has completely abandoned the enjoyment"—that is, the experience—of the *lū* sounds, namely the letter *lū* and the letter *ra*. The sense is that it has dispelled the *lū* and the *ra*.

Therefore, it is pure and absolute; as the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *śuddha* means 'absolute' in three senses: that which is flawless, that which is pure, and that which is such-and-such. It does not abandon its own meaning—the form of the *śrīphala* (bilva fruit)—which is described as having the three remaining letters, namely *mā*, *pha*, and *lā*, as its residual or final components. The phrase "even such as this" (*īdṛśam api*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. It does not forsake its own referent, the form of the auspicious fruit.

The word *mālūraphalam*, which conveys a certain meaning with its complete phonemes (*avikalavarṇa*), conveys that very same meaning even when there is a deficiency of phonemes according to the method described above. The point is that the words *mālūraphala* and *āphala* have the same referent (*ekārthakatva*). *Māphala* means *śrīphala* (the auspicious fruit). Furthermore, the status of the *bilva* as the *śrīphala* is established by scripture (*śruti*) in the passage, "O Vanaspati, you are the tree, namely the *bilva*," and is also established by the cited lexicon (*kośa*).

Regarding the word *śeṣa* here: it is called *śeṣa* because "it remains" (*śiṣyate*), derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). For this very reason, it possesses all genders (*bhedyaliṅgatā*). If the suffix *ghañ* were used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), there would be a restriction to the masculine gender alone. Therefore, the *Mahābhāṣya* states: "It continues as a relation. This is consistent with usages such as *śeṣaṃ rāmavat*, as well as with lexicographical works like the *Medinīkośa*, which begins with "The word *śeṣa* [is used] in the sense of Saṃkarṣaṇa and in the sense of remainder (*vadha*)" and concludes with "In other senses, it is not feminine. In this instance, the desired goal is achieved without any undesirable obstacle, like the fruit of the *mālūra* tree.
All of these are examples of the attainment of a purely desired object without anything undesirable.
The attainment of the desired through the avoidance of the undesired is as follows:
O Viṣṇu, the cloud that causes hatred toward Your glory, by shaking off its dense sins while falling headlong at Your feet, has become a cloud that possesses no sin.

O Viṣṇu! [The cloud] is a "ghanāghana," a rain-cloud of the monsoon; it harbors enmity toward your splendor (*śrī*), prosperity, and radiance. Shaking off—by means of that enmity directed at your splendor—the state of being a "ghanāgha," which consists of being burdened with incessant sin (the suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of "cause" according to Pāṇini 3.2.126; here "cause" means "result"; thus, the meaning is "for the purpose of shaking off the state of being a ghanāgha"), it falls headlong—that is, prostrating itself—at your feet, O Viṣṇu; for "Viṣṇu’s feet" refers to the truth that they are the celestial firmament. (Note: The term *ghanāgha* is a *karmadhāraya* compound: *ghana* meaning "dense" or "incessant," and *agha* meaning "sin" or "evil.")

*Ghanāgha* means that which is both dense (*ghana*) and evil (*agha*). One who does not possess such density of evil is *naghanāgha*; here, the negative particle *na-* forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound. He became so; the meaning is that he became one whose every impurity was cast away. "By suddenly prostrating before Kṛṣṇa upon the dusty ground, one becomes instantly free from stain through the decoration of dust upon the forehead."
O Vraja, avoid and shun that man who bows down in truth to Hari, whose lotus feet are worshipped by hosts of immortals,
for he is freed from all bonds of sin, like a fire drenched with clarified butter.

Thousands of such scriptural authorities (*pramāṇa*) are to be remembered. Regarding the term *ghanāghana* in this context, the analysis (*cheda*) is: "shaking the state of being a *ghanāghana*," that is, shaking the sequence of syllables *ghanāgha* which denotes intoxication; the meaning is "without even emitting [it]. "Falling head-first" means standing in a reverse order. Thus, the form *naghanāgha* is produced. Herein, there is the attainment of the desired end (*iṣṭasiddhi*), which consists in the removal of an undesirable state—the form *ghanāgha*—without the occurrence of an undesirable event for the *ghanāghana*.

O Hari, just as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) removes the fall from the bond of its own flowers for those who always serve it with good intent, so too does it remove that [fall] once they have attained the state of being your arms; what is appropriate is that which you do.

O hare! The wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru) always [prevents] the downward fall—meaning a fall into the lower world or a slipping toward the ground—from those who serve its own self: namely, from the wise ones (sumanas) who possess good minds, and from the flowers (sumanas). This is because of the connection to the bond of production (prasavabandhana), which refers both to the connection with birth in various wombs (*nānāyoni*) and to the stalk (*vṛnta*). As Amara states: "The stalk is the bond of production. (Amara-kośa 2.4.16)

To take away—that is, to dispel—your state of being an arm and your manifold forms, it is fitting that [the Kalpavṛkṣa] should remove the downward fall from the bond of the blossoms of those flowers (*sumanasaḥ*). Here, because of the exertion toward a desired end characterized by the avoidance of an undesirable result—namely, the downward fall from the bond of the blossoms of those flowers—the accomplishment of that [desired end] occurs without any undesirable consequence for the Kalpavṛkṣa. All these examples are indeed intermingled with the identification of non-difference through *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Furthermore, even in cases where there is the presence of an unexpectedly intense undesirable meaning, the figure of speech *samā* (similarity) is not obstructed if the intended meaning is understood through the power of *śleṣa* (punning). For example:

"O Lord, do not extend [the word] *muktamā* (freedom from pride) to me who am deluded by the power of Śrī; you served me, and you likewise act toward me as one who has extended [the word] *muktamā* (freedom from pride). (1342)

O Blessed One! You are one whose "vyāma"—defined by Amara as "the horizontal distance between the two outstretched arms" (*vyāmo bāhvossakarayostatayostiryagantaram*)—is "under the sway of Śrī" (*śrīvaśaga*), meaning that the space between his arms, extended on either side for the purpose of embracing as far as possible, is subject to the power of Lakṣmī. By this, it is illuminated that, through the strength of his presence in human form, you have disregarded the offenses of even those who are humble, and thus manifest a readiness to protect them.

Do not [say] "mā" to me, for since the substitution of "mā" is optional in cases where there is no subsequent reference (ananvādeśa), the form "mā" is used here. "Ātanu" means "make loose," that is, loosen the bond of worldly existence (*bhavabandha*). Alternatively, it refers to the delusion (*vyāmoha*)—an excessive state of mental distraction—rooted in wealth and under the sway of fortune (*śrīvaśaga*). Or rather, "O you who are under the sway of fortune" (*śrīvaśaga*) is an address to the Blessed One himself. Regarding "delusion" (*vyāmoha*), which is the infatuation caused by children, wife, wealth, and so forth: "āmukta" means "bound" (as Amara states: *āmuktaḥ pratimuktaśca*). Therefore, "mā tanu" means "do not make [it]."

This word is *mā*, not the prohibitive particle *māṅ*, which would have required the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. Thus, "you have served me" (*tvām āseve*) means that you, acting toward me as I have described, manifest yourself in exactly that way; this is a praise. Alternatively, "do not manifest me as bound" (*mā mām āmuktam*) refers to the delusion of being under the power of Śrī; this is a reproach.

This is the speech of reproach directed at You by a certain *prapanna* who, while serving Śrīnivāsa with the desire to attain liberation, recognizes that even the incidental worldly and otherworldly prosperity bestowed by Him has become an obstacle to that very goal. Here, although it might appear to be the figure of speech *viṣama* (incongruity) when there is an intention to express censure through praise in the form of *vyājastuti* (feigned praise), [the actual intent is as stated].

Nor should it be argued that this is not the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous) because worldly and otherworldly prosperity cannot be considered undesirable; for from the perspective of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), such prosperity is indeed undesirable, as stated in the words: "These, O dear one, are indeed hells compared to the abode of the Supreme Self. By this statement, since even otherworldly wealth is described as being like hell, the fact that worldly wealth is likewise [undesirable] is established by the logic of *kaimutya* (how much more so). Nevertheless, when the primary intended meaning (*vivakṣā*) is the praise expressed on the literal level (*vācya*), the figure of speech *sama* (the equalizing) is not precluded.

Thinking, "May I attain a state of prosperity that is utterly beyond description," I have taken refuge in you; yet, O Acyuta, the very prosperity bestowed by you is likewise utterly beyond description. (1343) "Utterly beyond description" (*sutarām uktividūrā*) means being outside the range of words, according to the scriptural teaching: "From whence words turn back. "Prosperity" (*saṃpat*) here refers to the hope that one might attain the sovereignty of liberation. The praise is this: thinking, "I have taken refuge in you with the expectation that such prosperity might be mine," you yourself have granted me a prosperity that is just as utterly beyond description.

The reproach is that prosperity which appears as exceedingly beautiful (*sutarām śobhanataratvena*) is far removed from liberation (*muktividūrā*), being distant from *mokṣa*. As it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "One who is attached to worldly wealth and well-being does not attain the supreme good," thus worldly prosperity is distant from liberation. Here, too, everything should be understood in the same manner as in the previous example.
O lotus-eyed one, just as I have always sought refuge in you with the thought, "May I be an eater of food," so too have you now, out of compassion, indeed made me an eater of food.

This is a statement of reproach, couched as a feigned praise, directed toward the Lord by a certain *prapanna* who—out of haste to attain the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and loathing even the experience of enjoying the fruits of commenced karma (*prārabdhakarman*)—finds the Lord experiencing worldly enjoyments exactly as before, even after his surrender.

For instance, O lotus-eyed one! the intention is that [the Lord] desires to attain the sovereignty of liberation, which consists of the bliss of experiencing the perfect Supreme Brahman, in order to ordain the singing of the *Sāman* according to the sequence stated in the Śruti—beginning with "He remains singing this Sāman" and continuing with "I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food"—by means of the chant "I am the eater of food. Regarding the two words "I" (*aham*) and "eater of food" (*annādaḥ*) found in the Śruti, the meaning is: "I" refers to the Supreme Self who has my body, and "eater of food" refers to Him who has the bodies of all enjoyers.

The commentary on that [verse] states: "The word 'I' (aham) culminates in the Supreme Self; likewise, the words 'food' (anna) and 'eater of food' (annāda), which denote the objects of enjoyment and the enjoyer, also culminate in Him. "I have come to You for refuge; I have surrendered myself. By Your grace, You have now—this very moment—acted in such a way that I have been made truly an eater of food, just as I requested. This is the first-person singular perfect form (*luṅ*) of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) used in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the past tense (*bhūta*). Alternatively, the construction may be read as "akāriṣi sāṃpratam," meaning "You have acted appropriately at this time. In that case, the sense is that what has been done is now fitting.

The *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *sāṃpratam* may mean 'now' (*adhuna*) or 'proper' (*yukta*). The particle *kila* is used here either to express probability or conciliation; as the *Viśvakośa* says: "The word *kila* is used in the sense of report (*vārtā*), probability (*saṃbhāvyā*), and conciliation (*anunaya*). Every point established here is intended for praise. The reproach is this: you were made merely an "eater of food" (*annāda*), a consumer of ordinary rice-mess (*odana*), and not one who is "free from hunger" (*vijighatsaḥ*)—as described in the Śruti—as devoid of such base qualities as hunger.

In this context, although there exists a powerful undesirable state consisting of worldly enjoyments for the seeker of liberation who has taken refuge, through the power of double entendre (śleṣa), there is the realization of the desired state consisting of the experience of liberated sovereignty.
O descendant of Raghu, just as the night-rangers desired your destruction for their own victory, you too, possessed of noble generosity, granted them that very destruction of the night. 1345.

"For your victory" means for the sake of overcoming those who oppose your deeds; "niśāraṇa" refers to a battle taking place at night. Likewise, "niśāraṇa" may mean a nocturnal battle exactly as desired. However, in reality, the meaning is: "for your victory," that is, for your own triumph consisting of their defeat, you granted the "niśāraṇa"—the destruction—of those night-stalkers (rajanicaras). According to Amara: *pramāpaṇaṃ nivarhaṇaṃ nikāraṇaṃ niśāraṇam*.

Here, although there exists an intense undesirable result in the form of the destruction of the night-stalkers, through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is the attainment of the desired object in the form of a night-battle.

Just as those who, through their defeat by you, desired to attain an immeasurable and desirable state—indeed, it was precisely that immeasurable and desirable state they obtained through their defeat by you (1346). O Blessed One! "Through your defeat" means through the humiliation caused by your actions. "Immeasurable" means unlimited; "desirable state" refers to a condition that is delightful due to its majesty. The same applies to the latter half of the verse. In that context, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the word *tvat* is to be understood as a separate term [meaning "by you"].

"From you"—that is, from defeat by you, which is a humiliation caused by one's own actions—there has been made an "amitā" (unmeasured) condition; that is, a "kanīyasthiti" (inferior state). Because of the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthayostādātmyāt*), the sense is that it is a state that is exceedingly base. The analysis of the compound is: "this is both inferior (*kanīyasī*) and a state (*sthiti*). By applying the suffix *īyasun* to the word *alpa*, the substitution *kan* occurs according to the rule "yuvālpayoḥ kananyatarasyām.

Here, although there exists an intense undesirable state in the form of an "inferior state," through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is the attainment of a desirable state in the form of a "beautiful state."

O Trivikrama, just as Bali performed sacrifices with the thought, "May I attain the status of the Lord of the Gods, or even the netherworld of the serpent Ananta," it was exactly so [attained] by you.

O Trivikrama! This [verse] is intended to manifest the unique nature of His incarnations regarding the subject matter introduced in this stanza. She attained the station of the Lord of the Gods—that is, the abode of Mahendra. The suffix *tṛn* is applied to the root *āp* preceded by *pra*. The particle *api* has the sense of "also. He is both the one who protects sufficiently (*alaṃ-pāt*) and the protector (*rakṣitā*). The suffix *tṛn* is applied to the root *pā*. Bali is the lord of the Daityas. Ananta is the world of those who enjoy the fruits of their respective actions—the best among the "enjoyers" (*bhoginām*)—extending as far as the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), that is, the entire universe (*viṣṭapa*).

Alternatively, "O Infinite One" (*ananta*) is an address to the Blessed Lord himself. The meaning regarding the world of the *bhogins* (enjoyers) has already been stated. Or else, "infinite enjoyment" (*anantabhoga*) refers to the experience of the Blessed Lord; that which possesses this is the "infinite-enjoyer" (*anantabhogī*), and that is the world (*loka*). Or, it means the world of those who possess infinite enjoyment—that is, those endowed with the experience of the Blessed Lord. "Even that" means even Śrī Vaikuṇṭha. "I may find" means "I may attain," while performing sacrifice—meaning while performing the ritual—with you, the one to be propitiated by sacrifice and the bestower of its fruit; such is the sense.

The meaning is that he was granted exactly the fruit according to his desire. In reality, however, although Bali attained the status of the Lord of the Gods, he was made to reach Pātāla—that which is so described as having *ananta* (the infinite) as its *bhogiloka* (world of serpents), that is, a multitude of snakes. Alternatively, if one intends *ananta* as an address to the Blessed One, the meaning is that he was made to reach Pātāla, known by that name, the world of *bhogins* (enjoyers), namely the world of the Nāgas.

In this case, although there exists the occurrence of an intense undesirable result—namely, falling into the netherworld—the attainment of the desired goal, consisting of reaching the worlds of those who have performed infinite merit, is nevertheless established; it should be understood that here the unexpectedness of the intense undesirable result is quite evident.

Even where, despite the presence of the attainment of a desired object, there is the perception of an undesired object that is non-existent due to the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is no impairment to the *samālaṅkāra* (simile), because the perception of the undesired object is merely apparent and does not reach a final conclusion.

Just as he had been told by his guru, who was most earnest in his instructions, that devotion to the Lord must be practiced, he performed that very devotion; yet, he did not transgress his guru’s command in any way whatsoever.

In this context, because he did not transgress the command of his guru under any circumstances, there is the manifestation of the figure of speech *virodhālaṃkāra* (contradiction). Even though there is an intention to employ another form consisting of a division of the three words in the expression *devenabhaktiḥ*, there is also indeed the figure of speech *samālaṃkāra* (simile), by adopting another form that conveys a different meaning through the single word *devenabhaktiḥ*: "devotion to the Lord of the gods (*devānām inaḥ*), the Sovereign (*svāmin*), the Blessed One (*bhagavati*)."
Just as the vow of Jayantī was declared by her father to be "the destruction of what must now be done," the boy acted exactly so; for who indeed would render the command of a father futile? (1349)

In this case as well, by the phrase "who indeed would render the father’s command false?", the figure of speech *virodha* (contradiction) is manifested. Even though there exists an intention to express a different form consisting of a single word in the term *nāśanam*, the figure of *samālaṃkāra* (simile/metaphor) remains entirely intact by resorting to another form that expresses a different factual meaning (*vastu-sad-arthāntara*) through the division of the two words *na* and *aśanam*, signifying: "Eating—that is, taking food—is not to be done; rather, fasting alone is to be observed."

In the previous example, there was the cognition of a non-existent, undesirable meaning through the division of three words, whereas there was the cognition of an existent, desirable meaning as a single word-unity. Here, however, the distinction is that there is the cognition of a non-existent, undesirable meaning as a single word-unity, while there is the cognition of an existent, desirable meaning through the division of two words.

The status of *samālaṅkāra* (the figure of equal pairing) should be understood even from the mere perception of the attainment of an unintended desired object through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), as seen in the previously cited examples such as "to serve him incessantly. By the word *mātra* ("mere"), the perception of an unintended object is excluded. For in those cases, there is merely the attainment of a desired object—such as the service of the moon by the blue lotuses and so forth—through the force of *śleṣa*, and not even the appearance of an unintended one; this is how it should be considered.

Regarding the definition of the figure of speech *viṣama* (the Uneven), where it is stated that "the production of a dissimilar effect from a cause, or the occurrence of something undesirable, as well as a discordant combination, constitute *viṣama*," and subsequently defining the figure *sama* (the Even) as its opposite: by the word "that" (*tat*) in the latter definition, only the final variety of *viṣama*—namely, the one consisting of a discordant combination—is intended, because it is only the opposite of this specific variety that possesses aesthetic charm.

However, the first two types of *bheda* (divergence) are not [included here], because they lack aesthetic charm (*cārutva*); for their causes consist respectively in the production of an effect contrary to its cause and the attainment of a desired object, both of which are established as actual facts (*vastu-siddha*). Thus, the figure of speech *samālaṃkāra* consists solely of a corresponding arrangement (*anurūpa-saṃghaṭanā*), and not, like the *viṣamālaṃkāra*, of three types of divergence; so it has been stated by the author of the *Alaṃkārasarvasva*.

That is not so; for even when cause and effect are inherently dissimilar, by means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other devices, their identity of attributes can be established to describe their conformity. Furthermore, even when something inherently undesirable is rendered identical with the desirable through that very same means, the description of the attainment of the desirable is shown here to possess aesthetic charm. Therefore, although it is "Equal" (*sama*), it is indeed threefold, appearing as if "Unequal" (*viṣama*).
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the Section on Simile (Samālaṅkāra), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Section on the *Vicitra* Ornament:
"If, for the sake of attaining a desired object, one should perform an action contrary to that [usual means], the wise call this the *Vicitra* ornament."

If an effort contrary to [the means for] some desired result were to be made, that constitutes the figure of speech *vicitrā* (the wonderful). This amounts to the performance of an action contrary to what is intended. Furthermore, "contrariety" (*viparītatva*) here signifies opposition (*pratikūlatva*).
Or rather,

O Hari, alas, you dwell upon the peak of the mountain of the serpent-king— a place difficult of access— even in order to rescue those submerged in the depths of the ocean of existence and lead them to the auspicious, excellent path.

*Suga* means "one goes easily here"; the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* by the rule *suduroradhikaraṇe*. *Supanthān* means "an excellent path"; the prohibition of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied by the rule *na pūjanāt*. *Durga* means "one goes with difficulty here."

In this context, with a view toward the fruit of rescuing people submerged in the depths of the ocean of existence—which is exceedingly low—and leading them to the excellent path, there is a description of an opposite effort consisting of remaining in a place that is difficult to reach, situated on the peak of a mountain abounding in high-rising serpents; the reality is that you practice dwelling upon the summit of the Śeṣa-mountain.

O Kṛṣṇa! In order to disregard the endless and insurmountable attachment to objects of enjoyment that ought to be abandoned, the virtuous worship you—who, alas, perform your dance even amidst those very objects of enjoyment that are to be shunned. O Kṛṣṇa! The virtuous worship you, who have performed your dance (i.e., are deeply attached) precisely to those objects of enjoyment that are to be abandoned—in other words, who are intensely immersed in them—in order to cast aside the contact with such objects of enjoyment that must be renounced. The word "alas" (hanta) expresses wonder.

In reality, however, the word *āheya* is to be split [as *ā-heya*]. *Āheya* means "born of a serpent" (*ahi-bhava*). "Dance performed there" refers to the dancing performed upon the hoods (*phaṇa*) of the serpent Kāliya. Regarding the term *āheya*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied to the word *ahi* in the sense of "originating from" according to the rule: *dṛtikukṣikalaśivastyastyaherḍhañ*. Here, with the aim of disregarding the contact with the body (*bhoga*) that is to be abandoned (*heya*), an effort characterized by the worship of the dancing performed upon that very body—which is the opposite of what is to be abandoned—is composed. Generally, the life-force (*jīvātu*) of this verse consists in the superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) based on paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
O Śrīnivāsa, it is no wonder to anyone that men climb the ridges of the winding mountain in order to descend from the peak of the mountain that bears the curved earth. 1352.

To descend from that mountain peak which is *vṛjina*—meaning crooked; or, in the alternative sense, *vṛjina* meaning sin itself, which is the "peak" (*dharādhara-śikhara*) [of the mountain of worldly existence]—such is the meaning. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *vṛjina* is neuter in the sense of impurity or sin, and masculine in the sense of hair; it is used in three genders when meaning 'crooked'. The actual state of affairs is that the edge or summit (*añcala*) of the mountain (*dharādhara*), which moves crookedly (*jihmaga*), refers to the peak of Śeṣācala. Amara states: "The words *arāla*, *vṛjina*, and *jihma* [all mean 'crooked']."

In this case, with the aim of the result characterized by descending from the peak of a mountain of crookedness, there is an effort consisting of ascending the summit of a mountain of crookedness, which is the opposite of that [result].

Just as sages, having restrained all their faculties, seek refuge in the Goddess Durgā when they must traverse difficult terrains—such as the inaccessible peaks of mountain ranges and formidable passes—so too do they seek refuge in the Divine (Daiva) when facing hardships and the hells. Regarding "difficult terrains" (*durgāṇi*): these refer to places that are hard to access due to mountains and the like, as well as miserable states and hells. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *durgā* refers to Gaurī and Kālī; *durga* refers to hell and a fortress; it also denotes a place on a mountain or similar inaccessible spot, and in three genders it means 'unassailable'. Another lexicon states: "*Durga* refers to hell and hardship. *Note on orthography:* The term *durgāṇi* is used here as a masculine plural form of *durga*, following the usage in the cited lexicographical sources. In standard Sanskrit, the feminine noun *durgā* would typically take the neuter plural *durgāṇi* when referring to places. However, the provided text uses the masculine form, which is consistent with the definitions given in the *Ratnamālā* and other cited authorities. The translation reflects the source text's specific phrasing.

There are also such usages as: "May everyone cross over all difficulties; may you quickly transcend these hardships. In these instances, there is a description of an effort characterized by taking refuge in a person situated in a difficult place—the very opposite of those difficulties—with the aim of the result consisting of crossing over those difficulties.
Or, for example:
O Śrī Paribṛḍha, the virtuous person who relies upon Your compassion for the sake of the protective glance that pacifies evil performs a wondrous feat: the very pacification of evil itself. (1354)

O Śrīparibṛḍha! A virtuous person is one who takes refuge in Your grace; whereas a "sinful" one—meaning a cruel one—is *śamana*, that is, Yama (as the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *śamana* is neuter in the sense of peace or killing, and masculine in the sense of Vaivasvata [Yama]"). For the sake of "obscuring the sight of him"—the sense being: "May I never have to behold Yama"—it is indeed strange that such a person regards and serves *pāpaśamana* alone, which is to say, the cruel Yama himself. However, the reality is that he actually spreads the pacification (*śānti*) of his own misdeeds.

In this case as well, everything is exactly as before. By the word "vicitram" (variegated), there is also an indication of the name of the figure of speech under discussion; thus, the distinction is that it is headed by the figure of speech called *mudrā*, which will be discussed later.
Or for example:

"O Leader of the family of the non-cool-rayed one (the Sun)! Alas, you who are possessed of policy, in order to personally seize the royal fortune (*rājyaśrī*) of the night-stalkers (*niśicara*), you instead gave that very same royal fortune to the younger brother of the night-stalkers (*yāminīcarakanīyasa*). (1355) O Leader of the family of the non-cool-rayed one! To seize the royal fortune—the prosperity—of the night-stalkers; in the alternative sense, the lack of fortune (*aśriyam*) belonging to the row of night-stalkers (*niśicara-rājeḥ paṅkteḥ*), namely the indecorousness resulting from being protected by the arms of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa)—to seize that very same royal fortune of the night-stalkers, you gave it to Vibhīṣaṇa, the younger brother of the night-stalkers. The rest is clear.

In this case, with respect to the result characterized by the seizing of the glory of the kingdom of the night-stalkers, there is an effort consisting of the giving of that very thing, which is the opposite of [the usual course].

O Lord of the Golden Mountain, whose majesty is eternal, may my mind always strive to diminish its excessive attachment to rebirth—this attachment to rebirth which, though sinless, finds delight in it—so that it may instead take delight in You alone. 1356.

He whose sovereignty (*vaibhava*) is eternal is called *sadātana-vaibhava*; the vocative of that is *nityavaibhava* (O You of Eternal Sovereignty). O *kanakagirīndra* (Lord of the Golden Mountain)! *punarbhavaruciḥ* means the desire for rebirth; *vihātuṃ tvat* is the word division [meaning "to abandon from you"]. O *anagha* (O Sinless One)—this is an adjective in the vocative case qualifying the Blessed One alone. *Tvat* means "from you"; *punarbhavaruciṃ* has the meaning already stated. *Sadā manasi tanavai* means "I shall always fashion [it] in my mind"—this constitutes the apparent contradiction (*virodha*). Alternatively, *tvadanaghapunarbhavarucim* is a single compound word.

"O Sinless One, I expand within my mind the luster—that is, the radiance—of those *punarbhavas* which are your nails; for Amara states, 'the nail is called *punarbhava*. This is the resolution [of the apparent contradiction]. Here, aiming at the fruit of abandoning the luster of rebirth (*punarbhava-ruci*), there is a contrary effort consisting of mental attention (*manaskāra*) toward the luster of rebirth. The distinction from previous examples is the presence of *yamaka* (paranomasia). However, the superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) based on the identity [of the two meanings] through the medium of *śleṣa* (punning) is common to all cases."
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Variegated (Vicitra), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on the Exceeding (Adhika):
"The statement that the contained is greater than its vast container [is the figure Adhika]."
Where there is a description of the contained being greater than its large container, there is the figure of speech named *adhika* (the Exceeding).
Now begins the section on the figure of speech *adhika* (the Exceeding): the description of the excellence of the contained as being greater than its vast container.
Where there is a description of the contained being greater than its container, there is the figure of speech named *adhika* (the Excessive). For example:

"Where the entire world was perceived by the world as being contained within the command 'Rule' (*adhikuru*), yet your compassion—which is intent on removing the calamities of Kṛṣṇā—did not find room within that body. (1357)

The term *adhikurusamiti* is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of a case ending, meaning "the assembly (*samiti*) or the battle (*saṃgara*) of the Kurus. The word *samiti* is employed here to include both [the assembly and the battle], since the Blessed One manifested His universal form (*viśvarūpa*) both in the assembly of the Kurus and in their conflict. As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *samiti* may refer to a future encounter, an assembly, or even a battle.

Here, by demonstrating the extreme vastness of the locus—wherein the entire world was beheld within the Blessed One’s divine body—the superiority of the contained object is described: that Your compassion does not extend to me within this divine body of Yours.

Just as the multitude of Your excellent qualities does not find room even within You, the Soul of the Universe and Sustainer of the World, so indeed this infinity of theirs arises from Your very own nature. 1358.

In the phrase "in the Universal Self, whose body is the entire phenomenal world," by stating "here too in the Universal Self," the extreme greatness of the substratum is demonstrated; thus, it is shown that the auspicious qualities do not fit within it, thereby illustrating the superiority of the attributes over the substrate.

Or for example: O Hero of the Raghus, as your fame—like the moon in its intensely brilliant light—expands on all sides, the sky takes on the agitation of [the moon's] dark spot. Or for example: O friend of Hari, the expanse of the sky, within the belly of the vast ocean of the light of your spreading fame, bears the graceful appearance of the form of the one whose banner is Garuḍa (Viṣṇu).
Or rather,

O Mother of all, for those who possess the fortune of Your glance, the fame of the Blessed One— flowing like the triple-pathed Ganges— somewhere in the celestial realm acts as a most clearly manifest blue lotus.
O Blessed One, the spreading renown of those who take refuge in you shines both within and without the cosmic egg, like the light of a clear lamp inside a crystal casket. 1362.

Among these four examples, the first two are mixed with *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile) embellished by *rūpaka* (metaphor). The latter two are combined with *upamā* (simile). In all cases, the description of the excellence of the *ādheya* (the contained) in relation to the *ādhāra* (the container) is identical. Furthermore, in three of the examples, there is a description that demonstrates the comparison between the sky and fame—the *ādhāra* and the *ādheya*—through a different mode of expression; however, in the last one, the distinction should be noted that the *ādheya* is fame alone, while the *ādhāra* is the entire universe (*brahmāṇḍa*).

Or rather, O Blessed One of immeasurable majesty, within the ocean of nectar that is the guise of your fame, large pearls shine forth, resembling the entire circle of the cosmic egg. (1363) The term *agaṇitavaibhava* is an epithet of the Blessed One. *Bhavadīyayaśaḥ* is either a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "your own fame," or a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the fame of your devotees (*bhāgavatas*). Alternatively, *agaṇitavaibhava* may be an epithet qualifying either the devotees or your fame.

"Under the guise of" (tannibhāt) means by way of that; the rest is clear. Here, the fame of Bhagavat, which is the object contained (*ādheya*), exceeds even the spheres of the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa-maṇḍala*), which serve as its substrates (*ādhāra*). In this case, the object contained is indeed the fame, and the substrate is indeed the spheres of the cosmic eggs. The distinction lies in the fact that it is infused with the figure of speech *kaitavāpahnuti* (concealment by pretext).
The second [section] is the statement regarding the superiority of the substratum, which is more extensive than the superstratum.
And that description of the receptacle as being greater even than the vast thing contained within it is indeed "the Exceeding" (adhika); such is the meaning.

To what extent is this mind of mine so vast—that it dwells within the abode of the world, which is the dwelling place of the wind-eaters (the gods), the expansive home of Śrī, and the seat of all blossoming? 1364.

"Expansive" means vast; "with expansion" means without confinement, as it truly is. Here, the superiority of the mind—which serves as the substratum for the form of Śrīnivāsa, who is the abode of the entire world—is established as distinct from that which is contained within it.
Or rather,
O Mādhava, I think that my mind is now sufficient for this great and wondrous expanse, wherein the Supreme Self, though greater than all the worlds, finds room.

I consider my mind to be exceedingly vast and wonderful. Intending to state the reason for this, he says "from all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*). The sense is that even though the Supreme Self is greater than all worlds—even within that mind which is [otherwise] atomic in form—He possesses a magnitude exceeding all worlds, according to the manner described in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, beginning with "This Self of mine within the heart is greater than the earth" and concluding with "greater than these worlds. The Supreme Self fits therein. This has the same meaning as the previous example; the distinction lies in the recognition of the scriptural passage cited.

Or rather, how does the Śruti speak of the self as "atomic"? Herein lies our doubt; for that very same scripture declares it to be the supreme Brahman, whose majesty is immeasurable and who dwells within. (1366)

The Śruti states that the Self, the inner self (pratyagātman), is atomic (aṇu), as in the passage beginning, "This Self is atomic. How then does it speak of that Supreme Brahman whose majesty—meaning its greatness—is "agaṇita," beyond the scope of calculation, being unsurpassedly vast in both essence and attributes? The meaning is that the same Śruti declares this very inner self to be "antara," situated within, as in the passage beginning, "He who is within the self. This is the sense.

Although in these examples praise is offered to the mind and the inner self (pratyagātman) as the two substrates, it should nevertheless be understood that this praise ultimately culminates in the praise of the subject under discussion—the Supreme Brahman. For even though the mind and the inner self are established as subtle, they are praised by conceiving them as the locus of the Supreme Brahman, which is greater than all worlds, possesses great majesty, and serves as the abode of the entire universe; thus, their praise results in the praise of the Supreme Brahman itself.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Excess (*adhikālaṅkāra*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of the Small (*alpālaṅkāra*):

"The smallness of the substratum (*ādhāra*) compared to the superstratum (*ādheya*), when the superstratum is subtle, is called 'the small' (*alpa*). That which is the subtlety of the substratum relative to its own superstratum—which is subtle—is the ornament named *alpa*. Here, "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) means slight; "subtlety" (*saukṣmya*) means thinness.

Just as for the slender-limbed daughter of the Lord of Mithilā, who dwelt beyond Laṅkā and was emaciated by intense separation, her nose-ornament, encircled by pearls, became a necklace around her neck. || 1367 ||

The phrase "mauktikavalayitanāsāmaṇḍanam" refers to a particular type of golden nose-ornament in the shape of a bracelet, encircled by pearls and fastened at the waist with pearls. Here, the aforementioned nose-ornament is slender; yet, because it was placed upon her neck by the blessed daughter of Janaka—who was emaciated by separation—due to the mental distress born of being parted from her beloved, it attained the state of a necklace (hāra) there. By this statement, the extreme slenderness of her neck is demonstrated; thus, one should infer the slenderness of the support from the slenderness of the object supported.
O Lord, as she, out of the agitation caused by the sight of you, fastens the ear-ornament of your beloved in the middle [of her waist], it becomes there an interwoven girdle.

Here too, the ear-ornament is exceedingly delicate; yet, due to the agitation caused by the sight of you, it was fastened upon the waist by your beloved Śrī, and thus, being there, it became like a girdle (*kāñcī*). By this statement, the extreme slenderness of her waist is revealed. Here, there is a specific gesture of love known as *vibhrama*.

According to its definition: "Vibhrama is the transposition of ornaments from their proper places due to haste at the [right] time. This poetic figure is the invention of Dīkṣita, as it was not noticed by earlier writers.

The subtlety of the supported arises from the subtlety of the support; due to the subtlety of the support, the subtlety of the supported would also be a minor ornament (*alpa-alaṃkāra*). It should be understood that this [ornament] is the opposite of the first *adhika* (excess), whereas the former [the previous one] was the opposite of the second.

Although this variety was not identified by the authors of the *Kuvalayānanda*, nevertheless, because it constitutes a superior counter-example, it must necessarily be admitted; thus, we have identified it, since even that which is "superior" (*adhika*) when occurring as a pair is of two kinds.

Just as the exceedingly slender belly of the daughter of Devaka was the supreme abode of Brahman, so too did it directly fulfill the meaningful intent of the Vedic revelation that [Brahman] is subtler than the subtlest. 1369.

The meaning is that this is according to the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad scripture: "It shines forth, subtler than the subtle. [The word] *anvarthā* means having a name that conforms to its actual significance. Here, by the extreme minuteness of Devakī’s womb, which serves as the locus (*ādhāra*), the subtlety of the Supreme Brahman, who is contained within it as the located (*ādheya*), is established.

Or rather: "This Supreme Self has dissolved within my heart, though it be but the size of an atom, as I bow before Him; I know this minuteness is appropriate, for His greatness is merely a figurative description. (1370)

Regarding the statement that "this Supreme Self is subtler," it is appropriate; for I know from the Śruti: "This Self of mine within the heart is subtler than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or even the kernel of a grain of millet. Thus, I consider it logical that He is most minute. If it is asked, "What then is the status of the Śruti passage stating, 'He is greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than heaven'?"—to this he replies: "His greatness is a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda)."

The sense is that the superiority of this Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended for glorification, and not a literal reality. Herein lies the distinction: although the Supreme Self is superior to everything, it is described as being subtler than its support—the subtle heart—which constitutes a form of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting in the statement of its lack of connection [to that support] despite its actual possession of universal superiority.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter on Minor Figures of Speech in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on the Figure of Mutual Ornamentation (*anyonyālaṅkāra*):
"The wise know mutual ornamentation to be the conferring of excellence upon one another."
The mutual conferring of excellence by two things upon one another is the figure of speech called *anyonya* (reciprocity). And this excellence takes the form of qualities, actions, and so forth.

Just as the splendor of the ruby on the bracelet becomes exceedingly crimson by the abundance of rubies on the hand, so too has the lotus-hand of the Mother of all beings become intensely red by the brilliance of that very ruby.

By the "abundance of redness" (*rāgabhūmnā*)—that is, by the extreme crimson hue—of the lotus-like hands; and by the "splendor" (*dhāmnā*), that is, the radiance, of those rubies (*padmarāga*) which are the bracelets (*karakaṅkaṇa*) on the hands. Here, there is a mutual conferring of excellence between the two qualities: the extreme redness of the lotus-like hands and the redness of the rubies of the bracelets.
Just as, for example:

"Between the chest [of Viṣṇu], the sky, and the sapphire that serves as the couch for the Lord who reclines upon the serpent—each rivaling the sun—the relationship of the adorned and the adornment became common to all through their mutual production of beauty. (1372)

The state of being the adorned and the adorning—the relationship between the object of ornamentation and the ornament—is common, being shared by both. Here, there is a mutual bestowal of excellence between the Lord’s chest and the Kaustubha gem through the action of producing splendor (*śrī*). This excellence consists in its being embellished by a simile (*upamā*).
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Mutual [Relation], in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on the Figure of Speech called *Viśeṣa* (Distinction):
*Viśeṣa* occurs when the substratum (*ādhāra*) is omitted while the superstratum (*ādheya*) is described.

The figure of speech *viśeṣālaṃkāra* consists in the description of the specific location of a contained object (*ādheya*) without its well-known container (*ādhāra*). This is of two kinds: the description of the contained as being situated in another container, and its description as being without a container at all.
Among these, the first is as follows:

Even though the moon has set and its light is exhausted, that dense moonlight spreads across the sky; yet upon your face, it diffuses the fragrance of blue lotuses, which is otherwise devoid of splendor.

The "excellent and beneficial fragrance" (*varaṃ hitaṃ ca āmodaṃ*) of the blue lotuses (*indīvarāṇām*); alternatively, in the phrase *dīvyantīvarahitam*, the word division is *dīvyantī ivarahitam*. *Ivarahitam* means "devoid of the *iva*" [particle], which refers to the fragrance of the *indirā* (Lakṣmī), i.e., *indirāmodam*. Regarding the term *indīvarāmodam*, even though the *ikāra* following the letter *da* is short and thus consists of two phonemes, when the subsequent *ikāra* is elided, the preceding *ikāra* remains, thereby producing that form.

Alternatively, the word division is simply *īvarahitam*; thus, *īvarahitam* means "the fragrance of the *indīvara* (blue lotus)," which is to say, "the fragrance of Indra" (*indrāmodam*). The point is that in the word *indīvarāmoda*, when the vowel *ī* following the letter *d* is elided along with the letter *v*, it is formed through the combination of the remaining *d* and *r*. It is well known in the Purāṇas and other texts that the moonlight of the Lord’s divine face bestows sovereignty over the three worlds, thereby producing the "fragrance of Indra."

The splendor of the Blessed One’s face, or the splendor of his smile, is superimposed as moonlight. Here, even though the well-known substratum in the form of the moon is absent, its attribute—moonlight—remains in a specific state by residing in another substratum, namely the Blessed One’s face. Or, for example: "Even when the sun has dissolved into the midst of the ocean, the entire mass of its rays, having entered the jewel residing in the breast of Kamalākṣa (Viṣṇu), constantly brings about the blossoming of the lotuses. (1374)

The "blooming of lotuses" refers both to the opening of lotus flowers and to the joy of Lakṣmī. Here too, although there is no conventional locus for the mass of the sun's rays, their specific location is stated to be in the Kaustubha gem, which is the subject of description.

Although in both of these examples, what are described as the moonlight and the mass of sunlight are actually of the same nature as the moonlight and the mass of sunlight that are the subjects of description, yet they are not those very things themselves; nevertheless, there is no fault because, through the power of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole)—which asserts non-difference despite difference—there is an identification (*adhyavasāya*) of them as one. In the case of the "fragrance of the blue lotus" and the "radiance of the lotus," however, the identification of them as one is based on the power of *atiśayokti* rooted in an identification of non-difference through the medium of *śleṣa* (punning). Nor should it be argued that in such cases there would be *atiśayokti* alone [and nothing else].

Because it bestows life upon all other ornaments, it is impossible for it to be sublated by them; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of numerous ornaments such as *śliṣṭa* (punning) and *paraṃparita* (metaphorical). As Bhāmaha has stated:
"This is *vakrokti* (poetic deviation) everywhere; by this, the meaning is brought to light.
Poets must exert effort in this regard—for what ornament could exist without it?"
Thus; "vakrokti" means "atiśayokti" (hyperbole).
The second type is as follows:

"With the luster of her eyes and the luster of her limbs, and with clouds in the sky and lightning from the slopes of the clouds, scattering them in every direction, she bestows nectar upon the wife of the jewel of the King of Serpents. (1375) Here, "nectar" refers to water and also to supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*). In this case, the clouds exist without the sky, and the lightning exists without the clouds; thus, they abide precisely without a physical support.

Just as all that is moving and unmoving has gone along with the hero of the Raghus and rests upon him, how little audacity is there in his fame, which wanders alone through the worlds without support?
The former was mixed with *rūpaka* (metaphor); this is either pure or mixed with *samāsokti* (speech of brevity).
The second variety [of *viśeṣa*] is where a single object of support (*ādheya*) is described as simultaneously residing in multiple loci; that too is proclaimed as a *viśeṣa*.

The second variety of *viśeṣa* is that in which a single object to be supported (*ādheya*), although situated upon a limited substrate (*ādhāra*), is described as simultaneously occupying multiple substrates; the word "simultaneously" (*yugapat*) is used to exclude the *paryāya* (successive) type which will be discussed later.

O lotus-eyed one, just as excellent virtues always dwell within the heads of those who perceive reality, in the minds of sages, and in the words of skilled poets, so too do they ever sport within you.

"May that pair of lotus feet of the Lord of the World—which shines upon the crest of the crown of the Śruti (the Vedas) as well as upon the crest of the excellent Vṛṣādri mountain—destroy the succession of my sins. Here, in the first verse, there is the simultaneous presence of the Lord’s auspicious qualities upon a single locus, while in the second, there is the simultaneous presence of the pair of lotus feet upon multiple loci.

Just as I behold this man on the Mountain of Serpents (Śeṣaśaila) who has taken refuge in a golden celestial chariot, I recognize him alone in the solar disc as one who possesses a golden abode, due to the distinction of his various forms.

I behold this very same Supreme Person whom I saw on Mount Ahicchatra residing in a golden celestial palace; I recognize Him as the one who, through a difference in manifestation—that is, a difference in mode—resides within the solar orb as the golden-hued one described in the scripture: "This golden person who is within the sun. I know that this one and the same Supreme Person is situated in both places.

The only difference in form (*vidhābheda*) here is that on Śeṣādri there is the color of a dark cloud, whereas in the solar orb there is the color of gold. In this context, because of the difference in form—specifically the distinction in the mere phonemes (*varṇa*) of the words *śritakanakavimāna* and *śritakanakadhāma*—the wonder lies in the fact that one perceives the word *śritakanakadhāma* as having the meaning "one who has resorted to a golden abode" (*śritakanakadhāman*); this is the distinction from the previous example.
The third variety [of *viśeṣa*] is that where, after the mere commencement of some task, another task even more difficult to accomplish is performed;
that too is accepted as *viśeṣa*.

The third variety of *viśeṣa* consists in the accomplishment of another task that was previously considered impossible or unachievable by one who has begun a certain undertaking. Thus, it should be understood that the general definition of the figure of speech *viśeṣa* is the state of being any one of these [three] varieties.

Just as even a cowherd boy, while placing his foot upon the mountain of Govardhana which served as a staircase, suddenly ascended the path beginning with the *arciḥ* stage—how could anyone here have any doubt about this? (1380)

Here, by means of the commencement of a minor action—namely, the placing of one's feet upon the first step of the Śeṣa mountain—the accomplishment of another, vastly improbable and seemingly impossible task, namely the crossing of the path beginning with the *arciḥ* [arcis], is depicted.

O Hari, it is indeed a marvel that you constantly wear upon your crest the head of the mountain that bears the best of Marut-eaters (the serpent Śeṣa), while the entire world, O Blessed One, becomes your crest-ornament by being called "bhavata" (your creation). 1381.

Here, by the commencement of a minor task characterized merely by adorning Śeṣagiri, the accomplishment of his status as the crest-jewel of the entire world—which is most difficult to achieve—is [described].

Or rather: O Sustainer of the Universe, while supporting you alone within my heart, I support this entire world. Indeed, consider this and tell me: are you the one skilled in sustaining the universe, or am I? 1382.

Here, by the commencement of the task of supporting a single Bhagavat, there is the performance of another task—supporting the entire universe—which is most difficult to accomplish. The distinction lies in the fact that the glory [of the Lord] is manifested through the "germinating parikara" (a poetic figure consisting of the employment of a significant epithet), namely the phrase "O Supporter of the Universe" (*viśvambhare*), which is an intentional application of a qualifying attribute.

Just as [the Creator] creates here Citrakūṭa—which is exceedingly fragrant, intoxicating the minds of people with the scent of most fragrant campaka flowers, and possessing mountain peaks made of jewels—many other mountains have likewise been fashioned on earth by Fate. In one sense, it is "atisurabhigandhamādanam": exceedingly fragrant (*atisurabhi*) and intoxicating (*mādana*) the minds of people with the scent of most fragrant (*atisurabhi*) campaka flowers. In the alternative sense, it refers to the mountain named Gandhamādana, which is exceedingly fragrant (*atisurabhi*) and exceedingly charming (*atimātra-manojña*), and which possesses jewel-encrusted peaks (*ratnasānu*). In the alternative sense, it refers to Sumeru, whose ridges (*sānu*) consist of jewels (*ratna*).
And the mountain named Citrakūṭa, which possesses variegated and wondrous peaks; by the Creator who fashioned such a great mountain, many other mountains were made and created upon the earth.
Just as the lotus-born Brahmā, while creating the mountain-like serpent Śeṣa— blissful, wind-like, facing all directions, pure, and vast— simultaneously created the other five elements.

*Khām* means the sky; *pavanaḥ* means wind; *sarvatomukham* means water; *śuciḥ* means fire; and *vipulā* means the earth—the collection of these is [the compound]. That which possesses this excellence is *sukhapavanasarvatomukhaśucivipulam*. Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound of the adjectives: *sukhapāni* (those which protect or preserve happiness, i.e., those that bring about happiness) refers to the *vanāni* (forests) in which they exist; *sarvatomukhaḥ* means possessing peaks on all sides; *śuciḥ* means pure; and *vipulaḥ* means vast. Thus, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇa-karmadhāraya*).

By the creator of such a mountain bearing hooded serpents—[the rest is easy to understand]. Here, the scriptural sequence regarding the simultaneous creation of diverse beings is not intended to be emphasized.

Just as the Creator, while fashioning the earth—which is rich with highly honored great undertakings, possesses manifold beauty, and has well-prepared regions—produced many apsarases; so too [is this city]. 1685.

[The city] was enriched by those who were honored by the great; [alternatively, it was enriched] by Rambhā, a celestial nymph (apsaras) of that name, who was honored and great. It possessed many grounds created by Bhābhṛt; [alternatively, it was] one where the celestial nymph named Kṛtasthalā resided, she who bears much splendor (bahuśobhābhṛt).

By the Creator, while fashioning the serpent-hill (Ahiśaila), the creation of many celestial nymphs (apsarases)—who are the courtesans of heaven—was accomplished; alternatively, the creation of many reservoirs of water (apsaras) was ordained. Here, in the three examples beginning with "atisurabhigandhamādanam," the accomplishment of another exceedingly difficult task—the creation of various mountains and so forth—is composed as being supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) through the commencement of a certain task, namely the creation of Śeṣādri. The distinction in the middle verse is that it is called *ratnāvalī*.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the Section on the Figure of Speech called Viśeṣa, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
By that very [work], O Lord of the Bull-Mountain, may you grant him abundant joy. (1386)

By that which is the source of great calamities, the birthplace of passion (*rajas*), and the abundance of the quality of *rajas*—by that very thing, meaning by that very abundance of the aforementioned quality of *rajas*, this world was shaken. (Alternatively, there is a word-break as *pakṣe pad-prabhava*: "that which originates from the foot"; *prabhavam* means that which comes forth; by the power of the dust (*rajas*) originating from the foot—that is, by the majesty of the pollen of one's own feet—you bestow intense bliss.)

Here, because that which is well-known as a cause of suffering—the manifestation of water, birth, and passion—is, through the power of paronomasia (śleṣa), identified with the manifestation of the dust of the Lord’s feet, and is then enjoined by the Blessed One as a means to bliss, there is a formal consistency with the definition [of poetic suggestion].
O King, those very enjoyments which were formerly regarded as nectar when you were not present before them, are indeed regarded by men as poison during the state of your presence.

The distinction here is that, whereas [in the previous case] the means of enjoyment were well-known as causes of pleasure, [in this case] they are established as causes of suffering; this is based on the opposite of what was stated before, it is incongruous, and it is mixed with a simile.
The second type is as follows:

Those wise ones who seek liberation by serving the lords of wealthy kings are the very same people who, when constantly practicing those same acts, all unintelligent ones, incessantly crave for worldly enjoyment. (88)

The wise, who know the truth, desire to be liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra through the service of the Lord Śrī Śeṣādri, the sovereign of the mountain-king of enjoyments; whereas the ignorant, who do not know the truth, desire to experience worldly enjoyments (bubhukṣante) through those very same services—namely, through the service of the sovereign mountain-kings (kṣmābhṛdadhīśvaras), the best of rulers, who are solely intent on enjoyment. This is the actual state of affairs. The ignorant desire to experience the enjoyments of worldly existence.

It should be noted here that the wise have adopted the service of the lords of the mountain-like kings of enjoyment as a means to liberation; however, by the unwise who rival them, these same services are turned into means for enjoyment contrary to that [liberation]. This transformation is sustained by the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole), which is rooted in the identification [of two things] based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the two meanings conveyed by the words "lord of the mountain-like king of enjoyment" (*bhogikṣmābhṛdadhīśvara*).

Just as you, O lotus-eyed one, burnt down the cities of your enemies with the Sudarśana discus, so too does that lotus-eyed woman bring prosperity to the cities of your enemies by means of that very same [discus]. 1389.

O Padmākṣa! That Sudarśana discus by which you burnt (adhākṣīḥ) the cities—such as Vāraṇāsī—of your enemies, Pauṇḍraka and others, by that very Sudarśana your lotus-eyed Lakṣmī brings (āvahati) the wealth of the city of your enemies; this is the apparent contradiction (*virodha*). The resolution (*parihāra*), however, is: "by that very Sudarśana"—meaning by that beautiful appearance (*sudarśana*) alone—"before" (*puraḥ*) means even before seeing him; thus it is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). The word "of those who have taken refuge" (*āśritānām*) is to be supplied as the object.

"Of enemies, *aprasrutām* means *akṣīṇām* (undiminished). From the root *rī*, belonging to the *divādi* class, in the sense of 'flowing' (*prasravaṇe*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the active voice (*kartari*). Because this [root] belongs to the *svādi* group, by the rule *svādaya oditaḥ*, it is marked with the *odit* designation; consequently, by the rule *oditaśca*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is changed to *n*. Amara states: *syannam, rīṇam, srutam, sutam*. It brings about (*āvahati*) *saṃpadam*, that is, prosperity (*śriyam*)."

In this passage, the Blessed One’s employment of the Sudarśana [discus], which he had accepted as the means for burning the cities of his enemies, as a means for Śrī—who is its adversary—to bestow prosperity that is the opposite of that [destruction], is composed with an excellence rooted in *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Or, for example: "The enemy of the cities (Śiva) scorched Pradyumna with the heat of his uneven glances; by that very same [heat], the Lord of the Bull-mountain (Śiva), the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), nourishes Pradyumna here. (1390)

Rudra, the enemy of the cities, scorched—that is, consumed by fire—the god of love, Pradyumna, with the splendor (dhāman) of his third, uneven (asama) eye; "pluṣ" is a root belonging to the Divādi class meaning "to burn. However, the Lord of the Bull and the Mountain [Śiva] [actually] did so with that very same splendor of his uneven eye—that is, with the brilliance of his eye, meaning his sidelong glance (kaṭākṣa); such is the actual state of affairs.

*Pradyumna* refers to Smara (the God of Love); *hiraṇya* means wealth or power—according to Amara, "hiraṇya, draviṇa, and dyumna" all signify wealth.
