He *puṣyati*, meaning he nourishes or sustains; the root *puṣ* (in the sense of nourishing) belongs to the *daivādika* class. The word "of those who have taken refuge [in him]" (*āśritānām*) is to be supplied as the object. Here, while the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) employed the very abode of his own incomparable glance as the instrument for the burning of Pradyumna, the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), acting as his adversary, employed that same thing as the instrument for his nourishment. The rest is as explained previously.

The second type of contradiction (*vyāghāta*) consists of an action performed by someone that is contrary to the effect desired by another. If it is composed with ease, that too is called a contradiction.

If, while an object is being presumed by someone to be capable of accomplishing a specific effect, another action that contradicts that effect is shown to be easily performed [by it], that too is a contradiction (*vyāghāta*). When there is ease in performing an action that contradicts the intended effect, the cause is all the more clearly shown to be conducive to that [contradictory] result.

If you regard me as a fool and thus remain indifferent, then for that very reason, O Hari, let there be a desire to show grace toward me. Alas! For women are objects of compassion, and indeed, living beings who are wretched and foolish are [the objects of concern] for the virtuous.

O friend! Here, the poet—who establishes the propriety of the Lord’s indifference by citing the scriptural authority, "Women are to be pitied by the virtuous, as are gifts and deluded beings," and thereby demonstrating that what was considered a cause for delusion is in fact a cause for His desire to show favor toward those very objects—supports this with reasoning; this is the second instance of contradiction (vyāghāta).

Or rather, O Lord, if you abandon me on the grounds that I am a fool, then follow me for that very reason; for the wise, by bringing a fool under their control, protect him by complying with his whims. 1392.

In this case as well, the poet—by demonstrating the maxim "one should abandon a fool by following his whims"—establishes the propriety of that [abandonment], supporting it through the presentation of the principle that what the Blessed One previously considered to be the cause for abandoning a devotee, namely foolishness, is in fact the cause for following the opposite of that [foolishness].
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter on the figure of speech *Vyāghāta* (Contradiction) in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.

In this manner, those figures of speech beginning with *Virodhābhāsa* (Apparent Contradiction) and ending with *Vyāghāta*, which are rooted in a contradiction manifested right at the outset through the superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) of some slight non-difference by means of devices such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole)—a contradiction that lasts only for a moment like a flash of lightning and consists merely of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*)—have been defined. Some maintain that these, while assuming various forms of variety, are merely subdivisions of *Virodhābhāsa* itself and not distinct from it, just as bracelets and other ornaments are not distinct from gold.

Others maintain that since figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *dīpaka* (illumination), which contain elements of comparison within them, would result in being mere varieties of *upamā* (simile), there would be excessive confusion; therefore, those figures that merely follow one another's shadow yet possess distinct aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) are indeed separate [from simile].
Others, however, maintain that there would be excessive distraction; thus, those whose distinctness follows merely the shadow of one another are indeed entirely separate.
Now, the Chain ornaments (śṛṅkhalālaṃkāra):
If, among meanings arranged in a sequence, there is a mutual connection of each preceding one with each succeeding one— or even the reverse— it is the Chain ornament.

When matters are arranged in the form of a series (*paṅkti*), the mutual connection of each subsequent element with each preceding one, or of each preceding element with each subsequent one, constitutes *śṛṅkhalā* (the chain). This takes various forms, such as cause-and-effect, qualifier-and-qualified, and so forth. Furthermore, this is not an independent figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), because its meaning is already encompassed by the varieties that will be described hereafter; for without this [chain], there is no distinct domain for those [varieties].

For instance, they say that just as in the case of metaphors (*rūpaka*) and the like, the aspect of non-difference or the aspect of common attributes—which exists as the vitalizing principle—is not a separate figure of speech, so it is in the present case as well. Others, however, do not tolerate this; for if [the *kāraṇamālā*] were merely a variety of metaphor through its sub-divisions such as "with parts" (*sāvayava*), or a variety of simile through its sub-divisions such as "complete" (*pūrṇā*) or "elliptical" (*luptā*), it would lack the status of an independent figure of speech. Therefore, the *kāraṇamālā* and its other varieties are indeed distinct from the chain-arrangement (*śṛṅkhalā*). We shall examine the truth of these two views further below.
Now, the "Garland of Causes" (kāraṇamālā) is a composition in which each preceding object serves as the cause for each succeeding one;
this garland of causes is also desired when the order is reversed.

When there is a weaving together of entities such that each preceding one serves as the cause for each succeeding one, or each preceding one serves as the effect of each succeeding one, that very thing constitutes the *śṛṅkhalā* (chain) form of the *kāraṇamālā* (garland of causes) ornament. In this regard, the first type consists of each preceding entity being the cause and each succeeding entity being the effect; the second type consists of each preceding entity being the effect and each succeeding entity being the cause.
Among these, the primary [sequence] is as follows:
by devotion, one goes to your mountain; by going to your mountain, one beholds you; by beholding you, O Lord, one immerses oneself within the ocean of perfect bliss. (1393)

*Nidhyāna* means seeing. As Amarasimha states: "But *nidhyāna* is gazing; it is also seeing, looking, and beholding. Here, the causal relationship is established such that each preceding element—devotion and the rest—is the cause for each subsequent element, beginning with the journey to Śeṣācala.
Just as from food indeed come the vital breaths of beings, from the vital breaths the mind, and from the mind discernment; from discernment comes bliss—thus do they uphold Brahman as the Light.

From food, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) sustain—that is, they bear—the radiance or light. This is the third person plural present indicative of the root *dhā* belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class. By means of the vital breaths, the mind (*manaḥ*) sustains—that is, it bears—the radiance. This is the first person singular present indicative of the root *dhā* belonging to the *bhūv-ādi* class; the same applies hereafter. Here too, the causal relationship of each preceding element—beginning with food—toward each succeeding element, beginning with the vital breaths, is interwoven.

The distinction here is that this [verse] follows the meaning of the Taittirīyaka Śruti: "From food, the vital breaths (prāṇas) arise for beings; from the vital breaths, the mind (manas); from the mind, consciousness (vijñāna); from consciousness, bliss—the womb of Brahman. This example is given to demonstrate that the poetic ornaments (alaṃkāras) have their foundation in the Śruti. "From food, the vital breaths"—that is, the senses (indriyas)—arise; the meaning is that the excellence of the senses and vital breaths conducive to hearing is produced.

*Manas* is the faculty of reflection; *vijñāna* is knowledge whose form is identical to perception; *ānanda* is the Supreme Brahman, the *parabrahma*, which comes to be—that is, it shines forth. The meaning of the Śruti is that through the sequence of hearing and so forth, rooted in the excellence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and culminating in profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*), the Supreme Brahman in the form of bliss is attained. Or as it is said: "Through the purity of food comes the purity of the mind; when the mind is pure, O Acyuta, your constant remembrance arises; and from that comes the liberation from all knots. (1395)

Here, in accordance with the scriptural passage, "When food is pure, the mind (*sattva*) becomes pure; when the mind is pure, there is constant mindfulness; upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is liberation from all knots," the causal relationship is established—just as before—between each preceding factor, such as purity of food, and each succeeding factor, such as purity of the mind. When there is purity of food—that is, when one partakes of *sāttvika* food—there is purity of the *sattva*, which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

And when that [meditation] exists, there arises constant mindfulness—a mindfulness whose form is identical to direct perception. When that mindfulness exists, there occurs the complete liberation from all "knots"—those things designated by the term "knots" because they are difficult to untie, namely ignorance, passion, and so forth; such is the meaning of the scripture.

Just as the conquest of the senses occurs through the steadiness of the mind, and from that comes the path of karma-yoga; from that comes knowledge, from that devotion, and from that liberation shall arise. (1396)
This is an undertaking based on the effect; the distinction is that the preceding ones, however, were undertakings based on the cause.
The second type is as follows:

"O Acyuta, [this world] exists because of the lack of taking refuge in the fresh lotus-pair of Your feet; that [lack of refuge] is due to the failure to discern the manifold miseries of existence; and even that is due to the non-attainment of the company of the virtuous. (1397) Here, the causality of each subsequent factor—such as the failure to take refuge—is established with respect to each preceding factor, such as the calamities of worldly existence.
Just as wealth is the cause of prosperity, the sidelong glances of Ramā are the basis of wealth; devotion is the cause of those glances, and the splendor of past merit is the cause of devotion. 1398.
The distinction is that in the previous example, the status of being a cause was conveyed by a case-ending (vibhakti), whereas here it is conveyed by words such as "hetu" (reason) and so forth.

Just as the taking of refuge at the feet of Hari occurs through the grace of a guru, that [grace] arises from the perfection of the quality of goodness (sattva), and that [perfection] arises from the glance of the Blessed One, while he [the glance] comes about through the power of spontaneous merit and the like. (1399)

This is the grace of the Guru. Here, at the outset, there is a distinction: whereas previously there was an introduction to the effect (*kārya*), here there is an introduction to the cause (*kāraṇa*). Furthermore, if in this context the mention of the cause alone is introduced at the beginning, then a "garland of causes" (*kāraṇamālā*) is appropriate—such as: "this is the cause of something, that too is the cause of something else," or "the cause of that, and the cause of that as well. However, when the mention of the effect is introduced at the outset, then it is appropriate [to say]: "this is the effect of something, that too is the effect of something else," or "the effect of that, and the effect of that as well."

In every case, that very word which was first employed to introduce the relationship between cause and effect must be carried through to the conclusion. Composing in this manner is pleasing because it accords with the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); otherwise, however, the sequence would be broken—this should be kept in mind. For example, there is a verse by the ancients:
"Control of the senses is the cause of modesty; excellence of virtue is attained through modesty;
people feel affection for a man who abounds in virtue; for prosperity indeed arises from the affection of the people."

In this context, having heard that mastery over the senses is the cause of discipline (*vinaya*), one might wonder what the cause of mastery over the senses is, or what the cause of discipline is; for the cause itself presents itself first by virtue of its being remembered.

The cause is known, but as for its effect, one might occasionally have an expectancy as to what that is; however, since "cause-ness" and "effect-ness" are relational categories, the understanding of the effect—dependent upon the cognition of one of the two related members—is to be reconciled by the hearing of the word "cause. Yet this expectancy is not universal. Thus, although the sentence "Excellence of qualities is obtained through modesty (*vinaya*)" effectively fulfills the expectancy "Of what is modesty the cause? in terms of its result, it nevertheless does so not directly, and is therefore not truly satisfying to the heart. Similarly, when there is the expectancy "What is obtained from excellence of qualities?"...

And [regarding the phrase] "in a person superior in qualities": here, the fault of *kathitapadatva* (repetition of a word) is not a defect; on the contrary, if that same meaning were expressed by another word, it would be a defect because it would obstruct recognition—just as in the case of an actor appearing in a different form—and because it would lack the unimpeded realization of the intended meaning. Furthermore, just as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) appears as a qualifier when an object is presented through a word, the word itself also appears as a qualifier. Thus it has been said: "There is no cognition in the world that does not follow from words."

Thus, they say that although the specific meaning of each respective word is non-different from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is nevertheless perceived as distinct; therefore, there is no fault of "repetition" (*kathitapadatva*). A detailed account, however, should be sought elsewhere.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the "Series of Causes" (*kāraṇamālā*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on the "Single String" (*ekāvalī*): when each preceding [term] becomes an adjective for each succeeding [term], that is the *ekāvalī*.
Or when they call this "Single-String" (ekāvalī) the qualified object (viśeṣya), then [it is so].

When each subsequent element is linked with each preceding one as either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a qualified (*viśeṣya*), that very [figure] is called *śṛṅkhalā-ekāvalī* (the chain-garland). This same figure is also called *gṛhītamukta-rīti* (the sequence of what is grasped and released). "Grasped and released" (*gṛhītamukta*) is a compound; its "sequence" (*rīti*) is a row (*paṅkti*). By means of that "sequence of what is grasped and released" (*gṛhītamukta-rītyā*), [it is so named]. The instrumental case is used here in the sense of non-difference (*abheda*). Consequently, its meaning is that *ekāvalī* is a sequence of what has been grasped and released.
Among those, the first is as follows:

"The serpent-mountain (Śeṣa), the abode of Hari (Vaikuṇṭha), and the mountain whose peaks are the jewels of the ocean-dweller’s playground—these, O Goddess born from the ocean, cause Your glory to rise upward and they indeed adorn the earth. (1400)

In this case, each subsequent element—such as Hari and the rest—functions as a qualifier for each preceding element—such as the serpent, the mountain, and so forth. Furthermore, this [type of *parikara*] is of two kinds, depending on whether the successive qualifiers establish or exclude [the object].
As it has been said: "Whether it is established or excluded, the succeeding member relates to the preceding one in turn."
Where an object functions as a qualifier, that is Ekāvalī; it is of two kinds.
Thus, the meaning is that where, as before, each preceding element is established, enjoined, excluded, or negated as a successive qualifier for each subsequent one, there it is called *ekāvalī*.

He who possesses discernment is wise; that which is discernment is the contemplation of reality; that which is reality is the supreme; and that supreme is the Brahman which shines as the ultimate essence. (1401)
In this context, each subsequent qualifier, such as "discrimination" (viveka) and so forth, serves to establish its preceding substantive, such as "the wise one" (budha) and so forth.
He is no man who is ignorant, and he is no scholar who does not know that Brahman; that is no Brahman which did not embrace the broad-chested Śiva on the Vṛṣādri mountain.

In this context, for each preceding substantive such as "human being" (*manuja*) and so forth, each subsequent qualifier such as "ignorant person" (*avidvat*) and so forth functions as an exclusion (*apohaka*). Although the function of establishing (*sthāpaka*) is also perceived in the former—for instance, in expressions like "one who is not discerning is not wise"—and the function of excluding is also perceived in the latter—for instance, in "one who is wise is a human being"—nevertheless, since those [functions] were not explicitly mentioned [in the definition], there is no fault.
The second type is the interweaving of each preceding element as a qualifier for each succeeding one. For example:
"Bhīṣma knows of Your glory; his mother purifies this world; O Acyuta, You lie with her who is dear to him; and Your virtues bring happiness to men. (1403)

Just as the Blessed Lord shines by means of Lakṣmī, so too does the Mountain of Serpents (Ahi-giri) become adorned with her as its crest-jewel; because of him, the Draviḍas are beautiful, and by them this Bharata-khaṇḍa is adorned. The term *dramiḍāḥ* refers to the country inhabited by the Draviḍas. According to the rule *so’sya nivāsaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form *drāviḍa*], which then undergoes elision (*lup*) according to the rule *janapade lup*; following this elision, the gender and number remain as they were when the suffix was present (*yuktavat*). In the first example, each preceding element—such as Bhīṣma and the rest—functions as an attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) for each succeeding element—such as the Gaṅgā and the rest.
In the second example, it should be understood that Lakṣmī and the others function as attributes for the Blessed Lord and the others respectively.
Thus ends the forty-ninth string, the *Ekāvalī*, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.

Here, this should be noted: in the second variety of *Ekāvalī*, if the assistance rendered by each preceding element to each subsequent one is of a uniform nature, then it is designated as *Mālādīpaka* (the Garland Lamp) by the ancients. As they have defined it:
"The first [variety] is *Mālādīpaka* if it conveys a quality progressively to each subsequent [element]."

Thus; the meaning is that the first [type] is the *dīpaka* (illuminator). In this context, by the word "garland" (*mālā*), a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*) is meant. By the word *dīpaka*, through the etymological derivation "like a lamp" (*dīpa iva*), that which is situated in one place yet benefits all is expressed. Therefore, the meaning of the two words [“garland” and “illuminator”] together is a chain characterized by an action or other qualities situated in one place that benefits everything.

Thus, in the section on the *dīpaka* ornament, one should not be deluded into thinking that this is a particular variety of *dīpaka* based on the definitions provided by the ancients; for it is universally accepted by all theorists of poetics (*alaṃkārikas*) that the former possesses an internal essence of similarity (*sādṛśya*). Here, however, there is no similarity whatsoever among the words that constitute the links of the chain. How then can we credit the terminology of "lamp-like" (*dīpaka*) application? They further state that this is because those words lack the nature of being both relevant (*prakṛta*) and irrelevant (*aprakṛta*).

In reality, however, since a single attribute is connected across various sentences, it possesses a particular strikingness (*vicchitti*) due to its similarity to the *dīpaka* (the "lamp" figure), as will be explained immediately below; therefore, it is proper that *mālādīpaka* (the "garland-lamp") be considered a distinct figure of speech. Otherwise, one would have to accept as separate figures even those varieties of chain-like figures such as *kāraṇamālā* (the "chain of causes"), simply because they possess some slight degree of strikingness—which would be untenable, according to others.

For this very reason, even the author of the *Sarvasva* has defined this ornament separately within this same section, stating: "When each preceding element brings about a quality in each succeeding one, it is *mālādīpaka* (the garland-like illuminator). Although earlier authors defined it immediately after *dīpaka* because it conforms merely to the nature of illumination, its distinct beauty—rooted in a chain-like structure (*śṛṅkhalā*)—has been defined in this very section by the authors of the *Kuvalayānanda*, the *Sarvasva*, and others.
Now, the "Garland-Lamp" (mālādīpaka) figure of speech:
this is the garland-lamp which arises from the combination of a lamp (dīpaka) and a single-stringed necklace (ekāvalī).

From the conjunction (*yuti*)—that is, from the union of the recurrence of a single attribute (*ekadharmānvaya*) with the manner previously described—the figure of speech named *mālādīpaka* arises. It is called *dīpaka* (the illuminator) because it resembles the *dīpaka* [figure] through the mere recurrence of one and the same attribute across different sentences; however, it is not the *dīpaka* figure mentioned earlier, since that [earlier] figure only occurs when the similarity (*aupamya*) between the relevant (*prakṛta*) and irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) subjects is implied.

Just as the necklace is adorned by the Kaustubha gem, and that gem by your chest, and your chest by Lakṣmī, and she by you, and you likewise by virtues such as excellent character— so too are they all mutually enhanced.

*Upaskriyate* means "it is adorned" or "it is embellished. This is the present tense (*laṭ*) in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*) from the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *upa*. By the rule *upātpratiyatne* (Pāṇini 6.1.139), the augment *suṭ* is added to *kṛ* when it signifies "improvement" (*pratiyatna*). Improvement here refers to the imparting of excellence. In this context, the single word *upaskriyate* connects with every part of the sentence: "The necklace is embellished by the Kaustubha gem, and that [gem] too is embellished by Your chest"—thus, due to its similarity to the figure of speech *Dīpaka* (the Illuminator), it is called *Dīpaka*. Because it employs the established method of composition, it is also an *Ekāvalī* (Single String); thus, there is a combination of *Dīpaka* and *Ekāvalī*.

Although the ancients defined this immediately after *dīpaka* because it conforms merely to the nature of that figure, its distinct beauty—rooted in a chain-like structure (*śṛṅkhalā*)—has been defined in this very section by the authors of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, the *Kuvalayānanda*, and others.
Now, the *mālādīpaka* (garland-lamp) figure:
this *mālādīpaka* occurs from the combination of *dīpaka* (lamp) and *ekāvalī* (single-string necklace).

From the conjunction (*yuti*)—that is, from the union of the recurrence of a single attribute (*ekadharmānvaya*) and the previously mentioned manner of expression—the figure of speech named *mālādīpaka* arises. It is called *dīpaka* because it resembles the *dīpaka* [figure] simply through the recurrence of one and the same attribute across different sentences; however, it is not the *dīpaka* figure described earlier, since that [earlier] figure only occurs when a comparison (*aupamya*) between the relevant (*prakṛta*) and irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) subjects is implied.

Just as the necklace is enhanced by the Kaustubha gem, and that gem by your chest, and that chest by Lakṣmī, and she by you, and you likewise by virtues such as excellent character— so too are they all mutually adorned.

*Upaskriyate* means "it is adorned" or "it is embellished. This is the present tense (*laṭ*) in the passive voice (*karman*) from the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *upa*. By the rule *upātpratiyatne* (Pāṇini 6.1.139), the augment *suṭ* is added to *kṛ* in the sense of "improvement" (*pratiyatna*). Improvement consists of the imparting of excellence. Here, the single word *upaskriyate* functions as a *dīpaka* (illuminator) because it connects with every sentence in the following manner: "The necklace is adorned by the Kaustubha gem, and that [gem] too is adorned by Your chest. Due to its similarity to *dīpaka*, it is called *dīpaka*. Because it possesses the nature of the style of composition previously described, it is also an *ekāvalī* (single-stringed ornament); thus, there is a combination of *dīpaka* and *ekāvalī*. As for example: [Example omitted per instructions]
The gods in heaven take refuge in Rudra; O Blessed One, Rudra takes refuge in Brahmā; Brahmā, for his part, takes refuge in you here, yet you never at any time take refuge in anyone.
This *mālādīpaka* (garland-like lamp), characterized by the combination of *āvṛttidīpaka* (repeated lamp) and *ekāvalī* (single-stringed necklace), differs from the previous example as follows:
"The gods have taken refuge in Rudra; Rudra has taken refuge in Brahmā;
Brahmā has taken refuge in me, O King; but I have not taken refuge in anyone."
Thus, the meaning of the words of the Blessed One from the Mahābhārata has been considered.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, on the *mālādīpaka* (chain-illumination), in the *Alaṅkāramāṇihāra*.
